en: One who is about to sacrifice with either the New Moon or the Full Moon oblation prepares the curdling agent for the oblation beforehand—
either one day or two days prior, according to the season.
Now, indeed, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage:
"He anoints with curd for the sake of being accompanied by Indra; he anoints over it with the remnants of the Agnihotra for the continuity of the sacrifice.
Having either failed to perceive the moon or having perceived it as full, he adds fuel to the fires.
He places three pieces of wood on the Gārhapatya fire, three on the Anvāhāryapacana fire, and three on the Āhavanīya fire.
They sweep around [the fires]. They thus produce the form of the Upavasatha day.
(1.1:1.7) Now, while he has undertaken the vow, he cuts a *parṇa* branch—either facing east or north, remaining silent, or at whatever place he thinks he will find it.
(1.1:1.8) That which is either eastern or northern, possessing many leaves and many branches, with its tips not dried up—that he cuts with the formula: "For food thee! For strength thee!
(1.1:1.10) With that branch, he drives away the calves, saying: "Ye are winds! Ye are approachers!"

Then he impels their mothers [the cows] with the formula: "May the god Savitṛ impel you toward the most excellent work! Swell, O inviolable ones, as the portion of the gods—full of vigor, full of milk, rich in offspring, free from disease, and free from affliction! Let not the thief nor the malevolent one master you; may the weapon of Rudra avoid you! Then he looks at the sacrificer with the words: "May you be many and firm in this lord of cattle."

(1.1:2.1) Then, having carried this branch around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, and having brought it in through the eastern door, he plants it behind the Gārhapatya fire, either on the pole-supporting beam or on the northern half of the fire-hall, with the words: "Protect the cattle of the sacrificer. This applies if he performs the *saṃnayana* offering;
however, if he does not perform the *saṃnayana*, it is simply the *barhis* grass that serves as the first item.

(1.2:2.5) Then, standing behind the Gārhapatya fire, he takes up either a butcher’s knife or a horse’s rib, saying: “At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee.
(1.2:2.7) Having taken it, he consecrates it, saying: “Thou art the proclaimer of the sacrifice.
He heats it over the Gārhapatya fire three times, saying: “Burnt away is the Rakṣas! Burnt away are the enemies! (1.2:2.7) Three times.

(1.2:2.8) Then he approaches the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "This prayer has gone forth toward the sacrificial grass, fashioned by Manu and adorned with the *svadhā* offering; the sages bring it from the east, acceptable to the gods. (1.2:2.11) With the words, "Here for the sitting upon the sacrificial grass," he looks toward the altar.
(1.2:2.11) Then he goes in that direction where he thinks he will find the sacrificial grass.
(1.2:2.12) He grasps a bunch of *darbha* grass, as much as he deems sufficient for the *prastara*, with the formula: "Thou art the portion set apart for the gods.

(1.2:2.13) Then he strokes it upward with the formula: "Thou art grown by rain. (1.2:2.14) He takes hold of it with a knife, saying: "O divine sacrificial grass, do not pierce me lengthwise nor crosswise; may I succeed in [cutting] thy joint."
(1.2:2.15) He cuts [the grass], saying: "May I, as the cutter, not come to harm.
(1.2:2.15) He touches the cuttings, saying: "O divine sacrificial grass, grow with a hundred shoots!
(1.2:2.16) Saying: "May we grow with a thousand shoots," he touches himself.
(1.2:2.17) He cuts this entire bunch at once.
(1.2:2.18) Having made it into a *prastara*, he lays it down with the formula: "Protect [us] from contact with the earth.
(1.2:3.1) From this point onward, he silently cuts off an odd number of handfuls.
(1.2:3.1) Three, or five, or seven, or nine, or eleven, or as many as he deems sufficient.
(1.2:3.2) Then, having wound the cord three times around it from left to right, he wraps it counter-clockwise with the formula: "Thou art the girdle of Aditi.
(1.2:3.3) Having laid it down with its ends pointing northward—
Upon that [altar], he gathers the prastara-bunch with the formula: "Well-gathered, I gather thee.
He binds it together with the formula: "The binding of Indrāṇī. He makes a knot with the formula: "May Pūṣan tie thy knot."
(1.2:3.6) "May it not rise against you," he says, as he covers [the fire] from behind while facing east.
(1.2:3.6) Then he lifts it up with the words, "I lift you up with the two arms of Indra" (1.2:3.7),
and places it upon his head with the words, "I carry you on the head of Bṛhaspati."
He approaches with the words, "Follow the wide mid-region.
Having approached, he places it not on the ground to the north of the Gārhapatya fire with the words, "Thou art going to the gods," and he sets it down as if above,
where he considers it to be secure.
(1.2:3.10) He silently cuts the eating-utensils;
(1.2:3.10) he cuts them for the ancestors in a single pull.

(1.2:3.11) Then, having likewise wound the cord three times around it, he binds the fuel-stick consisting of twenty-one pieces with the formula: "When you, having assumed the form of a black antelope, entered the trees, then I gather you together in twenty-one parts, well-assembled."

(1.2:3.14) He prepares the Veda-bundle: knee-high for one desiring cattle; shaped like a mortar for one desiring food; threefold for one desiring splendor; with its tip pointing upward for one desiring heaven. (1.2:3.15) He prepares the altar prior to the northern boundary-marking. (1.2:3.16) Then, in the afternoon, he performs the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
(1.3:3.17) Then, having cut off the leafy twigs from this branch, he scatters them in front of the Gārhapatya fire.
(1.3:3.18) Then, having stripped the bark from its lower part, he places it with its thickest end toward the rear of the Gārhapatya to serve as the *upaveṣa*.

(1.3:3.19) Then, having measured out a span (*prādeśa*) of it and wrapped it with blades of *darbha* grass, he makes a threefold branch-strainer (*śākhāpavitra*) with the verse: "The threefold *darbha* on the *palāśa* leaf, this much, measuring a span—may it act as the most excellent purifier in the sacrifice, making my milk and oblation pure."

(1.3:4.2) Then, after the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, having spread grass to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, he places upon it four items: the milking vessel, the strainer, the two pots for the *sāṃnāyya*, and the cooking pot.
(1.3:4.5) Then he sprinkles them with water, saying three times: "Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods.
(1.3:4.6) Then, sitting behind the *gārhapatya* fire, he pushes out the embers toward the north with the *upaveṣa* tool, saying: "Thou art the heat of Mātariśvan."
Upon them he places the *sāṃnāyya*-heating vessel with the formula: "Thou art heaven; thou art earth; thou art the all-sustainer; by the highest support, stand firm; do not waver.

Upon it he lays down a branch-strainer (*śākhāpavitra*) with its tip pointing eastward, with the formula: "Thou art the strainer of the Vasus, having a hundred streams; thou art the strainer of the Vasus, having a thousand streams.
Having taken hold of that [vessel], he remains seated, restraining his speech.

(1.3:4.11) Then he awaits the cows as they approach, [reciting]: "These come hither, yielding honey, prolific, glorious, and multiform; becoming many as they are born again—may Indra cause you, O cows, to delight here," or "May Mahendra cause you to delight here" if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra. (1.3:4.15) Then he says: "Announce to me when she has been mounted.
They announce her when she has been mounted.
He consecrates the cow while she is being milked with: "The drop is offered; the spark is offered.
(1.3:4.16) "To Agni, the great vault of heaven, Svāhā! To Heaven and Earth!
(1.3:4.17) Then, as [the milk] is being brought from the front toward the west, he asks: "Whom have you milked?"
(1.3:4.18) “That one,” the other replies.
(1.3:4.18) He addresses her with the mantra: “She is the life of all.
(1.3:4.19) When she is being brought for a second time, he asks: “Whom have you milked?”
(1.3:4.19) "That one [cow]," the other replies.
(1.3:4.20) He consecrates her with the mantra: "She is all-pervading.
(1.3:4.20) When he brings the third [milking], he asks: "Whom have you milked?"
(1.3:5.1) "That one," says the other in response.
(1.3:5.1) He consecrates her with the mantra: "She is Viśvakarman.

(1.3:5.2) When three [udders] have been milked, he releases his speech with the formula: "May she yield much for Indra and for the gods; may the oblation swell again. For the calves and for men, may she be fit for milking again. Or, "For Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra.
Having released his speech and without maintaining physical contact, he causes the subsequent [cows] to be milked silently.

Having poured water into the milking vessel, he pours in the wash-water with the mantra: "Be united, O you who follow the cosmic order (*ṛtāvarī*), you who are wavy and most rich in sweetness; you who are pleasant for the winning of wealth. Then, having heated it, moved it toward the north, and cooled it, he mixes it with curds through a strainer with the mantra: "I mix you with Soma as curds for Indra," or "for Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra.
He brings as much as he thinks will cause [the milk] to coagulate.
He pours the remnant of the Agnihotra over it [with the formula]: "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I continue thee, the continuity of the sacrifice.

Then he covers it with a bronze vessel or a cup containing water, [saying]: "Thou art unassailable; for Viṣṇu, for the sacrifice, I cover thee. With water, by means of a non-empty vessel, [I cover] those which lie purified around."
He places it as if above, where he considers it to be secure, with the formula: "O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation!
At this time, he silently drives away the calves for the morning milking using *darbha* grass.
(1.4:5.17) Then, after the morning *agnihotra* has been offered, he rubs his hands together with the formula: "May I be capable for you two for the sake of the work for the gods.
(1.4:5.18) These fires remain strewn around even from the night;
however, if they have not been strewn around, he first strews around the *āhavanīya* fire to the east, then to the south, then to the west, and then to the north.
In this very manner he strews grass around the Anvāhāryapacana fire;
likewise around the Gārhapatya fire.
Then, having spread grass in front of the Gārhapatya, he places the sacrificial implements upon them in pairs, with their openings facing downwards.

The wooden sword (*sphya*), the potsherds (*kapāla*), the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle, the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), the yoke-pin (*śamyā*), the mortar (*ulūkhalam*), the pestle (*musalam*), the lower grinding stone (*dṛṣad*), the upper grinding stone (*upalā*), the *juhū* ladle, the *upabhṛt* ladle, the *sruva* spoon, the *dhruvā* ladle, the vessel for the *prāśitra* portion, the *iḍā* vessel, the stirring-stick (*mekṣaṇa*), the flour-sifter (*piṣṭodvapanī*), the water-vessel for leading forward the waters (*prāṇītāpraṇayana*), the butter-pot (*ājyasthālī*), the *veda* broom, the wooden bowl (*dārupātrī*), the yoke-thong (*yoktra*), the trimming of the *veda* grass, and the fire-stirring stick (*dhṛṣṭi*) for cutting the fuel-wood (*idhma*).

Having arranged the *anvāhāryasthālī* and the *madantī* [water], as well as whatever other vessels there may be, in pairs in this very manner, and having seated the Brahman priest to the south, he spreads the *pṛṣṭhyā* line continuously from the *gārhapatya* fire to the *āhavanīya* fire, saying: "Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I spread thee for the continuity of the sacrifice; I spread thee for the continuity of the sacrifice."

(1.4:6.11) Then he prepares two strainers from the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), each a span (*prādeśa*) long, equal in size, with unbroken tips, and not cut by the fingernails, [reciting]: "May these two, Prāṇa and Apāna, move together, nourishing in every way the limbs of the sacrifice—the two strainers that purify the oblations."

(1.4:6.14) Then he wipes them with water, saying: "You are purifiers; you belong to Viṣṇu; you are worthy of sacrifice; you are purified by Vāyu; you are purified by the mind of Viṣṇu; you are the purifiers of the sacrifice. (1.4:6.16) Then, having sat down to the north of the Gārhapatya fire, he asks for either a bronze vessel or a wooden cup for carrying forth the *praṇītā* waters.
(1.4:6.17) Pouring water into it across the strainers, he says: "O Brahman, I shall carry forth the waters; O Sacrificer, restrain your speech."

(1.4:6.18) Being impelled, holding [the vessel] level with his breaths and not spilling it, having carried it around and placed it on *darbha* grass to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, and having covered it with *darbha* grass, (1.4:6.20) [having taken up the strainers], he turns to the right, runs back toward the west, and takes up the Agnihotra-ladle with his right hand and the winnowing basket with his left: "For service thee!
(1.4:7.1) Thus he heats them over the Gārhapatya fire three times, saying: "The Rakṣas is burnt away! The enemies are burnt away! (1.4:7.1) Thus three times.
(1.4:7.2) Then, behind the *gārhapatya* fire, there is a cart standing near the *agniṣṭha* post.

He touches its northern yoke-pole with the formula: "Thou art the yoke-pole (*dhūḥ*). Strike down (*dhūrva*) him who strikes us down! Strike him down who strikes us down; strike down him whom we strike down!"

He addresses the cart with the mantra: "Thou art the most liberal of the gods, the most fulfilling, the most beloved, the best bearer, the most excellent invoker of the gods; thou art the unerring vessel for the oblation. Be firm; do not waver."
Then, having stepped upon the southern end of the axle with the formula, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," and having mounted the forepart of the cart, he places the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) thereon.
In the winnowing basket he places the offering-spoon (*sruk*), and in the spoon the two strainers (*pavitra*).
Then he gazes at the grains for the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśīya*) with the formula: "I gaze upon thee with the eye of Mitra; do not fear, do not tremble, may I not harm thee."
(1.5:7.10) With the words, "Wide for the wind," he throws away either a blade of grass or a stalk of grain.

(1.5:7.11) Then, having touched water and explained the *daśahotṛ* formula, he addresses the sacrificer, saying, "I shall pour out the oblation," and pours it out with the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle provided with a strainer.

(1.5:7.13) If, however, there is no such [ladle], he places the wooden sword (*sphya*) behind the *gārhapatya* fire; upon the wooden sword he places the vessel, and into the vessel he pours the grains for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
(1.5:7.14) Then he touches the eastern half of the vessel with the formula: "Thou art the yoke-pole; injure him who injures us. (This portion is missing in Weber; it is found in BI, AnSS, and GOLS.)

"Crush him who crushes us! Crush him whom we crush! You are the most generous, the most fulfilling, the most beloved, the best bearer, and the best invoker of the gods among the gods. You are the unswerving vessel for the oblation. Be firm; do not waver! Thus [he says].
(1.5:7.18) Then he gazes at the materials for the sacrificial cakes, saying: "I gaze upon you with the eye of Mitra; do not fear, do not tremble, may I not harm you.
(1.5:7.19) Saying, "Wide open for the wind," he throws away a blade of grass or a stalk of grain.

(1.5:7.20) Then, having touched water and recited the *daśahotṛ* formula, he addresses the sacrificer, saying, "I shall pour out the oblation," and pours it out with the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle accompanied by the *pavitra*.
(1.5:8.1) “Oṃ, pour out!”—thus the sacrificer gives permission.

(1.5:8.1) Then he pours out [the grain] three times with this sacrificial formula: “At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out, acceptable to Agni. (1.5:8.1) Thus three times with this *yajus*.

(1.5:8.3) Having performed this very introductory verse once silently, he recites: "To Agni and Soma" at the full moon sacrifice; and "To Indra Vaimṛdha" as well. At the new moon sacrifice, for one who does not offer the *saṃnayya* (curds), he says: "To Indra and Agni"; for one who offers the *saṃnayya*, he says: "To Indra"; or "To Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra.
(1.5:8.6) Then he touches the poured-out portions with the formula: "This is for the gods."
(1.5:8.7) "And this of ours together"—with these words, he addresses those that remain.
(1.5:8.7) "For prosperity thee, not for misfortune!"—with these words [he addresses them].
(1.5:8.8) Then he gazes at the Āhavanīya fire: "May I behold the light of Vaiśvānara, the sun. With these words.
(1.5:8.9) Then he looks at the houses, saying: "May the dwellings be firm in heaven and earth. (1.5:8.10) Then, taking them up, he stands up. He goes forth, saying: "Follow the wide mid-region."
Having approached, he places [the vessel] to the north of the Gārhapatya fire with the words: "I place thee in the lap of Aditi.
He then consecrates the Gārhapatya fire with the words: "O Agni, guard the oblation."

(1.6:8.13) Then, having poured water across the strainers into this very ladle, he purifies it three times with the two strainers whose tips point northward, verse by quarter-verse: "May the god Savitṛ purify you with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya. (1.6:8.15) Then, magnifying them, he stands up [with the formula]: "O divine waters, flowing forward, moving forward, lead this sacrifice forward; place the lord of the sacrifice at the forefront. Indra chose you for the slaying of Vṛtra; you chose Indra for the slaying of Vṛtra."
(1.6:8.18) With water he sprinkles the waters, saying three times: "You are sprinkled; you are sprinkled.

(1.6:8.19) Then he sprinkles the grains for the sacrificial cakes, according to the respective deity, three times each, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni—for Agni-Soma, for so-and-so, for so-and-so. (The formula is supplemented by *devasya tvā savituḥ prasave 'śvinor bāhubhyāṃ pūṣṇo hastābhyām* and *amuṣmā amuṣmai*.)
Having turned the vessels face upwards, he sprinkles them three times with the formula: "Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods.

Having set aside the remaining sprinkling water, he shakes the black antelope skin while turning toward the north with its neck pointing upward, saying three times: "The *rakṣas* has been shaken off; the enemies have been shaken off."
(1.6:9.5) Then he spreads it out in front [of the mortar], with the neck facing west and the hair-side upward, saying: "Thou art the skin of Aditi; may the earth recognize thee.
(1.6:9.7) Upon that he places the mortar, saying: "Thou art the wooden pressing-vessel; may the skin of Aditi recognize thee.
(1.6:9.8) Into that he pours the grains for the sacrificial cake, saying: "Thou art the body of Agni, the release of speech; I take thee for the enjoyment of the gods."
He places the pestle down with the formula: "Thou art a stone, born of the tree; do thou prepare this oblation for the gods well-prepared.

Then he calls out to the preparer of the oblation three times: "O preparer of the oblation, come! O preparer of the oblation, come! [Aloud: "To strike together! Then he strikes the upper and lower millstones loudly with a bull's roar: "Proclaim food! Proclaim strength! Speak with splendor! May we conquer the assembly!"
Having threshed [the grain] and removed the husks, he holds the winnowing basket over to the north, saying: "Thou art increased by rain.

Into it he pours the grains for the sacrificial cake, saying: "May that which is increased by rain receive thee! Then, turning toward the north, he winnows them, saying: "The Rakṣas is winnowed away; the enemies are winnowed away."
Having struck the husks with his left hand, he throws them out in this direction, saying: "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases.
Then, having touched water, he winnows them, saying: "May Vāyu winnow you.
He causes the rice grains to fall into the vessel, saying: "May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you."
Handing [the rice] to the woman who husks it, he says: "To be thrice-husked; announce to me when they have been thrice-husked.

When they have been thrice-husked, they announce: "[They are] being thrice-husked. He pours the rinsing water of the rice grains either within the altar or toward the location of the rubbish-heap (utkara), saying: "Whatever husk remains, that is the portion of the Rakṣases; let the waters carry it away from here."
At this time, he milks the cows for the morning milking with a strainer whose fringes point north;
he does not curdle it here.

(1.7:10.6) Then, when the three [grains] have been husked, he likewise shakes the black antelope skin while facing north with its neck pointing upward, reciting three times: "Shaken off is the Rakṣas; shaken off are the enemies. (1.7:10.7) Then he spreads it out in front [of the mortar], with the neck toward the west and the hair side up, saying: "Thou art the skin of Aditi; may the earth recognize thee. (1.7:10.9) Upon it he places a yoke-pin with its thick end pointing north, saying: "Thou art the support of heaven; may the skin of Aditi recognize thee."
Upon that [altar], he places the lower grinding stone facing eastward with the formula: "Thou art the bowl, belonging to the mountain; may the support of heaven recognize thee.
Upon the lower grinding stone, he places the upper grinding stone with the formula: "Thou art the bowl, belonging to the daughter of the mountain; may the mountain recognize thee."

Upon that [skin], he pours out the grains for the sacrificial cakes: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour you out, acceptable to Agni; [acceptable] to Agni-Soma, to so-and-so, to so-and-so"—thus according to the respective deity.
He consecrates them: "You are grain; satisfy the gods; satisfy the sacrifice; satisfy the lord of the sacrifice; satisfy me, the performer of the sacrifice."
He grinds [the grain] with the formulas: "For out-breath thee! For in-breath thee! For diffused breath thee!
He looks at his two arms with the formula: "May I extend long through my offspring for the sake of life.
He causes the ground grains to fall upon the black antelope skin with the formula: "May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you."
(1.7:11.1) While handing over the oblation for grinding, he says: "Grind without mixing [the flour]; make it fine.
(1.7:11.2) They grind the materials for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and set aside the grains for the cooked rice (*caru*).
(1.7:11.3) If he intends to prepare a *caru* oblation, they should divide the grains intended for the *caru* and the *puroḍāśa* before the pouring of the grains.
(1.8:11.5) Then he places these washed potsherds behind the Gārhapatya fire:
eight to the south and eleven to the north.
(1.8:11.6) Then, having sat down behind the Gārhapatya, he takes up the fire-stirring stick with the formula: "Thou art the fire-stirrer; bestow spiritual power."
He addresses the Gārhapatya fire with: "O Agni, drive away the raw-eating Agni! (1.8:11.8).
With "Drive out the corpse-eater," he throws out a coal from the southern part.
Then he turns another [coal] toward [the fire] with: "Bring hither the one who sacrifices to the gods. (1.8:11.9)
He places it upon the middle of the southern potsherds with the formula: "Thou art firm; make firm the earth! Make firm life! Make firm progeny! Encircle the kinsmen for this sacrificer!
He then rolls a coal over it with the formula: "The Rakṣas is burnt away! The enemies are burnt away!"

(1.8:11.12) Then he lays down the one on the eastern side with: "Thou art the support; make firm the intermediate space; make firm the out-breath; make firm the in-breath; heap around the kinsmen for this sacrificer.
(1.8:11.14) Then he lays down the one on the western side with: "Thou art the foundation; make firm the sky; make firm the sight; make firm the hearing; heap around the kinsmen for this sacrificer."
(1.8:11.16) Then he lays down the one on the southern half with: "Thou art Dharma; make firm the quarters; make firm the womb; make firm offspring; heap around for this sacrificer his kinsmen.
(1.8:11.18) Then he lays down the first enclosing-stone with: "Ye are piled; heap around for him offspring, for him wealth, for this sacrificer his kinsmen.
(1.8:11.19) And then the other in the same manner.

(1.8:11.19) He places two [bricks] touching each other to the north, [saying]: "Ye are piled; bestow offspring upon him, wealth upon him, and kinsmen upon this sacrificer; heap them around. (1.8:12.2) Then he covers them with embers, [saying]: "Be heated by the heat of the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases.
(1.8:12.3) Then he yokes them with the *yoga* formula: "Those potsherds which the wise pile in the *gharma*, those of Pūṣan—may Indra and Vāyu yoke them for the sake of his service."
In this very manner he places the subsequent potsherds.
They kindle the potsherds;
they enkindle the vessel for the cooked rice offering.
They place the cooking vessels upon the fire and heat the water intended for mixing with the flour.

(1.9:12.8) Then, having sat down to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, restraining his speech, he pours the flour from the black antelope skin into the vessel across the strainer, according to the respective deity: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out, acceptable to Agni—for Agni and Soma, for so-and-so, for so-and-so. Thus [he does] according to the deity.
Then he says to the assistant: "Bring! Fetch water!

The one who issues the command brings [the water], having drawn from the *praṇītā* waters with the *sruva* spoon, supporting it with the *veda* grass-bundle or placing his hand between them. He does the same for the *madantī* waters.

As both [the flour and the water] are being brought together, he recites over them: "The waters have united with the waters; the plants with their sap. O wealthy ones, be united with the moving ones; be sweet with the sweet. Then he pours it around, saying: "You are born from the waters; be mixed with the waters. He mixes it, saying: "I mix you for the sake of generation."
Having mixed [the flour] and arranged it, he touches it, saying according to the respective deity: "For Agni thee! For Agni and Soma thee! For so-and-so, for so-and-so!
He forms a ball, saying: "Thou art the head of Makha.
Having pushed back the embers toward the southern border of the potsherds, he places it upon them, saying: "Thou art the Gharma, the life of all."
He spreads it out with the formula: "O wide one, spread yourself wide; may the lord of the sacrifice spread wide for you.
As he stretches it out, he makes it in the shape of a tortoise.
"He spreads over all the potsherds," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(1.10:13.3) Then, across the strainers, he pours clarified butter into the butter-pot, saying: "Thou art the milk of the great ones, the sap of the plants; of thee, undecaying, I pour out for the sacrifice to the gods. (1.10:13.5) Then, having drawn out embers mixed with ashes toward the north, he places [the pot] upon them.
(1.10:13.6) In this very same manner, he places the second sacrificial cake upon [the embers].

(1.10:13.6) Then [he takes] the boiled rice, then the curds. (1.10:13.6) Then, having poured water into a vessel, he causes the skin of the southern sacrificial cake to be taken up, saying three times: "Take the skin! Take the skin! (1.10:13.8) Then [he does so] for the northern one.
(1.10:13.8) Then he carries fire around [the sacrificial items], reciting three times: "The *rakṣases* are excluded; the enemies are excluded.

(1.10:13.9) Then he bakes the southern cake, [reciting]: "May the god Savitṛ bake thee on the highest vault of heaven; may Agni not burn thy body. (1.10:13.11) He addresses the Gārhapatya fire, [saying]: "O Agni, guard the oblation."

In this very manner, he bakes the northern cake. Then, having covered the southern cake with ashes, he covers it with the *veda*-grass mat, reciting three times: "Be united with the *brahman*; be united with the *brahman*.
Then [he does so] for the northern one.
(1.10:13.14) “Knowing [it], cook it!”—with these words he releases his speech.

(1.10:13.15) At this point, having heated this washing-water from the vessel over a coal from the Gārhapatya fire and having carried it forward, he pours it out westward upon three lines within the altar, saying: “Svāhā to Ekata! Svāhā to Dvita! Svāhā to Trita!”

(1.10:13.17) Then he takes up the Veda [grass-bundle] with the mantra: "This Veda has found the earth, which was hidden in secret, in the depths, in the caverns; may it find a world for the sacrificer; may it perform the flawless sacrifice, performing many rites.

(1.10:13.19) With the Veda, he sweeps around the altar three times, saying: "By means of the Veda they found the earth, the altar; that earth spread out over the earthly realms. She bears the embryo within the worlds; from her the sacrifice is born, providing all days."

(1.11:14.3) Then, standing behind the altar, he takes up the wooden sword (*sphya*) with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I take thee with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan.
(1.11:14.4) Having taken it, he consecrates it with the formula: "Thou art the right arm of Indra, thousand-edged, hundred-pointed."
(1.11:14.6) Then he whets it with sacrificial grass (*barhis*), saying: "You are Vāyu, of sharp brilliance; you are the hundred-edged weapon of the Lord of the Forest, the slayer of enemies.
(1.11:14.7) Then, within the altar (*antarvedi*), he lays down a blade of sacrificial grass with its tip pointing north, saying: "You are the armor of the earth; be an armor for the sacrificer.
(1.11:14.8) Upon that, he strikes with the wooden sword (*sphya*), saying: "O Earth, place of sacrifice to the gods! May I not harm the root of your plant."
"Araru is struck down from the earth," with these words he takes [the clod];
"Go to the fold, to the cow-pen," with these words he carries it;
he looks toward the altar, saying, "May the sky rain for you."

Having taken [the clod], he throws it onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) with the mantra: "Bind him, O God Savitṛ, in the furthest distance with a hundred fetters—he who hates us and whom we hate—do not release him from there. He strikes a second time with: "O Earth, place of sacrifice for the gods, may I not harm your root, O herb!
He takes [the clod] with: "Araru is driven away from the Earth, the place of sacrifice for the gods!"
"Go to the cow-pen, to the place for the cattle," he says as he carries [the earth];
he looks toward the altar, saying, "May the sky rain for you.

Having carried it, he pours it out on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), saying: "Bind him, O God Savitṛ, in the furthest distance with a hundred fetters—he who hates us and whom we hate; do not release him from there!"
He strikes the third [spot] with: "O Earth, place of sacrifice to the gods! May I not harm the root of your plants.
With "Araru, the non-sacrificer to the gods, is driven away from the earth," he takes [the clod], and with "Go to the fold, the stall of cattle," he carries it away.

(1.11:14.20) He gazes at the altar, saying: "May the sky rain for you. (1.11:15.1) Having carried [the earth], he scatters it upon the rubbish-heap (utkara), saying: "Bind him, O God Savitṛ, in the furthest distance with a hundred fetters—he who hates us and whom we hate—do not release him from there! Let not your Araru leap up to heaven! At this point, he continues [the recitation] silently; he carries the fourth portion together with the sacrificial grass (barhis).

(1.11:15.4) Then he performs the first tracing around: "May the Vasus trace you around with the Gāyatrī metre," thus on the south; "May the Rudras trace you around with the Triṣṭubh metre," thus on the west; "May the Ādityas trace you around with the Jagatī metre," thus on the north.

(1.11:15.7) Then he mutters the *karaṇa* formula: "O men, come and prepare this altar, rich in Vasus, rich in Rudras, rich in Ādityas, at the height of heaven, at the navel of the earth, so that this sacrificer may not come to harm.
(1.11:15.10) Then, with the wooden sword (*sphya*), he digs up the altar toward the east, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, the wise perform their work."
Then he says to the Āgnīdhra: "O Āgnīdhra, carry [the earth] from here three times.
Thereupon, the Āgnīdhra carries it three times.
When the Āgnīdhra has carried it three times, he then issues the command: "O Brahman, I shall perform the second tracing around."
(1.11:15.13) Having been impelled, he performs the subsequent tracing around: "Thou art *ṛta*," on the south; "Thou art the seat of *ṛta*," on the west; "Thou art the glory of *ṛta*," on the north.

(1.11:15.15) Then he smoothes the altar westward with the wooden sword (*sphya*), saying: "Thou art *dhā*; thou art *svadhā*. Thou art wide and thou art wealthy. O thou who art full of power, before the spreading of the cruel one! Having lifted up the earth, O giver of life, which they established in the moon by means of *svadhā*-offerings—looking upon that, the wise perform sacrifice."

(1.11:15.18) Then, having fixed the wooden sword (sphya) crosswise within the altar (antarvedi), he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters (prokṣaṇīḥ)! Place the fuel and the sacrificial grass (idhmābarhis) nearby! Clean the dipping-spoon (sruva) and the offering-ladles (sruk)! Gird the wife! Come forth with the clarified butter (ājya)!
(1.11:15.20) Having filled these sprinkling waters, they bring them forward;
the Adhvaryu, having poured them out upon the wooden sword to his south, sets them down in the track of the wooden sword.

(1.11:16.2) Then he strikes the wooden sword (sphya) into the mound (utkara) with the verse: "O gods, whoever hates me with the heart, with the mind, or with speech; whoever hates me with sacred knowledge (brahman) or with ritual action (karman); whoever [hates me] with learning or with a longing heart—with Indra’s thunderbolt, I cut off his head.

(1.11:16.4) Having washed his hands, he washes the wooden sword. (1.11:16.5) They set down this sacrificial fuel (idhma) and sacrificial grass (barhis), the fuel to the south and the grass to the north.
(1.12:16.7) Then he takes up these ladles: with his right hand the *sruva* and the *juhū* and *upabhṛt*, and with his left the *dhruvā*, the *prāśitraharaṇa*, and the scrapings of the *vedā*.
(1.12:16.8) He heats them over the *gārhapatya* fire, saying: "Burnt away is the Rakṣas! Burnt away are the enemies! With Agni’s most brilliant splendor I heat thee!
(1.12:16.10) Then he cleanses the *sruva* with the formula: "May I not wipe out the cow-pen; I cleanse thee, the vigorous one, the subduer of rivals."

Having wiped the handle three times on the inside and three times on the outside, and having likewise wiped it with the roots [of the grass], he touches it with water, heats it over the fire, and hands it back.
Then he wipes the *juhū* with the formula: "May I not wipe away speech or breath; I wipe you, the vigorous one, the subduer of rivals.
Having wiped it in that same manner, he touches it with water, heats it over the fire, and hands it back.
Then he cleanses the *upabhṛt* [ladle] with: "May I not wipe away sight or hearing; I cleanse thee, the vigorous one, the overcomer of rivals.
Having cleansed it in that same manner, having touched it with water, and having heated it, he hands it back.
Then he cleanses the *dhruvā* [ladle] with: "May I not wipe away offspring or the womb; I cleanse thee, the vigorous one, the overcomer of rivals."
In the same manner, having wiped it, touched it with water, and reheated it, he hands it back.
Then he wipes the *prāśitraharaṇa* [ladle] with the formula: "May I not wipe away the form and color from the cattle; I wipe you, the vigorous one, the subduer of rivals.
In the same manner, having wiped it, touched it with water, and reheated it, he hands it back.

(1.12:17.1) Then, having touched these wiping-sprigs with water, he throws them into the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "The craft of heaven has been spread out; it rests upon the peaks of the earth. By that [craft], which has a thousand branches, we destroy our rival, svāhā!
(1.12:17.4) Then, having strewn grass in front of the rubbish-heap (utkara) and having placed the offering-ladles (srucaḥ) upon them...

(1.12:17.5) Then, having led this wife between the *vedi* and the *utkara*, and having seated her to the south-west of the *gārhapatya* fire facing north, he girds her with the *yoktra* [with the mantra]: "Seeking goodwill, offspring, and fortune for thy body; being devoted to the vows of Agni, I gird thee for the sake of good deeds. (1.12:17.8) [Then he makes her recite: "May the rite be joined; may the prayer be joined to the desire."

(1.12:17.9) Then, across the strainer, he causes her to sip water with the mantra: "The plants are full of milk; the milk of the creepers is full of milk. Whatever milk belongs to the milk of the waters—with that, O Indra, unite me."

(1.12:17.11) Then he causes her to place fuel-sticks on the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall observe the vow; may I be able to do it; may it be successful for me, svāhā! O Vāyu, lord of vows! O Āditya, lord of vows! O lord of vows among vows, I shall observe the vow; may I be able to do it; may it be successful for me, svāhā! Thus he says.

(1.12:17.14) Then she sits down behind the *gārhapatya* fire with the verse: "With good offspring and as good wives, we have approached you, O Agni, the subduer of rivals, we who are undeceived, to you the undeceivable. May I be like Indrāṇī, not widowed; may I be like Aditi, rich in noble sons. For the sake of good progeny, I sit near you, O *gārhapatya*, so that this household shall not be destitute."

"My sons are slayers of enemies; moreover, my daughter is Virāj; and I am Saṃjāyā; the fame of my husband is supreme. (Thus he makes her recite this, and also: "May the deficiency be filled by the excess.")

(1.12:18.1) Then he makes her look at the Gārhapatya fire with [the words]: “O Agni, lord of the house, invite me; O wives of the gods, invite me. O wife, this is your place; homage be to you; do not harm me. (1.12:18.4) Then he makes her look at the clarified butter with [the words]: “You are the milk of the great ones, the essence of the plants; I look upon you with an undeceived eye for the sake of good progeny.”
(1.12:18.5) Then he places it over the Gārhapatya fire with the formula, "Thou art brilliance.
(1.12:18.6) Having placed a fuel-stick [on the fire], he carries it eastward with the formula, "Follow after brilliance.
(1.12:18.6) Then he places it over the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "May Agni not take away thy brilliance."
At this point, he places this fuel-stick in the middle of the Āhavanīya fire [with the formula "Svāhā"].

Then, having carried it around along the front of the *prokṣaṇī* waters and having placed it on the southern half of the altar, he causes the sacrificer to look at the clarified butter. "He should look while closing his eyes," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then, having carried it back in the same manner as it was brought and having placed it on the northern half of the altar, the Adhvaryu looks at it [with the formula]: "Thou art the tongue of Agni, well-being for the gods; for every domain, for the gods, for every sacrificial formula, become [ready]."
(1.12:18.12) Then, with two strainers whose tips point northward, he purifies it three times by moving them back and forth, [saying]: "Thou art the bright; thou art the light; thou art the radiance.
(1.12:18.14) Then he purifies the sprinkling waters, verse by quarter-verse: "May the god Savitṛ purify you with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya."

Having placed two strainers into the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling-water, he takes up the *sruva* ladle with his right hand and the *juhū* offering-ladle with his left; having set them down upon the *vedī*, he draws [the butter] into the *juhū* with the formula: "I take you, the bright one, for the bright one, for every station, for the gods, for every sacrificial formula. Having drawn four portions with this formula, he touches them together and hands them over.

(1.12:19.3) Then he takes [ghee] in the *upabhṛt* ladle with this formula: "Light, thee, in light; for every station, for the gods, for every sacrificial formula, I take thee. Having taken eight portions with this formula, while taking more draughts, he takes less ghee. (1.12:19.5) Having touched it in the same manner, he hands it over.

(1.12:19.6) Then he takes [the clarified butter] from the *dhruvā* vessel with this *yajus*: "I take thee for the flame, in the flame, for every abode, for the gods, for every *yajus*. Having taken four portions with this *yajus*, having filled [the ladle], and having touched it in the same manner as before, he hands it over.

(1.13:19.9) Then, having placed this butter-pot together with the *sruva*-ladle behind the altar, he stands up while pouring out the sprinkling waters, saying: "O divine waters, you who flow first, you who move at the head, lead this sacrifice forward; place the lord of the sacrifice at the head. Indra chose you for the slaying of Vṛtra; you chose Indra for the slaying of Vṛtra.
(1.13:19.12) With water, he sprinkles the waters themselves, saying three times: "You are sprinkled; you are sprinkled."
(1.13:19.13) Then, having untied the fuel, he sprinkles it with: "Thou art black, dwelling in the lair; for Agni, to thee, svāhā!
(1.13:19.14) He sprinkles the altar with: "Thou art the altar; for the sacrificial grass, to thee, svāhā!
(1.13:19.15) He sprinkles the sacrificial grass with: "Thou art the sacrificial grass; for the offering-ladles, to thee, svāhā!"

They bring this sacrificial grass (barhis) between the *praṇītā* waters and the *āhavanīya* fire. Having placed it within the altar with its knot toward the east, he sprinkles it: "For heaven, thee! over the tips; "For the intermediate region, thee! over the middle parts; "For earth, thee! over the roots.

(1.13:19.18) Having sprinkled the knot from the front toward the west together with the offering-ladle, he pours out the remaining *prokṣaṇī* waters from the southern hip to the northern hip [of the altar] with the formula: "Svadhā to the fathers! Be strength for those who sit on the sacrificial grass; go to the earth with strength! Having lifted up the vessel for the *prokṣaṇī* waters and loosened the sacrificial grass, he takes the *prastara* bundle from the front with the formula, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s tuft," (1.13:20.1) or silently;
he inserts the two strainers into it with the formula, "I place the out-breath and in-breath in the sacrificer," or silently.
He hands it over either to the sacrificer or to the Brahman priest. Then he stretches out these grass-bunches from the southern hip of the altar to the northern shoulder.
Then, at the southern edge of the altar, he spreads a handful of sacrificial grass with the formula: "O divine sacrificial grass, soft as wool, I spread thee, a good seat for the gods."
He spreads that thick grass in front, facing westward, in three layers, so as not to be seen through.

(1.13:20.6) Then, holding the *prastara* grass-bundle in his hand, having stepped forward toward the east, he lays down the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the formulas: "Thou art Gandharva Viśvāvasu; from every attacker, thou art the enclosing stick of the sacrificer, praised as *iḍā*," with this for the middle one; "Thou art the right arm of Indra; thou art the enclosing stick of the sacrificer, praised as *iḍā*," with this for the southern one; "May Mitra and Varuṇa lay thee around on the north with firm law; thou art the enclosing stick of the sacrificer, praised as *iḍā*," with this for the northern one.
(1.13:20.11) Then he encloses [the fire] from the east with the sun, saying: "May Sūrya protect you from the east against any curse.

(1.13:20.13) He places two fuel-sticks upright, saying: "O Sage, we kindle thee, the enjoyer of the oblation, the radiant one, O Agni, the great one at the sacrifice. Having silently added the southern stick and then the northern one, (1.13:20.14) he places two separating blades with their tips pointing northward across the altar, saying: "Ye two are the restrainers of the people."
(1.13:20.16) Upon the two *vidhṛti*-strainers, he places the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the formula: "Sit in the seat of the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas.
(1.13:20.17) Upon the *prastara*, he places the *juhū* ladle with the formula: "Thou art the *juhū*, dripping with ghee by name; by thy dear name, sit in the dear seat.
(1.13:20.18) To the north, he places the *upabhṛt* ladle with the formula: "Thou art the *upabhṛt*, dripping with ghee by name; by thy dear name, sit in the dear seat."
[He places] the northern *dhruvā* [ladle] with: "Thou art firm, dripping with ghee by name; by thy dear name, sit in the dear seat.

Then he touches the *sruk* ladles that have been set down: "These have sat down in the world of the well-done; protect them, O Viṣṇu! Protect the sacrifice! Protect the lord of the sacrifice! Protect me, the performer of the sacrifice! Then he consecrates the clarified butter with: "Ye are the forms of Viṣṇu; ye are the abodes of Viṣṇu; ye are the abodes of Prajāpati."
(1.14:21.4) Then he takes up with his right hand the vessel for clarified butter together with the *sruva*-ladle, and with his left hand the *pātrī* and the *veda*.

(1.14:21.5) Having taken these, having turned to the right, having hastened westward, and having sat down behind the *gārhapatya* fire, he spreads a double-layered base in the *pātrī* [with the mantra]: "I prepare a pleasant seat for thee; I fashion it well-favored with a stream of clarified butter. Sit upon it, O immortal one, be firmly established; O essence of rice, be well-disposed."
(1.14:21.8) Then, taking the *dhṛṣṭi* (stirring-stick), he pushes away the embers from the southern *puroḍāśa* cake, saying: "Here I push away the face of the attacking army.
(1.14:21.10) Then he shows it [to the sun], saying: "Shine forth with the light of the sun for great power!"

Having made it free from dust with the *veda*, he pours clarified butter over it, saying: "May Agni, whose source is ghee, swell; may he approve the oblations. Anoint the cavity, anoint the skin; I pour ghee over you, who are well-formed, a finder of wealth, and pleasing to Agni through the splendor of cattle.
Or [he uses the formula] belonging to whichever deity it is for.
Then he removes it [from the fire], saying: "Cooked, the progenitor of thoughts rises up."
He thoroughly satiates [the cake] with clarified butter, [reciting]: "Moist, spreading, the guardian of the world.
Having anointed it from above, he anoints it from below [with the formula]: "That self of yours which has entered into the animals—smear that!
In this very same manner, he removes the subsequent sacrificial cake.
Then [he prepares] the boiled milk, then the curd.

Then he adorns the *sāṃnāyya* with the formula: "That self of yours which has entered into the animals, which has spread throughout the abode of the gods—O Soma, having become possessed of a self and rich in ghee, go to the gods; find the light for me, the sacrificer. Having recited this, he removes the potsherds with the formula: "May nourishment, prosperity, and the essence of the earth not depart."
"He removes [the potsherds] after counting them, for the protection of the sacrificer," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, having filled the *sruva*-ladle with clarified butter, he places it between the two sacrificial cakes.
Then, grasping these together, he sets them down within the altar (*antarvedi*) with these *vyāhṛti*s: "Bhūr! Bhuvaḥ! Suvar!"
He places the two *puroḍāśa* cakes in the middle; the boiled milk (*śṛta*) to the south and the curd (*dadhi*) to the north.

Then, having carried the *sruva* spoon around the ladles from the front, he places it on the *prastara* grass-bundle to the south of the *juhū* with the formula: "Be pleasant for me, sit as one easy to sit upon on the earth! Spread me out with offspring and cattle in the world of heaven! Sit in the sky, on the earth, in the intermediate space! May I be superior; may my rivals be inferior to me!"

(1.14:22.8) Then, having carried it back around in the same manner as it was brought, he places it upon the *dhruvā* ladle with the formula: "Thou art the bull, belonging to the Śakvarī meters, the son of the *ghṛtācī*s; sit in thy dear seat with thy dear name."
(1.15:22.11) Then, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says: "Recite for the fire being kindled!
(1.15:22.12) Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting, "Forward your strengths, O heaven-reaching ones," at that point he places the first stick on the fire.
He places them on the fire at each *praṇava*.

Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting, "O Agni, kindled and invoked," he places a fuel-stick at the very end; he leaves one fuel-stick remaining. Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting, "Offer the oblation! Serve [the gods]!"—at that moment, he fans the Āhavanīya fire three times with this Veda-grass-bundle.

(1.15:22.16) When the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, having taken a portion from the *dhruvājya* with the *sruva* ladle and supporting it with the *veda* grass-bundle, he pours the *prājāpatya* oblation crosswise, [saying] mentally: "To Prajāpati, svāhā!
(1.15:23.1) Then he issues the command: "O *agnīdh*, cleanse the fires three times each!"

(1.15:23.2) Now this Āgnīdhra, having taken hold of the faggot-bundles with the wooden sword (sphyá), cleanses the enclosing-sticks (paridhís): three times the middle one, three times the southern one, and three times the northern one; he fans the Āhavanīya fire three times [with the formula]: "O Agni, winner of booty, I cleanse thee, the winner of booty, who art about to run, who art about to win booty, the vigorous, the winner of booty, for the winning of booty—Agni, the eater of food, for the sake of eating food."
(1.15:23.6) Then, in front of the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, he forms an *añjali* facing eastward, saying: "Thou art the world; spread thyself out! O Agni, O sacrificer, this is homage.
(1.15:23.7) Then he takes the *juhū* with his right hand, saying: "O *juhū*, come hither! Agni calls thee for the sacrifice to the gods.
(1.15:23.9) With his left hand [he takes] the *upabhṛt*, saying: "O *upabhṛt*, come hither! The god Savitṛ calls thee for the sacrifice to the gods."

Stepping across with his left foot, he mutters: "O Agni and Viṣṇu, may I not step upon you; move apart, do not burn me; O makers of space, create space for me. With the words, "Thou art the station of Viṣṇu," he prepares a place.

While the sacrificer maintains contact with him, he touches the middle enclosing stick and pours the straight *āghāra* libation continuously toward the east without interruption, [reciting]: “From here Indra performed heroic deeds; the sacrifice has been undertaken, rising up to touch the sky; the sacrifice of the lord of the sacrifice is unassailable, accompanied by Indra, *svāhā*!
Then, [reciting] “Great light!”, he lifts up the offering ladle.
(1.15:23.16) Then, without touching the two offering-spoons (*srucau*), he steps across toward the north and mutters: "Protect me, O Agni, from evil conduct; grant me a share in good conduct.
(1.15:23.17) With the *juhū* spoon, he anoints the *dhruvā* spoon three times, saying: "Thou art the head of Makha; may light anoint light with light.
(1.15:23.18) Then, having placed the two spoons in their respective places, he chooses the *pravara*.
(1.15:23.19) Having taken hold of the *utkara* mound, the faggot-binding cords, and the wooden sword (*sphya*), the Āgnīdhra priest clings to the back [of the altar].

(1.15:24.1) Then he calls for the announcement: "O, cause [the Hotṛ] to hear! "Let there be hearing! "May Agni, the divine Hotṛ, sacrifice to the gods—he who is wise and discerning, like Manu, like Bharata, like so-and-so, like so-and-so; may he bring [the gods] here together with the sacred formulation (*brahman*). May the Brāhmaṇas be the promoters of this sacrifice. He pronounces the name of the Hotṛ, saying, "So-and-so is the human [Hotṛ].
(1.15:24.4) Having stood up, the Hotṛ releases [the cord].
(1.15:24.5) Having been released, the Adhvaryu sits down;
he remains seated, awaiting the impulse.

Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ saying, "O Adhvaryu, take up the spoon full of ghee," he takes up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, steps across, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, "Recite the offering-verse for the *samidhs*.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering. Saying "Recite, recite," when about to sacrifice for the fourth time, he pours half of the butter from the *upabhṛt* into the *juhū*.

Having performed five fore-offerings (*prayāja*) and stepped across to the north, he sprinkles the oblations with the residue in successive order: first the *dhruvā* ladle, then the southern sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), then the *dhruvā*, then the northern sacrificial cake, then the boiled milk (*śṛta*), then the curds (*dadhi*), and finally the *upabhṛt* ladle.
Then, taking four portions of clarified butter (*ājya*), he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni.
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Offer the oblation to Agni."
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers [the oblation] in the eastern part of the northern half, facing the fire and extending his arms.
Then, having stepped across to the north while taking four portions of clarified butter, he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Soma.
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Soma."
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers [the oblation] facing it, extending his arms, in the eastern part of the southern half.
Then, having spread an underlayer of ghee, while taking a portion from the eastern half of the southern sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni!
Then he pays reverence to it, saying: "Do not fear! Do not tremble! May I not harm you! May your splendor not depart!"
(1.16:25.1) Then he touches it with: "Lift up Bharata; sprinkle after [the offering]. I shall cut portions for you in return; homage be to you; do not harm me.
(1.16:25.3) Having cut from the front half, he cuts from the rear half.

He pours clarified butter over it and anoints it back [with the remainder], saying: "Whatever I have done contrary to the proper order of my own self while cutting portions for you, I anoint that back again with clarified butter; may that swell for you once more."
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering.
Then, taking four portions of clarified butter, he says "For Prajāpati" in a low voice, and "Recite the invitatory verse" loudly.
Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says "Prajāpati" in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) and "Sacrifice! loudly (*uccais*). When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering.

Then, having spread an underlayer of ghee, while taking a portion from the rear half of the northern sacrificial cake, he says: "To Agni and Soma" on the full moon day; and also "To Indra Vaimṛdha. On the new moon day, he says "To Indra and Agni" for one who does not perform the *saṃnayya* offering, and "To Indra" for one who does perform the *saṃnayya*. Or he says "To Mahendra" if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra.
The standing near [the fire] is the same;
the touching is the same.
Having taken a portion from the rear half, he takes a portion from the front half.
He pours clarified butter over [the oblation];
the anointing is the same.
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Recite the offering prayer for Agni and Soma."

(1.17:25.14) He offers when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered. (1.17:25.14) Then, having spread an underlayer of ghee and taking two portions of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra," or "for Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra.
(1.17:25.16) He takes two portions of the cake, two of the boiled milk (*śṛta*), and two of the curd (*dadhi*).
He pours clarified butter over [the oblation] and anoints it back.
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Sacrifice to Indra," or "to Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra.
(1.17:25.18) He makes the offering when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered.
Then, having spread an underlayer of clarified butter, while taking a portion from the northern half of the southern *puroḍāśa*, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.

(1.17:25.20) He takes a single portion from the northern half of the southern *puroḍāśa*, once from the *dhruvā* butter, once from the northern *puroḍāśa*, once from the boiled milk (*śṛta*), and once from the curds (*dadhi*).
He pours clarified butter over [the oblation] twice;
he does not anoint it back.

When the *sviṣṭakṛt* portion has been cut off, he performs the two *pārvaṇa* offerings with the *sruva*-ladle: "We sacrifice to the bull, the vigorous one, the Full Moon; may he milk for us excellent heroism and thousandfold abundance of wealth. To the Full Moon, the giver of great riches, for the sake of out-breath, *svāhā*!"—thus at the full moon sacrifice.

(1.17:26.3) “The new moon is fortunate and very gracious; like a cow, she swells again and again. May she milk for us heroic vigor and thousandfold increase of wealth. To the new moon, the giver of good gifts, for the out-breathing—svāhā! Having recited this at the new moon sacrifice, he steps across, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, “Sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering in the eastern part of the northern half, passing over the previous offerings.
At this point, he throws this stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) into the Āhavanīya fire.

Having washed the *sruva* ladle, heated it, and filled it with water, he pours it out outside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the mantra: "This ocean, the hundred-streamed fountain, expanding in the midst of the world—Aditi, yielding clarified butter for the sake of mankind—O Agni, do not harm it in the highest heaven.
At this point, he pours all of that clarified butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle into the *juhū* ladle.

(1.17:26.15) Then, having set down the two offering-spoons (*srucau*) in their respective places, he cuts off the *prāśitra* portion from the northern half of the southern sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the size of a barleycorn—[not smaller] than a barleycorn—[with the formula]: "Let this be prepared for the piercing [of the enemy]; let us not injure the sacrifice; this oblation (*havis*) is pure and well-offered.

(1.17:26.18) Then, having sprinkled it with the handle of the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), having set it down behind the *praṇītā* waters, and having touched the handle of the dipping-spoon with water, he deposits it.
(1.18:26.20) Then he asks for a *kaṃsa* or a *camasa* as an assistant vessel (*upahavana*).

Having placed it within the altar (*antarvedi*), having spread an underlayer of ghee (*upastīrya*) in it, he breaks off a portion from the southern half of the southern sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and places it [in the vessel] with the formula: "I cut off the one-faced [portion], which was seen by Manu, which has ghee as its foot, and which is impelled by Mitra and Varuṇa, without breaking through the southern half.
(1.18:27.2) He cuts off the second portion after breaking through [the cake].

(1.18:27.3) Then, from the eastern half of the southern *puroḍāśa*, having well-saturated a piece three or four finger-breadths wide with clarified butter, he places the sacrificer’s portion in front of the *dhruvā* ladle.
(1.18:27.5) He takes two portions from the clarified butter in the *dhruvā*, twice from the northern *puroḍāśa*, twice from the boiled milk, and twice from the curds.
(1.18:27.6) He pours clarified butter over them.
Then he anoints the two fingers of the Hotṛ;
having smelled [the portion] with the nose, he cuts off four portions of the *avāntareḍā* (intermediate sacrificial food).
He spreads [the underlayer],
he places [the fuel] twice,
and he pours [the butter] over it.
The Adhvaryu, the Sacrificer, the Brahman, and the Āgnīdhra touch [the cake] together.

Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting, "The divine Adhvaryus are invoked; the human [Adhvaryus] are invoked," he divides the southern sacrificial cake into four parts and places it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting, "This sacrificer is invoked," at that moment the sacrificer, looking toward the Hotṛ, should meditate on Vāyu with his mind.
When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places the sixfold portion for the *agnīdh*.
He spreads [an underlayer of ghee], places [the portion], and pours [ghee] over it; he spreads [another underlayer], places [the portion], and pours [ghee] over it.
They consume [the portions].
They purify themselves.
Then he says, "Carry the *prāśitra* portion around for the Brahman.
They carry the *prāśitra* portion around.
(1.18:27.15) He follows the waters with the Veda, and [he follows] the portion for the Brahman.
(1.18:27.16) Then he asks for the Anvāhārya rice; they remove this sacrificial remnant.
(1.19:27.18) Then he issues the command: "O Brahman, we shall set forth; O Āgnīdh, having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, cleanse each of the fires once.
(1.19:27.19) Being thus impelled, he places this fuel-stick in the middle of the Āhavanīya fire.
(1.19:28.1) Then the Āgnīdhra cleanses the enclosing sticks with the wooden sword and the cord used for binding the fuel-wood—once the middle one, once the southern one, and once the northern one.

(1.19:28.2) He fans the Āhavanīya fire once, [reciting]: "O Agni, winner of the prize, I cleanse thee, the prize-winner, who hast run the race and won the prize, the vigorous one, the conqueror of the prize, for the sake of winning the prize—Agni, the eater of food, for the sake of food.

(1.19:28.5) Then, having touched these faggot-binders with water, he throws them after [into] the Āhavanīya fire, [reciting]: "He who is the overlord of beings, Rudra, the bull who moves along the threads: do not harm our cattle; let this be an oblation for thee, svāhā!"
Then, having taken up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles and stepped across, and having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to the gods.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering. He performs three *anūyāja* offerings directed westward, saying, "Sacrifice! Sacrifice! at each.
Having rinsed his mouth, he mixes [the flour].

Then, having stepped across toward the north and placed the two ladles in their respective places, he separates the two ladles with the two *vājavatī* verses: "By the impulse of strength, with the support, he has supported me.
With this, he lifts up the *juhū* with his right hand.
(1.19:28.12) "Then, by means of the *nigrābha*, Indra has made my rivals low," with these words he holds down the *upabhṛt* with his left hand.

(1.19:28.13) "The gods have increased the *udgrābha* and the *nigrābha* through sacred power (*brahman*)," with these words he moves the *juhū* forward. (1.19:28.14) "Then may Indra and Agni scatter my rivals in all directions," with these words he pushes back the *upabhṛt* toward the west.

(1.19:28.15) He anoints the enclosing sticks from the east: with "For the Vasus, thee! he anoints the middle one; with "For the Rudras, thee! the southern one; with "For the Ādityas, thee! the northern one.

(1.19:28.16) Then, having touched the *upabhṛt* with water and having placed the two ladles in their respective places, he anoints the *prastara* bundle in the ladles: (1.19:28.18) with "Licking what is anointed," he anoints the tips in the *juhū*; with "May the birds depart," the middles in the *upabhṛt*; and with "May I not wipe away offspring and the womb," the bases in the *dhruvā*.
(1.19:28.19) Then, having plucked a blade of grass from the *prastara* bundle, he places it into the *juhū* ladle.

(1.19:29.1) Then he causes the announcement to be made: "O, cause [the Āgnīdhra] to hear! "Let there be hearing! "The divine *hotṛ*s have been impelled for the auspicious utterance; the human [hotṛ] has been sent forth for the *sūktavāka*. Recite the hymns! Thus.

He hurls it forward as if above; he does not hurl it beyond the tip, nor does he cast it back from the front, nor does he let it strike against anything, nor does he scatter it in all directions, but he raises it upward with the mantra: "May the waters and the plants swell; you are the speckled ones of the Maruts; go to heaven, and from there send rain down upon us.
Then he looks toward the Āgnīdhra, saying, "O Āgnīdh!
To him the Āgnīdhra replies, "Converse [with the Hotṛ]!"
(1.19:29.7) "The Agnīdh has come," says the Adhvaryu.
(1.19:29.7) "He has come," says the Agnīdhra.
(1.19:29.7) "Make [them] hear! says the Adhvaryu.
"Śrauṣaṭ," says the Āgnīdhra. "Speak this," says the Adhvaryu.
"Throw [the firebrand] after [the oblation]," says the Āgnīdhra.
(1.19:29.9) He makes the supplementary offering with: "Go well to the divine *hotṛ*s; well-being to the human ones; pronounce the *śaṃyuvāka*.
(1.19:29.10) Then, having stood up, he worships the *āhavanīya* fire with: "O Agni, you are the protector of life; protect my life. O Agni, you are the protector of sight; protect my sight."
(1.19:29.11) Then he touches this [earth] with the words, "Thou art firm.

(1.19:29.12) He throws the middle enclosing-stick onto the fire with the words, "O divine Agni, that enclosing-stick which thou didst place around thee while being carried away by the Paṇis—I bring that very one back to thee according to thy pleasure, lest it should be alienated from thee. (1.19:29.14) Then he throws the other two together with the words, "Be united in the path of the sacrifice."
(1.19:29.15) Then he makes an offering over them with the residue.

He pours the residue from the *upabhṛt* ladle into the *juhū* ladle [with the formula]: "O great ones, you who have a share in the residue! O gods who stand upon the *prastara* and sit upon the *barhis* grass! All of you, welcoming this speech, sit down upon this *barhis* and rejoice—*svāhā*! Thus.

(1.19:29.18) Then, having turned clockwise and hastened westward, he unyokes the two offering-ladles upon the pole with [the formula]: "I set you two in the seat of Agni, whose house is secure; for the sake of favor, O ye full of favor, bestow favor upon me! O ye two bearers of the burden, protect the burden!
(1.19:29.20) But if there is no pole, he unyokes them on the rubbish-heap with the wooden sword (sphya), using this very same mantra.
Then, having taken the butter-pot together with the *sruva*-ladle in his right hand and the *juhū* in his left, and having handed the *veda* to the *hotṛ*,
they turn to the right and run toward the west.
The *adhvaryu* passes to the south of the *gārhapatya* fire, and the *hotṛ* to the north.
(1.20:30.3) They sit down behind the *gārhapatya* fire, facing eastward—the Adhvaryu on the south and the Hotṛ on the north.

(1.20:30.4) Then the Adhvaryu, having made the *veda* into an *upabhṛt* and taking four portions of clarified butter, says “for Soma” in a whisper, and “recite the invitatory prayer (*anubrūhi*)” loudly. (1.20:30.6) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says “Soma” in a whisper, and “sacrifice (*yaja*)” loudly.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.
While taking four portions of clarified butter, he says "To Tvaṣṭṛ" in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), and "Recite the invitatory verse" (*anubrūhi*) loudly.
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* response, he says "Tvaṣṭṛ" in a low voice, and "Sacrifice" (*yaja*) loudly.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.
While taking four portions of clarified butter, he says, "For the wives of the gods," in a low voice; "Recite the invitatory verse," loudly.
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "The wives of the gods," in a low voice; "Offer the oblation," loudly.
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers to the wives of the gods within the enclosed space.
Then, taking four portions of clarified butter, he says: "For Agni Gṛhapati," in a low voice; "Recite the invitatory verse (*anubrūhi*)," loudly.
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Agni Gṛhapati," in a low voice; "Sacrifice (*yaja*)," loudly.
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering in the eastern part of the northern half, passing over the previous offerings.
Then, having passed by the front of the *hotṛ*, he anoints the two fingers of the *hotṛ* twice;
having smelled them, he consumes [the portion].
He prepares the *iḍā* portion from the clarified butter itself in a four-handled vessel.
Both the Adhvaryu and the wife touch it together.
Once the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places the sixfold portion for the Āgnīdhra.
(1.20:30.17) Let them eat. (1.20:30.17) Let them sprinkle themselves.

Then, having taken four portions into the offering-spoon and turning away toward the left, he offers the expiation-oblation on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire: "Whatever has adhered to the mortar, to the pestle, and to the winnowing-basket; whatever to the grinding-stone and to the black antelope skin; whatever to the pot-sherd—those drops and splashes I offer together. May all the gods enjoy this oblation."
"Whatever drops there are in the sacrifice, many they may be—I offer them all, well-sacrificed and offered together into the fire, Svāhā! Thus [he says].

Having taken another fourfold portion and having placed the wood-shavings from the fire-drilling on the Anvāhāryapacana fire itself, and having poured in the husks, he offers the husk-oblation with: "O Agni, of unimpaired life-force, of cool body, protect me today from heaven; protect me from bondage; protect me from ill-sacrifice; protect me from bad food; protect me from evil conduct. Make our food free from poison; make our dwelling-place pleasant to sit in, Svāhā! Thus [he says].

(1.20:31.8) Then, having returned by the same way he came, he makes the sacrificer recite the Veda-mantra from "Thou art the Veda; thou art acquisition" until the end of the section. Having handed the Veda to the Hotṛ, he unties the wife with the mantra: "I untie this bond of Varuṇa, which Savitṛ, the kindly-minded, has bound. In the womb of Dhātṛ, in the world of good deeds, I make it pleasant for me together with my husband."

(1.20:31.12) Then, having placed her marriage-cord in her joined palms, he pours water from the vessel [over them] with the verse: "Be united with life, be united with offspring, O Agni, be united again with splendor! May I, as a wife, be united with my husband; may my self be united with my body. (1.20:31.14) Then she wipes her face with the verse: "O Sarasvatī, whatever honey is in your waters, in your cows, and in your horses—with that, O lady of plenty, anoint my face!"
"O Sarasvatī, cleanse [me]!"—with these words he pours out water.
"Having assumed the very form of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), he rises," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(1.21:31.18) Then, in the same manner, he causes her to sip water through the strainer with: "The plants are full of milk; the milk of the creepers is full of milk. Whatever milk is the milk of the waters—with that, O Indra, unite me. Thus.

(1.21:32.2) Then he causes her to place fuel-sticks on the Gārhapatya fire with the formulas: "O Agni, lord of vows, I have performed the vow; I was able to do it; it has been successful for me, svāhā! O Vāyu, lord of vows! O Āditya, lord of vows! O lord of vows among vows, I have performed the vow; I was able to do it; it has been successful for me, svāhā! (1.21:32.5) Then he causes her to go out by the way she entered.

(1.21:32.5) Then, having gone forward to the east, he causes the *dhruvā* ladle to swell with the formula: "May the *dhruvā* swell with ghee for every sacrifice performed by those seeking the gods; she is the udder of Sūryā in the lap of Aditi—broad-streamed Earth at this sacrifice."

(1.21:32.7) Then, dipping with the *sruva* ladle from the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), he offers the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta*) with the mantra: "That which was under-intoned and that which was over-intoned; that which was accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ*-call and that which was recited beyond measure in the sacrifice; whatever in the rite was redundant and whatever was deficient—may the sacrifice go forward, smoothing out and restoring its joints. May this offering, consecrated with *svāhā*, go to the gods! *Svāhā*! Thus.

(1.21:32.10) Then he offers the oblations for the prosperity of the sacrifice: "To those [sacrifices] successfully performed, svāhā! Vaṣaṭ to those not successfully performed, svāhā! A remedy for the ill-performed, svāhā! To expiation, svāhā! For misfortune, svāhā! To the divine bodies, svāhā! To success, svāhā! To complete success, svāhā! To universal success, svāhā! Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Suvaḥ svāhā! Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā! 'Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa' (RV 1.24.11); 'That I implore of thee' (RV 1.24.11)."

"O Agni, you are ours; O Agni, you are ours; O Agni, you are *ayās*. Being *ayās*, you are established by the mind. Being *ayās*, you have carried the oblation. Being *ayās*, bestow upon us healing, *svāhā*! And you, O Agni, are *ayās* and free from reproach. Truly, you are *ayās*. Held fast by an iron-like mind, you have carried the invocation with an iron-like [mind]. Being *ayās*, bestow upon us healing, *svāhā*! Whatever we have omitted in this rite, whether in respect of the mantra or the ritual action..."

"By this oblation, I pacify all that. May the gods be satisfied; may they rain down with clarified butter, svāhā! Whatever in this rite I have done in excess, or whatever I have done here deficiently—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make all that well-sacrificed and well-offered for me. To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, who has offered the well-offered oblations, the fulfiller of desires, svāhā! O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings."
"May that for which we sacrifice to you be ours; may we be masters of riches, svāhā! (1.21:33.5).

Then, having torn off portions from the stalks of the *barhis* grass, he anoints them upon the *dhruvā* ladle with the formula: "May the *barhis* be anointed with the oblation, with clarified butter; may it be anointed with the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Maruts; may it be anointed with Indra and all the gods. (1.21:33.7).
Then he throws it into the *āhavanīya* fire with the formula: "May it go to the celestial sky, svāhā!"

(1.21:33.8) Then, having risen and stepped onto the altar with his right foot, he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblation with the *dhruvā* ladle: "O gods who know the way, having found the way, go upon the way! O Lord of Mind, O God, place this sacrifice of ours among the gods, Svāhā! To Speech, Svāhā! To the Wind, place it, Svāhā!
(1.21:33.11) He lifts up the offering-ladle. (1.21:33.12) He pours out the *praṇītā* waters.
Having stood up, the sacrificer strides the Viṣṇu-strides with his right foot;
thus the New Moon or Full Moon oblation is completed.
(2.1:34.1) Now, regarding the formal declaration:

it is known from scripture that "At the beginning of a rite, one should desire for him whatever rite he desires; at the beginning of a constituent part of the sacrifice, one should desire for him whatever constituent part of the sacrifice he desires."

Having spread out Darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, the sacrificer sits upon it facing the east and mutters: "Those [waters] which flow from the front, those from above and from all sides—with these, purified by rays, I undertake faith and the sacrifice. O gods who know the way, find the way for the sacrifice! By the god who is the Lord of Mind, let the sacrifice be set in motion from the wind. [Then he says: "O Faith, come! I summon you with truth."
(2.1:34.6) He performs the act of knowing through intention: "For intention thee! For desire thee! For prosperity thee, I place before me, for immortality and for life!

(2.1:34.8) "I place his intention for protection, his desire for fulfillment; Indra’s thoughts they harness. (2.1:34.9) "I place the goddess Intention before my mind; may she, the mother of sacrifice, be easy for me to invoke. Whatever I desire with my mind, may I obtain that wish together with my heart, once it has entered therein."
(2.1:34.11) One mentally resolves three times and [utters] three times aloud:
(2.1:34.11) "Desiring all desires, I shall establish the fires," at the establishment of the fires;
(2.1:34.12) "Desiring heaven, I shall sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices," at the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
(2.1:34.13) “Desiring heaven, I shall sacrifice with the Cāturmāsya [seasonal sacrifices],” thus at the Cāturmāsyas;
(2.1:34.14) “Desiring heaven, I shall sacrifice with an animal,” thus at the Paśubandha;
(2.1:34.14) “Desiring heaven, I shall sacrifice with Soma,” thus at the Soma sacrifice.

(2.1:34.15) “Desiring heaven, I shall pile the fire-altar,” [he says] at the piling of the fire-altar. (2.1:34.16) At an Ahīna sacrifice or a series of days, he sacrifices according to his desire or for whatever purpose he desires: “May that be successful for me! May that be fully successful for me! May that be accomplished for me in my desire! Thus [he says].

Salt-earth, sand, mole-hill, ant-heap, clay from a pool, earth dug up by a boar, a lotus leaf, and gravel—these are the eight earthly materials.

(2.8:46.6) Having recited this section up to its end and having poured out the water, they cast away the vessel and return without looking back.
Having washed his hands and feet, and having returned by the same way he came, he causes the sacrificer to recite this section, "Pavamāna, the winner of heaven," while purifying him with water.

Having kindled the fuel from the *āmātya* fire at the time of the *anvāhāryapacana*, having set it down and cleansed it, and having strewn it around with sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he melts the clarified butter (*ājya*), purifies it, and places these items to the north: four water-pots, three stakes made of *udumbara* wood, a ladle (*darvī*) made of *udumbara*, and one *vapāśrapaṇī* (omentum-roasting fork) made of *udumbara* without a branch. To the south, he places all the other ritual implements belonging to the *sthālīpāka* for the ancestral sacrifice (*paitṛyajñika*), namely: the *eraka* grass mat and the pillow, collyrium and ointment, clarified butter, a handful of grass, the wooden sword (*sphya*), and the cord.
To the south, he prepares the gambling-ground (*adhidevana*).
Therein, he pours out forty-nine dice.

Then, taking up the wooden sword (*sphya*), he digs once toward the south, saying: "Struck down are the Asuras, the Rakṣases, and the Piśācas who dwell upon the earth! Let them go elsewhere, wherever their minds have gone!"
