(2.8:47.2) Then he sprinkles it with water, [reciting]: "May the lower, the higher, and the middle Soma-loving Fathers rise up! May those Fathers who have gone to the life-breath, who are harmless and knowers of the *ṛta*, protect us in our invocations! Thus.

(2.9:47.6) Then he takes up a firebrand with the verse: "The Asuras who, taking up their ancestral forms through the *svadhā*-offering, move about; those who carry away both the outer forts and the inner ones—may Agni drive them away from this sacrifice. (2.9:47.8) With that [firebrand], he heats the dug-out spot, saying: "May Agni Pāvaka, making the days auspicious, drive the Asuras far away from here, from their dwelling, they who, having assumed the color of the Pitṛs, desire a share here.
(2.9:47.10) Thereupon, he causes it to be extinguished right there.

(2.9:47.11) He drips a drop of clarified butter onto that firebrand. (2.9:47.11) He spreads the sacrificial grass with its tips pointing toward the south, [reciting]: "The sacrificial grass, once-cut, soft as wool, pleasant—I bring it for you, O Fathers. May my Fathers, worthy of Soma, sit upon this, along with their grandfathers and great-grandfathers. Thus he says.

(2.9:47.14) Then he invites the ancestors with: "May our Soma-loving fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers rise up and be present here, together with their followers—those who go to the breath of life, who are joined with truth, and who are free from malice. May the fathers come today to our invocation.
(2.9:47.17) "May the fathers come here to eat the oblation; having sat down upon the sacrificial grass at this sacrifice, may they not deprive us of a hero."

(2.9:47.18) Then he offers them a seat-cushion made of *eraka* grass, saying: "These are the seat and the bed; for these two, the Soma-drinkers have arrived. Having become dear to our people, be auspicious and bringers of well-being.
(2.9:47.20) Then he brings them drinks—either a drink of honey, a drink of milk, a drink of barley meal, or whatever else is available.
(2.9:48.1) He gives something else to the Brahmins.
(2.9:48.2) He pours another [portion] near [them], saying: "O fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, this is your drink.
(2.9:48.3) At this point, he sprinkles them silently with one water-pitcher.
(2.9:48.4) Then four people—the father and his sons—sit down around the dice.
The father stands in the east, the eldest in the south, the younger brother in the west, and the youngest in the north.
The father cuts off twelve seeds;
thereby he conquers.
Twelve are the elder;
that he conquers;
twelve are the younger.
That [fire] prevails.
Then, those [bricks] which remain, they pile up toward the smaller [side].
Now, if there are two [fires], the father has a double extent.
(2.9:48.8) Now, if there is only one wife, she is the third [participant].
(2.9:48.9) Or, if there are none at all, both husband and wife perform the two-day rite; (2.9:48.10) this same rule applies in the case of three [participants].
(2.9:48.10) This very same [procedure applies] to two [players].
(2.9:48.10) Saying, "The stake has been won," they depart.
(2.9:48.11) Having said, "A cow is the stake," they rise.

(2.9:48.11) Then, having taken sacrificial grass (*barhis*) from them, he dedicates the cow with the formula: "I dedicate you, who are dear, to the fathers, to the grandfathers, and to the great-grandfathers.
(2.9:48.13) According to some, [he does so] silently.
(2.9:48.13) Then he sprinkles it with water with the formula: "I sprinkle you, who are dear, to the fathers, to the grandfathers, and to the great-grandfathers."
"Silently," say some.
There, they cause her to be quieted with her head toward the west and her feet toward the south;
once she has been quieted, he silently causes her vital breaths to swell by sprinkling them with water.
Having silently extracted the omentum, he draws out the heart, the well-known portions, and the two kidneys; having placed these upon those very spits, they cook them on this very fire.
When the omentum is cooked, he offers five spoonfuls of oblations.

(2.10:49.4) "The waters that flow eastward and those from the north—with these waters, the sustainers of the entire world, I place another within me, away from my father. *Svadhā! Homage! Svāhā!* (2.10:49.6) "I place him within with the mountains, within with the great earth, with the sky, with the infinite quarters, and with protective aids; I place another within me, away from my grandfather. *Svadhā! Homage! Svāhā!*"

(2.10:49.7) "I interpose [him] with all the seasons, with days and nights well-joined, and with half-months and months; I place another between him and my great-grandfather. *Svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā!* (2.10:49.9) "Whatever my mother, acting contrary to her vows, has caused me to be confused—that seed let my father take back; let another man obtain it. *Svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā!*"

(2.10:49.11) “Whatever limb of yours the flesh-eater burnt while leading you away and carrying you to the worlds, O Jātavedas—that I cause to enter into you again. Be whole with all your limbs, O Fathers! Svadhā! Homage! Svāhā! Thus.

Having divided the omentum into three parts, he offers it with a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, saying: "To Soma, accompanied by the fathers, the impetuous one, we offer this oblation. O powerful one, enjoy this of ours; as one born of ourselves, [accept] the offering for the gods and the fathers. *Svadhā!* Homage!

*Svāhā!* I invoke Yama, who is accompanied by the Aṅgirases, for our protection, together with the fathers. O son of Vivasvat, eat this of ours; as one born of ourselves, [accept] the offering for the gods and the fathers. *Svadhā!* Homage! *Svāhā!* "

(2.10:49.18) “O Agni, Kavyavāhana, you who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*), worship the ancestors; carry the oblation to the gods, and offer the oblation to the ancestors according to your own nature. To the gods and the ancestors, *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*!

Having thus silently placed the wooden ladle (*darvī*) upon the fire, he offers these portions according to the procedure for the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*): first the heart, then the left kidney, then the right.

(2.10:50.2) "This for you, O father, [and] for those who follow you, and for those whom you here follow. This, O father, is your abode of *svadhā*. As great as the earth is, so great is your measure; this measure, having become such, I give to you. You are measured by the earth; do not perish for your father. Thus.

He gives the second [portion], saying: "This for you, grandfather N.N., and for those who follow you, and those whom you here follow. This, grandfather, is your abode of *svadhā*. As great as the intermediate space is, so great is your measure; this measure, being such, I give to you. You are measured by the intermediate space; do not perish for the sake of the grandfather."

He gives the third [portion], saying: "This for you, O great-grandfather [Name], and for those who follow you, and those whom you follow here; this, O great-grandfather, is your abode of *svadhā*. As vast as is the sky, so vast is your measure; I give you this measure as it truly is. You are measured by heaven; do not fail the great-grandfather!
Having said, "O ancestors, rejoice here according to your shares," he silently sprinkles [the remains] there with one water-pitcher.

(2.10:50.14) Then, having approached the cow from behind, he causes blood to flow [upon it] with the mantra: "Whatever *rakṣases* have a share in the blood, and whatever fathers (*pitaraḥ*) carry it away—let them disperse; let them be satiated with that blood of yours! Those miscarriages of ours who wait upon us as sharers of the blood—to them be their own portion, *svadhā*, and obeisance; let them be satisfied and rejoice! Those who are raw, those who are cooked, and those who fall upon us as corrupt ones..."

"To them, self-born, *svadhā*, obeisance! May they be satisfied and rejoice! Those who are boys, those who are women, and those unknown ones who fall upon us—to them, self-born, *svadhā*, obeisance! May they be satisfied and rejoice!
Having returned, he gives eye-ointment;
then he gives ointment for the body.
(2.10:51.2) Then he gives garments.
(2.10:51.3) Then he worships with six salutations in reverse order.
(2.10:51.3) Then he asks for a hero.
(2.10:51.4) Then, having raised them up and led them forward, he invokes the mind with three verses: "We summon the mind hither; may our mind return to us; O fathers, may the mind return to us.

(2.10:51.5) At this point, having given this unwashed garment to a Brāhmaṇa learned in this [rite], and having put on another garment to be worn, he goes toward the south and purifies himself with water.
(2.11:51.8) "In which both fragrances, tastes, and colors, as well as strength, are contained—may those waters be auspicious for me; may they carry away my evil deeds."

(2.11:51.9) "Those great waters sent by the gods, which pour forth vigor—may those waters be auspicious for me; may they carry away my evil deeds. Those from whose emergence this entire world is born—may those waters be auspicious for me; may they carry away my evil deeds. Those by whose splendor and glory these three worlds are encompassed—may those waters be auspicious for me; may they carry away my evil deeds."

"May those waters which flow—those to the east, those to the south, those to the west, those to the north, and those upward—rich, honey-sweet, and bright; may those waters be auspicious for me; may they carry away my evil deed. Having said this, he should remove the garment he was wearing at that time, put on another, and rise from the fire with the verse addressed to Prajāpati: "O Prajāpati, none other than you [has encompassed] these..."

(2.11:51.18) Then he throws back the firebrand with the verse: "Jātavedas has become the messenger of the oblation; having made the offerings fragrant, he has carried them away. He has given them to the Fathers, and they have eaten them with the *svadhā* call. Knowing the way, O Agni, come back again to the gods. (2.11:52.2) At this point, he gives these portions to the Brahmins: first the heart, then the left lung, then the right; he provides food according to his faith.
Having divided this cow into portions, he gives it as a boon to the Brahmins. Whosoever among them obtain a portion of its meat, they all indeed become sharers in the cow.
Having offered the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, he performs the *āmātya* oblations.
"This indeed is the Upavasatha day,
for the gods dwell near it [thinking], 'In the morning we shall win desirable wealth.
And that which is the eight-potherd cake for Agni is indeed the desirable wealth of the gods."
(2.11:52.9) "Desirable wealth indeed comes to him for whom one, knowing this, prepares this cow;
(2.11:52.10) he overcomes all evil;
he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin."
"He overcomes death again," so said Prajāpati. "These are indeed called the *Kūṣmāṇḍas*, or the *Kājavānis*, or the *Vāmātya-homas*, or the *Atīmokṣas*.
Whatever evil deed one performs in this world, from all that he is released; free from debt, he goes to the heavenly world," so said Prajāpati.

One who is about to establish the sacred fires procures eight earth-related materials: saline soil, sand, a mole-hill, the mound of an anthill, mud from a pool, earth dug up by a boar, a lotus leaf, and gravel.

(2.12:53.5) Now, the wooden items are: the *aśvattha*, the *udumbara*, the *parṇa*, the *śamī*, the *vikaṅkata*, a lightning-struck [piece of wood], and two kindling sticks (*araṇī*) made from *śamī* wood containing a *śamī* embryo; a nest of *muñja* grass; three moist fuel-sticks from a variegated *aśvattha* tree, each a span long, with their leaves and shoots intact and their tips not dried out; six pieces of gold—three of gold and three of silver; a horse that has drawn [the chariot] before; a chariot wheel; rice for the *brāhmaudana*; all kinds of herbs; a red bull's hide; new sacrificial vessels.

(2.12:53.11) Then he brings the two kindling woods for him [with the verse]: "The *aśvattha* tree that has grown from the womb of the *śamī*, which has climbed up together with you—that I bring to you by means of the sacred word (*brahman*), along with the sacrificial signs.
(2.12:53.13) Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*):
"One should establish the fire under the Kṛttikās."
(2.12:53.14) "One should establish the sacred fire under Rohiṇī;
(2.12:53.14) one should establish the sacred fire under the two Punarvasus; (2.12:53.15) [or] under the two Pūrvaphalgunīs."
(2.12:53.15) "Under the two later *phalgunī*s," (2.12:53.15) "under *citrā*.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the seasons.
(2.12:53.16) "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring; (2.12:53.16) a Rājanya in summer;
(2.12:53.17) a Vaiśya in autumn."
(2.12:53.17) “[The *rathakāra* [should establish the fires] in the rainy season,” so says Baudhāyana.
(2.12:53.17) But rather, whenever faith should come upon him, then he should establish them;
that indeed is his prosperity.
This [rite] is for one who is distressed or for one who possesses excessive faith. Now, indeed, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage:
"He who establishes the sacred fires under Rohiṇī prospers; he rises to all heights. Thus it is said.
"That new moon which occurs after the full moon of Vaiśākha coincides with the asterism Rohiṇī once a year; on that day one should establish the sacred fires. Thus it is said.
Now, prior to this, a house or a shed has already been constructed for him on a chosen sacrificial ground.
For that structure, they make two doors: one facing east and one facing south.
They prepare the site for the Gārhapatya fire in the middle; twelve paces to the east of that is the site for the Āhavanīya fire,
or else at a point marked by the range of vision.

To the south of the *viṣuvat* [line], he places the *anvāhāryapacana* fire. Or rather, so that two parts may be in the east and one in the west; having thus marked out three portions and sprinkled them with water, he shaves his hair and beard.
He trims his nails;
likewise the wife, with the exception of her hair. Both become adorned with human ornaments and clothed in new garments.
Then he has them cook the food for the commencement of the vow (*vratopāyanīya*).
Of that, two portions are eaten: one mixed with clarified butter and one mixed with milk.

(2.13:54.14) Then, when the sun has reached the top of the trees, he asks for all kinds of herbs, a vessel for clarified butter together with a *sruva*-ladle, a *sruk*-ladle, sacrificial grass (*barhis*), a garment, firebrands, and chips of wood.
(2.13:54.15) Having taken these, they go forth while remaining well-concealed toward either a frying pan (*ambarīṣa*) or a heating pan (*uttapanīya*).

(2.13:54.16) Having scattered firebrands upon it, having strewn it around with sacrificial grass, having melted the clarified butter and purified it, he offers the all-herbs mixture—previously spread out and sprinkled—with his joined palms, saying: "To Agni, who possesses all herbs, for nourishment and procreation, svāhā!"
(2.13:55.2) Then, having offered the *jayās*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, he offers the *amātya* oblations.

(2.13:55.3) Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter in the offering-spoon, he offers the oblation to Prajāpati with the verse: "O Prajāpati, none other than you [has encompassed] these [worlds].

(2.13:55.4) Having taken another four portions, he offers the *anukhyā* oblation with the verse: "Agni, the first Jātavedas, has looked along the vanguard of the dawns; he has looked along the days; he has extended along the many rays of the sun and along heaven and earth—svāhā!"

(2.13:55.7) Then the sacrificer takes these embers in either a vessel (*sata*) or a shallow bowl (*śarāva*), saying: "I take you for life; I take you for splendor; I take you for heat; I take you for vigor; I take you for Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
(2.13:55.9) Having taken them, he stands up, saying: "May life enter me; may prosperity enter me; may Vedic luster enter me.
(2.13:55.11) Having handed them over to the *adhvaryu*, they go out while the sacrificer maintains contact by holding on.
By this very same path he returns, goes around the north of the house, enters by the eastern door, and having piled [the fire] in the place of the Gārhapatya, he adds fuel to it.
They strew grass around it;
the Brahman and the sacrificer sit down to the south.
(2.13:55.14) Then he spreads this red bull-hide behind the fire with its neck to the east and the hair side up.
(2.13:55.15) At the place of the *vahasa* [the shoulder-hair], he pours out four measures of rice-grains, either with the formula, "I pour thee out, acceptable to the Brahman," or silently.
(2.13:55.17) Then he touches the poured-out grains with the formula: "For intention thee, for desire thee, for prosperity thee."
(2.13:55.18) Then, having poured these rice grains into a winnowing basket and sprinkled them with water, he carries them out upon a hide.
(2.13:55.18) Then, having placed the mortar and pestle upon that very hide, he threshes them.
(2.13:56.1) Then, with this same vessel, he pours in four vessels of water, provided that the cooking pot is sturdy.
But if it is not pressed, whether it be five or more [strokes],
it becomes equal to water.
Whosoever is skilled [in this] cooks it by means of a complete layering of fuel, bastes it with clarified butter, and removes it from the fire toward the north.
Then they announce it to the officiating priests as the "approaching cow.
These officiating priests approach him.

Then, having washed this vessel and spread a base of ghee within it, he draws the rice into it as if not striking it. Having made a cavity for pouring the clarified butter and having poured in abundant *ājya*, he then offers a portion of that very rice, or stands over it, [reciting]: "To the wise, the seer, the holy one, the bull, the vigorous one—may there be for us from him that fear which is free from fear. I sacrifice to the gods who are to be appeased; *svāhā*! Thus he says.

Then, having seated these four *ārṣeya* priests to the north, each facing his respective direction, and having had them sip water in succession, he pushes this [rice-mash] toward them while touching the ground and as if not cutting it off.
Having eaten it three times, they praise it, saying, "Your *brahmaudana* has been prepared. To them, he gives a young bull with testicles.
Then this Brāhmaṇa, sitting to the north, eats the scrapings of the embers;
to him he gives whatever may be available.

(2.14:56.14) Now, with whatever clarified butter remains, he anoints the fuel-sticks and places them [on the fire] with these *gāyatrī* verses: "Venerate Agni with fuel; awaken the guest with clarified butter. Offer the oblations into him—*svāhā*! O beloved Agni, let the ladles full of clarified butter, laden with oblations, approach you. Accept my fuel-sticks—*svāhā*! O Aṅgiras, we strengthen you with fuel and with clarified butter. Blaze brightly, O youngest one—*svāhā*! Thus for a Brāhmaṇa.
With *triṣṭubh* verses, for a *rājanya*: "I besprinkle Agni," "I besprinkle thee," "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation.
With *jagatī* verses, for a *vaiśya*: "The guardian of the people has been born, the watchful one," "Thee, O Agni, the human clans praise," "Seven are thy kindling-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues.
At the kindling-sticks, he gives a heifer.
(2.15:57.10) Then, handing over the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) to him, he says: "You shall restrain your speech; give your instructions regarding what you have to instruct.
(2.15:57.11) He replies: "Feed the Brahmins; guard the horse; set down the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*).
(2.15:57.12) His establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) becomes one of abundant provisions.
(2.15:57.13) There is prosperity in the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya).
Regarding this, they say: "One should not offer a cow at the establishment of the sacred fires, for it is of a terrible form.
One may indeed offer one, or one may not offer one.
(2.15:57.14) He may perform even many [offerings].
(2.15:57.14) "And he should follow this with a meritorious praise," says Kātya.
(2.15:57.15) Then he hands the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) to him.

He accepts them with the verse: "O great ones, mistresses of the people, in the seat of the Cosmic Order, come hither, you who are the sustainers of riches! Pregnant with the kinsman, O Jātavedas, you two generate him as the leader of the sacrifices. Ascend my ten fingers, O Agni, by means of the Truth, together with long life and splendor! May we live long through each successive year, so that I may perform the sacrifice at the new moon and the full moon."

(2.15:57.20) Then he takes hold of them [the two wives] with the formula: "You two are possessed of the season, having Agni as your seed; receive the embryo; I bestow it upon you both. That is the truth that you bear a hero; you shall give birth to a hero. Through me, you two shall procreate in the morning; once procreated, you shall cause me to procreate through offspring, cattle, and spiritual luster in the heavenly world."

(2.15:58.4) Then he leads him from untruth to truth, from the human to the divine, [with the words]: "Here I go from untruth to truth; I go from the human to the divine; I restrain my divine speech. (2.15:58.6) They remain sitting through the night, keeping him awake while he restrains his speech.
(2.15:58.7) On that night they kindle the fire with wood-shavings, [reciting]: "Kindling the fire with wood-shavings, may I win both worlds. Having prospered in both worlds, may I cross over death.

(2.15:58.8) To the north of the Gārhapatya’s hearth, he binds a spotted goat. With it, he causes the fire that is about to be established to look on, [reciting]: "O Agni, cause the offspring to dwell together; [cause] the quarters along with the cattle to dwell together. Bestow upon him the kingdoms which were present at the impulsion of Savitṛ."

(2.16:58.13) Then, having rushed forward in the latter part of the night, the Adhvaryu heats the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) with the mantra: "O Jātavedas, seed of the world, pour it here; from this austerity that which is to be born shall arise. Producing Agni, the bearer of oblations, from the *aśvattha* tree, and from the womb of the *śamī* tree—him who is the source of bliss.
(2.16:58.15) "This is your seasonal womb, from which once born you shone forth. Knowing it, O Agni, ascend it, and then increase our wealth.
(2.16:58.17) Then, having placed this fire in a vessel, they sit to the south keeping it aflame.

(2.16:59.1) Then he smears these fire-places with a lump of cow-dung. (2.16:59.1) Then, taking a third of the materials, he pours them out upon the site of the Gārhapatya fire with the verse: "That immortal [essence] of the earth which was produced together with thee—that Agni gave to Agni; let this [man] be placed therein. (2.16:59.4) Wherever he finds saline soil, there he mutters: "That which is black in the moon, let that also be here."

(2.16:59.5) Then he places them [on the fire] with: "With the vigor of heaven, with the greatness of earth, with the nourishment of the intermediate space, I place you, possessing all cattle. (2.16:59.6) Then he mixes them together with: "I unite your hearts; may your minds be united; may your breath be united.
Those bodies of yours which are dear, and your dear hearts—may your self be dear to you, and may your bodies be dear to me."

(2.16:59.10) Then he arranges them [with the formula]: "May heaven and earth be in harmony; may the waters and plants be in harmony; may the fires, being of one vow, be in harmony separately for my preeminence.
(2.16:59.11) "The fires that are of one mind between heaven and earth, adapting themselves to the two spring seasons, may they enter together as the gods enter Indra. Thus.

(2.16:59.13) Then, taking half of the remaining materials, having carried them out by the southern door, he pours them down in the place of the *anvāhāryapacana* fire with the mantra: "That immortal essence of the atmosphere which has come into being together with thee—that Vāyu gave to Agni; let this [essence] be placed therein.
(2.16:59.16) When he comes upon the saline soil (*ūṣa*), he mutters: "That which is black in the moon, let that also be here."
In that manner he places [the fire],
in that manner he mixes [the butter],
and in that manner he prepares [the offering].

(2.16:59.18) Then, having returned by the same way he came and taking the remaining materials, he carries them out by the eastern door and pours them down in the place of the Āhavanīya fire with the words: "That immortal [substance] which was produced from heaven, being together with thee—that the Āditya gave to Agni; in that may this [fire] be established."
When he comes upon the embers, he mutters: "That which is black in the moon, let that also be here.
He places [the fuel] in that manner;
he stirs it together in that manner.
He arranges [the fires] in that manner.
Then he gives instructions to the guardian:
"The fires have been separated; let no one pass between them. Thus he says.

(2.16:60.3) Then the Adhvaryu, having turned to the right and hastened westward, places a nest of *muñja* grass upon the materials at the site of the Gārhapatya fire. (2.16:60.4) Having placed the lower fire-drill (*araṇi*) upon it with its cutting edge facing westward, he places the upper fire-drill upon it while reciting the *Daśahotṛ* formula.
(2.16:60.6) He says: "Churn! (*manthata*).
The sacrificer churns first;
the sacrificer churns last;
he generates [the fire].

(2.16:60.7) Upon the birth [of the son], he releases his speech, saying: "I give a boon. (2.16:60.8) Then he pays homage to him with the verse: "Mortals have begotten the immortal, the one who does not falter, the swift one with strong jaws. May the ten sisters, the maidens moving together, embrace the newborn male."

(2.16:60.10) Then he breathes over him with: "By the breath of Prajāpati, I breathe over you with the nourishment of Pūṣan for me; for long life lasting a hundred autumns, for a hundred autumns of vitality, for life, splendor, living, and merit.

(2.16:60.12) "I place immortality in your breath, as an eater of food for the sake of food, as a protector for the sake of protection. (2.16:60.13) Then he says to the Udgātṛ, "Recite the Rathantara!"
(2.16:60.14) Then he establishes it with:

(2.16:60.14) <bhūr bhuvas> | <gharmaḥ śiras | tad ayam agniḥ | saṃpriyaḥ paśubhir bhuvat | chardis tokāya tanayāya yaccha |> (2.16:60.16) <"I establish thee, O lord of vows, by the vow of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases"— with these words, he should establish it for those of the Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras lineages.>

(2.16:60.17) “With the vow of the Ādityas, the gods, O Lord of Vows, I establish you,” [he says] for other Brāhmaṇa subjects. “With the vow of King Varuṇa, O Lord of Vows, I establish you,” [he says] for a king. (2.16:60.19) “With the power of Indra, O Lord of Vows, I establish you,” [he says] for a Rājanya. (2.16:60.20) “With the vow of Manu, the village-leader, O Lord of Vows, I establish you,” [he says] for a Vaiśya.
"O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of the Ṛbhus, the gods"— this is for the chariot-maker. Thus, according to the *ṛṣi* and according to the *gotra*,
[he establishes him] with the words, "With the *gāyatrī* metre."
To the north, he throws down a chip of gold with the words, "Be united with your own body. Then he hands over this silver [chip] to a Śūdra or an unknown person.
"He hands over misfortune itself," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(2.16:61.5) Then he worships him with: "I am yours; you are mine. This is [our bond]. You are my source; I am your source. Being mine alone, O Agni, carry the oblations, you who create the world for your father, O Jātavedas!

(2.16:61.7) May you, the good Gārhapatya, burning away the enemies, making each dawn more auspicious than the last, O Agni, driving away our rivals, bestow upon us abundance of wealth, food, and vigor! Thus.
(2.17:61.10) Now they take up this fire which has been gathered in the pan;

having carried it out by the southern door, he establishes the Anvāhāryapacana fire with the formula: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ! Vāta is the breath; may this Agni become dear to the cattle. Cook a well-dressed meal for our children and descendants.
(2.17:61.13) "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of these gods. Thus.
According to the ṛṣi and according to the lineage:
"With the Gāyatrī metre," he says. To the north, he throws down a piece of gold with the words: "Be united with your own body."
(2.17:61.15) Then he hands over this silver [vessel] to a Śūdra or an unknown person.
(2.17:61.16) "He hands over misfortune itself," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(2.17:61.17) Or rather, he establishes the Anvāhāryapacana fire directly from the Gārhapatya.

(2.17:61.17) “Prajāpati created Agni; he was afraid, thinking, ‘He will burn me up. He divided his greatness threefold for the sake of peace and to prevent burning. From this Brāhmaṇa [it follows]. (2.17:61.19) Then he worships him with: “May these riches wait upon me; may I dwell here together with these offspring. May Iḍā, possessing all forms, stand here; shine in the midst of wealth, O Jātavedas!
(2.17:61.22) Then, returning by the same way he came, he places the fuel for the leading forward of the fire.
He places that [fuel] on the fire in such a way that he thinks, "The Āhavanīya fire will be established just as the sun is half-risen";
it becomes so for him.
They prepare the supporting-bricks (*upayamanī*).
(2.17:62.3) This horse stands in front, washed clean from the east.

(2.17:62.3) Then he says to the Udgātṛ, "Recite the Vāmadevya! (2.17:62.4) Then he lifts him up with the formula: "I lift you up for vigor, for strength, for virility, for breath, and for luster. You are the overcomer of rivals, the overcomer of obstacles."

(2.17:62.6) "Whatever majesty of yours is in the gods, [bestowing] heaven; whatever self of yours has entered into the cattle; whatever prosperity of yours has spread among men—with that, O Agni, come to us, being well-pleased.

(2.17:62.8) "From heaven, from earth, from the intermediate space, from the wind, from the cattle, and from the plants—wheresoever, O Jātavedas, you have come into being—from there, O Agni, come to us, being well-pleased. Thus he says.
He first carries [the fire] this much.
(2.17:62.10) Then he moves it. (2.17:62.10) Then he moves it. (2.17:62.10) "He lowers the head further and further," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(2.17:62.10) "One should accomplish these measures while actually taking them up"—this is another [instruction].
(2.17:62.11) They lead the horse first.

(2.17:62.12) He addresses it with the mantra: "Go forward along the eastern quarter, O wise one; O Agni, may Agni be before you here. Shining forth, illumine all the quarters. Bestow strength upon our bipeds and quadrupeds. Thus.
At the Viṣuvat [day] they cease, saying: "Stride forth! You are great! O altar-seeker, for the sake of men, be watchful in the three worlds!

Then they pass by, saying: "Agni has looked along the vanguard of the dawns; as the first Jātavedas, he has followed the days. He has followed the many rays of the sun; he has extended across heaven and earth."
(2.17:62.17) Then, with this horse, he makes it step upon the sacrificial materials from the front toward the northern side, so that the embers of the fire once established may fall down upon them.
(2.17:62.19) Then, having turned it clockwise and sprinkled it with water, he releases it toward the north.
(2.17:62.20) This [horse] belongs to the Adhvaryu priest.
(2.17:62.20) He gives another [cow] to the Brahman priest.

(2.17:62.20) Then, having turned clockwise, he establishes the fuel-wood with the mantra: "Whatever is here of heaven, whatever is there of earth; the two worlds, being in agreement, have come together. Upon their back let Jātavedas sit—beneficent to offspring, pleasant to the body.
(2.17:63.3) "I establish you, the breath, according to the *ṛta*, as an eater of food for the sake of eating food, as a protector for the sake of protection. Thus.
Then he says to the Udgātṛ: "Sing the Bṛhat, the Vāravantīya, and the Śyaita!
Thus he gives all the directions.

While the *Bṛhat* is being sung, he establishes the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! The Arka is the eye; that is yonder sun, that is this Agni. May he be well-beloved by the cattle! O pure one, with that which is your pure luster, your pure body, your pure and imperishable light—with that shine for me; with that I establish you. With Agni, O Agni, through the sacred word (*brahman*). O Lord of Vows, I establish you by the vow of these gods. Thus [he establishes it] according to the *ṛṣi* and according to the *gotra*, [saying]: "With the *gāyatrī* metre."
(2.17:63.10) To the north, he throws down a chip of gold with the words: "Be united with your own body. (2.17:63.11) Then he hands over this silver [chip] to a Śūdra or an unknown person.
(2.17:63.12) "He hands over misfortune itself," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(2.17:63.12) Then he worships it [the fire], saying: "I have attained; I have pervaded; I have pervaded a full lifespan.
(2.17:63.13) At this point, he establishes these two fires: the *sabhya* and the *āvasathīya*.
(2.17:63.14) He rolls the chariot wheel continuously from the *gārhapatya* fire to the *āhavanīya* fire.

Having appeased the fires with all-herbs and the *vyāhṛtis*, he anoints five fuel-sticks each from various trees and places them upon the fires with these five verses beginning, "Being kindled, the first law... (*samidhyamānaḥ prathamo nu dharmaḥ*), omitting the verse, "O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation" (*āyurdā agne haviṣo juṣāṇaḥ*).

(2.18:64.1) Then, having turned clockwise and hastened westward, standing behind the *gārhapatya* fire, he worships with the [Tanū] formulas: "O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Virāj and the Svarāj—may they enter me; may they quicken me! O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Samrāj and the Abhibhū—may they enter me; may they quicken me! O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Vibhū and the Paribhū—may they enter me; may they quicken me!"
"O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the powerful and the abundant—may they enter me; may they quicken me. O Agni, with those bodies of yours which are auspicious, I establish you.
With these [formulas], he establishes the *gārhapatya* fire with all [the formulas]; with all [the formulas], the *anvāhāryapacana* fire.

(2.18:64.9) With all [the verses], he addresses the Āhavanīya fire. Then he assigns the terrible forms: "O Agni, with those forms of yours that are terrible, go to so-and-so. (2.18:64.10) At this point, he meditates mentally upon whomever the sacrificer hates.
(2.18:64.11) Then, having touched water, he worships with the Virāj-krama formulas:

(2.18:64.11) "O manly one, protect my offspring for the sake of immortality and life—those born and those yet to be born—established in immortality and truth," thus [he addresses] the Gārhapatya fire. (2.18:64.13) "O Atharvan, protect my food—its essence and its nourishment here for the sake of long life; O undeceived one, O cool-bodied one, make our food free from poison," thus [he addresses] the Anvāhāryapacana fire.

(2.18:64.15) "O Śaṃsa, protect my cattle—those that are two-footed and those that are four-footed, O Agni, those here with eight hooves and those that are one-hoofed and swift"—with these words he addresses the Āhavanīya fire. (2.18:64.17) "O Sapratha, protect my assembly hall; and those who are members of the assembly and its attendants, make them endowed with sensory power; may they attain a full lifespan"—with these words he addresses the Sabhya fire.

(2.18:64.19) “O Ahi Budhnya, guard my mantra—that which the seers who know the three Vedas know: the *ṛc*s, the *sāmans*, and the *yajus*’s; for that is the immortal glory of the virtuous. Thus [he recites] at the *āvasathīya*.

(2.18:65.1) Then, at the *gārhapatya*, having melted the clarified butter and purified it, and having taken four portions into the ladle, he offers a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the *āhavanīya* fire while it contains a fuel-stick, with the verse: “Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues...
(2.18:65.3) At the full oblation, he gives a choice gift.

(2.18:65.3) Then he places these washed Agnihotra vessels to the north of the Gārhapatya fire, either on a grass-mat or on a wooden block: the pot together with the dipping-spoon, the offering-ladle, the fire-brand for lighting, and a fuel-stick.
(2.18:65.6) Then, having stationed the Agnihotra cow to the south facing north, a Brāhmaṇa milks her; he should milk first from the two front udders.
One should milk two others;
one should not touch them together. "One should milk two for one who desires cattle," so it is said.
Having placed [the milk] on the fire, he pours the latter [portion] into it.

Then, having carried this *agnihotra* oblation around the front of the *āhavanīya*, having brought it in through the eastern door, and having set it down behind the *gārhapatya*, he performs the ritual procedure for the *agnihotra* therein; then, having approached with a fuel-stick, he carries it forward and sets it down on a grass-mat behind the *āhavanīya*.
(2.18:65.11) At this point, he silently places this fuel-stick in the middle of the Āhavanīya fire.
(2.18:65.12) "When it has been kindled, he offers twice facing it; he wipes upwards and he wipes downwards; thus he obtains both," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(2.18:65.13) Having tasted [the ghee] twice with his finger and having turned toward the north, he consumes [the remainder] with the ladle whose handle points eastward.
Having washed the ladle, heated it, and filled it with water, he pours it out toward the north.
"He thus gratifies the Seven Sages," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Having offered the oblation, he adds fuel for the kindling of spiritual luster.
"He pours out water; he has thus produced the form of the *avabhṛtha*," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(2.19:66.1) Then he sends a servant to cut the sacrificial grass (*barhis*),
or he prepares it with a *yajus* formula once it has been brought.
(2.19:66.2) Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, when he is about to offer the cake on eight potsherds for Agni, he should recite the *daśahotṛ* formula.
When about to recite the *sāmidhenī* verses, he should recite the *daśahotṛ* formula.
Having cooked [the oblation], he sets it down.
For that [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenīs*, five *prayāja*s, and two *ājyabhāga*s belonging to Vṛtrahan.
Then, for the oblation, he recites two *triṣṭubh* verses as the *saṃyājyā*s: "Agni is the head" and "Of the earth.
Having placed the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) belonging to the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*).
He gives [the dakṣiṇās] up to twelve; he may give more if he so desires. This sacrifice concludes with the pouring out of the *pūrṇapātra* and the *viṣṇukrama* steps.
He releases the vow.

Then, at that very moment, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni and a pap to Āditya. This pap is made with clarified butter.
When the milk has nearly boiled, he pours the clarified butter into it;
having cooked it, he sets it down.
For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja* offerings, and two *ājyabhāga* portions dedicated to Vṛtrahan.
Now, for the two oblations: for the offering to Indra and Agni, [the verses] are "O Indra and Agni, the lights of heaven" and "He pierced Vṛtra";
for the offering to Aditi, [the verses] are "May Aditi protect us" and "The great mother, indeed.
These two Triṣṭubh verses are the *saṃyājyā* offerings.
(2.19:66.14) Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice and then having drawn out this *caru* offering, four *ārṣeya* priests consume it.
(2.19:66.15) "He offers indeed in the light of the quarters," so says the Brāhmaṇa. (2.19:66.16) This sacrifice concludes with the *pūrṇapātra* and the *viṣṇukrama* steps.
He releases the vow.
At this point, he observes this vow for twelve days;
his vow is as follows:
he does not speak untruth.
He does not eat meat,
he does not approach a woman,
and they do not wash his garment with lye.
(2.20:66.19) Not drinking from earthenware vessels and not eating the leavings of a Śūdra, he washes his own feet (2.20:67.1) and does not eat salt.
(2.20:67.1) One may not engage in usury, except for sesame seeds.
(2.20:67.1) Before sunrise, while personally carrying fuel, he lies down near the fires. (2.20:67.2) These fires remain perpetually burning for him for twelve days.
No Brāhmaṇa stays in his house without having eaten.
Or, the sacrificer observes the vow of consuming only the remnants of the *agnihotra* offering; they bring food for the wife as well.
Then, when twelve nights have dawned, having spread the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna.
Having cooked it, he sets it down.
For this sacrifice, there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja* offerings, and two *ājyabhāga* portions belonging to Vṛtraghna.
Then, for the oblation, he uses two *triṣṭubh* verses as the *saṃyājyā*s: "O Agni, you purify the lives" and "O Agni, purify yourself.
Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives gold weighing thirty [mānas].
This sacrifice concludes with the *pūrṇapātra* and the *viṣṇukrama* steps;
he releases his vow.
Then, at that very moment, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pāvaka and to Agni Śuci.
Having cooked [the oblation], he sets it down.
For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja*s, and two *ājyabhāga*s dedicated to Vṛtra-slayers.
Then, for the two principal offerings (*havis*), [he recites]: "O Agni, purifier," "May he purify us," "Agni, most pure in his vows," and "Upward, O Agni, thy pure [flames]."
The two *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *triṣṭubh* metre.
Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives away two pieces of gold weighing thirty and forty *mānas*.
This sacrifice concludes with the pouring out of the *pūrṇapātra* and the *viṣṇukrama* steps.
He releases his vow.
(2.21:67.18) Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the *anvārambha* (the taking hold from behind).
(2.21:67.18) He performs the *anvārambha* of the full-moon sacrifice so that the day of preparation (*upavasatha*) is common to both.

(2.21:67.19) Then, in the morning, after the *agnihotra* has been offered and before the carrying forward of the waters, he melts the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, purifies it, takes four portions into the ladle, and, having mentally recited the *caturhotṛ* formula, offers it into the *āhavanīya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact from behind, saying: "Svāhā!"
Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers two oblations to Sarasvatī,
reciting "Full behind" and then offering with "O Agni and Soma.
Having taken another fourfold portion, he recites "The settling one, the gatherer of riches," and offers with "That share which the gods assigned to thee."

Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu, [and] a *caru* to Sarasvatī, [and] an oblation on twelve potsherds to Sarasvant.
Having cooked them, he sets them down.
For this sacrifice, there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja* offerings, and the two *ājyabhāga* portions belong to the Vṛtra-slayers.

Then, for the oblations, he recites as the two *saṃyājyā* verses the two *triṣṭubh*s: "O Agni-Viṣṇu," "O Agni-Viṣṇu," "Forward for us, O Goddess," "From heaven unto us," "The swelling breast of Sarasvatī," and "Those waves of yours, O Sarasvatī.
Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a pair of cattle.
This sacrifice concludes with the *pūrṇapātra* and the *viṣṇukrama* steps;
he releases his vow and then performs the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices.
The establishment of the fires is completed; the establishment of the fires is completed.

When one is about to re-establish the sacred fires, they say: "He has already performed the sacrificial formulas and gathered the materials; therefore, the materials need not be gathered again, nor should the sacrificial formulas be performed. However, it is also said: "Indeed, the materials must be gathered and the sacrificial formulas must be performed for the successful completion of the re-establishment of the fires."

He prepares a chariot that has been repaired, a garment that has been re-sewn, an ox that has been released for breeding again, a nest of *darbha* grass, three *visūrmi* needles made of *darbha*, and the well-known materials required for the establishment of the sacred fires (*āgnyādheya*).
"That new-moon day which occurs before the full moon of the month of Āṣāḍha coincides with the *punarvasu* constellation once a year; on that day he should establish the fires. Thus it is said.

On the day of preparation for that [sacrifice], having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), having moved down [to a new site], having churned out the fires, and having spread them out, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara, intending to extinguish the fires. Thus the well-known sacrifice is completed.
Then, at that very moment, having sprinkled the fires with water and having cooked the *brahmaudana* (the Brahmin’s rice-mess), he observes the fast.
(3.1:69.12) Then, in the morning, the ritual pertaining to the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) is performed.
(3.1:69.12) Only this much is different: (3.1:69.13) whereas there was a nest of *muñja* grass, here there is a nest of *darbha* grass.
(3.1:69.13) That which was the fuel for the carrying forward [of the fire] there, that here consists of darbha-grass stalks.
(3.1:69.14) He establishes the Gārhapatya fire with darbha-grass; he establishes the Anvāhāryapacana fire with darbha-grass; he establishes the Āhavanīya fire with darbha-grass.
(3.1:69.15) He establishes the Gārhapatya fire with darbha-grass.
At the fire-consecration, he recites the verses of the Sarparājñī.
(3.2:69.17) “The earth with its abundance, the sky with its expanse”—with these [verses], four are offered at the Gārhapatya fire and three at the Āhavanīya fire.
(3.2:70.1) The ritual procedure is the same up to the chariot wheel; only this much is different.
That which was the silent *agnihotra* there, here one offers with the verse, "Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues.
That which was the cake on eight potsherds for Agni there, here it is a cake on five potsherds for Agni.

(3.2:70.4) During the *prayāja* offerings, he inserts four case-forms: "O Agni, come for the feast! (*agna āyāhi vītaye*); "O Agni, let the kindling-sticks partake of the clarified butter! (*samidho agna ājyasya viyantu*); "We choose Agni as the messenger! (*agnim dūtam vṛṇīmahe*); "O Agni, let Tanūnapāt partake of the clarified butter! (*tanūnapād agna ājyasya vetu*); "By Agni, Agni is kindled! (*agnināgniḥ samidhyate*); "O Agni, let the *iḍā*-invocations partake of the clarified butter! (*iḍo agna ājyasya viyantu*); "May Agni strike down the Vṛtras! (*agnir vṛtrāṇi jaṅghanat*); "O Agni, let the sacrificial grass partake of the clarified butter! (*barhir agna ājyasya vetu*). (3.2:70.7) Thus, the final *prayāja* is naturally complete. (3.2:70.8) Now, therefore, follows the deliberation concerning the two *ājyabhāga* offerings.
Some say that the two *ājyabhāga* offerings should be those containing the word "slayer of Vṛtra" (*vārtraghnau*). Some say they should be those containing the word "increasing" (*vṛdhanvantau*).
Some say these two should be used: "Awaken Agni with a hymn" and "O Soma, you [are] for us."
(3.2:70.10) Some say that the two [verses] "O Agni, you purify the lives" and "O Agni, purify yourself" should be used;
for that which is the *pavamāna* is the form of Soma.
(3.2:70.11–12) The two *paṅkti* verses for the oblation are "O Agni, him today" and "For thus, O Agni."
Then, with the words, "And again with vigor, together with wealth," he offers two oblations on both sides of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
He pronounces the *sviṣṭakṛt* formula directed toward Agni. With the two *saṃyājyā* verses, "These [oblations] for thee today" and "With these our hymns," he sets down the *anvāhārya* rice.
He gives the sacrificial fee for the re-establishment of the fires: a chariot repaired again, a garment sewn again, and an ox released again.

(3.3:70.17) At its after-offerings (*anūyāja*), he inserts the case-forms: "O Agni, that mortal who has delighted in worship with prayers and thoughts—may he, the most excellent, truly enjoy food for our protection. May the divine sacrificial grass (*barhis*) partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of obtaining riches! O Agni, we meditate upon the hymn that is effective today, reaching unto heaven, for the sake of the god’s wealth. May the divine Narāśaṃsa partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of obtaining riches! Thus, the final after-offering is self-perfected.
This sacrifice concludes with the *pūrṇapātra* and the *viṣṇukrama* steps;
he releases his vow.
Then, at that very moment, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Varuṇa as a subsequent oblation (*anunirvapa*).
Having cooked [the oblation], he sets it down.
For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja* offerings, and two *ājyabhāga* portions dedicated to Vṛtra-slayers.
Then, for the principal oblation, [he recites] "Thou, O Agni, for us... and "So thou, O Agni, for us...".
The two *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
Having placed the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives an ox as a gift. This sacrifice concludes with the pouring out of the full vessel and the *viṣṇukrama* steps.
He releases the vow. "The re-establishment of the fires is completed," thus [it is called] the *vṛddhi-punarādheya* (the re-establishment for prosperity).
Now, indeed, it is said: "He who should establish the sacred fire after the time for the *punarādheya* has passed must offer these oblations."

(3.3:71.12) At the third establishment of the fires, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the cake on five potsherds for Agni, he offers oblations with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), saying: "Leka, Saleka, Suleka—may you Ādityas, enjoying the clarified butter, partake of it, svāhā! Keta, Saketa, Suketa—may you Ādityas, enjoying the clarified butter, partake of it, svāhā! Vivasvat, Aditi, Devajūti—may you Ādityas, enjoying the clarified butter, partake of it, svāhā! (3.3:71.17) Thus the third establishment of the fires is completed.
Now, for one whose fire has been stolen or whose kindling woods have been lost, he proceeds by means of the *brahmaudana* alone;
the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) is thus accomplished.
Before the setting of the sun, having added fuel to the *gārhapatya* fire and brought the *ānvāhāryapacana* fire, he draws out the flaming *āhavanīya* fire for the evening oblation.
Before the rising of the sun, having added fuel to the *gārhapatya* fire and brought the *ānvāhāryapacana* fire, he draws out the flaming *āhavanīya* fire for the morning oblation.

(3.4:72.6) "With speech as the Hotṛ, with breath as the Udgātṛ, with the eye as the Adhvaryu, with the mind as the Brahman, and with the ear as the Agnīdh—by means of these five divine officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), I lift you up. Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! While being lifted up, lift me away from evil—that which I have done unknowingly and that which I have done knowingly; whatever sin has been committed by day, from all that, once lifted up, release me! Thus at evening.

(3.4:72.10) "Whatever sin or evil has been committed during the night—release me from all of that! Thus he places the fire in the morning. (3.4:72.11) "I offer the immortal oblation into the immortal; I offer Agni upon the earth for the conquest of immortality. Through this, may we win from here our infinite desire, that which Prajāpati first won. I offer the immortal into Agni Vaiśvānara, Svāhā! Thus at evening.
(3.4:72.14) "I offer the immortal into Sūrya, into Agni Vaiśvānara, Svāhā! Thus in the morning.
The wife attends to this [fire] every evening and morning—some say "evening" [is sufficient].

Then he places these washed Agnihotra vessels to the north of the Gārhapatya fire: either on a grass-mat or on a wooden board—the pot together with the *sruva* spoon, the *sruk* ladle, the illuminator, and the fuel-stick.
(3.4:72.18) Then, having stationed this Agnihotra-cow to the south, facing north, a Brāhmaṇa milks her.

(3.4:73.1) "One should milk the two front udders for the eldest son of the eldest wife, or for one who has attained prosperity. (3.4:73.2) "One should milk the two rear udders for the youngest son of the youngest wife, or for one who desires to prosper."
"One should not touch [the two milks together]. One should milk two [cows] for one who desires cattle.
Having placed [the vessel] on the fire, he pours the latter [milk] into it.

Then, having carried this Agnihotra around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, having brought it in through the eastern door, and having set it down behind the Gārhapatya fire, he then sprinkles water around it.
(3.5:73.7) “I sprinkle you with *ṛta* by means of *satya*,” he says while sprinkling in the evening; (3.5:73.7) “I sprinkle you with *satya* by means of *ṛta*,” he says in the morning.
(3.5:73.8) Having offered in this very manner, he sprinkles [the fire].

Then, having turned clockwise, having hastened westward, and having sat down behind the Gārhapatya fire, he draws out the embers toward the north, spreads them apart, places [the vessel] upon them, and illuminates it with a lighting-stick, saying: "May your splendor not burn me.
With the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), he pours water back [into the vessel], saying: "Thou art immortality.
Having illuminated it once more, he carries fire around it three times, saying: "The *rakṣas* is excluded; the enemies are excluded."

Having made a path and carried [the fire] out toward the north, he pushes back the embers and takes up the *sruva* spoon with his right hand and the fuel-stick with his left, while holding the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle with his left hand. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee," he says.
He heats it over the *gārhapatya* fire three times, saying, "Burnt away is the Rakṣas! Burnt away are the enemies!
Then, having placed the ladle on the grass-bundle (*kūrca*), he addresses the sacrificer: "Om, I shall draw [the milk]."
(3.5:73.17) “*Om unnaya*,” with these words the sacrificer gives permission.
(3.5:73.18) Then he draws four spoonfuls [of ghee] from the vessel—either full or not full—reciting: “*Bhūr iḍā*, *bhuva iḍā*, *suvar iḍā*, *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar iḍā*.

(3.5:73.19) Having placed the spoon back into the vessel, he then touches those two [spoons] while reciting: “In harmony with the gods who come in the evening; may the gods who come in the evening bring me safely across together with cattle,” thus in the evening.

(3.5:74.1) “In unison with the gods who come at dawn; may the gods who come at dawn convey me safely across, together with my cattle. Thus, in the morning, having taken these fuel-sticks onto the handle of the offering-ladle, he places them on a grass-mat behind the *gārhapatya* fire, saying: “Homage to Īśāna! May my offspring and cattle increase; may I, the sacrificer, suffer no harm.”

Having hurriedly moved forward with the *daśahotṛ* formula, he carries it eastward, saying: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! Follow the wide mid-region! This is the broad path leading to the gods, by which the seers seeking heaven went; by that I go to the highest firmament, so that I may not be deprived of the presence of those who have performed good deeds. Thus he places it on a grass-bundle behind the *āhavanīya* fire, saying: "Homage to Īśāna! May my progeny increase! May I, the sacrificer, suffer no harm!"
At this point, he places this fuel-stick in the middle of the Āhavanīya fire.

(3.6:74.12) "I place you, the silver one, whose light is fire, possessed of wind, leading to heaven—the imperishable brick for the night—for the sake of the heavenly world. "I place immortality in the breath. May Prajāpati settle you. With these words, he performs the *tayādevata* rite: "By that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm! (3.6:74.14) Then he performs the *sūdadohas* rite: "The dappled ones, yielding milk for him, mix the Soma; they are the subjects at the birth of the gods, in the three bright realms of heaven. Thus [he recites] at evening.

Then in the morning [he says]: "Thee, the golden one, with the light of the sun, accompanied by Vāyu, leading to heaven—for the sake of the heavenly world—I place as an imperishable brick. I bestow immortality upon the downward breath. May Prajāpati settle thee.
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* verse.
When it has been kindled, he offers oblations facing it, saying at evening: "Agni is light, light is Sūrya; svāhā!"

(3.6:75.1) "Sūrya is the light, Agni is the light, svāhā!"—thus in the morning. (3.6:75.2) Thus indeed is the combined [offering]; now, the uncombined: (3.6:75.2) "Agni is the light, Agni is the light, svāhā!"—thus in the evening.

(3.6:75.3) “Sūrya is the light, the light is Sūrya, svāhā!”—thus in the morning. Then, having poured out [the butter] once and placed the ladle on the *kūrca* grass-mat, he turns to the right and gazes toward the Gārhapatya fire, saying: “Come hither, gather together! Let not the share of those who have shares be lost. Where the world of the seven seers, the doers of good deeds, is, there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer.
(3.6:75.6) Having passed over the first oblation, he kindles the fire further and offers the subsequent one with his mind, saying: “To Prajāpati, svāhā!”

Then, having moved the spoon over the grass-bunch three times and placed it upon the bunch, he wipes it downward; with his hand turned toward the west and lowered, he wipes the residue onto the plants, saying: "For the plants thee! Quicken the plants!

In this very same manner, having wiped it a second time, he wipes it onto the plants from the south while wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), saying: "For the ancestors thee! Quicken the ancestors!"—thus at evening.
Then, in the morning, having wiped upwards, he wipes the residue from [the vessel] onto the plants with his hand turned upwards and facing east, saying: "For the plants thee! Quicken the plants!

In the same way, having wiped downwards a second time, he wipes it onto the plants from the south while wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), saying: "For the ancestors thee! Quicken the ancestors!
Then, having touched water, he eats twice with his finger, saying: "Offspring, light!"
Then, having turned toward the north, he consumes [the remnant] with the ladle whose handle points eastward.

(3.7:76.5) “May this oblation be productive for me—ten-heroed, with a full host—for my well-being; may it gain for me self, progeny, cattle, fearlessness, worlds, and rain. (3.7:76.7) “May Agni make my progeny abundant; bestow upon us food, milk, and seed; may he maintain for us the increase of wealth, nourishment, and vigor—svāhā! Thus at evening.

(3.7:76.8) “May Sūrya make my offspring abundant,” [with these words] in the morning, having washed the *sruk* ladle, heated it, and filled it with water, he pours it out toward the north, saying: (3.7:76.9–11) “Delight the Seven Seers! Quicken the Seven Seers!
To the Seven Seers, *svāhā!*” [With this] he delights the Seven Seers themselves; so says the *Brāhmaṇa*.
(3.7:76.11) Then, behind the *gārhapatya* fire, he pours out water with the formula: "Here I offer immortality into Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā!

(3.7:76.12) With the formula, "In the imperishable [place], I offer an imperishable oblation, svāhā," he pours it out within the altar (*antarvedi*). (3.7:76.13) Having offered, he kindles [the fire] for the kindling of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
"He pours out water; he has thus produced the very form of the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha)," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(3.8:76.16) Then, when the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), having sipped water, and standing in the sacrificer’s place, he worships the *āhavanīya* fire with six verses in their proper metrical order, beginning with: “Approaching the sacrifice... (*upaprayanto adhvaram*).

With the six subsequent verses addressed to Agni-Pavamāna, he worships the Āhavanīya fire alone: "O Agni, you purify our lives"; "O Agni, purify yourself"; "O Agni, the purifier"; "As such, O purifier, [purify us]"; "Agni, most pure in his vows"; "Upward, O Agni, rise your pure [flames]."

Then he worships the Āhavanīya fire with: "O Agni, you are the giver of life; give me life. O Agni, you are the giver of splendor; give me splendor. O Agni, you are the protector of the body; protect my body. O Agni, whatever is deficient in my body, fill that up for me. Then he worships the night with: "O Citrāvasu, may I safely reach your end."

(3.8:77.6) Then he places a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "Kindling you for a hundred winters, may we, radiant, kindle you; full of vigor, O maker of vigor; full of glory, O maker of glory; possessing good heroes, [kindle] you, the undeceivable one, O Agni, the subduer of rivals, upon the highest firmament, svāhā!
(3.8:77.9) Then he pays homage to the Āhavanīya itself: "O Agni, you have united with the splendor of the sun, with the praise of the seers, and with your beloved abode."
(3.8:77.10) "O Agni, you possess the splendor of the sun; endow me with long life, splendor, and progeny. Thus [he says]. (3.8:77.11) Now it is indeed said:

(3.8:77.12) "Just as a man, a horse, or a cow grows old, so does the fire, once established, grow old. After a year has passed, one should worship it with the *agnipāvamānī* verses. Thus [it is said].
After a year has passed, he worships the Gārhapatya fire with the *āgnipāvamānī* verses.
"He thus makes it new again and ageless," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then he worships the house and the cattle [with the verse]: "I behold the offspring, the human progeny of *iḍā*; may they all be in our house."

(3.8:77.16) "You are water; may I partake of you as water. You are greatness; may I partake of you as greatness. You are power; may I partake of you as power. You are vigor; may I partake of you as vigor. O wealthy ones, rejoice in this world, in this stall, in this dwelling, in this womb. Remain right here; do not depart. May you become many for me. Thus [he says].

(3.8:78.1) Then he touches the calf of the Agnihotrī cow with the formula: "Thou art united, possessing all forms; enter me with vigor, with lordship over cattle, and with the increase of wealth! May I nourish you with thousandfold prosperity; may your riches rest within me.
(3.8:78.3) Then he worships the Gārhapatya fire with two-footed and three-footed verses: "O Agni, day by day, we come to thee, O illuminator of the darkness, bringing homage with our prayer."

(3.8:78.5) "Shining over the sacrifices, the guardian of *ṛta*, the radiant one, increasing in his own abode—(3.8:78.6) O Agni, be easy of access to us as a father is to his son; attend to us for our well-being.
(3.8:78.7) O Agni, you are our closest relative; be our protector, auspicious and providing a secure refuge."
"To thee, O most radiant one, O shining one, we now pray for the welfare of our friends. Agni is the Vasu, renowned as the Vasu; come hither, most glorious one, bestow wealth upon us.
With these words, he then pays homage to both the houses and the cattle.

(3.9:78.11) "I look upon you with vigor; look upon me with vigor. I look upon you with the increase of wealth; look upon me with the increase of wealth. You are the *iḍā*s, the makers of honey; enter me as pleasant ones, bringing delight. May I thrive through your thousandfold prosperity; may your riches rest within me.
(3.9:78.13) Then he worships the Āhavanīya fire with: "We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the god Savitṛ; may he impel our thoughts."

He worships the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "O Brahmaṇaspati, make me a winner of Soma, like Kakṣīvat, the son of Uśij. Then he worships the night with the verse: "Never art thou barren, O Indra; never dost thou fail the worshipper. More and more, O Maghavan, thy bounty as a god is increased."
Then he pays homage to the Gārhapatya fire with the verse: "O Agni, we set thee around us as a fortress, O wise one, O powerful one; thee of bold hue, day by day, the breaker of the treacherous."

(3.9:79.2) Then he worships the Gārhapatya fire with: "O Agni, lord of the house, may I be a good lord of the house through you as my lord of the house; may you be a good lord of the house through me as your lord of the house—for a hundred winters. I pray for this blessing, full of light, for myself and for so-and-so; I pray for this blessing for so-and-so and for so-and-so.
(3.9:79.5) He names as many sons as he has born, ending finally with the word "for progeny" (*tantave*).
(3.9:79.6) Now, indeed, there is this [text]:

(3.9:79.6) "Whoever stands facing the fire burns him; whoever stands with his back to it goes away from his offspring and cattle; therefore, one should stand as if sideways. (3.9:79.8) Thus, he stands as if sideways—neither facing it nor with his back to it.

(3.10:79.10) One who is about to perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña prepares: sacrificial grass cut in a single stroke, *darbha* blades for strewing, rice grains, a winnowing basket, a washed mortar and pestle, a cooking pot, a *sruva*-ladle together with its stirring-stick (*mekṣaṇa*), a mat (*erakā*) and a pillow (*upabarhaṇa*), ointment and unguent, a fringe of cloth (*daśā*), a wooden sword (*sphya*), a water-pot, and the sacrificial implements.
(3.10:79.13) Then he strews [grass] around the *anvāhāryapacana* fire.

To the north of that, he places each item separately: a mattress of *eraka* grass, a pillow, ointment for the eyes, ointment for the body, a fringe of cloth, the wooden sword (*sphya*), a water-pitcher, and the sacrificial implements.

Then, having arranged the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) and sitting behind the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, he pours out the rice grains into a pot containing a strainer, either with the formula, "I pour you out, acceptable to the ancestors," or silently. Having placed the pot so that half of it remains above [the strainer], and having set down the mortar and pestle upon this very skin, he threshes the grain only once while facing south.
(3.10:79.19) Then, without separating them,
(3.10:79.19) he pours water into this very pot across the strainer, places it over the fire, and pours the rice grains across the strainer.
(3.10:80.2) Then he pours out the clarified butter.
(3.10:80.2) Then he places the clarified butter on the fire.
(3.10:80.2) Having carried fire around both [the butter and the rice], he cleanses the stirring-stick and the dipping-spoon.
(3.10:80.3) Then, having cooked this sacrificial porridge and poured clarified butter over it, he removes it from the fire toward the north.

(3.10:80.4) Then, having placed the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder and having kindled the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he offers three oblations, taking portions with a stirring-spoon, in the eastern part of the southern half [of the fire] with the formulas: "To Soma, drunk by the fathers, svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā! "To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the fathers, svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā! "To Agni Kavyavāhana, the maker of good offerings, svadhā! Adoration! Svāhā! Thus [he offers].

Having silently placed the stirring-stick (mekṣaṇa) [on the fire], having arranged the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), having dug up the ground to the south of the Anvāhāryapacana fire with the wooden sword (sphyā), and having sprinkled it with water, he spreads sacrificial grass (barhis) with its tips pointing southward and purifies [the ancestors] with water, saying: "May the fathers be purified; may the grandfathers be purified; may the great-grandfathers be purified."

(3.10:80.11) Then, having spread a base of ghee with the *sruva* ladle and poured ghee over them, he gives three rice-balls, saying: "This for you, O father, [Name], and for those who follow you; this for you, O grandfather, [Name], and for those who follow you; this for you, O great-grandfather, [Name], and for those who follow you."
Having said, "O fathers, enjoy [the food] according to your portions," he turns toward the north and waits until the steam has subsided;
for they say, "The steam has subsided.
Then, turning back, he smells this sacrificial porridge.
(3.11:80.16) "Those ancestors who are equal and of one mind in the realm of Yama—for them is this world; *svadhā* and obeisance! May the sacrifice be prepared among the gods.
(3.11:80.17) "Those kinsmen who are of one mind, the living ones among the living who belong to me—may their prosperity be prepared for me in this world for a hundred years.
(3.11:80.19) Then, in the same manner, he purifies with water, saying: "May the fathers purify themselves; may the grandfathers purify themselves; may the great-grandfathers purify themselves."

(3.11:80.20) Then he gives collyrium, saying: "May the fathers anoint themselves; may the grandfathers anoint themselves; may the great-grandfathers anoint themselves. (3.11:80.21) Then he gives ointment, saying: "May the fathers anoint themselves; may the grandfathers anoint themselves; may the great-grandfathers anoint themselves. (3.11:81.1) Then he gives garments, saying: "O fathers, these are your garments; O grandfathers, these are your garments; O great-grandfathers, these are your garments."
"One should have the hair cut in the latter part of life," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(3.11:81.3) Then he worships with six salutations in reverse order: "Homage to you, O fathers, for the sap! Homage to you, O fathers, for the vigor! Homage to you, O fathers, for the life-force! Homage to you, O fathers, for the *svadhā*! Homage to you, O fathers, for the wrath! Homage to you, O fathers, for the terrible power! O fathers, homage to you! Those who are in that world, may they follow you; those who are in this world, may they follow me. You who are in that world, you are their [leaders]."
"May you be most excellent; among those in this world, may I be the most excellent among them.

Then he entreats for a hero: "O fathers, grant me a hero! O grandfathers, grant me a hero! O great-grandfathers, grant me a hero! May I be possessed of fathers through you! May you be possessed of good offspring through me!"

(3.11:81.12) Then he makes them rise with: "Arise, O fathers, go forth as heroes; follow the ancient path of Yama! Bestow upon us wealth and that which is auspicious; proclaim us as sharers among the gods!"

(3.11:81.14) Then he dismisses them with: "May the fathers go to their respective worlds with the speed of thought! Depart, O Soma-loving fathers, by the deep, ancient paths! Then go to the benevolent fathers who rejoice in the company of Yama.
(3.11:81.17) Then he invokes the mind with three verses: "We summon the mind hither; may our mind return to us; O fathers, let our mind return to us.
(3.11:81.18) At this point, he throws these rice-balls together with the sacrificial grass into the fire.
(3.11:81.19) Now they recite two [verses] each for these *śastra*s.

(3.11:81.19) Then, having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*), he worships the *gārhapatya* fire with the verse addressed to Prajāpati: "O Prajāpati, none other than you [created] these...
(3.11:82.2) At this point, he mutters this second [verse]: "That which is the intermediate space, the earth, and the sky..."
The Piṇḍapitṛyajña is concluded.
(3.12:82.4) When one is about to perform the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice of *śyāmāka* millet during the rainy season, (3.12:82.4) its *upavasatha* day is well known.

(3.12:82.5) Then, in the morning, after the *agnihotra* has been offered, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he pours out the oblation of *śyāmāka* millet for Soma.

Having released his speech with the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*), he melts the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, purifies it, takes four portions into the ladle, and offers the *ājyānī* oblations in the *āhavanīya* fire with the five verses beginning, "To him of a hundred weapons, of a hundred powers.
Having cooked the sacrificial cake, he sets it down.
For this sacrifice, there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja* offerings, and two *ājyabhāga* offerings dedicated to Vṛtra-slayers.
Then, for the oblation, he recites the two *saṃyājyā* verses in the *triṣṭubh* meter: "Swell up" (*āpyāyasva*) and "May [the milk] unite with thee" (*saṃ te*).
Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a garment as a gift.
(3.12:82.11) Then he eats the sacrificer’s portion with the mantra: “May Agni eat first; for he knows how the oblation is. May he, who dwells among all people, make the plants auspicious for us.
(3.12:82.13) This sacrifice concludes with the pouring out of the full vessel and the Viṣṇu-strides.
(3.12:82.14) He releases his vow.
(3.12:82.14) Now, when one is about to perform the *āgrayaṇa* offering of rice in autumn, (3.12:82.15) its *upavasatha* day is well known.

(3.12:82.15) Then, in the morning, after the *agnihotra* has been offered, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni, a pap for the Viśve Devās, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.

Having released his speech with the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he melts the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, purifies it, takes four portions into the ladle, and offers the *ājyānī* oblations into the *āhavanīya* fire with the verse: "To him who has a hundred weapons, who has a hundred powers... Thus there are five [offerings].
Having cooked [the sacrificial food], he sets it down.
For this sacrifice, there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja* offerings, and two *ājyabhāga* offerings belonging to the slayer of Vṛtra.

(3.12:82.21) Now, for the oblations: "O Indra and Agni, the luminous realms of heaven... you pierced Vṛtra" is the verse for the offering to Indra and Agni; (3.12:82.22) "All the gods... all the gods" is for the offering to the Viśvedevas;
(3.12:83.1) "May Heaven and Earth protect us... the two parents born of old" is for the offering to Heaven and Earth.
The two *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *triṣṭubh* metre.
Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives away the first-born calf.

Then he eats his portion of the sacrificial food with the mantra: "O gods, you have led us from good to better; through you as our protection, may we attain prosperity. Enter us, O food, as a source of delight; be auspicious and pleasant to our children and our bodies."
This sacrifice concludes with the *pūrṇapātra* libation and the *viṣṇukrama* steps;
he releases his vow.
Then, in the spring, he intends to perform the *āgrayaṇa* offering of barley.
(3.12:83.6) Its fast-day is well known. (3.12:83.7) The ritual procedure is the same as that of the *vrīhi-āgrayaṇa*.
(3.12:83.7) Only this much is different.

(3.12:83.7) Then he eats the sacrificer’s portion [with the verse]: “This very barley, mixed with honey, they ploughed upon the mind of Sarasvatī; Indra, the lord of a hundred powers, was the master of the plough, and the Maruts, the bounteous givers, were the ploughmen.
(3.12:83.10) This sacrifice concludes with the pouring out of the full vessel and the Viṣṇu-strides.
(3.12:83.11) He releases his vow.

(3.13:83.12) One who is about to go on a journey [from his fires] puts on the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*), sips water, goes around the front of the *āhavanīya* fire, and while standing in the sacrificer’s station, worships the *āhavanīya* with the mantra: “O Jātavedas, that name which my father and mother first gave me at the beginning—bear that for me again until I return; bearing your name, O Agni, I shall depart.
(3.13:83.15) Then, restraining his speech, he sets out.
(3.13:83.16) He releases his speech only when he is no longer in the vicinity of the fires.
He sleeps on the ground, abstains from meat, avoids women, and travels abroad; he does not travel abroad for more than twelve days,
nor does he bypass the day of preparation.
(3.13:83.18) On the path he prepares the fuel-sticks. (3.13:83.18) Having looked back at the fires, he restrains his speech.

He pays reverence only to the Āhavanīya fire with [the verse]: "O Jātavedas, my name and yours—we two who move about as if putting on two garments—let us exchange them again, you for long life and we for living, each according to our own way. Thus.

(3.13:84.1) Then he pays homage to the *gārhapatya* fire with: "Homage to Agni the unpierced, homage to the unassailable, homage to the sovereign! Agni is invincible, of great vigor, the all-conqueror; the Gandharva is the most powerful and the best. (3.13:84.3) Then he pays homage to the *anvāhāryapacana* fire with: "O Agni, the gods are your fathers; the oblations are yours, and the invocations are yours. Endow me with long life and with herds of cattle; establish me in well-being. (3.13:84.5) Then he pays homage to the *āhavanīya* fire.
"This Agni is the most excellent; he is the most venerable; he is the best winner of a thousandfold. May there be great heroic power for him."

(3.14:84.7) If they report to him a failure in the sacrifice, saying, "He has not offered for you," then, having melted clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the ladle, he offers the *saṃtanī* oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this interrupted sacrifice. Those dawns and those sunsets that have been offered, those I unite with the oblation of ghee, svāhā!
(3.14:84.11) Then he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumat.
(3.14:84.12) He gives a shallow cup as the sacrificial fee;
(3.14:84.12) that well-known sacrifice is concluded.
(3.14:84.13) Then he offers oblations for the transgressions.
(3.14:84.13) By means of this, indeed, the Vedic scholars of old—who were devoted to truth and desirous of splendor, fame, and spiritual luster—used to perform this worship.
(3.14:84.15) But that has now fallen into disuse because of the excessive difficulty of the vow.
Now, therefore, follows the worship using the Vairāja hymn alone.

(3.14:84.16) "O manly one, protect my offspring," [with these words] he addresses the Gārhapatya fire; (3.14:84.16) "O Atharvan, protect my food," [with these words] the Anvāhāryapacana fire; (3.14:84.17) "O Śaṃsya, protect my cattle," [with these words] the Āhavanīya fire.
