"O wide-extending one, protect my assembly hall," [with these words] he offers to the fire of the assembly hall; "O Ahi Budhnya, protect my mantra," [with these words] he offers to the fire of the dwelling house.
He then departs on a journey for an unlimited time.
(3.14:85.2) On his return journey, he prepares fuel-sticks on the road.
(3.14:85.3) Having looked back at the fires, he restrains his speech. Having arrived, he worships with this very [formula].
The expiation is the same.

Then, on the day of the Upavasatha, having placed the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, having sipped water, having gone around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, and having sat down in the sacrificer’s station, he sips water through the strainer with the mantra: "The plants are full of sap; the sap of the creepers is full of sap. That which is the sap of the sap of the waters—with that, O Indra, unite me."

Then he places fuel-sticks on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do it; may it be successful for me, svāhā! O Vāyu, lord of vows! O Āditya, lord of vows! O lord of vows among vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do it; may it be successful for me, svāhā! Thus he says.

Then, on the following day, when the oblation is being prepared, he consecrates it with the mantra: "I invoke Agni here, the Hotṛ; those gods worthy of sacrifice whom we call upon here. May the gods come with benevolent minds; may the gods partake of this my oblation.
Having recited this, he restrains his speech until the call for the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation).
Having released his speech at the call of the *haviṣkṛt*, he yokes the sacrifice with the formula: "Who yokes you? Let him yoke you."
At the proper time, he joins the potsherds with the formula: "The potsherds which the wise ones collect for the cauldron—may Indra and Vāyu join them together in the service of Pūṣan.

Of those potsherds that have been consecrated by the *yajus*, whatever is broken, he throws it onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) with the formula: "Unbroken is the cauldron, the giver of life; from where it was taken, there it has gone back again."

(3.15:86.1) Then, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the ladle, he offers the *saṃtanī* oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "The fuel, the altar, and all the enclosing sticks follow the life-span of the sacrifice. The thirty-three threads that have been stretched out—those who sustain this sacrifice through their own power—to them I restore what has been severed; *svāhā*! (3.15:86.5) Then he pours in another portion with the formula: "May the *gharma* go to the gods."
Now, it is indeed said:
"If [the cake] should be lost, one should offer a two-potherd oblation to the Aśvins and a single-potherd oblation to Heaven and Earth.
This sacrifice is completed in the well-known manner.

(3.15:86.7) Then, in the same manner, having melted the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the *sruva*-ladle, he offers the *saṃtanī* oblation into the *āhavanīya* fire with the verse: "The fuel, the altar, and all the enclosing sticks follow the life-span of the sacrifice. The thirty-three threads that have been stretched out, which sustain this sacrifice through the *svadhā* offering—of these, whatever has been severed, here I restore it; *svāhā*! (3.15:86.11) Then he pours in another portion with the formula: "May the *gharma* go unto the gods."

Now, if anything of the clarified butter or of the *sāṃnāyya* spills elsewhere than upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) before the final fore-offering (*prayāja*), he gathers its essence (*svadhā*).

(3.16:86.14) “I sprinkle you with the *yajus* for progeny, long life, and wealth; impelled by Bṛhaspati, may the sacrificer here suffer no harm,” with these words he consecrates what has been spilled.
Then he says: “To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā! Thus.

Then, having proceeded with what remains, he causes the sacrificer to look at the clarified butter (*ājya*): "Thou art clarified butter; thou art truth; thou art the overseer of truth; thou art the oblation for Vaiśvānara and for the All-gods, with purified vigor, possessing true power. Thou art might; thou art the subduing one; overcome the enemies; overcome those who act as enemies; overcome the hostile armies; overcome those who attack us. Thou art of thousandfold potency; quicken me! Thou art the clarified butter of clarified butter."

“You are the truth of truth; you have truth as your life-span; you have truth as your vigor. I sprinkle you with truth. May I partake of that of yours. Thus [he says]. Then [follows] the taking of the portions of clarified butter (*ājyagraha*).

Each time he has taken [the portions], he consecrates them with four formulas for the *juhū* ladle: "I take thee for the restraint and support of the five winds; I take thee for the restraint and support of the five seasons; I take thee for the restraint and support of the five directions; I take thee for the restraint and support of the five classes of men."

(3.16:87.7) With eight [verses] he takes the *upabhṛt* [ladle]: "I take you for the restraint and support of the five-holed vessel of the oblation; I take you for the splendor and restraint of the *brahman*; I take you for the vigor and restraint of the *kṣatra*."

With the four [verses]: "For restraint, for support, I take thee; for the people, for restraint, for support, I take thee; for heroic vigor I take thee; for good offspring I take thee; for the increase of wealth I take thee; for spiritual luster I take thee"—[he takes] the *dhruvā* [ladle]. With [the formula]: "The earth is ours; the oblation belongs to the gods; the blessings belong to the sacrificer; for the deities of the gods, I take thee."
He consecrates it as it is being filled with the mantra: "I take thee for desire.
He consecrates the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) as they are being laid around: for the middle one, "Thou art firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen, wise, observant, and a finder of wealth";
for the southern one, "Thou art fierce; may I be fierce among my kinsmen, fierce, observant, and a finder of wealth."
(3.16:87.17) “Thou art the conqueror; may I be a conqueror among my kinsmen, a conqueror, a perceiver, and a finder of wealth,” he says over the northern [fire].
(3.16:88.1) Then he yokes the fire with a formula: “I yoke thee with the divine prayer so that thou, O Jātavedas, mayest carry this oblation.
(3.16:88.2) As the two fuel-sticks are being placed upon it, he mutters: “Kindling thee, may we, possessing good offspring and brave sons, live long, offering tribute to thee.”

(3.16:88.4) Then he consecrates the oblations placed within the altar with the mantra: "O Agni, whatever of this sacrifice of mine may be damaged, or whatever of the clarified butter may be spilled, O Viṣṇu—with that I strike down my rival, the one difficult to kill; I cast him into the lap of Destruction. Thus.
(3.17:88.8) Then, with the words "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar," he should set down the *agnihotra* offering with these *vyāhṛtis*.
(3.17:88.9) "The *agnihotra* is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice, and these *vyāhṛtis* are the Brahman.
Thus, he places the Brahman at the very mouth of the sacrifice."
"When the year has come around, he should set them down with these very [verses].
By means of the Brahman, he encompasses the year on both sides"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, there is this [further statement]:
(3.17:88.11) "One performing the New and Full Moon sacrifices should set down the oblations with these *vyāhṛtis*.
(3.17:88.12) "The New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed the mouth of the sacrifice; these *vyāhṛtis* are the Brahman.
(3.17:88.13) "Thus, he places the Brahman at the very mouth of the sacrifice."
"When the year has come round, he should set them down with these very [verses].
'By means of the *brahman* alone, he encompasses the year on both sides,' so says the *Brāhmaṇa*.
Now, indeed, it occurs:"
(3.17:88.15) "One performing the Cāturmāsya sacrifices should set down the oblations with these *vyāhṛti*s.
(3.17:88.16) "The Cāturmāsyas are indeed the mouth of the sacrifice, and these *vyāhṛti*s are the Brahman.
(3.17:88.17) "Thus, he places the Brahman at the very mouth of the sacrifice."
"When the year has come around, he should set them down with these very [verses].
Verily, by means of the Brahman, he encompasses the year on both sides"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said:

(3.17:88.19) "Whatever part of the sacrifice is performed with a *sāman*, the blessing (*āśis*) of that sacrifice goes to the ruling class (*rāṣṭra*); whatever part is performed with a *ṛc*, the blessing of that sacrifice goes to the common people (*viś*). Thus, a Brahmin performs the sacrifice with one that lacks a blessing.
When about to recite the *sāmidhenī* verses, he should place these *vyāhṛtis* at the beginning."
"He makes the *brahman* itself the introductory step;
thus the Brāhmaṇa sacrifices with a sacrifice accompanied by a blessing. So says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said:
(3.17:89.1) "If one should desire, 'May the blessing of this sacrifice go to my rival sacrificer,' he should place these *vyāhṛtis* in the *puro'nuvākyā* for him.
(3.17:89.3) "The *puro'nuvākyā* indeed has the rival as its deity;
thus the blessing of his sacrifice goes to the rival," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, it is indeed said: "If he should desire of certain sacrificers, 'May the blessing of the sacrifice reach them equally,' he should place one of these *vyāhṛtis* at the half-verse of their *puro'nuvākyā*, one before the *yājyā*, and one at the half-verse of the *yājyā*.
Thus the blessing of the sacrifice reaches them equally. So says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"Just as Parjanya rains well when he has rained well, so does the sacrifice rain for the sacrificer.
They enclose water on dry ground.
"The sacrificer encompasses the sacrifice with a benediction," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

He begins for a Brāhmaṇa with the *vyāhṛtis*, for a Rājanya with the *hiṅkāra*, and for a Vaiśya with a *ṛc*; however, another view is that one should perform all three of these. He consecrates the fuel as it is being placed upon the fire.

(3.18:89.13) “O Agni, be swelling for the sacrificer; be withering to him who seeks to harm us. O Agni, kindled by the gods, kindled by the mind, sweet-tongued one!”—with these words he consecrates the *pravara* as it is being chosen. (3.18:89.14–16) “Upon the head of you, the immortal Hotṛ, I sprinkle [the clarified butter] for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for heroic vigor”—with these words he consecrates the *āghāra* oblation as it is being poured with the *sruva* ladle. “You are the mind belonging to Prajāpati; enter me with the mind that is existence. With these words he consecrates [the fire].
(3.18:89.17) He consecrates the *āghāra* libation being poured from the *sruc* with the mantra: "Thou art speech, belonging to Indra, the destroyer of rivals; enter me with speech and with power."

(3.18:89.19) He consecrates each of the *prayāja* offerings as it is offered: "I gratify the spring among the seasons; may it, being gratified, gratify me. I gratify the summer among the seasons; may it, being gratified, gratify me. I gratify the rains among the seasons; may they, being gratified, gratify me. I gratify the autumn among the seasons; may it, being gratified, gratify me. I gratify the winter and the cool season among the seasons; may they, being gratified, gratify me. Thus he says.
Having offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), he consecrates them with: "Through the sacrifice to the gods Agni and Soma, may I become possessed of sight.
He consecrates the offering made to Agni with: "Through the sacrifice to the god Agni, may I become an eater of food.
He consecrates the offering of the *upāṃśuyāja* that has been performed with: "Thou art the deceiver; may I be undeceived; may I deceive so-and-so."

(3.18:90.7) Here, he meditates in his mind upon whomever the sacrificer hates. (3.18:90.8) Then, having touched water, he consecrates the two offerings to Agni and Soma with the mantra: "Through the sacrifice to the gods, Agni and Soma, may I become a slayer of Vṛtra."

(3.18:90.9) He consecrates the sacrifice to Indra and Agni with: "Through the sacrifice to the gods, Indra and Agni, may I become possessed of power and an eater of food. (3.18:90.11) He consecrates the sacrifice to Indra with: "Through the sacrifice to the god Indra, may I become possessed of power.
(3.18:90.12) He consecrates the sacrifice to Mahendra with: "Through the sacrifice to the god Mahendra, may I attain victory and greatness."

(3.18:90.13) He recites the consecration formula over the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering: "By the sacrifice to the god Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, may I, long-lived, attain firm standing through the sacrifice. (3.18:90.14) While the *prāśitra* portion is being cut off, he murmurs: "May Agni protect me from ill-sacrificed rites; may Savitṛ protect me from evil speech. (3.18:90.16) Over the sacrificer’s share, he says: "Whoever acts as an enemy to me, whether near or far, may I conquer him with this."
He recites the mantra over the *iḍā* being brought forward, beginning with, "O thou of beautiful form and rain-like color, come! and continuing from there with, "O wealthy one.
He recites the mantra over the intermediate *iḍā* as it is being consumed: "Thou art delight; delight us! Thou art delightful to us; may I attain thy delight."

(3.18:90.19) Then, within the *antarvedi*, he purifies himself with water, [reciting]: "May the light of the mind enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this severed sacrifice. May Bṛhaspati extend this for us; may all the gods rejoice here.

(3.18:91.3) He consecrates the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) placed upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), [reciting]: "O radiant one, overflow; may there be no loss for me who gives; may there be no failure for me who acts. (3.18:91.4) Then he asks for the *anvāhārya* rice.
He addresses him as he sits within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*) with the mantra: "Thou art the portion of Prajāpati, full of vigor, full of milk," up to the end of the section.

(3.19:91.7) He consecrates each of the after-offerings (*anūyāja*) as it is offered with the formulas: "Through the sacrifice to the god Barhis, may I become possessed of offspring; through the sacrifice to the god Narāśaṃsa, may I become possessed of cattle; through the sacrifice to the god Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, may I, long-lived, attain a firm foundation through the sacrifice.

(3.19:91.9) Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ's recitation, "Agni has enjoyed this oblation," he causes the sacrificer to recite the formula for victory (*ujjiti*): "May I follow after the victory of Agni," according to the specific deity intended.
The spreading of the two *vājavatī* verses has been explained.

Now, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting, "This sacrificer, so-and-so, hopes," then he causes the sacrificer to recite the milking of the sacrifice: "These blessings have come, desiring to be milked; accompanied by Indra, we shall win; may we milk forth progeny and nourishment."

He consecrates the *prastara* grass-bundle as it is being thrown into the fire with the mantra: "May Agni cause you to go to the divinity by means of the red horse; may Indra cause you to go to the divinity by means of the two bay horses; may Sūrya cause you to go to the divinity by means of the dappled horse. He consecrates the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) as they are being released with the mantra: "I loosen your cords, I loosen your reins, I loosen the thongs and the fastenings. Bestow upon us wealth that is auspicious, and proclaim us as sharers among the deities."
Having recited the *śaṃyuvāka*, he follows it with the mantra: "Through the sacrifice to the god Viṣṇu, may I attain firm standing through the *śaṃyu*.
He then follows each of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings as they are performed with this same mantra.
"By the sacrifice to Soma, the god, may I beget noble seed; by the sacrifice to Tvaṣṭṛ, the god, may I nourish the form of cattle.
Then he combines the other two [formulas]: "The wives of the gods, Agni the lord of the house—this is the couple of the sacrifice. By the sacrifice to these two, may I prosper through their union."
At the Veda, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "Thou art the Veda; thou art acquisition; may I acquire. He continues thus until the end of the section.

He then consecrates the *dhruvā* ladle while it is being replenished with the mantra: "May the *dhruvā* swell with clarified butter for those seeking the gods at every sacrifice; [she is] the udder of Sūryā, in the lap of Aditi; a broad-streamed cow upon this earth at this sacrifice."

Then he eats the sacrificer’s portion with the formula: "The world of Prajāpati is named Vibhān; in it I place you together with the sacrificer," or with: "May the lord of the sacrifice be united with the blessing.
At this point, he asks for the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*).

Having placed it within the altar (*antarvedi*), he makes the sacrificer recite over the full vessel: "Thou art real; be real for me! Thou art all; be all for me! Thou art full; be full for me! Thou art imperishable; mayest thou not perish for me!"

(3.20:92.14) Then he purifies the quarters with: "May the gods, the officiating priests, purify me in the eastern quarter; may the months, the ancestors, purify me in the southern quarter; may the houses, the cattle, purify me in the western quarter; may the waters, the plants, the trees, purify me in the northern quarter; may the sacrifice, the year, and the lord of the sacrifice purify me in the upward quarter."
(3.20:92.18) Then he pours them out with the verse: "I send you forth to the ocean, O imperishable ones; go back to your own source. May I be unbroken in my progeny; may my milk not be spilled.
(3.20:93.1) Then, having stood up, he strides the Viṣṇu-strides with his right foot.

"Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of the adversary; with the Gāyatrī metre, I step along the earth. He whom we hate is excluded. With these four [verses], according to their respective metres, he steps out.
On the third [step], he repeats the fourth [verse];
he does not step out for a fourth [time].
He does not pass beyond the Āhavanīya fire.

Then, standing right there, he pays homage to the Āhavanīya with the formula: "We have gone to heaven; we have gone to heaven. May I not be cut off from your sight. Whatever heat is yours, may I not be deprived of it. Then he pays homage to the sun with the formula: "Thou art well-being, the best of rays. Thou art the bestower of life; grant me life. Thou art the bestower of splendor; grant me splendor."

(3.21:93.9) Then he excludes the rival from these worlds: "Here I exclude this rival from these directions, from this sky, from this intermediate space, from this earth, and from this food; excluded is he whom we hate. (3.21:93.12) Then, having touched water, he touches his own chest with the formula: "I have become united with light. (TS 1.6.6.2.e). He touches himself toward his chest.

(3.21:93.13) Then he turns around toward his right shoulder, saying: "I turn according to the turning of Indra. (3.21:93.14) Then he turns around toward the north, saying: "May I be united with offspring; may offspring be united with me; may I be united with the increase of wealth; may the increase of wealth be united with me.
(3.21:93.15) Then he places a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire, saying: "O Agni, being kindled, shine for me; may I, as your kindler, O Agni, shine—Svāhā!"
(3.21:93.17) Then he worships the Āhavanīya fire with: "May the sacrifice be wealthy; may I become more prosperous.
(3.21:93.18) Then he worships the Gārhapatya fire with two verses addressed to Agni and Pāvamāna: "O Agni, you purify our lives," and "O Agni, purify yourself."

(3.21:93.19) Then he worships the Gārhapatya fire with: "O Agni, lord of the house, may I be a good lord of the house through you as my lord of the house; may you be a good lord of the house through me as your lord of the house—for a hundred winters. I pray for this blessing, full of light, for myself and for so-and-so; I pray for this blessing for so-and-so and for so-and-so."
"As many sons as have been born to him," ending with the word "for offspring."
Now, indeed, it is said: "He who, having yoked the sacrifice, does not release it, becomes one without a firm foundation.
[Therefore, one should say: "Who has yoked you? Let him release you."
At the proper time, he releases the potsherds with the formula: "The potsherds which the wise ones collect for the cauldron—may Indra and Vāyu release them also within the domain of Pūṣan.

Then, having returned by the same way he came and sat down on the sacrificer’s seat, he sips water across the strainer in the same manner with the formula: "The plants are full of milk; the milk of the creepers is full of milk. Whatever milk belongs to the milk of the waters—with that, O Indra, unite me."

Then he places fuel-sticks on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "O Agni, lord of vows, I have performed the vow; I was able to do it; may it be successful for me, svāhā! O Vāyu, lord of vows! O Āditya, lord of vows! O lord of vows among vows, I have performed the vow; I was able to do it; may it be successful for me, svāhā! Thus [he says].

(3.22:94.12) Then, having stood up, he mutters the *punarālambha* formula for the sacrifice: "The sacrifice has come into being; it has come forth. It was born; it grew strong. It became the overlord of the gods. May it make us overlords; may we be masters of riches. (3.22:94.15) Then, having stepped forward toward the east, he mutters: "O Agni, this sacrifice is rich in cattle, rich in sheep, rich in horses; it has heroes as its friends, and is ever unassailable. O Asura, it is full of *iḍā*, rich in offspring, a long-lasting wealth, broad-based, and possessed of an assembly hall."
(3.22:94.17) Then he issues the command: "Now, let the Brahmins be gratified!"

(3.23:95.1) One who is about to perform the duties of the Brahman priest, having put on the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*) and sipped water, goes around the front of the Āhavanīya fire and, standing to the south facing north, pays homage to the seat of the Brahman with the formula: "Homage to Brahman! Homage to the seat of the Brahman! (3.23:95.3) Then, from his seat, he throws away a blade of grass with the formula: "O son of a remarried woman, stay away from here; sit on the seat of another who is more foolish than we. (3.23:95.4) He sits down with the formula: "May I go up from the depressions and up from the elevations."
(3.23:95.5) Then he gazes at them [the two fires], saying: "O Heaven and Earth, protect me this day."

Having sat down, he mutters: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! Who here shall be the Brahman? He [the breath] shall be the Brahman here. The vital breath is joined with Prajāpati. I am yoked by the Brahman, like a swift horse, like a draft-animal well-yoked to the pole, like a bull yoked to the yoke. I shall carry the oblation to the deities. I take refuge in Bhūḥ; I take refuge in Bhuvaḥ; I take refuge in Suvaḥ; I take refuge in Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ; I take refuge in Vāyu."

"I take refuge in Brahman; I take refuge in Kṣatra; I take refuge in the unbroken stone; I take refuge in Prajāpati’s treasury of Brahman; I take refuge in the unharmed deity, Speech; Om, I take refuge. Thus.

The sacrificer chooses that Brahman priest with the formula: "O lord of the earth, O lord of the world, O lord of the great being, we choose you as the Brahman; as the domestic priest for Vītahavya, by whom the Aṅgirases, the gods, went to the highest heaven, to the sky."

(3.23:95.14) Once chosen, the Brahman mutters: "I am the lord of the earth; I am the lord of the world; I am the lord of the great being. Impelled by the divine Savitṛ, I shall perform the office of the officiating priest. You have chosen me as your Brahman. [I choose] Vītahavya as my domestic priest, by whom the Aṅgirases, the gods, went to the highest heaven. O divine Savitṛ, they choose you, Bṛhaspati, as their divine Brahman. That I announce to the mind; the mind to the Gāyatrī; the Gāyatrī..."

The Triṣṭubh [is linked] to the Jagatī; the Jagatī to the Anuṣṭubh; the Anuṣṭubh to the Paṅkti; the Paṅkti to Prajāpati; Prajāpati to the All-gods; the All-gods to Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati to the Brahman; the Brahman to Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvar. "Bṛhaspati is the Brahman of the gods; I am the Brahman of men. O Bṛhaspati, protect the sacrifice! Thus [it is said].
When he says, "O Brahman, I shall lead forward the waters; O sacrificer, restrain your speech," then the Brahman gives the impulse.

(3.24:96.1) “O God Savitṛ, lead the sacrifice forward; cause these deities to prosper. May the sacrificer be upon the back of the firmament, in the world of heaven. Where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is, there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer. Om, lead it forward!
(3.24:96.3) Thus he remains restrained in speech while the *praṇītā* waters are being led forth, until the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*).
While the *sāṃnāyya* is being milked, he then says, "May she yield much milk as an oblation for Indra and the gods," or "for Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra.
He restrains his speech during the pouring of the grains until the placing of the potsherds;
he restrains his speech during the mixing until the covering with ashes.

(3.24:96.7) While the *stambayajus* is being carried forward, up until the placing of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, when he says, "O Brahman, I shall perform the second tracing of the altar," then the Brahman gives the impulse: "O Bṛhaspati, enclose the altar; with the sacred word (*brahman*), enclose this sacrifice. Where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is, there place this sacrifice and the sacrificer. Om! Enclose it! (3.24:96.11) While the clarified butter is being taken, he restrains his speech until the placing of the *dhruvā* ladle.
While the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, up until the *pravara* invocation; while the *puro’nuvākyā* has been recited, up until the *vaṣaṭ*-call;
while the *prāśitra* portion is being cut off, up until the impulse (*prasava*); they carry this *prāśitra* for him along the front of the *āhavanīya* fire.
He gazes upon it as it is being brought forward.
(3.25:96.16) "I gaze upon you with the eye of the Sun," he says.
(3.25:96.16) Then he receives it with both hands, saying, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I receive you with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan.
(3.25:97.1) Then he sets it down, saying, "I set you down on the navel of the Earth."

(3.25:97.2) Then he looks at it, saying: "I look upon you with the eye of Suparṇa, the Garutman. (3.25:97.2) Then, taking hold of it with his thumb and ring finger, and having passed over the teeth, he places it first on the tip of his tongue, saying: "I eat you with the mouth of Agni.
(3.25:97.4) Having eaten it and sipped water, he swallows it together with the water, saying: "With the belly of a Brāhmaṇa; with the sacred word of Bṛhaspati."

(3.25:97.5) Then, having sprinkled himself with water, he touches his vital organs: "May speech be in my mouth; breath in my nostrils; sight in my eyes; hearing in my ears; strength in my arms; vigor in my thighs; may all my limbs be uninjured; may my body be together with my self; homage be unto you; do not harm me. (3.25:97.8) Or [he says]: "In me are the breaths, in me are the breaths.
(3.25:97.9) He places the portion of the *brahmán* that has been brought back into the *prāśitra-haraṇa* vessel.
Then he asks for the Anvāhārya rice;
having been placed within the altar, he addresses it with a mantra.

(3.26:97.11) "O Brahman, you are the Brahman; homage to you, O Brahman, to the Brahman! Protect me from the unoffered today; may everything become offered for me. Thus [he says]. (3.26:97.12) Then, having taken a portion as large as that, he places it in the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel [with the words]: "You are prosperity (*śrī*); come toward me; may I be possessed of food and an eater of food. Thus [he says].

(3.26:97.13) Then, as he is being led northward in front of the offering-ladles, he addresses him with the mantra: "May the sacrifice ascend to heaven; may the sacrifice go to heaven; by that path which leads to the gods, may the sacrifice reach the gods. Thus.

When he says, "O Brahman, we shall set forth; having placed the fuel-stick, O Āgnīdhra, cleanse the fires once each," then the Brahman gives the impulse: "O God Savitṛ, this has been declared to you; impel it and perform the sacrifice. Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; protect the sacrifice; protect the lord of the sacrifice; protect me. Om! Be established!"—thus [he says] at the Pravargya rite, [commanding], "Proceed!"

He remains right there until the offering of the *samiṣṭayajus*. When the *samiṣṭayajus* has been offered, he rises and worships the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "Jātavedas has sacrificed the sacrifice of the oblation; being undeceived, he sat down first at its end. Winning the prize, release us with a good release! Bestow upon us wealth, O Jātavedas, and whatever is auspicious.
By this very [mantra] he becomes the Brahman priest for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the seasonal sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), and the Sautrāmaṇī.
Having set down the sacrificial oblations, he addresses the Hotṛ.
Wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder and having sipped water, he rubs his hands together, saying: "For your work; may I be able for the gods; for your power; for your good deed.
Then, with two verses, he takes the fire into himself: "I take Agni first into myself; that Agni who is ours..."

(3.27:98.8) Then, he enters between the altar and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), saying: "I resort to truth; I resort to *ṛta*; I resort to immortality; I resort to the dear, uninjured body of Prajāpati. With this fifteenfold thunderbolt, I trample upon my hateful rival—him who hates us and whom we hate. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar*. I stand in the station of Viṣṇu.
(3.27:98.12) Having stepped with his right forefoot across to the northern edge of the altar, he stands there.

When he recognizes [the signal], "Recite for Agni as he is being kindled," then he mutters this *hautra* formula: "I take refuge in Ka; I take refuge in him. That which is your shelter, O Prajāpati, the meter, in that I take refuge. As much as I know of you, O Viṣṇu, so much shall I perform for you. Impelled by the god Savitṛ, I shall perform the office of the officiant. Homage to Agni, the overseer; homage to Vāyu, the listener; homage to Āditya, the witness. Today, the beloved..."

"May I raise my voice for the gods; may it be worthy of being heard by men, possessed of *svadhā* for the ancestors, and a firm foundation for every living being. Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! O Praśāstṛ, through myself, my offspring, and my cattle, I take refuge in Prajāpati. May there be fearlessness for me. I shall recite the portion belonging to Prajāpati. I take refuge in speech; Speech shall perform the office of the officiating priest. For glory thee! For splendor thee! For sensory power thee! For prosperity thee!
May the Sacrifice and the Sacrificial Ground grant great protection! Thus he says.
In this case, having uttered the *abhihiṅkāra* three times, he joins the verse to the *abhihiṅkāra* without taking breath.
He recites the first verse three times: "Forward for you, O strengths, seeking the light" (*pra vo vājā abhidyavaḥ*), and the last verse three times.
(3.27:99.6) He exhales all [the breath] verse by half-verse.

(3.27:99.6) After the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, having invoked the deities and made a span-measure on the ground, he sits down, saying: "With this Gāyatrī metre, with the Trivṛt stoma, with the Rathantara sāman, with the *vaṣaṭ*-call as a thunderbolt, I thrust away my hateful rival. "The hater is thrust away," he says.
(3.27:99.9) He remains sitting looking at the Āhavanīya fire, or between the two, namely the *praṇītā* water and the fire.

He looks at [the fire], thinking either "no" or "yes. When he knows [it has been accepted], he becomes humble toward him. He mutters this: "Agni, the divine Hotṛ; O God Savitṛ, they choose you as Agni for the office of Hotṛ, together with your father Vaiśvānara."

(3.27:99.13) Then, having stood up, he touches the Adhvaryu on the right shoulder with his right hand, and the Āgnīdhra on the right shoulder with his left hand. (3.27:100.1) But if he himself responds to the call, he should touch him at the place of the *nīvi* on the right hip, [saying]: "We touch Agni, the domestic priest, in the choosing of the Hotṛ; by whom the gods and the Aṅgirases went to the highest heaven, to the sky."
(3.27:100.4) "O gods among gods, exert your prowess! May the first [be victorious] over the second, the second over the third! O thrice eleven, draw yourselves together!
(3.27:100.5) Then he announces his name to the Adhvaryu.
(3.27:100.6) Then he turns around toward his right shoulder, saying: "I turn according to the turning of Indra."
Then, while approaching the seat of the Hotṛ, he murmurs the following prayer.
"May the six wide ones protect me from distress: heaven and earth, day and night, water and plants. May they guard me; may they protect me; homage to them! Thus he says.
Then, from his seat, he throws away a blade of grass—either dry or with its tip broken off—along the junction of the southern and western directions, saying: "Parāvasu is cast out!
Then, having touched water and having spread [grass] underneath, he sits down, saying: "In this seat of Arvāvasu, I sit," while keeping his right hand uppermost.
Then, turning to the right, he gazes at the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra: "O Viśvakarman, you are the protector of the body; protect my body.

Both [the sacrificer and his wife] gaze at the Āhavanīya fire as well, [reciting]: "O Agni and Viṣṇu, may I not step between you two; do not consume my vigor; move apart so that you do not burn me; O makers of space, create a space for me.
With the words, "This is your space," he creeps slightly toward the north.

Then he mutters three verses: "O All-Gods, instruct me how, having been chosen as the Hotṛ and having sat down, I should think; tell me my portion so that I may carry the oblation to you by whichever path.
"May I today utter that first word of speech by which we gods may overcome the Asuras—O eaters of strength, O worthy of sacrifice, you five peoples, be pleased with my office as Hotṛ!"
"Homage to the great ones, homage to the small ones; homage to the young, homage to the aged. Let us sacrifice to the gods if we are able; O gods, may I not incur the reproach of my elders.
Having thus [recited], he causes the two offering-ladles to be taken up by means of the *srugādāpana* formula and sacrifices the oblation according to the respective deity.

Now follows the consecration formula for the *vaṣaṭ*-calls: "O *vaṣaṭ*-call, do not choose me; I invoke you with the great mind through Mātariśvan. [Do not take] my breaths or my speech. I carry the oblation to the gods. Might, force, force—speech is might.
If, however, the *vaṣaṭ*-calls are very close together, he consecrates with this much alone: "Might, force, force—speech. Then he anoints the two fingers of the Hotṛ twice.

(3.28:101.12) He wipes what was previously smeared onto the upper lip with the formula: "I consume thee, offered to Vācaspati; for food, for out-breathing. (3.28:101.13) With the formula: "I consume thee, offered to Sadasaspati; for strength, for down-breathing," he wipes it off onto the lower lip.
(3.28:102.1) Then, having touched water, he causes the *iḍā* to be cut four times with his hand not extended and not joined together.
He invokes the Iḍā, level with the mouth.

(3.29:102.4) "The Rathantara has been invoked together with the earth, together with Agni, together with food, and together with speech. "May the Rathantara invoke me together with the earth, together with Agni, together with food, and together with speech."

(3.29:102.6) <The Vāmadevya has been invoked together with the intermediate space, together with Vāyu, together with the breath, together with the cattle.> <May the Vāmadevya invoke me together with the intermediate space, together with Vāyu, together with the breath, together with the cattle.>

(3.29:102.8) “The Bṛhat has been invoked together with the sky, together with the Āditya, together with sight; may the Bṛhat invoke me together with the sky, together with the Āditya, together with sight.
(3.29:102.10) “The stationary world has been invoked; may the stationary world invoke me.”
(3.29:102.11) "The moving world has been invited; may the moving world invite me.

(3.29:102.12) "The seven officiating priests have been invited; may the seven officiating priests invite me. (3.29:102.13) "The cows with their curd-mixture have been invited; may the cows with their curd-mixture invite me."
(3.29:102.14) "The cow with the bull has been invited; may the cow with the bull invite me.
(3.29:102.14–15) The sacrificial food (*iḍā*) and the rain have been invited; may the sacrificial food and the rain invite me.
(3.29:102.15) The companion, the portion to be consumed, has been invited; may the companion, the portion to be consumed, invite me."
(3.29:103.1) “<Upahūtāṃ... upahūtāṃ... upahūtāṃ... upahūtāṃ ho iḍā>.
(3.29:103.1) Having uttered the portion inaudibly with “<Upahūtā he sāsi juṣasva meḍe>,” he invokes the explicit formula aloud.
(3.29:103.2) If he intends to consume the whole, having first consumed what is held in his hand, he should consume from the cup itself.

Now, if he should wish to give it away or set it aside, he should cut off a piece of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and eat it, saying: "Thou art the *iḍā*; thou art pleasant; thou art the maker of pleasure. Do thou place us in abundance of wealth and in good progeny. I eat thee for the glory of my mouth, so that my mouth may be fragrant.
Having eaten it and sipped water, he pours out a line of water toward the east or the north, silently. Such indeed is the rule regarding the clarified butter (*ājya*).
Then he mutters this prayer: "May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this severed sacrifice. May Bṛhaspati extend this for us; may all the gods rejoice here.

Having performed the after-offerings and uttered the *śaṃyuvāka*, he makes a reverential gesture with joined palms upon the sacrificial grass and confesses: "O Sacrifice, peace be mine and prosperity be mine! O Prajāpati, whatever in your sacrifice was deficient and whatever was redundant, that sacrifice is now in Prajāpati."
Then, having placed the *veda* grass-bundle on the southern half of the altar, he makes the sacrificer recite.

(3.30:104.4) "O God, by that means through which you became the Veda for the gods, as such, be the Veda for us! You are the Veda; you are acquisition. May I acquire offspring, cattle, and the heavenly world. You are action; you are the performance of action. May I perform meritorious action."
"You are a winner; you are a winner; may I win that [wealth]. "May the Veda grant the possessor of ghee, the nest-like abode, the thousandfold increase of wealth, and the prize-winning steed.

(TS 3.30:104.8) Having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings and the *phalīkaraṇa* oblation, he makes the wife recite over the *veda* grass-bundle: "You are the Veda; you are acquisition; may I acquire that [wealth]. (TS 1.6.4.4.v, supplemented by *aham adaḥ*).

"Thou art action; thou art compassion; may I obtain this through action. Thou art a giver; thou art a bestower; may I win that. May the Veda grant us wealth—abounding in ghee, providing a home, thousandfold, and full of vigor.
Having untied the Veda-bundle, he gives half of it to his wife.

The wife places them between her thighs or holds them down with her right thigh. Then, turning toward the east and spreading the other [blades], he goes forward, reciting: "Stretching the thread, follow the light of the mid-world; guard the luminous paths prepared by wisdom. Weave the work of the singers without flaw; become Manu and give birth to the divine folk. Then, those which remain over, he places upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), saying: "Thou art the filler; fill me with offspring and cattle."

Then, having gone out by the way he entered, having circumambulated the *āhavanīya* fire from the front, and standing to the south facing north, he worships the *āhavanīya*: "Jātavedas has sacrificed the sacrifice of the oblation, undeceived; sitting first at the end within this [fire], granting gain, release us with a good release! Bestow upon us wealth, O Jātavedas, and whatever is auspicious."

(3.30:105.9) "O Agni, grow strong by this *brahman*—whether by what we have done through our power or through our knowledge. And may you lead us toward greater prosperity; unite us with your benevolence that is rich in strength.

(3.30:105.11) "Those hundred, O Varuṇa, those thousand great sacrificial bonds of yours that are spread out—with them may Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and all the Maruts, who sing beautiful hymns, release us."
These indeed are the mutterings for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, for the seasonal sacrifices, for the animal sacrifice, and for the Sautrāmaṇī.
(3.31:105.15) Now, regarding the animals, they are placed [on the altar].

When he knows [the signal], "Recite for the fire being churned," then he mutters these two verses: "Whatever vows of yours we may violate, Whatever, with simple minds and feeble resolve, Mortals do not perceive of the sacrifice— May Agni, the Hotṛ, knowing the rite and discerning, As the best of sacrificers, worship the gods in due season. (Ṛgveda 10.2.5)

(3.31:105.19) While holding the staff of Mitrāvaruṇa, the Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite: "The cows have chosen you for kingship; the Maruts, who sing beautiful hymns, call upon you. Resting upon the height, at the peak of sovereign power, from there, O fierce one, distribute wealth to us.
(3.31:106.2) Having first grasped it, he hands it over to the Maitrāvaruṇa, saying: "By the command of Mitrāvaruṇa, the two directors, I give you [this staff]."
He receives it from the thick end [of the trunk] with the formula: "By the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the directors, I receive thee," holding it with the right hand uppermost.
Then he wipes it upwards with the formula: "May I become straight and free from disease.
Having taken it up, he issues the call: "Let the Hotṛ sacrifice to Agni, who is well-kindled with a good kindling-stick"—this concludes the section on the fuel for the animal sacrifice.

One is about to sacrifice with an animal victim. He prepares: enclosing-sticks of *pautudrava* wood; bdellium (*gulgulu*); fragrant reed-grass (*sugandhitejana*); a tuft of white wool from between the horns of a ram; two ropes, one double-stranded and one triple-stranded; two omentum-spits, one forked and one unforked; a heart-spike; enclosing-sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood; a staff for the Maitrāvaruṇa priest made of *udumbara* wood, reaching up to his mouth; sacrificial fuel and grass; fuel for the leading forward of the fire; a branch of the *plakṣa* tree; and barley for the *iḍasūna* vessels.
[He prepares] groats for the groat-oblation, curds for the speckled butter, and gold.

Then, having sacrificed with the New Moon oblation or under a [favorable] lunar mansion, he melts the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire, purifies it, takes four portions into the ladle, mentally recites the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula, and while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, he offers it into the Āhavanīya fire with the word "Svāhā!"

Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers the oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*) with the mantra: "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely; make wide room for our dwelling! Drink the clarified butter, O you whose source is butter! Further on and on the lord of the sacrifice, Svāhā!
Having taken another fourfold portion, he then requests the vessel of clarified butter together with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), gold, and a water-vessel.
They call for the carpenter along with his axe.

He says, "Come, O sacrificer," and having gone out by the eastern door, they go in that direction where his sacrificial post (yūpa) is visible, or where he thinks he will find it. He approaches a tree that grows on level ground, from a good soil, with many leaves and many branches, whose top is not withered, and which leans toward the west, [saying]: "I have passed others; I have not approached others. I have found you nearer than those further away, and further than those nearer. I choose you, who belong to Viṣṇu, for the sacrifice to the gods."
(4.1:107.18) Then he anoints it with clarified butter, [saying]: "May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey.
(4.1:107.19) He raises up a blade of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with its tip pointing upwards, [saying]: "O herb, protect him!
(4.1:107.19) With the axe, he strikes across it, [saying]: "O axe, do not harm him!"
(4.1:108.1) He sets aside that first chip which falls away, keeping it well-marked.
(4.1:108.2) Without splitting it, he cuts [the sacrificial post], ensuring it does not get caught on the axle.

(4.1:108.3) As it is being carried forward, whether eastward or northward, he addresses it with the mantra: "Do not scratch the sky with your top; do not injure the mid-region with your middle; be united with the earth."

(4.1:108.4) Then, having placed gold upon the stump where no tree grows and having strewn [grass] all around, he makes an offering with: "O Lord of the Forest, grow forth with a hundred shoots, svāhā!

(4.1:108.6) With the words, "May we grow forth with a thousand shoots," he touches himself. (4.1:108.7) He causes the branches to fall down in the direction of the tip with: "Thee, whom this whetted axe has brought forward for great good fortune."
"One should cut it for him to five cubits," so it is said.
This is the minimum for those who follow the Brāhmaṇa tradition;
he causes it to be trimmed at the time of the *caṣāla* to a maximum of a full embrace and a minimum of a span, with the formula: "May wealth, accompanied by heroic sons, be uncut."
(4.1:108.10) Of that which remains at the top, he cuts off four finger-breadths for the *caṣāla*.
Having made it either four-cornered or eight-cornered, he causes it to be brought down or has it brought down. Having brought it down, he completes [the post].
He makes the *svaru* from the very shavings of the wood.
Now, on the previous day, this altar for the animal sacrifice has already been measured out:
ten steps across at the back, twelve steps from west to east, and eight steps across at the front.
Having strewn it around, he performs the *stambayajus* rite.
This very [procedure] is established according to the *Pauroḍāśika* section:
three times with the *yajus* formula and a fourth time silently. He performs the first tracing of the altar.
He mutters the *karaṇa* formula. He digs up [the earth]. From the dug-up spot, the Āgnīdhra carries away [the earth] three times.
When the Āgnīdhra has carried [the earth] three times, he then asks for the wooden sword (*sphyá*), a water-vessel, sacrificial grass (*barhís*), and the *śamyā* peg.
Having taken these up, he says, "Come, O sacrificer!
To the north of the altar, at two or three steps' distance, having dug up the ground with the wooden sword and sprinkled it with water, he measures out the *cātvāla* pit with the *śamyā*.
(4.2:109.3) With the formula, "Thou art my path to wealth," he scratches inside with the wooden sword (sphya) using the front part of the vessel turned toward the north.
(4.2:109.4) With the formula, "Thou art my path to refreshment," he scratches inside with the wooden sword using the right side of the vessel turned toward the east.
(4.2:109.5) With the formula, "Protect me from distress," he scratches inside with the wooden sword using the back part of the vessel turned toward the north.
(4.2:109.6) With the words, "Deliver me from distress," he draws a line with the wooden sword (sphya) on the north side, inside the northern pitcher-mark.

(4.2:109.7) Then, having placed sacrificial grass (barhis) in the pit (cātvāla), he strikes it with the wooden sword while reciting: "May Agni know thee by the name Nabhas; O Agni Aṅgiras, thou who art upon this earth.
(4.2:109.9) He takes up [the grass] with the words: "Come with life by means of the name."

Having taken it, he pours it out upon the *uttaravedi* with the formula: "With that name of yours which is unassailable and worthy of sacrifice, I establish you. He strikes a second time with: "May Agni find Nabhas by name; O Agni Aṅgiras, you who are on the second earth.
He takes [the fire] up with: "Come with the name of Āyus."

Having taken it, he scatters it upon the *uttaravedi* with the formula: "With that name of yours which is unassailable and worthy of sacrifice, with that I establish you. He strikes the third [layer] with: "May Agni find Nabhas by name; O Agni Aṅgiras, you who are on the third earth.
He takes it up with: "Come by means of the name Āyus."
Having carried [the earth], he pours it down on the *uttaravedi* with the formula: "With that name of yours which is unassailable and worthy of sacrifice, with that I establish you.

He carries the fourth portion silently together with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Then the Adhvaryu digs up the loose soil from the *cātvāla* pit with the wooden sword (*sphya*). Then he says to the Āgnīdhra: "O Āgnīdhra, carry [the soil] from here three times."
Then the Āgnīdhra carries [the earth] three times.
When the Āgnīdhra has carried it three times, the Adhvaryu mixes the soil of the high altar (*uttaravedi*), saying: "Thou art a lioness; thou art a buffalo-cow.
He spreads it out, saying: "Spread wide! May the lord of the sacrifice spread wide for thee."

(4.2:109.20) He strikes it with the wooden sword, saying, "Thou art firm. (4.2:109.21) Then he sprinkles it with water, saying, "Be pure for the gods," or "Be beautiful for the gods. (4.2:109.22) He covers it over with sand.
Having finished that [altar] which is a span high and square, he measures it around with a yoke-pin.

Having raised the northern navel, and having covered it over, he takes up the spade with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee."
Having taken it up, he consecrates it with: "Thou art a spade; thou art a woman.

With it, he traces around the hole for the sacrificial post so that half shall be within the altar and half outside the altar, saying: "The *rakṣas* is traced around; the enemies are traced around. Here I cut off the neck of the *rakṣas*; him who hates us and whom we hate—here I cut off his neck."

(4.2:110.7) Then he says to the Āgnīdhra: "O Āgnīdhra, come! Dig this post-hole, measuring it by its upper part; let him throw out the loose earth toward the east; let him dig deeper than the upper part by four finger-breadths.
(4.2:110.9) He either digs it himself or has it dug.
For as long as the Adhvaryu is busy there, during that time the Pratiprasthātṛ places the fuel for the leading forward of the fire.
They prepare the *upayamanī* vessels from the *cātvāla*.
The Adhvaryu takes for himself the *prokṣaṇī* waters containing the sound of Indra;
he hands over to the *parikarmin* the clarified butter taken five times.
The ritual materials are placed upon the *brahman* priest.

Then he issues the command: "Recite for the fire being carried forward! O *āgnīdh*, follow along with the single wooden sword (*ekasphya*)! When this has been uttered three times, they lift [the fire] up.
They go to the Hotṛ’s station;
they proceed along the north side of the altar,
maintaining this fire.
Then the Adhvaryu sprinkles the high altar with sprinkling waters accompanied by the *indraghoṣavatī* verses.
"May Indraghoṣa protect you from the east with the Vasus," [he says] toward the east.
"May Manojava protect you from the south with the Pitṛs," [he says] toward the south. "May Pracetas protect you from the west with the Rudras," [he says] toward the west.
"May Viśvakarman protect you from the north with the Ādityas," [he says] as he [sprinkles] from the north.
Then, whatever remains of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he pours that out to the south of the high altar (*uttaravedi*),
for "whatever there is cruel, he pacifies that by means of this," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, having placed gold beneath her, he sprinkles her crosswise with fivefold-drawn butter:
with "Thou art a lioness, overcoming rivals, svāhā! on the right shoulder;
and with "Thou art a lioness, winning good progeny, svāhā! on the left hip.
(4.3:111.4) “Thou art a lion, winning increase of wealth, svāhā!”—thus on the southern hip. (4.3:111.5) “Thou art a lion, winning the Ādityas, svāhā!”—thus on the northern shoulder.
(4.3:111.6) “Thou art a lion; bring the gods for the god-loving sacrificer, svāhā!”—thus in the middle.
Then, with the words, "For the beings, thee," he lifts up the offering-spoon.
Then he lays down the enclosing-sticks made of *pūtudru* wood.
He places the middle one with the formula: "Thou art the life of all; make firm the earth."

(4.3:111.8) "Thou art firm-seated; make firm the intermediate space," [with this he places] the southern [brick]. (4.3:111.9) "Thou art unshakable-seated; make firm the sky," [with this he places] the northern [brick].
Then he pours out the remaining materials: bdellium, fragrant powder, and a tuft of white wool, [saying], "Thou art the ash of Agni; thou art the soil of Agni."

(4.3:111.11) Then he sprinkles them with the residue of the ghee. (4.3:111.11) Then, having turned to the right, he establishes the fuel: "O Sacrifice, be established in a good disposition, very gracious; may riches enter thee in many ways, creating long life for the sacrificer. "Then [he says], 'Anoint the singer with truth.
(4.3:111.14) Then, having loosened it and made it capable of bearing the oblations, he offers over it the *adhvara* oblations:
"May Agni, knowing, lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it. Proclaim the sacrifice to the gods; further on and on extend the lord of the sacrifice—*svāhā*! (4.3:111.15)

(4.3:111.16) "May Vāyu, knowing [the way], lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it. Proclaim the sacrifice to the gods; further extend the lord of the sacrifice—*svāhā*! (4.3:111.18) "May Sūrya, knowing [the way], lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it. Proclaim the sacrifice to the gods; further extend the lord of the sacrifice—*svāhā*!"

(4.3:111.19) "May the sacrifice, knowing [the way], lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it. Proclaim the sacrifice to the gods; further on and on extend the lord of the sacrifice—svāhā! Thus.

(4.3:112.2) Then the sacrificer himself offers these [oblations] with: "Agni, the eater of food, the lord of food, rules over food; may he grant me food, svāhā! Vāyu, the giver of breath, rules over breath; may he grant me breath, svāhā! Āditya, the giver of much, rules over the most numerous cattle; may he grant me the most numerous cattle, svāhā! Thus.

Having performed the second tracing around while it possesses fire, having leveled the ground, and having held the wooden sword (sphya) crosswise, he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass nearby; cleanse the dipping-spoon (sruva), the knife (svadhiti), and the offering-ladles (sruc); [cleanse] the vessel for the speckled butter silently; gird the wife; and bring the clarified butter and the curds."

When the *prokṣaṇī* waters have been brought, he wipes the wooden sword (*sphya*) with them, sets down the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*), turns to the right, and having hastened westward, he cleanses the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), the knife (*svadhiti*), and the offering-ladles (*sruk*); he cleanses the vessel for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājyagrahaṇī*) silently.

He girds the wife, goes out with the clarified butter and the curds, purifies the clarified butter and the *prokṣaṇī* waters in the established manner, and having taken the portions of clarified butter, he makes an under-layer of butter in the vessel for the speckled butter with the formula: "Thou art the milk of the great ones.
He makes a second under-layer with: "The body of the All-gods."

Having placed two blades of *barhis* grass in between, he pours curds [into the vessel] with the formula: "May I succeed today in the drawing of the speckled ones; you are the drawing of the speckled ones.
Having removed the two blades of *barhis*, he then bastes it with ghee, saying: "Thou art the heart of Viṣṇu.
With the formula, "One step of Viṣṇu has measured thee out for food," he bastes the second [portion].
Then, rising with the sprinkling waters, he sprinkles the fuel,

he sprinkles the altar, and he sprinkles the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass that has been set down and poured water over it, he takes the *prastara* bundle from the front.
Having strewn the fivefold sacrificial grass (*barhis*), holding the *prastara* in his hand, he steps forward toward the east and lays down the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood.
He places two upright fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and sets down two separating blades (*vidhṛti*) crosswise.
He places the *prastara* on the two *vidhṛtis*;
the *juhū* on the *prastara*;
and the other [ladles] on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

(4.4:113.4) Having touched them all over with the formula, "These have sat down," and having turned to the right, hastening westward, he calls for: water for sprinkling mixed with barley, a handful of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), a vessel for clarified butter together with the *sruva*-ladle, the cord for the sacrificial post, the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa, a chip from the sacrificial post, gold, and a vessel of water.

(4.4:113.6) Having placed these nearby, he washes the sacrificial post with the verse: "Whatever of thee the skillful carpenter has struck away with his hand by means of the axe—O Lord of the Forest, may the purifying waters drive that away."
This sacrificial post, washed, brought forward, and fitted with its top-ring (*caṣāla*), lies to the east of the pit.
Standing to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, facing away from it, he sprinkles it with water, saying: "For the earth thee! For the atmosphere thee! For the sky thee!
He pours water into the pit, saying: "May the world, the seat of the fathers, be purified."
He scatters barley grains with the formula: "Thou art barley; drive away from us our enemies; drive away the adversaries.
Having interlaced his hands holding the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he spreads it down with the formula: "Thou art the seat of the Pitṛs.
Then, having placed a piece of gold beneath it, he makes an offering with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) while saying: "Svāhā to the Pitṛs!"
(4.4:113.14) He inserts a chip of the sacrificial post [with the formula]: "Thou art easy of access, the first-goer among leaders; the Lord of the Forest shall stand upon thee; know him!
(4.4:113.16) Then he takes the vessel for clarified butter together with the dipping-spoon, the Svaru-chip, the rope, the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa, and a water-vessel.
(4.4:113.17) Having taken all this, he says: "Come, O sacrificer!"

The sacrificer follows behind, and the wife follows after him; having gone around the front of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), they stand to the south facing north—the Adhvaryu in front, the sacrificer behind him, and the wife furthest back.

Then, having pulled off the *caṣāla* (the wooden ring), he anoints the tip of the post with the formula: "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey," both inside and out. Having well-anointed it, he fixes the *caṣāla* on it with the formula: "For the plants that bear good fruit."
(4.4:114.4) Then, while pouring clarified butter with the *sruva*-ladle over the edge facing the fire (*agniṣṭhā aśri*), he says: "Recite for the sacrificial post as it is being anointed.
(4.4:114.5) He anoints it right to the end; indeed, he thus anoints the sacrificer himself with splendor. He does not anoint the upper part.
The wife anoints the end [of the post].
"He touches it all around; thus he bestows splendor upon it without leaving anything out," so says the Brāhmaṇa. As he raises it, he says: "Recite for the one being raised!"
He raises it with the formula: "Prop up the sky; fill the mid-region; make firm the earth with thy base.
Then he fashions it with two verses addressed to Viṣṇu: "Behold these thy stations," and "Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu"—with these two.

When he brings the edge facing the fire into contact with the Āhavanīya, he gazes at the top-ring of the Dhruva post with the verse: "That is the highest step of Viṣṇu, which the wise ever behold, like an eye fixed in the sky."

(4.4:114.12) Then he heaps earth around it from left to right with the formula: "I heap around you, the winner of the *brahman*, the winner of the *kṣatra*, the winner of good offspring, the winner of the increase of wealth.
(4.4:114.13) He compacts it with the staff of Mitrāvaruṇa, saying: "Strengthen the *brahman*; strengthen the *kṣatra*; strengthen the offspring; strengthen the increase of wealth.
(4.4:114.15) Having laid it down neither deficient nor excessive, he pours out a vessel of water.
(4.4:114.15) Then, having tripled this threefold girdle and winding it three times around at the height of the navel with the middle strand, he says: "Recite for that which is being girt.

(4.4:114.17) He winds it around three times clockwise, saying: "Thou art girt; may the divine subjects gird thee; may the increase of wealth gird this sacrificer, and men [gird him]. (4.4:114.19) At the ends, he interlaces them.
He causes it to enter to the end. He weaves the thick part over the thin part.
Then, to the north of the corner facing the fire (agniṣṭhā), he hides the sacrificial chip (svaru) in the middle loop with [the formula]: "I hide you on the ridge of the intermediate space."
He erects the sacrificial post provided with a wooden cup.
Then, having led this washed animal between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), he causes it to stand in front of the sacrificial post, facing west.

(4.5:115.2) Having taken two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the formula, "For food, thee," he performs the introductory dedication (*upākaraṇa*). "Thou art the one who approaches; the divine subjects have approached the gods, the carriers, the eager ones. O Bṛhaspati, bestow riches; may thy offerings be palatable. O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, enjoy the wealth; O wealthy ones, rejoice! Being born from Prajāpati—O Lord of Cattle, this animal is thine today. I dedicate thee, acceptable to Indra and Agni," or whichever deity it belongs to. (4.5:115.6)
Having set down two recognized blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he places the lower churning-wood block with the formula, "Thou art the birthplace of Agni.
He places two upper churning-sticks behind it with the formula, "Ye two are the testicles.
Then he takes up the two fire-drills with the formulas, "Thou art Urvaśī; thou art Āyu Purūravas."
(4.5:115.9) Then he anoints these two with the butter-pot, saying: "Anointed with ghee, do you two bestow virility.

(4.5:115.10) Then he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the formulas for procreation: "Be procreated according to the Gāyatrī metre; be procreated according to the Triṣṭubh metre; be procreated according to the Jagatī metre.
(4.5:115.12) Then he says: "Recite for Agni as he is being churned."
When [the fire] has been produced, he says, "Recite for the one that has been produced. As he strikes [the fire], he says, "Recite for the one being struck.
He strikes it with the words, "May you two be of one mind toward us."
Having struck [the post], he makes an offering with the verse: "Fire moves within fire, having entered it.

Then he takes up the rope with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take you. With that [rope], he binds the animal crosswise over the right half of its head with the formula: "O divine oblation, I seize you with the noose of Truth."

He joins the ends of the two-fold and three-fold [strands] together with the formula, "Be bold against men," and then fastens it. Then he sprinkles it with water, saying: "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to the waters, to the plants, and to Indra and Agni."
He causes [the animal] belonging to whichever deity it may be to drink [water], saying: "Thou art the drinker of waters.
Having sprinkled [it] from above with the words, "O divine waters, make this well-tasted oblation palatable for the gods," he sprinkles [it] from below.
"He makes it pure on all sides," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Having lifted up the vessel for the sprinkling water, he sets it down.
(4.6:116.4) Then, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says: "Recite for the fire being kindled!
(4.6:116.4) He places the faggot [on the fire].
(4.6:116.5) He leaves one fuel-stick remaining.
He fans [the fire] with the Veda-broom. When the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, he pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* spoon;
once it has been wiped clean, he pours the subsequent one with the two *sruc* ladles.
Then, without letting the two offering-ladles touch each other, having stepped across toward the north, he anoints the animal with the *juhū* ladle:
with the words, "May your breath unite with the wind," on the forehead;
and with the words, "May your limbs unite with those worthy of sacrifice," on the hump.
(4.6:116.9) "The lord of the sacrifice [is united] with his blessing," [with these words he places the cake] on the southern buttock.
(4.6:116.9) Then, having set down the two offering-spoons in their respective places, he chooses the *pravara*. He chooses the *hotṛ* in the established manner.

Then he causes the announcement to be made: "O, cause it to be heard! "Let there be hearing! "Mitra and Varuṇa are the two Praśāstṛs; from the office of the Praśāstṛ. [He says: "So-and-so is the human one," and thus he utters the name of the Maitrāvaruṇa. Then he causes the announcement to be made.

If he calls for the *atyāśrāvaṇa* here: "O, cause it to be heard! Let there be *śrauṣaṭ*! Agni is the leader of the divine clans, and this sacrificer is the leader of human beings. May their household-fire shine without fail for a hundred winters. May the two of you, as givers of wealth, be united in body yet not mingled in person. Having said this, the Hotṛ sits down and awaits the impulse.
(4.6:116.16) Having been urged, he takes up the two offering-spoons, steps across, causes the announcement to be made, and says, "Prompt for the kindling-sticks!

(4.6:116.17) When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering. Saying, "Prompt! Prompt! (4.6:116.18), while pouring together [the butter] at the fourth and eighth [calls], he pours it all together at the eighth.
He retains the remnants of the *saṃsrāva* for the sake of the *svāhākṛti* offerings.
Having performed the ten *prayāja* offerings and stepped across to the north, he asks for the *svaru* and the *śāsa*.
Having smeared those two on the *juhū* ladle, he anoints the animal with them, saying: "Anointed with ghee, may you two protect the animal."
He hands over the sword;
he hides the sacrificial post (svaru).
Then, having placed the two offering-ladles (srucau) in their respective places, he says: "Recite for the fire being carried around! (paryagnaye kriyamāṇāyānubrūhi).

(4.6:117.4) Then the Āgnīdhra, having taken a firebrand from the Āhavanīya, goes three times around [the victim] to the right, passing between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, to the north of the *śāmitra* site, in front of the victim, and behind the offering-ladles. (4.6:117.6) Then, following the circumambulation, he offers the *apāvya* oblations with the mantra: "The ancestors, knowing [the way], receive [the victim], over whom Paśupati has lordship; those who are bound after the one being bound, the wild animals of every form—releasing the seed of the world."
(4.6:117.9) Having set down the firebrand, the Āgnīdhra goes around three times again in the opposite direction as he came.
(4.6:117.10) Then they proceed with the firebrand in front;
the slaughterer follows behind with the animal.
The Adhvaryu takes hold of the animal with the two omentum-roasting spits;
the sacrificer takes hold of the two omentum-roasting spits.
Then, having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he issues the direction: "O Hotṛ, bring forward the oblations to the gods."

(4.6:117.12) Then, with two verses, he consecrates this animal as it is being led northward between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*: "The breath of the sacrificer is distinct from that of the animal; O wealthy ones, enter the lord of the sacrifice in a dear manner.

(4.6:117.15) When the Āgnīdhra places the firebrand there, he strews sacrificial grass (*barhis*) in front of or to the north of the place where the animal is to be slaughtered, saying: "Protect [the animal] from contact with the earth.
(4.6:117.17) Thereupon they slaughter this animal with its head toward the west and its feet toward the north.

(4.6:117.17) Having said, "Make him who makes no sound [bleat] conscious," they return by the same way they came and sit near the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter). With the mantra: "May offspring of every form rejoice here in this sacrifice, all-knowing and dripping with ghee; dwelling together in Agni as their home, may they favor us with milk and ghee," (4.6:118.2) they announce that he has been made conscious. (4.6:118.3) He offers the oblation for the one made conscious with the verse: "When the animal made a sound..."

(4.6:118.3) Then he approaches [the place] with the words, "O immolators, come hither! (4.6:118.4) He consecrates the animal being released from the noose with the mantra: "May Aditi release this noose.
(4.6:118.5) Having fastened it with a branchless twig, he casts it away toward this direction with the words: "I make him who acts as an enemy low; upon him whom we hate, I fasten the noose."

(4.6:118.6) Then the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife forward, having made her rise with a water-jar. (4.6:118.7) He then causes her to gaze upward at the sun, [saying]: "Homage to thee, O Expander! (4.6:118.8) Then, having gone out northward between the Cātvāla and the Utkara, while leading her eastward, he makes her recite: "Go forth, invincible; follow the stream of ghee, together with offspring, together with the increase of wealth."
When they have arrived, the Adhvaryu makes them recite over the waters: "O divine waters, seeking purity, pure yourselves, carry the gods; pure, may we, being served, be your servers.
He then causes the vital breaths of the animal to swell in their proper order: "May your speech swell," he says for speech.
"May your breath swell," [he says] regarding the breath;
"may your eye swell," regarding the eye;
"may your ear swell," regarding the ear.

He touches these very parts again with the formula: "That pain of yours which has gone to the breaths, that which [has gone] to the eye, that which to the ear; that which is cruel in you, that which is settled [within], may that swell for you; may that be purified for you by this.
With "May your navel swell," he touches the navel; with "May your anus swell," he touches the anus.
Having firmly grasped her feet, he washes them with the words: "Pure are the ways; peace to the waters; peace to the plants; peace to the earth.
With the words "peace to the two days," he pours out the remainder toward the south along the back [of the altar].
They lead away the wife.
They turn the animal over onto its back. Along the opening of its right flank, he lays down sacrificial grass with its tips pointing eastward, saying: "O herb, protect him!
He then places the knife across it, saying: "O knife, do not harm him!"
He cuts the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); he strips away its skin;
then he takes a small portion from this very same sacrificial grass.

Having smeared both ends of the thickest part with blood, he throws it out toward this direction, saying: "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases! Here I lead the Rakṣas into the lowest darkness—he who hates us and whom we hate; here I lead him into the lowest darkness.
Then, having touched water and covered himself more closely, he extracts the omentum, saying: "For food, thee!"
(4.6:119.10) With that [omentum], he covers the two omentum-spits, saying: "O Heaven and Earth, cover yourselves with ghee.
(4.6:119.11) Having pierced it with a branchless twig, he trims the fat from below, saying: "Uninterrupted be the wealth accompanied by brave sons.
(4.6:119.12) Then, having turned it to the right and sprinkled it with water, he heats it over the *śāmitra* fire.
(4.6:119.12) Then they set out, preceded by the firebrand.
The Adhvaryu follows with the omentum.
At this point, the sacrificer again takes hold of the two omentum-spits.
[The Adhvaryu] goes forth, saying: "Follow along the wide mid-region."

Having approached the edge of the Āhavanīya fire, he throws a tip of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) onto these embers while the omentum (*vapā*) is being heated over them, with the mantra: "O Vāyu, partake of the drops.
Then, having carried it between the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the Āhavanīya fire, the Pratiprasthātṛ cooks it from the south, facing north.
Then he makes an offering over it with a spoonful, with the mantra: "Thee they have established as the bearer of oblations."

Then he says, "Recite for the *stokīya* drops. When the *stokīya* verses have been recited and the omentum has been cooked, he takes the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, steps across, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, "Prompt for the *svāhākṛti*s.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.
(4.7:120.1) Then, having stepped across toward the north and having sprinkled the clotted butter with the residue of the offering, he sprinkles the omentum.

(4.7:120.3) Then, having spread an underlayer [of ghee] and scooping up the omentum twice with the dipping-spoon while cutting it off, he says: "Recite for the fat of the goat's omentum being cut off for Indra and Agni.
(4.7:120.4) He sprinkles it twice.
Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] regarding the fat of the omentum of the goat set forth for Indra and Agni.

Then, before the *svāhākṛti* offerings, he offers a spoonful with: "Svāhā to the gods! When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers the omentum with: "O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum; for you were the first Hotṛ. Increase their bodies with clarified butter; may the gods eat the oblation consecrated by Svāhā—Svāhā!"
Then, after the *svāhākṛti* offerings, he offers a spoonful with the formula: "To the gods, svāhā!

At this point, he throws the two omentum-spits into the fire—the one with a forked end facing eastward and the one without a fork facing westward—with the formula: "Svāhā! Go ye to the upward-moving wind of the Maruts!
Then he sprinkles them with the remains of the oblation.
Then, having stepped across toward the north and placed the two offering-spoons in their respective places, they step out and perform the ritual purification at the pit.

They call for the wife; they call for the *hotṛ*; they call for the *brahman*; they call for the *pratiprasthātṛ*; they call for the *praśāstṛ*; they call for the *āgnīdhra*, saying: "Come, O sacrificer! "O Waters, carry away this: whatever is blameworthy and whatever is impurity; whatever treachery and falsehood, and whatever curse I have uttered in anger. I release myself from the oath, and I release myself from Varuṇa."
"Release me from the fetter of Yama, from every sin against the gods, and likewise from sin against men.
Then, with his joined palms, he scoops up water, saying: "May the waters and plants be friendly to us.
He sprinkles that water toward the direction in which he has an enemy, saying: "May they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate."
(4.7:121.2) Then, having touched water, they sit down in their respective places.
(4.8:121.3) Then he issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, prepare the sacrificial cake for the animal sacrifice; O Pratiprasthātṛ, prepare the animal.
(4.8:121.4) This Āgnīdhra prepares the cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni.

(4.8:121.4) Then the Pratiprasthātṛ instructs the slaughterer regarding the victim: "O slaughterer, prepare the heart, the tongue, and the breast together; prepare the two kidneys and the two *matasna* together; prepare the left foreleg as a single portion; set aside the two sides separately; make the right hip the *adhyuddhi*; make the right foreleg, the left hip, and three parts of the rectum (*aṇimad-guda*) into three portions; set aside the large intestine (*vaniṣṭhu*) and the tail; [and prepare] much fat."
"Make [the organs] ready; move the animal forward three times; of the animal moved forward three times, make the heart the last.
When the animal has been cooked, he asks for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
Having placed it on the sacrificial grass and poured clarified butter over it, he removes it from the fire and sets it down within the altar (*antarvedi*).
(4.8:121.12) Then, while spreading [the butter] in the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, he says: "Recite for Indra and Agni as the cake is being portioned out.
(4.8:121.13) Having taken a portion from the eastern half, he takes a portion from the western half.
(4.8:121.14) He pours clarified butter over it.
He anoints [the ladle].
Then, for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he takes a single portion from the northern half of the *upabhṛt* and pours clarified butter over it twice.

He does not anoint [the offering]. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] regarding the cake set forth for Indra and Agni. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering.
(4.8:121.16) Then, while pouring together [the oblations], he says: "Recite for Agni.
(4.8:121.17) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Prompt for Agni!
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering in the eastern half of the northern half, passing over the previous offerings.
(4.8:121.18) Then, having stepped across toward the north and placed the two offering-spoons in their respective places, he cuts off the *prāśitra* portion and then cuts off the *iḍā* portion.
(4.8:121.19) When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places the sixfold portion for the *agnīdh*.
(4.8:121.20) They consume [the portions].
(4.8:121.20) They perform the purificatory sprinkling.
(4.8:122.1) Then he issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, place the northern sacrificial grass; O Pratiprasthātṛ, hold the dialogue regarding the animal sacrifice.
(4.8:122.2) Then this Āgnīdhra hides the *iḍasūna* in a branch of the *plakṣa* tree.
That [grass] becomes the northern sacrificial grass (*uttarabarhis*).

Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having divided the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) and poured it into the *juhū* ladle, goes out toward the north between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), and asks: "Is the oblation cooked, O Śamitṛ?
