At that moment, the Śamitṛ stands to the north, holding the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*).
He replies, "It is cooked.
Having stepped forward in the same manner for the second time, he asks him;
the other replies in the same manner.

Having stepped forward in that same manner for the third time, he asks him; the other replies in the same way. Then, taking the heart-spit from the *śamitr*, having pierced the heart with it, and handing it over to the *śamitr*, he bastes the heart with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), saying: "May your mind unite with my mind; may your breath unite with my breath. An offering pleasing to the gods, rich in ghee—*svāhā*!"

"Having separated [the fires], carry [the animal] away," he says; having returned by the same way they came, he spreads under [the ladles] in the four places for the *iḍā*-vessel: in the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*, in the *iḍā*-holder, and in that [spot] where he is about to take the fat-oblation.

They bring that animal, having carried it along between the *cātvāla* and the rubbish-heap, between the sacrificial post and the *āhavanīya* fire; he places it to the south with the *pañcahotṛ* formula.
By this same path they carry the sacrificial post.
By this very [formula] is the *iḍā* portion [taken].
Then, having placed the heart upon a branch of the *plakṣa* tree, while cutting off its tip with the knife, he says:
(4.9:122.17) "Recite for the *manotā* as the oblation is being cut off!
Thus [he says]. He first cuts off twice from the heart;

then from the tongue, then from the breast, then from the *taniman*, then from the two kidneys, then from the left foreleg, then from the right rib, then from the left, then from the right hip, and finally from the *adhyuddhi*.

Having divided the rectum into three parts, he places the thinnest part for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the thickest part for the *upayaj* offerings; having divided the middle part into two, he places it into the *juhū* ladle.
Then, having placed the fat of the *vṛkī* into the broth, he covers the *juhū* with it and sprinkles it with broth.
He pours clarified butter over [the portions].

Then, for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he takes a single portion from each of all the three limbs into the *upabhṛt* ladle. Having once cut off a piece of flesh from the right foreleg, he places it [in the ladle]; once from the left hip; and once from the small intestine of the rectum. Then, having placed the kidneys and the fat into the broth, he covers the *upabhṛt* with it.
He sprinkles it with broth and pours clarified butter over it twice.
Then, having placed the heart, the tongue, the breast, the membrane, the two kidneys, and the rectum together in a vessel, he sprinkles them with broth.
He pours clarified butter over it.
Then he takes the fat-oblation in either a bronze vessel or a wooden cup and sprinkles it with broth.
He pours clarified butter over [the portions].

Then he touches the cuttings of the victim with the formula: "May Indra’s out-breath settle in every limb; may Indra’s in-breath manifest in every limb. O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, let much of yours come together, since you, though of diverse forms, become uniform. May the mother and the fathers rejoice after you as you go to the gods for their protection, O friend."

(4.9:123.12) Then, with his right side [toward the fire], he stirs the fat-oblation from the pot [with the verse]: "Thou art glory; may Agni prepare thee; the waters have flowed together; for the gliding of Vāta, for the speed of Pūṣan, for the growth of the waters and the plants. (4.9:123.15) They carry away the tail of the slaughtered animal toward the west;
they carry the animal around.
(4.9:123.16) Then, taking up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for the oblation of the goat for Indra and Agni.
(4.9:123.17) Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Prompt the Hotṛ to recite the offering verse for the oblation of the goat set forth for Indra and Agni.
(4.9:123.18) The Pratiprasthātṛ stands to the north, holding the fat-offering (*vasāhoma*).

At the half-verse of the *yājyā*, he offers the *vasāhoma* with the mantra: "O drinkers of ghee, drink the ghee; O drinkers of *vasā*, drink the *vasā*. You are the oblation of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the oblation.

Following this offering, the *pratiprasthātṛ* offers to the quarters with the excess of the *vasāhoma* with the mantra: "The quarters, the intermediate quarters, the directed quarters, the distinct quarters, the upward quarters—svāhā to the quarters! Homage to the quarters, svāhā!"
Then, having turned clockwise and striking at the speckled butter with the *sruva* spoon, he says, "Recite for Vanaspati!
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prompt for Vanaspati!
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering in the eastern part of the northern half, passing over the previous offerings.
(4.9:124.9) Then, while pouring together [the portions], he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
(4.9:124.9) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Direct the call for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt!
(4.9:124.10) When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering in the eastern part of the northern half, passing over the previous offerings.
(4.9:124.11) Then, having stepped across toward the north and placed the two offering-spoons in their respective places, they lift up the *iḍā* portion of the fat for the Hotṛ.
(4.9:124.12) When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places the sixfold portion consisting of half of the *vaniṣṭhu* and then the other half of the *vaniṣṭhu* together with the fat upon the Āgnīdhra.
(4.9:124.13) They consume [the portions].
They perform the ritual purification.
Then he says, "Hand over the chest to the Brahman";
the Brahman accepts it.

(4.10:124.16) “O Soma, may we abide in thy service, bearing our minds within our bodies; may we, possessing offspring, attain prosperity. (4.10:124.17) Then he issues the command: “O Āgnīdh, bring the embers for the supplementary offerings! O Upayaṣṭṛ, sit down! O Brahman, we shall set forth! Having placed a fuel-stick, O Āgnīdh, cleanse each of the fires once!
(4.10:124.18) They bring these embers for the supplementary offerings from the Śāmitra fire.
He pours them out in front of the Hotṛ.
The Upayaṣṭṛ sits down with the third part of the rectum.
Then the Adhvaryu, having divided the speckled butter and poured it into the Juhū ladle, steps across, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the gods! (*devebhyaḥ preṣya*).

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers, saying: "Prompt! Prompt! In this very manner, the assistant offers the portions of the rectum (*guda*), with these eleven [formulas] beginning with: "Go to the ocean, svāhā! Finally, he throws everything after [the fire] with the formula: "Go to Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā!"
Then he wipes his hands on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the formula: "For the waters, for the plants; grant me mind and heart.
Then he gazes at its smoke with the formula: "May I attain body, skin, son, and grandson.

Having performed the eleven after-offerings (*anuyāja*), having stepped across toward the north and placed the *svaru* in the *juhū* ladle, he stands facing west in front [of the altar] and offers it with the formula: "May your smoke go to heaven, your flame to the intermediate space; fill the earth with ashes, *svāhā*!"
Then, having set down the two offering-spoons (*srucau*) in their respective places, he separates them with the two *vājavatī* verses.

Having scattered the *prastara* and the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) together with the *śaṃyu* formula, having poured out the remnants from the spoons, and having released the two spoons, they perform the joint offerings (*saṃyājana*) with the tail of the victim for the wives.
He offers only clarified butter to Soma and Tvaṣṭṛ.
He sacrifices to the wives of the gods with the tail-tendon turned upward; he sacrifices to Agni Gṛhapati with it turned downward;
from the tail-tendon turned upward, he cuts off the *iḍā* for the *hotṛ*.
He hands the six-portioned oblation to the Āgnīdhra from below. They both consume it and perform the ritual purification.

(4.10:125.14) Then, having taken four portions into the *sruva* ladle and turned away by stepping to the left, he offers an expiation on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire and does not proceed with the offering of the husks (*phalīkaraṇa*).

(4.10:125.15) Then, having gone forward to the east and replenished the *dhruvā* vessel, he offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations with the formula: "O sacrifice, go to the sacrifice; go to the lord of the sacrifice; go to your own womb, svāhā!
(4.10:125.17) With the *sruva* ladle itself, he makes a second offering with the formula: "This is your sacrifice, O lord of the sacrifice, accompanied by the *sūktavāka*, rich in heroes, svāhā!"

With the *sruva*-ladle he offers the third oblation, saying: "O gods who know the way, having found the way, go upon the way. O Lord of the Mind, O God, place this sacrifice of ours among the gods, *svāhā*! To Speech, *svāhā*! To the Wind, place it, *svāhā*!
He lifts up the ladle. Then he calls for the wooden sword (*sphya*), the water-vessel, and the heart-spit.
Having taken this up, he says, "Come, O sacrificer!

The sacrificer follows behind, and the wife follows after him. Having gone out toward the north between the *cātvāla* and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), and having dug up the ground in front of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with the wooden sword (*sphya*) and sprinkled it with water, he disposes of the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*) at the junction of dry and moist ground.
(4.11:126.7) “You are the burning pain; burn him who hates us and whom we hate.

(4.11:126.8) Then they purify themselves with water, saying: “From every station, O King, release us from here, O Varuṇa! Since we swear by the waters, the inviolable ones, saying ‘O Varuṇa,’ from that, O Varuṇa, release us.
(4.11:126.9) Then they return without looking back, for the sake of escaping from Varuṇa’s sight.
On the road, they prepare fuel sticks with the formula: "Thou art fuel; may we prosper.
Having arrived, he places them on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "Thou art a kindling-stick; thou art brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me.
Then they pay reverence to the Āhavanīya with the verse: "I have followed after the waters; we have united with their essence. Rich in milk, O Agni, I have come; endow me with splendor."

(4.11:126.14) Then, he burns the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) in the *aupayājika* fire with the mantra: "Whatever debt remains unpaid by me, for which I move about as a tribute to Yama—being right here, I discharge that; thus, O Agni, I become free from that debt.

(4.11:126.16) Then, with his joined palms, he offers parched grain flour (*saktu*), spread with clarified butter and sprinkled over it, into the forest fire (*pradāvya*) with the mantra: "O consumer of all, I offer thee, the consumer of all, *svāhā*!"

He shakes his two hands. He offers the second oblation with: "One has eaten from the cooked, one from the unoffered, one from the shared; may they provide us with healing, a seat, strength, and what is desirable. Then he says: "Whatever debts I have not yet repaid, for which I move about as a tribute to Yama—while remaining right here, we shall discharge them; living, we pay this back to the living, svāhā!"

He shakes his two hands. He offers the third oblation with the verse: "One from what is eaten, one from what is uneaten, one from what is shared—may they provide us with healing, a seat, strength, and that which is desirable.

And: "May we be free from debt in this world, free from debt in the next, and free from debt in the third world. May we overcome all paths—those leading to the gods and those leading to the fathers—being free from debt, svāhā!"

He rubs his hands together with the mantra: "One has eaten from the uneaten, one from the unoffered, and one from the shared portion; may they provide us with healing, a dwelling, strength, and what is desirable.
Then he worships the deities:
with the verse, "May this one come before us through the mist," he worships Agni; with the verse, "O Lord of the mist, do thou [grant] for us," he worships Vāyu.

(4.11:127.8) "O God, thou art the multiplier," [with these words] he worships the sun, and then he worships the sacrificial post [with]: "May I obtain excellent heroism, abundance of wealth, and possession of good horses; established with wealth by Bṛhaspati, as one for whom the Svagā has been pronounced, remain here for me, the sacrificer.
(4.11:127.10) Then he consigns the eastern fire into a wooden splinter [with]: "This is thy seasonal womb."
He throws it into the middle fire with two verses: "Being invoked," and "Awake, O Agni.
Then, having added fuel to the middle fire, he offers a full oblation into the middle fire with the verse: "Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues.
At the full oblation, he gives a choice gift.
"One should give either an excellent cow or an excellent bull," so said Baudhāyana. The animal sacrifice is concluded; the animal sacrifice is concluded.
One is about to sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva oblations on either the full moon day of Phālguna or Caitra.

Some say that the performance should be according to the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). Others say that one should perform it during the northern course of the sun, on an auspicious day of the waxing fortnight.

(5.1:128.3) He prepares a three-striped porcupine quill, a razor of red iron, four potsherds for the sacrificial cakes, four cooking-pots for the oblations, as many stirring-sticks, two portions of milk—one for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) and one for the curdling of the offering—and sacrificial grass tied in three bundles, which are then tied together as one, along with a *prastara* bundle of fresh shoots.
(5.1:128.7) Then, on the day of fasting, he performs the introductory sacrifice (*ārambhaṇīyā-iṣṭi*) consisting of two offerings: a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara and a pap for Parjanya.
That well-known sacrifice comes to a conclusion.
Then, on this day, the calves are driven away for the Viśvedevas;
having caused the milk for the Viśvedevas to be milked—either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* offering or silently—he observes the fast.

Then, in the morning, after the Agnihotra has been offered and before the carrying forward of the waters, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire, purified it, and taken four portions into the offering-spoon, he makes an offering in the Āhavanīya fire while mentally reciting the Pañcahotṛ formula, as the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying: "Svāhā!"

Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers an oblation on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Sarasvatī, a pap for Pūṣan, a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts, curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for the Viśve Devas, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.
At the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he releases his speech.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the pouring [of the grains].
Having poured [the flour] out, he places eight potsherds on the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire.
Then, having brought water across the strainers from the north, he places it over the *caru* for Soma.
Then, to the north, he places twelve potsherds for the offering to Savitṛ.
(5.1:129.1) Then, having poured water across the strainers from the north, he places [the milk] over the fire for the deities Sarasvatī and Pūṣan.
(5.1:129.2) Then, to the north, he arranges seven potsherds for the Maruts.
(5.1:129.2) Then, having poured milk across the strainers from the north, he places it over the fire for the sake of the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*).
(5.1:129.3) Then, on the north side, he places the cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.
(5.1:129.4) They kindle the potsherds;
they kindle the vessels for the cooked rice.
Having poured together the prepared flour and mixed it, he then places upon [the fire] a cake on eight potsherds for Agni.
Having placed the strainer across [the vessel], he pours the sacrificial grains for Soma into it;
then he places upon [the fire] a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ.
(5.1:129.7) He pours the grains for the offerings to Sarasvatī and Pūṣan across the strainers.
(5.1:129.8) Then he places the cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts.
(5.1:129.8) Across the strainers, he pours curds into the heated milk.
There is the *sāṃnāyya* curd-mixture.
Whosoever is skilled should cook it by means of a complete layering of fuel, remove the whey, and place it in a spot not exposed to heat.
Then he places upon it the single-potsherd cake for Heaven and Earth.
Having caused the sacrificial cakes to form a crust, having cooked them, having covered them, having gone eastward, and having poured out water for the Āpyas, he performs the *stambayajus* rite.
This very [procedure] is established as that of the *pauroḍāśika* [section].
He performs it three times with the *yajus* formula and a fourth time silently. He performs the first tracing of the altar.
He mutters the *karaṇa* formula. He digs up [the earth]. From the dug-up spot, the Āgnīdhra carries away [the earth] three times.

When the Āgnīdhra has carried [the earth] three times, then, having performed the second tracing of the altar, having leveled it, and having held the wooden sword (sphya) crosswise, he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the dipping-spoon (sruva) and the offering-ladles (sruc), and [cleanse] the vessel for the speckled butter silently; gird the wife; and bring the clarified butter and the curds."

When the sprinkling waters have been brought, he hands over the wooden sword (*sphya*) for purification, sets down the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmā-barhis*), turns to the right, and having hastened westward, he cleanses the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and the offering-ladles (*sruc*); he cleanses the vessel for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya-grahaṇī*) silently.

He girds the wife, goes out with the clarified butter and the curds, purifies the clarified butter and the sprinkling waters, and having taken the portions of clarified butter together with the speckled butter in the prescribed manner, he stands up with the sprinkling waters.
He sprinkles the fuel.
He sprinkles the altar;
he sprinkles the sacrificial grass (*barhis*);
having sprinkled the sacrificial grass that has been placed down and having poured water over it, he takes up the *prastara* bundle from the front, consisting of fresh shoots.
Having spread the sacrificial grass in three layers, holding the *prastara* bundle in his hand, he steps forward toward the east and lays down the enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood.
He places two upright fuel-sticks and sets down two separating blades crosswise.
On the two *vidhṛtis* he places the *prastara* made of *prasū* grass;
on the *prastara*, the *juhū* ladle;
and the other [ladles] on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

Having touched [the vessels] together with the formula, "These have settled," and having turned to the right and hastened back facing west, he removes the oblations in their proper order: the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), which have been spread with a base of ghee and sprinkled over, and the cooked rice dishes (*caru*), after having sprinkled them with ghee.
This is done in the established manner up to the Marut-oblation.
Then, having drawn out the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) into a bronze vessel or a wooden cup (*camasa*) and having brought the whey (*vājina*), he sprinkles it with ghee.
(5.2:130.13) Then, having removed the cake on one potsherd and having poured much [milk] over it, he makes its back exposed.
(5.2:130.13) Then, having taken hold of these [remains], he places them within the altar with these sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*): "Bhūḥ! Bhuvaḥ! Suvaḥ!
(5.2:130.15) Or he places the whey (*vājina*) either on the rubbish-heap or in the open space.
Then, he proceeds with the fire-drilled fire according to the ritual procedure for the fire-drilled fire,
having cast it forward and offered an oblation.
(5.3:130.17) Then, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says: "Recite for the fire being kindled!
(5.3:130.18) He places the faggot [on the fire] and leaves one fuel-stick remaining.
He fans [the fire] with the Veda. When the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, he pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* spoon;
once it has been wiped clean, he pours the subsequent one with the two *sruk* ladles.
(5.3:130.20) Then, without letting the two ladles touch each other, he steps across toward the north, anoints the *dhruvā* with the *juhū*, sets down the two ladles, and chooses the *pravara*.
(5.3:131.1) He chooses the *hotṛ* in the established manner.
(5.3:131.2) The *hotṛ* sits down.
He awaits the impulse;
once impelled, having taken up the two offering-ladles, stepped across, and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering-verse for the *samidhs*.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation. He offers with the calls "Recite! Recite! while pouring together [the butter] at the fourth and eighth [recitations].
In the eighth [offering], he pours together all [the butter].
Having performed nine fore-offerings (*prayāja*), he steps across to the north and, with the residue of the butter, sprinkles the oblations one after another.
Then he proceeds with the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) for Agni and Soma.
Then he proceeds with the oblations in their proper order. The procedure is well-established up to the *māruta* offering.

With the formula, "Recite for the Viśve Devas; sacrifice to the Viśve Devas," he proceeds with the *āmikṣā*. He proceeds silently with the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) with the formula, "Recite for Heaven and Earth; sacrifice to Heaven and Earth."
(5.3:131.9) Then he proceeds with the offering to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. (5.3:131.9) At this point, he throws these stirring-sticks into the Āhavanīya fire.
(5.3:131.10) Then he makes an oblation over them with the residue of the ghee.
Then, having stepped across toward the north and placed the two ladles in their respective places, he cuts off the *prāśitra* portion and then cuts off the *iḍā* portion.
When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places the sixfold portion for the *agnīdh*.
They consume it and perform the purification.
Then he says, "Carry the *prāśitra* portion around for the Brahman.
They carry the *prāśitra* around.
Following [the *prāśitra*] with water and following it with the *veda*-grass, they carry the Brahman’s portion.
Then he asks for the *anvāhārya* rice;
into it he gives the first-born calf. They remove this sacrificial remnant; they set down the *vājina*.
(5.4:131.17) Then he issues the command: "O Brahman, we shall set forth; O Āgnīdh, having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, cleanse the fires once each.
(5.4:131.18) Then the Adhvaryu, having divided the clotted butter and poured it into the *juhū* ladle, steps across, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, "Sacrifice to the gods!

(5.4:131.19) At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering. Having performed nine after-offerings (*anūyāja*) with the calls, "Sacrifice! Sacrifice!", he steps across to the north, places the two ladles in their respective positions, and separates the two ladles with the two *vājavatī* verses.

Having scattered the prastara-bunch and the enclosing-sticks with the *śaṃyu*-formula, having poured out the remnants from the two ladles, and having released them, he then asks for either a bronze vessel or a wooden cup that has not been smeared with clarified butter.
Having placed it within the altar, while pouring the *vājina* over the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) contained therein, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for the *vājins*."
Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the *vājins*.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering with, "To the *vājins*, svāhā!
Having offered at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* call, he carries away the portion for consumption.

(5.4:132.6) Having sought permission from as many officiating priests as there are, the sacrificer himself consumes [the portion] directly, saying: "Whatever semen of mine is emitted, whatever of mine increases, whatever is produced again, or whatever of mine takes firm root—with that, make me vigorous; with that, make me possessed of semen; with that, enter me auspiciously. Of that which is drunk by the *vājins*, drunk by the *vājins*... or: "Of the honeyed [portion], being invited, I consume it, having been invited."

(5.4:132.11) Then the Adhvaryu, having turned to the right, hastened westward, performed the offerings for the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*), and having gone eastward and replenished the *dhruvā* ladle, he offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations pertaining to the animal sacrifice with the formulas: "O Sacrifice, go to the Sacrifice! This is thy sacrifice, O Lord of Sacrifice! O gods who know the way!
(5.4:132.14) Then, having proceeded with the full-vessel rite and the *viṣṇukrama* steps, he releases his vow.

(5.4:132.15) Then, having performed the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices and having sat down in the sacrificer’s place, he shaves his hair and has it shaved all around with a three-striped porcupine quill and a razor of red metal, [reciting]: “The *ṛta* alone is the Supreme Lord; nothing whatsoever transcends the *ṛta*. Upon the *ṛta* the ocean is established; upon the *ṛta* this earth is supported. Agni with his sharp flame—heat has overcome the *uṣṇihā*.”

"The head has been placed upon the heat by the splendor of Vaiśvānara. By the *ṛta* I turn it back; by the *satya* I turn it around; by the *tapas* I follow it; by the auspicious (*śiva*) I cause it to turn toward me; by the powerful (*śagma*) I cause it to turn toward me. "That is the *ṛta*; that is the *satya*; that is the vow; may I be able to do that; by that may I be able; by that may I prosper. Having first [performed this] in the east, then in the south, then in the west, then in the north, and then from above, the Vaiśvadeva oblations are completed.
"He prays for prosperity lasting a year," thus he prays.
(5.5:133.6) Now, therefore, after four months, he is about to sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa oblations.

He procures a three-striped porcupine quill, a razor of red iron, four sets of potsherds for the sacrificial cakes, five cooking-pots, as many stirring-sticks, two kinds of milk—for the speckled butter and for curd—as well as the curd for seasoning the oblation, *śamī* leaves, flour of parched *karīra* fruit, a winnowing-basket made of reeds, and *karambha*-pots for each person made from barley grains that have been slightly heated and ground without being washed.
There are one extra [animals];
of these, they make one a ewe and one a ram.
The ram has horns, while the ewe is hornless.
The two of them are covered with white woolen threads;
there are two *adhvaryu* priests and two sets of sacrificial vessels.
The fuel and the sacrificial grass are twofold;
there are two altars:
of these, the northern one is like that for the animal sacrifice, and the southern one is like that for the new- and full-moon sacrifices.
These two altars are level behind and uneven in front, separated by a distance of one *pṛtha*.
On this day, two sets of calves are driven away: those for the Maruts and those for Varuṇa.
Having caused the milk of both sets to be milked—either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* or silently—he observes the fast.

Then, in the morning, after the *agnihotra* has been offered, having spread the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and carried forward the waters, he pours out the oblations: "To Agni, a cake on eight potsherds"—thus the five *saṃcara* offerings; "to Indra and Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds; to the Maruts, *āmikṣā*; to Varuṇa, *āmikṣā*; to Ka, a cake on one potsherd.
At the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he releases his speech.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the carrying of fire around the offerings (*paryagnikaraṇa*).

At this point, they carry fire around these *karambha* vessels, the ewe and the ram, the *śamī* leaves, the *karīra* fruits, the parched barley flour, the *aiṣīka* winnowing basket, and the scrapings from the sacrificial cakes.

Having caused the scrapings of the cakes to be taken, having cooked them, and having covered them, he goes eastward; having poured water for them, the two of them carry away the *stambayajus* grass-bunches.
The Adhvaryu carries his away on the northern altar, and the Pratiprasthātṛ on the southern one.
Of those two who are carrying [the oblations], the Adhvaryu goes first; of those returning, the Pratiprasthātṛ goes first.
This is the well-known procedure for the cake-offering (pauroḍāśika):
three times with the sacrificial formula (yajus), and the fourth time silently.
The two [priests] perform the first two enclosures.
The Adhvaryu alone mutters the Karaṇa formula.
It has been dug up.
The Āgnīdhra carries [the earth] three times from the two raised mounds.

When the Āgnīdhra carries it three times, the Adhvaryu, according to the procedure for the *cātvāla*, traces around the *cātvāla*. According to the procedure for the *uttaravedi*, he pours out the *uttaravedi*; having set aside the *uttaranābhi*, they both lead forward the two fires according to the procedure for the fire.
The Adhvaryu, having placed the fire on the northern altar, makes offerings over it with the oblations of the *adhvara*;
the Pratiprasthātṛ, having placed the fire on the southern altar, makes offerings over it silently.

Having performed the two subsequent enclosures while they possess fire, having leveled [the ground], and having fixed two wooden swords (sphya) crosswise, the Adhvaryu alone issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass nearby; cleanse the dipping-spoon (sruva) and the offering-ladles (sruk), and silently [cleanse] the vessel for the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya); gird the wife; and urge [the Agnīdh] regarding the clarified butter and the curds."

When the *prokṣaṇī* waters have been brought, he purifies himself with the two *sphya*s, places the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*) down, turns to the right, and having hastened westward, cleans the two *sruva* spoons and the *sruk* ladles; he silently cleans the *pṛṣadājya* vessel.
He girds the wife’s waist and they are urged on regarding the clarified butter and the curds.
Having purified both the clarified butter and the *prokṣaṇī* waters, the Adhvaryu takes the clarified butter together with the *pṛṣadājya* on the northern altar in the prescribed manner.
The Pratiprasthātṛ performs the rites pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices on the southern altar.
(5.6:135.6) Then they both rise up with the sprinkling waters;
they sprinkle the two fuel bundles; they sprinkle the two altars.
(5.6:135.7) They sprinkle the two bundles of sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
(5.6:135.7) When the two bundles of sacrificial grass have been set down, having sprinkled them and poured water over them, they take up the two *prastara* bundles from the front.
(5.6:135.8) The Adhvaryu spreads the sacrificial grass in five rows on the northern altar.
The Pratiprasthātṛ [places them] in three ways on the southern [altar].

Then, having moved forward with the prastara-bunches in their hands, they lay the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood around [the fires]. They place the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) upright.
He places the two separating blades crosswise; upon the separating blades, the two prastara-bunches;
upon the two prastara-bunches, the two juhū-ladles.
The others [are placed] on the two *barhis* grasses.
Having touched them together with the formula, "These have sat down," and having turned to the right, they run toward the west—the Adhvaryu from the south and the Pratiprasthātṛ from the north.
They remove the sacrificial oblations one after another in order.
The Adhvaryu removes the oblations beginning with those for Agni, in the established manner, up to the one for Indra and Agni.
The Pratiprasthātṛ, having drawn out the curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for the Maruts into a bronze vessel or a wooden cup, places a ewe therein.
Then he scatters into it *śamī* leaves, *karīra* fruits, parched barley flour, and the curdled milk.
Having brought the *vājina* (curd-whey), he then pours it over [the offering].
Likewise, the *adhvaryu* draws out the *āmikṣā* (coagulated milk) into either a bronze vessel or a wooden cup; having done so, he places a ram into it.
Then, for him, he scatters *śamī* leaves, *karīra* fruits, parched barley flour, and *āmikṣā*.
Having brought the *vājina* curds, he then pours ghee over it;
likewise, having removed the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) and brought much [milk] into it, he makes its surface visible.
Then, having grasped these together, they are placed within the altar (*antarvedi*).

The Adhvaryu places the oblations beginning with that for Agni on the northern altar, up to the one for Indra and Agni as is well known; the Pratiprasthātṛ places the offering for the Maruts on the southern altar;
and the Adhvaryu places the offering for Varuṇa and the single-potherd cake for Ka on the northern altar.
In the same way, whether at the *utkara* or in the sacrificial ground (*viśaya*) for the *vājina*,
the Adhvaryu alone proceeds with the rite of the fire churned by friction (*nirmanthya*), having offered the oblation after the fire has been cast [into the hearth].
(5.7:136.11) Then, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says: "Recite for the fire being kindled!
(5.7:136.12) He places two [fuel-sticks] into the fire and leaves two fuel-sticks remaining.
(5.7:136.12) They fan [the fires] with the two Veda-bundles.
(5.7:136.13) When the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, they both pour the two *āghāra* libations with the two *sruva* spoons.
(5.7:136.13) The Adhvaryu alone gives the call: "O Āgnīdhra, wipe the fires thrice each!"
The northern fire has been swept clean, while the southern one remains unswept.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ asks the wife, "Wife, who is your lover?
She replies, "So-and-so."
"May Varuṇa seize him!"—thus he points him out.
"If one does not speak of a paramour who exists, he obstructs a dear kinsman; let him point him out, saying, 'This man is my paramour.
By pointing him out, he causes him to be seized by the noose of Varuṇa"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(5.7:136.19) Having performed the paryagnikaraṇa rite around these *karambha* vessels, he places them together in a winnowing basket made of *aiṣīka* grass and hands them to the wife.
(5.7:137.1) The wife places them upon her head.

Then, having caused her to go out by the southern door and having led her around to the south of the *anvāhāryapacana* fire and around both altars, he leads her eastward and makes her recite: "We invoke the *praghāsya* Maruts, the carriers of the sacrifice, who are well-pleased with the *karambha*."
(5.7:137.4) Then, standing in front of the southern fire facing west— the Adhvaryu on the north, the sacrificer on the south, and the wife on the south—
the wife hands these *karambha* vessels to the sacrificer at this point;
the sacrificer places them upon his head.
Then he recites the invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*).

(5.8:137.8) “O God Indra, do not [forsake] us in battles; O Mighty One, let there be for you a propitiation. For great indeed is the bounty of this Bounteous One; the song of the Maruts, accompanied by oblations, praises him.

(5.8:137.9) Both the sacrificer and his wife recite the *yājyā*: “Whatever sin we have committed in the village, whatever in the forest, whatever in the assembly, whatever in our sensory power, whatever toward a Śūdra, whatever toward an Ārya, whatever against the law of another—for all that, you are the expiation, Svāhā!
(5.8:137.12) At this point, he throws this winnowing-basket made of reeds into the fire.
Alternatively, they eat after sprinkling [the food] with water.

As they disperse, the Adhvaryu consecrates them with the mantra: "The performers of the rite have performed the rite, together with the joy-bestowing speech. Having performed the rite for the gods, go home, O bounteous ones.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ cleanses the southern fire.
Both [priests] pour the two libations with the offering-ladles (*sruc*).
The Adhvaryu alone chooses the *pravara* (the invocation of the ancestral lineage);
he chooses the Hotṛ in the established manner.

The Hotṛ sits down, awaiting the impulse; when the impulse is given, having taken up the two offering-spoons, having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Recite the offering prayer for the *samidhs*."
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, they both offer, saying "Sacrifice! Sacrifice! while drawing together the butter at the fourth and eighth offerings.
At the eighth offering, the adhvaryu draws it all together, while the pratiprasthātṛ retains the residue for the after-offerings (*anūyāja*s).
Having performed nine fore-offerings (*prayāja*) and stepped across to the north, the two of them sprinkle the oblations in order with the remnants of the butter.
The Adhvaryu sprinkles those beginning with the offering to Agni, up to the one for Indra and Agni in the established manner;
the Pratiprasthātṛ sprinkles the offering to the Maruts.
The Adhvaryu [offers] the oblation to Varuṇa and a cake on one potsherd to Ka; then they proceed with the two portions of clarified butter for Agni and Soma.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ desists.
(5.8:138.6) Then the adhvaryu proceeds with the oblations in their proper order, [starting] from the one for Indra and Agni according to the established rule.
(5.8:138.7) Then the adhvaryu stops.
(5.8:138.7) Then the pratiprasthātṛ, while cutting portions from the offering for the Maruts, says: "Recite the invitatory verse for the Maruts!"
With the first portion he takes portions of the *śamī* leaves, the *karīra* fruits, the parched grain, and the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*).
With the second portion he places the *śamī* leaves, the *karīra* fruits, the parched grain, the curd-mixture, and the ewe.
He then pours clarified butter over them.
He anoints [the offering]. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the Maruts.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ desists.
Then the Adhvaryu, while taking portions from the oblation for Varuṇa, says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Varuṇa!
With the first portion, he takes portions of the *śamī* leaves, the juice of the *karīra* fruit, and the flour of parched grain, as well as from the *āmikṣā*.
With the second portion, he places the *śamī* leaf, the *karīra* fruit, the parched barley flour, the curdled milk (*āmikṣā*), and the ram;
he sprinkles them with clarified butter and anoints them in return.
Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sacrifice to Varuṇa.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering.
He proceeds with the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), saying, "Recite the invitatory verse for Ka," and "Sacrifice to Ka."
(5.8:138.16) Then they proceed with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
(5.8:138.16) The Adhvaryu cuts portions from the oblations beginning with that for Agni, while the portion from the one for Indra and Agni is well known;
(5.8:138.17) the Pratiprasthātṛ [cuts] from the one for the Maruts.
The Adhvaryu twice pours clarified butter over the vessel for Varuṇa and the cake on one potsherd from the *āśaya* vessel;
he does not rub them back.
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, they offer [the oblations] in the eastern part of the northern half, bypassing the previous offerings.
At this point, they throw these stirring-sticks (*mekṣaṇa*) into the two Āhavanīya fires.
(5.8:139.4) Then he makes offerings over them with the two *saṃsrāva* ladles.
(5.8:139.5) Then, having stepped across toward the north and set down the offering-ladles in their respective places, he cuts off the *prāśitra* portion and then cuts off the *iḍā* portion.
(5.8:139.6) The Adhvaryu cuts off portions starting from those for Agni; the procedure up to the one for Indra and Agni is well-established.
The Pratiprasthātṛ [pours butter] over the portion for Māruta,
the Adhvaryu over the portion for Vāruṇī, and over the cake on one potsherd from its receptacle;
he then pours [butter] over them.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ approaches the northern altar.
When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places the sixfold portion for the *agnīdh*. They consume it and perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*).
(5.9:139.11) Then he says, "Carry the *prāśitra* portion around for the Brahman.
(5.9:139.11) They carry the *prāśitra* around.
(5.9:139.12) Following the water, they follow the Brahman’s portion with the *veda*.
(5.9:139.12) Then he asks for the *anvāhārya* rice; into that he gives according to his faith. (5.9:139.13) They remove this sacrificial remnant.
They set down the *vājina* [curds].
The Adhvaryu alone gives the call: "O Brahman, we shall proceed; having placed the fuel-stick, O Āgnīdh, cleanse the fires once each.
Then the Adhvaryu, having divided the speckled butter and poured it into the *juhū* ladle, having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, says: "Sacrifice to the gods!"

When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, they both offer, saying, "Sacrifice! Sacrifice! Having performed the nine after-offerings (*anūyāja*s), they step across toward the north, set down the two ladles (*sruk*) in their respective places, and separate the ladles with the two *vājavatī* verses.

Having scattered the *prastara* and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) together with the *śaṃyu* formula, having poured out the remnants, and having released the ladles, they likewise ask for two vessels—either bronze bowls (*kaṃsa*) or cups (*camasa*)—that have not been smeared with clarified butter.
The performance of the two *vājina* offerings is identical.

The Adhvaryu alone, having turned to the right, hastened westward, performed the *saṃyāja* offerings for the wives, returned eastward, replenished the *dhruvā* ladle, and offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations pertaining to the animal sacrifice.
The Pratiprasthātṛ offers one, pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices, on the southern side.
(5.9:140.8) Then, having performed the rites of the full vessel and the Viṣṇu-strides, he does not release his vow.
(5.9:140.9) Then he requests: a vessel of clarified butter together with the dipping-spoon, a ladle, sacrificial grass, two garments for wearing, the remnants of the offering to Varuṇa, and husks.
(5.9:140.10) Having taken all this, he says: "Come, O sacrificer!"
The sacrificer follows behind, and the wife follows after him; having gone out northward between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), they go to where there is water.
The purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) is performed in the established manner, but he does not recite the *Sāman*, nor the verse: "O divine waters, this is your embryo."
(5.9:140.13) Then they go forward without looking back, for concealment from Varuṇa.
(5.9:140.14) On the way, they prepare fuel-sticks, saying: "You are fuel; may we prosper.
(5.9:140.15) Having arrived, he places them on the Āhavanīya fire, saying: "You are a kindling-stick; you are brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me."
Then they pay reverence to the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "I have followed the waters; we have united with their essence. Rich in milk, O Agni, I have come; unite me with splendor.
At this point, he releases his vow.

(5.9:141.1) Then, having performed the Full Moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices and sitting in the sacrificer’s place, he shaves his hair and has it trimmed all around with a three-striped porcupine quill and a razor of red-hot iron, [reciting]: "When Gharma turned back the ends of the earth and of heaven; Agni, ruling by his might, Varuṇa together with his prayers, Indra with his friends the Maruts. Agni with his sharp flame, the heat, the *uṣṇih* that has overcome."

"The heat has been placed upon the head by the splendor of Vaiśvānara. By means of *ṛta* I turn it back; by means of *satya* I turn it around; by means of *tapas* I follow it; by means of what is auspicious (*śiva*) I turn it toward [me]; by means of what is beneficial (*śagma*) I turn it hither. "That is the *ṛta*; that is the *satya*; that is the vow (*vrata*); may I be able to do that; through that may I be able; through that may I prosper. Thus [he recites] first in the east, then in the south, then in the west, then in the north, and then from above.
The Varuṇapraghāsa oblations are concluded;
he pronounces the blessing: "He invokes the well-being of the year. Thus he invokes.

(5.10:141.12) Now, therefore, after four months, he becomes one who is about to sacrifice with the Sākamedha oblations. He procures a three-striped porcupine quill, a razor of red iron, four sets of potsherds for the sacrificial cakes, four cooking-pots, as many stirring-sticks, and curds for the speckled butter.
Then, on the fast-day of the full moon, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Anīkavant, together with the rising sun.
That well-known sacrifice is completed.
Then, at midday, he offers a caru-oblation to the Maruts Sāṃtapanas;
that well-known sacrifice is completed.
Now, on this day, the calves are driven away from their mothers for the Maruts Gṛhamedhins.

Then, after the evening Agnihotra has been offered, having cooked the Gṛhamedhīya caru-oblation in the milk of all the cows over the Gārhapatya fire, he pours clarified butter over it and removes it toward the north.
Then, having washed that vessel and spread a layer of ghee in it, he draws the oblation into it as if without striking it.
Having prepared a vessel for pouring the clarified butter and having brought a large quantity of *ājya*, he places it within the *vedī*.
Then he proceeds with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings for Agni and Soma.
Then, having spread an underlayer of butter, while taking a portion from the eastern half of the *caru*, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhins."
Having cut a portion from the eastern half, he cuts a portion from the western half;
he pours clarified butter over it and anoints it back.
Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhins.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation.
Then he proceeds with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
The Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice concludes with the *iḍā*.
He leaves behind the residue of the charred crust for the sake of the full ladle.
They cook the neighbor's portion for the women and children.
They have eaten their fill;
they anoint themselves;
they smear themselves with unguents.
They let the calves stay with their mothers;
on this very night, they bind the calf of two cows that share the same womb.
Then, at the approach of the latter part of the night, the Adhvaryu hastens there and offers the Agnihotra oblation with the milk from a cow that has her calf with her.
Then, having cleansed this ladle and spread a base of ghee in it, he places all of that charred scrap into it;
he pours ghee over it twice.
Then he recites the invitatory verse: "O ladle, fly away full; fly back again well-filled. Let us trade like merchandise, O Lord of a Hundred Powers, for food and strength."
He sacrifices with: "Give to me; I give to thee; bestow upon me; I bestow upon thee; bring to me what is brought; I bring to thee what is brought—svāhā!
He should sacrifice at the bellowing of a bull with: "O bull, come!
This other [formula], "The *hiṃ*-utterance of Brahman," is also [an option].
He offers in the *gārhapatya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying: "Svāhā!

Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on seven potsherds to the sporting Maruts at the time when the sun has risen; that sacrifice is concluded in the established manner.

Then, at that very time, having spread the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he pours out [the oblations]: "To Agni, a cake on eight potsherds"—thus five *saṃcara* offerings; "To Indra-Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds; to Indra, a pap; to Viśvakarman, a cake on one potsherd.
Having caused the cakes to form a crust, having baked them, having covered them, having gone eastward, and having poured out water for the *āpyas*, he performs the *stambayajus* rite.
This is the well-known procedure according to the *Pauroḍāśika* section.
Three times with the *yajus* formula and a fourth time silently; he performs the first tracing of the altar and mutters the *karaṇa* formula.
He digs up [the earth]. From the dug-up spot, the Āgnīdhra carries it away three times.
When the Āgnīdhra has carried it away three times, he then traces around the *cātvāla* pit according to the procedure for the *cātvāla*.
Following the procedure for the *uttaravedi*, he pours out the earth for the *uttaravedi*.

Having raised the *uttaranābhi*, he leads forward the fire according to the procedure for the fire. Having performed the second tracing around [the altar] while it contains the fire, having leveled it, and having held the wooden sword (*sphya*) crosswise, he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*) nearby; cleanse the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and the offering-ladles (*sruc*); silently [cleanse] the vessel for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*); gird the wife; and bring the clarified butter and the curds."

When the sprinkling waters have been brought, he wipes the wooden sword (*sphya*), sets down the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmā-barhis*), turns to the right, and having hastened westward, he cleanses the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and the offering-ladles (*sruc*); he cleanses the vessel for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) silently.
He girds the wife, and having come forward with the clarified butter and the curds, and having purified the clarified butter and the sprinkling waters, [the rite] proceeds in the established manner.
It concludes in the same way as the Vaiśvadeva oblations, except for the whey-offering (*vājina*).
Then, having performed the rites with the full vessel and the Viṣṇu-strides, he does not release his vow.

(5.11:143.17) Intending to perform the Mahāpitṛyajña, he prepares rice and barley, six potsherds, the milk of a cow that suckles another's calf, a half-vessel, two new vessels, a stalk of sugarcane, three leaf-cups, sacrificial grass with its roots, a larger kindling-wood bundle than the usual *idhma*, the enclosing sticks from the *idhma*, a mattress and pillow, ointment and unguent, a fringe of cloth, the wooden sword (*sphya*), two water-pitchers, and the sacrificial implements.
(5.11:143.20) Then he strews grass around the Gārhapatya fire.
To the north of that, he places each item separately: the cushion and the pillow, the ointment and the salve, the fringe, the wooden sword, the two water-jars, and the sacrificial implements.
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder and sat down to the north of the Gārhapatya fire, he pours out the oblation with the Agnihotra-ladle containing the strainers, [reciting]:
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out, acceptable to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs. Thus he pours out four handfuls of rice.
Having performed this same introductory formula, he offers four portions of barley with the words: "I offer what is pleasing to the Pitṛs seated on the sacrificial grass.
Having performed this same introductory formula, he offers four portions of barley with the words: "I offer what is pleasing to the Pitṛs consumed by fire.
For these, he causes the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*) to be raised over the rice alone.
They gather the barley; he releases his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*); the ritual procedure is the same up to the pouring over (*adhivapana*).
Having poured [the grains] out, he places six potsherds on the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire-altar.

Then, having pounded these barley grains in a mortar and having placed a single potsherd on the Gārhapatya, they roast them; having made the parched grains (*dhānā*) multiform, half of those grains remain.
Then they prepare the other parched grains (*saktu*). Having poured together the prepared and ground flour and mixed it, he places upon it a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) on six potsherds.

Then, having drawn out embers mixed with ashes toward the north and placed a new vessel upon them, he pours clarified butter across the strainer and, across the strainer, scatters the roasted grains (*dhānā*).
Then he asks for half a vessel of milk from the cow that suckles her calf;
having poured groats into it across a strainer, he stirs it with a single cane-stick,
stirring toward the south.
"He stirs it without beginning," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, having drawn out embers mixed with ashes to the north and placed [the vessel] upon them,
and having caused the skin of the sacrificial cake to form and covered it, he pours [the water] right here for the aquatic beings.
To the south, this level sacrificial mound has been prepared;
there he merely draws out this square altar, but does not dig it.
Having kindled the Anvāhāryapacana fire in the middle of it, he performs the Stambayajus rite.
This very procedure is established according to the *Pauroḍāśika* [Kalpa].
He performs it three times with the *yajus* formula and the fourth time silently.
He performs the first tracing of the altar.
He mutters the Karaṇa formula. He digs up [the earth]. From the dug-up spot, the Āgnīdhra carries away [the earth] three times.

When the Āgnīdhra has carried [the earth] three times, [the Adhvaryu], having performed the second tracing of the altar, having leveled it, and having held the wooden sword (sphya) crosswise, issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters! Place the fuel and the sacrificial grass (idhmābarhis) nearby! Clean the dipping-spoon (sruva) and the offering-ladles (sruk)! Come forth with the clarified butter!

Once the sprinkling waters have been brought, he throws away the wooden sword, purifies himself, places the fuel and the sacrificial grass nearby, turns to the right, hastens back toward the west, and cleans the dipping-spoon and the offering-ladles.

He rises with clarified butter; having purified both the clarified butter and the sprinkling water, and having taken the clarified butter in five or six ladlings in the established manner, he stands up with the sprinkling water.
He sprinkles the fuel and he sprinkles the altar.
He sprinkles the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass that has been placed down and having poured water over it, he silently takes up the *prastara* bundle from the front, including its roots.
Then, having arranged the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), he goes around three times, strewing [the grass] counter-clockwise.
(5.12:145.16) First, more closely together;
(5.12:145.16) then further apart;
(5.12:145.16) then further apart.
Then, having placed the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, he goes around three times again in the opposite direction.
Then, holding the *prastara* grass-bundle in his hand, he lays down two enclosing sticks— the middle one and the southern one— and places two fuel-sticks upright.
He places the two *vidhṛti* grass-blades crosswise.
Upon the two *vidhṛtis*, he silently lays down the *prastara* bundle together with its roots.
Upon the *prastara*, he places the *juhū* ladle.

Having touched the two *barhis* blades with the formula, "These have sat down," he turns to the right, hastens back facing west, and takes down the oblations in order: the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) which has been spread with a base of ghee and sprinkled over, the parched grains (*dhānāḥ*), and the groat-mash (*karambha*).
Of these, they take them up one by one, following the sequence.
He places the sacrificial cake to the south;
the parched grains to the north;
and the groat-mash to the north.
To the south, he places this enclosure, a cushion and a pillow, ointment and oil for anointing, a fringe, and the wooden sword (sphyam).
To the north are two water-pitchers.
The Brahman and the sacrificer sit to the south, while the Adhvaryu and the Āgnīdhra sit to the north.
(5.13:146.9) Then, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says: "Recite for Agni, for the gods, for the fathers, as he is being kindled.
(5.13:146.10) He places the faggot [on the fire] either once or thrice; he leaves one fuel-stick remaining.
He fans [the fire] with the Veda. When the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, he pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* spoon;
once it has been wiped clean, he pours the subsequent one with the two *sruc* ladles.

(5.13:146.12) Then, without letting the two offering-spoons touch each other, having stepped across toward the north and having anointed the *dhruvā* with the *juhū*, and having set down the two spoons, he chooses the *pravara*.

(5.13:146.13) Then he causes the announcement: "O, cause [the Āgnīdhra] to hear! "Let there be hearing! "May the divine Agni, the Hotṛ, sacrifice to the gods and the Pitṛs; sit down!"—this much is the *pravara*.
(5.13:146.15) The Hotṛ sits down.
He awaits the impulse;
once impelled, having taken up the two offering-spoons, stepped across, and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering-verse for the *samidhs*";
when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation.

Having offered four fore-offerings (*prayāja*) excluding the one for the *barhis* grass with the call "Sacrifice! Sacrifice!", he steps across to the north and pours the residue of the oblation over the sacrificial offerings in their proper order.

Then he proceeds with the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) for Agni and Soma. Then, having stepped across to the north and placed the two offering-spoons (*sruk*) in their respective places, they arrange themselves with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*).
These officiating priests move around;
they transpose the oblations.
He places the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) to the north.
To the south is the *karambha* [gruel]; the parched grains (*dhānā*) are placed on the seat itself. To the north sit the Brahman and the sacrificer; to the south, the Adhvaryu and the Āgnīdhra.
(5.13:147.6) Then they enclose it. (5.13:147.6) They make its door face north.
(5.13:147.7) He says to one who is strong: "Go around [the fire] three times from right to left, sprinkling with this water-pitcher in a continuous stream."
He does so;
having set down the pitcher, he circumambulates it three times again in the same manner as before.
Then, having spread an underlayer of ghee, while taking a portion from the eastern half of the sacrificial cake, he says:
"Recite the *anuvaṣaṭ* for Soma accompanied by the ancestors, *svadhā*!"— with these words,
he cuts a portion from the eastern half of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and from the eastern half of the parched grains (*dhānā*).
From the eastern half of the *karambha*,
he pours clarified butter over it and then anoints it back.
Having taken the portion from the south, he steps across toward the north.
He calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* with "O Svadhā!
The response is given with "Let there be Svadhā!"
"Make the Soma for the ancestors with the *svadhā* call," he says.
"Those who [offer] *svadhā*" is the *āgūr*; or "those for whom we offer *svadhā*";
with "Svadhā! Homage! he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.

Then, having spread an underlayer of ghee, while taking a portion from the middle of the parched grains (*dhānā*), he says: "For the Fathers seated on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad*), [say] *svadhā*!
He takes a portion from the middle of the parched grains.
From the middle of the *karambha* and from the middle of the *puroḍāśa*,
he pours clarified butter over them.
He anoints [the offering]. Having cut off the portion from the south, he steps across toward the north.
He causes the announcement to be made with: "Oṃ! Svadhā!"
"Let there be *svadhā*," he responds. "Make *svadhā* for the *pitṛ*s seated on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad*)," [the Adhvaryu says].
"Those to whom *svadhā* [belongs]," is the *āgūr*; or, "We invoke those to whom *svadhā* [belongs]."
"svadhā namaḥ"—with these words he pronounces the *vaṣaṭ* call;
when the *vaṣaṭ* has been pronounced, he makes the offering.
Then, having spread an underlayer of ghee, while cutting off a portion of the *karambha* from the rear half, he says: "For the *agniṣvātta* fathers, svadhā!"
He cuts a portion from the rear half of the *karambha*;
from the rear half of the *puroḍāśa*; and from the rear half of the parched grains.
He pours clarified butter over it,
anoints it back,
and having cut off a portion from the south, he steps across toward the north.
"O Svadhā!"—thus he causes the announcement to be made.
"Let there be Svadhā!"—thus he responds.
"Make the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs [the offering] Svadhā!"—thus [he says].
With the exclamation "Ye svadhā," or "We offer svadhā," or "Svadhā,
obeisance," he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call;
when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering.
(5.14:148.12) Then, having spread an underlayer of ghee, while cutting a portion from the southern half of the sacrificial cake, he says: "For Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, [pronounce] *anu svadhā*!
(5.14:148.13) He cuts a portion from the southern half of the sacrificial cake, and from the southern half of the parched grains.
From the southern half of the *karambha*,
he pours clarified butter over it twice;
he does not anoint it back.
Having made the portioning from the south, he steps across toward the north.
He causes the announcement to be made with "O! Svadhā!
The response is given with "Let there be Svadhā!"
(5.14:148.16) “Make Agni Kavyavāhana the Sviṣṭakṛt; pronounce *svadhā*!”—thus [the Adhvaryu says].
(5.14:148.17) “Those to whom *svadhā* [belongs],” is the *āgūḥ*; or “We offer *svadhā* to those,” is the *āgūḥ*.
(5.14:148.18) He utters the *vaṣaṭ* with “*Svadhā namaḥ*!”
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering in the eastern part of the southern half, passing over the previous offerings.
At this point, he throws that stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) and the splinter (*śalākā*) into the fire. Then he pours the remnants of the oblation (*saṃsrāva*) over them.

Then, having stepped across to the south and placed the two offering-spoons (*srucau*) in their respective places, they put on their sacred threads (*yajñopavītāni*). These officiating priests (*ṛtvijas*) move around;
they transpose the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*).
(5.14:148.22) He places the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) to the south. (5.14:149.1) To the north, he places the groats (*karambha*); the parched grains (*dhānā*) remain in the vessel itself.
The Brahman and the sacrificer sit to the south, while the Adhvaryu and the Āgnīdhra sit to the north. Then, having cut off the *prāśitra* portion, he cuts off the *iḍā* portion.
When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places the sixfold portion for the *agnīdh*.
Having consumed it with the *nighra*, they set it down on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), he mixes together the sacrificial cake, the parched grains, and the groats in a vessel.
He places three balls of food upon the three corners of the leaf-enclosures:

on the southern hip with the formula, “This for you, O father, [Name], and those who follow you”; and on the right shoulder with the formula, “This for you, O grandfather, [Name], and those who follow you.”

(5.15:149.9) “This for you, O great-grandfather, N.N., and those who follow you,” he says over the northern shoulder. (5.15:149.10) He wipes the smear on the northern hip, saying: “This is yours, this is ours; may we, living and alive, follow along after this [lineage].”

Having said, "O Fathers, rejoice here according to your portions," they go out toward the north, put on their sacred threads over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*), and worship the *Āhavanīya* fire with the verses: "O Maghavan, may we gladden thee who art fair to behold; now indeed, O thou whose chariot-seat is full, being praised, thou goest according to thy will; yoke now, O Indra, thy two bay steeds.
They worship until the fire goes out.

Then they pay homage to the Gārhapatya fire with the verse: "They have eaten, for they have rejoiced; they have shaken off their dear [impurities]. The self-luminous inspired ones have praised you with a most recent hymn. Now, O Indra, yoke your two bay steeds! (TS 1.8.5.1d).
They continue to pay homage until the fire goes out.

Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), they approach the *Anvāhāryapacana* fire, reciting: "The fathers have eaten; the fathers have rejoiced; the fathers have been satisfied; the fathers have cleansed themselves. Depart, O Soma-loving fathers! (5.15:150.5). They remain standing there until the fire goes out. Then he says to one who is strong: "Go around [the fire] three times from right to left, sprinkling a continuous stream of water with this water-pitcher."
He does so;
having set down the jar, he circumambulates it three times again in the same direction.
He gives him a mattress and a pillow, as well as collyrium and ointment, as if for the pleasure of bringing them back.
Then he gives garments.
Then he worships with six salutations in reverse order.
Then he asks for a hero.
(5.15:150.10) Then, having raised them up and led them away, he invokes the mind with three verses: "We summon the mind hither; may our mind return to us again; O fathers, [give] us back our mind.
(5.15:150.11) At this point, he throws these rice-balls together with the leaf-cups into the fire.
(5.15:150.12) They dismantle the enclosure.
(5.15:150.13) Then they put on their sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*).
(5.15:150.13) Then he issues the command: "O Brahman, we shall set forth; O Āgnīdh, having placed a fuel-stick (*samidh*) on the fire, cleanse the fires once each.
(5.15:150.14) Then, taking the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, stepping across, and having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Sacrifice to the two gods! (*devau yaja*).
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.

Having performed two after-offerings (*anūyāja*) without the *barhis* grass while saying "Sacrifice! Sacrifice!", he steps across to the north, places the two ladles (*srucau*) in their respective positions, and separates the two ladles with the two *vājavatī* verses.

Having scattered the *prastara* and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) together with the *śaṃyu* formula, having poured out the remnants from the ladles, and having released the ladles, he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* right here.
(5.15:151.1) Now they recite two [verses] each for these *śastra*s.

(5.15:151.1) Then, having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*), they worship the *gārhapatya* fire with the verse addressed to Prajāpati: "O Prajāpati, none other than you [has encompassed] these...
(5.15:151.3) At this point, he mutters this second [verse]: "That which is the intermediate space, the earth, and the sky..."
The Mahāpitṛyajña is concluded.

While the Adhvaryu is busy there, the Pratiprasthātṛ bakes the *traiyambaka* cakes on single potsherds—one for each person plus one extra—on the Gārhapatya fire. Having baked them, he removes them without pouring clarified butter over them and sets them aside in a vessel, a pan, or the hollow of an old leather bag, and then waits.
Then he asks for two threads, blue and red, the last leaf [of the *parṇa* tree], a firebrand from the edge of the house, and a water-pot.

Having taken this [fuel], they pay homage to the *gārhapatya* fire with the words: "As many as we are who belong to the household, for them I have performed [this rite]. You are the shelter of cattle; you are the shelter of the sacrificer; grant me shelter.
Then, having gone out toward the north, they proceed in that direction where a well-known, permanent crossroads exists;
or, if such one does not exist, they depart by means of a cart or a chariot.

Having kindled this single firebrand and strewn grass around it, he takes a single portion from each of all the *traiyambaka* cakes upon the edge of a *parṇa* leaf and offers them with the formula: "Rudra is indeed one; he does not stand for a second. The rat is your animal, O Rudra; accept it! This, O Rudra, is your share, together with your sister Ambikā; accept it! A remedy for the cow, for the horse, a remedy for man, and also a remedy for us—a good remedy!"

"Just as [it was] for the ram and the ewe, so may we ward off Rudra, O Mother; ward off the god Tryambaka. So that he may make us better, so that he may make us wealthier, so that he may make us possess cattle, so that he may cause us to prosper—Svāhā!
At this point, he throws this final leaf into the path of the cattle of one whom he hates;
however, if he does not hate anyone, he throws it into a molehill.
Then he hands out one of these *traiyambaka* cakes to each of the officiants and two to the sacrificer.

Then they walk three times around this fire from left to right, striking their right thighs, [reciting]: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity; like a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from death, not from immortality. Having walked around once, they stand to the north.
They dig it up with the formula, "For Bhaga thee! and they desire to obtain it.
In this very same way, they go around a second time.
In this same way, he performs it a third time.

Then she, desiring a husband, walks around three times counter-clockwise, striking her left thigh, [reciting]: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the bringer of a husband; like a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from here, not fall [into misfortune].
Having walked around once, she stands facing the north.
He digs it up with the words, "For Bhaga, thee! and thus he desires to obtain it.
In this very same manner, he goes around a second time.
In this manner, he does so a third time; then he pours them into the joined palms of the sacrificer.

"‘I unite you with offspring, as one unites surā with *māsara*’—with these words, the sacrificer pours them into the joined palms of his wife. ‘I unite you with offspring and cattle, as one unites surā with *māsara*’—with these words, the wife pours them into the hands of her daughter who desires fortune (*bhaga*), saying: ‘I unite you with fortune, as one unites surā with *māsara*’."

(5.17:153.1) Then, having placed them in a sack and tied them with two threads, one blue and one red, he fastens them to a dry stump or to a forked branch [of a tree], saying: "This, O Rudra, is your portion; enjoy it. With this favor, pass beyond the Mūjavat mountains, with your bow unstrung, the Pināka in hand, clothed in a skin.
(5.17:153.4) They remain standing there until the embers have gone out.
(5.17:153.5) Then, having poured the water together and cast aside the vessel, they return without looking back.
Having washed his hands and feet, he returns by the same way he came and, having returned, offers a *caru* oblation to Āditya.
"Aditi is indeed this [earth]; it is upon her that they find firm support," so says the Brāhmaṇa. That sacrifice concludes in the established manner.
(5.17:153.8) Here he releases his vow.

Then, having performed the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices, he sits down in the sacrificer’s place and, with a three-striped porcupine quill and a razor of red iron, he has the hair on his head cut short and shaved all around, [reciting]: “He who turned this great earth around according to the seasons; he who, upon the skin of this earth, causes the plants to grow—Agni, ruling by his might, Varuṇa together with his prayers, Indra with his friends the Maruts.”

With a sharp flame, Agni, burn the heat that has seized the *uṣṇih* [head]. The head is placed upon the heat by the splendor of Vaiśvānara. By the cosmic order (*ṛta*) I turn it back; by truth (*satya*) I turn it around; by austerity (*tapas*) I follow it; with auspiciousness (*śiva*) I turn it toward me; with power (*śagma*) I turn it hither. Of the head...

"That is the cosmic order (*ṛta*); that is the truth (*satya*); that is the vow (*vrata*). May I be able to accomplish that; may I be able by means of that; may I prosper through that. Having first [recited this] in the east, then in the south, then in the west, then in the north, and then above, the *Sākamedha* oblations are completed.
"He invokes the well-being of the coming year," thus he invokes.
(5.18:153.20) Now, therefore, after four months, he is about to sacrifice with the Śunāsīrīya oblations.

(5.18:154.1) He procures a three-striped porcupine quill, a razor of red copper, five sets of potsherds for the sacrificial cakes, five vessels for the cooked rice offerings, as many stirring-sticks, and curds for the speckled butter.
(5.18:154.3) Then, on this night, the calves are driven away from their mothers for Vāyu.
In the morning, he causes the milk for Vāyu to be milked either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* or silently.

Then, after the morning *agnihotra* has been offered, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he pours out the oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, and so forth—the five *saṃcara* offerings; a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra-Agni; a pap for the Viśve Devas; a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra Śunāsīra; the milk for Vāyu; and a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya.
Having caused the sacrificial cakes to take on their crusts, having cooked them, and having covered them, he goes eastward, pours out water for the Āpyas, and performs the *stambayajus* rite.
This is the well-known procedure pertaining to the sacrificial cakes (*pauroḍāśika*).
He recites the formula three times and performs the fourth time silently.
He performs the first tracing around;
he mutters the *karaṇa* formula;
he digs up [the earth].
The Āgnīdhra carries [the earth] three times from the dug-out place.
If he prepares the *uttaravedi*, the rite is concluded in the same manner as the *mahāhavīṃṣi*;
but if he does not prepare the *uttaravedi*, it is concluded in the same manner as the *vaiśvadevahavīṃṣi*, with the exception of the *vājina* offering.
(5.18:154.14) Then, having performed the rites of the full-vessel and the Viṣṇu-strides, he releases his vow.

(5.18:154.15) Then, having sacrificed with the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha offerings, he sits down in the sacrificer’s place and, with a three-striped porcupine quill and a razor of red metal, he shaves the hair on the crown of his head and has the rest of his hair shaved all around, [reciting]: "The Supreme Lord released one month for the sake of creatures; thereby he brought great bounty to them—immortality to mortals. You are born after your offspring; that indeed is your immortality among mortals."

By which [the months, the half-months, the seasons, and the years were turned back]; by which, O Prajāpati, they turned back those [limbs] of yours while you were sacrificing—by that sacred word (*brahman*) do I turn this [head] back for the sake of living. Agni with his sharp flame, the *uṣṇih* meter has overcome the heat; the head is placed upon the heat.

By the splendor of Vaiśvānara, by *ṛta* I turn it back for him, by *satya* I turn it around for him, by *tapas* I follow it for him, by the auspicious I bring it near for him, by the powerful I turn it toward for him. [Of the head...]

“That is the cosmic order; that is the truth; that is the vow. May I be able to accomplish it; may I be able through it; may I prosper through it. Having first [recited this] in the east, then in the south, then in the west, then in the north, and then from above, the Śunāsīrīya oblations are completed.
“He invokes the well-being of the year-long cycle,” thus he invokes.

One who is about to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma procures a black antelope skin, a black antelope horn, a garment, and a girdle; this girdle is made of broad braided hair, threefold and with a single loop on one side. He also procures twenty-two bunches of *darbha* grass, fresh butter, collyrium, a reed-shaft with its tuft intact, a staff of *udumbara* wood, a wooden cup (*camasa*), and a vessel for the offering of the vow-food (*vrata*) together with a sling and a stirring-stick.
These are the thirteen items for the sacrificer.

An equal number of items are placed on both sides of the wife: a water-pot (*kumba*), a head-net (*kurīra*), a garment, a girdle, and an unlimited number of bundles of *darbha* grass; furthermore, fresh butter, collyrium, a reed with its tuft, a vessel made of clay, a wooden pin, and a cooking-pot provided with a sling and a stirring-ladle.

A sacrificial hall has been constructed on a site for the sacrifice that is pleasing to the gods. One should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice on a site for the sacrifice where the oblation is offered first; he should choose whichever of these [sites] he prefers.
The sacrificial hall has its ridge-pole facing east, with openings on all sides, and it is higher toward the south.
They construct four doors for it: facing east, south, west, and north.
To the south they construct the fire-hall for cooking the ritual fast-food (*vrata*), and behind it the women’s quarters (*patnīśāla*).
Now, if the water-place is at a distance, they construct two straw-covered enclosures to the north of the hall— the eastern one for the sacrificer and the western one for his wife—
and they provide two doors facing east in them;
there he causes two water-jars to be placed.
(6.1:156.15) Then, having sacrificed with either the new-moon oblation or under an auspicious constellation, he consigns the fires into the two kindling woods and proceeds toward the hall.

(6.1:156.17) Having gone around the north side of the hall and entered it by the eastern door, he churns the fire in the hearth of the Gārhapatya, spreads the fires, and they tie up the King Soma upon the central beam; they then strew grass around it.
The Brahman and the sacrificer sit down to the south.

Then, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the *sruva* ladle, he offers it into the Āhavanīya fire with the mind reciting the *Saptahotṛ* formula while the sacrificer maintains contact [with him], saying: "Svāhā!
Having taken another four portions, he offers the oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*), if he performs this offering at this point.
In the forenoon itself, they tie up the two calves of the two cows that provide the sacrificial food.
Then he has the food for the commencement of the vow cooked for them; they both eat of it, mixed with clarified butter and mixed with milk.
(6.1:157.5) Then the Adhvaryu asks for the materials for the bathing-place.
(6.1:157.6) Then he says, "Come, O sacrificer!
Having gone out by the eastern door, they go to where there is water.
Then, while he faces the east, he moistens his right godāna lock with water.
