"May the waters moisten you for life, for long life, and for splendor. With these words, he raises the blade of *barhis* grass with its tip pointing upward. "O herb, protect him!
With this, he places the axe across it, saying, "O axe, do not harm him!"
He shaves [the hair] with the formula: "O God, may I be renowned; I shave these.
With the formula: "May I attain prosperity in what follows," he touches the area where the shaving has ended.
By this same procedure, he moistens the hair for the subsequent *godāna* ceremony, either with the *yajus* formula or silently.
Handing the razor to the barber, he says: "O barber, report to me when my hair and beard have been shorn and my nails have been clipped.
He reports to him accordingly.
Then he sprinkles him with water, [reciting]: "May the waters, our mothers, purify us; may those who cleanse with ghee purify us with ghee."

Having rubbed [the garment] thoroughly, he washes away the dust with the mantra: "May they carry away all our impurity. He steps out with the mantra: "I rise up from these [waters], pure and cleansed.
Covering himself with the edge of his garment, he sips water.
"He eats water," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then he puts on an unwashed garment from left to right, saying: "Thou art the body of Soma; protect my body.
Now, fresh butter, having been separated [from the cream], lies upon a vessel of water for him.
Having rubbed his hands together, he first anoints his face with them, saying: "Thou art the milk of the great ones; thou art the bestower of splendor; bestow splendor upon me.
Another anoints his back, following the direction of the hair down to the feet.

Then this collyrium, ground on a stone slab, lies ready along with a tufted reed-shoot. Sitting behind him while he faces eastward, he anoints his right eye with his left hand three times without blinking, [saying]: "Thou art the pupil of Vṛtra; thou art the protector of the eye; protect my eye! He does so twice for the other [eye].
(6.2:158.6) "He also anoints five times," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(6.2:158.6) He anoints the right [hand] five times and the left five times. (6.2:158.7) Then he purifies him with twenty-one bunches of *darbha* grass, [saying]: "May the Lord of Thought purify you; may the Lord of Speech purify you; may the god Savitṛ purify you with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the bright sun. Thus.

He causes the sacrificer to recite: "O Lord of the filter, with that filter of yours, for whatever purpose I purify myself, may I be able to accomplish that. Then, having placed him upon his left hand, he leads him into the hall [with the words]: "O gods, we approach you at this sacrifice, you whose laws are true; O gods worthy of worship, since we call upon you at the invocation.
He causes him to enter the hall by the eastern door [with the words]: "Indra and Agni, Heaven and Earth, Waters, and Plants."

Then, having led him around the front of the Āhavanīya fire and seated him to the south facing north, he makes him look at the Āhavanīya, saying: "Thou art the lord of consecrations. And [he makes him look] at himself, saying: "Protect me while I am here."
While the Adhvaryu is busy there, the Pratiprasthātṛ silently moistens the wife’s right armpit with water;
he silently raises a blade of sacrificial grass with its tip pointing upward,
and he silently places the axe across it.
He sows silently;
he touches the area where it has been sown silently.
By this same procedure, he moistens the other armpit with water, silently indeed.
Handing the razor to the barber, he says, "Barber, report back to me when her armpits have been shaved and her nails have been clipped.
He reports to him accordingly.
Then he sprinkles her with water silently.
Having run through [the dust] silently, he washes away the dust silently;
he rises from the water silently.
Having covered himself with the edge of his garment, he sips water.
Silently he puts on an unwashed garment, turning it from left to right;
silently he anoints himself; silently he applies collyrium.
(6.3:159.4) Then he purifies her with an unlimited number of bunches of *darbha* grass, silently each time.

(6.3:159.4) Then, having brought her in and caused her to enter the hall by the western door, while leading her toward the east, he makes her recite: "Let the wife of Brahmanaspati go forward; let her sit upon the altar with splendor. And I, following my desire, shall enter here into my own world."

(6.3:159.7) Then he sits down behind the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra: "O Agni, we, possessing good offspring and good wives, have approached you, the subduer of rivals, the undeceivable one, whom none may deceive.
(6.3:159.8) Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice consisting of a cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni and Viṣṇu.

For this [offering], ten items are omitted: one does not lead the sacrificer to the vow-food; one does not gird the wife; one does not prepare a portion for the sacrificer, nor a portion for the Brahman priest, nor a cake placed on the sacrificial grass; one does not request the *anvāhārya* rice; one does not perform the oblation of the husks; one does not offer the *samiṣṭayajus*; one does not cause the sacrificer to recite over the full vessel; and one does not take the steps of Viṣṇu.

Then the Adhvaryu, having turned to the right and hastened westward, having performed the offerings for the wives, having gone eastward, having replenished the *dhruvā* ladle and poured it back into the *ājya-sthālī*, offers the *dīkṣā* oblations by dipping with the *sruva* spoon from the *ājya-sthālī*.
(6.4:159.18) “To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā! To Medhā, to Manas, to Agni, svāhā! To Dīkṣā, to Tapas, to Agni, svāhā! To Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Agni, svāhā! Thus.

(6.4:159.19) Then, having taken four portions into the ladle, he offers the fifth oblation with the ladle: “O divine waters, vast, bringing welfare to all; O Heaven and Earth, the wide atmosphere; may Bṛhaspati increase us with the oblation, svāhā! Thus.

Having taken another fourfold portion of clarified butter, he offers a full ladle as the *audgrahaṇa* oblation with the verse: "Every mortal should choose the friendship of the God who leads; everyone seeks wealth from him; let him choose glory so that he may prosper—svāhā!
At this point, he pours out this full vessel within the altar.

(6.4:160.6) Then, having carried it around in front of the Āhavanīya fire, he hands over to the sacrificer the black antelope skin, the black antelope horn, the garment, the girdle, the Udumbara staff as the fifth, and the turban as the sixth.
(6.4:160.8) Then the Pratiprasthātṛ hands over to the wife the water-pot, the head-net, the garment, the yoke-thong, and the peg.
Then, on the sacrificer’s seat, he spreads a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair facing upward.

He touches its white and black parts; his thumb rests on the white part and his finger on the black part, saying: "You two are the artistic forms of the *Ṛg* and *Sāman* verses; I take hold of you both; may you two protect me until the conclusion of this sacrifice."

(6.5:160.13) Then, bending his right knee, he creeps forward [toward the fire], reciting: "O God Varuṇa, sharpen this prayer of one who strives, sharpen his will and skill! So that we may cross over all difficulties, may we board a ship that provides a good crossing.

(6.5:160.15) Then, making a lap, he winds the girdle around himself from left to right, saying: "Thou art vigor, belonging to Aṅgiras, soft as wool; grant me vigor. (6.5:160.17) Saying, "Protect me; do not harm me," he ties a knot that can be untied.
At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ girdles the wife with a cord, reciting the two verses: "Seeking goodwill... and "I gird you.
Then he covers the sacrificer with a garment, saying: "Thou art Viṣṇu’s protection; thou art the sacrificer’s protection; grant me protection.
He causes him to recite over the openings of the garment: "Protect me from the gaze of the stars."

(6.5:160.22) Having tucked in the ends of his garment, he wraps his head with a turban from left to right, saying: "I wrap your head with glory, for the sake of glory, fame, and Vedic splendor. (6.5:161.1) At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ silently places a braid of hair upon the wife's head.
(6.5:161.2) Now, she has this black antelope horn, which has either three or five ridges, bound with a hempen cord and tied like a circular ornament.
He hands it to the sacrificer with the words, "Thou art the womb of Indra.
The sacrificer receives it with the words, "Do not harm me.
Having tied it to the fringe at the edge of his garment, he digs up a clod of earth within the altar with it, saying, "For the sake of agriculture, for good crops."
(6.5:161.7) With the words, "For the plants with good fruit for thee," he scratches the hair-parting on the right side.
(6.5:161.8) At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ ties a wooden pin to the wife [of the sacrificer] with the words, "Scratch yourself with this.
(6.5:161.9) Then he hands him a staff of Udumbara wood with its tip pointing upwards, reaching up to his mouth, with the words, "The divine Vanaspati is well-established."
(6.5:161.10) “Standing upright, protect me from the [sacrificial] residue,” with these words the sacrificer receives [the vessel].

(6.5:161.11) Then he causes him to recite the formula for the taking hold of the sacrifice: “Svāhā! I take hold of the sacrifice with the mind; svāhā! from heaven and earth; svāhā! from the wide atmosphere; svāhā! I take hold of the sacrifice from the wind. (6.5:161.13) At this point, he closes his fists and restrains his speech.

Then he says: "This Brahmin, so-and-so by name, of such-and-such a lineage, the son of so-and-so, the grandson of so-and-so, the great-grandson of so-and-so—him we announce to Indra, to Indra and Agni, to the Vasus, to the Rudras, to the Ādityas, to the Viśve Devas, and to the Soma-drinking Brahmins.
Having said this three times in a low voice, he has indeed announced him to the gods.
Having gone out three times with a loud voice, [he says],
"He has indeed announced him to both the gods and the men," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then he instructs him.

(6.6:162.4) "You are consecrated; speak as one who is consecrated. Speak only the truth, not untruth. Do not smile; do not scratch yourself; do not uncover yourself. If you should smile, smile with your mouth covered; if you should scratch yourself, scratch yourself with a black antelope horn; if you should release speech, recite a verse addressed to Viṣṇu. Let not the sun rise over you while you are elsewhere than in the consecrated shed, nor let it set over you. [Recite] those names which are the names of the deities..."

"Tell me those names as they have been told. Then, while telling those names which do not belong to the deities as they have been told, place the *vicakṣaṇa* [brick] at the top; speak speech that is pleasing and full of insight; do not cut yourself off from the black antelope skin nor from the staff. Thus he performs all this exactly in that manner.
Then, at the time of adding fuel, standing to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, he issues the command: "Make the fires luminous! O consecrated one, restrain your speech! O wife, restrain your speech!"
Having given the command, the two who are observing silence milk the two portions for the *vrata* (fasting-food).

Then the Adhvaryu, having gone out by the eastern door and having caused the milking, returns by the same way he came; having performed the Agnihotra procedure at the Gārhapatya fire, having heated the milk, moved it northward, cooled it, and having either poured it into a vessel or not poured it, he hangs it on a sling in the northern part of the shed.

(6.6:162.17) Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having gone out by the southern door and caused [the milk] to be milked, returns by the same way he came; having heated it over the vessel for boiling the *vrata*-milk, having removed it toward the north, and having cooled it, he pours it out—either having poured it out or not—and hangs it on a sling in the southern section of the shed.

(6.6:163.1) Then, when the stars have risen, the sacrificer, having fastened his black antelope skin and gone out by the eastern door, stands in front of the shed and releases his speech three times, saying: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! Prepare the *vrata*! Prepare the *vrata*!"
Then he approaches the guests;
he utters speech that is pleasing and far-sighted.
If he should encounter anything impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; the Sun is the best of lights. O consecration, do not abandon me!"
Now, if it rains upon him, he mutters there: "O flowing waters, bestow strength; bestow vigor; bestow strength; do not destroy my consecration, do not destroy my austerity.

These two *yajus* formulas of his remain in use until the conclusion of the rite. Then, at the time for the falling [of the rain], he spreads a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and its hair side upward in the sacrificer’s station.
If there is a great deal spread out, he lies down directly upon the black antelope skin without anything intervening;
then he mutters the formula for lying down.

(6.7:163.12) "O Agni, do you keep watch well; may we rejoice well. Protect us for our welfare; give us back for our awakening. Thus [he says]. (6.7:163.13) "He lies on the south side; this indeed is the resting place of the sacrificer. He lies in his own resting place, having turned toward the fire; he lies having turned toward the deities and the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(6.7:163.15) Then the wife lies down silently behind the Gārhapatya fire.

(6.7:163.16) Then, having hastened there at midnight, the Adhvaryu makes him recite the awakening-formula: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows, a god among mortals; you are to be praised in the sacrifices. (6.7:163.18) Then he sips water, saying: "We meditate upon the divine thought, the most gracious, for our aid—the bestower of splendor, the carrier of the sacrifice; may it lead us safely across to our will.
(6.7:164.1) Then, having poured [milk] into a bronze cup or a wooden bowl, he gives it to him as his vow-food (*vrata*).

Having enclosed that space to the south, he partakes of the fast-food (*vrata*) with the formula: "O gods born of mind, yoked by mind, very skillful, sons of Dakṣa—may they protect us; may they aid us; homage to them; to them, svāhā!
Having partaken of as much as the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) permits, he partakes further in silence.
At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours [the remainder] into the wife's vessel and gives her the fast-food.
Having enclosed that [space], he observes the vow in silence.
Having washed the vessels, they hand them over.
Then, in the same manner as before, prior to the disappearance of the stars, having issued the summons, the two who have restrained their speech cause the milk for the vow to be drawn.

(6.7:164.8) Then, when the sun has risen, the sacrificer, having fastened on the black antelope skin and having gone out by the eastern door, standing in front of the hall, releases his speech three times, saying: "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar! Make the vow! Make the vow!

(6.7:164.10) The release of speech is the same; the formula for lying down is the same; the formula for waking up is the same; the sipping of water is the same; the taking of the vow is the same. (6.7:164.12) Then he sends out the collectors of the sacrificial gifts.

(6.7:164.12) He first sends a messenger to one whom he thinks will not refuse him, [saying]: "May all the gods turn toward me; may Pūṣan with his gain, Soma with his bounty, and the god Savitṛ, the giver of wealth, [turn toward me].

(6.7:164.15) Upon seeing him bringing [the gift], he mutters, but not if he is not bringing it: "O Soma, grant this much; bring more! May I not fail in my fulfillment while bestowing; may I not fail in my life!
(6.7:164.16) He accepts it according to its form.
(6.8:164.18) "Thou art the moon," [with these words] he addresses the gold; (6.8:164.18) "Thou art a garment," [with these words] the cloth; (6.8:164.18) "Thou art a cow," [with these words] the cow.
(6.8:164.19) With "Thou art a horse," [he addresses] the horse; with "Thou art a goat," the goat; with "Thou art a ram," the ram.
Now, if anything is not specifically assigned by the Brāhmaṇa, he accepts it with the words: "Thou art dedicated to Prajāpati; be for my enjoyment.
Having gathered them together, they guard them.
Of those [animals], whichever perishes or dies, he assigns it to Vāyu with the words: "To Vāyu, thee!"
(6.8:165.1) That which dies in water or in a snare, [he addresses] with: "For Varuṇa, thee! (6.8:165.2) That which perishes or falls into a pit, [he addresses] with: "For Nirṛti, thee!
(6.8:165.3) That which a snake or a tiger kills, [he addresses] with: "For Rudra, thee!"
Of those, three are directed away.
Now, as for this one that has been lost—if they should find it, what should be done?
It should be treated exactly as prescribed; this is one view.
"Who might find for her a recipient more worthy than this?
One should give her away together with the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*); this is one view.
'One should sacrifice with her using a *vāyavyā* [offering]; this is another."
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the departure.
Either security and well-being are found for the consecrated one elsewhere than at the sacrificial ground, or he undergoes consecration there.
They mix the two portions of the *vrata* milk, and they tie together the two calves of the two *vrata*-milking cows.
They establish whatever is to be established: the Gārhapatya fire in the interior of the cart and the Āhavanīya fire on the front part of the pole.
Alternatively, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), he sets out with a verse addressed to Bṛhaspati: "Go forth from good to better; let Bṛhaspati be your forerunner.
Now, if someone should approach him while he is traveling at the time of his vow, he places the two kindling woods to the north, encloses the area to the south, and performs the vow.
Silently, he seeks grass and water.

Then, if he comes upon water that is not for crossing, he mutters: "O divine waters, O son of the waters, that wave of yours which is fit for oblation, full of power, most intoxicating—may I not step upon it; may I follow the unbroken thread of the earth.
He either plunges into it or crosses over it.
"Having made a bridge, he passes beyond," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then, where he intends to stay, he takes up residence with the words: "Now, having taken up residence in this choice place on earth.
Then he worships the rising sun with the words: "Drive away the enemies, O you who possess all heroes!"

Then he proceeds with the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) for Agni and Soma.
He proceeds with the principal offering (*havis*) in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), [with the calls]: "Recite the invitatory verse for Viṣṇu! and "Sacrifice to Viṣṇu!"
(6.18:177.9) Then he proceeds with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
(6.18:177.9) The guest-offering (*ātithya*) concludes with the *iḍā*.
(6.18:177.10) At this point, he pours out this full vessel within the altar (*antarvedi*).

At this point, having caused the clarified butter in the *dhruvā* vessel to swell, he asks for either a bronze cup or a wooden ladle; having placed it within the altar, he pours that *tānūnaptra* mixture into it.
"I take thee for the one who falls; I take thee for the one who falls around; I take thee for Tanūnapāt; I take thee for Śākvara; I take thee for the mightiest in power. Thus [he says].

Then as many officiating priests (ṛtvij) as there are, they touch it together, saying: "Thou art unassailed, unassailable, the vigor of the gods, a protector against imprecation, beyond the reach of imprecation."
He causes the sacrificer to recite: "May the Lord of Consecration approve my consecration; may the Lord of Austerity approve my austerity. May I attain truth directly. Place me in prosperity.
Having sought the invitation from as many officiating priests as there are, the sacrificer himself smells it three times, saying: "I offer you in Prajāpati, in the mind.
Then, having poured water over it, he sprinkles it to the north.
Then he says: "The waters rejoice for the fires.
"The divine, immortal waters, increasing the cosmic order, rejoice.
"Run hither with them."

(6.19:177.21) Then, having touched the *madantī* waters, having stood up, having untied [the vessel], and having placed gold within, they cause the King [Soma] to swell, [saying]: "O divine Soma, may every stalk of yours swell for Indra, the winner of the single prize! May Indra swell for you; may you swell for Indra! Thus.
He causes the sacrificer to recite: "Swell with abundance for our friends through wisdom; O divine Soma, may I attain well-being at the pressing.
Then, having touched water, they sit down in their respective places.
Then the Adhvaryu separates the two offering-ladles with the two *vājavatī* verses.
Having torn off the *prastara* from the two *vidhṛtis*, he anoints it three times without crushing it; he does not call for the *āśrāvaṇa* for the *prastara*, nor does he throw the *barhis* after it.

Having placed it on the southern half of the altar, they perform the *nihnuvana* over it from south to north, [reciting]: "Desired are riches for the impulse, for fortune; truth for those who speak truth; homage to heaven, homage to earth! (6.19:178.10) He places small wood-shavings upon the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) upon the *prastara*, and having untied the cord with which it was tied, having carried it across the *āhavanīya* fire, and having sprinkled it with water, he sets it down to the north.

Then he leads the sacrificer into the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*) with the formula: "O Agni, lord of vows, you are the lord of vows among vows. That body of mine which is here, let it be in you; that body of yours which is here, let it be in me. O lord of vows, may the vows of us two who observe the vow be common."

(6.19:178.14) Then he instructs him: "Tighten your girdle more closely; clench your fists more tightly; be one whose vow is heated; purify yourself with the *madantī* waters. Release first the previous vow. With that body of yours, O Agni, which belongs to Rudra, protect us; to that body of yours, *svāhā*! From this point forward, he should observe his vow. Thus he performs all of this.
(6.20:178.19) Then he proceeds with the Pravargya rite according to the procedure for the Pravargya.
(6.20:178.19) Now, taking up the wooden sword (sphya), he says: "O Agnīdh, place the boiling waters on the fire; place the oblation on the fire; come, sit down!
(6.20:178.20) Into these very boiling waters, he pours more water.
He places the clarified butter on the fire;
that is the oblation.
Then, from this very sacrificial grass that has been spread out, he cuts off a portion around the edges.
He carries away the *stambayajus*.
This is the well-known procedure pertaining to the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika*).
He does so three times with the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) and a fourth time silently.
He performs the first tracing of the altar,
mutters the *karaṇa* formula,
and digs up the earth.
From the *uddhata* [spot], the *āgnīdhra* carries [the earth] three times.

When the *āgnīdhra* has carried it three times, [the Adhvaryu], having performed the second tracing (*parigrāha*), having leveled [the ground], and having held the wooden sword (*sphya*) crosswise, issues the call: "Set down the boiling waters! Place the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*) nearby! Clean the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and the offering-ladles (*sruc*)! Bring the oblation!"

When the *madantī* waters have been brought, having wiped the wooden sword (*sphya*) for him and having set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmā-barhis*), he turns to the right, hastens back toward the west, and cleanses both the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and the two offering-ladles (*sruk*).
He comes forward with the oblation;
having purified both the oblation and the *madantī* waters, he takes eight portions into the *juhū* ladle.
He pours four portions into the *upabhṛt* ladle.
Having poured a third portion from the *ājyasthālī* vessel, he stands up with the *madantī* waters.
He sprinkles the fuel wood (*idhma*).
He sprinkles the altar;
he sprinkles the sacrificial grass;
having sprinkled the sacrificial grass that has been placed down and poured water over it, he takes up the Prastara-bunch made of *aśvavāla* grass from the front.
Having spread the sacrificial grass in a single layer, holding the *prastara* in his hand, he steps forward toward the east and lays down the enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood.
He places two upright fuel-sticks;
he sets down two crosswise separating-blades made of sugarcane.
(6.20:179.14) On the two separating blades (*vidhṛtī*) he places the *prastara* of *aśvavāla* grass; (6.20:179.14) on the *prastara*, the *juhū* ladle;
(6.20:179.14) on the other two [blades], the *barhis* grass.

Having touched [the fire] with the formula, "May these sit down," having turned to the right, having hastened westward, and having sat down behind the Gārhapatya, he recites the verses concerning the wives of the gods.
Then, having returned by the same way he came, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says, "Recite for the fire being kindled.
He places the faggot on the fire either once or thrice.
He does not leave any fuel remaining; he fans the fire with the Veda. When the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, he pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* ladle.
When the [sacrificial ground] has been swept, he does not [use] the two offering-ladles for the subsequent [rite].
Then he chooses the *pravara* (the ancestral invocation).
Then he causes [the *āgnīdhra*] to announce: "O, cause to hear! "Let there be hearing! "Sit down, O Hotṛ!"—this much constitutes the *pravara*.
The Hotṛ sits down;
he awaits the impulse.
Being impelled, taking up the two offering-spoons, he says:
(6.21:180.1) “For Agni,” he says in a whisper; “Recite the invitatory verse,” he says aloud.
(6.21:180.1) Having stepped across and caused the announcement to be made, he says, “For Agni,” in a whisper; “Sacrifice,” he says aloud.
(6.21:180.2) When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers in the eastern half, at the halfway point.
Then, standing right there, he says "For Soma" in a low voice; "Recite the invitatory verse" loudly.
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says "Soma" in a low voice; "Offer the oblation" loudly.
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering in the middle.
(6.21:180.4) Then, while bringing [the butter] together, he says "For Viṣṇu" in a low voice; "Recite the invitatory verse" loudly.
(6.21:180.5) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says "Viṣṇu" in a low voice; "Sacrifice" loudly.
(6.21:180.6) When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers the whole [oblation] from behind.

Then, having stepped across toward the north and set down the two offering-spoons in their proper places, he says: "O Agnis, the waters rejoice!"— "The divine, immortal waters rejoice, increasing the cosmic order."—
"Run hither with them!"

(6.21:180.8) Then, having touched the *madantī* waters, having stood up, having loosened [the Soma], and having placed gold within it, they cause the King [Soma] to swell, reciting: "O divine Soma, may every stalk of yours swell for Indra, the winner of the single prize! May Indra swell for you; may you swell for Indra!
(6.21:180.11) He causes the sacrificer to recite: "Make your friends swell with gain and wisdom! O divine Soma, may I attain well-being at your pressing.
(6.21:180.12) Then, having touched water, they sit down in their respective places.
Then the Adhvaryu separates the two offering-spoons with the two *vājavatī* verses.
Having plucked the *prastara* bundle with the two separating-blades (*vidhṛti*), he anoints it three times without crushing it;
he does not call for the *āśrāvaṇa* regarding the *prastara*.
He does not throw the *barhis* after [the oblation].

Having placed it on the southern half of the altar, they perform the *nihnuvanam* over it from south to north, saying: "Desired riches for the impulse, for fortune; truth for those who speak truth; homage to heaven, homage to earth!"

Having turned the *prastara* toward his left hand and having dipped the *sruva* ladle into the *ājya*-pot, he offers the first *upasat* oblation with the mantra: "O Agni, that body of yours which lies in the abyss, which lies in the dust, which lies in the flame—the most exalted, dwelling in the depths—with it I have struck down the fierce word, I have struck down the dazzling word, *svāhā*! (TS 1.2.11.2.f).

(6.21:180.20) He places the wood-shavings upon the enclosing-sticks and the sacrificial grass upon the *prastara*-bundle, loosens them with a cord to the required extent, washes them over the *āhavanīya* fire, sprinkles them with water, and sets them down to the north.
(6.21:181.2) Then, having gone out, he issues the command: "O *subrahmaṇya*, invoke the *subrahmaṇyā*; give the three-breasted vow-food.
(6.21:181.3) The *subrahmaṇya* priest invokes the *subrahmaṇyā*.
He bestows the Tristanavrata.
Then, in the afternoon, he proceeds with the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites;
the performance of these two is identical, differing only in this respect.
(6.21:181.5) They conceal [the offering] with the left hand uppermost.
(6.21:181.6) Then, having gone out, he issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; have the three-teat milk for the vow.
(6.21:181.7) The Subrahmaṇya invokes the Subrahmaṇyā, and they have the three-teat milk for the vow.
He presents it at midnight.
Then, having hastened there in the latter part of the night, the Adhvaryu gives the instruction: "Cause the two-teat *vrata* milk to be milked.
At dawn, when the sun has risen and speech has been released, he proceeds with the middle *pravargya* and *upasad* rites;
at this point, he offers the oblation in the *rajāśayā* vessel.
Then, having gone out, he issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; give the two-breast vow.
The Subrahmaṇya invokes the Subrahmaṇyā, and he gives the two-breast vow.
From the Āhavanīya fire itself, he first strides six steps eastward;
there he drives in a peg.
That is the Śālāmukhīya peg.
From the *śālāmukhīya* peg, he strides thirty-six steps toward the east;
there he drives in a peg,
which is the peg for the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭīya*).
From the *śālāmukhīya* peg, he strides fifteen paces to the south and fifteen to the north;
there he drives in two pegs—
those are the two hips (*śroṇī*).
From the peg at the sacrificial post-hole, he strides twelve steps to the south and twelve to the north;
there he drives in two pegs.
These two are the shoulders.
Then, having measured it diagonally with the measuring-cord, he encloses it on all sides with a rope;
he stretches the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord.
From the peg marking the hole for the sacrificial post (*yūpāvaṭīya*), he strides twelve small steps westward along the rope.
That is the middle *śaṅku* of the Uttaravedi.
From the middle *śaṅku* of the Uttaravedi, he strides five small steps to the south and five to the north;
there he drives in two *śaṅkus*.
From the peg at the sacrificial post-hole, he strides four small steps toward the south and four toward the north;
there he drives in those pegs.
Those two are the shoulders.
Then, having measured it diagonally with the measuring-cord, he encloses it all around with a cord and stretches the *pṛṣṭhyā* line across.
(6.22:182.8) Measuring along from the middle *śaṅku* of the northern altar-ground, he strides six steps westward and a seventh to the south. (6.22:182.10) There he places the wooden sword (*sphya*);
that is the location for the *uparava* holes.
Then, from the northern corner-post of the great altar (*mahāvedi*), he strides twelve steps westward along the edge of the altar and a thirteenth step toward the north.
There, the Āgnīdhra sits down;
that is the time for the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
Then, from the time of the sounding-holes, he carries away the Stambayajus.
This very [procedure] is established according to the *Pauroḍāśika* [Kalpa].
He performs it three times with the sacrificial formula (*yajuṣ*) and the fourth time silently.
He performs the first tracing of the altar (*parigrāha*).

He mutters the *karaṇa* formula: "O men, come and prepare this altar, rich in Vasus, rich in Rudras, rich in Ādityas, rich in Viśvedevas, at the height of heaven, at the navel of the earth, so that this sacrificer may not come to harm. He digs it up.
From the *uddhata* [spot], the *āgnīdhra* carries [the earth] three times.

When the *āgnīdhra* has carried it three times, then standing in front of the hall, he issues the command: "O altar-makers, prepare the altar! Break up the high places! Fill in the hollows! Cast away the chaff! Complete the altar so that it slopes toward the east and the north! They act according to this command.
(6.23:182.21) Then, from the northern shoulder-mark of the great altar, he strides three steps westward along the edge of the altar and a fourth step northward.
(6.23:183.1) Following the procedure for the *cātvāla* pit, he traces out the *cātvāla*.
(6.23:183.2) Following the procedure for the high altar (*uttaravedi*), he pours out the earth for the high altar.
Having removed the northern navel and covered it, he proceeds with the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasad* rites.
Then, having gone out, he issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; have the two-teat *vrata*-milk milked.
Thereupon, the Subrahmaṇya priest invokes the Subrahmaṇyā.
He causes a two-teat cow to be milked for the vow;
he offers that at midnight.
(6.24:183.7) Then, having hastened there in the latter part of the night, the Adhvaryu gives the instruction: "Milk the *ekastana* cow for the vow.
(6.24:183.8) When the sun has risen in the morning and speech has been released, he proceeds with the two final *pravargya* and *upasad* rites;
at this point, he offers the oblation on the *harāśaya* brick.
(6.24:183.9) Then, having gone out, he issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; give the half-breast vow-food.
(6.24:183.10) The Subrahmaṇya invokes the Subrahmaṇyā;
[the Adhvaryu] gives the half-breast vow-food.

Then, at that very time, having combined the afternoon *pravargya* and *upasada* rites and gone out, he issues the command: "O *subrahmaṇya*, invoke the *subrahmaṇyā*! O *pratiprasthātṛ*, set down the *pravargya* according to the procedure for the *pravargya* for the purpose of its removal.
They divide this place into three parts:
one third [of the vessel] they place on the *gārhapatya* fire, one third in the supporting ladles (*upayamanī*), and they deposit the remaining third.
Then, according to the procedure for the *pravargya*, he puts away the *pravargya* vessel.
According to the procedure for the fire, he leads forward the fire.

Having performed the second tracing of the altar while it contains the fire, having leveled it, and having held the wooden sword (*sphya*) crosswise, he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters! Place the fuel and the sacrificial grass! This much constitutes the call.
Right here he spreads this sacrificial grass (*barhis*), stroking it along once only.

Regarding this, some say that this very *idhmābarhis* (fuel and grass) should remain lying there for the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma. Now, his two wagons, washed, brought forward, and made ready, stand on both sides of the hall.
Of these two, the southern one is larger and the northern one is smaller.
The southern one has its plank removed, while the northern one has its plank not removed.
That which is bound to the axle of those two is left as it is.

(6.24:184.3) Then they bring them back within the altar. (6.24:184.3) Then, having placed a cord on both sides at a distance of one cubit in front of the hall, (6.24:184.4) he sprinkles them with the formula: "O you two belonging to Viṣṇu, be purified for Viṣṇu!"

Then he says, "Come, O sacrificer," and having led him into the hall by the eastern door, he melts the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, purifies it, takes four portions in the ladle, and while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, he offers the oblation to Savitṛ on the *śālāmukhīya* fire with the verse: "The inspired priests of the great inspired one, the wise, harness their minds and harness their thoughts; he alone, knowing the sacred ways, ordains the priestly offices—great is the praise of the god Savitṛ, Svāhā!"
Having taken another fourfold portion, he then requests: "The vessel for the clarified butter together with the dipping-spoon, the wooden sword, the water-vessel, the sacrificial grass, and the gold.
Having taken these up, he says: "Come, O sacrificer!"

The sacrificer follows behind, and the wife follows after him. Taking one-third of a footprint, he goes out by the eastern door, creeps behind the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, and on the southern track, having dug up the earth with the wooden sword (*sphya*), sprinkled it with water, and placed gold upon it, and having strewn grass all around, he makes an offering with the verse: "Viṣṇu strode through this; in three places he planted his foot; gathered together is his dust in the footprint—*svāhā*! Then he pours half of these footprint-dusts into the joined palms of the wife.
Then he sprinkles them with the residue of the ghee.
With his right hand turned upward, he anoints the southern axle-peg, saying: "May a hero be born to us for our work, whom we all may live upon, who shall be the controller of many."

Having taken another fourfold portion and having crept behind the axle of the northern *havirdhāna* cart, he digs up [the earth] on the northern track with the wooden sword (*sphya*), sprinkles it with water, places a piece of gold upon it, strews [grass] all around, and offers an oblation over it, [reciting]: "O you two, be full of nourishment, rich in cows, abounding in good pasture, and glorious for mankind! Viṣṇu has propped apart these two worlds; he has supported them."
"By his rays he has supported the earth on all sides, svāhā! (TS 1.2.13.2.f).
At this point, the wife pours all these foot-dust particles into her joined palms.
Then she sprinkles them with the residue of the oblation.
With his palm turned upward, he anoints the northern axle-pin; the act of anointing is the same for both.
Then he hands these implements over to the Pratiprasthātṛ.
They lead the wife and call upon the Hotṛ; then, having taken hold of them both together, he issues the formal command.
"Recite for the two *havirdhāna* carts as they are being moved forward.
When this has been said three times, they move them forward with the words: "Go forward, fashioning the sacrifice; lead the sacrifice upward; do not falter!
Now, if the axle creaks, he murmurs there: "O God of fair speech, announce [us] to the dwellings!"

Then the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ approach them directly. Having gone around the north of the two *havirdhāna* carts and having passed by the two front [posts], they step three steps westward along the cord from the middle *auttaravedika* peg.
There, they cause the two [chariots] to rest upon their front parts as if on the nave, with the formula: "Rest here on the summit of the earth!"
Then, with the verse containing the word *āśis*, "Whether from heaven, O Viṣṇu, or from the earth," the Adhvaryu drives in the wedge to the south of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.
Then he secures it firmly with a cord, [reciting] "I shall now proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu.
In the same manner, the Pratiprasthātṛ drives in the wedge to the north of the northern *havirdhāna* cart.
(6.25:186.1) Then he fastens it firmly with a cord using this same mantra.
(6.25:186.2) Then the Adhvaryu, having measured one cubit eastward from the chin of the southern *havirdhāna* cart and having fixed the mark on the ground, causes a pit to be dug there.
(6.25:186.3) Then, having measured a fore-arm's length eastward from the southern end of the yoke and having fixed the mark on the ground, he causes a pit to be dug there.
He causes both of them to dig another pit to the north. In the same manner, the Pratiprasthātṛ digs three pits to the north; likewise to the west.
Upon them they erect pillars with their ears turned toward the east; upon these they project two beams directed toward the north.
They place the forehead-ornament in front, saying: "Thou art the forehead of Viṣṇu."

With the words, "Thou art the back of Viṣṇu," he lays down the middle roof-panel; with the words, "Ye two are the corners of Viṣṇu," those which are on both sides. They enclose it from the south and from the north.
They make two doors, one facing east and one facing west.
Then, having placed a handful of *kuśa* grass against the southern door-post, he weaves a needle through it, and the cord through the needle, saying: "Thou art the needle of Viṣṇu.
With the words, "Thou art the firm [stake] of Viṣṇu," he makes a knot.
Having loosened it at that very moment, he says: "Complete [the work] by making knots with your manual skill.
In this same way, he completes the northern door-post; in this same way, he completes the other two door-posts.
(6.25:186.14) Then he touches it, saying: "Thou art belonging to Viṣṇu; for Viṣṇu thee!
(6.25:186.15) Then the Adhvaryu, having turned to the right and hastened westward, strides six steps eastward along the cord from the peg at the front of the hall, and a seventh step to the south.
(6.25:187.2) There he lays down the wooden sword (abhri).
At the time for the Audumbarī post,
he takes up the spade from the place where the Audumbarī post will stand.
(6.26:187.4) “At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee.
(6.26:187.5) Having taken it, he consecrates it: “Thou art a spade; thou art a woman.

(6.26:187.5) With that [spade], he traces a circle around the pit for the Udumbara post: “The Rakṣas is encircled; the enemies are encircled. Here do I cut off the neck of the Rakṣas. Whoever hates us and whom we hate—here do I cut off his neck. Thus he says.
Then he says to the Udgātṛ: "O Udgātṛ, come! Dig this pit for the Audumbarī post; throw out the earth toward the east.
He either digs it himself or has it dug. From that very spot, he measures out the Sadas.
Just as there are three roof-coverings across, so [should they be] toward the east;
just as there are three roof-coverings lengthwise, so [should they be] toward the north.
Or alternatively, so that two parts should be to the north of the cord and one to the south.
He causes three-tiered pits to be dug for it.
Having run from there toward the east, he measures out the *uparava* holes in front of the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart; they are a span wide at the mouth, a span deep, and a cubit long.

Then he says to the *unnetṛ*: "Come, O *unnetṛ*, dig these *uparava* holes—a span wide at the mouth, a span deep, a cubit long, facing downward, without breaking through [the bottom], and connected above and below."
He digs them himself or causes them to be dug.
Then he pours their soil in front of the support of the southern *havirdhāna* cart;
he makes that mound (*khara*) four-cornered.
(6.26:188.4) Then he makes it [the mortar] covered with sand.
(6.26:188.4) Then, from the place of the *uparava* pits, he takes up the spade with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee.
(6.26:188.6) Having taken it, he consecrates it: "Thou art a spade; thou art a woman."

With that [cord], he traces around the pit for the sacrificial post (*yūpāvaṭa*) so that half of it shall be within the altar (*antarvedi*) and half outside the altar (*bahirvedi*). He says: "The *rakṣas* is traced around; the enemies are traced around. Here do I cut off the neck of the *rakṣas*; whoever hates us and whom we hate—here do I cut off his neck. Then he says to the *Āgnīdhra*: "O *Āgnīdhra*, come! Dig this pit for the sacrificial post, measuring it by its upper part, throwing out the loose earth toward the east. Dig it deeper by four finger-breadths than the upper part."

He digs it himself or causes it to be dug, as much as the Adhvaryu is occupied there; meanwhile, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having measured the Udumbara post together with the sacrificer, leaves a portion unburied at the bottom, saying: "Uninterrupted is wealth accompanied by brave sons.

Then the Adhvaryu, having turned clockwise and hastened westward, makes a request for the sprinkling water containing barley, a handful of sacrificial grass, the butter-pot together with the *sruva*-ladle, the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa, gold, and a vessel of water.
Having taken hold of this, he says, "Come, O sacrificer!
This post of Udumbara wood, having been washed and brought forward, lies near the eastern hole;
he sprinkles it from the far side toward himself.
"For heaven thee! For the atmosphere thee! For the earth thee!"—with these words he pours water into the pit, saying, "May the world, the seat of the Fathers, be purified.
He scatters barley-grains, saying, "Thou art barley; keep away from us our enemies; keep away our adversaries."
Intertwining the sacrificial grass held in his hand, he spreads it out with the formula: "Thou art the seat of the Pitṛs.

Then, having placed a piece of gold underneath it, he makes an oblation upon it with the dipping-spoon, saying: "Svāhā to the Pitṛs! Then he raises it up, saying: "Prop up the sky; fill the mid-region; make firm the earth!"
(6.27:189.3) Then he fixes it with its ear turned toward the east, saying: "May Dyutāna Māruta fix thee by the firm law of Mitra and Varuṇa.

(6.27:189.4) Then he piles earth around it from left to right, saying: "I pile thee around as the winner of the Brahman, the winner of the Kṣatra, the winner of good progeny, and the winner of the increase of wealth.
(6.27:189.6) He compacts it with the staff of Mitrāvaruṇa, saying: "Strengthen the Brahman! Strengthen the Kṣatra! Strengthen the progeny! Strengthen the increase of wealth!"

Having set down [the vessel] neither deficient nor excessive, and having poured out the water-vessel, he then places gold upon its two prongs and makes an offering with the dipping-spoon, saying: "O Heaven and Earth, fill yourselves with clarified butter, svāhā!
He pours the remainder down until it reaches the end.
"He anoints the sacrificer himself with splendor to the very end," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then they announce her to the Udgātṛs;
they perform upon her whatever rites they know.
Following the raising of this [post], they raise pillars with their tops turned toward the east; upon them, they project the rafters toward the north.
They lay on the middle roof-covering with the formula: "Thou art the seat of Indra."
"The shadow for all people"— this refers to those [enclosures] that are on both sides.
"One desiring splendor should erect one with nine roofs"—
thus, all [the enclosures] consist of exactly three [roofs] each.
“He makes the southern ones northern. He thus makes those which were southern northern. “He makes intermediate ones for the sake of distinction,” it is said.
He throws grass-bundles at the joints;
these are the internal partitions.

Then they enclose it with the verse: "O lover of songs, may these songs encompass thee on every side; may they be increases following the increase of thy life; may they be acceptances, acceptable to thee."
They enclose it on the south and on the north;
they make two doors, one facing east and one facing west.

Then, having grasped a handful of *kuśa* grass at the southern door-post, he weaves a needle through it with the formula: "Thou art the needle of Indra. Through the needle, he passes a cord with the formula: "Thou art the seam of Indra."
(6.27:190.4) With the words, "Thou art the firm foundation of Indra," he makes a knot;
having immediately loosened it at that very moment, he says, "Complete [the work] by making knots with manual skill.
In the same manner, [he treats] the upper door-post.
In this manner, he fashions the other two door-posts.
Then he touches it, saying: "Thou art Indra's; for Indra, thee!
Then, from the northern shoulder-mark of the great altar, he strides eighteen steps westward along the edge of the altar.
He measures out that Āgnīdhra shed so that half of it shall be within the altar and half outside the altar. Then, having gathered the materials, they enclose it; they make its door on the south side.
The side-measure of the Āgnīdhra shed is five aratnis.
By this, the Mārjālīya shed is explained;
they make its door face north.

(6.28:190.12) Then, standing right there, he asks for a wooden shovel, sprinkling-water containing barley, sacrificial grass held in his hand, a vessel for clarified butter together with the dipping-spoon, the pressing-skin, two pressing-boards, six pegs, a pressing-stone, gold, and a water-vessel.
(6.28:190.14) Having taken all this, he says, "Come, O sacrificer!
Having caused him to enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, he spreads this skin within the interior of the southern *havirdhāna*.
They set down the other [implements] in front of the axle.
Then, from the place of the *uparava* holes, he takes up the spade with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee.
Having taken it, he consecrates it with: "Thou art a spade; thou art a woman."

With that [cord], he traces around the *uparava* holes, beginning with the southern one of the two in front: "The *rakṣas* is traced around; the enemies are traced around. Here I cut off the neck of the *rakṣas*; him who hates us and whom we hate—here I cut off his neck.
He does this for all of them in successive order. He digs them all in successive order, saying: "I dig the *rakṣas*-slayers, the *valaga*-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu."

Then he scatters dust over them [with the words]: "Here I dig up that hidden spell (*valaga*) which an equal or an unequal has buried for us; here I cast him down who, whether equal or unequal, acts as an enemy against us—with the *gāyatrī* metre!
With the words, "The spell is struck down," he scatters dust from the right foot of the sacrificer under his feet, from the southern side of the two eastern [stakes].
With the words, "With the *triṣṭubh* metre," he scatters [dust] from the southern side of the two western [stakes].
"With the *jagatī* metre," [he says] over the northern of the two rear [lines]. "With the *anuṣṭubh* metre," [he says] over the northern of the two front [lines].
At this point, he throws these foot-dusts away in a place free from traffic.
At this point, the sacrificer meditates mentally upon whoever he hates.
Then, having touched water, both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer touch these [stakes]; the Adhvaryu touches the southern one of the two front ones, and the sacrificer touches the northern one.
Then the sacrificer asks: "O Adhvaryu, what is here?"
"May it be auspicious," [he says].
"May that be for us both together.
Then the Adhvaryu asks: "O Sacrificer, what is there?"
"May it be auspicious," [he says];
"may that be ours together.
Whatever [portion] the Adhvaryu leaves behind, that the sacrificer touches.
(6.28:191.15) Of the two southern [cords], the Adhvaryu touches the rear one first, and the sacrificer the front one.
(6.28:191.16) Here the Adhvaryu asks,
and then the sacrificer.
The Adhvaryu touches the northern of the two rear [stones], and the sacrificer the southern one.
Here the sacrificer asks,
and then the Adhvaryu.
Regarding the two subsequent [vessels], the Adhvaryu touches the first one and the Sacrificer the latter.
Here, the Adhvaryu asks first,
and then the Sacrificer.
The sacrificer asks first, and the sacrificer asks last.

Then he touches them all in succession, saying: "Thou art the Virāj, the slayer of rivals; thou art the Samrāj, the slayer of enemies; thou art the Svarāj, the slayer of the malevolent; thou art the Viśvārāj, the destroyer of all destructive powers. Thus he addresses them all in order.

(6.28:192.1) Then he sprinkles them with water, [saying]: "I sprinkle you, the Rakṣas-slayers, the spell-destroyers, belonging to Viṣṇu," over all of them in due order. (6.28:192.3) Then he pours water upon them, [saying]: "I pour down upon you, the Rakṣas-slayers, the spell-destroyers, belonging to Viṣṇu," upon all of them in due order.
(6.28:192.4) Then he scatters barley-grains upon them, [saying]: "Thou art barley; drive away from us those who hate us; drive away our enemies," upon all of them in due order.

(6.28:192.5) Then he strews sacrificial grass over them with the formula: "I strew [you], the Rakṣas-slayers, the spell-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu," doing so for all of them in due order. (6.28:192.7) Then, having placed gold between himself and them, he makes an oblation over them with the dipping-spoon (sruva) with the formula: "I offer [you], the Rakṣas-slayers, the spell-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu, svāhā! doing so for all of them in due order.
(6.28:192.8) Now, these two sounding-boards (phalaka) of his are perforated in a long Soma sacrifice, but not perforated in a one-day (ekāha) sacrifice.
He places them so that they touch each other with the formula: "I place you two, the Rakṣas-slayers, the charm-destroyers, belonging to Viṣṇu.
Then he fixes them around with stakes—two in front, two behind, and two on either side—to prevent them from slipping away.
Then he heaps earth around them from left to right with the formula: "I heap around you two, the Rakṣas-slayers, the charm-destroyers, belonging to Viṣṇu."
(6.28:192.13) Then he strews sacrificial grass around them with the formula: "I strew you, the two Rakṣas-slayers, the two Valaga-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu.
(6.28:192.14) Then he touches them with the formula: "The two Rakṣas-slayers, the two Valaga-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu.
(6.28:192.15) Then he spreads this skin over the two boards, with the neck pointing eastward and the hair facing upward, either with the formula "O Sacrifice, be established! or silently.
(6.28:192.17) He causes the pressing-stones to resound upon the wooden board covered with a skin.
"Thou art great, O great pressing-stone; utter a great voice for Indra!"—
with these words he spreads this skin upon the seat and places a pressing-stone among the stones.
(6.29:193.1) Then, in front of the support of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, he ties down a handful of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the sake of the hymns of praise (*stotra*).
(6.29:193.2) Then he asks for the wooden sword (*sphya*), a water-pot, earth from the pit (*cātvāla*), and sand.
(6.29:193.3) Having taken all this together, he says: "Come, O sacrificer!"

Having hastened to the Āgnīdhra shed, having dug up with the wooden sword and sprinkled [the ground], he pours down earth from the *cātvāla* pit along with sand, saying: "Thou art pervasive, the carrier; protect me, O Agni, with thy fierce aspect; carry me across; do not harm me.
He makes that hearth (*dhiṣṇiya*) circular, and then he makes it shining with sand.
Then, within the *sadas*, he pours out the hearth-mounds (*dhiṣṇiya*), first that of the Hotṛ with the formula: "Thou art the bearer, the carrier of oblations.
To the south, that of the Maitrāvaruṇa with: "Thou art the invigorating one, the wise. To the north, that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin with: "Thou art Tutha, the all-knowing."
(6.29:193.10) “You are the eager one, you are the sage,” [he says] to the north of the Potṛ.
(6.29:193.11) “You are the swift one, you are the Bambhāri,” [he says] to the north of the Neṣṭṛ.
(6.29:193.11) “You are the seeker of aid, you are the worshipper,” [he says] to the north of the Acchāvāka.
Then, at the southern edge of the altar, he pours out the *mārjālīya* hearth with the formula: "Thou art the purifier, the *mārjālīya*.
In all cases, he continues [the procedure] with the verse addressed to Rudra.
Finally, he pours it out at the *āgnīdhra* shed, [standing] facing north.
(6.29:193.14) "He has poured down eight [grains]," he says.
(6.29:193.15) Then he assigns eight [of them],
and (6.29:193.15) with the words, "Thou art the sovereign, O Kṛśānu," he worships the Āhavanīya fire.
(6.29:193.16) "Thou art the one to be honored, O Pavamāna," [with these words] he addresses the Āstāva;
(6.29:193.16) "Thou art the swift-moving, the wind-like," [with these words] the Cātvāla;
(6.29:193.17) "Thou art unswept, the preparer of the oblation," [with these words] the Paśuśrapaṇa.
Then, standing at the door of the *sadas*, he worships the Audumbarī post with: "Thou art the abode of Truth, the light of heaven. With:
"Thou art the light of Brahman, the abode of heaven," he worships the seat of the Brahman priest.
Then, remaining in that very place, he worships the Gārhapatya fire with: "Thou art the one-footed goat."
(6.29:194.2) "Thou art the serpent of the deep," [he says] over one whom they are about to abandon.

(6.30:194.4) Then, standing right there, he issues the direction: "Strew the sacrificial grass! Offer the *vrata* milk! Summon those who share in the *vrata*. Strew the *āstāva* thickly! Strew the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds thickly! O *unnetṛ*, having placed the ten-stranded filter upon the *daśāpavitra* in the *droṇakalaśa*, set down the pressing-stones and the vessels for the *vāyavya* cups in the wife’s hall! O *agnīdh*, place the clarified butter on the fire! O *pratiprasthātṛ*, cleanse the offering-spoons! Come forth with the clarified butter!
Bring curds for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*)! Thus.
They perform according to the directions.
Then, at the southern edge of the altar, he spreads a handful of sacrificial grass with the formula: "O divine sacrificial grass, soft as wool, I spread thee, a comfortable seat for the gods.
They proceed, spreading it thickly from the east towards the west.
(6.30:194.11) Then, having taken the clarified butter mixed with clotted curds (*pṛṣadājya*) inside the hall and handed it over to the attendants, he hands the King Soma over to the Brahman priest.
(6.30:194.12) Having taken him, the Brahman stands to the north.

Standing to the north, he leads the fire forward [with the verse]: "Arise, O Agni; rise after me, being in harmony with all the gods worthy of sacrifice. Place the sacrificer in the world of heaven; do not abandon this oblation for which we approach you. (6.30:194.13) Thus he says.
Then he places the fuel for the leading forward of the fire. They prepare the supporting-bricks from the *cātvāla* pit.

When those who have taken the vow have touched him and the area is covered, having melted the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire and purified it, and having taken four portions in the ladle, he offers the *vaisarjana* oblations on the *śālāmukhīya* fire with the verse: "O Soma, you are the one who provides wide protection against the bodily injuries and the hostilities caused by others; svāhā!"
With the *sruva*-ladle, he causes [the butter] to splash into [the fire], saying: "May the swift one, enjoying the clarified butter, partake; *svāhā*!
Having taken another fourfold portion, he issues the call: "Recite for Agni and Soma as they are being led forward. When this has been recited three times, they lift up [the ladles].
They go according to the will of the Hotṛ.
Now, it is indeed said:
"They carry the fire forward; they lead the wife away; they cause the entrails to be moved along."
Whatever sacrificial implement he has here, with that they first settle down by the fire.
Then, preceded by the fire, they set out; following behind are the King (Soma), the clarified butter, and the pressing-stones along with the Vāyavya cups.

They go out through the eastern door, [reciting]: "May this Agni create wide space for us; may he go before us, shattering our adversaries. May he, exulting, conquer the enemies; may he win the prize in the contest for booty."

Having gone around the north of the *sadas* and having placed the fire in the *āgnīdhra* shed, he offers an oblation in the *āgnīdhra* with a verse containing the word "lead": "O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God who knows all ways; keep away from us the crooked sin; we shall offer to thee the most abundant speech of homage, Svāhā!
At this very spot, having set down the pressing-stone for the *vāyavya* cup, they pass by with the King Soma and the clarified butter.

He offers a spoonful of oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely; make wide room for our dwelling. Drink the ghee, O you whose source is ghee! Further on and on the lord of the sacrifice, Svāhā! Thus.
Then he rises with the sprinkling waters;
he sprinkles the fuel and he sprinkles the altar.
He sprinkles the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass that has been placed down and having poured water over it, he takes the *āśvavāla* grass as the *prastara* from the front.
Having spread the sacrificial grass in five rows, holding the *prastara* in his hand and moving forward toward the east, he lays the enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood around the fire.
He places two fuel-sticks upright.
He lays down two separating-blades made of sugarcane crosswise,
and upon the two separating-blades, the prastara-bunch made of *aśvavāla* grass.

He places the *juhū* on the *prastara*, and the other two ladles on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Having touched them all together with the formula, "These have sat down," and having touched water, he takes the King [Soma] from the Brahman and causes him to enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door with the verse: "Soma goes forth, the knower of the way; he goes to the appointed place of the gods, to sit upon the womb of *ṛta*."

Then, he spreads a black antelope skin in the interior of the southern *havirdhāna* cart with the formula: "Thou art the seat of Aditi. With the formula: "Sit on the seat of Aditi," he places the King [Soma] upon the black antelope skin. Then he hands him over to the deities with the formula: "O divine Savitṛ, this is your Soma; guard him; let him not deceive you."

The tradition continues: "{F etat}{FN TS.1.3.4.2.i. Weber: et;aṃ. BI, AnSS, GOLS: et;at.}{TSw et;aṃ}{TSgols et;at}{BI etat} O Soma, you, a god, have approached the gods; here I, a human, [approach] humans, together with offspring, together with the increase of wealth.
Saying "Homage to the gods," he makes a *añjali* gesture facing eastward; saying "Svadhā to the ancestors," he lowers it toward the south.
Then he steps out [of the enclosure], saying: "Here I release myself from the noose of Varuṇa.
Then he worships the Āhavanīya fire, saying: "May I behold the light of Vaiśvānara, the heavenly light."

(6.31:196.18) Then he releases the sacrificer from the intermediate consecration with the formula: "O Agni, Lord of Vows, you are the lord of vows among vows. That body of mine which was in you, let it now be in me; that body of yours which was in me, let it now be in you. O Lord of Vows, according to our respective natures, let the vows of us two who have observed the vows be fulfilled."

(6.31:196.21) Then he instructs him: "Untie your girdle; loosen your fists; hand over the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa; let them address you as 'Sacrificer' by calling your name; let the Subrahmaṇya priest invoke the Subrahmaṇyā for you along with your fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, sons, and grandsons. He does all this exactly in that manner. (6.31:197.3) Then, having offered the oblation for the sacrificial post, he prepares the post with the Yajus formula.
He prepares the pit for the sacrificial post with a *yajus* formula;
this concludes the section on the pit for the sacrificial post.
Then he erects the sacrificial post according to the procedure for the post.
Having set aside the post provided with a wooden cup (*svaru*), he dedicates the animal to Agni and Soma.
Having performed the rite with its omentum in the established manner and having thrown the two omentum-spits into the fire, they step out and purify themselves at the *cātvāla* pit.
Then he asks for that firm jar. Having taken it, they go out toward the north between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, and proceed to where there is water;
he does not pass over the waters as they flow toward their end.
He does not take [the water] from stationary sources;
he takes it while standing against the current;

he takes it at the junction of shade and sunlight, [reciting]: "These waters are rich in oblation; the divine sacrifice is rich in oblation; he seeks to win with oblation; may Sūrya be rich in oblation."

Then, having taken them up, having turned to the right, and having placed them on his left shoulder, he returns by the same way he came, goes around the north of the Āgnīdhrīya fire, goes around the north of the Sadas, enters the hall by the eastern door, and places them behind the Gārhapatya fire on the Aupasadā altar, touching them together, with the formula: "I place you in the seat of Agni whose house is secure; O gracious ones, for the sake of grace, bestow grace upon me."
(6.32:197.17) Then he offers the sacrificial cake for the animal victim.
(6.32:197.18) The sacrificial cake for the animal victim concludes with the *iḍā* invocation; the animal sacrifice concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Some say that it ends with the *hṛdayaśūla* (the rite for the heart-piercing).
Then, about to carry around the *vasatīvarī* waters, he says: "Step aside; let me not carry them around you.
The sacrificer sits down in the sacrificer’s station, and the wife sits behind the *gārhapatya* fire.

Then, having taken them up, having carried them out by the southern door, having placed them on his left shoulder, having gone around the south of the *sadas*, and having carried them around the south of the *mārjālīya* hearth, he sets them down to the south, touching the sacrificial post, with the formula: "You are the portions of Indra and Agni."

Then, having taken them up, turned toward the north, and placed them on his right shoulder, he returns by the same way he came, goes behind the Gārhapatya fire, and sets them down in contact with one another upon the *aupasadā* altar, saying: "You are the portion of Mitra and Varuṇa."

Then, having taken them up and carried them out by the eastern door, having placed them on the southern shoulder [of the altar], having gone around the north of the *sadas*, and having carried them around the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth, he sets them down to the north, touching the sacrificial post, with the formula: "You are the portions of all the gods.

Then, having taken them up, having turned clockwise, having placed them on his left shoulder, and having returned by the same way he came, he sets them down behind the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth, touching it, with the formula: "Be watchful at the sacrifice."

(6.34:198.15) Then he assigns the milks: "From that cow which yields for the *samrāj*, prepare curds for the *dadhigharma*; from that which belongs to the sacrificer, [prepare] curds for the *āmikṣā*; from that which belongs to the wife, [prepare] milk for the *āśira*. Prepare both milk and parched grain flour. Prepare curds for the *ādityagraha* as a mixture with boiled milk. Prepare the flour for the sacrificial cakes. Prepare parched grains for the *hāriyojana* cup. Prepare four *ambhṛṇa* vessels, three *udacana* vessels, and uneven numbers of *ekadhana* jars, with three being the smallest."

"Prepare eleven sets of four cords each, four omentum-spits, two bundles of fuel and sacrificial grass, and large enclosing-sticks of Udumbara wood; let the Subrahmaṇya priest invoke the Subrahmaṇyā. Thus they act according to the directions.
Then he causes these Ambhṛṇa vessels to be brought forward.
The *ādhavanīya* [vessel] is in the interior of the northern *havirdhāna* cart;
the *pūtabhṛt* [vessel] is on the front beam (*prauga*);
their water-fetching vessel is common to both.
One [pot] with its lid is at the Āgnīdhra fire;
one [pot] with its lid is at the Mārjālīya fire. On this night, the sacrificer sleeps at the Āgnīdhra fire.
They guard the King [Soma] in the two Havirdhāna sheds.
(7.1:200.1) Now, therefore, they wake up at the very dead of night.

They awaken these officiating priests: the Adhvaryu, the Hotṛ, the Brahman, the Udgātṛ, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Prastotṛ, the Praśāstṛ, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Acchāvāka, the Neṣṭṛ, the Potṛ, the Sadasya, the Unnetṛ, the Āgnīdhra, the Grāvastut, the Subrahmaṇya, and the Pratihartṛ, as well as whatever other assistants there may be.
Having washed their hands and feet, they approach the sacrificer in the Āgnīdhra shed.
(7.1:200.6) Then the Adhvaryu rubs his hands together, saying: "May I be capable for you two for the sake of the work for the gods.

(7.1:200.6) Then, standing right there, he issues the command: "O Unnetṛ, having placed the pressing-stones and the Vāyavya cups along with the fringe-filters in the Droṇakalaśa, set them down in front of the axle of the southern Havirdhāna cart. O Agnīdh, place the clarified butter on the fire. O Pratiprasthātṛ, wipe the offering-spoons. Come forth with the clarified butter. Bring curds for the speckled butter."
They act according to the directions.

Then the Adhvaryu touches the Āgnīdhra shed with a verse addressed to Agni: "Agni is the head of heaven... He touches the Havirdhāna shed with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu: "O Viṣṇu, you are our nearest relative..."

With a verse addressed to Agni, he offers with the *sruva* ladle: "This Agni [is the lord] of thousands. With a verse addressed to Vāyu, he offers the *vāyavya* cups: "O Vāyu, a hundred bay horses [are yours].
With a verse addressed to Indra, he offers for the *sadas*: "All have made Indra grow great."
Then, having taken the portions of clarified butter mixed with clotted butter, he rises with the sprinkling waters;
he sprinkles the fuel and he sprinkles the altar.
He sprinkles the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Having sprinkled the sacrificial grass that has been placed down and having poured water over it, he takes up the *prastara* bundle from the front.

Having spread the sacrificial grass in a single layer, holding the *prastara* in his hand, he moves forward toward the east and lays down the large enclosing sticks (*mahāparidhi*) made of *udumbara* wood with the standard formula for laying them down.
Then he yokes them with a formula:
"I yoke the earth for thee together with light," [he says] for the middle one;
"I yoke Vāyu for thee together with the intermediate space," [he says] for the southern one.
(7.1:200.20) "I yoke your speech together with the sun," he says over the northern [ladle].
Then he touches the placed ladles, saying, "I yoke the three distinct ones for you, the sun.
Then, having touched water, he says, "Come, O sacrificer."

Having caused [the Soma] to enter the Havirdhāna shed by the eastern door, he then spreads this skin upon the two planks with its neck toward the east and the hair upward, either with the formula, "O Sacrifice, be established," or silently.

Having placed the pressing-stones facing each other upon it, he brings down the King [Soma] between the two poles of the southern Havirdhāna cart with two verses: "For the heart thee! For the mind thee! O King Soma, come, descend!
Then he announces him to the Udgātṛs.
In that [place], they perform whatever rites they know. Then, having touched water, he says, "Come, O sacrificer.

Having run to the Āgnīdhra shed and taken four spoonfuls into the offering-ladle, he recites the Pañcahotṛ formula mentally and offers it into the Āgnīdhra fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying, "Svāhā!"
Having taken another fourfold portion, the Āgnīdhra offers it into the mouth [of the fire] with the formula: "Protect me from the curse of the mouth, from every imprecation, svāhā!
Then he silently places a chip of wood smeared with ghee onto the Āhavanīya fire. Then, standing right there, he issues the call.

(7.2:201.12) "O Hotṛ, recite for the gods who travel at dawn! O Brahman, restrain your speech! O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā! O Agnīdh, pour out the oblations for the *savanīya* [sacrificial cakes]! O Pratiprasthātṛ, arrange the vessels on the mound!
Thus they act according to the directions.
Then the Hotṛ begins the *prātaranuvāka*.
The Brahman restrains his speech;
the Subrahmaṇya priest invokes the Subrahmaṇyā formula.
When that has been invoked, the Brahman releases his speech.
The Āgnīdhra offers these Savanīya cakes for Indra on eleven potsherds.
He causes the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*) to be raised specifically over the rice grains. They then take up the barley.
(7.2:201.18) Then the Pratiprasthātṛ arranges the vessels on the mound.

(7.2:202.1) He places the Upāṃśusavana stone on the front half of the mound with its head toward the south. To the south [of that] he places the Upāṃśu vessel, and to the north the Antaryāma vessel, so that they are touching;
however, for one practicing sorcery, they should not touch.
(7.2:202.3) Behind [the Āgrayaṇa vessel], following in sequence, are the vessels for the two deities: the cup for Indra and Vāyu, the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa, and the cup for the Aśvins.
(7.2:202.4) Behind those, the cups for the Śukra and Manthin are placed side by side: the Śukra cup to the south and the Manthin cup to the north.
(7.2:202.5) In front of the Manthin cup are the two Ṛtu cups.
Behind [the Āgrayaṇa vessel], he places the Āgrayaṇa-sthālī.
On the southern buttock of the mound, he places the Āditya-sthālī together with its supplementary cup (upaśaya);
on the northern buttock of the mound, he places the Ukthya-sthālī together with its supplementary cup.
In front of the support of the northern *havirdhāna* cart, on ground that has not been strewn with sand, he places the *dhruva* vessel;
between the *pūtabhṛt* and the *ādhavanīya*, the cups; and behind the axle of the southern *havirdhāna*, the *droṇakalaśa* and the two *daśāpavitra* strainers. He sets them down.
(7.2:202.10) Then he touches them with ten formulas, one for each: "Agni is the deity; the Gāyatrī is the metre; thou art the cup of the Upāṃśu.
(7.2:202.11) Then the Adhvaryu either enters [the cart-shed] or remains watching over the ritual acts.

(7.3:202.13) Now, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting: "The Dawn has appeared with her white cattle; Agni has been laid down in due season. Your immortal chariot, O wonder-workers, rich in stallions, has been yoked. O lovers of sweetness, hear my call!"—then, having taken four spoonfuls into the *pracaraṇī* ladle, he offers it into the Āhavanīya fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "May Agni hear my call with his fuel; may the Waters and the divine Dhiṣaṇās hear."
"Listen, O pressing-stones, to the sacrifice of the wise; may the god Savitṛ hear my invocation, Svāhā!

Having taken another fourfold portion and taken the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he issues the command: "O Hotṛ, send forth the waters! O Camasādhvaryu of the Maitrāvaruṇa, come hither! Ekadhanins, come! O Neṣṭṛ, lead up the wife! O Agnīdh, receive [the water] at the Cātvāla pit with the Hotṛ’s cup and the Vasatīvarī waters!
They act according to the command.
The Neṣṭṛ leads the wife forward, taking the Pānnejana vessel, with this liturgical formula: "Go forth! Come up!

Having caused her to go out by the eastern door, having led her around the north of the Sadas, and having led her around the north of the Āgnīdhra hearth, they exit between the Cātvāla pit and the Utkara mound toward the north and proceed to where there is water.

(7.3:203.4) Then, having thrown sacrificial grass (*barhis*) into the water, he makes an offering over it with the formula: "O divine waters, O Son of the Waters, that wave of yours which is fit for oblation, powerful, and most intoxicating—that, bestow among the gods in a godly manner, pure for those who drink the pure, you whose portion we are;
*svāhā*! (7.3:203.7) With the cup of Maitrāvaruṇa, he causes the offering to float away with the formula: "Thou art the furrower; [drive] away the enemy of the waters.
(7.3:203.8) Having placed two blades of sacrificial grass in between, he draws up [the water] with the formula: "For the imperishability of the ocean, I draw you up."
(7.3:203.8) Then he draws the Ekadhana cups, either with the formula, "I draw you, acceptable to Indra," or silently.

(7.3:203.9) Then he draws the Pannejani waters with the formula, "I draw the Pannejani waters for the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Viśve Devas; I draw you, the Pannejani waters, for the sacrifice. (7.3:203.11) Having handed them over to the wife, they rise up.

When the sacrificer has taken hold [of him], having returned by the same way they came, he touches together the *hotṛ*’s cup and the *maitrāvaruṇa*’s cup at the *cātvāla* pit and pours out the *vasatīvarī* waters.
He fills the *hotṛ*’s cup and causes water to splash into the *maitrāvaruṇa*’s cup.

Then, having placed together the *hotṛ*’s cup, the *vasatīvarī* waters, and the *maitrāvaruṇa*’s cup—these three—he anoints them with the *pracaraṇī* spoon according to the respective *stomas*, [reciting]: “May light be anointed with light; may the bright be anointed with the bright; may the oblation be anointed with the oblation; may the lord of the sacrifice be anointed with the blessing.
Then the wife, having returned by the same way she came, places them silently, touching them together on the *aupasadā* altar behind the *gārhapatya* fire.
Then the Adhvaryu goes toward the signal-call of the Hotṛ.
The Hotṛ asks the Adhvaryu: "Adhvaryu, have you seen [them]? "I have seen them," he replies. "They have bent down; look at them! the other replies.

(7.4:203.21) Now, if it is an *agniṣṭoma*, he offers with the verse: "O Agni, the mortal whom you protect in battles, whom you urge on in the contests for booty—he shall be the master of eternal refreshments, *svāhā*!

(7.4:204.1) And if it is an *ukthya*, he wipes [the ladle] on the middle enclosing-stick with this very same formula. (7.4:204.2) And if it is an *atirātra*, he enters [the sacrificial ground] while reciting this very formula.
"For the sake of distinguishing the sacrificial rites," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, having drawn these cups belonging to the Hotṛ through the space between the two poles of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, he sets them down in the *nīḍa*.
Then, having turned the *ādhavanīya* vessel upside down, he pours out all the contents of the cups belonging to the Maitrāvaruṇa.
He pours out a third of the *vasatīvarī* waters; he pours out a third of the *ekadhana* waters.
He places the *vasatīvarī* waters in front of the axle.
(7.4:204.7) Behind the axle, he places the Ekadhana jars. Then, having sat down between the two *havirdhāna* carts, he asks for a four-cornered vessel made of *udumbara* wood.

(7.4:204.8) Having placed two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) within it, he draws the *dadhi-graha* for Prajāpati, [saying]: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, the luminous, for the luminous Prajāpati; for Dakṣa, the increaser of skill; offered to the gods who have Agni as their tongue, who live by truth, whose chief is Indra, whose king is Varuṇa, whose breath is Vāta, and whose soul is Parjanya. Thus.
