(9.7:275.3) Then he touches this [earth] with: "Thou art the mare of Manu, having many sons; protect me from all destructive powers; mayest thou be easy of access to me; do not harm me.

(9.7:275.5) Then, with the two poking-sticks, he draws out the embers toward the north with: "O Agni, burn up the enemies within thee; burn the curse of the hostile stranger. O Vasu, being wise, burn those who are mindless; let thy ageless, unwearied flames spread abroad."
With these [bricks], he encloses it to the right, saying: "You are piled; you are piled around! Svāhā! Be enclosed by the Maruts!
Then the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ enclose it with thirteen enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *vikaṅkata* wood.
The Adhvaryu places two [sticks] pointing eastward, saying: "Thou art the measure."
(9.7:275.11) "Thou art the measure," says the Pratiprasthātṛ, moving northward;
they both proceed in this very same manner with the interlocking formulas: "Thou art the counter-measure," "Thou art the equal-measure," "Thou art the distinct-measure," "Thou art the upward-measure.
(9.7:275.12) Then he fixes the thirteenth enclosing-stick on the south side with its tip pointing upward, saying: "Thou art the interior space of the atmosphere."
(9.7:275.14) Then he covers it with a golden plate, [saying]: "Protect the sky from heat!
(9.7:275.14) Then he pays homage to it, [reciting]: "With these songs," "One of thy forms is bright," and "Worthy, thou carriest arrows and bow.
(9.7:275.16) When it has flared up, he removes the golden plate.

(9.8:275.17) Then he takes up the fans: with "Thou art the Gāyatra," he takes one; with "Thou art the Triṣṭubh," another; and with "Thou art the Jāgata," another. (9.8:275.18) With these, bending his knee, he fans him from behind toward the east, saying, "Honey, honey, honey. (9.8:275.19) He hands two fans to the Pratiprasthātṛ standing to the north.
(9.8:276.1) He hands one of the two to the Āgnīdhra.
(9.8:276.1) Then they walk around him three times clockwise, fanning [the fire] at each *praṇava*. Having walked around three times, they stand to the north.
(9.8:276.2) Then he takes up the fans.
(9.8:276.3) Having walked around by the rear, he gives two fans to the Pratiprasthātṛ standing to the north. (9.8:276.4) Of those two, he hands one over to the Āgnīdhra.
Then they sit down around him:
the Adhvaryu sits behind, facing east,
and the Pratiprasthātṛ sits in front, facing west.
To the north, the Āgnīdhra sits facing south.
In this very manner, they remain fanning [the fire] at every *praṇava*, keeping the embers together and causing the *mahāvīra* to swell.

Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ’s recitation, "With those [rays] by which you released the swallowed quail," the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer rise toward him and cause it to shine with this section: "Ten rays toward the east, ten thou shinest toward the south."

(9.8:276.10) Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting, "O Aśvins, may our speech be effective," at that moment they lift up the fans. (9.8:276.11) Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting, "The dappled one, the foremost, has caused the dawn to shine," at that point, having said, "The Gharma has shone," they walk back around three times in the same manner as they came, setting down the fans.
They worship while looking at the openings [of the fire-places], beginning with the verse, "I have seen the Herdsman," and continuing until the words, "May we enjoy thee; do not harm me."

(9.8:276.15) Then he worships the Gārhapatya fire with: "O Agni, you are the lord of the household of the clans, of all human clans. O youngest one, protect us from distress with a hundred fortresses for a hundred winters! May there be gifts right here for the one who kindles you, for the tireless one, for the one who possesses a heart of compassion! Thus.
When [the Adhvaryu] has disappeared, the Pratiprasthātṛ causes the wife to recite from the Veda: "May I consort with thee, O thou who art accompanied by Tvaṣṭṛ," up to the end of the section.
At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the southern Rauhiṇa cake with the formula: "May the day, as light, be pleased with its banner; may the fair-lighted one [be pleased] with light, svāhā!"
(9.9:277.1) Then he takes up the girdle with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee.
(9.9:277.2) Having taken it, he consecrates it with: "Thou art the girdle of Aditi.
(9.9:277.3) The Pratiprasthātṛ, having gone around behind, [takes] the milking vessel and the two *pinvana* bowls.
Then he calls this cow that yields the *gharma* three times in a whisper by the names of the deities: "O *Iḍā*, come! O *Aditi*, come! O *Sarasvatī*, come!
Three times he calls aloud, having gone out through the southern door, using whatever name she may have: "O so-and-so, come! O so-and-so, come!
Then he ties her with the rope, saying: "Thou art the turban of Aditi."
(9.9:277.7) With the words, "Vāyu art thou, belonging to the Ṛg-verses," he touches the calf of the Gharma-cow.
(9.9:277.8) Then he lets it loose with the words, "May Pūṣan let thee loose; cause [the milk] to be given to the Aśvins."

He addresses the calf as it suckles: "That breast of thine which is inexhaustible, which is refreshing, by which thou nourishest all desirable things; that which bestows jewels, finds wealth, and is a liberal giver—O Sarasvatī, bring that here for it to suck.
When [the milk] has been offered, he pours it out, saying: "O Dawn, warm the *gharma*! O Dawn, drink the *gharma*! Warm [it] for the *gharma*!"

Having joined and aligned [the ladle], he approaches it with the formula: "May Bṛhaspati approach you. He touches the breasts [of the vessel] with: "You are givers, you are flowing; you are encompassed on all sides by blood.

Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ's recitation, "With ten [fingers] from Vivasvat," he causes her to swell in the two milking vessels with: "Swell for the Aśvins; swell for Sarasvatī; swell for Pūṣan; swell for Bṛhaspati; swell for Indra; swell for Indra."
(9.9:277.17) He causes the remainder to be milked into a bronze vessel.

(9.9:277.17) At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ silently milks the she-goat into the *pinvana* vessel. (9.9:278.1) Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting, "Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati," he hands over the two portions of milk to the Pratiprasthātṛ and returns by the same way he came. He takes up the hoof-supports: [he takes] one with the formula, "Thou art Gāyatra," and the other with, "Thou art Traiṣṭubha"; [he takes] the supporting tray with, "Thou art Jāgata."

(9.9:278.4) Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting, "Come near with milk, O milker of the cow, hither!"—at that moment, as the two portions of milk are being brought forward, he consecrates them with: "Come toward me with a share of vigor; O Indra and Aśvins, drink the Gharma of the honeyed *sāragha* [bees' honey]; O Vasus, sacrifice, *vaṭ*!
(9.9:278.7) Then, having sat down to the east facing westward, both the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ pour the two portions of milk into the Mahāvīra vessel.
The Adhvaryu first pours in the cow’s milk with the formula: “Svāhā! I offer thee for the rain-winning ray of the sun, svāhā!
Then he gazes at its steam with the formula: “Thou art honey, the oblation; heat the heat of the sun!
At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ silently pours in the goat’s milk.
Having brought both together, the Adhvaryu pours a third portion into them.

At this point, he pours whatever milk was in the bronze vessel into the supporting ladle, having pushed back the embers; then the Adhvaryu grasps the Mahāvīra vessel used for the ritual performance with its two handles.

"By means of heaven and earth, I enclose thee," with these words he wipes beneath [the fire] with the *veda* grass-bundle and supports it with the supporting-stand, saying, "By means of the intermediate space, I support thee. Then, taking it up, he stands up, saying, "Permitted by the gods and the ancestors, may I be able to carry thee."

He carries it forward with: "Thou art brilliance; follow after brilliance! May Agni protect me from the earth, Vāyu from the intermediate space, and Sūrya from the sky! Do not harm me, O toucher of the sky; do not harm me, O toucher of the intermediate space; do not harm me, O toucher of the earth! Thou art *suvar*; grant me *suvar*; grant me the sky; protect me from the sky! Then he recites the names of the winds: "To the ocean-like wind, svāhā!"—thus five times without pausing. In the same way, he recites two further [formulas].

(9.10:279.6) There are six subsequent [oblations], according to the order of their occurrence: "To Agni, accompanied by the Vasus, svāhā! To Soma, accompanied by the Rudras, svāhā! To Varuṇa, accompanied by the Ādityas, svāhā! To Bṛhaspati, accompanied by the Viśve Devas, svāhā! To Savitṛ, accompanied by the Arbhus, the Vibhus, the Prabhus, and Vāja, svāhā! To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Pitṛs, svāhā!
(9.10:279.9) With the words, "May all the quarters be occupied by the sacrificial fee," he gazes at the Brahman seated to the south.

"Viśvān devān ayāḍ iha"—with these words [he addresses] the Hotṛ seated behind. Stepping across with his left foot, he murmurs: "O Aśvins, drink of the honeyed Gharma consecrated by Svāhā! Svāhā to Agni worthy of sacrifice! May there be well-being through the Yajus-formulas! With this, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "O Aśvins, drink the Gharma that gladdens the heart, day after day with your aids! May Heaven and Earth approve of you both."
Having called out loudly, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the Gharma. When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the oblation, saying, "Svāhā to Indra!"

(9.10:279.16) Having offered at the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call with the words, "Svāhā! O Indra! Vaṭ!", he causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "O Aśvins, you have drunk the Gharma that gladdens the heart, day by day with your aids. May Heaven and Earth approve of you both. As is fitting, protect that which is to be protected. Homage to Heaven! Homage to Earth! Place this sacrifice in heaven! Place this sacrifice in heaven! Go to heaven! Go to the intermediate space! Go to the earth! Go to the five directions!"
"Go to the gods who drink the Gharma; go to the ancestors who drink the Gharma.
At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having dipped the milking vessel into the supporting tray, fills the Mahāvīra vessel used for the performance.

(9.10:279.22) Then the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ together cause it to swell inside the enclosing sticks, saying in a whisper: "Swell for food; swell for strength; swell for the Brahman; swell for the Kṣatra; swell for the waters; swell for the plants; swell for the trees; swell for heaven and earth; swell for well-being; swell for spiritual luster; swell for the sacrificer; [swell] for me. Having said this, he says aloud: "Swell for preeminence!"
(9.10:280.5) Then he causes himself to swell toward each of the quarters with the formulas: "For brilliance thee! For splendor thee! For power thee! For prosperity thee!
(9.10:280.6) At this point, whatever milk is in the *mahāvīra* vessel, he pours it into the supporting tray (*upayamana*).
(9.10:280.7) Then, having stepped across to the north, he places that supporting tray within the altar (*antarvedi*) with its opening facing east.
At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ hides the silver plate on the mound at the Udvāsanīya fire;
upon it he places the Mahāvīra vessel used for the ritual performance.

(9.11:280.11) “You are Dharma, O good Dharma! Uphold our sacred formulations (*brahmāṇi*), uphold the powers of the nobility (*kṣatrāṇi*), uphold the common people (*viśam*). May the wind not cause you to fall! Thus [he says]. (9.11:280.12) Now, if he should practice sorcery, [he says]: “I place you in the breath of so-and-so! Go forth to ruin along with him who hates us and whom we hate! Thus [he says].
Then, having touched water, he asks for six chips of Udumbara wood.
Having taken one from each of them with the supporting ladle, he lets it drip onto the eastern part of the Āhavanīya fire, saying: "To Pūṣan, the sap, svāhā!
Then he places it, touching it, within the ointment between the middle enclosing-sticks.

In the same manner, having dipped the second [wick] into the supporting tray (*upayamana*), he lets it drip onto the eastern half of the *āhavanīya* fire with the formula: "To the pressing-stones, svāhā!
He then places it so that it touches the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) at its inner end.
In the same manner, having dipped the third [wick] into the supporting tray, he lets it drip in the middle of the *āhavanīya* fire with the formula: "To the Pratirebhas, svāhā!"
He places that very same inner ointment, touching it, upon the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*).

In the same manner, having taken a portion from the supporting-wood (*upayamana*) with the fourth [ladle], he lets it drip onto the rear half of the *āhavanīya* fire, saying: "To Heaven and Earth, svāhā!
Then he hides this upper ointment within the ashes.

In the same manner, having struck [the fire] with the fifth splinter from the supporting grass-bundle (*upayamana*), he lets it drip onto the southern half of the *āhavanīya* fire, saying: "Svāhā to the fathers who drink the *gharma*!
Then he places it, so that it touches the southern enclosing-stick (*paridhi*), outside the area of the ointment.

Then, having anointed this sixth splinter with all the residues and finally striking it from the supporting grass-bundle, he lets it drip onto the northern half of the *āhavanīya* fire, saying: "Svāhā to Rudra, whose Hotṛ is Rudra!"
(9.11:281.10) Then, looking after him through an opening to the north of the hall, he throws [the wood] out with the formula: "Go away to ruin along with that one who hates us and whom we hate.

(9.11:281.12) Then, having touched water and having moistened the remaining chips with water, he throws them into the Āhavanīya fire. (9.11:281.13) At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the northern Rauhiṇa cake with the formula: "May the Day enjoy the light with its banner; may the fair-lighted one [enjoy] the lights, svāhā!"
At this point, he silently places this fuel-stick in the middle of the Āhavanīya fire.
When it has caught fire, he makes two offerings facing it with the formula: "bhūḥ svāhā.
Then, having placed this supporting ladle within the altar with its opening facing east, he performs the ritual procedure for the Agnihotra over it.

Having sought the invitation from as many officiating priests of the *pravargya* rite as there are, the sacrificer himself consumes [the portion] directly, saying: "The oblation has been offered, the honeyed oblation in Agni, who is most like Indra. You are our father; do not harm me! O divine *gharma*, may we partake of you, who are honeyed, full of vigor, full of nourishment, belonging to the Aṅgirases, and possessed of the *svadhā*-call. May we enjoy you; do not harm me!"

(9.11:282.2) Then, having cleansed this supporting tray (*upayamana*) either on the mound of remains (*ucchiṣṭakhara*) or by the Āgnīdhra, and having placed it within the altar with its opening facing east, they cast into it two plates, one of gold and one of silver; then, having brought the boiling waters (*madantīr apaḥ*), they purify themselves with verses containing the word "gold" (*hiraṇyavatībhiḥ*).

With the four verses beginning, “Golden-colored, pure, purifying,” he pours out the boiling water right there. Then, dipping the spoon into the vessel of clarified butter, he offers the expiations for the *gharma* with these two sections: “To Prāṇa, svāhā! To Pūṣan, svāhā!

Having placed this supporting tray within the altar with its opening facing east, while completely extinguishing all that pertains to the *gharma*, he says: “Recite for the *gharma* as it is being set down.”

(9.12:282.10) Then, having carried this supporting tray around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it on the black antelope skin upon the Samrāḍ-āsandī to the south, with its opening facing east, [saying]: "Svāhā! To thee for the rays of the sun!
(9.12:282.12) Then they perform the subsequent pacification, [saying]: "May the wind, Mātariśvan, blow auspiciously for us!
(9.12:282.13) Then, in the afternoon, he proceeds with the afternoon Pravargya rite.
Whatever has been prescribed for that [northern Rauhiṇa cake] is indeed prescribed for this [southern one] as well;
the ritual action is the same up until the offering of the southern Rauhiṇa cake.
Then he offers the southern Rauhiṇa cake with the mantra: "May Night, the light, be pleased with the banner! O fair-lighted one, with light, svāhā!"
In the same manner, he offers the northern *rauhiṇa* oblation. The ritual procedure is identical up to the placing of the fuel-sticks (*samid*).

At this point, he places this fuel-stick in the middle of the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra: "You have carried me across from day to night; protect me! This is your fuel, O Agni; be kindled by it! Grant me long life; anoint me with splendor! Thus at evening. At dawn, [he says]: "You have carried me across from night to day; protect me!"

From that point forward, he adds fuel to the fire in the forenoon with the morning mantra and in the afternoon with the evening mantra. When it has been kindled, he makes two offerings facing it: "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā!"—thus in the evening.
"Sūrya is the light, the light is Sūrya, svāhā!"—thus at dawn. The ritual procedure is the same up to the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*).

Then, having carried this supporting ladle (*upayamana*) around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it on the black antelope skin upon the royal throne (*samrāḍāsandi*) to the south, with its opening facing west, saying: "Svāhā! Thee for the constellations!"*
Then they perform the subsequent pacification rite with the verse: "May Vāta Mātariśvan blow auspiciously for us.
In this very manner, he proceeds with the Pravargya ceremony for three days, six days, twelve days, or a year, or for four months in the case of the Tāpaścita fire-altar.
Having consumed the *pravargya* offering, one should not eat meat for a year;
one should not approach a woman;
and one should not drink from an earthen vessel.
"Rāma, one should not drink the remnants of this [offering];
it consumes his very vital energy," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(9.13:283.15) Intending to remove the *pravargya* vessel, he prepares three fire-sticks (*śālāka*), fuel-sticks (*idhma*), three hundred [blades of grass], two water-pitchers, curds mixed with honey, a handful of *grumuṣṭi* grass, a bundle of *avakā* plants, twenty fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood, cuttings of *muñja* grass, flour for the *rauhiṇa* cakes, and sand for the mounds (*khara*). (9.13:284.2) At this point they perform the first pacification rite with the mantra: "Homage to speech! Having spread grass in front of the *āhavanīya* fire, they place all these items belonging to the *parigharma* together upon it.
"Here [is] the royal throne-seat, here the pillar for the milking-vessel, and here the peg for the she-goat.
Then, having poured the remnants separately into these two *khara* mounds, they set them down together right here.

Then either the attendant or the *Āgnīdhra*, having poured the remnants of the *ucchiṣṭa-khara* into a vessel, carries it out through the southern door and pours it out in the region of the *Mārjālīya*.
(9.13:284.7) Then, having returned by the same way they came, they cause the Śūdras to go out.
(9.13:284.8) They call the wife;
they call the Hotṛ.
They summon the Brahman priest; they summon the Pratiprasthātṛ;
they summon the Prastotṛ.
They summon the Āgnīdhra.
They enclose the doors.
Then they shield this wife with a garment having its fringes pointing northward.
They strew [the grass] around.
The Brahman and the sacrificer sit down to the south. At this point, they perform the first *śānti* rite for those for whom it has not yet been performed.
Then, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire, he purifies it.
At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having kindled a faggot of Śālāka wood on the Āhavanīya fire and holding it at the height of his mouth, stands in front facing west.

The Adhvaryu, standing behind him facing east, makes an oblation with the dipping-spoon (sruva), saying: "O Gharma, that heat of yours which is in heaven, which is in the Gāyatrī metre, which is in the Brāhmaṇa, and which is in the Havirdhāna shed—by means of this, I appease that of yours; svāhā!"
Having thrown that very [fuel] into it and having kindled another, he stands in front facing west, holding [the vessel] at the height of the navel.

The Adhvaryu, standing behind him facing east, makes an offering with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), saying: "O Gharma, whatever heat of yours is in the intermediate space, in the *triṣṭubh* metre, in the *rājanya*, and in the *āgnīdhra*—that of yours I appease with this; *svāhā*!
Having thrown that very [fuel] into it and having kindled another, he stands in front facing west, holding [the vessel] at the height of the knee.

The Adhvaryu, standing behind him facing east, makes an oblation over it with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), saying: "O Gharma, that heat of yours which is in the earth, which is in the *jagatī* metre, which is in the Vaiśya, which is in the assembly—by means of this, I appease that of yours; *svāhā*!

Having thrown it right there and opened the doors, they then take up the Pravargya vessel and go out by the eastern door, reciting the two verses: "May Anumati favor us today... and "O Anumati, you indeed have favored us..."
Then, having stepped onto the great altar (mahāvedi), he says to the Prastotṛ, "O Prastotṛ, sing the Sāman!
The Prastotṛ follows with the Sāman;
he reaches the finale (nidhana) three times.
"Every person attains the *nidhana*," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then they step forward.
"From heaven, protect me from the one who seeks to harm us; guard the bodies of the intermediate space. By the law of the earth, we follow after thee for new prosperity.
With these words, at the *viṣuvat* [central day], they perform the second *nidhana*.
Then they step forward with the mantra: "For the protection of the *brahman*, guard the body of the *kṣatra*; we follow you according to the law of the *viś* for new prosperity."
At the time of the *uparava* holes, they perform the third *nidhana*.
Then they step forward [saying]: "For the protection of breath, guard my body; for sight, guard my limbs; by the law of hearing, we follow after thee for new prosperity."
(9.14:285.17) Then they stop to the north of the *uttaravedi*. He says to one who is strong: "Go around three times to the right, sprinkling a continuous stream from this water-pitcher.
He does so.

While the water is being sprinkled around, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "Thou art auspicious, for the bestowing of peace; a child for the nourishing of men. Bring us peace and bring it all around.
Having set down the jar, he goes back around three times in the same manner as he came.

(9.14:286.2) Then he touches the *uttaranābhi* with the mantra: "The four-cornered navel of Order, the seat, all-encompassing life, the wide-extending shelter—away from hatred, away from crookedness; we have followed another vow of the Law. (9.14:286.4) Then he scatters these two mounds to the north of the *uttaranābhi*.
With two pokers, he makes the hearth long from east to west and high;
having placed gold upon it, he spreads out a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and its hairy side upward.
Then, having scattered the flour of the *rauhiṇa* cakes over it, having covered it with cuttings of *muñja* grass, he scatters sand over it.

(9.14:286.8) Then the Adhvaryu, grasping the Mahāvīra vessel intended for use with two hooves, fills it with curds mixed with honey, saying: "O Gharma, this is your food, this is your nourishment; through this, grow and swell! May we also grow and may we also swell! (9.14:286.11) Then he pours into it [the milk], saying: "You are the milk of the great ones, ordained among the gods; you are the light of the trees and the essence of the plants; as those possessing strength, we pour you, who possess strength."
Then he places it on the front half of the sacrificial seat with the mantra: "The mind is directed upward toward heaven."
(9.15:286.15) Then, having taken these two *upaśaya* Mahāvīras and filled them with curds mixed with honey, he places them so that they touch the front of the *pracaraṇīya* Mahāvīra.
(9.15:286.17) Then, having filled this *pracaraṇī* with curds mixed with honey, he places it upon the Mahāvīras with its opening facing westward.
(9.15:286.18) Then, having anointed these two gold plates (*rukma*) with curds mixed with honey, he places them so that they touch the *pracaraṇīya* Mahāvīra on both sides.
(9.15:286.19) Then, having filled these two *pinvana* vessels with curds mixed with honey, he places them on either side of the *pracaraṇīya* *mahāvīra*, touching it, with their openings facing west.
(9.15:287.2) Then, having untied this *mauñja* cord, he anoints its tip with curds mixed with honey and spreads it out, touching the *mahāvīras*, with its tip pointing westward.

(9.15:287.4) Then, having anointed these two *śaphas* with curds mixed with honey, he places them behind the *pracaraṇīya* *mahāvīra*, their tips crossing transversely, interlaced, and touching one another.
(9.15:287.5) Then, having anointed these two Rauhiṇa-offering ladles with curds mixed with honey, he places them down so that their tips touch each other and point westward.
(9.15:287.7) Then, having anointed these ten Udumbara fuel-sticks with curds mixed with honey, he spreads them out behind the two Rauhiṇa-offering ladles, touching one another and pointing westward.

(9.15:287.9) Then, having untied this Veda made of Kuśa grass and anointed it with curds mixed with honey, he spreads it out behind the Mahāvīra vessel used for the performance, touching it and pointing westward.
(9.15:287.11) Then, having anointed these two posts with curds mixed with honey, he places them behind the two hoof-marks, touching each other with their tops pointing westward.
(9.15:287.12) Then, having filled this supporting vessel with curds mixed with honey, he places it above the two posts with its opening facing westward.
(9.15:287.13) Then, having untied this cord-material and anointed it with curds mixed with honey, he lays it down right there upon the supporting vessel.

(9.15:287.15) Then, having loosened these enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood, which serve as handles for the fans, and having anointed them with curds mixed with honey, he spreads them out above the supporting-wood (*upayamana*), with their tips turned crosswise, interlaced, and touching one another.
(9.15:287.17) Then, having anointed this hoe (*abhri*) with curds mixed with honey, he places it behind the two pillars, with its tip turned crosswise and touching [them].
(9.15:287.18) Then, having anointed these two fire-stirring sticks (*dhṛṣṭi*) with curds mixed with honey, he places them with their tips turned westward, touching the tips of the hoe.
(9.15:288.1) Then, having anointed these two fans with curds mixed with honey, he places them behind the *dhṛṣṭī* so that they touch each other.

(9.15:288.3) Then, having anointed these ten fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood with curds mixed with honey, he spreads them out behind the two fans with their tips pointing westward, so that they touch one another.
(9.15:288.4) Then, having filled this vessel of clarified butter with curds mixed with honey, he places it behind the wooden shovel (*abhri*) so that it touches it.
Then, having anointed this fan with curds mixed with honey, he covers the butter-pot with it.
Then, having anointed these two Rauhiṇa potsherds with curds mixed with honey, he places them behind the butter-pot so that they touch it.

Then, having filled this dipping-spoon (*sruva*) with curds mixed with honey, he places it behind the butter-pot, between the two Rauhiṇa potsherds, so that its bowl faces westward and it touches them.

(9.15:288.10) Then, having untied this mat made of *kuśa* grass and having anointed it with curds mixed with honey, he spreads it behind the vessel of clarified butter, with its tips pointing westward, so that it touches [the other items].
(9.15:288.12) Then, having untied this stool and having anointed it with curds mixed with honey, he places it right here to the north, so that it touches [the other items].
(9.15:288.13) Then, having anointed the remaining clay with curds mixed with honey, he pours it down between the two thighs.
(9.16:288.15) "O Gharma, this is your food, this is your soil; grow by it and swell with it; may we also grow and may we also swell," he says.

(9.16:288.16) Then, having scattered sand over it and covered it with cuttings of *muñja* grass, and having scattered the flour of the *rauhiṇa* cakes, he covers it with a black antelope skin, with the neck pointing eastward and the hair side up.
Or rather, he encloses the great vessel (*mahāvīra*) used for the ritual performance on all sides, like the disk of the sun.

(9.16:288.19) Then he worships it with: "O you who exist in the form of a person, you do not stand within my mouth; neither above nor across. I am fashioned according to your fashion; you are fashioned according to my fashion. Who you are, that I am; who I am, that you are. Ascend to the firmament together with the sacrificer."

Then, taking a handful of clods of earth, he sprinkles them with curds mixed with honey, saying: "The sky has flowed down to the earth; the young bull has flowed down to the cows. May all these worlds flow; may the sacrifice that has flowed forth cause procreation. It has flowed, it was born, it has been procreated. From what has flowed, the bull is born; from what has flowed, may we procreate."

Then he says to the Prastotṛ: "O Prastotṛ, sing the Vārṣāhara Sāman and the Iṣṭāhotrīya. He says this to one who is strong: "With this water-pitcher, sprinkling a continuous stream, go around three times keeping your right side toward [the fire]. While it is being sprinkled, he causes the sacrificer to recite the Gandharva-formulas, beginning with: "Ranti by name art thou, the divine Gandharva," and continuing up to: "Indra recognized Dakṣa as the unimpaired."
Having set down the pitcher, he circumambulates it three times again in the reverse direction.

Then he pays homage to it with the formula: "O divine Gharma, as a god you have gone to the gods; here I, a man, go to men. Follow after my Soma-draught, together with offspring and with abundance of wealth.
Then, with joined palms, he takes water, saying: "May the waters and plants be friendly to us."
He sprinkles water toward that direction in which he has an enemy, saying: "May they become ill-disposed friends to him who hates us and whom we hate.
Then, having touched water, he worships the sun with the *jyotiṣmatī* verse: "Up from the darkness we have risen... and so forth.
(9.16:289.17) Then, having covered it with a load of *avakā* grass, he instructs the guardian: "Guard the *mahāvīra* from birds.
(9.16:289.18) He says to the *prastotṛ*: "O *prastotṛ*, follow along with the *śyeta* chant.
(9.16:289.19) Then, having returned by the same way he came, he offers two *sruva*-ladle oblations on the *gārhapatya* fire with the verses, "Upwards that one" and "The bright one."
Then they worship the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "O Agni, announce this most recent Gāyatra gift to us among the gods.
Then, having hastened to the place of the Āgnīdhra, they perform the subsequent *śānti* rite at the Āgnīdhra's station with the words: "May the wind, Mātariśvan, blow auspiciously for us."
(9.17:290.5) Now, therefore, we shall explain the expiations for the *gharma* ceremony.
(9.17:290.5) Now, if the sun should set while the *pravargya* has not yet been performed, one should offer three spoonfuls of oblations in the *gārhapatya* fire with the words: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ.
(9.17:290.7) Having performed the *upasad* rites, one should perform the *pravargya* on the following day.
(9.17:290.7) Now, if the sun should set while the *pravargya* has been commenced, one should offer three spoonfuls of oblations on the *gārhapatya* fire with the words: "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar.
(9.17:290.9) Then, having tied a piece of gold with a cord at the western door, one should proceed.
(9.17:290.10) And if the [vessel] should fall over while the *pravargya* is in progress, one should offer three spoonfuls of oblations on the *gārhapatya* fire with the words: "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar."
(9.17:290.11) Then he raises it with two verses: "Upward indeed for our protection... and "Standing upright, protect us from distress.
(9.17:290.12) Then he fills it with clarified butter with [the verse]: "Him the sages anoint, as if spreading him out...

(9.17:290.13) Now, if a crack or a fissure occurs, one should mix powdered stone with goat's milk, sprinkle that over it, and heat it with a firebrand while reciting the two verses: "The wandering moon... and "Even when apart from the embrace... (9.17:290.13).
He indeed regrows.

However, if it should break entirely, he grinds these very potsherds without adding any liquid, mixes them with that clay which lies set aside for the expiation, kneads it, shapes it, bakes it, cools it, and sets it down.
Then he prepares another *mahāvīra* vessel for use.
(9.17:290.18) Now, if they pass by [the fires] while distracted, one should offer three spoonfuls of oblations in the *gārhapatya* fire with: "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar.
(9.17:291.1) Then they pass back again with: "punar ūrjā saha rayyā.
(9.17:291.2) Now, if the [fire] being lifted should fall, one should offer three spoonfuls of oblations in the *gārhapatya* fire with: "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar."
(9.17:291.3) Then he touches it with two verses: "O Gharma, do not cause us distress; do not cause us to tremble; do not [afflict] us with our provoked intentions.

(9.17:291.5) Now, if a bird should alight and discharge its excrement upon either the milk-cow of the Gharma or the Mahāvīra vessel, one should wash those two with warm water, reciting: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, protect us here."

(9.17:291.7) Then he should offer nine spoonfuls of oblations in the *gārhapatya* fire with [the verses]: “Hear this my call, O Varuṇa”; “That I implore of thee”; “O Agni, be thou our nearest friend”; “So be thou, O Agni, unto us”; “Thou, O Agni, art the messenger”; “Up from the darkness we have risen”; “Upwards that [sun]”; “The bright [face]”; and “The birds with beautiful wings.
(9.17:291.9) Now, if he cannot find a cow that yields the *gharma* milk, he should cause another cow to be milked.
(9.17:291.10) And if he cannot find another, he should cause a she-goat to be milked.

(9.17:291.11) Now, if he should not find a goat, he should proceed with the milk of the *arka* plant. (9.17:291.11) If he should not find the milk of the *arka* plant, he should mix together barley flour, rice flour, or millet flour with water and proceed with those.
He may even proceed with water alone.
But one must certainly not fail to perform the rite.

Having recited, "Thou art the milk of the great ones," the pouring into the *mahāvīra* vessel is performed; then, having recited, "The sky has spilled upon the earth," he performs the consecration over what has been spilled.

(9.17:291.15) Now, if lightning should strike, one should offer a spoonful of oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire with these mantras according to their respective forms: "The lightning that struck from the east... and so forth. The expiations for the *gharma* have been stated as: "To breath, svāhā! To Pūṣan, svāhā! and so on.

If anything should go wrong during the performance of the *gharma* rite, one should offer these oblations: "Homage to thee, O Gharma, Lord of the Earth! Svāhā! Homage to thee, O Gharma, Lord of the World! Svāhā! Homage to thee, O Gharma, Lord of Beings! Svāhā! To Gharma, Svāhā! To the Aśvins, Svāhā! To Indra, Svāhā! To Bṛhaspati, Svāhā! To Prajāpati, Svāhā! To Brahman, Svāhā! Thus.
Then, having laid down the *āṣāḍhā* brick, marked with three lines and bearing the northern characteristic, he lays down here the *gharmeṣṭakā* and the *kulāyinī*.
With the verse, "Up from his vigor [arose] the light," he lays down the *gharmeṣṭakā*; with the verse, "Those which are your moist wombs, O Agni, those... he lays down the *kulāyinī*.

Having worshipped the piled fire with Sāmans and recited over it with an Uktha, he touches the fire while standing on the northern corner of the hip, using this Anuvāka: "Thou art Agni; thou art Vaiśvānara.
At this point, he gives the sacrificial fee to the Adhvaryu: either a hundred or a thousand cows, or one for each brick.
At the *soma* sacrifice accompanied by the *pravargya*, they consume the *dadhigharma* with this section: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar; in me be that great power (*indriya*) of Indra.
Then he assigns the terrible forms (*ghorās tanūḥ*):
"O Agni, those terrible forms of thine which are *snik*, *snīhī*, *snīhiti*, and *snīhiti*"; these are the terrible forms.
“*Dhuni* and *Dhvānta*”—this is the group for the Rājasūya sacrifice. “*Ugra* and *Dhuni*”—this is for the piling of the fire-altar (*āgnicitya*).
Now, if a thief should steal either the Gharma-milch cow or the Mahāvīra vessel, one should offer a spoonful in the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra: “May Day and Night drive him away from you.”
"Khaṭ!"—these are cruel words.
Now, if a one-eyed dog should bark, he addresses it with the mantra: "O Indra, as you wander about, look out for the cows.
Then he should throw a firebrand blazing at both ends toward him, saying: "O Agni, converse with Agni; O Death, converse with Death."
(9.18:292.17) Then he pays homage to it with: "Once to thee, O Agni, is homage; twice to thee is homage; thrice to thee is homage.
(9.18:293.1) Now, if a vulture should cry out, he addresses it with: "With blood on its mouth, indistinct with gore.
(9.18:293.2) And if distressed speech should arise, he addresses it with: "Since this, having become a wolf..."
(9.18:293.3) Now, if a jackal, a crow, or a partridge should cry out, he addresses it with the mantra: "Whether impelled or seeking its own desire.
(9.18:293.5) If a female hyena should cry out, he addresses her with the mantra: "Long-snouted one, foul-jawed one.
(9.18:293.6) If an owl or a female owl should cry out, he addresses it with the mantra: "Thus has the owl flown down."

(9.18:293.7) Now, if an insane voice should arise, he addresses it with the mantra: "That which has entered into these beings... (9.18:293.8) Then, if a bird should fly down upon the Gharma-milking cow or the Mahāvīra vessel, he addresses it with the mantra: "Spreading out your thighs, you fall... (9.18:293.9) Then, if worms should infest the Gharma-milking cow or the Mahāvīra vessel, he should wash them away with water, saying: "With Atri, I kill you, O worm!"
Now, if an enemy should approach while the *pravargya* rite has been set in motion, he should offer a spoonful (*sruvāhuti*) in the *gārhapatya* fire, saying: "Bring it! Cut off [the portion]!
Then, when he is about to address him with a curse, he should address him, saying: "I curse you by means of the *brahman*!"

Then, he should shake the right door-post of one whom he hates, [saying]: "Strike, O you who are born of the *śimi*! (9.18:293.14). If anyone other than these should low, he should throw a flaming brand at him from both sides, [saying]: "Strike, O you who are born of the *śimi*! (9.18:293.16).

Then, if the wind should blow as if shaking everything, he addresses it with the mantra: "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ! Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ! Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ! The world has been established! The world has been established! The world has been established! (9.18:293.16–17).

Now, if he should enter the hall uninvited, he should enter with this verse: "By these songs, whatever of ours is deficient here. But if he is already invited, he should enter with this very same verse.

(9.19:294.4) Now, therefore, we shall explain the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*). During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having had his hair and beard shaved, and having performed the introductory rite as before, he goes out from the village toward the east or the north. Having established the fire on a barren spot where no roof is visible, having strewn grass around it, having placed the boiling water (*madantī*) over the fire, and having performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the first Anuvāka, he prepares seats for the deities of the Pravargya ceremony with *darbha* grass.

To the east of the fire, [he says]: "I prepare for the Pravargya; I prepare for the Gharma; I prepare for the Mahāvīra; I prepare for the Sovereign. To the south of the fire, [he says]: "I prepare for Brahman; I prepare for Prajāpati. To the north of the fire, [he says]: "I prepare for the Ṛṣis, the makers of mantras, the lords of mantras; I prepare for the gods who drink the Gharma."

(9.19:294.12) Then, on the south side, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he says: "I prepare [the portion] for the ancestors who drink the Gharma; I prepare [the portion] for Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors.

(9.19:294.14) Then, having touched water, on the north side, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), he says: "I prepare [the portion] for Rudra, whose Hotṛ-priest is Rudra. (9.19:294.15) Then, having touched water, he says: "I prepare [the portion] for all the deities of the Pravargya."

Having sprinkled water around the fire from left to right and having placed fuel sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood upon it with the *vyāhṛtis*, he satisfies the deities of the *pravargya* rite with the *madantī* waters.
In front of the fire, [he says]: "I satisfy the *pravargya*; I satisfy the *gharma*; I satisfy the *mahāvīra*; I satisfy the sovereign (*samrāj*).
To the south of the fire, [he says]: "I satisfy the *brahman*; I satisfy Prajāpati."

To the north of the fire, with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he says: "I satiate the seers, the makers of mantras, the lords of mantras; I satiate the gods who drink the *gharma*. Then, to the south, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), he says: "I satiate the ancestors who drink the *gharma*; I satiate Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Pitṛs.
Then, having touched water, to the north, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, he says: "I satiate Rudra, the Hotṛ of Rudra."

Then, having touched water, [the teacher] makes [the student] recite while he causes him to place four fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood—whose tips are not dried out and which have been anointed with clarified butter—with the formula: "I satiate all the deities of the *pravargya*," followed by each of these mantras one by one: "The earth is the fuel-stick."

Then he pays homage to the deities: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the Śukriya vow; may I be able to do so; may it be successful for me. O Vāyu, lord of vows; O Āditya, lord of vows; O lord of vows among vows, I shall perform the Śukriya vow; may I be able to do so; may it be successful for me."
(9.19:295.14) Then he causes him to recite the opening verses of these sections, or those of the first and the last.
(9.19:295.15) Then he instructs him: "Close your eyes and restrain your speech.

(9.19:295.15) Then, with an unwashed garment, he wraps his head three times from left to right so that it faces forward, saying: "You are piled up, you are piled around; Svāhā! Be enclosed by the Maruts!"

Having sprinkled water around the fire from left to right, having placed fuel sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood with the *vyāhṛtis*, and having gratified the deities of the *pravargya* with the *madantī* waters, he performs the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the final *anuvāka*.
Then, after the sun has set, they return to the village. He should remain silent that night, whether standing or sitting, or even lying down.

Then, at dawn when the sun has risen, having gone out from the village toward the eastern or northern direction, having established the fire on a barren plot where no roof-covering is visible, having strewn grass around it, having placed the boiling water over the fire, and having performed the *śānti* rite with the first *anuvāka*, he prepares seats for the deities of the *pravargya* ceremony with *darbha* grass and, reciting "The birds, the fair-winged ones," removes his garment.
Then he causes him to behold six things: fire, water, the sun, a cow, a Brahmin, and gold.

Having first displayed three [of the implements], and having displayed the others as they are available, he should sprinkle water around the fire from left to right, place fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood upon it with the *vyāhṛti*s, satisfy the deities of the *pravargya* rite with the *madantī* waters, and perform the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the final section (*anuvāka*).
Then he should instruct him in the observances of his vow:
"He must not mount a vehicle."
(9.19:296.8) He shall not climb a tree. (9.19:296.8) He shall not descend into a well. (9.19:296.9) He shall not carry an umbrella.
He shall not wear sandals; he shall not sleep on a couch;
he shall not converse with a woman nor with a Śūdra.
If he should converse, he should converse with a Brāhmaṇa;
he should not eat in the evening;
if he should eat in the evening, he should eat only when the fire has been extinguished.
He shall not bathe.
He shall fast on the eighth day and on the days of the lunar festivals, and he shall bathe on those days.
Restraining his speech, he shall remain standing during that night, or he may sit or lie down.
Upon seeing impurity, blood, a corpse, or a vessel containing refuse, he should gaze at the heavenly bodies.
Having seen impurity, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; the Sun is the best of lights. O consecration, do not abandon me!
Now, if it rains upon him, he mutters: "O flowing waters, bestow strength! Bestow vigor! Bestow strength! Do not destroy my consecration, do not destroy my austerity!"
One should observe this vow for a year,
for the vow does not extend beyond a year.
However, one may study it during that very year.
If, however, he has not studied during this year, he should observe this vow for as long as his study lasts.
Then, when the year has elapsed, he may teach or cause [the student] to hear [the texts].

Having performed the introductory rite (*upākaraṇa*) as before, having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, having established the fire on a waste plot where no roof is visible, having strewn grass around it, having placed the boiling water (*madantī*) over the fire, and having performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the first *anuvāka*, he prepares seats for the deities of the *pravargya* ceremony with *darbha* grass.
Then he performs the expiation for a violation of the vow (*avratyaprāyaścitta*) with two verses: "Whatever deficiency has occurred in my self," and "Agni has given back my sight.

Having sprinkled water around the fire from left to right, having added fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood with the *vyāhṛtis*, and having gratified the deities of the *pravargya* rite with the *madantī* waters, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite while four fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood—with undried tips and anointed with clarified butter—are being placed upon the fire, using these mantras one by one: "The sky is the fuel," and so forth.

(9.20:297.12) Then he worships the deities: "O Āditya, lord of vows, I have performed the Śukriya vow; I was able to do it; may it be successful for me. O Vāyu, lord of vows! O Agni, lord of vows! O lord of vows among vows! I have performed the Śukriya vow; I was able to do it; may it be successful for me. Thus.

Having sprinkled water around the fire from left to right, having placed fuel sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood with the *vyāhṛtis*, and having gratified the deities of the *pravargya* rite with the *madantī* waters, he should perform the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the final anuvāka and then teach its periods of non-study (*anadhyāya*).
He should not study when the sun has set.
Not when the sun has not yet risen,
nor when it is obscured by spray,
nor when it has turned away.
(9.20:298.1) Not in the shade of a cloud;
(9.20:298.1) not near domestic animals, nor near wild animals.
Neither at the edge of water, nor while looking at green barley, nor at mansions.
Not having seen bodies or blood spattered, nor having eaten meat.
(9.20:298.4) Having eaten at a *śrāddha* feast, nor having had his hair and beard shaved,
nor having let his hair hang loose.
He does not brush his teeth,
he does not apply collyrium,
and he does not anoint himself with oil.
(9.20:298.6) not with a wet garment;
(9.20:298.6) "not wet," so it is said.
Then he should study his sacred recitation (*svādhyāya*).
Sitting to the west of the fire on *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* grass in his hands, he should study the *svādhyāya* with his face turned away [from the fire].
Whenever he perceives anything that has not been consecrated by a rite of pacification (*śānti*), he should perform the pacification again and then study.

Having studied [the Veda] and having gone out for the Pravargya ceremony with the highest [teacher], one should not study anything else until one has re-entered the village; should one study something else, [he must perform the penance].

(10.1:1.1) One who is about to collect the materials for the fire-pan (*ukhā*) prepares a horse and a donkey; for these two, two reins made of *muñja* grass or of *kuśa* grass; a wooden shovel (*abhri*) well-finished by a Brāhmaṇa; clay that has been prepared and is ready to be worked; a mound from an anthill; a black antelope skin and a lotus leaf; a yoke-halter; a water-pitcher; gold; potsherds from a deserted dwelling; gravel; unground collyrium; wool from a black sheep; hair from a black antelope skin; a Vaiśya seventeen years of age who is skilled in the construction of the fire-pan.

(10.1:1.6) Then, having performed either the New Moon sacrifice or a sacrifice under a [favorable] lunar mansion, he causes a pit to be dug in front of the hall at the point where the *śamyā* is placed.
(10.1:1.7) He coats that with prepared clay. (10.1:1.8) He makes it level with the opening.
He places near it a black antelope skin, a lotus leaf, a yoke-tie, a water-pitcher, and gold.
Then, at the midpoint, having dug up with the wooden sword and sprinkled [the ground], he deposits a mound of earth from an anthill.
A Vaiśya sits to the south, guarding it.
Then, having dug up the northern portion of the shed with the wooden sword (sphya) starting from the front, and having sprinkled it with water, he pours sand down.
He makes that mound circular. Then he makes it radiant by covering it with sand.
Having covered it with young *kuśa* grass and knots of *dūrvā* grass, they then enclose it;
they make its door face north.

He places near it potsherds from a deserted site, pebbles, ointment-free ground powder, black antelope hair, hair from a black antelope skin, a slaughter-ground, a support for the cauldron, and a well-baked cauldron.

(10.1:1.16) Then these two, the horse and the donkey, stand washed in front of the hall. (10.1:1.17) He places the wooden spade within the altar and the two ropes at the northern edge of the altar. (10.1:1.18) They strew grass around the altar.
The Brahman and the sacrificer sit down to the south.

Then, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the offering-spoon, he offers the Sāvitra oblations into the Āhavanīya fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him.

(10.2:1.22) “Harnessing the mind first” (*yuñjānaḥ prathamaṃ manaḥ*)—these six verses follow immediately. “O God Savitṛ” (*deva savitaḥ*) is this *ṛc*; “This [gift] for us, O God Savitṛ” (*imaṃ no deva savitaḥ*) is this *yajus*. One satisfies [the sacrifice] either with a *ṛc* or with a *yajus*. (10.2:2.1) Having offered the ninth oblation, he stands in worship with the words: “With a *ṛc*, perfect the hymn of praise” (*ṛcā stomaṃ samardhaya*).
