(10.2:2.2) Then he takes up the spade with four sections, beginning: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ...
(10.2:2.3). Having carried it around in front of the Āhavanīya fire, he hands it to the Brahman priest seated to the south.
(10.2:2.5) Then he takes up the rope with [the verse]: "They grasped this rope of Order..."
With that [rope] he fastens the horse, saying: "O courser, run forward!
In this very same way, he takes up a second rope; with that he fastens the donkey, using two verses: "Yoke ye both the donkey," and "At every yoking, the most powerful."
They lead the horse first;

he addresses it with: "Come forward, overcoming the curses. He follows behind the donkey with: "With Pūṣan as thy companion, from the common dwelling-place of the earth, come hither for Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras."
They circumambulate the Vaiśya from left to right.
The Vaiśya asks, "O men, what do you seek? They reply, "We seek the Agni Purīṣya in the manner of the Aṅgirases."

(10.2:2.12) Then he worships the ant-hill with the formula: "We shall bear Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras. (10.2:2.13) Then they walk around it with the verse: "Agni Jātavedas, the first, has looked along the forefront of the dawns; he has followed the days; he has extended his rays in many directions toward the sun; he has stretched across heaven and earth.

(10.2:2.15) Then he causes the horse to step upon the clay while facing eastward with two verses: "The prize-winning steed, having come from the path," and "Having stepped upon the earth, O prize-winning steed."

(10.2:2.16) Then he strokes its back with the verse: "Heaven is your back, the earth your seat; the atmosphere is your soul, the ocean your womb. Having looked around with your eye, trample down those who attack you.

(10.2:2.18) At this point, whoever the sacrificer hates, him he meditates upon as being beneath the horse's feet. (10.2:2.19) Then he makes it step forward facing the east with two verses: "Step forth! He has stepped forth!"
(10.2:2.20) Then he pours water over this foot-print.

(10.3:2.21) “O divine waters, release the honeyed ones for the health of the offspring; let the plants with good fruit spring up from their place. (10.3:2.22) Then, having taken four spoonfuls in the *sruc* ladle and having placed a piece of gold on the southern intermediate hoof-print, and having strewn grass around it, he makes an offering over it with the verse: “I sprinkle Agni with mind and with clarified butter.”

Having taken another fourfold portion of ghee and having placed gold in the northern intermediate hoof-print, he offers an oblation over it after having strewn grass around it, with the verse: "I sprinkle thee with speech and with ghee.

(10.3:3.4) Having removed the gold and taken up the spade, he traces around the footprint with three verses: "The sage, lord of booty," "O Agni, we [place] thee within a fort," and "Thou, O Agni, with thy days.
(10.3:3.6) He digs with two formulas: "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ" and "Thee, O Agni, full of light, of fair countenance."

(10.3:3.7) Then, having strewn grass with tips pointing eastward upon the north side of the ritual materials, he spreads a black antelope skin over them with its neck toward the east and the hairy side upward.
(10.3:3.9) Then, [reciting] "Thou art the back of the waters," he brings a lotus leaf.
(10.3:3.10) Having placed that on top of the black antelope skin, he then touches both of them together with two verses: "May you two be a refuge" and "May they clothe themselves."
Having set aside the lotus leaf, he carries away the earth with eight verses.
"Thou art the earth-dweller, the sustainer of all," with this [verse]—
of which four are *gāyatrīs* and four are *triṣṭubhs*— he carries away each individual clod of earth with its respective verse.

Alternatively, he carries away a single *piṇḍa* with eight [verses]. Then, having filled this pit with all the loose soil, he pours water over it with the mantra: "May Vāyu Mātariśvan join together for thee that which was torn from the heart of the outstretched one; to him who moves by the breath of the gods, O Goddess, let there be *vaṣaṭ* for him and for thee!"

(10.4:3.17) Then, having placed a lotus leaf upon the clay above and having gathered together the edges of the black antelope skin, he ties them with a cord, [reciting]: "Well-born together with light, you have sat down as a protection and a refuge, O heaven! Clothe yourself in your all-shaped garment, O Agni, O radiant one!
(10.4:3.20) Then, taking it up, he stands up with two verses: "Arise, O performer of good sacrifice! Stand upright for our protection! Thus with these two.

(10.4:4.2) Then he brings it [the fire] with the verse: "Born as an embryo of the two worlds, O Agni, thou art lovely, distributed among the plants; a brilliant infant, anointed against the darkness, thou hast come forth from thy mothers, bellowing toward the cows.
(10.4:4.4) Then the donkey sets it down with the formula: "Be firm, with strong limbs; be swift, a prize-winning steed; be broad, easy to mount; thou art the carrier of Agni’s soil."
(10.4:4.6) Then he worships it with: "Be auspicious toward offspring, O Aṅgiras; do not burn against the human beings! Do not scorch heaven and earth, nor the atmosphere, nor the trees!
(10.4:4.7) They lead the horse first; (10.4:4.8) he addresses it with: "Let the prize-winner go forward, neighing loudly."
(10.4:4.8) Behind [the cart] follows the donkey: "The braying donkey, flying along, bearing the Agni of the soil—may he not fall before his full span of life.
(10.4:4.10) "The braying donkey, well-yoked to your chariot, O you two bulls—he, the swift messenger, shall carry from here for you both the Agni of the soil.
(10.4:4.11) "Bearing the bull Agni, the son of the waters, the one born of the ocean; O Agni, come for the feast! Thus [he says].
(10.4:4.12) Then he gazes at them, saying: "The *ṛta*, the truth; the *ṛta*, the truth. (10.4:4.13) They move clockwise around the Vaiśya.
(10.4:4.13) The Vaiśya asks: "O men, what do you carry?"
(10.4:4.14) "We bear Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras," thus the others respond. (10.4:4.15) Then they bring him down onto the mound with two verses: "O plants, receive this Agni; O plants, rejoice in him.
(10.4:4.16) Having sprinkled him with water, they release the horse and the donkey.
(10.4:4.16) They throw the two cords into the water, or else they consume them after sprinkling them with water.
(10.5:4.18) Then he loosens it with the verse: "Shining forth with broad radiance... (10.5:4.18).
Then he pours water over it with the three verses in their proper meter beginning: "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss... (10.5:5.2).

Then he mixes it with potsherds from a deserted site, pebbles ground down, goat hair, and the hair of a black antelope skin with the two verses: "Mitra, having mixed the earth... and "I mix thee for freedom from disease. (10.5:5.2)
(10.5:5.4) Then he gathers it together with the formula: "The Rudras, having gathered the earth...
(10.5:5.5) He forms a lump with the formula: "Thou art the head of Makha. (10.5:5.5) With the formula: "Ye two are the feet of the sacrifice," he presses it down with his two thumbs.
(10.5:5.6) Then, having cut off a third portion from the clay, he makes three lumps.
(10.5:5.7) He gives one of them to the one who fashions the fire-pan, with the words: "United with the Vasus and the Rudras.
(10.5:5.8) He consecrates it with the formula: "May the Vasus fashion thee with the Gāyatrī metre."
He gives half of the remaining clay with the words, "O Sinīvālī, she of the beautiful braids.
He consecrates it with the formula, "May the Rudras fashion you with the Triṣṭubh metre. Finally, he gives him all the clay with the words, "Let her fashion the fire-pan according to her ability."
He consecrates it with the formula: "May the Ādityas fashion you with the Jagatī metre; may the All-gods, belonging to all men, fashion you with the Anuṣṭubh metre.
Now, it is indeed said:
"With some [formulas] he restrains [the breath], and with others he consecrates; this is for the sake of pairing."
(10.5:5.14) "He makes it three-peaked," it is said.
(10.5:5.14) Since he carries [the earth] three times and anoints it three times, by that it becomes three-peaked.
(10.5:5.15) He makes it a span high, and of unlimited extent across.

(10.5:5.16) Then, at a distance of three or four finger-breadths from this [altar], he lays around the girdle (*rāsnā*) with the formula: "Thou art the girdle of Aditi. (10.5:5.17) Then, toward each of its directions, he raises eight corners;
and at the junctions of the girdle and the junctions of the corners, he forms eight breasts.
"One should make it nine-cornered for one practicing sorcery," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
He makes the ninth [corner] without a breast.
Then he takes its hollow with the formula: "May Aditi take your hollow with the Pāṅkta metre."
(10.5:5.20) Then he places it on the mound with the verse, "Having fashioned that great fire-pan," reciting the rest of the section to its end.
(10.5:6.1) In this very same way he makes a second one, and likewise a third; [he prepares] five *carṣabha* bricks and three *maṇḍala* bricks silently.

(10.6:6.3) Then, with the clay that remains over, he causes it to dry in a windy place by exposing it to the wind. (10.6:6.4) When they have been dried in the wind, he prepares twenty-one balls of dung from a stallion, as well as a spade and a fire for baking. (10.6:6.5) Then, having kindled a horse-dung firebrand, he fumigates the primary cauldron, beginning with: "May the Vasus fumigate thee with the Gāyatrī metre," and continuing until: "May Varuṇa fumigate thee," both inside and outside.
Having fumigated it well, he places it down.

In the same way he fumigates the second, and likewise the third. [He places] five *carṣabha* bricks and three *maṇḍala* bricks silently. Then, to the north of the hall, he has a pit dug that is wide at the top, with the formula: "May the goddess Aditi, favored by all the gods, dig you as a pit in the lap of the earth, in the manner of the Aṅgirases."

Having spread that [clay] with cooked [dough], he places the principal fire-pan (*ukhā*) upon it with the formula: "May the divine wives of the gods, who are associated with all the gods, place thee, O pan, like Aṅgiras, in the lap of the earth.
In this very same way he places the second [pan], and likewise the third. He silently lays down five *carṣabha* bricks and three *maṇḍala* bricks.
He arranges them so as to face either the east or the north.
(10.6:6.14) Then, having covered them from above with a baking vessel, he coats them with clay.
(10.6:6.15) He leaves an excess of four finger-breadths on each side for the purpose of kindling. (10.6:6.16) Then he sets them near the fire.
(10.7:6.17) With "The *dhiṣaṇās* thee! he [places them] in the east; with "The *gnās* thee! in the south; with "The *varūtrīs* thee! in the west; with "The *janayas* thee! in the north.

(10.7:7.1) Then he entrusts them [to Mitra], saying: "O Mitra, bake this fire-pan (*ukhā*). May it not break. I entrust this to you so that it may not break. (10.7:7.2) They are baked either by day or by night.
(10.7:7.3) If he fasts in the morning, he enters [the ritual] in the evening; if in the evening, [he enters] in the morning.

(10.7:7.4) When those [milk products] have been cooked, he prepares cow’s milk, goat’s milk, a stirring-stick, a stone for grinding, a ladle, tongs, a winnowing-basket, a sling, and a black antelope skin.
(10.7:7.5) Having taken all this together, he approaches [the fire], reciting: “By his greatness, Mitra has become co-extensive with this heaven, and by his glory, with the earth.”
(10.7:7.7) “The glory of the god Mitra, the supporter of the people, which wins booty; his splendor, most wonderful in fame.

(10.7:7.8) Then, taking the fire-stirring stick (*dhṛṣṭi*), he scatters the embers from the principal fire-pan (*ukhā*) with the formula: “May the god Savitṛ scatter you, he of the good hand, the good finger, and the good arm, with his power.
(10.7:7.10) Then he raises it up with the formula: “Arise, become great; stand upright, you who are firm.”

(10.7:7.11) Then he establishes it in the pan with [the verse]: "O Earth, not sinking, fill the regions and the quarters. (10.7:7.12) Then, having grasped it with the tongs and placed it in the vessel, he heats it over a goat's milk.

"May the Vasus anoint you with the Gāyatrī metre," with these words he begins; "May the Viśve Devas, belonging to all men, anoint you with the Ānuṣṭubh metre"—having thus anointed [the brick] both internally and externally, he causes it to overflow with cow's milk. In this very same way he anoints the second, and likewise the third; silently [he anoints] five *ṛṣabha*-bricks and three *maṇḍala*-bricks.

(10.8:7.18) Now, if a crack or a fissure occurs, one should sprinkle powdered stone into goat’s milk, moisten [the vessel] with that, and heat it over a firebrand; it will surely heal. (10.8:7.19) But if it breaks entirely, one should grind those very shards into powder, mix them with the clay that was set aside for the expiation, knead it, bake it, let it cool, and set it down.
When their breathing has ceased, he places them together in a wooden chest, covers them from above with a black antelope skin, and hangs them on a sling in the northern part of the shed;
they remain there until the appointed time.
(10.9:8.6) Now, during this very same first fortnight, he performs a sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Vāyu.

(10.9:8.6) For that sacrifice, the following is prepared: the heads of a horse and a Vaiśya who have been killed in battle by one intending to sacrifice with an animal; (10.9:8.8) while they play at dice, they cook a bull, a ram, and a goat.

(10.9:8.8) They bring this serpent’s head. (10.9:8.9) Now, on the very previous day, this altar for the animal sacrifice has already been measured out for him. (10.9:8.10) Having strewn it around, he performs the *stambayajus* rite.
This very [procedure] is established according to the Pauroḍāśika [Kalpa].
He draws [the lines] three times with the Yajus formula and a fourth time silently. He performs the first tracing of the altar.
He mutters the *karaṇa* formula. He digs up [the earth]. From the dug-up spot, the Āgnīdhra carries away [the earth] three times.
When the Āgnīdhra carries [the earth] three times, then he traces around the *cātvāla* pit according to the procedure for the *cātvāla*.
According to the procedure for the *uttaravedi*, he pours out the *uttaravedi*.
Having set aside the *uttaranābhi*, he leads forward the fire according to the procedure for the fire.

Having performed the second tracing around while it possesses fire, having leveled the ground, and having held the wooden sword (sphya) crosswise, he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass (idhmābarhis) nearby; cleanse the dipping-spoon (sruva), the knife (svadhiti), and the offering-ladles (sruc); [cleanse] the vessel for the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) silently; gird the wife; bring the clarified butter and the curds; O Pratiprasthātṛ, prepare the heads of the victims.
The Adhvaryu alone performs the well-known ritual actions pertaining to the animal sacrifice.
(10.9:8.19) Then the Pratiprasthātṛ requests twenty-one beans, a *parṇa*-branch, a lump of clay, a water-vessel, a clod of earth dug up from a mole-hill with seven holes, and a pair of tongs.
(10.9:9.2) Having taken these, he approaches the animal heads.
(10.9:9.3) To the south lies this head of a human being, in front of the others.
Then, having arranged the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), he scatters seven beans around the human head and sweeps it three times counter-clockwise with a leafy branch.
"Day after day leading away cattle, horses, men, and all that moves, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is not yet satiated with these five classes of men.

Having scattered [the grains] with seven other verses, he draws them around, saying: "Before King Yama, the son of Vivasvat, those people are separated—those here who desire the truth and those who are speakers of untruth."
Having scattered it with seven others, he draws it around, saying: "O King, they are sifted here; then they come unto you—those who pay homage to the gods and honor the Brahmins.

Then, taking the ant-hill mound with his right hand and the human head with his left hand using tongs, and having brought the vital breaths together with the vital breaths, he places the ant-hill mound in its receptacle.

(10.10:9.13) Then, having sprinkled this human head, scraped it, and washed it, he coats it with clay, taking care not to coat the vital breaths. (10.10:9.14) Then they prepare the other [bones] in the same manner; having scraped them and washed them, they coat them with clay, taking care not to coat the vital breaths. (10.10:10.2) Then he places them down after sprinkling them with water.
They remain lying there until the [proper] time.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the *sāmidhenī* verses of the animal sacrifice:
the eleven verses beginning with "pra vo vājā abhidyavaḥ," and the ten verses beginning with "samās tvāgna ṛtavo vardhayantu."
Having extracted the *jyotiṣmatī* verse from among them, he places nine verses in the position of the *dhāyyās*.
Then he places two *dhāyyās* containing the word "broad-footed" (*pṛthupāja*).
Then he places this verse: "Yoke, indeed, those who best invoke the gods."
These verses, being recited continuously, amount to twenty-four;
however, he recites the *jyotiṣmatī* as the very last one. Then he pours the *āghāra* libation with the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning.
Now, therefore, follows the deliberation concerning the *āprī* verses.
(10.11:10.10) “His fuel-sticks rise upward,” thus [he says]; there are twelve [verses].

(10.11:10.11) Having extracted from them the *tānūnapātī* verse, he places the *nārāśaṃsī* verse for the Vasiṣṭhas. (10.11:10.11) Having extracted the *nārāśaṃsī* verse, he places the *tānūnapātī* verse for those of other lineages (*gotra*).

(10.11:11.1) Now, if [the sacrifice] is mixed, [the invitatory verses are]: for the omentum, "O you whose food is fat," and "For wealth, him who..."; for the animal cake, "He who breathes," and "He who gives himself"; for the oblation, "Toward Vāyu," and "With your teams, come to us. (10.11:11.3) But if it is indeed entirely dedicated to Vāyu, then of these [verses], "O you whose food is fat" and "For wealth, him who..."—two are for the omentum, two for the animal cake, and two for the oblation.

Now, if it is indeed a sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati for all [the victims], then from the verses beginning "He who breathes" and "He who is self-given," two are used for the omenta, two for the animal cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), and two for the oblation (*havis*).
They perform the complete conclusion of the animal sacrifice. Then, having carried fire around these heads of the animals, he hangs them in carrying-slings on the northern part of the shed.
Then, having tied this serpent’s head with a cord, he knots it to the loop of the sling;
these remain there until the appointed time.
Then the second half of the month is determined. He prepares the bricks and the sacrificial fees for the fire-altar, if he intends to pile it after having maintained it for a night;
however, if he has maintained it for a year, he need not concern himself with the "long journey" [of the bricks].

He prepares a principal throne-seat made of Udumbara wood; its legs are a span high, its head-boards and side-boards are a cubit long, it is woven with single-strand ropes of Muñja grass, covered with planks, and smeared with clay. He also prepares a sling of Muñja grass with six or twelve strands, a nest-like basket of Muñja grass, a Krumuka stick mixed with clarified butter, two fuel-sticks—one of Vikankata wood and one of Śamī wood—seven fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood, three fuel-sticks of various trees, and a gold plate with twenty-one knobs.
The materials for the Agniṣṭoma are well known.

A sacrificial hall has been constructed on a chosen site for the sacrifice to the gods. Then, having brought him from the bathing-place and purified him, he performs the Agnidīkṣaṇīyā offering consisting of three oblations: a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap in ghee for Aditi, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara.
Of that [offering], as many [portions] are omitted as there were for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice.

Then the Adhvaryu, having turned to the right and hastened westward, having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, having gone eastward, having replenished the *dhruvā* ladle and poured it back into the *ājyasthālī*, offers the *agnidīkṣā* oblations by dipping with the *sruva* spoon from the *ājyasthālī*.

(10.13:12.12) < To Ākūti, Agni, the impeller, svāhā! To Manas, Medhā, Agni, the impeller, svāhā! To Citta, Vijñāta, Agni, the impeller, svāhā! To Vāc, Vidhṛti, Agni, the impeller, svāhā! To Prajāpati, Manu, svāhā! To Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā! > Thus [he says].

(10.13:12.15) Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter into the *sruva*-ladle, he offers the full ladle as the *audgrahaṇa* oblation with the mantra: "All [beings] choose the friendship of the god, the leader; all seek wealth; let him choose glory so that it may prosper—*svāhā*! (10.13:12.17) At this point, he pours out this full vessel within the altar (*antarvedi*).
(10.13:12.18) Then, having carried it around in front of the *āhavanīya* fire, he hands it over to the sacrificer.
(10.13:12.18) Then he asks for the principal fire-pan (*ukhā*).

(10.13:13.1) Having scattered dung-clods and rotten grass into it, and having cast a spoonful of clarified butter into it, he sets it upon the outermost embers of the *āhavanīya* fire with two verses: "Do not break! Be firm! (10.13:13.3) Then he entrusts it [to Mitra] with the formula: "O Mitra, heat this pan; let it not break. I entrust this to you so that it may not break."
Now, it is indeed said: "If [the vessel] should break, he should mix it again with those very same potsherds.
If it breaks, having ground these very potsherds without adding water, and having mixed them with that clay which was set aside for the expiation, he kneads it, bakes it, cools it, and sets it down.
(10.13:13.7) Then he chooses another [priest]. (10.13:13.7) Now, indeed, it is said: (10.13:13.8) "For one who desires food, he should take [the portion] from a frying pan. Thus.
Now, indeed, it is said: "If one should desire of a sacrificer, 'May I produce a rival for him,' he should bring [the wood] from elsewhere and place it [on the fire].
Now, indeed, it is further said:

"One for whom prosperity has departed, one should place [the fire] into him after churning it," so it is said. Now, indeed, it is further stated: "For one who desires prosperity, whoever should prepare the fire-pan (*ukhā*), he alone should be his [officiant]."

(10.13:13.12) Whatever [fire] is produced from the heat of the fire-pan (*ukhā*), into that he places a nest of *muñja* grass, saying: "O Agni, that vigorous body of yours which has entered into the plants—by means of this I propitiate it for you, svāhā!
(10.13:13.14) Then he places a piece of *krumuka* wood soaked in clarified butter, saying: "We who have wood as our food, whose libation is ghee.

(10.13:13.15) Then he places two fuel-sticks, one of *vaikaṅkata* wood and one of *śamī* wood. He places the *vaikaṅkata* stick with: "From the highest gathering-place," and the *śamī* stick with: "From the furthest distance."
Then, with the three verses beginning, "Sit down upon the lap of this mother," he worships the newborn child. Then he places five fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood upon the fire.

(10.14:14.1) "O Agni, whatever [deeds] there are... "Whatever the woodpecker eats... "Night after night, without ceasing... "In the navel of the earth... "Those armies that are attacking... Thus [he recites]. (10.14:14.2) Then he worships him with the five-verse *rākṣoghnī* hymn: "Make your power wide like a net... and so forth.

Then he anoints three fuel-sticks from different trees and places them on the fire: one made of *aśvattha* wood with [the verse], "With your two tusks, [seize] the thieves"; one made of *vaikaṅkata* wood with [the verse], "Those who are thieves among men"; and one made of *śamī* wood with [the verse], "He who would act with hostility toward us.
Then, while making the sacrificer recite [the verses], "Sharpened is my sacred prayer" and "I have raised up their arms," he places the final fuel-stick made of *udumbara* wood on the fire.
At this point, he makes the sacrificer recite over the black antelope skin.
He neither clenches his fists nor restrains his speech.
Then he places this stool, with its loops and cords untied, behind the Āhavanīya fire. Upon it, having grasped the fire-pan with two fingers, he sets it down.
"As a mother her son, the earth bears Agni, the one born of the soil, in her own womb—the fire-pan. May Prajāpati Viśvakarman, in harmony with all the gods and the seasons, yoke it. Thus [he says].
(10.15:14.13) Then, while seated, he fastens the gold plate upon the northern support with the verse: "The gold plate, shining forth...
(10.15:14.14) Then he fastens the sling-loop with two verses: "The seer puts on all forms; Night and Dawn...
(10.15:14.15) He silently places the black antelope skin over it.

(10.15:14.15) Then he gazes at it: "You are the fair-winged Garuḍa; the Trivṛt is your head; the Gāyatra is your eye; the Stoma is your body; the Vāmadevya Sāman is your torso; the Bṛhat and Rathantara are your wings; the Yajñāyajñīya is your tail; the meters are your limbs; the Dhiṣṇiya hearths are your hooves; the Yajus formulas are your name.
(10.15:14.18) Then he lifts it up: "You are the fair-winged Garuḍa; go to heaven; fly to the light of heaven!"
(10.15:14.19) Previously, these long loops for the sling have been made for it. (10.15:15.1) He either steps onto it here, or he lifts it up.

(10.16:15.3) “Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of the adversary; ascend the Gāyatrī metre; stride along the earth; excluded is he whom we hate. With these four verses, according to their respective metres, he strides. (10.16:15.5) On the third [step], he repeats the fourth [verse];
he does not stride for a fourth [step].
He does not pass beyond the Āhavanīya fire.

Then, having recited the verse, "He cried out," he turns around toward his right shoulder, reciting the four verses: "O Agni, you who turn back," "O Agni Aṅgiras," "With strength again," and "Together with wealth.
Then, having turned toward the north and loosened the black antelope skin, he unties the loop of the sling with the verse, "O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond from us."
(10.16:15.9) Then he brings it forward with two verses: "I have brought thee hither; O Great One, thou hast stood upright before the dawns.
(10.16:15.10) At this point, if he should desire of a Rājanya, "May he possess a kingdom," he should meditate upon him in his mind.
(10.16:15.11) "He indeed becomes possessed of a kingdom," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(10.16:15.12) Then, having carried it back around in the same manner as it was brought, he places it within the altar with the four *ṛc*-verses beginning, "Sit thou in the lap of this mother. (10.16:15.13) At this point, he closes his fists and restrains his speech.
(10.16:15.14) Then, intending to give him the vow-food, he either places upon the fire a fuel-stick dedicated to Annapati or mutters: "O Lord of Food, give us food!"
(10.16:15.15) Then he kindles the *ukhya* fire with [the verse]: "By which the gods went upward, ascending by light.

(10.16:15.16) As many times as he is about to give him the fast-food (*vrata*), in that same manner he either places a fuel-stick for the Lord of Food (*annapati*) upon the fire or mutters [the formula], and likewise he kindles the *ukhya* fire.
(10.16:15.18) Then, in the morning when the sun has risen and speech has been released, he worships with the *Vātsapra* hymn consisting of eleven verses, beginning: "From heaven Agni was first born."
In this very manner, he sets out on the previous day and performs the ritual worship on the following day;
then, on the Upavasatha day, his Vātsapra recitation is completed.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation concerning the departure.
When one who is consecrated finds security (*yogakṣema*) elsewhere than at the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), or when he is consecrated [elsewhere],
they mix the two portions of the *vrata* milk and tie together the two calves of the *vrata*-cows.
They place whatever is to be placed: the Gārhapatya fire in the interior of the cart and the Āhavanīya fire on the front part of the pole.

Then he lifts up the Ukhya fire with the verse, "May all the gods lift thee up. Then he sets it down on the front part of the cart together with the four *saṃsā* verses, beginning with, "Sit thou in the lap of this mother."
Then they fasten these legs of the throne firmly to the wooden boards;
they tie the sling-loop to the middle beam.
Or else, having consigned the fires into the two kindling-sticks (*araṇis*), he sets out with the two verses: "Go forth from good to better," and "Go forward, O Agni, full of light."

(10.17:16.13) Now, if the axle creaks, he recites this verse: "He cried out... (RV 10.98.1). Then, when [the rite] has concluded, he places upon the fire a fuel-stick anointed with clarified butter, using the Gāyatrī verse for a Brāhmaṇa: "Worship Agni with fuel; awaken the guest with clarified butter; pour the oblations into him, Svāhā! (RV 8.44.1), and using the Triṣṭubh verse for a Rājanya: "Agni is heard far and wide among the Bharatas" (RV 6.15.19).
As many times as he is about to depart, he performs all this in exactly the same way.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation concerning excessively increased *bhasman* (ash).
If the *bhasman* increases excessively, he prepares a hundred [measures], an iron ladle, and a pair of tongs.
Having taken these things, they go to where there is water; that is the *sokhya*.

(10.18:17.1) Then, having grasped this fire with tongs and placed it in the vessel, he causes the ashes to enter the water with the wooden spoon, reciting three verses in their proper meter: "O divine waters, receive these ashes; O Agni, your seat is in the waters; you are the embryo of the plants. (10.18:17.4) Then he places it back [upon the embers] with two verses containing the word "light": "Having settled in the womb with the ashes, having sat down again in your seat and in the waters... with these two.
Then, with the two verses, "Again with vigor, together with wealth," he rises again. Then he adds fuel to the *ukhya* fire with [the verse], "May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle you again.
Then, having carried it back around as it was brought, standing in the sacrificer’s station, he worships it with the section beginning, "Be awake! May he be awake! until the end of the *anuvāka*.
As many times as the ashes increase, in that very manner he performs all this.
Now, therefore, he lies down for the sake of the time [of the ritual] until the materials are gathered.
Now, therefore, follows the fast-day (upavasatha) pertaining to the purchase [of the Soma].

He prepares five hundred bricks, an unlimited number of *apasyā* bricks, black *nairṛtī* bricks, three baked with husks, ashes, loose earth (*purīṣa*), saline soil (*ūṣā*), and sand. Then, on the day of the fast-day, he settles upon the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) with two verses: "We have come hither; depart! (VS 10.19).

(10.19:17.14) Then he measures out the great altar (*mahāvedī*). Having stepped out these same larger steps and having measured by a diagonal measurement, he encloses it on all sides with a cord and stretches the *pṛṣṭhyā* line.
(10.19:17.16) Then he measures this fire-altar westward from the peg at the post-hole using a bamboo rod one man’s length long, making it symmetrical in its wings and tail.
The two wings become longer by one *aratni*.
Whether he intends to build it as sixfold, sevenfold, twelvefold, or however many-fold it may be,
he then measures it diagonally with a measuring-line and encloses it all around with a cord.
Having stretched the cord, he draws the line.
Having removed the cord, they dig the trenches.
They erect the water-channels.
They make them higher toward the south and toward the west.
Only this much ritual action is performed on this day;
they remain for this night.
(10.19:18.4) Then, having hastened there during the latter part of the night, the Adhvaryu gives the instruction: "Milk the *tristanavrata* cow.
(10.19:18.5) Then, having poured this fire into a vessel, they sit to the south keeping it burning.
(10.19:18.6) Then he smears this fire-place with a lump of cow-dung.
Upon that [altar], he lays down four bricks facing east: two joined together in front and two joined together behind.
Then he encloses it from left to right with thirteen bricks. Alongside each brick, he draws a line.
Having removed the bricks, they cause the trenches to be dug.
They raise the *apasyā* bricks;
they make them higher toward the south and toward the west.
Then, with two verses, he takes the fire into himself: "I take Agni first within me; that Agni who is ours...
With the verse, "O Agni, those logs of thine, those abodes...", he mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula.
Having touched a white horse, he lays down this brick amidst the gravel with the words: "May Prajāpati settle thee; by that deity, like Aṅgiras, sit thou firm."

(10.20:18.14) Here he pours down the ritual materials: with "Thou art the ash of Agni," the ash; with "Thou art the soil of Agni," the soil; with "Thou art recognition, the upholder of desires," the saline earth; with "May thy upholding of desires be in me," the sand. (10.20:18.17) Then he mixes them together with: "Those bodies of yours which are dear, may your hearts be united; may your self be dear to you, and may your bodies be dear to me."
(10.20:18.19) Then he arranges them with: "May heaven and earth be in order; may the waters and plants be in order; may the fires be in order separately, sharing the same vow for my preeminence.
(10.20:18.20) Then he lays down the upward-facing bricks with: "You are piled, you are well-piled; being upward-facing, take your place! By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm!"

Then he arranges [the bricks] along: with the *gāyatrī* verse, "Swell up," for a Brāhmaṇa; with the *triṣṭubh* verse, "May thy milks unite," for a Rājanya. He arranges them according to the [proper] order and according to the gravel. Upon that, he lays down four bricks facing eastward, belonging to the Yajus formulas.

"This is that Agni; O Agni, you go toward the flood of heaven; O Agni, that splendor of yours which is in heaven and on earth; the Agnis of the soil"—with these two verses, facing each other, he places [the bricks] in the east. With "O Agni, the *iḍā*," he places the southern one; with "This is your seasonal womb," the northern one. With "You are the *cit*," he places the southern one in the west; with "You are the *paricit*," the northern one.

(10.21:19.8) Then he encloses it with thirteen *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks, moving from left to right, [with the formula]: "Fill the world, fill the gap; and sit down, you who are auspicious. May Indra, Agni, and Bṛhaspati seat you in this womb. (10.21:19.11) He performs the *tayādevata* rite [with the formula]: "By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm."
(10.21:19.12) Then he performs the *sūdadohas* verse: "These dappled ones, yielding milk for him, mix the Soma; they are the clans at the birth of the gods, in the three luminous realms of heaven.
(10.21:19.14) Then, having descended and touched a black horse, he places the *tanūpurīṣa* earth with the verse: "He who is praised in heaven...
(10.21:19.15) Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* verse. Thus, indeed, this first layer is completed.
In this very manner the second [oblation] is poured out, in this manner the third, in this manner the fourth, and in this manner the fifth.
If the sun should rise while they are being prepared, the sacrificer, remaining silent, takes hold of the Adhvaryu.
The Adhvaryu takes up the fire-pan (*ukhya*), and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes up the fuel for rekindling.
Facing each other from the east, they pour together [the ashes] with the four verses beginning, "Be united.
Then he takes down the fire-pan from the sling.

"As a mother her son, the earth has carried the Agni of the soil into his own womb—the fire-pan. May Prajāpati Viśvakarman, in harmony with all the gods and the seasons, release him. Thus [it is said].
"One should not look at it," they say, "for it is indeed full of heat."

Looking elsewhere at that [spot], he throws drops of curd, either with the formula, "I place that pure [substance] for you," or silently. Then, having filled it with sand and covered it from above with curd, he places it in the northern part of the shed.
In this very same way he fills the second one, and likewise the third.
These remain lying there until the appointed time.
(10.22:20.7) Then, with a verse addressed to Vaiśvānara, he takes up the sling: "That bright light which was born beyond this region—may it carry us across our enemies.

(10.22:20.9) Then he asks for three black Nairṛta vessels baked with husks, a stool, the fastening of the gold plate, and a vessel of water. (10.22:20.10) Having taken all this, having gone out by the southern door, they go in that direction where there is a natural salt-flat or a cleft in the ground clearly visible.
He lays down that sling with its loop facing away, saying: "O Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā!

Along the cord of the sling, he places bricks belonging to Nirṛti facing away, saying: "Homage to you, O Nirṛti of all forms! What you, O Goddess Nirṛti, have bound, I offer as an oblation into the cruel mouth of this [Nirṛti] of yours. He then hangs the stool, which serves as the fastening for the gold plate.
Then he worships with two verses: "Seek him who does not press [the Soma], who does not sacrifice; I, praising the divine Nirṛti," and so on.
Then, having poured the water together and cast aside the vessel, they return without looking back.
Having washed their hands and feet, they return by the same way they came and worship the Gārhapatya fire with the verse: "The dweller, the gatherer of riches."
Some, however, pay homage to the Āhavanīya fire, [thinking]: "From here on, this shall be the Gārhapatya."
Then he proceeds with the Prāyaṇīya offering;
having proceeded with the Prāyaṇīya, he proceeds with the footprint ritual;
having proceeded with the footprint ritual, having purchased and brought back the King Soma, he offers the Ātithya.
Having performed the *ātithyā* [offering], he proceeds with the first two *pravargya-upasad* rites.
Then, having gone out, he issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; give the three-breasted *vrata*-milk.
Thereupon, the Subrahmaṇya invokes the Subrahmaṇyā.
He bestows the *tristanavrata* vow.
Starting from the tail-end itself, he strides four steps westward and a fifth step to the south;
there he places the wooden sword (*sphya*).
That is the time for the *uparava* holes.
Then, from the northern corner-stake of the great altar (*mahāvedi*), he strides twelve steps westward along the edge of the altar and a thirteenth step toward the north.
At that point, the *āgnīdhra* priest takes his seat.
That is the time for the *utkara*.
Then, from the time for the *uparavas*, he carries away the *stambayajus*.
This [procedure] is well known.
(10.23:21.13) He performs the rite pertaining to the sacrificial cake three times with the *yajus* formula and a fourth time silently.
(10.23:21.14) He performs the first tracing of the altar and mutters the *karaṇa* formula.
From the *uddhata* [earth], the Āgnīdhra carries it away three times.
When the Āgnīdhra has carried it away three times, then, standing in front of the hall, he issues the command: "O altar-makers, prepare the altar!
They act according to that command.

(10.23:21.17) Then they put on sandals made of black antelope skin: the Adhvaryu with the formula, "For the piled one, thee!"; the Pratiprasthātṛ with, "For the piled-up one, thee!"; the Brahman with, "For the mind-piled one, thee!"; and the sacrificer with, "For the heat-piled one, thee! Or rather, all of them may do so with the formula, "For the piled one, thee! For the piled one, thee! (10.23:21.19) Alternatively, [they may do so] silently. Then he asks for a bow with arrows, four stones, an Aindra brick, a Vibhakti brick, a vessel of water, a bunch of Darbha grass, Dūrvā grass, and a pot of clarified butter together with a dipping-spoon.
Having taken this up, they place it on the northern hip-end.
Then, with two verses—“I take Agni first within me” and “The Agni who is ours”—he takes the fire into himself.
He mutters the *svayaṃcit* verse: “Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes...”
Having touched a white horse, he places this [brick] within the gravel with the formula: "May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!
Then he takes up a bow with four arrows and a stone.

Having taken all this, having gone around the fire-altar by the south from behind, and standing in front of the peg for the sacrificial post-hole, he strings the bow and, stretching it forward, strikes the arrow into the ground within the gravel.
"Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra; protect our bodies, O far-seeing one!
With these words, having pulled it out, he places a stone down with the formula: "May he who seeks to harm us from the east, may he strike this stone!
Then, on the southern side of the right wing, at the edge where the wing meets the body, he drives in an arrow containing gravel.

Having dug it out, he places a stone [upon it] with the formula: "He who [attacks us] from the south... Then, at the rear of the tail, on the tail-support, having reached the edge, he drives in an arrow containing gravel.
Having dug it out, he places a stone [upon it] with the formula: "He who [attacks us] from behind..."
Then, on the northern side of the northern wing, he drives in an arrow with pebbles inside it at the end of the wing-extension.
Having pulled it out, he places a stone upon it with the mantra: "He who [is] from the north. "He places them in the quarters," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.

Then he places this *aindrī* brick upon the stepping-stone with the mantra: "May he protect it—he who is the possessor of the *ṛjīṣa*, the overcomer; he who is the fair-cheeked bull, the lord of prayers; he who is the breaker of the cow-pens, the wielder of the thunderbolt, who stands upon the bay horses; may that Indra pierce through for us manifold spoils. Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.
Then, on the south side, he lays down the *vibhakti* brick with the verse, "O Agni, come for the feast.
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula.

Then, having stepped upon it, having pulled out the peg from the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, and having poured out a vessel of water, he lays down a clump of *darbha* grass, either with the formula, "May Vāc lay thee down in the ocean," or silently.

(10.24:23.9) Then he makes offerings over it with spoonfuls, using five [verses] beginning: "In harmony with the year, with the months... (10.24:23.10) Then he lays down a blade of *dūrvā* grass with [the verse]: "At thy coming and thy departure, may flowering *dūrvā* grow; may a spring arise there, or a lake adorned with lotuses.
(10.24:23.12) Having performed the *tayādevatam* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formulas.
Now, prior to this, a pair of ploughs made of udumbara wood has already been prepared for him.
[He prepares] a team of six oxen or a team of twelve oxen.
He touches their leather thongs with two verses: "Bind the thongs; prepare the well-dug pit.
He yokes [the oxen] with two verses: "The seers yoke the ploughs and the yokes; yoke the ploughs."
He ploughs with two verses: "The ploughshare, tipped with iron... and "May the ploughshares be auspicious for us.
He inspects the furrow with two verses: "O yielder of desires, milk forth desire... and "May the furrow be filled with ghee.
Starting from the tail-end, he first ploughs three furrows directed toward the east.
Three [lines] toward the right shoulder from the northern hip;
three toward the left shoulder from the southern hip;
three toward the left wing from the right wing.
(10.25:24.6) Then, having unyoked them, turned to the right, and sprinkled them with water, he releases them toward the north.
(10.25:24.7) These [animals] belong to the *adhvaryu* if he performs a sacrifice accompanied by sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
(10.25:24.8) But if it is a sacrificial session (*sattra*), they distribute them according to their respective shares.
Wherever the oxen are, there is that pair of yokes and the plow.

Then, to the east of this [spot], there is a trough made of udumbara wood, in which all kinds of herbs have been mixed together with curds and clarified butter. He first sows three furrows toward the east from the tail [of the animal] with the three verses beginning, "The plants that were born," according to their respective meters.
(10.25:24.12) With three [verses], he [covers] from the northern hip toward the right shoulder. (10.25:24.12) With three [verses], [he covers] from the southern hip toward the left shoulder.
(10.25:24.13) With five [verses], [he covers] from the right wing toward the left wing.
"He shaves with fourteen [blades]," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then he collects clods of earth from the various directions.
Having run forward from that very spot toward the east, he takes a clod of earth from outside the pebbles.
He places it down with gravel inside.
"May he who is the progenitor of the earth not harm us.
Then, having run along the right wing, he takes a clod of earth from outside the pebbles and places it inside the pebbles with the words: "Turn toward us, O Earth."
Then, having recited over the tail, he takes a clod of earth from outside the gravel;
he places it inside the gravel with the formula: "O Agni, that which is your bright [form] and that which is your shining [form].
Then, having recited over the left wing, he takes two clods of earth from outside the gravel with the formula: "Food and strength I take from here."
(10.26:25.6) Of those two, he places one inside with gravel, [reciting]: "May it enter into our cattle and plants.
(10.26:25.7) He throws the other away in that direction in which his enemy resides, [reciting]: "I abandon exhaustion, lack of food, and disease.
(10.26:25.8) One view is that he should complete this while still taking up [the earth] toward that direction.
"One should exchange one *yajus* for another *yajus*"; this is another [instruction].
Then, from the northern shoulder-mark of the Great Altar (*mahāvedi*), he strides three steps westward along the edge of the altar and a fourth step toward the north.
There, according to the procedure for the pit (*cātvāla*), he traces out the pit.
Following the procedure for the *uttaravedi*, he pours out the earth for the *uttaravedi*.
Having leveled the *uttaranābhi*, he pours sand over it with six verses in their respective meters, beginning: "O Agni, yours is glory and vigor...

Then he lays down the upward-facing bricks (*ūrdhvacit*) with the formula: "You are piled; you are piled around. O upward-facing ones, take your place! By that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm!"

Then he arranges [the grains] along: for a Brāhmaṇa, with the Gāyatrī verse, "Swell up" (*āpyāyasva*); for a Rājanya, with the Triṣṭubh verse, "May thy milks unite" (*saṃ te payāṃsi*). He arranges them according to the quality of the soil and according to the nature of the gravel.

(10.27:25.18) Then they pile up this great altar (mahāciti) in front of the hall, either on a raised platform or on a hide: twenty-two bunches of *darbha* grass, water for sprinkling, clarified butter for sprinkling, the horse, the materials for the high altar (*auttaravedika*), thirteen *bārhaspatya* bricks, as many pieces of gold, a jar of water, a lotus leaf, a gold plate, a golden man, two offering-ladles, a serpent’s head, and everything else.

Having placed upon the *payaḥprokṣa* (the sprinkling with milk) twenty-two bunches of *darbha* grass—the naturally perforated stone (*svayamātṛṇṇā*), the ten *skandhyā* bricks, the *avakā* plants, and whatever others he is about to lay down—he sprinkles them with these, mixed with curds and honey. He also places a tortoise, a mortar and pestle made of *udumbara* wood, all kinds of herbs, the fire-pan (*ukhā*), and the heads of the sacrificial animals. Then, with the formula, "I sprinkle you, the fires, acceptable to the fires," or silently, he performs the sprinkling with clarified butter while reciting: "By fire is fire kindled. (10.27:26.7–26.9)

(10.27:26.10) Then he issues the command: "Recite for the fires being led forward. (10.27:26.11) If the Hotṛ does not desire to do so, the sacrificer himself recites this single verse, "The fires dwelling in the soil," three times; then they proceed with the fire at their head. (10.27:26.12) Then he hastens forward with this horse facing the east.
(10.28:26.14) “He has overcome all hostile armies,” [he says].
(10.28:26.14) Then he consecrates with the mantra, “When you first cried out as you were being born,” [as the horse] steps upon the right shoulder.
(10.28:26.15) They settle it down at the northern edge of the buttock.
Then, with two verses, he takes the fire into himself: "I take Agni first into myself," and "The Agni who is ours.

He mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes... Having touched the white horse, he mounts it with two verses: "This is the gathering-place of the waters; homage to thee! and [the second verse].
Then he places a hundred [bricks] at the joint of the tail and at the joint of the body.
Then he pours out the water-pitcher.

He takes the pitcher with his right hand and the pot with his left; having filled them from the *sata* and having thrown two chips of gold into them, he lays them down crosswise along the spine on those [bricks] which run from the southern shoulder toward the *svayamātṛṇṇā*.
"Golden-hued, pure, purifying, in whose midst King Varuṇa moves"— with these two verses,

having filled [the pits] in this very manner and having thrown [the earth] back in this way, he places them along the furrows at the Viṣuvat, using the third and fourth verses, over those which run toward the naturally perforated stone from the northern hip.

In this very manner, having filled [the space] and having thus leveled it, he lays down those [bricks] which run toward the *svayamātṛṇṇā* from the right hip, along the furrows at the *viṣuvat*, with the fifth and the sixth verses.

In this very manner, having filled [the space] and having thus leveled it, he lays down those [bricks] which run toward the *svayamātṛṇṇā* from the left shoulder, along the furrows at the *viṣuvat*, with the seventh and the eighth verses.

In this very manner, having filled [the space] and having thrown [the earth] back in this way, he lays down those bricks which run from the southern wing toward the *svayamātṛṇṇā* along the transverse line at the *viṣuvat*, using the ninth and the tenth verses.

In this very manner, having filled [the space] and having thrown [the earth] back in this way, he lays down those bricks which run from the northern wing toward the *svayamātṛṇṇā* along the transverse line at the *viṣuvat*, using the eleventh and the twelfth verses.

Of those [bricks], he places the one belonging to Bṛhaspati in the middle with the formula: "Rest in heaven; strive in the intermediate space; arise from the earth! You are spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); for spiritual luster, you! Thus it is said.
"He places them along the furrows," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.
Then, having performed the ritual procedure for the *uttaravedi*, he adorns the *uttaravedi*.
Then, upon the *uttaravedi*, he places a lotus leaf (*puṣkaraparṇa*) with the formula, "Thou art the back of the waters. Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.
(10.30:28.7) Then, upon the *uttaravedi* itself, he places the gold plate (*rukmá*) on the northern support (*uttaranirbādha*) with the verse, "The Brahman was born first.
(10.30:28.8) Then he sprinkles it crosswise with five ladlings of clarified butter, [chanting], "Make your path wide like a net.
(10.30:28.9) Then, to the south, he places a golden man facing eastward with the verse, "In the beginning, the Golden Germ (*hiraṇyagarbhaḥ*) came into being."
Then he touches it with the verse, "The drop has fallen" (*drapsaś caskanda*).

Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* verses. Then, at the distance of a step to the north, he places two offering-spoons: one made of *kārṣmarya* wood, filled with clarified butter; and one made of *udumbara* wood, filled with curds—the *kārṣmarya* one to the south and the *audumbara* one to the north—with the formulas, "Thou art this" for the *kārṣmarya* one, and "Thou art so-and-so" for the *audumbara* one, [the latter] by means of the mind alone.
Having performed the *tayādevatam* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* verses.
Then, on the right side of the forehead, he places a serpent’s head with the three verses beginning with "Homage be to the serpents," according to their respective meters;
or rather, wherever he perceives danger arising from the people of the countryside.
Having performed the tayādevata rite, he performs the sūdadohas rite.

(10.31:28.19) Then he prepares the naturally perforated stone with the *yajus* formula: "Thou art firm, a supporter; thou art unsubdued by Viśvakarman, well-fashioned. May the ocean not destroy thee, nor the eagle; remaining unshaken, support the earth! Thus.

(10.31:29.1) Then, having made the horse smell it, he runs toward it together with an unlearned Brāhmaṇa and lays it down so that its vital breaths may be joined with the vital breaths of this person, and not be shut off: "O Earth! May Prajāpati settle you," having recited this; "May Agni protect you with great well-being, with a most peaceful shelter; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras. (10.31:29.5) "Having laid down the first *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, one should breathe over it. Thus he breathes over it.
(10.31:29.5) Now this Brahmin gives a boon.

(10.31:29.6) Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter in the offering-spoon, he offers it in the space of the naturally perforated stone (*svayamātṛṇṇā*) with the formula: "I offer consciousness with mind and with ghee.
(10.31:29.7) Having caused [the sacrificer] to touch him with both thumbs, he makes him recite the ascent: "I have stepped upon the earth; may my breath not forsake me."
In another cavity, he places a golden brick with the formula: "Thou art brilliance; grant me brilliance; grant me the earth; protect me from the earth.
Behind that, at the limit of the steps, he places a circular brick with the formula: "The earth, filled with food, has become a fortress.
To the south, he places the *retahsic* brick with the formula: "The earth is the *retahsic*; may she bestow seed upon me; may she cause seed to be produced in me."
Having performed the tayādevata rite, he pronounces the sūdadohas verses.
(10.32:29.15) Then he lays down these ten *skandhyā* bricks facing east: two *ṛtavyā*s, two *dviyajuṣī*s, the *virāj*, the *viśvajyotis*, the *sayuj*, the *aṣāḍhā*, and two *saṃyānī*s.
(10.32:29.17) He lays down the two *ṛtavyā*s with the formula: "Madhu and Mādhava.
He then lays down a blade of *avakā* grass with the formula: "Thou art the womb of Agni."
Then he lays down two *dviyajuṣ* bricks with two verses: "Growing up from joint after joint, you who spread yourself out by a hundredfold," [and] "O Dūrvā brick.

Then he lays down the *hiraṇyamūrdhnī* brick with [the verses]: "Those splendors of yours, O Agni, which are in the sun; those splendors of yours, O gods, which are in the sun. Then the *virāj* and the *viśvajyotis* bricks: "The *virāj* has established the light; may Bṛhaspati settle you"—thus the upper one.
(10.32:29.22) Then he lays down the *sayuj* brick with: "I yoke thee, the companion, for Indra and Agni, as a yoke-fellow.

(10.32:30.1) Then he lays down the *aṣāḍhā* brick, marked with three lines and having its characteristic mark on the north side, with: "Thou art the invincible Aṣāḍhā, the subduing one. (10.32:30.2) Then he lays down the two *saṃyānī* bricks with: "Thou art the path of Agni; thou art the path of the gods, O Agni."
Having performed the tayādevata rite, he pronounces the sūdadohas verses.
(10.33:30.4) Then, having sat down to the north of the three-lined [brick], he asks for curds mixed with honey and a tortoise.

(10.33:30.5) He anoints it with the curds mixed with honey, reciting the three verses in their proper meters beginning with, "The winds are honey for the one who follows the cosmic order" (*madhu vātā ṛtāyate*).

(10.33:30.6) Then, having wrapped it in a bundle of *avakā* plants, he places it facing westward in front [of the altar] with two verses beginning, "May the great heaven and earth... and "May the four quarters and the fires proceed."
(10.33:30.8) Then they fix it around with pegs on all sides so that it cannot slip away.

(10.33:30.9) Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* formula. (10.33:30.9) Then, standing right there, he asks for a mortar and pestle made of udumbara wood and all kinds of herbs.
This mortar is one span in measure, and the pestle is one cubit in measure.

In it he threshes all the herbs, [saying]: "Thou art the portion of vigor; thou art the purifier of vigor; vigor is food, for the sake of eating food. Then he places it to the north at the distance of a step, [saying]: "That is the highest step of Viṣṇu."
To the north, he places a pestle as the *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick;
having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he recites the two *sūdadohas* verses.
Then he asks for the principal fire-pan (*mukhyā ukhā*).
Within that [space], he offers two spoonfuls of oblations with a *sruc* ladle that flow inward:

"O Agni, yoke those which are yours" (*agne yukṣvā hi ye tava*)—he offers this in the southern cavity; "Yoke those who best invoke the gods" (*yukṣvā hi devahūtamān*)—he offers this in the northern one.
Then, to the north, at the distance of a step, he lays down [the brick] with: "Thou art firm, O Earth; overcome those who attack us."
He places the other [bricks] to the north of the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks. Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he recites the *sūdadohas* verses. Then he asks for this human head.
He throws pieces of gold into his vital breaths.
With the verse, "A drop has fallen," he places one into the mouth;
with the verse, "This has become the vigor of the entire world," he places one into the right nostril.
With the formula, "Of Agni Vaiśvānara," he places [the gold plate] on the northern [eye];
with "Agni is radiant with light," on the southern eye;
and with "The golden disk is resplendent with luster," on the northern.
With the words, "For the Ṛc, thee," he [pours] into the right ear;
with the words, "For the Ruc, thee," into the left.
Then, having taken four portions into the offering-spoon (*sruva*), he makes an oblation into the right eye with the verse: "The brilliant face of the gods has risen up."
Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers it on the northern axle with the verse, "The bright [glory] of the gods...
(RV 1.115.1). "He offers with a common [verse]," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

With these words, he mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes... Having touched the white horse, he mounts it with two verses: "This is the gathering place of the waters; homage to thee..."
Then, having stepped forward, he offers two *saṃcita* oblations on the third layer with the verses, "O Agni, worthy of the house" (*agne gahya*) and "That I entreat of thee" (*tat tvā yāmi*).
To the south, he lays down the *vibhakti* brick with the verse, "May Agni strike down the Vṛtras.
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula.
Then he stretches out these five *skandhyā* bricks facing eastward: two *ṛtavyā*s, two *sayuj*s, and one *saṃyānī*.
He lays down the two *ṛtavyā*s with the formula: "Saha and Sahasya.
He then places a blade of *avakā* grass upon them with the formula: "Thou art the womb of Agni."
Then he lays down two *sayuj* bricks with the formulas: "I yoke thee with the *stomas* as a companion; I yoke thee with the *chandases* as a companion.
Then he lays down the *saṃyānī* brick with the formula: "Thou art the aerial path of the gods.
Having performed the *tayādevatam* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.

(10.42:40.6) Then he lays down the *akṣṇayāstomīya* bricks. (10.42:40.6) With the words, "The Swift is the Trivṛt," he lays one down in the east; with "The Sky is the Saptadaśa," in the south; with "The Supporter is the Ekaviṃśa," in the west; and with "The Radiant is the Pañcadaśa," in the north. (10.42:40.8) With the words, "The Onset is the Aṣṭādaśa," he lays one down in the east; with "The Overturning is the Triṃśa," in the south; with "Splendor is the Dvāviṃśa," in the west; and with "Austerity is the Navadaśa," in the north.

(10.42:40.10) He places [the bricks] in front with the words, "The womb is the twenty-fourfold"; to the south with, "The embryos are the twenty-fivefold"; behind with, "Vital power is the twenty-sevenfold"; to the north with, "The gathering is the twenty-threefold. (10.42:40.12) He places [the bricks] in front with the words, "The ritual intention is the thirty-onefold"; to the south with, "The station of the sun is the thirty-fourfold"; behind with, "The foundation is the thirty-threefold"; to the north with, "The vault of heaven is the thirty-sixfold."

With the formula, "Thou art the portion of Agni," he places one in the east; with "Thou art the portion of the Nṛcakṣases," in the south; with "Thou art the portion of Mitra," in the west; and with "Thou art the portion of Indra," in the north.

With "Thou art the portion of the Vasus," he places one in the east; with "Thou art the portion of the Ādityas," in the south; with "Thou art the portion of Aditi," in the west; and with "Thou art the portion of the god Savitṛ," in the north.

(10.42:40.19) “The *dhartra* is the *catuṣṭoma*,” with these words he places one in the east; “Thou art the portion of the Yavas,” with these words [he places one] in the south; “Thou art the portion of the Ṛbhus,” with these words [he places one] in the west; “The *vivarta* is the forty-eightfold [stoma],” with these words [he places one] in the north.
(10.42:40.22) “He places them in a different order from that in which they are recited,” so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* verses.

(10.42:41.1) Then he lays down the Sṛṣṭi bricks with [the formulas]: "With one they praised; creatures were produced," and so on, seventeen in number. (10.42:41.2) He lays down four on the southern shoulder, then three, then three, then three, then four.
(10.42:41.3) From the southern shoulder he extends them toward the southern hip.
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula.
Then he lays down the *vyuṣṭi* bricks with the words, "This indeed is she who first shone forth," fifteen in total—
three in each of the quarters and three in the middle.
The layer is completed with the *vyuṣṭī* bricks;
having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he recites the *sūdadohas* verses.

(10.43:41.8) Then he piles the fire-altar facing in all directions; the limbs of the fire, the brick dedicated to Prajāpati, the bull, and the space-filling bricks (*lokaṃpṛṇā*). (10.43:41.9) Here he gives the impulse with a space-filling brick facing north; they cover the fire-altar completely with bricks facing north.
He draws it across while it is well-covered with a *palāśa* branch, saying: "Fill the world; fill the gap.
Then he touches the layer with the *citiklpti* formula: "May the wise one distinguish between thought and lack of thought.
Having touched this layer with an *āgneyī* verse in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, he descends with two verses: "May speech be in my mouth; may the breaths be in my nostrils."
Then he proceeds with the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites.
On this day, only this much ritual action is performed;
they stay for that night.
Then, on the eighth day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites;
the laying down of the loose earth is the same.
Then, on the ninth day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites.
(10.44:41.18) All put on sandals made of black antelope skin.

(10.44:41.19) Then he asks for the vessel of clarified butter together with the dipping-spoon, the *vibhakti* brick, a water-pot, and everything belonging to the *svayamātṛṇṇā* and the *nikopa*; as well as the seven *skandhyā* bricks, the *avakā* plants, and whatever other bricks he is about to lay down.
(10.44:42.1) Having taken all this, they set it down at the northern corner of the hip.
Then, with two verses, he takes the fire into himself: "I take Agni first into myself," and "The Agni who is ours.

He mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "O Agni, those logs of thine, those abodes... Having touched the white horse, he mounts it with two verses: "This is the gathering-place of the waters; homage to thee! and [the second verse].
(10.44:42.5) Then, having stepped forward, he offers two *saṃcita* oblations on the fourth layer with the verses, "O Agni, Kiṃśila! That I beg of thee," and "O Agni, we meditate upon the hymn.
(10.44:42.6) To the south, he lays down the *vibhakti* brick with the verse, "O Agni, we meditate upon the hymn.
(10.44:42.7) Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula.

(10.44:42.7) Then he lays down these seven *skandhyā* bricks facing east: two *ṛtavyā*s, the *svarāj* and the *viśvajyotis*, one *sayuj*, and two *saṃyānī*s. (10.44:42.9) He lays down the two *ṛtavyā*s with the formula: "Heat and the month of heat. (10.44:42.10) He places an *avakā* plant upon them with the formula: "Thou art the womb of Agni. He lays down the *svarāj* and the *viśvajyotis* with the formula: "The self-ruling one has established the light; may Prajāpati settle thee," [placing] the northern one.
Then he lays down the *sayuj* brick with the formula: "For prosperity, for nourishment, for pre-eminence among one's kinsmen; with me as thy companion and ally, I yoke thee.
Then he lays down the two *saṃyānī* bricks with the formulas: "Thou art the intermediate space; for the intermediate space, thee!
Having performed the *tayādevatam* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.
(10.45:42.16) Then he lays down the *asapatnā* bricks.

(10.45:42.16) With the words, "O Agni, drive away our born enemies," he lays one down in the east; with the words, "those born by force," he lays one down in the west. With the words, "The forty-fourfold hymn-form (*stoma*)," he lays one down in the south; with the words, "The sixteenfold hymn-form," he lays one down in the north.
(10.45:42.18) Of these, he places the one containing loose soil in the center with the words, "Thou art the soil of the earth, named Apas."
Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.
Then he lays down the *virāj* bricks with the formulas, "The *evaś* metre," "The *varivaś* metre," and so on; forty of them, ten in each direction, but not in the middle.
"He lays them down diagonally," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses. Then he lays down the *stomabhāga* bricks with [the formulas]: "Thou art a ray; for the dwelling-place thee; quicken the dwelling-place," thirty-one in total—seven in each of the directions and three in the middle.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.

Then he lays down the *nākasad* bricks with [the formulas]: "Thou art the queen; thou art the eastern quarter; the Vasus are thy gods as overlords. Thus he places five in each of the directions and one in the middle.
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.

Then he lays down the five *pañcacoḍā* bricks above the *nākasad*s with [the formulas]: "This one in front is the golden-haired, with sun-like rays," and so on—five in each of the directions and one in the middle.
To the west of those [bricks], he lays down the last one facing eastward.
At this point, he meditates in his mind upon whoever the sacrificer hates.
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.
(10.45:43.9) Then he lays down the *chandas* meters. From the section beginning "Agni is the head of heaven," he lays them down three by three according to the traditional recitation.
He lays down *gāyatrī*s in the east, *triṣṭubh*s in the south, *jagatī*s in the west, *anuṣṭubh*s in the north, and *bṛhatī*s in the middle.
He lays down *uṣṇih*s in the east, *paṅkti*s in the south, *akṣarapaṅkti*s in the west, *aticchandas* in the north, and *dvipadā*s in the middle.
Alternatively, having placed two *dvipadā* verses in the middle with an *aticchandas* verse to the north, and having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.
Then, on the southern shoulder, he lays down the *kṛttikās*, seven in number, made into clusters, with the formulas: "Thou art Ambā by name; thou art Dulā by name."
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.

Then he lays down the *vṛṣṭisani* bricks with the formulas, "Thou art the winner of the east wind," "Thou art the winner of the clouds," and so on—five of them, one in each of the quarters and one in the middle.
"He sets them down while moving around [the altar]," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.
Then he lays down the Āditya bricks with the formulas, "For the ocean thee! For the flowing one thee!"—eight in all, two in each of the quarters, but not in the middle.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.
(10.45:43.21) Then he lays down the ghee-bricks with the formulas: "For the Ṛc, thee! For radiance, thee!"—five bricks, one in each of the directions and one in the middle.
(10.45:43.22) "He settles them by moving around [the altar]," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(10.45:44.1) Having performed the tayādevata rite, he pronounces the sūdadohas verse over them.
Then Yaśodā lays down five bricks—one in each of the quarters and one in the middle—with the formula: "I settle thee, the glorious Yaśodā, in glory.
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.
Then he lays down the Bhūyaskṛt bricks with the formulas: "Thou art the maker of abundance; thou art the maker of wide space," placing them one in each of the quarters and one in the middle.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.
Then he lays down the *apsuṣad* bricks with the formulas: "Thou art seated in the waters; thou art seated in the hawk,"—five of these, one in each of the quarters and one in the middle.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.
Then he lays down the Draviṇodās bricks with the formula, "I set thee in the wealth of the earth," five in each of the directions and one in the middle.
Having performed the tayādevata rite, he pronounces the sūdadohas verses.
Then he lays down the Āyuṣya bricks with the formulas, "Protect my out-breath," "Protect my in-breath," and so on—seven in each of the directions and three in the middle.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.
Then he lays down the bricks named after the seasons with the formula, "The Yāvas and Ayāvas," and so on; there are seven [bricks] placed one by one in the directions and three in the middle.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.
(10.46:44.14) Then he lays down the bricks of Indra’s body with the formula, "By Agni, the all-conquering," twenty-two in number—five in each of the quarters and two in the middle.
Having performed the tayādevata rite, he pronounces the sūdadohas verses.

(10.46:44.15) Then he lays down the bricks of the sacrifice’s body with the formula, "Prajāpati, blind in mind, [was] the perceiver," thirty-three in number—eight in each of the quarters and one in the middle.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.

Then he lays down the *jyotiṣmatī* bricks with the formula, "I settle thee, the luminous one," twelve in number—three in each of the directions, but not in the middle. Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.

(10.46:44.20) Then he lays down the *bhūteṣṭakā* bricks with the formulas: "To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā!"—twelve in all, three in each of the directions, but not in the center. Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse. (10.46:44.22) Then he lays down the *ājyānī* bricks with the formula: "To him who has a hundred weapons, who has a hundred powers"—five in all, one in each of the directions and one in the center.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.
Then he lays down the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* bricks with the formula, "O glorious Agni, endow this man with glory," four of them—one in each direction, not in the middle.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses.
Then, on the right shoulder, he lays down the Paurṇamāsī brick with the formula, "Full in the west. Having performed the tayādevata rite, he pronounces the sūdadohas verse.
Then, on that same right shoulder, he lays down the Nakṣatra bricks with the formula, "Kṛttikā is the lunar mansion; Agni is the deity."

(10.46:45.6) Then he causes them to shine with the formula: "O Agni, you are the light of Prajāpati, Dhātṛ, and Soma; for the sake of the Ṛc you, for the sake of radiance you, for the sake of splendor you, for the sake of brilliance you, for the sake of light you.
(10.46:45.8) Then he extends this path of the constellations, beginning from Rohiṇī up to Viśākhā;
he extends it from the right shoulder to the right hip.
(10.46:45.10) Then, at the joint of the tail and at the joint of the body, he lays down the New Moon brick with the verse: "That portion which the gods assigned to thee...
(10.46:45.11) Then he extends this path of the constellations, beginning from Anurādhā and ending with Apabharaṇī.
(10.46:45.12) He extends it toward the northern shoulder from the northern hip.
(10.46:45.12) Then, on the northern shoulder itself, he lays down the Paurṇamāsī brick with the formula: "Full behind.
(10.46:45.13) "He lays them down so that they do not touch one another," so says the Brāhmaṇa. (10.46:45.14) The layer is completed by means of the Nakṣatra bricks.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.
Then, having descended and touched the black horse, he places the *tanūpurīṣa* brick with the words, "He who is questioned in heaven.
Having performed the *tayādevata* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.

(10.46:45.17) Here he piles the sixth layer with [the bricks]: "Saṃyac and Pracetas," five in each of the directions and one in the middle. (10.46:45.18) Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verses. Then he piles the fire-altar facing in all directions, [consisting of] the limbs of Agni, the *prājāpatyā*, the *ṛṣabha*, and the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks.
(10.46:46.2) Here, he gives the impulse with a *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick facing east.
(10.46:46.2) They cover the fire-altar with bricks facing east; then with those facing north.
(10.46:46.3) However, they complete it by means of the eastern bricks.
(10.46:46.3) To whatever height he intends to build, to that height he piles it.
(10.46:46.4) Then it remains untouched by the *citikḷpti* formula.
(10.46:46.5) He asks for these four *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks.

He places them in the quarters: "For breath, for sight, thee! By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! For the diffusive breath (*vyāna*), for sight, thee! By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! For the downward breath (*apāna*), for sight, thee! By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! For speech, for sight, thee! (TS 5.5.5.4 is expanded).

[The formula] is expanded: "By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! (10.46:46.9). Then, having caused the horse to smell the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone, he runs forward together with a Brāhmaṇa who does not know [the ritual] and lays it down, reciting: "O Sky! I set thee in the seat of the earth," and following this with: "May Sūrya protect thee with great well-being, with a hundredfold shelter; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! (10.46:46.12).
"Having laid down the third, he should breathe over it. (10.46:46.12)
He breathes out. Then this Brāhmaṇa gives a boon.
Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter into the ladle, he offers it into the cavity of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone with the formula: "I offer thought with mind and with ghee."
Having caused [the sacrificer] to touch [the hole] with both thumbs, he makes him recite for the ascent: "I have ascended to heaven; we have gone to the light.
He places a golden brick in the other hole with the formula: "Thou art the light; grant me the light; grant me heaven; protect me from heaven.
Behind that, at the limit of the strides, he places a circular brick with the formula: "The unconquered heaven has been entered by means of the cosmic order."
To the south, he lays down the *retaḥsic* brick with the formula: "The sky is the *retaḥsic*; may it bestow seed upon me; may it cause my seed to be produced.
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.
Then, to the north, at the distance of a step, he lays down the *vikarṇī* brick with the formula: "Like a snorting horse eager for pasture..."
Having performed the *tayādevatam* formula, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.
Then he lays down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with the words: "Fill the space, fill the gap.
Then he touches them with the *citiklpti* formula: "May the wise one distinguish between thought and lack of thought..."
Having touched this layer with an Āgneyī Paṅkti verse, he descends with two verses: "May speech be in my mouth; may the vital breaths be in my nostrils.
Then he proceeds with the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites.
Only this much ritual action is performed on this day.
They stay for this night.
Then, on this very ninth day, he prepares for the tenth day a thousand pieces of gold;
some say they should be more than three, being unlimited. If there are a thousand, two hundred each are placed upon the leaf-veins.
Then, on the tenth day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites;
the laying down of the loose earth is the same.
