Then, having poured water into a vessel and scattered pieces of gold, he sprinkles [the earth] with two hundred [pieces] at a time: with the formula "Thou art the measure of a thousand," over that which is to the east of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; with "Thou art the image of a thousand," over that which is to the south of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; with "Thou art the dimension of a thousand," over that which is to the west of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; and with "Thou art the extent of a thousand," over that which is to the north of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*.
(10.47:47.18) Then he sprinkles the middle with two hundred [bricks], saying: "Thou art thousandfold; for a thousand thee!

(10.47:47.19) Then, standing at the northern corner of the hip, he transforms the bricks into milch-cows, reciting from "O Agni, may these bricks of mine be milch-cows" until the end of the section. Then he proceeds with the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites.
Only this much ritual action is performed on this day.
They stay for this night.

Then, on this very tenth day, he prepares for the eleventh day: a leaf of the *arka* tree, goat’s milk, a pap of *gāvīdhuka* seeds, a bow with three arrows, a stone, a water-pitcher, a frog, *avakā* plants, a branch of reed, a clump of darbha grass, a vessel for clarified butter together with a dipping-spoon, a long bamboo pole, and a twelfth [item].
Then, on the eleventh day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the *pravargya* and the *upasad* rites.
Having fixed the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) into the long bamboo tube, he offers two oblations upon the final layer of the piling with the verses: "O Agni of the forest" and "That I beg of thee."
While the Adhvaryu is occupied there, the Pratiprasthātṛ stops at the last brick of the northern wing, having removed the loose earth from it.
Then, having made a funnel out of this Arka-leaf so that it filters inward, standing facing north and holding it at the level of his mouth, he says: "Bring! Fetch!
When he reaches the Dhareṣṭakā, he begins there, reciting this section of the text beginning with "Homage to thee, O Rudra, to thy wrath," up to its end; then the second [and] third [times].

At the fourth [section], when he recognizes the words, "Homage to the charioteers," he utters *svāhā*. Turning back from that very spot toward the east and holding [the vessel] at the level of his navel, he begins with, "To the charioteers," recites the remainder of the section, and then the fifth and sixth [sections].
At the seventh [section], when he recognizes the words, "Homage to the one belonging to the rain," he utters *svāhā*.

Turning from there toward the south, holding [the water] at knee-height, he begins with the words, "And for those who do not rain," and recites the remainder of the section, including the eighth, ninth, and tenth [verses], and of the eleventh [section] as far as he recognizes the words, "As many as these and even more. At that point, he utters *svāhā*.
Turning back from there toward the west, holding [the water] at ankle-height, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "Homage to the Rudras who are on the earth."

Holding [the vessel] at the level of the navel, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "Homage to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space. Holding it at the level of the neck, he causes the sacrificer to recite: "Homage to the Rudras who are in heaven.
At this point, he throws that *arka* leaf onto the path where the cattle of the one whom he hates pass.
If, however, he does not hate anyone, he deposits it in a rat's hole.

At this point, he places this *gavīdhuka* oblation (*caru*) on the final brick with the words: "The Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants; the Rudra who has entered all beings—to that Rudra let there be homage.
Then he asks for this triple-bow (*tisṛdhanva*).
Standing at the northern corner of the hip, he worships it;

or rather, he does so while walking around it [in a clockwise direction]: "O Rudra, that bow which is yours in front, may the wind blow after it for you; to that [bow] of yours, O Rudra, I pay homage with the year. "O Rudra, that bow which is yours to the south," "that bow which is yours to the west," "that bow which is yours to the north," "that bow which is yours above"—thus [he says].
Then he gives it to a Brāhmaṇa without having asked for it.
(10.48:49.12) Now, this water-pot of his lies touching a stone at the northern corner of the buttock.
(10.48:49.13) He says to one who is strong: "Go around three times to the right, sprinkling with a continuous stream from this water-pot.

While the water is being sprinkled around, he makes the sacrificer recite: "The strength that rests upon the rock, in the mountain, in the wind, in Parjanya, in the impulse of Varuṇa; that which has been gathered from the waters, from the plants, and from the trees—grant us that food and strength, O Maruts, acting in concert.
Then he sets down this jar so that it touches the stone, saying: "Let hunger be in the stone; let your pain reach him whom we hate."
Having set down the pitcher, he circumambulates it three times again in the reverse direction.
Then, upon this very long bamboo pole, he fastens a frog, an *avakā* plant, a branch of cane, and a clump of *darbha* grass.
With that, he draws across what lies to the east of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone, [saying]: "With the *avakā* plant of the ocean; with the afterbirth of the snow."
With two [formulas] from the east, with two from the south, with two from the west, and with two from the north—
<he draws it out with eight>, so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then,
having cut these very black-antelope-skin sandals and this long bamboo pole, they throw them together into the *cātvāla* pit.

(10.49:50.7) Then, [thinking] "the fire is extinguished," (10.49:50.8) having taken the butter-pot together with the *sruva*-ladle and having run forward, he offers the serpent-oblations (*sarpāhuti*) by dipping with the *sruva* from the butter-pot:
(10.49:50.9) "Thou art named Samīcī, the eastern quarter," saying this, sitting behind [the altar], he offers into the eastern hole.
(10.49:50.10) "Thou art the vigorous one, the southern quarter," saying this, sitting in the north, he offers into the southern hole.

(10.49:50.11) "Thou art the forward one, the western quarter," saying this, sitting in the east, he offers into the western hole. (10.49:50.13) "Thou art the stable one, the northern quarter," saying this, sitting in the south, he offers into the northern hole.
(10.49:50.14) Then, having returned by the same way he came, he offers two oblations at the very place where he first offered. [He says: "Thou art named Adhipatnī; thou art named Vaśinī.
(10.49:50.15) Then, having descended, he worships the fire with Sāman chants.

He worships the front part with the *gāyatra*; the right wing-tip with the "Heart of Agni" (*agner hṛdaya*); the right wing with the *rathantara*; the right hip with the *vāravantīya*; the tail with the *yajñāyajñiya* of the seasonal stations (*ṛtusthā*); the left hip with the *śyaita*; the left wing with the *bṛhat*; the left wing-tip with the "House of Prajāpati" (*prajāpater gṛha*); and the middle part with the *vāmadevya*. Then he says: "O Hotṛ, recite the *uktha* for Agni after [the offering to] Agni."

(10.49:51.2) If the Hotṛ does not desire [to recite], the sacrificer himself, having spread grass behind the tail [of the sacrificial animal] and sat down upon it, recites the *uktha* for Agni after Agni with the formula: "Father Mātariśvan has placed flawless steps; the eager ones have fashioned flawless steps. May Soma, the all-knowing leader, lead us; may Bṛhaspati recite the hymns of praise and the intoxicating songs—Om! This he does either once or thrice. Then he makes him recite the "milking" of the *stotra* and *śastra*: "The sacrifice has been offered by the Bhṛgus..."
"May I partake here of the wealth of that which has been offered and consumed, through the blessings of the Vasus.
Then he proceeds with the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites.
On this day, only this much ritual action is performed.
They stay for this night.

Then, on this very eleventh day, he prepares for the twelfth day: a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, a wooden trough (*droṇa*) of *udumbara*, a pouring-vessel (*praseka*) of *udumbara*, and a *vitaṣṭi* (a hollowed-out piece of wood) of *udumbara*; in it there is clarified butter taken five times. There is a cup of *udumbara* full of curds, three fuel-sticks of *udumbara*, three of various trees, a faggot of various trees, curds mixed with honey, a handful of grass (*grumuṣṭi*), a bundle of *avakā* plants, a speckled stone, and a second sprinkling-vessel for the clarified butter.

The Hotṛ priest, the reciter for the Apratiratha hymn, two or three jars of melted and purified clarified butter, grains of rice for the Brāhmaudana cooked for the Brahman, all kinds of herbs, a red bull's hide, milk from a black cow that has a white calf, a chariot with its pole-tie for the Caṣāla-offering, and chips of wood for the enclosing sticks—these are the materials.
Then, on the twelfth day, when the sun has risen, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites.
(10.50:51.19) Then, having gone out, he issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā; give the half-breast vow-food.
(10.50:52.1) The Subrahmaṇya invokes the Subrahmaṇyā, and [the Adhvaryu] gives the half-breast vow-food.

(10.50:52.1) Then he takes fivefold-drawn clarified butter, curds mixed with honey, a handful of *grumuṣṭi* grass, and a bundle of *avakā* plants. (10.50:52.2) Having taken these together and hastened forward, he sprinkles the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone crosswise with the fivefold-drawn butter, saying: "To the one sitting among men, vaṭ! To the one sitting in the waters, vaṭ! To the one sitting in the forest, vaṭ! To the one sitting on the sacrificial grass, vaṭ! To the one who has found the light of heaven, vaṭ! (10.50:52.5) With this very ladle, dipping it out, he offers the Gandharva-oblations with curds mixed with honey.

"You are the darts; your dwellings are in the east"—sitting behind [the fire], he offers in the eastern cavity. "You are the smearing ones; your dwellings are in the south"—sitting from the north, he offers in the southern cavity.
"You are the wielders of the thunderbolt; your dwellings are in the west"—sitting from the front, he offers in the western cavity.
(10.50:52.10) "You are named the 'Abiding Ones'; your houses are in the north"—saying this, sitting to the south, he makes an offering into the northern hole.
(10.50:52.11) Then, having returned by the same way he came, he makes two offerings at the very place where he first offered: "You are named the 'Overlords'; you are named the 'Flesh-eaters'.
(10.50:52.13) Then he says, "O Pratiprasthātṛ, prepare this fire so that it has the spots of a tortoise."
He makes that [spot] marked with a tortoise-pattern; he does not step upon it unless it has been sprinkled.
Then, taking a handful of loose soil, he sprinkles it with curds mixed with honey, saying: "Those gods who [are] of the gods," and "Those gods who attained godhood among the gods."

With two [formulas] he sprinkles in front, with those two from the south, with those two from the west, and with those two from the north. "He sprinkles around it in successive order," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then, having covered it with a load of Avakā plants and having instructed the guardian, he hastens back and proceeds with the afternoon Pravargya and Upasad rites.

(10.51:52.20) Then, having gone out, he issues the command: "O Subrahmaṇya, invoke the Subrahmaṇyā! O Āgnīdh, pour out the oblation for Vaiśvānara and the Maruts! O Pratiprasthātṛ, set down the Pravargya according to the procedure for the Pravargya, for the purpose of pouring it out.
(10.51:53.2) They divide this footprint into three parts: one third they place on the Gārhapatya fire, one third in the supporting ladles, and one third he deposits [on the ground].

(10.51:53.3) Then, having raised the *pravargya* vessel according to the procedure for the *pravargya*, he places upon it an oblation for Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds and oblations for the Maruts on seven potsherds.

(10.51:53.4) Then, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the offering-spoon, he offers the *anīkavant* oblation in the Āhavanīya fire.
Having recited "Agni with his sharp flame... and continuing with "...may he, the benevolent one, [be] with his army for us," he makes the offering.

Having taken another portion of four ladlings, he offers the Vaiśvakarman oblations in the Āhavanīya fire itself, having recited "He who, sacrificing, [created] all these worlds... and continuing with "For Viśvakarman, the god, was born."

Having taken another fourfold portion and having recited, "The Father of the eye," he offers with the words, "O Viśvakarman, with the strengthening oblation. "He offers with two separate hymns; he bestows the power of the two hymns separately," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then he places three fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood, [reciting]: "Lead him upward," "O Indra, make him more prosperous," and "In whose house we prepare the oblation."
(10.51:53.13) Then he places the fuel for the leading forward of the fire.
(10.51:53.14) They prepare the supporting-bricks from the *cātvāla* pit.
(10.51:53.15) Then he issues the call: "Recite for the fire being led forward! O *Āgnīdh*, follow along with the single wooden sword! Let the second *Hotṛ* recite the *Apratiratha* hymn! Thus.
(10.51:53.16) This second Hotṛ priest begins with the *Apratiratha* hymn: "Swift, sharpening [his weapons]... (10.51:53.17) "It consists of ten verses," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(10.51:53.18) Then, together with this very fire, they take up a speckled stone, clarified butter for sprinkling, a vessel full of curds made of Udumbara wood, three fuel-sticks from different trees, and sacrificial chips as enclosing sticks.
(10.51:53.20) Then he lifts it up with [the verse], "May all the gods lift thee up.
(10.51:53.20) "He carries [it] with six [verses]," so says the Brāhmaṇa. (10.51:54.1) Of these, two contain the word *parigṛhya*.

(10.51:54.1) Then, at the time of the *viṣuvat* [central day], at the station of the *āgnīdhra*, he places a spotted stone with two verses: "This is the measurer of heaven; the bull, the ocean... (10.51:54.3).
Then, with four verses beginning with "All have magnified Indra," he goes as far as the tail.
They maintain this fire.
Then he sprinkles that piled altar with the sprinkling of clarified butter.

"May the Vasus with the Rudras protect you from the east," [he says] toward the east; "May the Fathers, whose king is Yama, with the Pitṛs protect you from the south," [he says] toward the south; "May the Ādityas with all the gods protect you from the west," [he says] toward the west; "May Dyutāna Māruta with the Maruts protect you from the north," [he says] toward the north; "May the gods, of whom Indra is the eldest and Varuṇa is the king, protect you from below and from above," [he says] toward the zenith.

(10.52:54.10) Then, with this very fire, he hastens forward with five [verses]: "Go forth, knowing, along the eastern quarter"; "Stride toward the vault with Agni, the fire-pan"; "From the earth I have ascended to the mid-region"; "Going to heaven, they look not back"; "O Agni, go forth as the first of those seeking the gods. (10.52:54.13) They hold up this fire;
then he offers a ladle made of Udumbara wood, filled with curds, upon the naturally perforated stone.
Having recited the *puro’nuvākyā* verse, “Night and Dawn,” he offers the oblation with the verse, “O Agni, thousand-eyed.
Then, having turned to the right, he establishes the fuel with the verse, “You are the fair-winged Garuḍa. “He settles it with three [verses],” so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(10.52:54.16) Then, having untied it and made it capable of bearing the oblations, he makes additional offerings with the *adhvara* oblations: "May Agni, knowing [the way], lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it; announce the sacrifice to the gods; further extend the lord of the sacrifice—*svāhā*! May Vāyu, knowing [the way], lead the sacrifice; may Sūrya, knowing [the way], lead the sacrifice; may the Sacrifice itself, knowing [the way], lead the sacrifice; may those who destroy the sacrifice not find it; announce the sacrifice to the gods; further extend the lord of the sacrifice—*svāhā*! Thus.

(10.52:54.21) Then, having stepped down and performed the second tracing around [the altar] while it possesses the fire, having leveled it, and having fixed the wooden sword (sphya) across [the altar], he issues the command: "Set down the sprinkling waters! Set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass!"

(10.52:55.1) Then, having stepped forward, having laid the enclosing-sticks of *śakala* wood, having anointed the fuel of various trees, and having placed it on the fire with the utterance of *svāhā*, he places three fuel-sticks of various trees: with the verse, "O Agni, kindled, shine before us," he places one of *udumbara* wood; with the verse, "We would worship thee in thy highest birth, O Agni," he places one of *vaikaṅkata* wood; and with the verse, "That wonderful [gift] of Savitṛ, the most excellent," he places one made of *śamī* wood. (10.52:55.5) Then he offers two oblations of clarified butter with the verses, "I offer consciousness" and "O Agni, him today."
(10.52:55.6) Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter into the *sruva* ladle, he offers the full *sruca* with the verse: "Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues.
(10.52:55.8) While offering here, he should meditate on the quarters with his mind;
thus he wins them from the very quarters.
He offers curd first and ghee afterwards.
"He bestows brilliance and sensory power upon him in a unified manner," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, standing right there, he calls for a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara and cakes on seven potsherds for the Maruts.
Then, having spread the underlayer of ghee all around and placing the portions for Vaiśvānara upon it, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Vaiśvānara.
He pours ghee over them twice.
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Offer the oblation to Agni Vaiśvānara."
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers in the middle.
Then he makes additional offerings over it with ladle-oblations (*sruvāhuti*) using five [mantras], beginning with: "Like the sun is the Gharma, svāhā!
Thereafter, he proceeds with the Maruts.
Having recited the *paryupastāra* formula in the manner of a *darvihoma*, namely, "Such-like and other-like," he offers with the words, "Śukrajyotis and Citrajyotis.
Having recited, "Śukrajyotis and Citrajyotis," he offers with the words, "Ṛtajit and Satyajit. Having recited, "Ṛtajit and Satyajit," he offers with the words, "Ṛta and Satya."

Having recited "Ṛta and Satya," he recites the group that is to be recited in the forest and offers the oblation; having recited that group which is to be recited in the forest, he offers the oblation with "Such as these, like these.
Having recited "Such as these, like these," he offers the oblation with "Measured and well-measured for us."
Having recited, "Both the measured and the well-measured for us," he offers with, "The like and the unlike.
He piles them around Vaiśvānara on both sides; having recited each group [of verses] after the other, he offers.
"He causes the announcement for Vaiśvānara loudly; he offers the oblations to the Maruts in a low voice"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(10.54:56.8) Then he places this sprinkling-vessel upon the fire, either to the south facing north, or behind facing east.
(10.54:56.9) Its eastern half is like the front part of a ladle;
its middle is exactly the same.
The base is like a *camasa* cup;
upon it, spreading four [spreads of ghee], he says: "Bring [the stream] continuously and without interruption; I shall recite the *Vasordhārā*.
When the stream reaches the fire, he begins with: "O Agni and Viṣṇu, being in harmony," and continues the entire *Vasordhārā* until its conclusion.
At this point, he throws the pouring-spoon into the fire. Then he makes an offering over it with the residue of the oblation.
Then, in whatever clarified butter remains, he cooks the *brahmaudana* (the rice-mess for the Brahman).
Four Brāhmaṇas eat it;
"To them he should give four milch-cows," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, previously for him, there is a vessel made of Udumbara wood containing all kinds of herbs, mixed together with curds and clarified butter.

With a sruva-spoon made of udumbara wood, he offers the *vājaprasavīya* oblations over what has been placed [therein], reciting: "This impulse of strength was first born; may strength [fill] the seven directions for us. Thus, fourteen spoonfuls of oblations.
He leaves over the remainder for the sake of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Then, having covered it, he sets it down in a known place.
(10.54:56.19) Then, with the verse, "O Night and Dawn," he offers the milk of a black cow that has a white calf.

(10.54:57.1) Then he offers the six *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations with [the formulas beginning] "The one who conquers through truth, whose abode is truth. (10.54:57.2) With the formula, "O Lord of the World," he offers five oblations at the front of the chariot.

Then he offers three *ruce* oblations with [the verses]: "O Agni, those splendors of yours which are in the sun," "O gods, those splendors of yours which are in the sun," and "Bestow splendor upon us among the Brahmins."

Then, having poured clarified butter into the offering-ladle, he offers oblations to the names of the winds, taking portions with his joined palms: "Thou art the ocean, full of moisture, the giver of rain; bringing welfare and joy, blow upon me, svāhā! Thou art the Marut, the host of the Maruts; bringing welfare and joy, blow upon me, svāhā! Thou art the seeker of aid, the worshipful one; bringing welfare and joy, blow upon me, svāhā! Some, indeed, think that they are offering to the wind itself.
At this point, he throws these enclosing-sticks made of *śākala* wood into the fire.
This [section] ends with the Śākala.
Then he erects the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds.
Having erected the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*, he pours out the *adhvara-dhiṣṇiya* hearths.

Upon them, he lays down the *agni-dhiṣṇiya* hearths: at the *āgnīdhra* hearth, he places one *yājuṣī* brick with the verse, "O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations," and seven *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks.
(10.55:57.14) Then, on the *dhiṣṇiya* of the Hotṛ, there is one *yājuṣī* brick and eleven *lokaṃpṛṇā*s. (10.55:57.15) Then, on the others, there is one *yājuṣī* brick and seven *lokaṃpṛṇā*s each.
(10.55:57.16) Then, on the *mārjālīya*, there is one *yājuṣī* brick and five *lokaṃpṛṇā*s.
(10.55:57.16) Then he leads forward Agni and Soma.
(10.55:57.17) Having led forward Agni and Soma, he raises the sacrificial post according to the procedure for the post.
(10.55:57.18) Having set out the sacrificial post equipped with a wooden cup, he dedicates the animal victim to Agni and Soma.
Having performed the well-known rite with the omentum of that [animal], and having thrown the two omentum-spits into the fire, he takes up the *vasatīvarī* waters.
Then he offers the sacrificial cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for the animal; following it are the eight *devasū* oblations, beginning with "To Agni Gṛhapati. These are they.
They tie them up separately,
cook them separately,
and they consist of different grains.

The call for the animal-cake offering is "Recite! and "Sacrifice! for the other oblations. When he says, while cutting portions from the offering to Varuṇa, "Recite for Varuṇa, the Lord of Law," then he cuts once from the northern half of each of all [the portions] into the *upabhṛt* ladle for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, and he pours clarified butter over them twice.
He does not anoint [the offering]. Having stepped across and caused the announcement to be made, he says, "Sacrifice to Varuṇa, the lord of dharma.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation.
Now it is indeed said:

"Varuṇa has been sacrificed to, but Sviṣṭakṛt has not yet been sacrificed to; then the Brahman takes his hand. Thus, when Varuṇa has been sacrificed to and Sviṣṭakṛt has not yet been sacrificed to, then the Brahman takes his hand.

"May Savitṛ impel you among those who impel; Agni among householders; Soma among the lords of the forest; Rudra among cattle; Bṛhaspati among speeches; Indra among the eldest; Mitra among the truthful; Varuṇa among the lords of dharma."

All this is as follows: "O gods who are the impellers of the gods, do you impel this [man], the son of such-and-such a father, for freedom from enemies, for great sovereignty, for great overlordship, for great lordship over the people.
Then, while he stands in the sacrificer’s station, he says to those for whom he has become the chief: "This is your king. The others reply: "Soma is the king of us Brāhmaṇas."
Then he releases his speech with the words, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ.
He wipes his face with two verses: "That sovereignty has been established; all the hosts have become Varuṇa's.
He steps the Viṣṇu-strides, which are Gāyatra in nature, with the formulas: "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu; thou art the step of Viṣṇu; thou art the wide-stride of Viṣṇu."
Then he proceeds with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering;
he does not cut off the *iḍā* portion from the oblation for Rudra.
They cause him to be cast into the deepest part of the waters.
The cake offerings conclude with the *iḍā* invocation;
the animal sacrifice concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings;
some say it concludes with the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*).
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and having set aside the milks, they observe the fast.
(10.57:59.7) Now, therefore, they wake up at the very dead of night.
(10.57:59.7) The ritual procedure is the same up to the placing of the offering-ladles (*sruk*).

(10.57:59.8) Having placed the ladles, he yokes the fire with the formula for yoking: "I yoke Agni; these two are your wings; you are conscious, you have the ocean as your womb"—with these three verses.
Then, having brought down the King [Soma], he begins the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*).
When the morning litany has been concluded, he goes toward the waters. He emerges from the waters.
He enters that very sacrifice;
the pressing is performed in the established manner,
and the cups are drawn in the established manner.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup.

Having drawn the Āśvina cup and taken eleven cords, he approaches the sacrificial post. Having set aside the post provided with a wooden chip (*svaru*), he dedicates the eleven animals: a black-necked goat for Agni; a ewe for Sarasvatī; a brown one for Soma; a dark-grey one for Pūṣan; a white-backed one for Bṛhaspati; a speckled one for the Viśvedevas; a ruddy one for Indra; a dappled one for the Maruts; a composite one for Indra-Agni; a dark-bellied one for Savitṛ; and a ram for Varuṇa.
Having performed the well-known ritual with their omenta, they proceed to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).
That [pressing] concludes in the regular manner. They proceed to the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*).

Whenever it is midday, having filled this golden vessel with honey, he looks at it with a verse addressed to Sūrya containing the word "variegated" (*citravatī*), causes the horse to smell it, and gives it to the Brahman priest.
The pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner;
the cups are drawn in the established manner.
The ritual procedure up to the offerings for the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) is the same.
Having offered the *dakṣiṇā* oblations, he proceeds with the three *marutvatīya* cups.
The *nārāśaṃsa* goblets, having been replenished, are set down below the rear support of the southern *havirdhāna* cart for the sake of the *māhendra* cup.
(10.57:60.6) Then, prior to the consecration, he offers six *pārtha* oblations with the formulas: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā!
(10.57:60.8) Then, on the sacrificer’s seat, he spreads out a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair upward.
(10.57:60.9) Having seated the sacrificer there facing eastward and having placed gold and silver plates around him, he sprinkles him from the front toward the west with all medicinal herbs.
He sprinkles him from the head down, letting the water flow down as far as the mouth.

"On the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the controller of speech—with the imperial sovereignty of Agni, I consecrate you; with the imperial sovereignty of Indra, I consecrate you; with the imperial sovereignty of Bṛhaspati, I consecrate you.

When he has been wiped clean, they cry out together: "This one, [name], of such-and-such lineage, the son of such-and-such, the grandson of such-and-such, the great-grandson of such-and-such, has been consecrated by means of the Agnisava!"
Then, with the words "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar," he releases his speech;
he wipes his face with two verses;
he takes the Viṣṇu-strides according to the Gāyatrī meters.
Then, after the consecration, he offers six oblations pertaining to the earth.
"Oblation to Indra! Oblation to Ghoṣa!"—with these words he offers twelve oblations to the beings (*bhūtānām aveṣṭīḥ*), [and then] "Oblation to Earth! Oblation to the Intermediate Space!
With this, the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinam savanam*) concludes in the regular manner.
They proceed to the third pressing.
Having performed the established rite with the Āditya cup, he draws the Āgrayaṇa cup.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Pavamāna laud.
Having performed the Pavamāna rite, he proceeds with the animal sacrifices in their own place.

For these, there are separate *manotās*, separate deities, separate touchings, and separate *vasā-homas*. The *vanaspati* offering is common, as is the *sviṣṭakṛt* accompanied by the *praisha* calls; the *iḍā* is common, and the directions are common.
Some say the directions are separate.
The ritual procedure is the same up until the *yajñāyajñiya* stotra.

When the *yajñāyajñiya* stotra has been commenced with the first [verse], he then touches the fire with two verses: "Homage be to thee; do not harm me; give us water, cleave the ocean. The ritual procedure is the same up until the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

Having performed the *saṃyāja* offerings for the wives, having gone forward to the east, having replenished the *dhruvā* ladle, and having offered the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations belonging to the *adhvara*, he offers ten oblations pertaining to the fire-altar with the verse: "That which flowed forth from intention... The ritual procedure is the same up to the *avabhṛtha*.
Then, at this *avabhṛtha*, he offers the second *avabhṛtha* oblation with the formula: "To the ocean, the guide, to the lord of the rivers, obeisance!"
The *avabhṛtha* rite is well known.
Having performed the *udayanīya* sacrifice, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.
For that cow, there is curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa, from which portions are to be cut off.
(10.59:62.2) They perform the complete ritual for the animal sacrifice.

Then, having melted the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire and purified it, and having taken four portions of the butter into the ladle, he offers the ladle full of butter as the "unloosing" (vimoka) oblation to Agni with the verse: "Suck this breast, rich in vigor, of the waters. (10.59:62.4) Then he pays homage to it with the formula: "Those fires which belong to the soil..."
(10.59:62.5) Then he worships him with the Āpti verses: "O Agni, may we obtain you with our mind," and so on, with nine verses according to their respective meters.
(10.59:62.6) Then he performs the Udavasānīyā sacrifice;
then he performs the Devikā offerings.
Then he performs the Traidhātavīya sacrifice;
then he performs the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice;
for a year he does not descend toward anyone.
He does not eat the flesh of the head, nor the flesh of birds.
Having piled the fire-altar, he should not approach a woman with whom sexual intercourse is forbidden; one who has piled the fire-altar should not run while it is raining.
If he should run, he must return [to his place].
"He turns toward food itself," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
One is about to perform the Vājapeya sacrifice.

He procures a black antelope skin, two gold plates—one of gold and one of silver—a goat skin, a hundred-measure weight of gold, seventeen gold *kṛṣṇala* seeds, a golden vessel filled with honey, a chariot wheel of *udumbara* wood with seventeen spokes, a wooden frame consisting of seventeen planks, a sacrificial post that is hornless, four-cornered, and seventeen cubits long, a bundle of wheat, a turban, seventeen measures of wild rice (*naivāra*), and seventeen bags of herbs.

Seventeen vessels for the Vāyu offerings with broad bases and handles, a hundred and a tail-hair [whisk], seventeen gold neck-ornaments (*niṣka*), seventeen garments, seventeen loads of clothing, seventeen chariots, seventeen drums, seventeen elephants, seventeen female slaves, seventeen harnessed oxen, and seventeen hundred cows— or perhaps of each kind of age— or seventeen thousand, for in that [sacrifice] all ages are contained.
Twenty-four animals and fifty-one horses; a pole made of *khadira* wood, split and bound with thongs.
The materials for the *agniṣṭoma* are well-known.
He undergoes initiation during the final days of summer, prior to the full moon of the month of Āṣāḍha.

For this [sacrifice], there are thirteen initiation days (*dīkṣā*), three pressing days (*upasad*), and the Soma-pressing on the seventeenth day. Alternatively, there are seventeen initiation days, three pressing days, and the Soma-pressing on the twenty-first day.
Or again, there are exactly three initiation days, three pressing days, and the Soma-pressing on the seventh day.
Now, indeed, it is said: "One offers the *sāvitra* oblation before each and every ritual act.

Thus, when about to prepare the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, he offers the *sāvitra*: "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice for his prosperity. May the divine Gandharva, the purifier of intentions, purify our intention. May the Lord of Speech make our speech sweet today. Svāhā! Thus.
(11.2:64.7) When about to offer the initiation oblations, he offers to Savitṛ;
(11.2:64.8) when about to pour out the Prāyaṇīyā oblation, he offers to Savitṛ;
(11.2:64.9) when about to offer while holding gold between [his fingers], he offers to Savitṛ.
He proceeds step by step.
Having proceeded step by step and having purchased and carried away the King Soma, when he is about to offer the *ātithya* oblation, he offers the *sāvitra* oblation.
When he is about to proceed with the first *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, he offers the *sāvitra* oblation.
At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having caused a pit to be dug in the southern section of the hall, prepares the *vājapeya* surā.
Intending to perform the first tracing of the great altar (*mahāvedi*), he offers the oblation to Savitṛ.
Intending to lead forward the Āhavanīya fire, he offers the oblation to Savitṛ.
(11.2:64.14) When about to measure out the *sadas* and *havirdhāna* sheds upon the chariot-stand, he offers an oblation to Savitṛ.
(11.2:64.15) When about to lead forth Agni and Soma, he offers an oblation to Savitṛ.
Thus he has offered ten times within the hall.
Now, therefore, the Āgnīdhra priest shall indeed offer the oblation.
When he is about to erect the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), he offers the oblation to Savitṛ.

When the Adhvaryu and the Sacrificer move forward from the east toward the west, anointing [the post], then the Pratiprasthātṛ moves up from the west toward the east, wrapping it with cloths; or he ties on strips of cloth with their fringes pointing northward, or he winds strips of leather from a bow around it.
At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having made a sheaf of wheat equal on both sides, ties it with a turban.
Upon that [sheaf], they perform whatever rites are performed upon the *caṣāla*.
Having set aside the sacrificial post provided with a *svarka* ring, he offers the oblation to Savitṛ, intending to bring forward the animal victim for Agni and Soma.
(11.2:65.7) Having performed the well-known ritual with its omentum, when about to take the *vasatīvarī* waters, he offers an oblation to Savitṛ.
(11.2:65.9) When about to pour out the sacrificial cake for the animal victim, he offers an oblation to Savitṛ. There are three [offerings] at each pressing.
Those [oblations] are seventeen.
Alternatively, one may offer them at each pressing; this is another view.
Then he offers the sacrificial cake for the animal sacrifice.

The eight Devasū oblations follow it: "To Agni Gṛhapati," and so forth; their performance has been explained as that of the fire-altar's installation. The cake offerings conclude with the *iḍā* invocation, and the animal sacrifice concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
(11.2:66.1) Some say it ends with the heart-spit-offering.

(11.2:66.2) At this point, he has these drums suspended according to the directions: five on the southern hip, five on the northern hip, four on the right shoulder, and three on the left shoulder. "In this way, they secure speech for him from the quarters," so said Baudhāyana. Āñjīgavi says that they should be fastened in clusters in front of the Āgnīdhra shed.
Kātya says that [the sacrificers] sit around [the fire].
Then, having carried the *vasatīvarī* waters around and having set aside the milks, they fast.
(11.3:66.8) Now, therefore, they wake up at the very dead of night;
having taken the morning portions of clarified butter and having brought down King Soma, he begins the morning litany (prātaranuvāka).
When the morning litany has been concluded, he goes toward the waters.
The Adhvaryu runs toward the water.

At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having strained the Vājapeya surā and taken it along with the vessel, carries it out through the southern door, goes around the south of the *sadas*, carries it around the south of the Mārjālīya hearth, brings it into the *havirdhāna* shed by the western door, and places it behind the axle of the southern *havirdhāna*.
Then the Adhvaryu emerges from the water.
He undertakes all the sacrifices;
the pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner,
and the cups are drawn in the established manner.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āgrayaṇa draught.
Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he draws the five *atigrāhya* draughts for Indra with these five [formulas]: "Thou art taken with a support; thee, the one seated among men, seated in wood... and so forth.
(11.3:66.17) Then he places them, arranged in clusters, upon the eastern part of the southern half of the mound.

(11.3:67.1) While the Adhvaryu is occupied there, the Pratiprasthātṛ purifies the *surā* with a woolen filter whose fringes point northward, [reciting]: "May the daughter of Sūrya purify your *parisrut*, the *soma*, with her eternal, continuous fleece.
(11.3:67.4) The Adhvaryu takes the cup for Vāyu, and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the *upayāma*.

The Adhvaryu, standing to the east, takes the Soma-cups from the Droṇakalaśa with a vessel dedicated to Vāyu. Having recited, "By this station, generating mighty deeds," he says, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Prajāpati.
Having wiped it around, he sets it down, saying, "This is thy womb; for Prajāpati, thee."

(11.3:67.8) Then the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the Surā-cups with the *upayāma* formula, reciting: "O, surely, those who possess barley... and so on. Having recited this, he takes [the cup] with: "Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati, thee!
(11.3:67.10) He deposits it with: "For Prajāpati, thee!
He neither makes it acceptable (*juṣṭam*) nor [places it] in its womb (*yonim*).
In this very manner, the two of them draw the cups in an interlocking sequence, seventeen each.
The Adhvaryu arranges the Soma cups in two rows or three rows toward the north in front of the axle;
the Pratiprasthātṛ arranges the Surā cups in two rows or three rows toward the north behind the axle.
(11.3:67.14) Then he draws the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. Having recited, "Mount the chariot, O slayer of Vṛtra," he says, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra, the *ṣoḍaśin*.
(11.3:67.16) Having wiped it around, he sets it down with, "This is thy womb; for Indra, the *ṣoḍaśin*, thee. (11.3:67.17) Then he draws the *ukthya* cup.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup.
Having taken the Āśvina cup and having taken six cords, he approaches the sacrificial post.

Having set aside the post provided with a wooden chip (svaru), he then dedicates these animals: one for Agni, one for Indra-Agni, one for Indra, a cow barren of calves for the Maruts, seventeen dark-colored and uniform animals for Prajāpati, and finally one for Sarasvatī.
Then he proceeds with the fire produced by friction according to the ritual procedure for the fire of friction (*nirmanthya*).

Having struck [the victim] and offered the oblation, he then fastens these animals dedicated to various deities separately with double-stranded cords and binds them individually to triple-stranded ropes.

Then, having fastened these animals dedicated to the same deity separately with double-stranded cords, he binds them to a single sacrificial post; or alternatively, he attaches one animal to another animal.
Having finally yoked a Sarasvatī cow, he then sprinkles them, makes them drink, sprinkles [the ground] around them, and pours out the water from the vessel for sprinkling.
(11.4:68.10) Then, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says: "Recite for the fire being kindled! (11.4:68.11) He places the faggot on the fire;
he leaves one fuel-stick remaining.
(11.4:68.11) He fans [the fires] with the Veda-bundle. (11.4:68.12) When the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, he pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* spoon;
once it has been wiped clean, he pours the second [libation] with the two *sruk* ladles.

Then, without letting the two offering-ladles touch each other, having stepped across toward the north and having anointed the animals with the *juhū* ladle, he sets down the two ladles and chooses the *pravara*.
He chooses the officiating priests in the established manner.
The *hotṛ* priest sits down.
He awaits the impulse;
once impelled, having taken up the two offering-spoons, having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Prompt for the *samidh*s!
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers, saying, "Prompt! Prompt!"
Pouring together [the butter] at the fourth and eighth [fore-offerings], he pours it all together at the eighth;
he retains the residue for the *svāhākṛti* offerings.
Having performed ten fore-offerings and stepped across toward the north, he anoints the victims with the *svaru* and the splinters.

These animals have different deities, different sounds, and different directions. Now, these animals have the same deity, the same sounds, and different directions; their ritual procedure is identical up to the carrying of fire around them (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
Then they proceed northward with the animals around which fire has been carried.
Of these, the one for Sarasvatī is on the northern side;
the one for Agni is by way of proximity.
The Adhvaryu takes hold of the two omentum-roasting spits specifically for the victim dedicated to Agni.
The other assistants lead the other victims separately toward the north, one after another, without letting them cross paths.
The Adhvaryu throws down sacrificial grass for the victim dedicated to Agni as it is being slaughtered, but separately for the others.

Then they strike down the others, either toward the east or toward the north, saying: "Make them cry out; cause them to fall into a swoon. Having said this, they return by the same way they came and sit near the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter), reciting: "May offspring of every form rejoice here in this sacrifice, all-knowing and dripping with clarity; dwelling together in Agni as their home, may they favor us with milk and clarity.
When the animals have been struck down, he offers the oblation for those struck down, reciting: "That the cattle have cried out... (TS 3.1.4.3).
Then he approaches with the words, "O immolators, come hither! He consecrates the animals as they are being released from their bonds with the mantra: "May Aditi release these bonds."

Having fastened it separately with branches that have no twigs, he casts it away toward this direction [the south] with the mantra: "I make him who acts as an enemy low; upon him whom we hate, I cast the snares."
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife forward, having caused her to lift up the water-jar;
he causes the vital breaths of the animals to swell in due order. Following behind, the Adhvaryu goes along, extracting the omenta.
(11.5:70.2) The Adhvaryu begins with the omentum of the offering to Agni alone; they bring the others in succession.
(11.5:70.4) While the omentum of the offering to Agni alone is being heated, he throws the tip of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) into it; they hold the others over it.
(11.5:70.5) He makes an oblation with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) over the omentum of the offering to Agni alone; they hold the others over it.

Then, having proceeded with the *svāhākṛti* call, he sprinkles the clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with the residue of the offering and sprinkles the omentum of the animal for Agni alone; they hold out the others. Then, having offered a spoonful before the *svāhākṛti* calls, he proceeds with the omenta of these animals dedicated to various deities, [saying] "Recite the invitatory prayer" and "Give the command."

(11.5:70.9) Then, while gathering together the omenta of these animals that share the same deity, he says in a whisper, "For Prajāpati," and aloud, "Recite for the fat of the goats' omenta as it is being cut. He [pours ghee] as much as the ladle can hold.
(11.5:70.11) Then they lift up the others with a vessel or with the *veḍasūna* [ladle].
(11.5:70.12) He pours ghee over them twice.
Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says in a whisper, "For Prajāpati," and aloud, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] regarding the offered omentum and fat of the goats.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the omentum; he proceeds with the omentum of Sarasvatī in a whisper.
Then, having offered the *svāhākṛti* oblation with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) and having thrown the omentum-spits into the fire, they step out and purify themselves at the *cātvāla*.
(11.5:71.4) Then he gives instructions regarding the animals, saying, "O *śamitr*, cook that which is not to be cut off from the portion for the Maruts separately.
(11.5:71.5) Then, having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, they proceed to the morning pressing (11.5:71.6);
that concludes in the regular manner.
(11.6:71.7) Then, having offered the *sāvitra* oblation, they proceed to the midday pressing with the formula: "O divine doors!

(11.6:71.8) Having recognized that they have proceeded from this very point upwards, the Adhvaryu, moving eastward, says: "Fix the chariot-wheel in the *cātvāla*; place the chariot on the *rathavāhana*; wash the horses; whatever you intend to give as a sacrificial fee, place that to the south; come, O pressers! Call the *grāvastut*; come, O sacrificer! (11.6:71.11) The pressing is performed in the established manner.
The cups are drawn according to the established rule.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āgrayaṇa cup.
Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he draws the Ṣoḍaśin, reciting: "Indra indeed his two bay horses carry," and following this, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Ṣoḍaśin Indra."
Having wiped it around, he sets it down with the formula: "This is thy womb; for Indra Ṣoḍaśin thee.
Then he draws the Ukthya cup;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the offerings for the Dakṣiṇās.
(11.6:72.4) When about to offer the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he asks for a vessel of clarified butter together with a *sruva* ladle and a *sruk* ladle, as well as a garment.
(11.6:72.5) To the fringe at the end of this very garment, a gold necklace is tied.
(11.6:72.6) Having taken all this, he says: "Come, O sacrificer!"
Having gone around to the north of the Āgnīdhrīya fire and having gone around to the north of the Sadas, he stands in front of the hall and hands these Śastra-texts to the Pratiprasthātṛ.
Then he says, "Come, O Sacrificer!
This chariot has been placed upon the chariot-stand at the southern corner of the altar.
He brings it down with the formula: "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra; through thee may this man slay Vṛtra.

Then they turn it, held by the pole, toward the interior of the altar with the verse: "In the impulse of strength, we celebrate with our speech the great Mother named Aditi, in whom this entire world has entered; may the god Savitṛ impel for us the righteous order within her."
(11.6:72.13) Then he washes the horses in the waters with the verse: "In the waters is immortality, in the waters is healing; and in the praises of the waters, O horses, become swift winners.

(11.6:72.15) Then he yokes the southern horse with the formula: "Whether Vāyu has yoked you, or Manu has yoked you, or the twenty-seven Gandharvas—they first yoked the horse; they placed speed in him."
(11.6:73.2) Then he cleans its back [with the mantra]: “O Son of the Waters, swift-moving one, may this one win the prize with that wave which is humped, surging, and most effective in winning booty.
(11.6:73.3) In the same way, he yokes the second draft-animal; in the same way, he attaches the side-horse to its left side; in the same way, he cleans the backs of those two.
Following the yoking of this [central horse], everything is yoked in the manner of a team of oxen.
They place additional girth-bands on the elephants;
they cause loads of clothing to be carried in; and they tie knots with cords made of gold at the fringes of the garments.
(11.6:73.7) He causes the sacrificial fees to be brought in by groups.
(11.6:73.7) Then he offers two oblations on the Gārhapatya fire with two verses addressed to Sūrya.
(11.6:73.8) He offers an oblation on the Āgnīdhra fire with a verse containing the word *naya*.
The sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) are released by way of the southern path.
Whatever he gives, he gives with gold as the foremost.
Then there are garments, yoked oxen and horses, and finally elephants and men.
(11.6:73.11) These very chariots, though not yet given, pass over [the goal];
they do not run the race while belonging to another.
(11.6:73.12) With the mind alone he gives his own chariot to the *adhvaryu*; having mentally assigned them, the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇās*) are distributed.
He proceeds with three offerings to Marutvat;
the Nārāśaṃsa cups, having been replenished, are set down below the rear support of the southern Havirdhāna cart for the sake of the Mahendra cup.
(11.7:74.1) Then he asks for seventeen *śarāva*-measures of wild rice (*naivāra*).
(11.7:74.2) This is cooked in milk;
with it he performs the offering, [saying]: "Recite the invitatory verse for Bṛhaspati! Sacrifice to Bṛhaspati! Thus.
Having covered that [oblation] before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering has been made, he sets it down in its known place.
Now, previously for him, there is a vessel made of *udumbara* wood containing all kinds of herbs, mixed together with curds and clarified butter.
Taking portions from this with a ladle made of *udumbara*, he offers seven oblations of food with the mantra: "The impulse of strength brought forth this in the beginning... and so on.
He leaves over the *prareka* for the sake of the consecration.
Then, having covered it, he sets it down in its known place.
Then, prior to the consecration, he offers six *pārtha* oblations with the formulas: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! and so forth.
Then, on the sacrificer’s seat, he spreads out a black antelope skin with its neck toward the east and the hair upward.
Having seated the sacrificer there facing eastward and having placed gold and silver plates around him, he sprinkles him from the front while facing westward with a mixture of all herbs.

He sprinkles [the water] from the head down to the mouth, letting it flow down over him, [saying]: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech—with the sovereignty of Agni, I sprinkle you; with the sovereignty of Indra, I sprinkle you; with the sovereignty of Bṛhaspati, I sprinkle you.

When he has been wiped clean, they shout out together: "This one, so-and-so, the son of such-a-one, the grandson of such-a-one, the great-grandson of such-a-one, has been consecrated by means of the Vājapeya!"
Then, with the words "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ," he releases his speech;
he wipes his face with two verses;
he takes the Viṣṇu-strides according to the Gāyatrī meters.
Then, after the consecration, he offers six *pārtha* oblations with the formulas: "To Indra, svāhā! To Ghoṣa, svāhā!
He offers twelve *aveṣṭi* oblations for the beings with the formulas: "To the Earth, svāhā! To the Intermediate Space, svāhā!
At this point, he performs the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of this cake for Bṛhaspati.
(11.7:75.3) Then, taking it, he goes out northward between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*.
(11.7:75.3) To the north, these chariots stand with their horses harnessed.

(11.7:75.4) There he makes those horses, yoked by the *yajus*, smell [the vessel]: "O swift ones, winners of the prize, about to run for the prize, about to win the prize, smell the portion of Bṛhaspati! Thus.
(11.7:75.6) Then, having covered it, he sets it down in a known place.
(11.7:75.6) Then he approaches the chariot, saying: "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu; thou art the step of Viṣṇu; thou art the wide-stride of Viṣṇu.
(11.7:75.7) Then he touches the two sides of the chariot, saying: "The two hooks, the two descending ones, which are on both sides of the chariot."
He mounts the chariot with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may I win the prize through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize.
At this time, the Brahman ascends the marked chariot wheel;
he consecrates it from that very spot with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, may I ascend the highest firmament through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize."

(11.7:75.12) Then, having mounted the sacrificer, he makes him recite the *ujjitī* verses: "Agni won speech with the one-syllable [meter]," and so on, seventeen verses. (11.7:75.14) Then he hands him a horse-whip, [saying]: "O horse-whip, powerful one, rich in power, make the horses powerful in battles! (11.7:75.15) With it, he strikes the horses as is appropriate.
(11.7:76.1) "Thou art a courser," [he says] for the southern one; (11.7:76.1) "Thou art a steed," for the middle one; (11.7:76.1) "Thou art a racer," for the northern one.

(11.7:76.1) Then he causes these race-horses to look on [the goal], saying: "O prize-winners, run for the prize! Conquer in the impulse of the Maruts! Measure out the distances! Steady the paths! Go to the goal!
(11.7:76.4) This post made of Udumbara wood is fixed at seventeen throws of the yoke-pin.

They call it "the wood. "O you who run the race, do not pass beyond it; do not turn back without reaching it. Having placed it between your flanks and holding it with your left hands, turn around with your right hands; do not creep away before you have finished. Thus he says.

Then he says, "Come hither, O sacrificer; I shall draw the cup for Mahendra. While the sacrificer has taken hold of him, he draws the cup for Mahendra, reciting, "Great is Indra who [is great] in might," and then, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Mahendra.
Having wiped it around, he sets it down, saying, "This is thy womb; for Mahendra, thee!"
(11.8:76.11) He then sets down these five *atigrāhya* cups dedicated to Indra together.

(11.8:76.12) Then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), restraining his speech, he hastens westward and introduces the chant (11.8:76.13) for the *māhendra* hymn as they chant.

When the *sāman* has been introduced, he issues the command: "O Brahman, sing the *sāman* of the *vājina*s; O racers, run the race! Beat the drums! Pressers, press the soma! O Āgnīdh, pour out the milk-mixture and make the mortar resound! O Pratiprasthātṛ, offer the cake on one potsherd for Varuṇa; attend to the offering for Soma!
They act according to the command, and the Brahman sings the *sāman* of the *vājina*s.
Whosoever among the attendants binds him [with the cord],
the race-runners run,
and they beat the drums.
The voices cry out; he consecrates the voices that have cried out with the mantra: "Speak the word for Indra! Make Indra win the prize! Indra has won the prize!
Then he consecrates the racing chariots with the four verses in their proper meters, beginning: "O swift steeds, protect us in every contest!"
"The sounds cease for the sake of the weapon;
for the Hotṛ: 'This is the last,' they say. After the time of the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu turns away.
The Hotṛ calls out to him; the Adhvaryu responds;
[the Hotṛ] recites the *śastra*.
He responds.
Having responded to the *uktha* in the established manner, he goes forward and lifts up this cup for Mahendra;
the others lift them up after him.
They lift up the *nārāśaṃsa* cups;
then he causes [the Āgnīdhra] to announce: "O, cause to hear! "Let there be hearing! "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice the *soma*!
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.
Then they offer these five *atigrāhya* cups for Indra together;
they offer twice, both at the *vaṣaṭ*-call and at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*-call.
In the same manner, they cause the *nārāśaṃsa* vessels to vibrate twice each.
The Māhendra cup, offered twice, remains set aside.
The chariots approach.
Seeing that the chariots have arrived, he requests the vessel of clarified butter together with the *sruva* ladle.

If they report to him that the chariot has met with an accident, the Āgnīdhra offers this oblation: "And even as he runs, speeding along... With both [verses], he offers the oblation for unyoking the chariot: "May the impulse of strength come to me."
(11.9:78.8) Then he asks for seventeen śarāva-measures of wild rice, seventeen gold kṛṣṇalas, and a golden vessel filled with honey.
(11.9:78.9) Having taken these, he goes out toward the north between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*.
(11.9:78.10) To the north, these yoked chariots stand ready.

(11.9:78.11) He causes these horses, yoked by the *yajus*, to smell [the vessel] with the formula: "O prize-winning, prize-conquering steeds, having run for the prize and having won the prize, wipe yourselves in the portion of Bṛhaspati!
(11.9:78.13) Then, having covered it, he sets it down in a known place.
(11.9:78.13) Then he addresses the chariots as they are being unyoked: "This has become that true compact of yours, which you made with Indra."
(11.9:78.15) He consecrates the drums as they are being sounded with the mantra: "O trees, cause Indra to win; be unyoked for the prize!
(11.9:78.16) Thus he unyokes this chariot harnessed by the *yajus* formula, while they turn the others back as they were given. (11.9:78.17) These race-runners approach him.
He gives one *kṛṣṇala* to each of them;
having taken those together with a half, he presents them all at once to the Brahman priest, saying, "A golden vessel full of honey."
The Brahman, having taken hold of it, descends.

Then he says: "O race-runners, having passed along the southern path, take your station at the southern hip; O Maruts, having gone around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, take your station at the southern shoulder.
Thereupon, they drive them away from the two sheds.
Then he says, "Come, O sacrificer," and having caused the sacrificer to enter the Havirdhāna shed by the eastern door, he causes him to stand near the Soma cups.
"Ye are united; unite me with what is auspicious," he says. "Ye are separated; separate me from evil," he says, regarding the cups of *surā*.
Then, taking this *surā* along with its residue and these cups of *surā*, they offer them to the race-winners (*ājisṛt*).
Drinking it, they remain there, rejoicing and exalting themselves.
Whatever portion of the offering for the Maruts is unfit for consumption, he places that between the two groups upon branches of the *parṇa* tree;
having cried out together, they tear it to pieces.
(11.11:79.11) Then he asks for the vessel of clarified butter together with the dipping-spoon, a garment of silk-cotton (*tārpya*), and one made of *darbha* grass.
(11.11:79.11) Having taken these up, he says: "Come, O sacrificer!
(11.11:79.12) The sacrificer follows behind, and the wife follows after him.
(11.11:79.12) He offers twelve spoonfuls of oblations into the Āhavanīya fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "Vāja and Prasava... and so forth.
(11.11:79.14) Then he causes the sacrificer to put on a linen garment [with the formula]: "Thou art the caul of the Kṣatra.
(11.11:79.14) [With the formula: "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra," he causes the wife to put on one made of Darbha grass.
(11.11:80.1) Then he extends this cord from the sacrificer’s station toward the east or the north, reaching up to the sacrificial post.
(11.11:80.2) Then he addresses his wife: "O wife, come; let us two ascend to heaven. (11.11:80.3) "Let us two indeed ascend to heaven," the other replies.
"I shall ascend to the world of heaven for both of us," says the sacrificer;
"Do you ascend to the world of heaven for both of us," says the wife. He ascends it with ten formulas: "May life be perfected by the sacrifice."
Having reached the end, he raises his arms and says: "We have gone to the heavenly world, O gods; we have become immortal; we have become the offspring of Prajāpati.

Then he looks toward this world, saying: "May I be united with offspring; may offspring be united with me; may I be united with the increase of wealth; may the increase of wealth be united with me. Then he descends upon it, thinking: "As far as they think they will reach, so far shall they rejoice."
Then they strike him with bags of dust.

(11.12:80.11) “For food, thee!”—with these words the Adhvaryu [strikes] from the east; “For the eating of food, thee!”—with these words the Brahman from the south; “For strength, thee!”—with these words the Hotṛ from the west; “For the winning of strength, thee!”—with these words the Udgātṛ from the north.
(11.12:80.12) But if these do not desire to do so, then the Adhvaryu alone strikes from the east, the Pratiprasthātṛ from the south, the Āgnīdhra from the west, and the Unnetṛ from the north.
Their distribution [of the blows] is according to that of the drums.
At this point, he places a stool for him to descend upon;
upon it he spreads a goat-skin, and on the goat-skin he places a hundred-māna weight of gold.
Then he steps down onto the gold with his right foot, saying: "Thou art immortality."
"Thou art nourishment; thou art procreation," [he says] as he places the left [foot] upon the goat-skin.
Then they carry him to the seat with this same couch, or he goes there himself.
These cups follow after him.
At this point, he invokes the *iḍā* of this offering to Bṛhaspati.
Once the *iḍā* has been invoked, both the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu consume the cup for Mahendra, as well as the *nārāśaṃsa* goblets with the portion drunk by Narāśaṃsa.
In this case, having poured the remnants of these *atigrāhya* cups together into the principal cup, the sacrificer himself consumes them directly.
Alternatively, they may pour all of them into the *camasa*s and consume them; this is another option.
These three, having invited one another, consume the *hotṛ*’s *camasa*.
(11.12:81.11) According to their respective cups,
they touch themselves with the formula, "Impel [the breath] for me," but they do not cause the cups to swell.
(11.12:81.12) Having consumed all [the portions], they perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*).
(11.12:82.1) Then, with the formulas "For Indra thee! For Indra thee!", he proceeds in this manner through the three *ukthya* rounds.
(11.12:82.2) The midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinaṃ savanam*) is concluded.

Then, having offered the *sāvitra* oblation, they proceed to the third pressing. Having performed the rite with the *ādityagraha* in the established manner, he draws the *āgrayaṇa*. Then he draws the *ṣoḍaśin*, reciting: "The Soma has been pressed for you, O Indra," followed by: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra, the *ṣoḍaśin*."
Having wiped it around, he sets it down with the formula: "This is thy womb; for Indra, thee, the Ṣoḍaśin.
Then he draws the Ukthya cup;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the Pavamāna laud.
Having performed the Pavamāna rite, he proceeds with the animal sacrifices in their own place.

For these, there are separate *manotās*, separate deities, separate touchings, and separate *vasā-homas*. The *vanaspati* offering is common, as is the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering accompanied by its *praisha*; the *iḍā* is common, as are the directions.
Some say the directions are separate.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the *dhruva*-like cups (*camasa*).
Having performed the rite with the *dhruva*-like cups, he proceeds with the three *ukthya* rounds, [offering] to Indra-Varuṇa, to Indra-Bṛhaspati, and to Indra-Viṣṇu.
Then he proceeds with the *ṣoḍaśin*.
Then, as they go forward toward the east, he says: "Fill the cups following the Hotṛ’s cup! O Unnetṛ, draw up the entire King [Soma]; do not leave any remainder!
Thus, they first fill the Hotṛ’s cup, and the others as they come along.
Having drawn up the entire King [Soma], they set them down upon the Uttaravedi.
(11.13:82.17) They set these Prājāpatya [vessels] down together.
(11.13:82.17) Then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), restraining his speech, he hastens westward and introduces the chant (*stotra*).
(11.13:83.1) They chant the hymn.
They perform this Bṛhat-sāman on the twenty-one-fold stoma over verses addressed to Viṣṇu containing the word *śipiviṣṭa* for the Hotṛ.
"This is the last [verse]," they say. From the time of the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu turns away.
The Hotṛ calls out to him; the Adhvaryu responds;
[the Hotṛ] recites the *śastra*.
He responds.
Having responded to the *uktha* in the prescribed manner, he goes forward and lifts up this *hotṛ*-cup while the others lift up their respective cups after him.
They lift up the cups;
then he causes the announcement to be made: "O, cause it to be heard! "Let there be hearing! "O reciter of the hymns, sacrifice the Soma-draughts!
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.
Then they offer these oblations to Prajāpati together;
he offers twice, at the *vaṣaṭ* call and at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* call.
In the same manner, they offer all the *camasa* cups twice each.
(11.13:83.8) Then they run toward the west with the portions for consumption, according to the formula for the consumption at each pressing: "Of that which has been drunk by Prajāpati.
(11.13:83.9) At this point, having poured together the residues into the principal cup of these [vessels] belonging to Prajāpati, the sacrificer himself consumes them directly.
(11.13:83.11) Alternatively, they may pour all of these entirely into the cups and consume them; this is another option.
In this regard, he offers that portion of the Māruti [oblation] which is not to be cut off to the officiating priests. Having divided this into equal portions, they consume it;
these three, having invited one another, consume from the Hotṛ’s cup alone.
According to their respective cups,
they touch themselves with the formula, "Impel me," but they do not cause the cups to swell.
Having consumed all [the portions], they purify themselves.

Then he issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, bring the embers for the supplementary offerings (aupayaja); O Upayaṣṭṛ, sit down; O Brahman, we shall set forth; having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, O Āgnīdh, cleanse each of the fires once.
They then bring these embers for the supplementary offerings from the Āgnīdhra hearth.
He pours them down in front of the Hotṛ.
The Upayaṣṭṛ sits down with the third portions of the entrails.
At this point, having divided these third portions of the entrails into eleven parts, the Upayaṣṭṛ performs the secondary offerings.
From this point onward, the procedure is the same.
The Vājapeya sacrifice is concluded.
Having performed the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Pratyavarohaṇīya Agniṣṭoma.
The Vājapeya is completed; the Vājapeya is completed.

One is about to perform the Rājasūya sacrifice. Prior to the full moon of Phālguna or Caitra, having sacrificed with the New Moon oblation, he undergoes initiation. For that [sacrifice], there are three days of initiation and three days of Upasad; on the seventh day, the Soma-pressing begins.
This Prāyaṇīya Agniṣṭoma, consisting of four stomas and involving a thousand-fold sacrificial fee, concludes with the Udavasānīyā offering.
Then, on the eighth day, he offers the Ānumata oblation; at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he releases his speech.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the pouring [of the grains].
Having poured them, he places eight potsherds on the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire; the Pratiprasthātṛ places one to the north for the oblation to Nirṛti.
While handing over the grain to be ground for the oblation, he says: "Grind it, making it fall both eastward and westward."
(12.1:85.8) Those grains which fall to the east of the *śamyā* peg, the Adhvaryu collects them, mixes them together, and cooks them for Anumati.
(12.1:85.10) Then those grains which fall to the west of the *śamyā* peg, the Pratiprasthātṛ collects them, mixes them together, and cooks them for Nirṛti.

(12.1:85.11) He takes this offering for Nirṛti—already spread with a base of ghee and sprinkled with ghee—as well as a black garment with a black fringe, a firebrand from the edge of the house, and a vessel of water.
Having taken this, he offers a spoonful of oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire with the formula: “Vīhi! Svāhā! May you enjoy the oblation!

Then, having gone out by the southern door, they go toward that direction where his own natural salt-flat (*iriṇa*) or a cleft in the ground is clearly visible. Having kindled a single firebrand there, strewn grass around it, and grasped it with both thumbs, he offers the oblation to Nirṛti with the formula: “This is your portion, O Nirṛti; you are possessed of the sacrificial offering. Release him from distress, svāhā!”
(12.1:86.3) Here he gives a black garment with a black fringe.

(12.1:86.3) Then, having poured out the water and cast aside the vessel, they depart without looking back. Having washed their hands and feet and returned by the same way they came, he offers a spoonful in the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra: "Svāhā! Homage to him who has done this! (12.1:86.6) Then he completes the rite with the *anumata* offering.
He gives a milch cow.
Then, on the ninth day, he offers a caru-oblation to Āditya and gives a boon.
Then, on the tenth day, [he offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu.
He gives a dwarf horse as the sacrificial gift.
Then, on the eleventh day, there is an offering to Agni and Soma on eleven potsherds;
he gives gold as the sacrificial gift.
Then, on the twelfth day, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and gives a draft bull as a gift.
Then, on the thirteenth day, [he offers] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and curds to Indra.
(12.2:86.12) He gives a bull that draws the cart.
(12.2:86.12) Then, having passed over the Āgrayaṇa oblations, on the fourteenth day he offers to Sarasvatī last;
(12.2:86.13) he gives a heifer.
Then, on the fifteenth day, he offers a pap to Sarasvatī; he gives a young bull as the sacrificial fee.
However, if the fast-day falls on the fourteenth day itself, then on that very day he should sacrifice with these two offerings using separate sets of sacrificial grass.
(12.2:86.16) Now, on this day, the calves are driven away from all the gods.
Having caused the milk for the Viśve Devas to be milked—either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* or silently—he observes the fast.

(12.2:87.1) Then, on the following day, having sacrificed with the oblations for the Viśve Devas and having sacrificed with the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha offerings, he proceeds with the established ritual.
Then, on the following day, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Sutrāman.
A chariot is presented, with its two shafts intact and its armor complete, yoked either with mares that are pregnant or with stallions; a gold necklace is wrapped around it, and he gives that away.
Then, on the following day, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Āmhomuc.

He gives a chariot that has not been driven before, which is without shafts and without armor, yoked either with mares that have not yet brought forth or with gelded horses, and a smooth gold ornament.
These two are called the *saṃtanī* sacrifices.
Then, on the following day, he begins with the two *saṃtanī* sacrifices themselves.

In this very manner, performing the *saṃtanī* sacrifices alternately day by day, the sacrificer proceeds for four months—whether by means of an *iṣṭi*, or a *paśubandha*, or the first-fruits offering (*yavāgrayaṇa*) as desired.

Then, when four months have elapsed, having performed the *saṃtani* sacrifice, having sacrificed with the *varuṇapraghāsa* oblations, and having sacrificed with the *paurṇamāsa* and *vaimṛdha* offerings, he concludes the rite in the established manner.
Then, on the following day, he begins again with the two *saṃtanī* sacrifices.

Performing the sacrifices in this very way with the two *saṃtanīs* in alternation day by day, he passes the remaining four months; at his pleasure he may sacrifice, at his pleasure perform an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), or at his pleasure perform the *śyāmāka-āgrayaṇa*.

Then, when four months have elapsed, having performed the *saṃtani* sacrifice, having sacrificed with the *sākamedha* oblations, and having sacrificed with the full-moon and *vaimṛdha* offerings, he concludes the procedure in the established manner. Then, on the following day, he begins again with the two *saṃtanī* offerings.

Sacrificing in this very way with the two *saṃtanī* offerings in alternation day by day, he passes another four months, performing at will an *iṣṭi*, at will an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), or at will the first-fruits offering of rice (*vrīhyāgrayaṇa*).

Then, when four months have elapsed, having performed the *saṃtanyā* sacrifice, having sacrificed with the *śunāsīrīya* oblations, and having sacrificed with the *paurṇamāsa* and *vaimṛdha* offerings, he concludes the procedure in the established manner.
Then, on the following day, he begins again with the two *saṃtanī* sacrifices.

Performing the sacrifices in this very way, alternating the two *saṃtanī* sacrifices day by day, the sacrificer proceeds for seven days—either at will with an *iṣṭi* or at will with an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*).
Then, on the eighth day, he offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap of *gāvīdhuka* grain for Rudra, curds for Indra, and a pap of barley for Varuṇa.
Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a milch-cow that has recently calved as a gift.
Then, at that very moment, he proceeds with the rite of the five fuel-sticks (*pañcedhmīya*).

Having drawn out the embers in five places, he places five fuel-sticks upon them: one made of *parṇa* wood in the east, one of *naiyagrodha* wood in the south, one of *āśvattha* wood in the west, one of *audumbara* wood in the north, and one of *plākṣa* wood in the center.

(12.4:88.19) Then he sprinkles them with clarified butter: "O gods who sit in the east, led by Agni, slayers of demons (*rakṣohan*), may they protect us; may they favor us; homage to them! To them, *svāhā*! O gods who sit in the south... O gods who sit in the west... O gods..."
"Ye gods who sit above," [he says].
Then, with the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick), he sweeps away the embers, saying: "The *rakṣas* is swept away; the *rakṣas* is burnt up. Here I utterly burn up the *rakṣas*.
Then he makes offerings over them with five spoonfuls, saying: "To Agni, the slayer of *rakṣases*, svāhā! and so forth.

(12.4:89.5) Here he gives away a chariot drawn by a dappled horse. (12.4:89.5) Then he asks for a ladle made of *parṇa* wood, flour of *apāmārga* plants, a garment to be worn as a lower cloth, a firebrand from the edge of the house, and a water-pot.
(12.4:89.7) Having taken these, they go out toward the north and proceed in that direction to where there is a natural depression or a cleft in the ground clearly visible.

Having kindled this single firebrand and strewn grass around it, he offers groats of *apāmārga* with a ladle made of *parṇa* wood, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I offer the slayer of the Rakṣas; svāhā!
Having said this, he throws the ladle after [the oblation] with the words, "The Rakṣas is slain! He then stands over [the fire] with the words, "We have struck down the Rakṣas!"
(12.4:89.12) Here, he gives away what he is wearing.

(12.4:89.13) Then, having poured the waters together and cast aside the vessel, they return without looking back; having washed their hands and feet, (12.4:89.14) they go back by the same way they came and perform the conclusion with the *aindraturīya* [offering].
Then, on the ninth day, he offers the first Devikā oblations: a pap for Anumati, a pap for Rākā, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Dhātṛ.
Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a heifer as a gift.
Then, on the tenth day, he offers the subsequent Devikā oblations: a pap for Sinīvālī, a pap for Kuhū, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Dhātṛ.
Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a young bull as a gift.
Then, on the eleventh day, he begins with the *triṣaṃyukta* offerings: he offers an oblation to Agni and Viṣṇu, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Viṣṇu, and a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu.
He gives a dwarf, draft-bull as a gift.
Then, on the twelfth day, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Soma, and a pap to Soma;
he gives a brown horse as a gift.
Then, on the thirteenth day, he offers a pap to Soma and Pūṣan, a pap to Indra and Pūṣan, and a pap to Pūṣan.
He gives a dark-colored animal.
Then, on the fourteenth day, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara;
he gives gold as the sacrificial gift.
Then, on the fifteenth day, he gives a sacrificial pap made of barley to Varuṇa and a horse as a gift.
(12.5:90.12) Then, while he is performing the New Moon oblation, the Ratnins encamp him—either from the south facing north, or from behind facing east.

(12.5:90.13) Once they have encamped, the Brahman priest stands either on the southern side or the western side. (12.5:90.14) Whatever is used for the consumption of the sacrifice remains in the house of the Brahman alone.

(12.5:90.15) Then, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, having settled at the house of the Brahman priest, having churned out the fires and spread them out, he offers a *caru* oblation to Bṛhaspati in the house of the Brahman priest.
