(12.5:91.2) He gives a white-backed animal as a gift. (12.5:91.2) Then, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, he proceeds toward his own fire-places.
As he is departing, he addresses him with the mantra: "May this king, the slayer of Vṛtra, having become king, slay Vṛtra.
Then, having settled upon his own fire-places, churned the fires, and spread them out, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Sutrāman.
Now, on that day, having caused milk to be milked from a white cow with a white calf and having mixed it together, he sets it aside.

Then, on the following day, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, having settled in the house of a Rājanya, and having churned out the fires and spread them out, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra in the house of the Rājanya;
he gives a bull as a gift.
Likewise, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, he sets out toward his own fire-places.
As he proceeds in that very manner, he consecrates him with the mantra:
"In whosever house he sacrifices, he consecrates him [with]: 'May this king, the slayer of Vṛtra, having become king, slay Vṛtra.
Then, having settled upon his own fire-places, kindled the fires by friction, and spread out the fires, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Ām̐homuc.
On this very day of his birth, having caused the milk of a white cow with a white calf to be milked and having curdled it together, he sets it aside.
Then, on the third day, he gives a *caru* offering to Āditya in the house of the Mahiṣī and presents a milch-cow.
Then, on the fourth day, he offers a pap of cooked rice to Bhaga in the house of the favorite wife; he gives a cow that has miscarried and is barren as the sacrificial fee.
Then, on the fifth day, he offers a pap of black rice, split by the fingernails, to Nirṛti in the house of the discarded wife.
He gives a black, hornless cow.
Then, on the sixth day, at the house of the commander of the army, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and gives gold as the sacrificial gift.
Then, on the seventh day, he gives a cake on ten potsherds for Varuṇa at the house of the charioteer; a large castrated bull is given as a gift.
Then, on the eighth day, he gives a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts at the house of the village headman.
He gives a speckled cow.
Then, on the ninth day, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ in the house of the Kṣattṛ; he gives a dappled cow.
Then, on the tenth day, he gives a cake on two potsherds for the Aśvins in the house of the charioteer; he gives two cows that breathe together.
Then, on the eleventh day, he gives a pap for Pūṣan in the house of the tax-collector.
He gives a dark-colored [animal].
Then, on the twelfth day, in the house of the Akṣāvāpa, he gives a spotted, overflowing pap of Gavidhuka grain dedicated to Rudra.
(12.5:92.9) This day for him is indeed well-established: having caused milk to be milked from a white cow with a white calf and having curdled it together, he sets it aside.
(12.5:92.11) Then, on the thirteenth day, there is an offering to Mitra and Bṛhaspati.
(12.6:92.12) Now, indeed, it is said:

"In ghee that has solidified by itself, churned by itself, from the milk of a white cow with a white calf, one should separate the husked and unhusked rice grains in a four-cornered vessel made of *aśvattha* wood from a branch that has fallen of its own accord. (12.6:92.14) Now, indeed, it is further said:

"The altar is self-made; the sacrificial grass is self-gathered; the fuel is self-prepared. Thus, this king is honored by his own deeds. He himself prepares the altar; he himself binds the fuel and the sacrificial grass; he himself fashions a four-cornered vessel of *aśvattha* wood; and from a branch that has fallen of its own accord, he separates the rice grains that have reached the ears from those that have not.
Now, it is indeed said:
"Those [grains] that have ears are for Bṛhaspati in milk; those that are earless are for Mitra in clarified butter.

Then, having drawn out embers mixed with ashes toward the north, and having placed a new vessel upon them, and having poured clarified butter across the strainer, and having scattered the earless grains across the strainer, he covers the portion for Bṛhaspati with that [butter].
He places that [offering], likewise covered, within the altar.
The ritual procedure up to the *prayāja* offerings is the same.

Having performed five *prayāja* offerings, having stepped across to the north, and having sprinkled the offering to Bṛhaspati with the residue of the clarified butter, he sprinkles the offering to Mitra.
He proceeds first with the offering to Bṛhaspati and then with that to Mitra.
He cuts off the portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt of the former offering to Bṛhaspati, and then of that to Mitra.
He cuts off the Iḍā-portion of the former offering to Bṛhaspati, and then of that to Mitra.
Having set down the *anvāhārya* mess of rice, he gives away this very white cow with a white calf;
thus the oblation to Mitra and Bṛhaspati is concluded.
(12.7:93.12) Now, during this very same first fortnight, he undergoes initiation for the consecration-rite consisting of the Ukthya sacrifice.
(12.7:93.13) Its initiatory period is of unlimited duration, and there are six Upasad days.
(12.7:93.13) He purchases the King Soma in such a way that he thinks, "My pressing will coincide with the new moon day, the day fit for sacrifice."
He becomes successful through that.
Then he performs the Prāyaṇīya offering;
having performed the Prāyaṇīya, he performs the rite with the footprint.
Having proceeded with the *pada* ritual, having purchased the King [Soma] on a red hide, he carries him away and performs the *ātithya* offering.
Having performed the *ātithya*, he then proceeds day by day with the *upasad* rites. Then he leads forward the *āhavanīya* fire.
Having led forward the Āhavanīya fire, he erects the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds upon the chariot-stand.
Having erected the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds upon the chariot-stand, he leads forward Agni and Soma.
Having led forward Agni and Soma, he raises the sacrificial post according to the procedure for the post.
Having set out the sacrificial post provided with a *svaru*, he dedicates the animal for Agni and Soma.
Having performed the well-known ritual with its omentum, he takes the *vasatīvarī* waters.
Then he offers the sacrificial cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) belonging to the animal sacrifice.

These are followed by the eight oblations of the Devasū sacrifice: "To Agni Gṛhapati," and so forth. Their performance has been explained as being according to the procedure for the [Agni] Pavamāna offerings; the sacrificial cakes conclude with the *iḍā* invocation.
The animal sacrifice concludes with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings;
some say it concludes with the heart-spit.
At this point, he fastens these drums in every direction.
(12.7:94.12) Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and having set aside the milks, they observe the fast.
(12.7:94.13) Thereupon, at the very dead of night, they awaken; having taken the morning clarified butters and having brought down King Soma, he begins the *prātaranuvāka*.
(12.7:94.14) When the *prātaranuvāka* has been concluded, he goes toward the waters.
He emerges with water;
he enters the Ukthya rite; the pressing is performed in the established manner.
The cups are drawn in the established manner;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup.
Having drawn the Āśvina cup and having taken two ropes, he approaches the sacrificial post.

Having set out the sacrificial post provided with a *svaru*, he dedicates an animal for Agni; for that [animal], one for Indra and Agni is to be seized as a secondary victim. Having proceeded with the two omenta in the established manner, they advance toward the morning pressing.
That concludes in a straightforward manner;
they proceed to the midday pressing,
and the pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner.
The cups are drawn in the established manner;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the offerings for the *dakṣiṇā* priests.
When about to offer the *dakṣiṇā* oblations, he requests a vessel for clarified butter together with the *sruva*-ladle, a *sruk*-ladle, and a cloth.
At the end of this garment, at its fringe, a cord for the neck-ornament (*niṣkara*) has been tied.
Taking hold of this, he says, "Come, O Sacrificer!
Having gone around to the north of the *Āgnīdhrīya* fire and having gone around to the north of the *Sadas*, he stands before the hall and hands over these ritual implements to the *Pratiprasthātṛ*.
Then he says, "Come, O sacrificer!
This chariot has been placed upon the chariot-stand at the southern corner of the altar;
he brings it down with the formula: "Thou art the thunderbolt of Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra; through thee may this man slay Vṛtra."
(12.7:95.9) Then they turn him, who holds the pole, toward the interior of the sacrificial altar silently.
(12.7:95.10) Then he washes the horses in the water silently.
(12.7:95.11) Then he yokes the right-hand draft-animal with the formula: "By the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the directors, I yoke you with the yoking of the sacrifice."
(12.7:95.12) Then he rubs its back silently. (12.7:95.13) In this very same manner, he yokes the next draft-animal. (12.7:95.13) In this very same manner, he yokes the side-horse to its left.
In this very manner, he rubs the backs of those two [horses].
Following the yoking of this [chariot], everything is yoked like a horse-drawn vehicle.
They make the elephants wear extra girth-bands.
They cause bundles of garments to be brought in; they tie cords for the necklaces to the fringes of the clothes;
he causes the sacrificial gifts to be brought in in groups.
(12.7:95.17) Then he offers oblations on the Gārhapatya fire with two verses addressed to Sūrya.
(12.7:96.1) He offers on the Āgnīdhra fire with a verse containing the word "lead" (*naya*). The sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇās*) are released by way of the southern path.
Whatever he gives, he gives beginning with gold.
Then garments, then yoked cattle and horses, and finally elephants and men.
These chariots are indeed not given away for the sake of mere transit.
These do not run the race for another;
with the mind alone he gives his own chariot to the *adhvaryu*,
and with the mind he assigns the four-footed cattle and the field to the *brahman*.
Having assigned [the portions] mentally, he proceeds with the three Marutvatīya offerings.
The Nārāśaṃsa goblets, having been replenished, are set down below the rear support of the southern *havirdhāna* cart for Mahendra.
(12.8:96.9) Then he asks for a droṇakalaśa made of reeds and sixteen cups for Vāyu.

(12.8:96.10) Now, these waters of his, collected from the quarters in sixteen portions, have already been placed there beforehand; they lie deposited behind the eastern axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, extending westward toward the supporting posts.
Of these, those on the eastern side are flowing (*vahantī*), and those on the western side are belonging to Sarasvatī (*sārasvatī*).

He makes offerings into the flowing waters with the mantra: "You are worthy of sacrifice; they have taken up the divine waters, the honey-sweet, the strength-bestowing, gathered for the Rājasūya. Those with which they consecrated Mitra and Varuṇa, those with which they led Indra beyond his enemies.
You are the givers of kingship; grant us kingship, svāhā! Thus he says.
He takes [the water] with a vessel made of *parṇa* wood, saying: "You are the givers of sovereignty; grant sovereignty to so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, the grandson of so-and-so.
Then he takes the waters of the ocean belonging to Apāmpati, saying: "You are the lord of waters," whether from a male-named ox or from the sea.
Then he takes the waters of the waves, saying: "You are the male wave."
(12.8:97.9) With "Thou art Vṛṣasena," [he takes] those from a pond; with "Ye dwell in the cow-pen," those from a well;
with "Ye are the vigor of the Maruts," those from a pool.
"Ye are sun-bright," [he says] over those that are visible; "Ye are sun-skinned," [he says] over those that rain during sunshine;
"Ye are gladdening," [he says] over the hailstones.
"Ye are the lowing ones," [he says] regarding the dappled cows; "Ye are the powerful ones," regarding the cow's udders; "Ye are the all-sustaining ones," regarding the milk.

(12.8:97.12) "You are the supporters of people," [with these words] he takes the curd. (12.8:97.13) "You are the brilliance of Agni," [with these words] the clarified butter. (12.8:97.13) "You are the essence of the waters and the plants," [with these words] the honey.

Then he makes offerings with the Sarasvatī verses: "The divine waters have taken up the honeyed, the strength-filled, being gathered for the Rājasūya—those wherewith they consecrated Mitra and Varuṇa, and those wherewith they led Indra beyond his enemies.
You are the givers of kingship; grant us kingship, svāhā! Thus.
He draws [the water] with a vessel made of *parṇa* wood, saying: "You are the givers of sovereignty; grant sovereignty to so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, the grandson of so-and-so.

Then he pours them together into a wooden trough (*droṇakalaśa*) made of *veta* wood, saying: "O divine waters, flow together, full of sweetness with those full of sweetness, winning great splendor for the kṣatriya."

(12.8:98.7) Then he places them between the *dhiṣṇiya* of the Hotṛ and that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin with the formula: "Sit down, unassailable, full of vigor, bestowing great splendor upon the Kṣatriya. (12.8:98.9) At this point, they carry away to the residence those vessels belonging to the Adhvaryu which contain solid food (*arthya*). Then they throw away those vessels which do not contain solid food (*anarthya*) into the water.
They set aside the Vasatīvarī waters of the Sarasvatī for the Daśapeya sacrifice from those that have not yet been offered.

(12.9:98.12) Then, standing right there, he asks for a hollow stalk of *darbha* grass, a hundred-māna weight of gold, four vessels made of different kinds of wood, a linen garment (*tārpya*) and a turban, one hundred and one tufts of *darbha* grass, curds, an *udumbara* branch, young grass shoots, a bow, and arrows.
(12.9:98.14) He ties the hundred-māna weight of gold to the hollow stalk of *darbha* grass with [the formula]: "Thou art uncrushed, the kinsman of speech, born of heat.
(12.9:98.16) Then he places it into a trough-shaped cup (*droṇakalaśa*) made of *veta* wood with [the formula]: "Thou art the gift of Soma."

He purifies [the waters] with gold, saying: "O bright ones, I purify you with the bright; O radiant ones, with the radiant; O immortal ones, with the immortal—svāhā! For the Rājasūya, for those who have been gathered."

He draws [the water] with a vessel made of *parṇa* wood, [reciting]: "Sharing the feast, O brilliant ones, these [waters], undecaying and active, he has taken as his garment. Varuṇa has made his dwelling-place in the dwellings; the infant of the waters is within the most motherly ones."

Having taken it with this same [formula], he hands it to the Brahmin seated in the east; having taken it with this same [formula], he hands it to the Rājanya seated in the south with a vessel made of Udumbara wood; having taken it with this same [formula], he hands it to the Vaiśya seated in the west with a vessel made of Aśvattha wood;
having taken it with this same [formula], he hands it to the Janya seated in the north with a vessel made of Nyagrodha wood.
(12.9:99.8) Then, having carried this *prareka* to the Āgnīdhra and covered it, he sets it down in a known place.
(12.9:99.9) Then he causes the sacrificer to put on a *tārpya* garment with the formula, "Thou art the caul of the Kṣatra.
(12.9:99.10) With the formula, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra," he fastens the *tārpya*.
He winds the turban around as if over a central navel.
Then he purifies him with one hundred and one tufts of darbha grass using the standard purification rite. Then, wiping him, he causes him to consume curd, an udumbara fruit, and young grass shoots.

(12.9:99.13) Then he leads him eastward with the *āvida* formulas: "Agni Gṛhapati has been found for us," and so on, with seven verses according to their meter. (12.9:99.14) Then, as he stands in the sacrificer’s place, he addresses him: "This is your king, O Bharatas!
(12.9:99.16) To those of whom he is the chief, they reply: "Soma is the king of us Brāhmaṇas!"

(12.9:99.16) Then he hands him a bow with the formula: "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra; through thee may this man slay Vṛtra. With the formula, "Ye are the repellers of enemies," [he hands] the arrows.

"Drive away my enemies," says the other as he receives [the water], adding: "Protect me from behind; protect me from the side; protect me from the front; protect me from the quarters; protect me from all destructive powers.
Then, with the *triṣṭubh* verse, "The golden-hued ones at the dawning of the dawn," he raises his arms upward.
(12.9:100.5) Then he instructs him: "Proceed toward the quarters with the mind alone; rise upward following the mind.
(12.9:100.6) Then he makes him recite.
"Stand upon the fuel-stick! Stand upon the fierce one! Stand upon the Virāj! Stand upon the northern direction! Stand upon the upward direction! Thus he says.

Then, standing right there, he calls for a cake on twenty-one potsherds for the Maruts and curdled milk (āmikṣā) for the Viśve Devas. Of that [cake], the middle potsherds are placed with the group of verses recited in the forest; the others are with the two groups [of verses] from the Rājasūya.
He proceeds with those two [oblations] with the calls: "Recite for the Maruts! Sacrifice to the Maruts! and "Recite for the Viśve Devas! Sacrifice to the Viśve Devas!
Having covered these two oblations before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering has been made, he sets them aside in their designated places.
Then he asks for a tiger skin, a gold and a silver plate, boar-skin sandals, lead, and red iron.
(12.10:101.2) A eunuch sits to the south.
Then, prior to the consecration, he offers six *pārtha* oblations with the formulas: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā!
(12.10:101.3) Then, on the sacrificer’s seat, he spreads a tiger skin with its neck to the east and its hair upward, saying: "Thou art the splendor of Soma; may my splendor be like thine."
Having seated the sacrificer facing eastward, he places two gold and silver plates around him.

With the words, "Thou art immortality; protect me from death," he places the silver plate below; with the words, "Protect me from the lightning-flash," he places the gold plate above, which has a hundred holes. Then, with the words, "May the biting serpents be driven away," he pierces with lead a eunuch sitting to the south.
With his left foot, he casts away a piece of red iron, saying: "The head of Namuci is cast away!
At this point, they bring forth the consecration waters for him, and he gazes upon them.
"May King Soma, Varuṇa, the gods, and those who impel the Law—may they inspire your speech; may they inspire your breath; may they inspire your sight; may they inspire your hearing.
Having taken the vessel of the Brahman priest, he consecrates [the sacrificer] with it.

The Adhvaryu alone mutters the sacrificial formula (*yajus*), while the others sprinkle [him], saying: "With the splendor of Soma I sprinkle thee; with the brilliance of Agni, with the luster of Sūrya, with the power of Indra, with the heroism of Mitra and Varuṇa, with the might of the Maruts. Thou art the lord of the ruling powers (*kṣatra*) among ruling powers. Protect beyond the sky, O so-and-so!"* *The name of the consecrated person is inserted here.*

(12.11:101.17) Then, when the upward streams have been wiped away, [he recites]: "They have turned back from below toward the north, following Ahi Budhnya as they move along; upon the back of the bull-like mountain, those ships move about, self-pouring as they go.

(12.11:102.3) At this point, having poured the remnants of these consecrations into the primary vessel, he goes to the house of the appointed deputy. (12.11:102.4) Then, while the deputy and the queen maintain contact with him, he offers an oblation with: "O Prajāpati, none other than you possesses these things."

(12.11:102.5) Here, this appointed representative gives him a boon. (12.11:102.6) Then, handing over the vessel to the representative, he says: "This vessel shall be your inheritance; when I consecrate you, let this be yours. (12.11:102.7) Then, returning by the same way he came, he offers the *prareka* oblation in the *āgnīdhra* fire with: "O Rudra, that which is your supreme name, the buyer—unto it you are offered; you are sacrificed to Yama, svāhā!"

At this point, he hands him the bow, if it has not already been handed over previously. When he has been wiped clean, they shout out: "This one, so-and-so, the descendant of such-a-one, the son of such-a-one, the grandson of such-a-one, the great-grandson of such-a-one, is being consecrated by means of the Rājasūya!
Then, with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ," he releases his speech.
He wipes his face with two [verses].
He takes the Viṣṇu-strides with Gāyatrī verses. Then, after the consecration, he offers six Pārtha oblations with the formula: "To Indra, svāhā! To Ghoṣa, svāhā! and so forth.
He offers twelve oblations to the elements with the formula: "To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā!
At this point, he performs the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering for these two oblations. Then, having covered them, he sets them aside in their designated places.
Then he puts on two boar-skin sandals with the formula, "Thou art the wrath of cattle," on the right foot, and with "May my wrath be like thine," on the left.
Then he touches this earth with the formula, "Homage to Mother Earth.
He places his right foot upon it with the formula, "May I not harm Mother Earth," and his left foot with the formula, "May Mother Earth not harm me."
Then, between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap, he steps out toward the north, saying: "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu; thou art the step of Viṣṇu; thou art the wide-stride of Viṣṇu.
To the north, these chariots stand yoked;
as soon as he sees them, the *pratihitṛ* stands still.
Then, having taken up the bow of the deputy and strung it, he mounts the chariot, saying: "May I conquer by the impulse of the Maruts.
Saying, "The mind has reached [its goal]," he leans over the pole. At that very moment, the deputy follows after him, saying: "O much-invoked one, you have overcome the enemies."

"He takes hold [of the bow] with a *triṣṭubh* verse," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then, handing the bow to his deputy, he says: "This Kṣatriya has been defeated by a thousand [cows] at thirty-six throws of the *śamyā*-stick; shoot an arrow at him! Strike him down! Having conquered him, drive him away along the southern path!"
The nobleman alone is instructed: "The prince will shoot an arrow at you; he will miss you. Therefore, wipe it with the upper part [of the garment] and hand the arrow to him.
He does so.

Then he says: "Come near, O sacrificer; I shall draw the Māhendra cup. When the sacrificer has taken hold of him, he draws the Māhendra cup, reciting: "Great is Indra who [is great] in might," and then: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Mahendra.
Having wiped it around, he sets it down, saying: "This is thy womb; for Mahendra, thee!"
(12.13:104.7) Then he asks for these beads—a silver one, an udumbara one, and a golden one. (12.13:104.8) These are woven into separate threads.

(12.13:104.9) Having tied them to the middle beam of the northern *havirdhāna* cart, having touched water, and having taken two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he proceeds westward while restraining his speech and introduces the chant (*stotra*).

They chant for the Mahendra cup. When the *sāman* has been introduced, he issues the call: "O race-runners, run the race! Beat the drums! Pressers, press the Soma! O Āgnīdh, pour out the milk-mixture and make the mortar resound! O Pratiprasthātṛ, offer the cake on one potsherd to Varuṇa; attend to the offering for Soma! They perform according to these instructions.
The race-competitors run;
they beat the drums,
and voices cry out together.
He recites the mantras over the sounds that have arisen:
"The noises fall silent for the sake of the *śastra* of the Hotṛ; this is the last," they say.
After the time of the *hotṛ*, the *adhvaryu* turns away;
the *hotṛ* calls out to him, and the *adhvaryu* responds.
He recites the *śastra*;
he responds with the *pratigara*.
Having responded to the *uktha* in the established manner, he goes forward and lifts up this cup for Mahendra.
While they lift the other [cups], they lift up the Nārāśaṃsa cups;
then he causes the announcement to be made: "O, cause to hear! "Let there be hearing! "O reciter of the hymn, offer the oblation of Soma! Thus he says.
At the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ*, he makes two offerings.
In the same manner, they twice each touch the *nārāśaṃsa* cups.
The *māhendra* cup, having been offered twice, remains [unconsumed].
The chariots approach.
Seeing the chariots arrived, he mutters: "May I be united with sensory power and vigor; may sensory power and vigor be united in me.
Then he goes out toward the north between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap.
To the north, these chariots stand yoked;
as soon as he sees them, the deputy stops.
Then, taking the deputy’s bow and stringing it, he mounts the chariot, saying: "May I conquer by the impulse of the Maruts."
"Mind is obtained," [he says] as he mounts the pole.
At that very moment, the attendant stands behind him [saying], "O much-invoked one, you have overcome the enemies. "He takes hold with a *triṣṭubh* verse," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(12.13:106.2) Then, handing over the bow to the deputy, he says: "This bow shall be yours as an inheritance when I consecrate you; this shall be yours.

(12.13:106.4) Then, returning by the same way he came, passing between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, having caused him to enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, and having turned the chariot eastward, he stands still.
(12.14:106.7) He asks for these three amulets: one of silver, one of udumbara wood, and one of gold.

He fastens the silver one on his left hand with the formula: "Thou art this much; thou art life; bestow life upon me. On the right [hand] he fastens the one of udumbara wood with: "Thou art vigor; bestow vigor upon me. On the right [hand] indeed he fastens the golden one with: "Thou art a yoke-mate; thou art luster; bestow luster upon me.
At this point, he brings him the *āmikṣā* curd-mixture.
Over her right hand he places [his own] right hand with the words, "Thou art Mitra"; over her left hand, "Thou art Varuṇa. Then he touches her with the words, "May I be united with all the gods.
Then, having covered her, he sets her down in a well-known place.
(12.14:106.13) He strings these beads onto a single cord, placing one made of *udumbara* wood in the middle.
(12.14:106.14) Having fastened them around his necks, he returns by the same way he came, turns the chariot eastward in front of the *āgnīdhra* shed, and stands there.
(12.14:107.1) Then, at the *āgnīdhra* shed, he offers the oblations for unyoking the chariot with four spoonfuls, saying: "To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā! and so forth.
Then, prior to this, the chariot-stand—facing east, with its shafts ready and its equipment prepared—is already standing in front of the Āgnīdhra shed.
Upon it, together with the charioteer, he places the chariot.
Thus, he interposes it from the heavenly world.
"He is a swan, dwelling in purity"—with these words he places [the fire];
verily, by means of the Brahman, he brings it down, and by means of the Brahman he establishes it.
"He establishes it with the Aticchandas metre"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(12.14:107.7) Now, prior to this, a shed has been caused to be constructed behind the Āgnīdhra fire-hall, measuring four or eight steps [in size].

(12.14:107.8) In its center, he erects a throne-seat made of Udumbara wood with the formula: "Thou art the navel of the kṣatra. (12.14:107.9) Upon it, he spreads an upper cover of woven wool with the formula: "Thou art the womb of the kṣatra."
(12.14:107.10) Then he sits down upon her.
(12.14:107.10) As he is sitting down, he addresses her with the mantra: "Sit on what is pleasant; sit on what is comfortable; may it not harm you.
(12.14:107.12) "May it not harm me," the other replies.
He addresses the one seated nearby with the mantra: “Varuṇa, of firm vows and wise intent, has sat down among his subjects for the sake of sovereign rule.
Then the officiating priests sit around him:
the Adhvaryu sits to the east, the Brahman to the south, the Hotṛ to the west, and the Udgātṛ to the north.
Then the possessors of the treasures go either eastward or northward;
he addresses the Adhvaryu.
"O Brahman!
[Thus he calls. "You, O King, are the Brahman," says the Adhvaryu. "You are Savitṛ, of true impulsion.
[Thus he addresses] the Brahman.
"You are the king, you are the Brahman," says the Brahman priest. "You are Indra, of true might," [he says] to the Brahman.
"O Brahman! [he says] to the Hotṛ priest. "You are the king, you are the Brahman," says the Hotṛ priest. "You are Mitra, the most gracious," [he says].
"O Brahman! [he says] to the Udgātṛ.
"Thou art the Brahman, O King," replies the Udgātṛ; "Thou art Varuṇa, whose law is truth," [the King replies].
"O Suśloka, [O Suślokas]," [he says] to the Kṣattṛ.

(12.15:108.9) “O King, you are one of good renown,” says the *kṣattṛ*. (12.15:108.10) “O [you] of auspicious fortune! he says to the charioteer (*saṃgrahītṛ*). (12.15:108.10) “O King, you are one of auspicious fortune,” says the charioteer.
(12.15:108.11) “O King Satyarāja! [he says] to the tax-collector.

(12.15:108.12) “You, O King, are indeed King Satyarāja,” says the tax-collector. Having approached seven persons with auspicious names, he hands him the wooden sword (*sphya*), saying: “You are the thunderbolt of Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra; with it, prosper me.”
"May I prosper through that for you," says the other as he receives it.

He hands it over to the charioteer (*sūta*) and the village headman of the charioteers (*sūtagrāmaṇin*), to the kinsman (*sajāta*) and the village headman of the kinsmen (*sajātagrāmaṇin*), to the charioteer (*saṃgrahītṛ*), and finally to the two dice-players (*akṣāvāpa-govyaccha*).
With that [chariot], those two, having dug up the middle of the gaming ground (*adhidevana*), pour down three fifties of golden dice.
(12.15:109.1) Then, having cut off five dice from him, he hands them over [with the words]: "He has become the king over the quarters.
(12.15:109.3) He immediately throws them back onto the dice. (12.15:109.3) Then they announce this boiled rice.
The Brahman and the sacrificer receive separate shares; the charioteer and the village headman receive equal shares; the steward and the charioteer of the herd receive equal shares.

Now, he who is like one skilled at dice, having sat upon the king’s seat and cast four hundred dice, says, "The king has won! Having made those very dice appear as if slightly bent all around, he says, "The Brahmin has won!"

(12.15:109.8) Then they announce this rice-porridge: the Brahman and the sacrificer share it equally; the charioteer and the village headman do not share it; the attendant and the charioteer do not share it. He who loses the game, for him the attendant cooks this [portion] in his own household.
While this rice is being cooked, the Hotṛ causes the Śunaḥśepa legend to be recited while seated upon a golden cushion;
the Adhvaryu responds to him while seated upon a golden mat.
"Oṃ, Hotṛ! So be it, Hotṛ! Truth, Hotṛ!
We have succeeded, Hotṛ!"—if indeed the Hotṛ does not know [the response], another who is an expert in the recitation of the *hotrā* formulas recites for him, and the Pratiprasthātṛ responds to him.
"It consists of more than a hundred," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
When this rice-porridge has been cooked, he then takes it out all at once and offers it to the Brahman. To him he gives these very amulets, a hundred [cows], a crossroads, and a four-sided field.
Then he gives to the Hotṛ a hundred [cows], a carriage drawn by a single horse, and a golden cushion.
Then he gives to the Udgātṛ a hundred [cows] and a carriage drawn by a single horse.
Then he gives to the Adhvaryu a hundred [cows], a carriage with its own team of horses, fifty golden dice, and a golden seat.
At this point, having won this [stake] from them, they give a thousand [cows], divided into four parts.
Then they carry him to the *sadas* on this very seat, or he walks there himself.
These cup-bearers follow after him.
At this point, he invokes the *iḍā* for these two oblations.
Having invoked the *iḍā*, both the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu consume the *māhendra* cup.
They consume the *nārāśaṃsa* cups with that which has been drunk by Narāśaṃsa.
These three, having invited one another, consume from the *hotṛ*’s cup alone; they consume from their respective cups according to the cup.
With the words, "Impel me," they touch themselves.
They do not swell the cups;
having consumed everything, they perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*).
Then, with the formula "For Indra thee! For Indra thee!", he proceeds with the three *ukthya* rounds in this manner.
The midday pressing is concluded.
They proceed to the third pressing.
Having performed the established rite with the Āditya cup, he draws the Āgrayaṇa draught.
(12.16:111.1) Then he draws the Ukthya cup.
(12.16:111.1) The ritual procedure is the same up to the Pavamāna laud.
(12.16:111.2) Having performed the Pavamāna rite, he proceeds with the two animals at their own place.

For these two, there are separate *manotā* hymns, separate deities, separate touchings of the omentum, and separate offerings of the fat; the *vanaspati* offering is common, as is the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering accompanied by the *praisha* call, the *iḍā* portion, and the directions.
Some say the directions are separate; the ritual procedure up to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) is common.

(12.16:111.5) Now, at this purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), they put on sandals with leather wings. Having floated away the boar-skin sandals, he emerges with the two leather-winged sandals. At the edge of the waters, he offers an oblation, saying: "To the grandson of the waters, svāhā!"
At the Viṣuvat, he offers on a bunch of darbha grass with the formula: "To the Son of Strength, svāhā! Having returned, he offers on the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā!
The avabhṛtha rite is performed in the established manner.
Having performed the *udayanīyā* offering, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.
Having proceeded with its omentum in the established manner, he neither shaves his beard nor his hair.

This *ukthya* consecration sacrifice (*abhiṣecanīya*) is thus completed; it has thirty-four *pavamāna* chants, a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and concludes with the *udavānīyā* offering.
(12.17:111.14) Now, for him, a hall has already been caused to be built on a chosen sacrificial ground, at a distance of seven throws of the *śamyā* from the front.
(12.17:111.15) Right there, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni;
he gives gold as the sacrificial fee.
Having moved away after the casting of the wooden pin (śamyā), he dwells there and offers a sacrificial pap (caru) to Sarasvatī;
he gives a heifer as a gift.
On the second day, having moved away after the placement of the *śamyā* markers, he dwells there;
he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ and gives away a soiled garment as a gift.
On the third day, having moved the sacrificial ground after the placement of the *śamyā* markers, he dwells there;
[he offers] a pap of cooked rice to Pūṣan and gives a dark-colored animal as a gift.
On the fourth day, having moved the sacrificial ground after the placement of the *śamyā* markers, he dwells there;
[he offers] a pap of cooked rice to Bṛhaspati and gives a white-backed animal as a gift.
On the fifth day, having moved the sacrificial pegs and retired, he dwells there;
he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and gives a bull as a gift.
On the sixth day, having moved away after the placement of the *śamyā* markers, he dwells there;
[he offers] a cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa and gives a large castrated bull as a gift.
Then, on the seventh day, he settles in the hall.
On this very day he undergoes initiation.
Now, it is indeed said:
(12.17:112.9) "They consecrate him immediately; they purchase the Soma immediately; he gives him a lotus-wreath.
(12.17:112.10) Then, having brought him from the bathing-place and purified him, and having led forward the one wearing the lotus-wreath, he performs the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering.
(12.17:112.12) When that [offering] has been completed, he neither closes his fists nor restrains his speech.
They set aside for him this remnant of the oblation as his portion of the vow; then he performs the Prāyaṇīyā offering,
and he releases his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation.
At this point, they give him this sacrificial remnant as his portion of the vow-food (*vratabhājana*).
Then he performs the *prāyaṇīya* offering;
having performed the *prāyaṇīya*, he proceeds with the footprint rite (*pada*).
Having driven about with one foot and having purchased the King Soma with ten hornless young bulls, he brings him home and prepares the *ātithya* offering.
Having performed the *ātithya*, he offers the *saumya* pap before the *upasad*s.
He gives away a brown bull as a gift.
Then, between the two middle *upasad* offerings, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Tvaṣṭṛ;
he gives a *śuṇṭha* as a gift.
Then, after the *upasad* offerings, there is a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu.
He gives a dwarf [as a gift].
Then he leads forward the Āhavanīya fire.
Having led forward the Āhavanīya, he erects the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds.
Having measured out the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds, he leads forward Agni and Soma.
Having led forward Agni and Soma, he raises the sacrificial post according to the procedure for the post.
Having set up the post provided with a wooden cup (*svaru*), he dedicates the animal victim for Agni and Soma.
Having performed the well-known ritual with its omentum, he takes the *vasatīvarī* waters for Sarasvatī. Then he offers the sacrificial cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) belonging to the animal sacrifice.
The offering of the sacrificial cake concludes with the *iḍā* portion.
The animal sacrifice ends with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings;
some say it ends with the *hṛdayaśūla* (heart-spit).
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milks, they fast.

(12.17:113.7) Now, therefore, they wake up at the very dead of night. Having taken the morning portions of clarified butter and having brought down King Soma, he begins the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*).
When the morning litany has been concluded, he goes toward the waters.
He rises up with water.
He enters upon the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; the pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner,
and the cups are drawn in the established manner.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup.
Having taken the Āśvina cup and having taken two ropes, he approaches the sacrificial post.
Having set aside the sacrificial post provided with a wooden chip (*svaru*), he dedicates the animal victim for Agni.
For that [sacrifice], a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati is to be offered.
Having performed the ritual with the omenta of those two in the established manner, they proceed to the morning pressing.
At the eastern door, the charioteer and the village headman wait; at the western door, the attendant and the charioteer.
They ask those who are moving forward and questioning: "Who is your mother? Who is your maternal grandmother?
If one completes [the lineage] up to the tenth generation, they let him pass.
But as for one who does not complete it, they push him away with a long bamboo pole.

(12.18:114.2) As for him who says, "A Vaiśya woman is my mother; she is Sāvitrī," they release him while saying, "The subjects are the guardians of the marriages. (12.18:114.4) Here, ten men each take charge of a cup. The morning pressing concludes in a straightforward manner.
They proceed for the midday pressing;
the pressing is performed in the established manner,
and the cups are drawn in the established manner.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the offerings for the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

Having offered the *dakṣiṇā* oblations, he gives two mirrors to the Adhvaryu, a garland to the Udgātṛ, a golden ornament (*rukma*) to the Hotṛ, a horse to the Prastotṛ and Pratihartṛ, twelve four-year-old cows to the Brahman, a barren cow to the Maitrāvaruṇa, a bull to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, two garments to the Neṣṭṛ and Potṛ, a single-yoked ox laden with barley to the Acchāvāka, and a draft-ox to the Agnīdh.
The Hotṛ belongs to the Bhṛgu lineage.
The Śrāyantīya is the Brahman’s chant; the Vāravantīya is the Agniṣṭoma chant. The midday pressing concludes in the regular manner.
They proceed to the third pressing.
Having proceeded with the well-known Āditya cup, he draws the Āgrayaṇa.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Pavamāna laud;
having proceeded with the Pavamāna, he proceeds with the two animal offerings in their own place.

For these two, there are separate *manotā* hymns, separate deities, separate touchings of the omentum, and separate offerings of the fat; the *vanaspati* offering is common, as is the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering accompanied by the *praisha*, the *iḍā* portion is common, and the directions are common.
Some say the directions are separate. The ritual procedure up to the *avabhṛtha* bath is common.
The *avabhṛtha* rite is well known.
Having performed the *udayanīya* offering, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.
Having proceeded with its omentum in the established manner, he shaves only his beard at the southern edge of the altar, not his hair.
This Agniṣṭoma, the Daśapeya with seventeen stomas and a thousand-fold sacrificial fee, concludes with the Udavasānīyā offering.
Then he performs the *diśām aveṣṭi* sacrifice consisting of five oblations:
he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, a pap to the Viśve Devas, curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) to Mitra and Varuṇa, and a pap to Bṛhaspati.
Now, it is indeed said:

(12.19:115.8) < Having sacrificed each oblation, he pours clarified butter over the offering to Bṛhaspati.> (12.19:115.9) Having sacrificed each oblation, he pours clarified butter over the offering to Bṛhaspati.
(12.19:115.10) Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives these prescribed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Then he performs the animal sacrifice with two animals.
He offers a dewlapped, pregnant ewe to Aditi, and a speckled heifer of four years of age to the Maruts.
The one for Aditi is pregnant, while the one for the Maruts is not pregnant.
He proceeds with the offering to Āditya first and with that to Marut second.
He causes the announcement for the offering to Āditya to be made loudly and for the offering to Marut in a low voice.
It concludes in the same manner as a Paśubandha sacrifice involving two animals.

Then he sacrifices with the oblations for the Sātyadūtas. He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to the Aśvins and Pūṣan, a pap to Sarasvatī of true speech, and a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ of true impulsion. Having set down the Anvāhārya rice, he gives away a bow with three arrows and a dry leather water-bag.
He sends it to rival kings; he who accepts it, he knows, "He is my friend";
and he who does not accept it, he knows, "He is my enemy."
Then he performs the sacrifice with the former Prayuj offerings.

He offers an oblation on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, an oblation on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Bṛhaspati, an oblation on eight potsherds for Tvaṣṭṛ, and an oblation on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara.
Having set down the Anvāhārya mess of rice, he gives as the sacrificial fee a draft animal that draws a chariot-stand.
Then, having performed the Full-moon sacrifice and the Vaimṛdha sacrifice, he sacrifices with the subsequent Prayuja oblations.
He offers a pap to Sarasvatī, a pap to Pūṣan, a pap to Mitra, a pap to Varuṇa, a pap to Kṣetrapati, and a pap to Aditi.
Having set out the Anvāhārya mess of rice, he gives away the northern horse of the chariot-pole as a gift.
During this time, he observes this twelve-day vow:
he anoints himself,
but does not brush his teeth.
He anoints himself,
he does not rejoice, yet he fights when battle arrives.
The sacrificer either observes the vow of consuming the remnants of the *agnihotra* or his wife brings him food.
Now, for him, three halls have already been prepared on a chosen sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) to the east.

Having settled in the southern half of the hall, kindled the fires, and spread them out, he undergoes initiation for the Atirātra sacrifice known as the Keśavapanīya, which has its stomas directed westward.
Its initiation period is of unlimited duration, with twelve Upasad days.
He purchases the King Soma in such a manner that he thinks: "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the day of the full moon sacrifice."
It succeeds for him in that manner;
he proceeds from the fast-day with the well-known ritual.
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and having set aside the milks, they observe the fast.

(12.20:117.5) Now, therefore, they wake up at the very dead of night. Having taken the morning portions of clarified butter and having brought down King Soma, he begins the morning litany (prātaranuvāka).
When the morning litany has been concluded, he goes toward the waters.
He enters upon the Atirātra sacrifice; the pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner,
and the cups are drawn in the established manner.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the *avabhṛtha* bath;
the *avabhṛtha* is performed in the established manner.
Having performed the *udayanīyā* sacrifice, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.
Having performed the offering of its omentum in the prescribed manner, he has his hair shaved on the southern edge of the altar, whatever hair there may be.
This Keśavapanīya Atirātra sacrifice, characterized by the Praticīnastoma and involving a thousand-fold sacrificial fee, concludes with the Udavasānīyā offering.
Then, having settled in the middle hall, churned the fire, and spread out the sacred fires, he undergoes initiation for the Vyuṣṭi Dvirātra sacrifice.
His consecration period is unlimited and there are twelve *upasads*.

He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks: "Since this is for me a two-night sacrifice, may the first day coincide with the fast-day (*upavasatha*) of the new moon, and the second day on the following day.
Thus concludes the *vyuṣṭi*-two-night sacrifice.

Then, having settled in the northern hall, kindled the fires by friction, and distributed the sacred fires, he undergoes initiation for the *udayanīya* *agniṣṭoma*. For this sacrifice, there are three days of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and three days of fasting (*upasad*); the pressing of the Soma juice occurs on the seventh day.
This *udayanīya* *agniṣṭoma*, characterized by four stomas and requiring a thousand-fold sacrificial fee, concludes with the *udavasānīyā* offering.
Then he sacrifices with the Devikā oblations;
then he sacrifices with the Traidhātavīya;
then he sacrifices with the Sautrāmaṇī.
The Rājasūya is completed in sixteen and a half months;
the Rājasūya is completed; the Rājasūya is completed.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the *iṣṭi* sacrifices.
For these, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices is prescribed as being performed once [for all].
The preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) belongs to the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
All [the oblations] are first, all are middle, and all are last.

One should offer those whose places are specified according to the proper time on the Parvan day. Now, as for those whose places are not specified—namely, the auspicious days (*puṇyāha*) of the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*)—these are the points of access (*tīrtha*) for those *iṣṭis* that are not performed in times of distress.
Now, those *ārteṣṭi* offerings which are performed at the time of an accident are as follows:
namely, the *abhyuddhṛta*, the *abhyudita*, the *abhinimrukta*, and the *avijātā*.
The adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) has been explained.
The undertaking of the vow is constant.
One should perform the duties of the sacrificer until completion, except for the deities of the *āvāpa*;
among those, those that have secondary names (*sopanāmāḥ*) are recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
(13.1:119.9) Now, as for the others, because they are taught in a loud voice:

(13.1:119.10) one should know that there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; that one should make the two *mānavī* verses the *dhāyyās*; the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* verses the *dhāyyās*; the two *triṣṭubh* verses the *saṃyājyās*;
and the two *vārtraghna* verses the *ājyabhāgas* during the first fortnight.
Aupamanyava says that the two [offerings] containing the word *vṛdh* belong to the second fortnight.
One should understand that those oblations which are separated by either a specific desire (*kāma*) or a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must indeed have separate sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

Only by specific instruction does an oblation separated by a sacrificial fee come to have the same sacrificial grass; as in the case of the *Diśām Aveṣṭi*, the *Iṣṭis* do not follow the sequence of the *Upāṃśuyāja*.
The *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses belong to the same deity as the oblation (*havis*).
Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, there are the secondary offerings (*upahoma*), which are those for which [specific] secondary offerings have been prescribed.
The optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) for which no specific sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has been enjoined have clothing as their fee.
The animal sacrifice has a cow as its sacrificial fee;
the *anvāhārya* rice mess is obligatory. Thus, indeed, these offerings have been explained.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni.
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "O you both, Indra and Agni," and "For I have heard..."

"One contending for land or among one's kinsmen should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni"—for this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "O Indra and Agni, the luminous realms of heaven" and "He pierced Vṛtra.
"One about to set out for battle should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni."
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "O Indra and Agni, [you broke] ninety forts," and "The pure hymn of praise...

(RV 8.92.1). "Having won a battle, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni"—for this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Both of you, O Indra and Agni," and "For we have heard... (RV 6.60.13).

"One intending to go to a settlement should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni"—these two [verses] belong to that [offering]: "O Indra and Agni, the luminaries of heaven" and "He pierced Vṛtra.
"One should subsequently offer a pap to Pūṣan."
For that [offering], these two [verses] are used: "We indeed [choose] thee, O Lord of the Path," and "From every path.
"One should offer a *caru* of wild rice (*kṣaitrapatya*) upon arriving at a settlement";
for that, these two [verses] are used: "With the Lord of the Field" and "O Lord of the Field."
"One should subsequently offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni"— for this [offering], these two [verses] belong to those who have won a battle.
"One who, being a regular performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, should omit either the new moon day or the full moon day, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt.
Intending to sacrifice with this offering, he prepares sacrificial grass from a nearby path and an ox. For this sacrifice, these two [verses] are used: "O Agni, lead us" and "To the gods..."
Having placed the *anvāhārya* rice mess down, he gives an ox as a gift.

"One who, having established the sacred fires, should behave as if violating his vows, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati"—for him these two [verses] are used: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows" and "Whatever vows of yours we may violate."
"One who is beset by demons should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, the slayer of demons.
Now it is further said: "He should offer it at nightfall; he should cause the sacrifice to be performed within an enclosed space."
Having risen during the deep of night, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Rakṣohan.
He causes the sacrifice to be performed in an enclosed space.
He recites fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses from this section beginning with "kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ prasitiṃ na pṛthvīm," proceeding straight through them.
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong: "The slayer of Rakṣases" and "With light, apart.
Then, prior to the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he offers an oblation with the spoon, [reciting]: "And may the roarings of Agni reach unto heaven."
"One practicing exorcism should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni accompanied by Rudra"—for this [rite], these two [verses] belong to it: "O Agni, you are Rudra" and "To you the king.
"One whose cattle or men have died, or who is afraid, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Surabhimat."
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Agni is the Hotṛ;
he has performed well," and "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat when a battle is joined.
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Agni has roared" and "In thee are all treasures."
Now, indeed,
it is said: "He surely overcomes those whose ancestors and descendants die one after another in succession,
for the human oblation is his most beloved."
"One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat.
These two [verses] belong to that [offering].
Now, indeed, it is said:
"He indeed cries out against the house of him whose house they enter.
He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat.
These two [verses] belong to that [offering].
Now, indeed, it is said:
"One whose desire does not come to pass should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kāma.
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong: "To thee, O best of Aṅgirases... and "May we attain that desire, O Agni."

"One who is contending for land or among kinsmen should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Yaviṣṭha. For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "O most youthful one, O Bhārata, the best... and "He, the shining one...
"One who is being subjected to malevolent magic should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Yaviṣṭha."

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "One who desires, 'May I attain a full lifespan,' should offer a cake on eight potsherds to the life-sustaining Agni. For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Life for you," and "O Agni, giver of life."

"One desiring prosperity should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jātavedas"—for this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "To him, to thee" and "From heaven. "One desiring luster should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Rukmat."
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong: "The pure purifier," and "Appearing as a golden ornament.

"One desiring splendor should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tejasvat. For this [offering], these two [verses] belong: "When for food [he approaches] the lord of men," and "He with greater splendor."

"One desiring to conquer should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Sāhantya. For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "O Agni, bring the conquering [wealth]," and "That wealth, O Agni, which conquers in battles."
(13.6:123.1) "He who desires, 'May I be possessed of food,' should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Annavat.
For him, these two [verses] are used: "For the bull-food, for the cow-food," and "For you, O Son, are words...
(13.6:123.2–3) "He who desires, 'May I be an eater of food,' should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Annāda."

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "He who desires, 'May I become a lord of food,' should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni, the Lord of Food. For this [offering], these two [verses] are used.
"One who has been ill for a long time should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna, to Agni Pāvaka, and to Agni Śuci.
Intending to perform this sacrifice, he procures gold.

For this sacrifice, these are the [offering verses]: "O Agni, you purify our lives"; "O Agni, purify yourself"; "O Agni, the Purifier"; "May he, the Purifier, [purify us]"; "Agni, whose vow is most pure"; "Upward, O Agni, rise thy pure [flames]."
Having set out the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives gold.
"One who desires sight should offer this very [oblation]," it is said;
for that [offering], these [verses] are used.

"One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Putravat and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Putriṇ; for this [sacrifice], these are the verses: ‘He who, thinking of thee with a humble heart...’; ‘For which well-doer, O Jātavedas...’; ‘In thee, O son of strength...’; ‘At every hymn, Soma gladdened Indra...
One who desires, ‘May I be full of essence,’ should offer a pap cooked in goat’s milk to Agni Rasavat.”
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "O Agni, with thy sap... and "...I have followed the waters.
(13.7:123.17) "He who desires, 'May I be possessed of wealth,' should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vasumat.
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "The Wealthy One, the Lord of Wealth... and "Thee, O Agni, the Lord of Wealth among riches... (13.7:123.18)

"One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vājasṛt when a battle has been joined"—for this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Thee, O Agni, best winner of booty" and "This Agni of ours. "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Agnivāt when they should carry fire into another fire."
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong: "By fire is fire kindled," and "For you, O Agni, are kindled by fire.
"One whose fire, having been taken out, should go out before the *agnihotra* has been offered, should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat.
They say that one should take another [fire] from a burning [source] and carry it forth."
(13.7:124.3) "That should not be done. [The objection:
'If the first portion is drawn out for its own share, why should another be drawn out?
[The reply: One should churn the fire by placing those very same embers together."
Having set down those very embers, he churns [the fire] with:
"From here Agni was first born, Jātavedas from his own womb; may he, knowing [the way], carry the oblation to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī.
Thus, "He generates him from his own womb by means of the meters," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat.
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "Upward, O Agni, thy pure [flames]" and "With light, [thou hast shone forth]."
Now, indeed, it is said:
"One who is being accused should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara, a pap to Varuṇa, and a pap to Dadhikrāvan.
Intending to sacrifice with this offering, he prepares gold.

For this [offering], these are the verses: "Vaiśvānara with his aid," "Thou, O Agni, shining with thy flame," "Away from us thy wrath," "Up, the highest," "I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan," and "Hither hath come Dadhikrās.
Having placed the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives gold as a gift. "One desiring offspring should perform this very [offering]," so it is said.
For her, these [verses] are used:
"One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born. For her, these two [verses] are used: "From the manifestations of Vaiśvānara" and "When you were born, O Agni."

"One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara after having omitted either the new-moon or the full-moon sacrifice. For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Vaiśvānara with his aid... and "He who is questioned in heaven...".
"One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when one intends to extinguish the sacred fires."
For this [offering], these are the verses: "Agni is the head," "Of the earth," "Vaiśvānara with his aid for us," and "O Agni, shining brightly with thy flame.
"One desiring a village should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara and one on seven potsherds to the Maruts.
Now, indeed, it is said:

"One places the Vaiśvānara [oblation] on the Āhavanīya fire and the Māruta [oblation] on the Gārhapatya fire; while the [Śastra] is being recited, one sets them down. Thus, at the proper time, he sets down the Vaiśvānara facing westward.
While the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, he offers an oblation to the Maruts;
for this [offering], these [verses] are used: "Vaiśvānara with his aid," "He who is asked in heaven," "O Maruts, when from heaven," and "Those shelters of yours."

"One should offer a *caru* oblation to Āditya when about to set out for battle"—for this [rite], these two [verses] are used: "May Aditi protect us" and "The great mother, indeed. "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara after reaching the camp"—so it is said.
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong: "May Vaiśvānara come to us with aid," and "O Agni, maintain our wealth among the generous patrons.
"Having eaten the food of two people who are at enmity, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara"—for this [offering], these two [verses] belong:
"May Vaiśvānara come to us with aid," and "The upholder of Truth."
"One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara after having committed an offense against an equal who was the first [to do so]. For this [offering], these same two [verses] are used.
"One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara after having accepted a sheep as a gift."
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Vaiśvānara with his aid... and "O Agni, you, shining brightly with your flame...
(13.9:125.17). "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara after receiving back an animal that has teeth in both jaws, whether it be a horse or a human" (13.9:125.18);
for this [offering], these same two [verses] are used.

"One intending to go for a prize should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara"—for this [offering], these two [verses] belong: "May Vaiśvānara come to us with his aid," and "May we abide in the good-will of Vaiśvānara."
Now, it is indeed said: "He who, having engaged in the year-long rite, does not release it, becomes indeed without a firm foundation.
"Having returned, he should offer this very Vaiśvānara sacrifice again. Thus [it is said].
Having returned, he offers this very Vaiśvānara sacrifice.
"Whatever [offering] he employs, that he releases by means of its portion, for the sake of stability," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"One should send away to one's rival that rope with which one drives away the best cow.
Having sent away to his rival that rope with which he drives away the best cow, he casts it down in the rival's cow-pen.
"Verily, he sends away Destruction (Nirṛti) unto him," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
For this [sacrifice], these two [verses] are used.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"One desiring cattle should offer a caru-oblation to Indra.
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "Indra for you from every side" and "Indra, the men."

"One desiring cattle should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, the possessor of power (*indriyāvat*). For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "The powers of the hundred-fold wise one," and "It was granted to you. "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, the possessor of heat (*gharmavat*)."
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "In whom the seven Vasus... and "Into the raw cows you placed the cooked... (RV 8.69.2–3).
"One desiring food should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Arkavat.
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "The singers sing loudly to Indra indeed" and "The Gāyatrins sing to you" (RV 8.97.11; 8.16.1).

"One desiring prosperity should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Gharma-vat, to Indra Indriyāvat, and to Indra Arkavat. For this [sacrifice], these [verses] are used: "In whom the seven Vasus... "Thou hast placed the cooked within the raw... "The powers, O Śatakratu... "It has been granted to thee... "The singers sing loudly to Indra indeed... "The Gāyatrins sing to thee... Thus.
"One who is seized by evil should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Aṃhomuc.
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "To the deliverer from distress... and "Since he has entered me...".
"One whom enemies might cause to tremble, or whose kingdoms might come together against him, should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Vaimṛdha."

For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: “O Indra, strike away our enemies; like a terrifying wild beast,” and “One who is bound or besieged should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Protector. For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: “Indra the Protector” and “Do not deliver him over to this one, O powerful one.”

"One whose great sacrifice does not succeed should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra, the possessor of the *arka* and the horse-sacrifice. For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Thy chariot, O unvanquished one," and "That which for thee, the bull..."
"One desiring a village should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Anvṛju.
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "The months follow him," and "It was granted to thee.
"One whose army is as if unsharpened should offer a pap to Indrāṇī."
Now, indeed, it is said:
"One should bind *balbaja* grass to the fuel;
one should place them on the fire together with the fuel."
He places them on the fire together with the fuel-sticks (*idhma*).
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Among these women, O Indrāṇī... and "O Indrāṇī, I have not found delight...
It is said: "When a battle has been joined, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Manyumat Manasvat."
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "He who, as soon as born... and "Indra, the fierce one, has surpassed your greatness.
(13.13:127.15) "One who is as if dejected in mind should offer this very same [oblation]," it is said.
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used.
"One who is as if himself sinful should offer this very [oblation]"— for this [offering],
these same two [verses] are used.
"One who desires, 'May my subjects be desirous of giving,' should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Giver (*dātṛ*).
For him, these two [verses] are used: 'Do not neglect us' (*mā no mardhīḥ*) and 'Bring it hither' (*ā tū bhara*).
"One for whom something has been offered as if it were to be given, yet is not actually given, should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Bestower (*pradātṛ*)."
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "We invoke the giver; the wielder of the thunderbolt, the giver.

(13.14:127.22) "One who has been expelled or is being expelled should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Sutrāman"—for this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Indra Sutrāman; may we be in the good favor of him, the worthy of sacrifice. (13.14:128.1)
"One who, though worthy of prosperity, remains equal to his peers—for him one should offer this cake on eleven potsherds to Indra.
Now it is further said: "The invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*) is a *revatī* [verse], for the sake of peace and to prevent burning; the offering verse (*yājyā*) is a *śakvarī* [verse]."
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "The wealthy ones for us" and "Forward for him, the chariot."
Now, indeed, it is said:
"One practicing exorcism should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu;
Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter."
(13.15:128.8) "A *caru* for Bṛhaspati," it is said. Now, indeed, it is also said:
"Those who practice sorcery against one from afar, they in turn practice sorcery against him."
"One should employ two *puro'nuvākyās* for each [verse] to ensure successful application.
Thus, he recites the *puro'nuvākyā* twice for each,
and cuts portions of the oblations three times for each.
For this [offering], these are the verses: "O Agni and Viṣṇu," "O Agni and Viṣṇu," "Forward for us, O Goddess," "To us from heaven," "O Bṛhaspati," and "Thus to the Father.
"One who is being subjected to malevolent magic should sacrifice with this very [offering]"—for this, these same [verses] are used.
"One whose sacrifice does not succeed should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu"—for this [sacrifice], these two [verses] are used: "O Agni and Viṣṇu," and "O Agni and Viṣṇu.
"One who desires sight should offer a pap cooked in ghee to Agni and Viṣṇu."
For this [offering], these same two [verses] are used.
Now, it is indeed said:
"The rival sacrificer appropriates the power and vigor of one who does not sacrifice when he sacrifices. One should perform the Adhvarakalpa offering when a rival is sacrificing."
"It does not take away his sensory power or vigor. "One should offer [the oblation] before speech is uttered.
Thus, he rises during the deep of night, before speech is uttered.
"One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu at the time of the morning pressing;
Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter;
there should be a pap for Bṛhaspati. Thus it is said.
For this [offering], these are the verses: "O Agni and Viṣṇu," "O Agni and Viṣṇu," "Forward for us, O Goddess," "From heaven unto us," "O Bṛhaspati," and "Thus to the Father.
One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu at the time of the midday pressing;
Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter.
"A rice-oblation for Bṛhaspati"— for this [offering],
these same [verses] are used.
"One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu at the time of the third pressing."
(13.16:129.4) "Sarasvatī should have the portions of clarified butter;
there should be a sacrificial pap for Bṛhaspati"—
these same [verses] belong to her.
"One should offer a cake on one potsherd to Mitra and Varuṇa at the time of the barren cow.
These two [verses] belong to it: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, come to us," and "Stretch forth your arms."
(13.17:129.7) "For one who should desire spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he should offer this *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra on the full moon of the month of Tiṣya.
Thus, he who should desire spiritual luster offers the *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra on the full moon of the month of Taiṣya;
he causes the sacrifice to be performed within an enclosed space.
Now, indeed, it is said: "The clarified butter is churned from the milk of a white cow with a white calf; the clarified butter is for sprinkling;
they purify themselves with clarified butter."

(13.17:129.11) "Whatever constitutes spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he produces all of that. (13.17:129.12) "They say, 'Spiritual luster is being produced in excess,' [and] 'He is liable to become afflicted with skin disease.'"
"One should employ two verses of Manu as *dhāyyā*s," so it is said.
Of the verses beginning with "Swift is the chariot of the god-favored one," he places two in the position of the *dhāyyā*s;
these two belong to that [section]: "O Soma and Rudra, tear asunder in all directions," and "O Soma and Rudra, you two [remove] these."
“If one should fear, ‘I shall become afflicted with skin disease,’ he should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Pūṣan.
For this [rite], these two [verses] are used: “O Soma and Pūṣan,” and “These two gods.
“One desiring offspring should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra.”
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "O Soma and Rudra, tear asunder in all directions," and "O Soma and Rudra, you two [remove] these.
"One practicing exorcism should offer a pap of cooked rice to Soma and Rudra"—for this [offering], these same two [verses] are used.
"One who has been ill for a long time should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra.
Intending to perform this sacrifice, he prepares a bull for the *hotṛ*.
For this [sacrifice], these same two [verses] are used.
Having set out the *anvāhārya* rice, the Hotṛ gives away a bull as a gift.
"He who desires, 'May I produce a rival for him in his own domain,' should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra.
Having settled upon the boundary of another's field, having churned the fire, and having spread the fires, he offers the *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"Having enclosed the altar, one should sweep up half [of the earth] but not the other half; one should spread half of the sacrificial grass but not the other half."
"One should place half of the fuel on the fire, but not the other half;
thus one generates a rival for him in his own abode"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
These two [verses] belong to that [rite].
(13.19:130.10) Now, indeed, it is said:
(13.19:130.10) "One desiring a village should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts.
(13.19:130.11) And now, indeed, it is said.
(13.19:130.11) "He places the offering for Indra over the Āhavanīya fire and that for the Maruts over the Gārhapatya fire; he sets them down while the invitatory verse is being recited.
Thus, at the proper time, he sets down the offering for Indra facing westward.
While the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, the offering to the Maruts is performed;
for this [offering], these [verses] are used: "Indra for you from every side," "Indra, the men," "O Maruts, since from heaven," and "Whatever shelter is yours.
One who desires, "May I create discord between the nobility and the common people," should offer this very [oblation].
(13.19:130.16) While cutting portions for Indra, he should say: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra!
(13.19:130.16) He recites: "O Indra, [protect us] from all sides...
(13.19:130.17) Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Sacrifice to the Maruts!"

He performs the offering with the verse, "That which is your shelter" (*yā vaḥ śarma*). While cutting off the portions for the Maruts, he should say, "Recite the invitatory prayer for the Maruts" (*marudbhyo 'nubrūhi*).
He recites the response with the verse, "O Maruts, that which indeed from heaven... (*maruto yad dha vo divas*).
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Indra!
He performs the offering with the verse, "Indra, the men... [RV 8.93.2]. "He creates discord among them regarding their own share; they stand apart, separated," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"One who desires, 'May they be in harmony,' should offer this very [oblation].

Having cut portions according to the respective deities, he should sacrifice according to the respective deities. Thus, by means of their own shares, he brings them into harmony, each in his proper place."
“They indeed become fit,” so says the Brāhmaṇa.
For this [offering], there are those same [verses] which belong to the previous one.
"One desiring a village should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Indra and one on twelve potsherds to the Viśve Devas.
Regarding this sacrifice, one who is about to perform it prepares a garment that has never before been worn by a teacher.
Now, it is indeed said:
"One should take a portion from the offering for Indra and then take a portion from the offering for the Viśve Devās;
then, [one takes] from above the portion for Indra.
Having taken a portion from the offering for Indra, he takes two portions from the offering for the Viśve Devās.
(13.20:131.7) Then, after [the offering] to Indra:
(13.20:131.7) "By means of power itself, he encompasses his kinsmen on both sides for him," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(13.20:131.8) For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Indra in battles... and "May he exhilarate us..."
Having set out the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a garment that has never before been used as a teacher’s fee (*upādhāyya*).
[The injunction states: “One who desires a village should offer a pap of millet cooked in the milk of a spotted cow to the Maruts.
Now, it is indeed said:

"The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are those containing the word 'dear' (*priyavatī*)," it is said; these two belong to that [rite]: "I invoke your dear names, O swift ones," and "For glory, with your splendors.
"One who is at variance with his own kin should be made to sacrifice with this *saṃjñānī* [rite]," it is said.
When those with whom he wishes to consult have assembled, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni accompanied by the Vasus;

[he offers] a pap to Soma accompanied by Rudra, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and a pap to Varuṇa accompanied by the Ādityas. For this [sacrifice], these two [verses] belong to it: "May Agni, the first, protect us with the Vasus; may the god unite us with the Vasus."
"One desiring prosperity should offer a *caru* oblation to the Ādityas who are accompanied by the word *bhuvat*.
For this [rite], these two [verses] are used: "The sacrifice of the gods... and "Pure is the work...".
"One who has been expelled or is being expelled should offer a *caru* oblation to the Ādityas who are accompanied by the word *dhārayat*."
(13.21:132.2) Then, [saying] "O Aditi, give your consent," he who is being expelled takes the dust from the footprints of the one expelling him.
(13.21:132.3) Having taken them, he carries them forward [with the words]: "Come hither, O Maruts, bounteous givers, together with this lord of the people, toward that king.
(13.21:132.4) Then he pours them into the joined palms of the sacrificer [with the words]: "May the blessing be true!"
(13.21:132.5) “*Manas* here,” he says, and thus he restrains [his breath].
(13.21:132.6) At this point, he scatters these foot-dusts in a place where there is no passage.
(13.21:132.6) At this point, he meditates mentally upon whoever the sacrificer hates.
For this [rite], these two [verses] are used: "The Ādityas uphold... they uphold the three earths.

(13.21:132.8) "One should fetch rice from the house of whoever might be a speaker of vulgar speech beyond [the boundary]; one should separate the white and the black [grains]. (13.21:132.9) Thus it is said.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"If there should be white [grains], one should offer a caru-oblation to Āditya. For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Those Kṣatriyas... and "...no sacrificial fee."
"The Viś is indeed the Ādityas by deity; thus he approaches the Viś," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is also said: "His Viś has been won, but his Rāṣṭra has not been won," they say.
"One should offer that *vāruṇa* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) which consists of black grains.
For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa" and "That I implore of thee.
The kingdom indeed belongs to Varuṇa.
"He attains both the people and the kingdom," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
