Now, it is indeed said: "If he should not obtain [the consent], he should offer [the oblation] with the formula: 'I offer this portion to the Ādityas so that they may obtain [it] from such-and-such a person, for such-and-such a clan. Having offered it, he desists. Thus [he acts].
Then, when he has understood [the time], he piles them together.
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to him: "The sacrifice of the gods," and "With the newest favor of the Ādityas.
Regarding this, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "The Ādityas themselves, seeking their own portion, cause him to enter among the people."
Now, it is indeed said:
"If he should not succeed, he should fix seven stakes of *aśvattha* wood upon the middle shaft.
Having stationed the cart with its pole facing eastward, he fixes seven stakes of *aśvattha* wood upon the middle shaft.

Having struck the middle one, he stretches out three towards the west and three towards the east, [saying]: "Here I bind the Ādityas so that they may descend from such-and-such for such-and-such a people. "The Ādityas themselves, their heroes bound, cause him to enter the people," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, it comes to pass:
(13.22:133.9) "If he should not understand [the meaning], he should offer this very oblation of cooked rice to Āditya. (13.22:133.9) He should also bind the splinters onto the fuel-bundle;
(13.22:133.10) he should place them on the fire together with the fuel-bundle. Thus it is said.
He places them on the fire together with the fuel-sticks.
"He thus approaches [them] without being excluded," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said:
(13.22:133.11) "They are made of *aśvattha* wood.
(13.22:133.12) "The *aśvattha* is indeed the vigor (*ojas*) of the Maruts; by means of that very vigor, he enters among the people."
"There are seven;
for the Maruts consist of seven groups. Verily, by means of the groups, he enters among the people," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
For this [offering], these same two [verses] are used.
Now, it is indeed said: "He who fears death should offer this *prājāpatya* sacrifice consisting of a hundred *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces.
One intending to perform this sacrifice prepares a hundred *suvarṇa* *kṛṣṇala* pieces, a new vessel, and abundant clarified butter.

Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he pours out four handfuls of *kṛṣṇala* berries with the formula, "I pour out what is pleasing to Prajāpati. Having released his speech at the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he places a new vessel over the *gārhapatya* fire, pours clarified butter through the strainer, and throws the *kṛṣṇala* berries into it across the strainer. Then he pours out the clarified butter.
Then, having placed the clarified butter on the fire and having carried fire around both [the butter and the meat], he sets them down within the altar.
Now, it is indeed said:
"He cuts off four *kṛṣṇala* seeds each, for the attainment of the fourfold portion."
(13.23:134.4) He cuts eight portions for the deity, four for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, eight for the *iḍā*, four for the intermediate *iḍā*, one for the *prāśitra*, and one for the sacrificer.
(13.23:134.6) They offer ghee while offering;
they consume ghee while consuming.
Then, having drawn them up one by one, he offers them to the Brahman priest;
for this [offering], these two [verses] belong to him: "Hiraṇyagarbha" and "Prajāpati."
(13.24:134.9) "For one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he should offer this *saurya* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*).
(13.24:134.10) One who is about to sacrifice with this offering prepares five gold *kṛṣṇala* seeds and two plates, one of gold and one of silver.

(13.24:134.11) Then, having cooked that *caru*, having poured clarified butter over it, having removed it from the fire toward the north, and having grasped it with the gold and silver plates, he places it within the altar (*antarvedi*).
The ritual procedure is the same up to the *prayāja* offerings. Now, it is indeed said: "At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala*."

At each *prayāja* offering, he places a *kṛṣṇala* seed upon it and offers it, while reciting these two [verses]: "Upwards that one" and "The bright. Having set down the *anvāhārya* mess of rice, he gives away two plates, one of gold and one of silver.
"One who desires, 'May I find gold; may gold come to me,' should offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, one on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ, and a pap to Bhūmi.
Intending to sacrifice with this *iṣṭi*, he procures gold. For this sacrifice, these are the verses:

"He, as of old... (RV 5.44.1); "Downward his poetic insights... (RV 7.9.3); "The golden-handed for aid... (RV 7.85.1); "The lovely thing today, O Savitṛ... (RV 7.38.1); "Truly, thus among the mountains... (RV 8.40.5); "Hymns [praise] you, O far-reaching one... (RV 8.68.1).
Having set out the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives gold as a gift.
"One should perform this very [offering] after having obtained gold," so it is said;
for that [offering], these same [verses] are used.
"One should offer this very [oblation] for whom gold might be lost"— for that [offering],
these same [verses] are used.

(13.25:135.6) "For one who vomits *soma*, one should offer this *śyāmāka* oblation to Soma and Indra. These two [verses] belong to it: "With the soft-bellied one" and "Whose wrath has been appeased. (13.25:135.7-8) "One person indeed is a *somavāmín*, while another is a *somātipavita*."
"For one who has over-poured the Soma, one should offer this *śyāmāka* oblation of boiled rice to Soma-Indra.

For that [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Being pressed," and "O you, with your companions. "One desiring cattle should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni the Giver, and a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Bestower."

One who is about to sacrifice with this *iṣṭi* procures curds, honey, clarified butter, water, and barley. Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he pours out four handfuls of rice with the words, "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni Dātṛ. Having performed that same introductory formula, he pours out exactly four handfuls of rice with the words, "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra Pradātṛ."
Having performed this very same introductory rite (*pratipad*), he says, "I offer what is pleasing to Prajāpati," and pours out four handfuls of barley.
He causes the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*) to be raised over those [barley grains] while they are actually over the rice.
They then lift up the barley.

He releases his speech with the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*). The ritual procedure is the same up to the pouring [of the grains]. Having poured them, he places eight potsherds on the southern half of the *gārhapatya* fire and eleven on the northern side.

(13.25:136.2) Then, having pounded these barley grains in a mortar and placed a cake on one potsherd upon the *gārhapatya* fire, they roast the parched grains (*dhānā*). When he places these two oblations upon the fire, then he sprinkles these parched grains with four things: with curds, honey, clarified butter, and water. These are his [verses]: "O Agni, give wealth to the donor"; "Give us, O Agni, hundreds"; "We invoke the giver"; "The wielder of the thunderbolt is the giver"; "Like purified butter"; "Both, O bright one, of the clarified butter."
(13.26:136.8) "For one who has failed in a sacrifice, he should offer this *iṣṭi*: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, and a pap for Soma.
(13.26:136.9) Now, it is indeed said:
"One should cause the portions of the offering for Agni and the offering for Soma to be joined together in that for Indra."
(13.26:136.10) He joins the [verses] dedicated to Agni and those dedicated to Soma with the one dedicated to Indra.
(13.26:136.11) "He bestows brilliance and spiritual luster upon him in a unified manner," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(13.26:136.12) For this [rite], these [verses] are used: "He, as of old"; "Downward the poetic insights"; "Indra for you from every side"; "Indra, the men"; "Thou art ours, O Soma"; and "Those which are thy abodes."

"One whose desire does not come to fruition should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma"—for this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "O Agni and Soma, you who possess common wealth" and "You two [have bestowed] these.
"One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and Soma."

(13.26:136.16) He who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a cake on eight potsherds of *śyāmāka* millet to Agni and Soma; for this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "O Agni and Soma, this [oblation] of mine... and "O Agni and Soma, of the oblation set forth... (13.26:137.2). "He who fears impotence should offer a pap of *śyāmāka* millet to Soma Vājin. Thus [it is said].
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: "Swell up" and "May [the milk] unite with thee.
"One desiring a village should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Bṛhaspati," so it is said.
Now, indeed, there is also this [further rule]:
"The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses contain the word 'host' (*gaṇa*)," it is said; these two belong to that [offering]: "We invoke thee, the Lord of hosts, of all hosts," and "He, with his folk.
One who desires, "May I destroy the common people (*viś*) within the sacred formulation (*brahman*)," should offer this very [oblation].
"One should employ the invitatory and offering verses for the Maruts," it is said; these two belong to that [rite]: "O Maruts, since from heaven... and "That shelter which is yours..."
"One desiring heaven should offer a *caru* oblation to Aryaman"—for this [rite], these two [verses] are used: "Aryaman comes" and "O Aryaman, those which are yours.
"One who desires, 'May my offspring be fond of giving,' should offer a *caru* oblation to Aryaman."
For her, these two [verses] are used:
"He who desires, 'May I go safely to the assembly,' should offer a pap to Aryaman.
For him, these same two [verses] are used.
(13.27:137.13) "For a kṣatriya who is inferior to his younger brothers, one should offer this cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Indra-Anuṣūk. Thus it is said.
Now, moreover, it is stated:
(13.27:137.14) "The invitatory and offering verses are those containing the words 'depth' (*budhna*) and 'summit' (*agra*). Thus it is said.

For this [offering], these two [verses] belong: “From the base, the summit is being praised by the Aṅgirases; from the base, he has measured out the summit with measures. “If there should be a Brāhmaṇa who is younger than his elder brothers, for him one should offer this *ānuṣūka* oblation of cooked rice to Bṛhaspati.
Now, indeed, it is said:

(13.27:137.18) “The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are ‘having a foundation’ (*budhnavatī*) and ‘having a summit’ (*agravatī*). Thus, these two belong to it: “The Great One propped up the earth,” and “He who from the foundation reaches the summit by his might.”
Now, indeed, it is said: "For one who is seized by *pāpayakṣman*, he should offer this *āditya* oblation of cooked rice on the new moon day.
For that [sacrifice], these two [verses] are used: "He becomes ever new as he is born," and "The stalk which the Ādityas cause to swell."

(13.28:138.1) "If he should desire of someone, 'May he be an eater of food,' for him he should offer this three-layered oblation: a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra the King, for Indra the Overlord, and for Indra the Self-Ruler.
(13.28:138.4) Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he pours out four handfuls of rice with the words, "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra the King."
Having performed this very introductory rite, he offers four handfuls for each deity— [saying] "To Indra the Overlord" and "To Indra the Self-Ruler"—
and releases his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*).
The ritual procedure up to the pouring [of the grain] is the same.
Having poured [the grain] onto the Gārhapatya fire, he places eleven potsherds with their faces turned upwards.
Now, it is indeed said:
"He places [the vessel] upon the potsherds with their faces turned upwards, so that there may be no loss of vigor."
(13.28:138.10) "There are three sacrificial cakes;
these worlds are three.
This is for the attainment of these worlds."
"Each subsequent one becomes greater," it is said;
thus he makes each subsequent one indeed greater.
"He cuts off while making [the portions] reach all [of them]," it is said.
While cutting the portion, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra the King.

Having recited, "In the eastern quarter you are Indra, the king," he offers the oblation with: "Indra shall conquer; he shall not be defeated. While cutting the portion, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra the Overlord."

Having recited, "Indra shall conquer; he shall not be defeated," he performs the *yajyā* with, "His majesty indeed exceeds [all]. While cutting the portion, he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra, the self-ruling king.
Having recited, "His majesty indeed exceeds [all]," he performs the *yajyā* with, "In the eastern quarter, you, O Indra, are the king."
"One recites them alternately to prevent burning," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"One who desires sensory power (*indriya*) or vigor (*vīrya*), for him one should perform this sacrifice with all the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras].

One intending to sacrifice with this *iṣṭi* procures a horse, a bull, a ram, and a goat. Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he pours out four handfuls of rice with the words, "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra associated with the *rathaṃtara*."

Having performed this very introductory rite, he takes four handfuls for each of the deities— [reciting] "For Indra Bārhatas," "For Indra Vairūpas," "For Indra Vairājas," "For Indra Śākvaras," and "For Indra Raivatas"—
and releases his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*).
The ritual procedure up to the pouring [of the grains] is the same.
Having poured [the grain] onto the Gārhapatya fire, he places twelve potsherds with their faces upward.
Now, it is indeed said:
"He places [the vessel] upon the potsherds with their faces upward, for the sake of non-exhaustion."
(13.29:139.6) "The sacrificial cake is on twelve potsherds for the sake of its being dedicated to the Viśvedevas. (13.29:139.7) "He cuts portions from all sides," it is said.
While cutting, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra associated with the Rathantara-sāman!"
Having recited, "We praise thee, O Hero," he performs the *yajyā* with, "For we invoke thee indeed.
While cutting off the portion, he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra Bārhata.
Having recited, "For we invoke thee indeed," he performs the *yajyā* with, "O Indra, as many as are the heavens for thee..."
While cutting the portion, he says: "Recite for Indra Vairūpa.

Having recited, "O Indra, that which [is] of yours, O Heaven," he performs the offering with, "Drink the Soma; O Indra, let it exhilarate you. While cutting the portion, he says: "Recite for Indra Vairāja."
Having recited, "Drink the Soma, O Indra; let it exhilarate thee," he performs the *yajyā* with, "Never art thou barren. While cutting the portion, he says, "Recite for Indra Śākvara.
Having recited, "Never art thou barren," he performs the *yajyā* with, "May the wealthy ones be our companions at the feast."

While cutting [the portion], he says: "Recite for Indra Raivata! Having recited the verse, "The wealthy ones are our companions at the feast," he offers with the verse, "We cry out to thee, O Hero. "He recites them alternately to prevent burning," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Having placed the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a horse, a bull, a stallion, and a goat.
"One who is being falsely accused should sacrifice with this very [rite]"—
this is the same as the one previously mentioned.
(13.30:139.20) "For one who desires sight, he should offer this sacrifice: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Bhrājasvat, a pap for Sūrya, and a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Bhrājasvat.
(13.30:140.3) For this [sacrifice], these [verses] are used: "Upward, O Agni, thy pure [flames]," "With light," "Upward that," "The bright," "Upward, O Agni, thy pure [flames]," and "With light.
When the *iḍā* has been invoked, there remains [an oblation] unoffered for the *agnīdh*.

(13.30:140.5) Then he gives three balls of food to the sacrificer. (13.30:140.5) Reciting, "Upwards that Jātavedas," "The seven bay mares [draw] you in the chariot," and "The brilliant face of the gods has risen," he gives the balls of food. (13.30:140.7) Thus he bestows sight upon him.
"That which belongs to him is indeed that," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"One desiring a village should offer the *vaiśvadevī* *sāṃgrahaṇī* oblation.
Thus they cook the *vaiśvadeva* rice-pap (*caru*) as if gathering it together.
Then he lays down the enclosing-sticks with the formula: "Thou art firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen.
For this [rite], these two [verses] are used: "O All-Gods," and "O All-Gods.
Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers three spoonfuls with the formulas: "Thou art the mind," and "O Gods, of the mind."
Now, it is indeed said:
"The fire indeed goes to his body, the Soma to his vital sap;
Varuṇa seizes him with the noose of Varuṇa, Sarasvatī [seizes] his speech, and Agni-Viṣṇu [seize] the self of him who is long ill."
"One who has been long ill, or one who desires, 'May I live the full span of life,' for him he should offer this sacrifice.
Intending to perform this sacrifice, he prepares a new vessel made of *khadira* wood, fresh butter as the clarified butter, and a *pravarta* [earring] of such a measure as he thinks he will live for.

Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on ten potsherds for Varuṇa, a pap for Sarasvatī, and a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu. The ritual procedure is the same up to the inspection of the clarified butter. At the inspection of the clarified butter, he recites: "That which was new became fresh butter."
The ritual procedure is the same up to the placing of the offering-spoons (*sruc*).

Having placed the spoons, he then places this *pravarta*—anointed with clarified butter and spread over with a new vessel made of *khadira* wood—together with the sacrificial oblations within the altar-ground.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the *prayāja* offerings.
Having performed the *prayāja* offerings, he proceeds with the principal oblations (*havirbhiḥ*).

For this [offering], these [verses] are used: "May life be thine," "O Agni, giver of life," "Swell up," "Gather together for thee," "Avert thy wrath," "Up the highest," "The goddess [has led us forward]," "From heaven to us," "O Agni and Viṣṇu," and "O Agni and Viṣṇu.
Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers oblations from the *sruva*-ladle.

(13.32:141.9) “You are the breath of the Aśvins; may they two grant it to you, whose breath you are—svāhā! You are the breath of Indra; may he grant it to you, whose breath you are—svāhā! You are the breath of Mitra and Varuṇa; may they two grant it to you, whose breath you are—svāhā! You are the breath of the Viśve Devas; may they grant it to you, whose breath you are—svāhā!

Having offered these oblations one after another, he pours the remnants over the Pravarta stone with the formulas: “You are the ruler (rāṭ); you are the far-ruler (virāṭ); you are the sovereign ruler (samrāṭ); you are the self-ruler (svarāṭ).”
(13.32:141.14) Then, having carried this Pravarta around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it to the south.

(13.32:141.15) Then he causes the sacrificer to gaze at the clarified butter with [the words]: "The stream of ghee, the path of immortality, bestowed by Indra and presented by the Maruts—Viṣṇu beheld that for you; that the Iḍā impelled for you with the cows. Thus.

Then, having taken hold of the hand of the Brahman priest, the officiating priests (ṛtvij) lead him around, saying: "By the *pāvamāna* hymn, by the course of the *gāyatrī*, by the power of the *upāṃśu* cup—may the god Savitṛ release you for life, for the sake of living! By the hymn of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*, by the course of the *triṣṭubh*, by the power of the *śukra* cup—may the god Savitṛ release you for life, for the sake of living! By the measure of Agni, by the course of the *jagatī*, by the power of the *āgrayaṇa* cup—may the god Savitṛ release you for life, for the sake of living! Thus they say.
Then he drinks the clarified butter from the gold vessel.

As he drinks, [the teacher] addresses him with the mantra: "O Agni, make this man fit for long life and splendor; O King Varuṇa and Soma, make his seed dear. Like a mother, O Aditi, grant him protection, so that he may reach old age, O All-Gods!
Then, having washed this earring with water, he fastens it on the right ear with the mantra: "Bestowing long life upon you from every side."
Then he causes him to turn around [the fire] with the words: "Thou art life; thou art all-encompassing life; thou art complete life; thou art entire life.
Then the Brahman priest takes his hand, reciting from "Agni is long-lived" until the end of the section.

"One should offer as many four-potherd oblations to Varuṇa as one might receive horses, with one additional [oblation]"—for this [rite], these two [verses] are used: "Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa" and "That I implore of thee.
"If one should receive more [horses], one should subsequently offer a one-potherd oblation to Sūrya."
For this [sacrifice], these two [verses] are used: "Upwards that one" and "The bright one.
Then he goes down to the waters for the *avabhṛtha* bath.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"One should return and offer a *caru* oblation to Aponaptr.
These two [verses] belong to it: "O Son of the Waters," and "The others come together.
"One for whom [the disease] has been seized by evil should offer this curd-mixture (*payasyā*) to Indra and Varuṇa. Thus [it is said].
One who is about to sacrifice with this offering prepares curds, milk, and *āmikṣā*.

Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he pours out four handfuls of rice with the words, "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra and Varuṇa. He releases his speech at the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*).
The ritual procedure is the same up to the pouring [of the grains].
Having poured them, he places eleven potsherds on the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire-altar.
When he pours this sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) upon [the potsherds], at that time he cooks this *āmikṣā* on the Gārhapatya fire.

Then, having taken out this sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), which has been spread with a base of ghee and sprinkled over with ghee, and having covered it completely with the curd-mixture (āmikṣā), he places it within the altar (antarvedi).
Now, it is indeed said: "He places the sacrificial cake upon the curd;
thus he endows it with a body."
"Moreover, [he piles it] as having a foundation;
he arranges it in four ways;
verily, he finds firm support in the quarters."
"He gathers it together again," he says.

Having divided the *āmikṣā* and the *puroḍāśa* into four parts, he distributes them, saying: "O Indra and Varuṇa, that body of yours which is to be restrained—by that, release this man from distress! O Indra and Varuṇa, that body of yours which is powerful, protective, and brilliant—by that, release this man from distress! He gathers them together again, saying, "Having gathered them together, he cuts off the portions."
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to him: "O Indra and Varuṇa, I... and "O Indra and Varuṇa, you two for our sacrifice...

Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers eight spoonfuls with [the formula]: "O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever offense we have committed against you in the fire, that I expiate for you with this. Thus [there are] eight.

Now, indeed, it is said: "He who has rivals, being in competition, should sacrifice with this offering; he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni the Impetuous, to Agni the Repeller, and to Agni the Facing One.

For this [sacrifice], these are the verses: "This Agni has gone forth"; "I worship for thee, I send forth my thought for thee"; "Becoming manifest with thy power"; "With thy light"; "O Agni, thou with thy face"; "Him who is fair-faced, fair-looking, and swift-moving."

(13.35:144.4) "He who has rivals, being in competition, should sacrifice with this offering: he should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Deliverer from Harm, to Indra the Dispeller of Enemies, and to Indra the Possessor of Power. Thus it is said. Furthermore, it is indeed stated: "He offers a cake on thirty-three potsherds."
(13.35:144.8) Those very same three cakes on eleven potsherds that were mentioned previously are these ones;

for this sacrifice, these are the verses: "O deliverer from distress," "When he has entered me," "Unbind for us, O Indra," "Indra, the dominion," "The powers, O Śatakratu," and "It has been granted to thee.
(13.35:144.10) He who has rivals should, while contending, perform this sacrifice; he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Saṃvarga.
"One should touch that [oblation] when it has been cooked and placed [on the fire] with this *yajus*," so it is said;

he touches that cooked oblation when it has been placed there with this *yajus*: "Thou art vigor, thou art power, thou art strength, thou art radiance, thou art the abode of the gods by name; thou art the All, the life of the All; thou art the Whole, the life of the Whole, the overcomer. By means of this oblation, may I overcome such-and-such a rival.
He recites seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses from the section beginning with "Harness, indeed, those who best invoke the gods," moving forward through them.
For her, these two [verses] are used: "O friends, together for you... and "Thou, O bull, dost don them all together."

(13.36:144.19) "For one who desires offspring, he should offer this *gārmuta* oblation to Prajāpati. For this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "O Prajāpati," and "He knows. (13.36:144.20) "For one who desires cattle, he should offer this *gārmuta* oblation to Soma and Pūṣan. Thus it is said.
For this [sacrifice], these two [verses] belong to it: "O Soma and Pūṣan," and "These two gods.
"One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā";
thus, on the following day, he observes the fast with the thought, "With the Citrā."

Then, in the morning, he offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on eight potsherds for Tvaṣṭṛ, a pap for Sarasvatī, a pap for Sarasvant, a pap for Sinīvālī, and a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra.

For this [offering], these [verses] are used: "Through Agni may he obtain wealth"; "O Agni, rich in cattle"; "Swell up"; "Gather together for thee"; "Here, Tvaṣṭṛ, the foremost"; "That seed of ours"; "Forward for us, O Goddess"; "To us from heaven"; "The swelling [milk] of Sarasvatī"; "Those waves of thine, O Sarasvant"; "O Sinīvālī"; "She who has beautiful hands"; "Indra for you from every side"; "Indra, the men."
Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers oblations with the *sruva*-ladle, [reciting] the five verses beginning with "O Agni, come to us with cattle," and two *yajus* formulas.

One who is about to perform the Kārīrī sacrifice prepares a black garment with a black fringe, a black horse, a black halter, a black antelope skin, black honey, groats of *karīra* fruit, a black jar that is half-baked, a black three-pole cart, a black ewe, a stalk of black *varṣāhū* grass, and fuel and sacrificial grass of reeds. Then, he places the black garment with the black fringe upon the sacrificer’s seat.

(13.37:145.15) Then, having tied a black horse with a black halter in front of the Āhavanīya fire, he pours out black honey, *karīra* fruits, and parched barley flour upon a black antelope skin within the altar.
(13.37:146.1) He buries a cooking pot in the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).
(13.37:146.2) Then, having stationed a cart with its pole pointing eastward in front of the rubbish-heap, he ties a black sheep in front of its supporting pillar.
To the north of the Āhavanīya fire, he places a black *varṣāhū* stalk or a cane branch as the fuel and sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*).
Then the sacrificer puts on a black garment with a black fringe.
"You are of the Maruts; you are the vigor of the Maruts! Split the stream of the waters!"—with these words he fans the wind from behind, saying, "O Maruts, cause the swift falcon to rest.
Thus he generates an easterly wind for the attainment of rain; so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Then, having released this horse from its tether, he tosses it about with the *uttaravargya* formula: "Roar! Thunder! Deposit the embryo! (13.38:146.10). If it shakes itself, if it urinates, or if it voids dung, one knows for certain: "It will rain. Then he offers the oblations to the names of the winds: "The east wind, raining, invigorating, turning [the waters]—svāhā! and so on, eight times.

(13.38:146.12) Then, within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*), he mixes honey with the flour of *karīra* fruits upon a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) with the mantra: "The refreshing, the longing, the pure, the swift; the luminous, the dark, the moistening, the well-foaming; the supporters of Mitra, the supporters of Kṣatra, the good kingdoms—bring them here for one like me!

(13.38:146.14) Having formed three balls and gathered them together, he binds the edges of the black antelope skin with a cord, saying: "Thou art the tethering-rope of the stallion; I bind thee for the sake of rain."
Then he fastens them to the first pole of the cart.
"O gods who possess wealth, O Agni, Soma, and Sūrya!"—with these words he halts for a day and night;
on the second [day], he fastens [the garment] with: "O gods who grant protection, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman!"
He ceases at the very end of the day and night;
on the third [night], he ties [the horse] with the mantra: "O gods who drink together, O Son of the Waters, swift-moving one!
He ceases at the very end of the day and night.
Now, it is indeed said:
"If it should rain, one should offer only that much.

Whether it rains or not, in either case, he offers the *piṇḍīs* with the *sruva*-ladle, having spread a base of butter and poured butter over them, [reciting]: "Even by day they create darkness," "Him whom the men [invoke]," and "O Maruts, you who raise him up from the ocean."
(13.39:147.6) Then he observes their smoke, [reciting]: "The dark-colored ones, the tawny ones, the fair-winged ones...
(13.39:147.7) "If it should not rain, on the following day he should offer the oblation;
he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Dhāmacchat, a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts, and a cake on one potsherd to Sūrya. (13.39:147.8) Thus it is said.

For this [offering], these are the verses: "Thou indeed, O Acyuta," "O Agni Jātavedas, many are thine," "O Maruts, grant us rain from heaven," "The bounteous Maruts make the waters swell," "Upwards that [sun]," and "The bright one.
Then, prior to the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he offers three oblations with the wooden spoon, [reciting]: "Like Aurva and Bhṛgu, I invoke the pure one; like Apnavāna... and so on.
Then he fills this jar with water, saying: "Release the rain from heaven; fill the ocean with water.
If it cracks or breaks, one knows for certain: "It will rain.
Then he makes an offering over two sheepskins, saying: "Thou art born of the waters, the first-born; thou art the strength of the ocean."
If she shakes herself, or if she urinates, or if she voids excrement, one knows: "It will rain.
Then he offers an oblation upon a clump of *varṣāhū* grass.
"Make the earth swell; split open this divine sky. Grant us of the divine water; as the lord, release the leather bag.

Then he throws it into the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "The golden-haired one in the expanse of the atmosphere. Then he gazes at its smoke with the verse: "Thy well-winged birds have followed thy course."

(13.40:148.4) Then, standing within the altar-ground (*antarvedi*), he shakes the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) while reciting from "O gods who have their share in heaven" (*ye devā divibhāgāḥ*) until the end of the section. (13.40:148.5) The Kārīrī sacrifice concludes here.
Now follows the Añjaḥsava-Kārīrī.
He offers an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni; having cooked it, he sets it down.
For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses, five *prayāja*s, and two *ājyabhāga*s belonging to the Vṛtra-slayer.
Then, for the principal oblation: "Agni is the head," and "Of the world."
The two *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
Those [verses] with which he fastens the balls of rice, those with which he offers the oblations, and those with which he gazes at the smoke—these succeed.
The *añjaḥsava-kārīrī* sacrifice is concluded.

Now, indeed, it is said: "One should sacrifice with the Traidhātavīya when practicing sorcery, or when being subjected to sorcery, or when intending to sacrifice with a thousand, or when having sacrificed with a thousand, or one who, having said 'I shall sacrifice,' does not sacrifice.
One who is about to sacrifice with this offering prepares a thousand pieces of gold, a garment of silk (*tārpya*), and a cow.

Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he pours out four handfuls of rice with the words, "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra and Viṣṇu. Having performed that same introductory formula, he pours out four handfuls of barley with the words, "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra and Viṣṇu. Having performed that same introductory formula, he pours out exactly four handfuls of rice again with the words, "I pour out what is pleasing to Indra and Viṣṇu."
(13.41:148.19) He causes the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*) to be raised specifically over the rice.
(13.41:149.1) They lift up the barley; he releases his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the pouring [of the grains].
Having poured them, he places twelve potsherds on the *gārhapatya* fire.
Now, it is indeed said:
(13.41:149.3) "There is a cake on twelve potsherds. (13.41:149.3) "These [twelve] are three sets of four potsherds each," (13.41:149.4) "for the sake of threefold prosperity."
(13.41:149.4) "There are three sacrificial cakes.
(13.41:149.4) There are these three worlds.
(13.41:149.5) It is for the attainment of these worlds."
(13.41:149.5) “Each subsequent one becomes larger,” it is said.
Thus, he makes each subsequent one indeed larger, with the barley-meal cake in the middle.
Now, there is also this [text]: (13.41:149.6) //
(13.42:149.8) "All the meters are to be recited in this sacrifice," they say.
(13.42:149.8) "The *kakud* is indeed the vigor of the *triṣṭubh*;
the *uṣṇih* is that of the *jagatī*."
"In that he recites the *uṣṇih* and the *kakubh*, by that very means he wins all the meters"—thus [it is said].
With the verses beginning "Forward, O Agni, with your aids," he places two *dhāyyā*s in their proper place.

Then, with the verse containing the word "three," "O Agni, three are your strengths, three your stations," he performs the concluding rite (*paridhāna*) for the sake of uniformity—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"Cutting off portions while making them available to all," it is said;
for this [offering], these two [verses] are used: "Together with your work... and "Both of you have conquered...".
Having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a thousand pieces of gold, a garment of silk (*tārpya*), and a cow.
"If one should desire of a Rājanya: 'May he be born unconquered; may he go about slaying his enemies,' for him one should offer this oblation to Indra and Bṛhaspati.
Intending to sacrifice with this offering, he prepares a golden girdle.
For this [sacrifice], these two [verses] are used: "O Indra and Bṛhaspati, [be] with us... and "May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind."
Having set out the Anvāhārya rice, he gives a golden girdle.

"One who, having eaten new grain before performing the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, or one who should sacrifice in another's fires, or one in whose fires another should sacrifice—such a person, having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇis*), having moved away, having churned out the fires, and having spread the fires, offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to it: ‘Vaiśvānara with his aid,’ and ‘He who is praised in heaven.’"
"One whose Agnihotra has been interrupted should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumatya, if he should desire: 'May the thread of my progeny not be severed.

Having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, having moved away from the dwelling, having churned out the fires, and having spread them out, he should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumatya."

For her, these two [verses] are used: "O Agni, you are our thread and our bridge; you are the path that leads to the gods. With you, O Agni, may we ascend to the back [of heaven], and then may we rejoice in the banquet with the gods. "Making for oneself an easy path, free from weariness... [TB 2.4.2.6]
"Unwavering, the sharp-horned bull, blazing brightly, beholding his ancient dwelling place, Agni has stretched out the celestial thread," thus [it is said]. (See TB 2.4.2.5.)

The two *saṃyājyā* verses for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering are: "We invoke Agni Sviṣṭakṛt—the bearer of oblations, the overcomer of hostility, the slayer of Rākṣasas, the victor in battles, the radiant, the shining one, the wise fulfiller of desires."
"O Agni, make that well-sacrificed; O God, overcome all hostile armies. Shining forth, show us a wide path; bestow upon us a radiant and undecaying life. (Thus it is said:
"He who, having established the sacred fires, should shed tears, shall offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratabhṛt."
For this [offering], these two [verses] belong to him: "O Agni, you who bear the vows, pure one, seat the gods here for the sake of carrying the oblation.

"Now bearing the vows, O protector of vows, undeceivable, sacrificing to the gods, ageless, and possessing excellent heroes; bestowing jewels, O Agni, easy to find—protect us so that we may live, O Jātavedas! Thus.

Now, if one’s fires should become mixed with common fires, or with each other, or with the fires of another, he should consign the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), move away, churn out the fires, spread them out, and offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vivici. [He offers] to Agni Vratapati. For this sacrifice, these are the verses: "O Agni, thy flames, driven by the wind, spread in all directions"; "Thee, O Agni, the human tribes praise"; "Thou, O Agni, art the guardian of vows"; and "Whatever of our vows we have violated."
The sacrifices are completed; the sacrifices are completed.
Now, it is indeed said: "Prajāpati desired, 'May I create offspring.
He performed austerity."
(14.1:152.2) He created serpents. (14.1:152.2) He desired, "May I create offspring. (14.1:152.3) He performed fervor for a second time.
(14.1:152.3) "He created birds. (14.1:152.3) "He desired, 'May I create offspring. (14.1:152.4) "He performed austerity for a third time."
"He saw this speech of the consecrated;
he spoke it, and from that indeed he created offspring.
Regarding this, they ask: "What is that austerity, having performed which one speaks the speech of the consecrated?"
Now, it is indeed said:
"The Aṅgirases, when going to the heavenly world, caused consecration (*dīkṣā*) and austerity (*tapas*) to enter into the waters.
Therefore, one bathes in the waters.

"One should say: 'He directly obtains consecration and austerity'—this is what that means. Now, it is indeed said: "When one who is consecrated sees something impure, the consecration departs from him."
"His blue-black hue departs.

Thus, having seen something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; the Sun is the best of lights. O consecration, do not abandon me! He says this so that the consecration does not depart from him.

"Neither his dark nor his tawny [complexion] departs," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said: "When it rains upon one who is consecrated, the unappeased celestial waters strike away his vigor, strength, consecration, and ascetic heat."

While being showered upon, he mutters: "O flowing waters, bestow strength; bestow vigor; bestow strength. Do not destroy my consecration (*dīkṣā*), do not destroy my austerity (*tapas*). Thus he says. "He thus places all this within himself;
neither his vigor nor his strength, nor his consecration, nor his austerity do they destroy," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"Agni is the deity of the consecrated one;
he [Agni] is, as it were, hidden from him when he goes forth."
Having ascended from this [fire], he becomes as if hidden.
Having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, he sets out with a verse addressed to Bṛhaspati:
"Go forth from the auspicious toward what is more auspicious; may Bṛhaspati be your forerunner," he says.
"Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods;
he [the sacrificer] takes hold of him;
he carries him across to the further shore. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
(14.1:153.4) [The rule] for the joint journey of the waters has been explained;
(14.1:153.4) that for the settling [of the fires] has been stated.
Now, indeed, it is said:

(14.1:153.5) "He who purchases King Soma after having caused him to go to the world of sovereignty attains sovereignty over his own people. (14.1:153.6) "The meters, indeed, are the world of sovereignty for King Soma.
(14.1:153.7) "One should address him with this mantra before the purchase of Soma," so it is said.
Before the purchase of the Soma, he addresses it with this mantra.

(14.2:153.10) “‘This is your Gāyatra portion,’ say this for me to Soma; ‘This is your Triṣṭubh portion,’ say this for me to Soma; ‘This is your Jagatī portion,’ say this for me to Soma; ‘Go to the sovereignty of the Chandomas,’ say this for me to Soma. (14.2:153.13) Having thus caused him to go to the world of sovereignty, he purchases [Soma];
“He attains the sovereignty of his own people,” so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said: "He who knows the foundation of the *tānūnaptra* ritual stands firm.
The exponents of the Veda say: "They do not consume [the remainder], nor do they offer it as a libation; where, then, does the *tānūnaptra* find its foundation?"
"One should say, 'In Prajāpati, in the mind,' and he should smell [it] three times.
Thus, he smells it three times, saying: "I offer you in Prajāpati, in the mind."
"This indeed is the foundation of the *tānūnaptra* rite;
he who knows thus stands firm. So says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is also said:

(14.2:153.19) "O Adhvaryu, he who knows the firm foundation of the Adhvaryu stands firm indeed. (14.2:153.20) "From whatever place he thinks, 'I shall offer without stepping forward,' from that place, standing, he should cause the announcement to be made.
Thus, from whatever place he thinks, "I shall offer without stepping forward," from that place, standing, he causes the announcement to be made.
"This indeed is the firm foundation of the Adhvaryu;
he who knows thus stands firmly. So says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is also said:
"If one were to offer while stepping forward, he would depart from his firm foundation;
therefore, the offering should be made by one standing in the same place for the sake of stability.
This rule applies to all sacrificial offerings except for the *haviryajñas*.
"One offers while stepping forward," so it is said in the Haviryajñas. Now, indeed, it is also said: "He who knows the property of the Adhvaryu becomes possessed of property."
"The *sruk* is his own; the *vāyavya* cup is his own; the *camasa* ladle is his own.
If he were to call for the *āśrāvaṇa* without grasping either the *vāyavya* or the *camasa*, he would depart from his own.
Thus, he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* while grasping both the *vāyavya* and the *camasa*.
"He does not depart from his own [self]," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said:

"He who introduces the stotra without having established the Soma—his Soma becomes unestablished, the stoma becomes unestablished, the ukthas become unestablished, the sacrificer becomes unestablished, and the adhvaryu becomes unestablished."
"The wind is indeed the support of the *soma*; the cup is its support; the *soma* is the support of the *stoma*; the *stoma* is the support of the *ukthas*.
"One should begin the *stotra* either after having drawn a *graha* or after having filled the cup.
For filling the cup is indeed the drawing of it.
Having either taken up the draught-cup or poured out the contents of the *camasa*, he introduces the *stotra* with the words:
"He establishes the Soma against [the enemy], the *stoma* against [them], the *ukthas* against [them];
the sacrificer stands firm against [them], and the *adhvaryu* stands firm against [them]. So says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"In that they collect the footprint of the Soma-purchase cow, they are collecting the sacrifice itself;
the mouth of the sacrifice is in the two Havirdhāna sheds."
"When they move the two *havirdhāna* carts forward, then one should smear the axle with it.
When he moves the two *havirdhāna* carts forward, then with that third of a footprint he smears the axle-end of the wife.
"He thus continues the sacrifice at the very mouth of the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, it is indeed said: "They carry the fire forward; they lead the wife away; they move the sacrificial dishes after her. Then this hearth of hers is left behind; it broods upon her, and being capable of becoming Rudra, it is liable to destroy the offspring and cattle of the sacrificer.
Therefore, when they lead the consecrated animal toward the north, one should take its fire for cooking the meat.
When they lead the consecrated animal northward, he then carries away its cooking-vessel;
"By that very act, he makes it a sharer [in the sacrifice]," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, there is this [further statement]:
"The Āhavanīya fire is indeed the sacrificer.
When they carry the animal-cooking fire from the Āhavanīya, they are thereby dragging the sacrificer away.
Therefore, that [original Āhavanīya] should remain, or one should produce a new fire by friction. Thus it is said.
If he is about to perform [the rite] with him, he does not bring him [the fire] along.
Even so, this [fire] remains burning, lying unextinguished.
But if he does bring him along, then at the time for the animal sacrifice, having taken a firebrand and grasped the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), he goes forward before the animal.
(14.3:155.13) Here they cook the animal victim with fire produced by friction.
(14.3:155.14) They bring that [animal] together with the omentum and the fire-drilling wood-blocks, "for the sake of the sacrificer’s selfhood," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(14.3:155.15) Now, it is indeed said:
"If a portion of the animal should be lost, one should cut [the portion] from clarified butter as a substitute," so it is said.
As many portions of the animal as are lost, that many times he cuts [the portion] from clarified butter as a substitute;
"that itself is the expiation for that," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, it is indeed said: "If they should tear apart the sacrificial animal, and someone should desire, 'May they meet with misfortune,' he should offer an oblation in the Āgnīdhra fire with a verse containing the word 'namas' and the words 'kuvid aṅga'. Thus, he offers in the Āgnīdhra fire with the verse containing the word 'namas' and the words "kuvid aṅga."
"He appropriates their very act of reverence;
they swiftly meet with misfortune," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Or, if he churns [the fire] while alone, he offers this oblation at the Śāmitra fire.
(14.3:156.4) The procedure for the introductory offering is well known.
(14.3:156.5) The performance of the *apāvya* offerings has been explained.
The subsequent [portion] is the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said: "He who performs a sacrifice not according to its deity is cut off from the deities and becomes worse off;
he who performs it according to its deity is not cut off from the deities and becomes better off."

"One should touch the *āgnīdhra* shed with a verse addressed to Agni, the *havirdhāna* shed with one addressed to Viṣṇu, the ladles with one addressed to Agni, the *vāyavya* cups with one addressed to Vāyu, and the *sadas* with one addressed to Indra.

Thus, he touches the *āgnīdhra* shed with a verse addressed to Agni, the *havirdhāna* shed with one addressed to Viṣṇu, the ladles with one addressed to Agni, the *vāyavya* cups with one addressed to Vāyu, and the *sadas* with one addressed to Indra.
"In this way, he attends to the sacrifice according to its respective deities."
"One is not cut off from the deities; one becomes more prosperous"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Thus the laying of the large enclosing-sticks made of Udumbara wood has been explained;
the placing of the offering-spoons has been explained.
The touching of the vessels has been explained. Now, it is indeed said:
"The Adhvaryu is the one who incites the sacrifice for the sacrificer."

(14.4:156.15) "Indeed, the one who has sacrificed perishes before the one who has not sacrificed. (14.4:156.15) "Protect me from the mantra of the mouth, from every curse!"—thus he should offer an oblation before the *prātaranuvāka*.
(14.4:156.17) Before the *prātaranuvāka*, having risen in the deep of night, the *āgnīdhra* offers in the mouth [of the fire]: "Protect me from the mantra of the mouth, from every curse, svāhā! Thus.

(14.4:156.18) "The Adhvaryu binds that skin over himself from the front for the sake of non-injury," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is also said: (14.4:157.2) "He who indeed overcomes by means of the meters, he overcomes those two who are pressing [the Soma]."

(14.4:157.3) When the two have finished pressing the Soma, he rises during the last watch of the night and offers three *abhibhūti* oblations in the *āgnīdhra* fire: "For lying down, for sitting down, for the overcoming of the *gāyatrī*, svāhā! For lying down, for sitting down, for the overcoming of the *triṣṭubh*, svāhā! For lying down, for sitting down, for the overcoming of the *jagatī*, svāhā! Thus.
Then he offers two oblations of breath: "O out-breath and in-breath, protect me from death! O out-breath and in-breath, do not abandon me!
Now it is indeed said:
"Those for whom the Soma is prepared strive against one another regarding the deities of the out-breath and in-breath."
"‘For repose thee! For rest thee! he says.
The meters, indeed, are repose and rest.
Verily, by means of the meters he appropriates his meters; so says the Brāhmaṇa."
Now, indeed, it is said:
"They say that he whose sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) are more numerous appropriates the deities.
"If the *soma* sacrifice beyond [this point] should be an *agniṣṭoma*, one should perform an *ukthya*."
He enters upon the Ukthya sacrifice;
[it is said]: "If it should be an Ukthya, one should perform an Atirātra.
Thus, he enters upon the Atirātra sacrifice.
(14.4:157.14) “By means of the sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) he appropriates the deities for himself; he becomes more prosperous,” so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(14.4:157.15) Thus [is it] from the perspective of the Adhvaryu. Now, from the perspective of the Chandoga:
(14.4:157.16) "The *ājya* verses are 'calling forth' (*pretivant*) and 'praising' (*caitivant*), for the sake of victory.
(14.4:157.16) The introductory verses (*pratipad*) contain [the word] 'Marut,' for the sake of conquest.
(14.4:157.17) Both the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* [sāmans] are employed."
Thus, indeed, according to the Chāndogas.
Now, according to the Hotṛ:
"The *sajanīya* is to be recited; the *vihavya* is to be recited; Agastya’s *kayāśubhīya* is to be recited. Thus, indeed, for one who performs the sacrifice on a single day (*ekāha*).

Now, for the performers of the *sattra* sacrifice, the rising at the dead of night is the same; they perform the five *abhibhūti*s and two *prāṇāhuti*s. They proceed according to their specific resolve (*kratu*), and they enter upon the days as they have been prescribed.
The recitation over the *nigrābhya* waters has been explained.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"The plants are indeed the subjects (*viś*) of Soma."
"The subjects indeed have the power to bestow [the Soma] upon the king;
the Soma belongs to Indra.
Thinking thus, when he is about to press it, he begs the King from the plants.

"I have increased you with my mind, O well-born ones; born of *ṛta*, may we be sharers in your portion. O divine plants, in harmony with Indra, grant your consent for the pressing of the Soma," he says.
"Verily, having caused him to be surrendered to the plants, to his own people, and to his own deity, he presses [the Soma]," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, there is this [further passage]:
(14.4:158.11) "The first shoot of the Soma that is being pressed which falls away is capable of destroying the sensory power, vigor, offspring, and cattle of the sacrificer.
(14.4:158.12) "He should address it with a mantra," so [it is said].

(14.4:158.13) He should address that first shoot of the Soma which is being pressed with the mantra: "Let it fall back to me along with offspring, along with the increase of wealth; do not destroy my sensory power and vigor!"
"He thus invokes this very blessing for the sake of sensory power, vigor, progeny, and the non-destruction of cattle"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Here follows this *drapsānumantraṇīyā* verse;
we shall recite it together with the others.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"He who indeed endows the gods with the glory of the gods and men with the glory of men becomes possessed of divine glory among the gods and possessed of human glory among men.
"Those cups which he should draw prior to the Āgrayaṇa, those he should draw silently;
those which are subsequent, those he should draw with audible sound," so it is said.
Those cups which he draws prior to the Āgrayaṇa, those he draws silently;
those which are subsequent, those he draws with a loud sound.
"Thus he endows the gods with the glory of the gods and men with the glory of men."

"He becomes renowned among the gods as one who honors the gods, and renowned among men as one who honors men"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. When they are about to perform the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant, while they have all taken hold of one another, he offers a spoonful of oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "May Agni Vaiśvānara, who brings welfare to all, protect us at the morning pressing by his greatness; may that purifier bestow wealth upon us. May we be long-lived, sharing the draught together, Svāhā!"

During the midday *pavamāna* chant, while they have likewise taken hold of one another, he offers a spoonful (*sruva-āhuti*) into the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra: "May all the gods, the Maruts, and Indra not abandon us at this second pressing. May we, long-lived and speaking what is pleasing to them, abide in the favor of the gods, *svāhā*!"

During the Ārbhava Pavamāna, while they have likewise taken hold of one another, he offers a spoonful on the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "This is the third pressing of the seers, those who by means of the Truth set the cup in motion; may those sons of Sudhanvan, having attained heaven, lead our well-offered sacrifice toward greater prosperity, Svāhā!
Now it is indeed said:
"Some oblations are offered with a fixed abode, others without a fixed abode."
(14.5:159.18) "Those [cups] that have the *āghāra* libation are those that have a fixed abode; those belonging to Soma are without a fixed abode.
(14.5:159.19) "Having taken the cup for Indra and Vāyu, he should perform the *āghāra* libation.

Thus, having taken the cup for Indra and Vāyu, he performs the *āghāra* libation with the formula: "O Gods, may this sacrifice be a peaceful rite (*adhvara*) for our plants, for our cattle, and for our people. For every living being you are the peaceful rite. Swell, O divine Soma, rich in ghee! *Svāhā*! (The variant reading is corrected from *syāhā* to *svāhā*).
(14.5:159.22) "Thus he makes those oblations gentle and provided with a foundation.
(14.5:160.1) "He who knows thus becomes possessed of a foundation. Moreover, he anoints heaven and earth with clarified butter."
(14.5:160.2) "These two, when explained, become a source of livelihood. (14.5:160.2) "He who knows thus becomes a source of livelihood," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(14.5:160.3) Then the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the residue of the *manthin* cup on the northern half of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "This, O Rudra, is your portion, that which you requested; accept it! May we obtain lordship over cattle, abundance of wealth, and heroic strength for a full year—*svāhā*! (14.5:160.6) Now, it is indeed said: "Manu divided his inheritance among his sons."
(14.5:160.6) He excluded Nābhānediṣṭha while he was living as a student of sacred knowledge.
He returned,
and [Nābhānediṣṭha] said, "Why have you excluded me?"
"I did not exclude you," he said.
"These Aṅgirases are performing a sacrificial session;
they do not know the world of heaven."
"Tell this Brāhmaṇa to them:
'When they go to the heavenly world, they will give you those animals which belong to them.
He said this to them.

Regarding this, they ask: "What did he say to them? [The answer is: the *apāvya* verses, the *santanī*s, the *drapsānumantraṇīya*s, the *acchāvākīya*s, the *stotrīya*s, and the *śastrīya*s—[he said to them]: "Speak the truth! Let not your faith depart from you! This is what he said to them. "When he was moving about with the sacrificial animals on the sacrificial ground, Rudra approached him"—this is a restatement of that ritual action which has been mentioned. Then he offers two *pravṛtāhuti* oblations.
"May I be beloved of speech; fulfill the hymn with the Ṛg-verse"—this is the third [verse] following that;
we shall explain it in that very place.
Then he consecrates the drops with the mantras: "The drop has fallen," "That drop of thine," "The drop which," and "That drop of thine."
Now, it is indeed said:
"The Adhvaryu is the first of the officiating priests to be yoked; by him the *stoma* is to be yoked.
When they proceed toward the *bahiṣpavamāna*, the Adhvaryu proceeds first, bowing low and holding two blades of *barhis* grass.
"May speech go first, going straight to the gods, bestowing glory upon me, vital breaths upon the cattle, and offspring upon me and the sacrificer," he says.
"Thus he yokes speech at the mouth of the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, there is this [further statement]:
(14.5:161.5) "The very foundation of the sacrifice is established when, having drawn the cups, they proceed to the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant;
for they go forward,
and they chant with verses directed forward."
"One returns and worships with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu. Thus he returns and worships with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu;
for Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice.
"He has indeed performed the sacrifice.
"'O Viṣṇu, you are our nearest; grant us protection, O Conqueror! Your streams, dripping with honey, milk out an inexhaustible spring,' he says.
Whatever of him dries up while he lies [in the womb], that very thing he causes to swell by means of this [verse]," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said: "He who, knowing the ascents of the *pavamāna* [stotras], performs the sacrifice, ascends after the *pavamānas*;
he is not cut off from the *pavamānas*."

At the *bahiṣpavamāna*, when the fifth [verse] has been introduced, he makes [the sacrificer] recite: "Thou art a falcon, having the *gāyatrī* metre; I take hold of thee; carry me safely across. At the midday *pavamāna*, when the eighth [verse] has been introduced, he makes him recite: "Thou art a well-winged bird, having the *triṣṭubh* metre; I take hold of thee; carry me safely across."

During the *ārbhava-pavamāna* chant, when the ninth [verse] has been introduced, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "Thou art united, having the *jagatī* as thy metre; I take hold of thee; convey me safely across," so he says. These indeed are the ascents of the *pavamāna* chants;
he who, knowing thus, sacrifices, ascends after the *pavamāna* chants.
"One is not separated from the *pavamāna* [stotras]," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said:
"He who knows the continuity of the *pavamāna* reaches a full lifespan."
(14.6:162.2) < He does not die before his full lifespan;
he becomes possessed of cattle; he obtains offspring.>

(14.6:162.3) "The cups for the Pavamāna are drawn; now, these [vessels] of his remain undrawn: the *droṇakalaśa*, the *ādhavanīya*, and the *pūtabhṛt*. If he were to commence [the rite] without having drawn them, he would cut off the Pavamāna.
If that [Pavamāna] were cut off, the breath of the Adhvaryu would follow after it and be cut off."
"Thou art taken with a support; for Prajāpati, thee!"—with these words he should touch the *droṇakalaśa*. Thus he touches the *droṇakalaśa* with "For Prajāpati, thee.
"For Indra, thee!"—with these words [he touches] the *ādhavanīya*.
"From all the gods, thee!"— with these words he pours into the *pūtabhṛt* vessel; thus he extends the *pavamāna* chant and attains a full lifespan.
"He does not die before his full lifespan;
he becomes possessed of cattle; he obtains offspring"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"There are truly three pressings;
yet they omit the third pressing and perform it without a *soma* stalk."
(14.6:162.12) "Having offered the *upāṃśu* [cup], one should pour the *aṃśu* stalk into the *upāṃśu* vessel; having mixed it at the third pressing, one should press it.
(14.6:162.13) Thus, that very *aṃśu* stalk which has been placed in the *upāṃśu* vessel, he mixes with the *ṛjīṣa* of the midday pressing and presses it.
(14.6:162.15) "In that he causes it to swell, by that it possesses the *aṃśu*."
"In that he presses [the Soma], by that it becomes possessed of the *arjīṣa*.
Thus he makes all the pressings (*savana*) possessed of stalks (*aṃśumat*), possessed of pure juice (*śukravat*), and equal in potency. So says the Brāhmaṇa.
(14.7:162.18) Now, therefore, follows the investigation concerning those [vessels] that have cracked or leaked.

If the *droṇakalaśa* has cracked or leaked, having taken four spoonfuls in a vessel, he offers them into the *āhavanīya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "The moon, fleeing in the assembly of many, though young, was swallowed by the grey-haired one. Behold the wisdom of the god through his greatness! Today he has died, for yesterday he was still the same—svāhā! Thus.

Then, having poured water from the *vasatīvarī* jars into the *hotṛ*'s cup, he gathers its essence with the formula: "May prosperity increase through Soma; may the wealth of that which has been sacrificed and consumed come to me.
He consecrates what has been spilled with: "To the Lord of Being, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā! If it has indeed become cracked, he smears it over.

If, however, [the Soma] has already begun to flow, he raises it up, places two blades of *barhis* grass in between, and pours the *svadhā* offering; then, having removed the two blades of *barhis*, he causes [the Soma] to overflow from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel.

If the *ādhavanīya* jar is cracked or leaking, he likewise takes four spoonfuls in a vessel and offers them into the *āhavanīya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "Two oceans, vast and undecaying, revolve like feet within a belly; beholding one of them, they pass over it; not beholding the other, they pass over it by means of a bridge, svāhā! Thus.

(14.7:163.11) Then, having poured water from the *vasatīvarī* waters into the *hotṛ*’s cup, he collects its own residue in the same manner, [reciting]: "May prosperity increase through Soma; may the wealth of that which has been sacrificed and enjoyed come to me.
(14.7:163.14) He consecrates what has spilled with: "To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Creatures, Svāhā!"
If it has indeed burst, he smears it [with clay].

If, however, it has sprung a leak, having lifted it up and placed two blades of *barhis* grass between, he pours the *svadhā* offering; then, removing the two blades of *barhis*, he causes the liquid to flow out from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel itself until it is reached.

If the *pūtabhṛt* vessel is broken or leaks, he likewise takes four spoonfuls into a vessel and offers them into the *āhavanīya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "The one, the long-haired one, knowing all beings, clothes himself in two continuous garments; covering himself, he goes wearing black; he takes up the bright [light], having left the old behind—svāhā! Thus.

(14.7:164.2) Then, having poured water from the *vasatīvarī* waters into the *hotṛ*’s cup, he prepares its *svadhā* offering in the same manner: "May prosperity increase through Soma; may the wealth of that which has been offered and consumed come to me.
(14.7:164.5) He consecrates what has been spilled with: "To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā!"
(14.7:164.6) If it has indeed burst, he smears it [with clay].

(14.7:164.7) But if it has indeed leaked, having lifted it up and placed two blades of *barhis* grass in between, he pours the *svadhā* offering; then, having removed the two blades of *barhis*, he causes the remainder to flow out from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel itself.

If the Āgrayaṇa vessel is cracked or leaks, one offers with its *puroruc* verse, lifts it up, places two blades of *barhis* grass between [itself and the ground], and pours the *svadhā* offering. Having removed the two blades of *barhis*, one causes the liquid to flow back from the *droṇakalaśa* itself for the sake of replenishment. Now, if another cup (*graha*) is cracked or leaks, one offers with that very same *puroruc* verse, lifts it up, places two blades of *barhis* grass between [itself and the ground], and pours the *svadhā* offering. Having removed the two blades of *barhis*, one causes the liquid to flow back from the Āgrayaṇa vessel itself for the sake of replenishment.
Now, it is indeed said: "Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did that too. Then the gods perceived this Great Sacrifice (mahāyajña).
(14.8:164.15) < They wove that [web].> (14.8:164.15) <They performed the Agnihotra as their vow.> (14.8:164.16) <Therefore, one should observe two vows.>
(14.8:164.16) "For they offered the Agnihotra twice; they performed the Full Moon sacrifice as the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma,
and they performed the New Moon sacrifice as the animal sacrifice to Agni."

"They performed the Vaiśvadeva as the morning pressing, the Varuṇapraghāsas as the midday pressing, and the Sākamedhas, the Pitṛyajña, and the Tryambakas as the third pressing. Thus it is said. Regarding this, they ask: "Which one is that great sacrifice?"
This very [rite] is called the *cāturmāsya* Soma sacrifice.
Furthermore, whatever *saumya* sacrifice there may be, that is the *mahāyajña*.
"The Asuras sought to follow after this sacrifice of theirs."
They did not follow him.
They said, "These gods have indeed become worthy of the *adhvara*. That is the reason for the name *adhvara*.
"Then the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with Soma, prospers in himself; his rival is defeated. So says the Brāhmaṇa.

(14.8:165.5) Then he worships the King [Soma] in his entirety with: "Encompassing Agni, encompassing Indra, encompassing all the gods, encompass me with spiritual luster! Flow pure for us, bringing peace to the cattle, peace to the people, peace to the horses, and peace, O King, to the plants! May we be givers of undiminished wealth, O Lord of riches, of heroic power, and of the increase of prosperity. Grant me of that; may I partake of that which is yours; of that of yours, I wipe this away. Thus.
There are four desires fulfilled by those endowed with Brahmanic power; whichever of these desires he wishes for, that he designates and then wipes away.
Then he proceeds with the *avakāśa* formulas:
"O giver of splendor, purify yourself for splendor for my vital breath"—with this, he gazes at the *upāṃśu* cup.
(14.8:165.12) “For out-breathing,” [he offers] the Antaryāma cup; (14.8:165.13) “For diffused breathing,” [he offers] the Upāṃśusavana stone;
(14.8:165.13) “For speech,” [he offers] the Aindravāyava cup.
"To Dakṣa and Kratu," [he addresses] the Maitrāvaruṇa cup;
"To Śrotra," the Āśvina cup;
"To the two eyes," the Śukra and Manthin cups.
"To the self," [he offers] the Āgrayaṇa;
"to the limbs," the Ukthya;
"to life," the Dhruva.
"For stability," he says regarding the ṛtupātra at the midday pressing,
but not at the morning pressing;
"for vigor," he says while looking at either the *atigrāhya* cup or the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.
(14.8:165.18) With the words, "Thou art the belly of Viṣṇu," he looks at the *droṇakalaśa*. (14.8:165.18) With the words, "Thou art the belly of Indra," [he looks] at the *ādhavanīya*.
(14.8:165.19) With the words, "Thou art the belly of the All-gods (*viśve devāḥ*)," [he looks] at the *pūtabhṛt*.

(14.8:165.19) Then he worships the King [Soma] in his entirety: "Who art thou? What is thy name? For whom [do I offer] thee? To whom [do I offer] thee? Him whom I have satisfied with Soma; him whom I have gladdened with Soma—may I be rich in offspring through offspring, rich in heroes through heroes, rich in splendor through splendor, and well-nourished."

"O well-nourishing one! From all my forms, O bestower of splendor, flow pure for the sake of splendor; grant that to me; may I partake of that of yours; with this of yours, I wipe myself clean. Thus [he says]. There are four desires fulfilled by the Brāhmaṇa; whichever of those desires he wishes for, having designated it, he wipes himself clean, saying: "I wipe myself clean for long life; I wipe myself clean for prosperity; I wipe myself clean for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); I wipe myself clean for the breath of so-and-so; I wipe myself clean for this."

"Whomever he satisfies, he, being satisfied, departs from him through the out-breath and in-breath, through speech, through skill and resolve, through the two eyes, through the two ears, through the limbs of the self, and through life;
he quickly perishes," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
The worship of the *sphya* and *vighana* has been explained;
the ritual of the *saṃprasarpaṇa* has been explained;
the recitation concerning the consumption of the sacrificial portions (*bhakṣānuvāka*) has been explained.
The taking of the *pṛṣadājya* in its unmodified form has been explained;
the *dadhigharma* has been explained.
Now, indeed, it occurs as follows:
(14.9:166.12) "If a black bird should touch the speckled butter, his Śūdras will be liable to die;
if a dog should touch it, his four-footed cattle will be liable to die;
if it should spill, the sacrificer will be liable to die. Thus [it is said].
Now it is indeed said:
"The speckled butter is cattle;
cattle, indeed, fall away from him whose speckled butter spills."
"That he takes up the speckled butter again, he thereby takes up the cattle for him again," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said:
"The speckled butter is indeed the breath."
"The vital breath indeed spills away from him whose *pṛṣadājya* spills.
In that he takes up the *pṛṣadājya* again, he recovers his vital breath for him. He takes it up after having placed gold [within]. Thus [it is said].
When the *pṛṣadājya* has been spilled, he asks for either a bronze vessel (*kaṃsa*) or a cup (*camasa*).

Having placed it within the altar (*antarvedi*), he collects its essence (*svadhā*) with the formula: "May prosperity increase through curds and ghee; may the wealth of that which is sacrificed and enjoyed come to me. He consecrates the spilled portion with the formulas:
"To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Creatures, Svāhā!"
(14.9:167.5) Then he places a gold piece weighing a hundred mānas into this ladle.

(14.9:167.6) During the regular taking up [of the offering], he recites the verse addressed to Viṣṇu: "O Viṣṇu, you are our nearest... (14.9:167.7) Having removed the gold and having made the horse smell it, he sets it down.

(14.9:167.7) Now, therefore, regarding that which has become impure—such as what has been smelled by a dog, wiped over by a crow, infested by insects, or whatever else one considers impure—one should entirely immerse this ladle in water; then, one places a piece of gold weighing a hundred mānas into another ladle.
In the case of the regular drawing of the Soma, he recites the verse addressed to Viṣṇu: "O Viṣṇu, you are our nearest [kinsman]. (14.9:167.10) Thus it is said.
Having removed the gold and having made the horse smell [the butter], he sets it down. Now, it is indeed said: "The sacrifice of him whose *pṛṣadājya* spills is rent asunder."
"He takes it up again with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu.
Thus he takes it up again with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu;
for Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice.

(14.9:167.14) "By means of sacrifice alone one continues the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa. (14.9:167.15) When they are about to proceed inside the hall, he says: "O Brahman, we shall proceed; O Hotṛ, recite for the Gharma."

Then the Brahman gives the impulse: "O God Savitṛ, he has declared this to you; impel it and perform the sacrifice. Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; protect the sacrifice, protect the lord of the sacrifice, protect me. Om, proceed! Thus, at the word "establish," it occurs in the case of the Haviryajñas.

(14.9:168.1) When [the Adhvaryu] says, "O Brahman, we shall chant; O Praśāstṛ," then the Brahman gives the impulse: "O God Savitṛ, he has announced this to you; impel it and perform the sacrifice! Bṛhaspati is the Brahman. Do not depart from the long-lived Ṛc, nor from the body-protecting Sāman. May your blessings be true, may your intentions be true. Speak Ṛta and Satya. Chant at the impulse of the god Savitṛ: 'Bhūr! With Indra, chant! Thus at the morning pressing."
(14.9:168.6) At the midday pressing, he says, "O you accompanied by Indra, praise for the sake of *bhuvas*!

(14.9:168.6) At the third pressing, he says, "O you accompanied by Indra, praise for the sake of *suvar*! (14.9:168.7) Once the praise has been performed, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the milking of what has been praised: "Thou art the praise of the praised; may the praised milk strength for me; may the praise of the praised come to me."

At the *śastra*, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the milking of the *śastra*: "Thou art the *śastra* of the *śastra*; may the *śastra* milk strength for me; may the *śastra* of the *śastra* come to me. He causes him to recite the repetition of both these [formulas]: "Possessing power, we win; may we milk offspring and nourishment. May this my true blessing be among the gods; may spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) come to me."

Then he mutters the *punarālambha* formula of the sacrifice: "The sacrifice came into being; it has come into being. It was born; it grew. It became the overlord of the gods. May it make us overlords; may we be masters of riches. Now it is indeed said:
"The sacrifice milks the master of the sacrifice, or the master of the sacrifice milks the sacrifice."
(14.9:168.16) "If one performs a sacrifice without knowing the milking of the *stotra* and *śastra*, the sacrifice milks him;
having sacrificed, he becomes worse off.
But if one performs a sacrifice knowing the milking of these two, he milks the sacrifice."
(14.9:168.18) "Having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous.

(14.9:168.18) "'Thou art the laud of the laud; mayest thou milk strength for me; may the laud of the laud come to me. Thou art the recitation of the recitation; mayest thou milk strength for me; may the recitation of the recitation come to me,' so he says.
(14.9:168.20) This, indeed, is the milking of the laud and the recitation."
"He who, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice, indeed milks the sacrifice;
having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Thus has been stated the satiating of the Hotrakas.
The rites for Vaiśvakarman have been declared;
the pouring of the *āśira* mixture has been declared;
and the performance regarding the *dhruva* vessel has been declared.
Now, indeed, it is said:
(14.10:169.4) "When the Hotṛ calls out toward the Adhvaryu, he hurls a thunderbolt at him.

(14.10:169.4) Having responded to the morning pressing, he says, "O reciter of the hymn (*ukthaśas*). (14.10:169.5) Or rather, having responded to each individual hymn, he says, "O reciter of the hymn," or [he says it] after each pressing.
"‘The hymn has been spoken,’ he says after responding to the midday pressing;
‘The hymn has been spoken for Indra,’ he says after responding to the third pressing.
These [formulations] consist of seven syllables."
"The Śakvarī consists of seven steps;
the thunderbolt is of the Śakvarī nature.
By means of the thunderbolt, he places the thunderbolt within himself at the third pressing. So says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"The exponents of sacred knowledge say:

'He should be the Adhvaryu who would bring the meters into correspondence with the *pratigara* at each pressing—[thinking] that he might place splendor in himself at the morning pressing, sensory power at the midday pressing, and cattle at the third pressing.'"

"O reciter of the *uktha*," he says, having responded to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). "The *uktha* has been spoken," he says, having responded to the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinaṃ savana*). "The *uktha* has been spoken for Indra," he says, having responded to the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*).
"These seven syllables;
the *śakvarī* consists of seven feet; cattle are associated with the *śakvarī*."
"The third pressing belongs to the Jagatī.
"At the third pressing itself, he brings the meters into correspondence during the *pratigara* response.
"Moreover, the Jagatī is indeed cattle."
"The third pressing belongs to the cattle;
verily, he places cattle within himself at the third pressing," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, it occurs:

(14.10:170.1) "When the Hotṛ calls out toward the Adhvaryu, he places a ram's wool upon him. If he were not to drive it away, his household would fall into ruin before the end of the year. "‘Śoṃsā mod iva!’—with these words he responds," so it is said.
When he is called out, he responds with "Śoṃsā modīva. "By that very means he drives away evil," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:

(14.10:170.5) "Just as one awaits a long-drawn-out [person], so does the *adhvaryu* await the response (*pratigara*). If he were to respond prematurely, it would be just as if one were to collide with a long-drawn-out [person]. If [the response] were to be omitted at the half-verse, it would be just as if one were left behind by those who are running."
Regarding this, they say: "One should not be an *āśāpratigara* (one who responds with the *ā-śā*).
For an *āśāpratigara* either responds prematurely or causes the half-verse (*ardharca*) to be lost.
