One should simply breathe out when it is time to breathe out, and one should simply breathe in when it is time to breathe in."
"He who, knowing thus, responds [with the *pratigara*], becomes an eater of food;
a vigorous one is born among his offspring"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it occurs as follows:
"This one is indeed the Hotṛ, that one is the Adhvaryu. When he recites while seated, the Hotṛ does not depart from this [earth], for she (the earth) is, as it were, seated.
(14.10:170.12) "Moreover, by that means the sacrificer milks this very [earth].
(14.10:170.13) "In that the Adhvaryu responds while standing, he does not depart from yonder [heaven];
for yonder [sun] stands, as it were."
(14.10:170.14) "Furthermore, by that means the sacrificer milks that very [world] itself.
(14.10:170.14) "Because he recites while sitting, therefore the gods subsist on what is offered from here.
Because he responds while standing, therefore human beings subsist on what is offered from there."

(14.10:170.16) “Because he recites while sitting facing east and the *pratigara* is responded while standing facing west, therefore the seed is deposited facing eastward and offspring are born facing westward,” so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, there is this [further passage]: (14.10:171.1–2) ... 14.10.3.1–5. The *Ṣoḍaśin* cup. The *Ṣoḍaśin* cup is offered at the midday pressing. It is offered with sixteen verses. Therefore it is called the *Ṣoḍaśin*. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in man. One attains these sixteen parts of man. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the year. One wins these sixteen parts of the year. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the body. One wins these sixteen parts of the body. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the sacrificial animal. One wins these sixteen parts of the sacrificial animal. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Sāman*. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Sāman*. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Brahman* priest. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Brahman* priest. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Adhvaryu* priest. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Adhvaryu* priest. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Yajus* formula. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Yajus* formula. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Ṛc* verse. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Ṛc* verse. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Sāman* chant. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Sāman* chant. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Prastāva* section. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Prastāva* section. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Udgītha* section. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Udgītha* section. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Pratihāra* section. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Pratihāra* section. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Nidhana* section. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Nidhana* section. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Gāyatrī* meter. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Gāyatrī* meter. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Triṣṭubh* meter. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Triṣṭubh* meter. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Jagatī* meter. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Jagatī* meter. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Anuṣṭubh* meter. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Anuṣṭubh* meter. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Paṅkti* meter. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Paṅkti* meter. It is offered with sixteen verses. There are sixteen parts in the *Dvipadā* meter. One wins these sixteen parts of the *Dvipadā* meter. It is offered with sixteen verses. Having offered, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "Thou art the winner of heaven; may heaven not forsake me; may I not forsake heaven; may heaven not forsake me. He consumes [the remnant], saying: "May Sūrya bestow wisdom upon me, offspring upon me, and radiance upon me.

(14.17:182.4) "The *rāṣṭrabhṛts* are indeed the kingdom;
verily by means of the kingdom he wins the kingdom for him."
"He indeed becomes the kingdom," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is also said:
"The oblations are to be offered for oneself."

(14.17:182.6) One who intends to sacrifice for himself, having kindled a fire in vain, offers the Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations at night with two *svāhā* utterances while using a yoke-pin as the enclosing sticks:
(14.17:182.7) "The Rāṣṭrabhṛts are indeed the kingdom; the subjects are the kingdom. (14.17:182.8) "The kingdom is the subjects."
"The kingdom is cattle;
since he who is the best among his peers possesses the kingdom, by means of the kingdom itself he secures the kingdom;
he becomes the most excellent among his equals. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said: "They should be offered for one who desires a village.

Intending to offer for one who desires a village, he piles up a common fire on the gambling-ground and, at night, offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations twice with the *svāhā*-utterance while using a wooden pin as the enclosing sticks.
(14.17:182.12) "The *rāṣṭrabhṛt* [bricks] are indeed the kingdom;
the kinsmen are the kingdom.
By means of the kingdom itself, he wins for him the kingdom and his kinsmen."
"He becomes truly domestic," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is also said:
"He offers the oblation on the gambling-ground."
(14.17:182.14) “Verily, on the gambling-ground itself he wins his kinsmen;
those [kinsmen], being won, wait upon him,” so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it occurs:
(14.17:182.16) "The front of the chariot (*rathamukha*) is to be offered for one desiring vigor.

(14.17:182.16) One who is about to offer for one desiring vigor, having held the front of the chariot over the fire at night upon the yoke-pins used as enclosing sticks (*śamyā-paridhi*), offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations twice with the utterance of *svāhā*.
(14.17:182.18) "Vigor, indeed, is the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*."
"The chariot is vigor. "By means of vigor, he secures vigor for himself;
he indeed becomes vigorous," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"For one who has been expelled from his kingdom, oblations should be offered for him.
He should say to as many chariots as he may have, 'Yoke them!'"
"He thereby yokes the kingdom for him," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said:
"The oblations of one whose kingdom is not in order are themselves not in order."
"One should lift the right wheel of one's own chariot and offer oblations upon the axle-rod.

Thus, having lifted the right wheel of his own chariot and held the chariot-axle over the fire at night, he offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations twice with the utterance of "svāhā" upon the yoke-pin serving as the enclosing sticks.
"He thus prepares the oblations for him."
"When these [waters] of his are being prepared, the kingdom is prepared accordingly"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now it is indeed said:
"When a battle is joined, [the oblations] are to be offered.
When a battle is joined and he is about to offer, he prepares a fuel-stick (*idhma*) of *māndhuka* wood.

(14.18:183.10) Then, having established the fire against the enemy and having anointed fuel-sticks of *māndhūka* wood, he places them on the fire with the utterance of *svāhā*. At night, using pins as enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations twice with the utterance of *svāhā*. (14.18:183.12) "The embers themselves, turning back, turn back the army of his enemies," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(14.18:183.14) Now, indeed, it is said:
"For one who should go mad, [oblations] are to be offered for him.
Intending to offer for a madman, he prepares [fuel] from the Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Plakṣa trees.

Then, having kindled a common fire and having anointed this fuel, he places it on the fire with the utterance of "svāhā. At night, using a yoke-pin as a sacrificial enclosure-stick, he offers the Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations twice with the utterance of "svāhā."
"These indeed are the dwellings of the Gandharvas and Apsarases;
he pacifies them in their own abode," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is also said:
"One who performs malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) should offer the oblations in reverse order. Thus it is said.

One about to perform malevolent magic, having established a fire at will in a self-made salt-flat or a cleft in the ground, facing away from that [victim], offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations at night with two *svāhā* utterances, using a wooden pin as the enclosing sticks, while reciting:
"Whatever is cruel in speech, with that he utters the *vaṣaṭ*."
"He cuts him with the cruel edge of speech;
he immediately meets with misfortune"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"Regarding one for whom he should desire, 'May I take away his food,' he should lie down on his back in that person's assembly hall and gather blades of grass while reciting, 'O Lord of the World!
Thus, for one for whom he should desire, "May I take away his food," he lies down on his back in that person's assembly hall and gathers blades of grass with the words, "O Lord of the World!
Then, having taken them, he carries them away.
"I take away the food of so-and-so, the son of such-and-such," he says;
thus he takes away his very food.
"He takes it away with six [verses]," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(14.18:184.9) Then he entrusts these [gifts] either to his own assembly or to his own kinsmen.
(14.18:184.10) "By means of Prajāpati himself, having taken away his food, the seasons bestow it upon him," so says the Brāhmaṇa. (14.18:184.11) Now, indeed, it is said:

(14.18:184.11) "If there should be an elder kinsman who has been deprived [of his inheritance], having settled him on dry land and having cooked a *brahmaudana* of four *śarāva*-measures, one should offer it to him.

(14.18:184.13) Thus, if there should be an elder kinsman who has been deprived, having settled him on dry land and having cooked a *brahmaudana* of four *śarāva*-measures, he offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations at night with two *svāhā* utterances over the *śamyā* as the enclosing-stick.
(14.18:184.15) "The *rāṣṭrabhṛts* are indeed the height."
"The height, the plateau.
"By means of height itself, he causes him to attain the height among his equals," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, there occurs [this]:
(14.18:184.17) "It consists of four measures; thus he finds firm support in the quarters. It is prepared in milk."
(14.18:184.18) "Verily, he bestows luster upon him. (14.18:184.18) "He draws it out for the sake of being cooked. (14.18:184.18) "It contains clarified butter for the sake of purity."
"Four of noble lineage partake [of the food];
he offers into the very light of the quarters," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said: "One desiring offspring should offer the Devikā oblations.
Thus, for one desiring offspring, he first performs the rite for Dhātṛ.
(14.19:185.2) First for one desiring cattle; (14.19:185.2) from the middle for one desiring a village; (14.19:185.3) from the middle for one who has been long ill.
The first [is for] one who is about to sacrifice;
the last [is for] one who has already sacrificed;
the first [is for] one desiring wisdom.
In the middle of the wooden cart-pole,
these [oblations] are cooked in milk. If he were to pour out all of them together, they would be liable to burn him up.
(14.19:185.6) "Having offered two of the first [portions], one should offer the third element; likewise one should offer the subsequent ones;
thus they do not burn him."

"Furthermore, whatever desire for which it is offered, that very one he attains through these [verses]," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, it is said: "In that the sacrificer offers the Agnihotra morning and evening, he is actually laying down sacrificial bricks as those oblations."
"The days and nights are indeed the bricks of him who has established the sacred fires.
When he offers the evening and morning oblations, having obtained the days and nights and made them into bricks, he lays them down. He offers ten times in one place."
"The *virāj* consists of ten syllables.
Having obtained the *virāj*, he places it down after having made it into a brick.
Moreover, he thereby obtains the sacrifice within the *virāj* itself.
(14.19:185.12) "Each of his [altars] becomes possessed of a site (citya).
Therefore, wherever he departs after having stayed for ten nights, that is the sacrificial ground (yajñavāstu); whatever is prior to that is indeed without a site (avāstu). Thus it is said.
When, having stayed for ten nights, he is about to depart, they gather together upon the cart standing near the Āhavanīya fire whatever of his there is to be gathered.
That which is prior to that is indeed without a dwelling.
For Rudra is indeed Vāstoṣpati.
"If one were to depart without having offered the oblation to Vāstoṣpati, Agni, having become Rudra, would rise up after him and slay him.
He offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati;
verily, he pacifies him with his own portion."
"The sacrificer does not come to ruin," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"If one were to offer when [the fire] has been yoked, that would be exactly as if one were to offer an oblation at a dwelling where [the owner] has already departed."
"If one were to offer the oblation while [the chariot] is unyoked, it would be exactly as if one were offering an oblation while at rest.
His offering to Vāstoṣpati would remain unoffered, for the right [ox] is yoked while the left is unyoked.
Therefore, he offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati. Thus [it is said].

When the right [ox] is yoked and the left is unyoked, he should take four spoonfuls in a ladle made of *parṇa* wood, and having drawn them back, he offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati in the Āhavanīya fire, reciting: "O Lord of the Dwelling, recognize us," and having recited this, he offers with: "O Lord of the Dwelling, with thy auspicious assembly...
At this point, having set down the ladle and yoked the left [ox], he departs.
"He performed both. "He pacifies it without omission," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, it is said:
"If one were to offer with a single [verse], one would perform a *darvihoma*.
Having recited the *puro'nuvākyā*, one offers with the *yājyā* for the sake of providing a deity. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it occurs:
"If he were to take up what has been offered into the fire, he would cause Rudra to mount after his house.
If he were to depart without having extinguished the embers, that would be exactly like a sacrificial ruin or a conflagration.
[Therefore,] he causes the fire to mount into the two kindling woods with the verse: 'This is thy womb, fit for the season.'"
"This, indeed, is the womb of Agni;
he causes him to ascend into his own womb.
Now, they say: 'If [the fire] that has been ascended into the two kindling woods should be lost, his fire would perish; it would have to be established again.'"
"O Agni, that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice, come with that; ascend!"—with these words, he causes [the fire] to ascend into himself. Thus it is said.
He causes himself to ascend with [the verse]: "O Agni, that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice—with that come hither! Ascend, O Self, unto yourself! Toward the treasures...
"Bestowing upon us many heroic riches—having become the sacrifice, sit upon the sacrifice, O Jātavedas, in your own womb; being born, come to your dwelling. Thus [he says].

(14.19:186.19) Then he makes him descend with [the verse]: "Descend again, O Jātavedas; knowing [the way], carry our oblation to the gods. Bestow upon us life, progeny, and wealth; shine for us unceasingly in our home.
(14.19:187.1) "The sacrificer is indeed the womb of Agni;
thus he causes him to ascend into his own womb," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
The *anvārambha* has been explained.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"The seers did not see Indra face to face."
Vasiṣṭha saw him face to face.

He said, "I shall tell you, O Brāhmaṇa, that by which your subjects will be propagated with you as their domestic priest; but do not speak of this to other Ṛṣis. To him he then spoke these Stomabhāga formulas.

(14.20:187.6) "Then the subjects were born with Vasiṣṭha as their domestic priest. Therefore they say, "The office of the *brahman* belongs to a descendant of Vasiṣṭha. When [the *hotṛ*] says, "O *brahman*, we shall chant; O *praśāstṛ*," then the *brahman* gives the impulse (*prasauti*) after making this the introductory formula: "O God Savitṛ... Having taken each [verse] one by one from this section beginning with "Thou art a ray; for dwelling thee; quicken the dwelling," he gives the impulse.

In this very manner, while giving the impulse, he impels the *agniṣṭoma* with twelve [verses], the *atyagniṣṭoma* with thirteen, the *ukthya* with fifteen, the *ṣoḍaśin* with sixteen, the *vājapeya* with seventeen, the *atirātra* with twenty-nine, and the *aptoryāma* with all [of them].
When they move forward for the *rathaṃtara* *sandhi*, he says: "Thou art Vasuku; thou art Veṣaśri; thou art Vasyaṣṭi.
In this very manner he impels [the rites] up to the *aptoryāma*.
(14.20:187.15) Now, therefore, concerning the strides themselves:

one who practices sorcery, being beset by rivals and contending with them, should perform the rites for sorcery and, having undertaken the ritual arts of sorcery, should stride for a year with these steps.

(14.20:187.16) "With the god Agni I conquer the hostile armies; with the Gāyatrī metre, the Trivṛt-stoma, the Rathantara-sāman, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call as my thunderbolt, I cast down my previously born rivals. I press them down, I drive them away from this dwelling, from this world of earth—him who hates us and him whom we hate. By the stride of Viṣṇu, I step over them."

With the god Indra I conquer the armies; by means of the *triṣṭubh* metre, the fifteenfold hymn-form (*stoma*), the *bṛhat* chant, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call as my thunderbolt, I cause my co-born rivals to fall low. I press them down, I drive them back, in this abode, in this world of earth—him who hates us and him whom we hate. By the stride of Viṣṇu, I step over them.

"With all the gods I conquer the battles; with the Jagatī metre, the seventeenfold Stoma, the Vāmadevya Sāman, and the Vaṣaṭ-call as my thunderbolt, I cast down my younger rivals. I crush them, I drive them back—to this dwelling, to this world of earth—him who hates us and whom we hate. By the stride of Viṣṇu, I step over them. Thus he says.
Or rather, it may be continued in the *abhicaraṇīya* sacrifices.
Or else, having set aside the other sequences, one should proceed for a year with these sequences.
The mounting of the *śukra* and *manthin* vessels has been explained.
Now, therefore, regarding the *atīmokṣas*:

having offered the *vaiśvakarmaṇa* oblations, having melted clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire and purified it, and having taken four portions into the ladle, he offers it into the *gārhapatya* while the sacrificer maintains contact with him.
(14.21:188.13) "O gods who destroy the sacrifice, who dwell upon the earth—may Agni protect me from them; may we, the doers of good, go [to heaven], svāhā!

Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers it in the Gārhapatya fire itself: "O gods who steal the sacrifice, who dwell upon the earth—may Agni protect me from them; may we, the doers of good, go [to heaven], svāhā!"

Then he proceeds toward the Āgnīdhra fire with the verse: "We have come, O Mitra and Varuṇa, to that which is yours, the desirable portion of the nights; grasping the firmament in the world of the well-performed deed, upon the third back in the luminous realm of heaven."

(14.21:188.19) Then, having run to the *āgnīdhra* and taken four portions of clarified butter in the *sruva*-ladle, he offers it in the *āgnīdhra* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "O gods who destroy the sacrifice, who dwell in the intermediate space—may Vāyu protect me from them! May we, the doers of good deeds, go to heaven! Svāhā!"

Having taken another fourfold portion, the Āgnīdhra himself offers it with: "O gods who steal the sacrifice, who sit within the intermediate space—may Vāyu protect me from them; may we, the doers of good deeds, go to the world of heaven, svāhā!"

Then he approaches the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "O Savitṛ, those nights of yours which travel between heaven and earth along the path of the gods—may we, ascending to the light of heaven together with all our households and offspring, cross over the regions."

(14.21:189.7) Then, having hastened to the Āhavanīya fire and taken four portions into the offering-spoon, he makes an oblation in the Āhavanīya while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "O gods who destroy the sacrifice, who dwell above in heaven—may Sūrya protect me from them; may we go to those who have performed good deeds, svāhā!"

Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers it in the Āhavanīya fire itself with the mantra: "O gods who steal the sacrifice, who dwell above in heaven—may Sūrya protect me from them; may we, the doers of good deeds, go to the world of the righteous, svāhā!"

Then he pays homage to the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "O Jātavedas, by that supreme oblation wherewith you brought together the milks for Indra—by that, O Agni, do thou cause this man to prosper; bestow upon him preeminence among his kinsmen.
For there are gods who destroy the sacrifice and those who steal the sacrifice.
(14.21:189.14) "They sit upon these worlds, seizing and plundering the property of him who gives and him who sacrifices.
(14.21:189.15) "'Those gods who are slayers of the sacrifice, who dwell upon the earth, those in the intermediate space, and those in heaven'—so he says.
(14.21:189.16) 'Having crossed over these very worlds, he goes to the heavenly world together with his household and his cattle,' so says the Brāhmaṇa."
Alternatively, he offers three oblations on the Gārhapatya fire, three on the Āgnīdhra fire, and three on the Āhavanīya fire.
Or else, reciting [the formulas], he should move from the Gārhapatya to the Āhavanīya. The Udavasānīyā sacrifice has been explained.

(14.21:189.20) At this point, he offers this third *pravṛtāhuti* oblation with the formula: "May the god Sūrya protect me from the gods; may Vāyu protect me from the intermediate space; may Agni, the sacrificer, protect me from sight—*svāhā*!

(14.21:190.1) Now, one practicing exorcism offers milk into a vessel made of *kārṣmarya* wood from a brown cow that has a brown calf, with the formula: "O impetuous one, O vigorous one, O Savitṛ, you who belong to all people! With these names of yours, O Soma, we shall worship you; with those names of yours, O Soma, we shall worship you—*svāhā*! (14.21:190.1) Thus.
Having directly pierced his heart, he shall tear out his entrails;
he surely overcomes that rival.
Now, regarding whichever officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) with whom he may have rivalry, he says to him: "Let him not approach my cup; I shall perform the touching."
With this very mantra, he should offer the cup. That [Soma] flows through the filter either upwards or downwards.
The mixing of the *pātnīvata* [cup] has been explained.
The lifting up of the Āditya cup has been explained;
the spoonful-offering of the Prāyaṇīya sacrifice has been explained;
[and] that of the Udayanīya has been explained.
The worship of the sacrificial post has been explained.
The *patnīyajus* formulas have been recited. These ladles (*sruk*) are exactly as described in this Brāhmaṇa.
The *dadhigraha* has been explained.
Now, it is indeed said:
"One should take a portion of clarified butter for one who desires splendor.
Having placed two blades of *barhis* grass in between, he takes the portion of clarified butter.
"One should draw a soma-cup for one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Having grasped the stalks (*aṃśu*), he draws the soma-cup.

Then, on the Mahāvrata day, he draws this additional cup (*atigrāhya*) dedicated to Prajāpati, reciting: "All [the gods] encompass your power," and then: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Prajāpati."
Having wiped it around, he sets it down with: "This is thy womb; for Prajāpati, thee.
Now, therefore, follows the taking up of the Prāṇagrahas themselves.

Having piled the king [Soma] together so that it is well-satisfied, he stretches out new stalks toward the east: "This one is Bhuvas; his breath is Bhauvāyana; spring is Prāṇāyana; the Gāyatrī belongs to spring; from the Gāyatrī comes the Gāyatra; from the Gāyatra comes the Upāṃśu cup; from the Upāṃśu comes the Trivṛt stoma; from the Trivṛt comes the Rathantara Sāman; from the Rathantara comes the seer Vasiṣṭha. With thee, taken by Prajāpati, I take the breath for the subjects. Thus he says.
"This one to the south is Viśvakarman"—with these words, he extends nine [lines] toward the south. "This one behind is Viśvavyacas"—with these words, he extends nine toward the west.
"This one above is the sun"—with these words, he extends nine toward the north.
"This is the higher thought," he says; thus, from above, he causes them to proceed clockwise.

He counters them with the *apānabhṛt* verses: "The eastern direction of the directions; spring of the seasons; Agni the deity; the Brahman the wealth; the *trivṛt* hymn-form; it has the fifteenfold as its track; the three-year-old steer the age; the Kṛta throw of the dice; the easterly wind the wind; Sānaga the seer. Thus [he recites].

He causes [the ancestors] to recite: "O fathers, grandfathers, those further and those nearer," for those who are in the east; "The southern quarter," for those who are in the south; "The western quarter," for those who are in the west.
"Of the quarters, the northern one"—with these words, those that are on the north;
"of the quarters, the upward one"—with these words, those that are above; they proceed around clockwise.
These [cups] are indeed prescribed for the Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya days on the tenth day.
However, in the case of Rātrisattras, one who is ill or has been afflicted may take them even at the Agniṣṭoma;
he will certainly become free from disease.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"Both these were created from Prajāpati," so says the Brāhmaṇa. And "O Aśvins, [drink] the Surā-mixture," this occurs specifically in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"This [earth] is the Agnihotra-cow;
this earth, indeed, settles down for him whose Agnihotra-cow settles down."
"One should make her rise," it is said.

He makes that Agnihotra cow rise upon which she has sat down, [reciting]: "The goddess Aditi, of all forms, has risen; she has bestowed long life upon the lord of the sacrifice, preparing a portion for Indra, and for Mitra and Varuṇa.
Now, indeed, there is this [text].
"If the Agnihotra cow sits down after being let loose, she sits down having perceived the exhaustion or the evil of that [sacrificer].
"Having milked her, one should give her to a Brāhmaṇa whose food one would not eat.
Thus, when the Agnihotra cow sits down after being let loose, he milks her right then and there and gives her to a Brāhmaṇa.
And from that time forward, he does not eat food.
Now, it is indeed said:
"The milk of him whose *agnihotra* spills while being milked enters the earth."

"One should consecrate that [milk] with a mantra. Thus, when his *agnihotra* milk spills while being milked, he consecrates it with: "Whatever milk today has clung to the earth, whatever has flowed into the plants, whatever into the waters—may there be milk in my houses, milk in the cows, milk in the calves, and may that milk be in me. So he says.
"He places milk itself within himself, in his house, and in his cattle.
"He pours water [into it]. "Verily, by means of water he obtains this," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"If one joins that which is afflicted with the unafflicted part of the sacrifice, then both of them become afflicted.
Indeed, this *agnihotra* becomes afflicted when, while being milked, it spills; [therefore] one should not milk over it.
If one's *agnihotra* milk spills while it is being milked, he does not milk that same cow again.
"Whatever it may be, in whatever condition it is, it should be offered as an oblation. Then, having milked another cow, he should offer the oblation once more.
"By means of that which is itself unafflicted, he repairs the affliction of the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is further said: "If [the oblation] of one who has run forward should spill, and if he were to go back again without having offered it from there, he would cut off the sacrifice."
"Where it spills, there he should sit down and take it up again.

Thus, wherever it spills, he should set down the vessel right there, pour in what remains, and having poured more [milk] back into it, he should offer that very same [substance], however it may appear;
or else, having milked another [cow], he should offer again.
"He repairs the injury of the sacrifice by means of that which is itself uninjured," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"The sacrifice of him is rent asunder for whom a dog runs between while the Agnihotra is placed upon the fire."
(14.23:193.10) "Agni, indeed, is Rudra. If one were to turn [the fire] back toward the cow, he would deliver the cattle over to Rudra;
the sacrificer would become destitute of cattle."

"If he were to sprinkle water [over the fire], he would place that which is inedible for Agni—the water—upon these two [fires]; it would be inedible for them. Taking ashes from the *gārhapatya* fire, [he recites]: "Over this Vishnu strode."
"Thus, with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, he should run forward while causing the Āhavanīya fire to fall away.
So, with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, he runs forward while causing the Āhavanīya fire to fall away.

"Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; by means of the sacrifice itself, he continues the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Then, "He also scatters ashes over the footprint of the dog for the sake of pacification," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now it is indeed said:
"The Āhavanīya fire of one whose sun sets while the fire has not been lifted desires the Gārhapatya, and the Gārhapatya desires the Āhavanīya.
For such a person, one should carry gold tied with a blade of *darbha* grass in front, then the fire, and then the Agnihotra offering."

(14.24:193.20) If the sun sets while his fire has not been lifted up, an assistant, having tied gold with a blade of *darbha* grass, goes forward first; following him comes a Brahmin of Ṛṣi lineage, followed by the fuel, and then by himself with the *agnihotra*.
(14.24:194.2) Then, having placed this gold in the site of the *āhavanīya* fire and removed the gold, he turns to the right and establishes the fuel.
Now, it is indeed said:
(14.24:194.4) "Having set down the *agnihotra* oblation, he should remain seated until the sun has set.
(14.24:194.4) "He who is exhausted follows after his violated vow as if in death. (14.24:194.5) "Indeed, he who faints goes to the end of his own life."
"He reaches the end of the sacrifice whose fire the sun sets upon while it has not yet been carried forth. He offers again after making [the fire] blaze up;
thus he repairs the end of the sacrifice by means of the end," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"Varuṇa seizes the sacrifice of him whose fire the sun sets upon while it has not yet been carried forth.
"He should offer a *caru* oblation to Varuṇa."
"By that very [means] he redeems the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"The Āhavanīya fire of one whose sun rises while his fire has not been lifted out desires to go down into the Gārhapatya; the Gārhapatya desires to go down into the Āhavanīya."
"One should carry forth four ladlings of clarified butter first, then the fire, then the Agnihotra," so it is said.

If the sun rises while someone's fire has not yet been carried forth, the assistant first takes his place with the four ladlings of clarified butter; following him comes the Brāhmaṇa of the Ṛṣi-lineage with the fuel-wood, and following him the sacrificer himself with the Agnihotra.
Then, having placed this clarified butter in the site of the Āhavanīya fire and having removed the butter, he establishes the fuel-wood.
Now, it is indeed said:
"The dawn indeed dawns turned away from him for whom the sun rises while his fire has not been lifted."

“May Uṣas with her banner favor the sacrifice accompanied by the gods; [may she favor] the most honey-sweet [offering] for the gods, Svāhā!”—having sat down facing west, he should offer with clarified butter. “Thus he causes her to dawn for him facing west,” so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said:
(14.24:194.19) "Having set down the *agnihotra*, one should remain seated until the sun has set.
One who dies after [the vow] is indeed following the slain vow. He who faints goes to the end of his own self."
"He reaches the end of the sacrifice for whom the sun rises while his fire has not been lifted up," [it is said]. "Having kindled it again, he offers;
by means of the end, he repairs the end of the sacrifice. So says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"Mitra seizes the sacrifice of him whose fire the sun rises over while it has not yet been carried forward.
[Therefore] one should offer a pap to Mitra.
"By that very [means] he redeems the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"If the Gārhapatya fire should go out while the Āhavanīya has not gone out, if one were to churn the Gārhapatya without having first extinguished the Āhavanīya, he would cause a rupture."
"He would produce a rival for him.
"Whatever belonging to the sacrificial site (*vāstavya*) is performed at the sacrifice, Rudra follows after that.
If he were to settle down first, he would be worshipping a sacrificial fire belonging to the site."
"Rudra might become one who slays his cattle";
"having extinguished the Āhavanīya fire, he should churn the Gārhapatya.
Thus, having extinguished the Āhavanīya, he churns the Gārhapatya.

"From here Agni was first born, Jātavedas from his own womb; may he, knowing [the way], carry the oblation to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī. Thus [it is said]. "Verily, by means of the meters he causes him to be born from his own womb," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, there occurs [this]:
"He churns the *gārhapatya* fire.
Indeed, cattle attend upon one who has established the *gārhapatya* fire;
when it goes out, the cattle depart after it. Thus [it is said].
(14.24:195.12) Then he worships it with: "Rejoice for the sake of food, for wealth, for power, for splendor, for vigor, and for lordship.
(14.24:195.13) Then he kindles it with: "May the two Sarasvatī springs kindle thee; thou art the sovereign ruler (samrāj), thou art the far-shining one (virāj)."
Now, it is indeed said:
"The wheel is a thunderbolt.
"The thunderbolt cuts through the sacrifice of him whose wagon or chariot passes between the two fires."
(14.25:195.16) "Having extinguished the Āhavanīya fire, one should draw it out from the Gārhapatya," so [it is said].

Having extinguished the Āhavanīya fire, he takes out a fuel-stick from the Gārhapatya with the verse: "O Agni, that footprint of yours which was first set down, and which extended along the rays of the sun—bring that back here, the abode of wealth; unite us with your favor that brings strength. Thus [it is said]: "By means of his former sacrifice, he continues the sequence of the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(14.25:195.20) Then he pays homage to him with: "O Agni, you are far-reaching; you are the beloved, the chosen Hotṛ. Through you they extend the sacrifice.
(14.25:195.21) "Agni is all the deities; by means of the deities he continues the sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
(14.25:195.22) Then he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt.
Having placed the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives a bull as a gift; that sacrifice concludes in the well-known manner.
Now, indeed, it is said:

(14.25:196.2) "If the Soma at the morning pressing is left over, overflowing while desiring the midday pressing," so it is said. (14.25:196.4) When the Soma is left over at the morning pressing, as he goes forward, he says: "Fill the cups following the Hotṛ's cup! O Unnetṛ, draw up the King [Soma] in its entirety; do not let any remain! (14.25:196.6) They fill the Hotṛ's cup first, and the others as they come along.
Having raised the king [Soma] from all sides, they place him upon the high altar (*uttaravedi*).
Then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he, restraining his speech, runs westward and introduces the chant (*stotra*);
they chant it.

This is the Gāyatra Sāman in the fifteenfold form. They perform it for the Hotṛ with the verses containing the word *dhayat*, beginning with "The cow yields milk for the Maruts. They say, "This is the last [verse]. From this point onward, the procedure is the same.
Now, it is indeed said: "If at the midday pressing the Soma overflows, it overflows desiring the third pressing for the Ādityas.
When the Soma has overflowed at the midday pressing, he, walking eastward, says: "Fill the cups following the Hotṛ's cup! O Unnetṛ, draw up the King [Soma] entirely; do not let any remain!"
They first draw the *hotṛ*’s cup, and the others as they happen to be available.
Having drawn the entire King Soma, they set them down on the *uttaravedi*.
Then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he, restraining his speech, runs westward and introduces the chant (*stotra*).
They chant the *gaurīvīta* *sāman*, which is seventeenfold; they perform it upon these verses beginning, "O Sūrya, you are great indeed.
To the *hotṛ* they say, "This is the last [verse]."
(14.25:196.19) From this point onward, it is the same.
(14.25:197.1) Now, indeed, it is said: "If at the third pressing the soma should be left over, one should perform the *ukthya*."
"If one should have a surplus at the Ukthya, he should perform an Atirātra.
That which has a surplus at the Atirātra is indeed difficult to discern.
When there is a surplus at the Atirātra, moving forward, he says: "Fill the cups following the Hotṛ's cup! O Unnetṛ, draw up the entire King Soma; do not let it remain in excess!"
They first draw the *hotṛ*’s cup, and the others as they come along. Having drawn the King [Soma] entirely, they set them down on the *uttaravedi*.
Then, having touched water and taken two blades of *barhis* grass, restraining his speech, he hastens westward and introduces the *stotra*.
They chant;
they perform this Bṛhat Sāman on the twenty-one-fold stoma upon verses addressed to Viṣṇu containing the word *śipiviṣṭa* for the Hotṛ. They say to him: "This is the last verse."
From this point onward, it is the same.

Thus, when the Chandogas and Bahvṛcas desire [the draught], if they should not so desire, then at the morning pressing, when there is a surplus, he pours the Āgrayaṇa vessel over that jar which he considers sufficient for the King [Soma] who remains; he holds it underneath and lets it flow down three times.
As he pours it out and restrains it, it becomes entirely the Āgrayaṇa draught.
Having uttered the *abhihiṃkāra* over it three times and wiped it around, he sets it down.

At the midday pressing, when there is a surplus, he takes the vessel which he considers sufficient for the King [Soma] that remains over; having poured the Āgrayaṇa over the top of that vessel, he supports it from below.
He causes it to overflow three times;
as it overflows, it becomes entirely the Āgrayaṇa vessel.
Having likewise uttered the *abhihiṃkāra* over it three times and wiped it, he sets it down.
When the third pressing has been exceeded, one causes the *hāriyojana* cup alone to overflow here;
for there is no further drawing [of Soma].
Now, therefore, follows the investigation regarding the *dhruva* cup that has been depleted.
Having enclosed it with two verses addressed to Indra and Agni, he should offer it;
for Indra and Agni are indeed the gods among the gods whom we worship again and again—this is one [view].
Having enclosed it with two verses addressed to the Aśvins, he should offer it.
"The Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods; by means of them, he prepares a remedy for him"—this is one [view].
He should offer the oblation after enclosing the victim with two verses addressed to Viṣṇu.
"Whatever is redundant in the sacrifice, that is redundant with respect to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa"—this is another [view].
(14.26:198.6) He should throw it into the water together with the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath).
(14.26:198.7) "Just as my other vessels smeared with Soma [are disposed of], so shall this one be for me"—this is one view.
(14.26:198.8) Or he should burn it up together with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
"This forest fire is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara.
This [fire] is taken for Agni Vaiśvānara so that it may be offered into the Vaiśvānara fire as something stable; this is another [reason].
Then he undergoes initiation again: "The sacrifice, indeed, is the expiation for the sacrifice"— this is for one who performs a one-day sacrifice.
Now, regarding the performers of the sacrificial session (*sattra*):
having prepared a runoff channel on the *mārjālīya* mound that possesses a downward slope, they pour it out there;
for on the following day, they are about to perform the *savana* extraction.
The *saṃsava* has been explained.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"Those among the consecrated for whom one dies go to ruin."
"If they were to cast him out, their world would become like that of evildoers. "Bring it! Burn it! he should say.
If the consecrated one (*dīkṣita*) should suffer from a disease, he should indeed lie on the *āgnīdhrīya* bed.
They bring him portions of food as much as he deems sufficient for eating. If he recovers from his illness, he returns;

but if he indeed passes away, they should remove the embers from all the fires, consign the fires into the two kindling woods, carry them out between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, and cremate him with them.

Having cooled it for three nights, they should pile it up; having done so, they should wait for the conclusion of the six-day rite. Then, when the six-day rite has concluded, he asks for a jar for the bones.

Having placed the collected [fire] upon it and having set it down to the south of the altar, they should praise it with the verses of the Serpent Queen (*sarparājñī*). "This earth, indeed, is the queen of those that creep. By means of these [verses], they entrust him to her.
(14.27:199.9) "They say that what has been praised but not recited after [the *śastra*] is unsuccessful.

(14.27:199.10) "The *hotṛ*, as the first, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), should circumambulate the *mārjālīya* fire while reciting the *yāmī* verses and proclaiming the *sarparājñī* verses.
(14.27:199.11) When they have thus circumambulated, the *adhvaryu* goes around last.

(14.27:199.12) Then, having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder, they walk around three times again in the same manner as before. As they have thus circumambulated, the *adhvaryu* goes around first. (14.27:199.13) Then, taking him [the deceased], having placed him between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), and having set down the stone and the jar of bones, he sprinkles them with water, saying: "May the evil be burnt away from us. (TS 4.1.2.4)
At that [sacrifice], they draw the cups beginning with those for Mitra and Varuṇa.
Then they remain seated for the remainder of the sacrificial session.
At the time of its purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), having placed a jar of bones there, he sprinkles it with water.
This indeed becomes his *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath); or rather, he should consecrate (*dīkṣayet*) him in the place of whoever may be his nearest kinsman.
In the course of a year, they cause the bones to perform the sacrifice.
Now, it is indeed said:
"The cattle and the virility depart from him who makes the sacrificial post sprout, thereby creating a demonic appearance for him.
'He should offer an animal of many colors to Tvaṣṭṛ,' so it is said.
If the sacrificial post of those performing a *sattra* should sprout, they should cut off its top-ring (*caṣāla*) and perform the offering of an animal to Tvaṣṭṛ at the *savanīya* sacrifice."

"Alternatively, having cooked the *brahmaudana* for Tvaṣṭṛ, they should cut down these branches or have them carved. Alternatively, having offered the spoonfuls (*sruvāhuti*) for Tvaṣṭṛ, they should cut down these branches or have them carved.
Or rather, one should simply say, 'For Tvaṣṭṛ, for Tvaṣṭṛ. Thus [it is said].
Now, it is indeed said:
"Those for whom the consecrated fire goes out go to ruin. "If the Āhavanīya fire should go out, if one were to churn it [back], he would cause a break in the continuity."
(14.28:200.10) "He would produce a rival for him.
(14.28:200.10) "If the Āhavanīya fire should go out, one should take it from the Āgnīdhra fire. (14.28:200.11) If the Āgnīdhra fire should go out, one should take it from the Gārhapatya fire."
(14.28:200.11) "If the Gārhapatya fire should go out, one should churn it again from that very same place.
(14.28:200.12) "For it is indeed here that it lies hidden; and when they see it hidden in its highest [place], then they seek it."
"One should make the two kindling sticks (*araṇi*) from whatever wood it may have gone out;
one should also make the *krumuka* stick.
Having made the two kindling sticks from that very wood from which it has gone out, and having placed a chip of *krumuka* beneath them, he should churn while keeping those very embers together.

Having placed those very embers together, he churns them with the mantra: "From here Agni was first born, Jātavedas from his own womb; may he, knowing [the way], carry the oblation to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī. Thus, "He procreates him from his own womb by means of the meters," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(14.29:201.4) "Now, if both the Āhavanīya and Gārhapatya fires should go out, one should churn the Gārhapatya fire and then draw out the Āgnīdhrīya fire from it for the Āhavanīya. (14.29:201.5) If both the Āgnīdhrīya and Gārhapatya fires should go out, one should churn the Gārhapatya fire and then draw out the Āgnīdhrīya fire from it.
(14.29:201.6) Now, if both the Āgnīdhrīya and Āhavanīya fires should go out, one should draw out the Āgnīdhrīya fire from the Gārhapatya and then draw out the Āhavanīya fire from that."

(14.29:201.7) "Now, if all [the fires] should go out, one should churn the *gārhapatya*, then, having drawn out the *āgnīdhrīya*, from that one should draw out the *āhavanīya*. (14.29:201.9) Now it is indeed said: "One churns the *gārhapatya*."
"The Gārhapatya fire is indeed the womb of Agni; he thus generates him from his own womb; he does not generate a rival for him. So says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said: "If one's *soma* should run out, he should divide a piece of gold into two parts; he should shake one part over the *ṛjīṣa* and offer the other.
Thus, when his *soma* runs out, he divides that gold into two parts; he shakes one part over the *ṛjīṣa* and, having placed the other part into the principal cup (*mukhya-camasa*), he offers it.
"He presses Soma indeed; he offers Soma," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is further said:
"Of the Soma being pressed, the dear body went forth."
"That became gold, that [became] golden coin (*hiraṇya*); when they make it of gold, they endow him with his own dear body," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, it is said:
(14.29:201.18) "If they should carry off one's un-purchased *soma*, he should indeed purchase it; that itself is the expiation for that," so says the *Brāhmaṇa*. Now, indeed, it occurs [in the text]:
(14.29:201.19) "If they should steal what has been purchased, one should press *ādāra* plants and *phālguna* plants.
(14.29:201.20) *Ādāras* are small grasses;
*phālgunas* are those from the Himālayas.
In the absence of those white ones (*śvetaka*), there is a substitute. It is known from scripture: "In the third heaven from here, Soma was."
The Gāyatrī brought it;
its tip was broken off,
and that became the parṇa tree.
(14.29:202.3) "That is the reason for the leaf-nature of the *parṇa* tree.
(14.29:202.4) "Therefore, the pressing of the Soma must be performed using only *parṇa*-shoots.
(14.29:202.4) "One should mix it with boiled milk at the morning pressing."
"This has been boiled," [it is said];
"with curds at midday"— thus this becomes curds.
"At the third pressing, with the mixed curds" (14.29:202.6)—
they say this refers to the butter churned from milk along with the *pilaka* [curd-mass], drawn out before it has reached the state of fresh butter (14.29:202.7).
"The Soma sacrifice should be an Agniṣṭoma, having the *Rathantara* as its *sāman*."
(14.29:202.8) "Those very officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who have been chosen should perform the sacrifice for him.
Thus it is said; those same ones perform the sacrifice for him.
(14.29:202.9) "He should give one cow as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Thus it is said.
He gives one cow here as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Whatever he intends to give here, that he gives there.
"One should purchase Soma again."
(14.29:202.11) "By means of sacrifice alone he seeks that sacrifice; that itself is the atonement for it," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, it occurs:

(14.29:202.12) "Verily, he who pledges himself for the sacrificial session (*sattra*) pledges himself for all deities, for all desires, for all hymns-of-praise (*stoma*), for all meters (*chandas*), and for all *pṛṣṭha* chants."
(14.29:202.14) "A man is indeed only as great as his wealth; he should sacrifice with all his possessions.
Thus [it is said]. They perform the Atirātra Viśvajit;
then, on this occasion, he gives away all his possessions.
"His Soma sacrifice should have all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras;
thus he ransoms himself from all deities, from all desires, from all stomas, from all meters, and from all *pṛṣṭhas*," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"Pavamāna, [the one] who wins the light of heaven"—this [verse] occurs in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice;
the subsequent portion is the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, it is said:

"Therefore, when performing the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the sacrificer should pray: 'I pray for well-being lasting for a year. Therefore, when performing the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, the sacrificer should pray: 'I pray for well-being lasting for a full year. Therefore, when performing the Sākamedha sacrifices, the sacrificer should pray: 'I pray for well-being lasting for an idāvatsara year.'"
"Therefore, by means of the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice, the sacrificer prays for prosperity year after year"—thus he should pray.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"The Kṛttikās belong to Agni; the bright [light] is above, the light is below. Thus they say that one may optionally use the Nakṣatra-bricks.
Now, it is indeed said:
"One should perform the *vaṣaṭ* at that auspicious constellation just before dawn";
one should perform it in the morning.
One should perform it at the time of *saṃgava*; one should perform it at midday;
one should perform it in the afternoon.
One should perform it in the evening;
as far as the sun goes there, where one can see the last [object], so far one should perform it. Whatever he may do, he performs it on an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). Thus it is said.
The Brāhmaṇa is in the north; the Brāhmaṇa is in the north.

A king who has conquered all and rules over the whole earth is about to perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice. He chooses this sacrificial ground: one that is favorable to the Aśvins in the east, favorable to the Aśvins in the south, favorable to the Aśvins in the west, and favorable to the Aśvins in the north. They cut down trees, break up the high ground, fill in the low ground, and remove the parched husks of grain.
They create bathing places for rivers on all sides, as well as springs and ponds.
Then, he selects two lakes in the middle of the sacrificial ground—those that flow out, do not dry up, and have auspicious names—if they find such.
However, if they do not find such, they dig them and fill them with water brought from elsewhere or carried there by means of water-courses.

In such a way that they remain leak-proof, non-depleting, and bear auspicious names, he then, to the west of that, selects the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) from the middle, twice as wide as the width of the fire-altar.
They construct a hall there with its ridge-pole facing east, with openings toward the quarters, and higher on the south side.
To the south of that [shed], they construct a stable for horses;
there they make a horse-pen from *aśvattha* wood using wedges with their points directed downwards.

(15.1:204.13) Now these materials are prepared for him: a handsome horse, which is the best among his excellent steeds; other than that, an unlimited number of draft-oxen, castrated and without testicles; a black four-eyed dog; two slaves, the son of a concubine and the son of a secondary wife; an old couch; a mattress of reeds; a pestle made of *saidhraka* wood; the son of an unchaste woman; four hundred guards: one hundred princes fit for the couch, one hundred non-princes who are fierce, and one hundred [others].
There are a hundred charioteers and village leaders, four *kṣattṛ*s and collectors, and four great officiating priests (*ṛtvij*);
others follow them, and at the proper time they bring them together on foot.
(15.2:205.7) Up to the *subrahmaṇyā* call:

four kinds of water collected from the quarters; four thousand *niṣkas*; two ornaments, one of gold and one of silver; two other pieces of gold; two lute-players; a Brāhmaṇa and a Rājanya; two cords, one made of *muñja* grass and one made of *kuśa* grass, both thirteen cubits long.
With these things prepared, he waits for the arrival of Citrā.

(15.2:205.10) Then, [reciting] "With the *citrayā* [offering]," he causes the fires to ascend into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) and proceeds toward the hall, [reciting]: "O Savitṛ, those paths of yours which are ancient, dustless, and spread out in the mid-air—by those easy-to-traverse paths, protect us today and speak for us, O God."

Having gone around the north of the hall and entered the hall by the eastern door, he churns fire in the place of the *gārhapatya* fire, spreads the fires, and worships the *gārhapatya* with: "Homage to Agni, who dwells on earth and fills the world; grant a world to this sacrificer. [He worships] the *anvāhāryapacana* fire with: "Homage to Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space and fills the world; grant a world to this sacrificer."

(15.2:206.2) "Homage to Sūrya, who dwells in heaven, the protector of the world! Grant a world to this sacrificer!"—with these words [he addresses] the Āhavanīya fire. (15.2:206.3) Now, to the west of this [fire], behind the horse-stable, a small shed with a single exit has been constructed for him. (15.2:206.4) Having kindled a common fire there, he offers ninety oblations with the formula, "To Death, svāhā! To Death, svāhā! and eleven with the formula, "To Prayāsa, svāhā! etc.
"A man has a life-span of a hundred years and a strength of a hundred; the self is the one hundred and first. To the extent that he is a man, from that he wards off death"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, having had his hair and beard shaved, having gathered his body hair, having clipped his nails, and having cleansed his teeth, the two bathe and put on two unwashed garments.
Both are adorned with human ornaments and wear unwashed clothes.
Then he has them cook the food for the commencement of the vow for these two; they eat of it mixed with clarified butter and mixed with milk.
Then, in the afternoon, pieces of gold are placed upon their mouths.
The sacrificer [takes] gold; the wife, silver; or, if there are many wives, they take silver.
Then, while he remains silent, he offers the evening Agnihotra.
These royal attendants approach him—the charioteers, the village overseers, the chamberlains, the collectors, and the artisans.
To them he gives a four-year-old cow that has miscarried.
While they cook it, they remain seated, delighting in it and keeping watch.
Then, in the morning, while sipping water for rinsing, they snap their fingers at the gold.
The son of a woman married while her husband was still living takes those [spoons].

Then they worship the rising sun with the formula: "Homage to the seer, homage to the overseer, homage to the observer; homage to the proclaimer, homage to the one who proclaims nearby, homage to the one who proclaims after; homage to the hearer, homage to the one who hears nearby, homage to the one who hears after; homage to the existent, homage to the non-existent; homage to the born, homage to the one about to be born; homage to the past, homage to the future. Then he offers the *vaiśvadevī* *sāṃgrahaṇī* oblation.
That well-known sacrifice is completed.
While the Adhvaryu is occupied here, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having cooked the *brahmaudana* in the fourfold waters, pours clarified butter over it and sets it aside toward the north.
Then, having washed this vessel and spread a base of ghee within it, he places that washed silver plate into it.
(15.3:207.6) Having made a vessel for pouring ghee and having brought a large quantity of clarified butter, he raises it from that [spot] as if not striking it.
(15.3:207.7) Then, on top of it, he places a washed golden plate.

(15.3:207.8) Then, having seated the great officiating priests to the north, each in his respective direction, and having caused them to sip water in succession, he pushes this [gold plate] toward them while touching the ground, as if without breaking the connection.

He said, "May the Brahmins and the kings bring me safely to completion by means of this sacrificial horse, for the sake of the supremacy of the Brahman. To him, the others replied, "So be it; we shall bring you safely to completion by means of this sacrificial horse, for the sake of the supremacy of the Brahman.
Then they agreed with him regarding that supremacy of the Brahman.
(15.4:208.1) Then he instructs them: "Having each eaten once, hold [the portions] without touching them.
(15.4:208.2) Then, having soaked the two cords in this vessel for pouring ghee, he hands it to the attendant.
(15.4:208.3) Having eaten a second time, they praise him, saying: "Your Brahmaudana has been successfully prepared."
To them he gives four thousand gold coins (*niṣka*s), as well as two plates, one of gold and one of silver.
At this point, those who are the consecrators of the *kṣatriya* consecrate the *adhvaryu*.
He says: "O Brahmins and kings, the *adhvaryu* shall be king for these two years; serve him! Whoever does not serve him, they shall deprive him of all his property."
(15.4:208.8) Now, for these two years the Adhvaryu is the king;
they call the other the sacrificer.
(15.4:208.9) He says: "O Brahman, I shall bind the horse fit for sacrifice for the gods and for Prajāpati; may I prosper through it."
"Bind it! the other replies; "May you prosper through this for the gods and Prajāpati."
(15.5:208.12) Then he takes up the cord with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee.
(15.5:208.13) Having taken it, he consecrates it with: "They have grasped this cord of Order."

With that [rope] he binds the horse, [saying]: "Thou art a binder; thou art the world; thou art the restrainer; thou art the supporter. Go to Agni Vaiśvānara, who is far-extending, consecrated by Svāhā upon the earth! Thou art the restrainer, the ruler; thou art the restrainer, the controller; thou art the supporter, the sustainer.
In this very same manner, he takes up a second rope and with it binds the horse in the same way.
(15.5:208.17) He fills in along the back of the horse.
(15.5:208.18) At this time, the son of the younger sister and the son of the woman who was given as a supplementary gift both place a dog against two dog-tethers.
(15.5:208.19) Then this son of a harlot, having wrapped his left knee with a piece of old cloth, stands behind the dog with a pestle made of Sidhraka wood.
(15.5:209.1) Then the Adhvaryu proceeds from the east together with a hundred princes of the royal lineage who are entitled to a couch.
(15.5:209.3) The Brahman proceeds from the south together with a hundred fierce men who are not kings.
(15.5:209.3) The Hotṛ proceeds from the west together with a hundred charioteers and village leaders.
To the north, the Udgātṛ stands together with a hundred attendants, both charioteers and collectors; in the middle are the horse and the dog;
then they proceed toward the southern pool.

(15.5:209.5) With the three sections beginning, "Heaven is your back," "The steed has stepped forth with his strides," and "The steed has stepped up," they cause the horse to run over [the altar] as far as the chest. (15.5:209.7) Standing to the east facing west, the Adhvaryu sprinkles it, saying: "Having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, may the king slay Vṛtra.
Following that sprinkling, one hundred princes entitled to the couch sprinkle it.

The Brahman priest, standing to the south facing north, sprinkles [the horse] with the formula: "Having sacrificed with this pure horse, may the king be unassailable. Following that sprinkling, one hundred fierce non-kings sprinkle it.

The Hotṛ, standing behind and facing east, sprinkles [the horse] with the formula: "Having sacrificed with this pure horse, may this king [be] for this people possessing much cattle, much horses, much goats and sheep, much rice and barley, much beans and sesame, much gold, much elephants, and [much] male and female slaves."
"May she be possessed of many male slaves, possessed of wealth, possessed of nourishment, possessed of abundant increase of riches, and possessed of all kinds of great wealth—may she be a queen!
Thus [he says]; following this, they sprinkle her, and a hundred charioteers and village headmen sprinkle her.
Standing to the north of the *udgātṛ* and facing south, he sprinkles [the horse] with the mantra: "Having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, may the king attain a full lifespan.
Following that sprinkling, a hundred attendants (*kṣattṛ*s) and charioteers (*saṃgrahītṛ*s) sprinkle it, according to the Brāhmaṇa passage: "They sprinkle the horse from all directions."
(15.5:209.19) Now, this son of a harlot has been instructed for him thus: "When I have bound you, then you shall strike the dog.
(15.5:210.1) Having been bound, this son of a harlot strikes the dog with a pestle made of Sidhraka wood.
(15.5:210.2) He consecrates it right there with the following mantra.

“He who seeks to strike down the courser—Varuṇa attacks him,” [he says]. Having placed that [stone] beneath the horse's feet, he causes it to float away toward the south with the words: “Away, O mortal! Away, O dog! Then the Brahman or the sacrificer takes his hand, saying: “I and you, O slayer of Vṛtra, have come together for the sake of gains. Even the ill-wisher, O wielder of the stone, shall acknowledge us; O Hero, Indra’s gifts are auspicious.”
At this point, he fastens this bundle of reeds at both ends with two cords of muñja grass;
it is then bound together with a branch of cane.
By means of this, one hundred princes of the royal lineage are separated.

Following their separation, the other two [groups] take one hundred [bricks] at one end and two at the other end. Then he instructs them: "With this eṣīka-reed support, as if lifting it up, you should cause the horse to gallop from the east toward the west with a wave."

While the chariot is being driven forward, the Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite: "O Indra, by your wisdom you have prevailed upon the earth; your greatness has pervaded the realms. For with your own power you have slain Vṛtra; no enemy has found the limit against you in battle.
Then, having wrapped it up, he causes it to float away toward the south.

(15.6:210.16) Then, having turned this horse clockwise, he leads it to the hall with [the verse]: "When the wind went to the waters, the beloved body of Indra—O singer, by this path, turn this horse back for us.
(15.6:211.1) The Adhvaryu follows it with the preceding *stokīyā* verses: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! with this section, repeating the invocation again and again until its drops cease.

(15.6:211.3) Then, having stationed this horse facing east in front of the hall and having entered [the sacrificial ground], he offers the oblations for the horse dedicated to Savitṛ: "To Agni, svāhā! To Vāyu, svāhā!"—thus seven times. (15.6:211.5) Then, in the morning, he offers a cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Savitṛ. Having set it down, he offers the preliminary portions: "To Agni, svāhā! Svāhā to Indra and Agni!"—thus five times.
Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he performs eighty-three oblations of the horse’s behaviors with the formulas: “To the sound *īm*, svāhā! To that which has been uttered as *īm*, svāhā!
He performs thirteen oblations of the gallops before they have been completed with the formulas: “To the coming, svāhā! To the departure, svāhā! That well-known sacrifice then concludes.
Then, having turned this horse clockwise and having led it into the hall through the eastern door, he stations it facing east within the sacrificial ground and says:
Regarding this, they say: "At every step, indeed, the Adhvaryu offers an oblation for the sacrificial horse. We shall offer it right here so that for us there will be an offering at every step.

For its feet, he offers the *dhṛti* oblations, either diagonally or in a circumambulatory manner: "Here is support, svāhā! Here is separation, svāhā! Here is delight, svāhā! Here is rejoicing, svāhā! Thus.

(15.7:211.15) Then, having made him step forward toward the east, he sprinkles him: with "For Prajāpati thee," from the front; with "For Indra and Agni thee," from the south; with "For Vāyu thee," from the back; with "For the Viśve Devas thee," from the north; with "For the gods thee," from below; and with "For all the gods thee," from above.

(15.7:211.18) Then he sprinkles it with a further sprinkling: "For cultivation thee! For security thee! For wealth thee! For prosperity thee! For the earth thee! For the intermediate region thee! For the sky thee! For the existent thee! For the non-existent thee! For the waters thee! For the plants thee! For all beings thee! (15.7:212.1) Then he offers its forms: "To the one with white spots, svāhā! To the one with spotted thighs, svāhā! To the black one, svāhā! To the white one, svāhā!"—with these two sections.

(15.7:212.3) Then, having risen after him, he murmurs the names of horses into his right ear: "Abundant through thy mother, powerful through thy father; thou art a horse, thou art a steed, thou art a racer, thou art a man, thou art a runner, thou art a courser, thou art a prize-winner, thou art a bull, thou art one whose mind is directed toward men, thy name is 'the Swift'.
(15.7:212.5) Then he pays homage to it with: "Follow the flight of the Ādityas!"

(15.7:212.6) Then he releases it from the two reins with the formula: "Thou art the earth; for the past thee, for the present thee, for the future thee, for that which is to be thee, for all beings thee.

(15.7:212.7) Then he entrusts it to the deities: "O gods, guardians of the quarters, protect this horse, consecrated for sacrifice, for the gods. (15.7:212.9) At this point, they release for him these unlimited draught-animals, castrated and marked.
Then these four hundred guardians, having put on their armor and spread out their shields, question him just as they would for battle;
to them he gives leave to eat cooked food.
He said, "O Brahmins and kings, do not speak ill of him whose cooked food these shall carry away, even if he has not been authorized by me.
He said, "O Brahmins and kings, drive your vehicles outside the sacrificial ground! Whosoever is joined with mares, they shall seize his entire property.
Thus, they drove their vehicles outside the sacrificial ground.
They move about with stallions and mules,
but not with mares nor with female mules.
Then these two lute-singers take hold of them from behind.
(15.8:213.1) Then this Brahmin, the lute-player, sings: “Thus you gave,” “Thus you sacrificed,” “Thus you cooked”—in this way, three mixed verses.
(15.8:213.3) There is freedom of movement for the horse; they guard him both from bathing and from being ridden.
(15.8:213.4) Now, if a calamity befalls the horse, there is an offering on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, an offering on eight potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Pūṣan, and a pap for Rudra.
(15.8:213.5) And if he does not find it, there is an offering on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara at a deer’s burrow.
(15.8:213.7) And if it is joined by mares, there is an offering on eight potsherds for Agni Aṃhomuc, milk for Sūrya, and a portion of clarified butter for Vāyu.
If it blows fiercely, it belongs to Rudra;
if there is a flow, it belongs to Pūṣan;
if it is in the waters, it belongs to Varuṇa.
(15.8:213.9) If he is one-eyed, it belongs to Sūrya.
(15.8:213.10) Whichever of these misfortunes he encounters, the expiation is performed only once.
Then he releases that one among his excellent horses which is the best. Thereafter, he proceeds with the two reins;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the handing over.
Having released the horse, they immolate the animals dedicated to the Viśvedevas; the oblations for the Viśvedevas follow their animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśa*), or rather,
the animal-cake offerings themselves become the oblations for the Viśvedevas.
The middle *Sāvitrī* follows them; the animal sacrifices conclude in the established manner.
Then, in the afternoon, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ Āsavitṛ.
That well-known sacrifice is completed.
Then, having performed the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices, he returns to the established procedure.
Then these two lute-players take up their positions.
Then this royal kṣatriya, accompanied by a lute-singer, sings: "Thus you were clothed in skins," "Thus you fought," "Thus you slew that battle. These are the three mixed verses.
When the morning *agnihotra* has been offered, the Brāhmaṇa lute-singer sings; when the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, the Rājanya sings. In this very manner, the two sing for a year.
(15.9:214.7) Then, in the morning, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Savitṛ.
(15.9:214.8) Having placed it down, he makes offerings to the shares [of the gods] in front;
before the sun has risen, he offers the *dhṛti* oblations and he offers the *pradrāva* oblations.
That well-known sacrifice is completed.
Then, at midday, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Savitṛ Prasavitṛ; that well-known sacrifice is completed.
(15.9:214.11) Then, in the afternoon, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ Āsavitṛ; that sacrifice concludes in the established manner.
(15.9:214.13) Then, on the following day, he begins with the [oblations] dedicated to Savitṛ.
In this very manner, performing the Sāvitrī offerings day by day, the sacrificer proceeds for four months—performing at will an *iṣṭi*, at will a *paśubandha*, and at will the *yavāgrayaṇa*.
Then, when the four months have elapsed, having performed the Sāvitrī sacrifice, they immolate the animals for the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings.
The Varuṇapraghāsa oblations follow those animal-cake offerings;
indeed, for these [offerings], the Varuṇapraghāsa oblations themselves become the animal-cakes.
The middle Sāvitrī follows them.
The animal sacrifices conclude according to the established procedure.
Then, in the afternoon, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ Āsavitr; that sacrifice concludes according to the established procedure.
Then, having performed the Full-moon sacrifice and the Vaimṛdha sacrifice, he concludes the rite in the established manner. Then, on the following day, he begins with the Sāvitra offerings.

Performing the sacrifices in this very same way day after day with the Sāvitra offerings, the sacrificer passes the remaining four months—whether by means of an *iṣṭi*, or a *paśubandha*, or the *śyāmākāgrayaṇa* as desired.
Then, when four months have elapsed, on the fast-day of the full moon, he immolates an animal dedicated to Agni Ānīkavat. The oblation for Agni Ānīkavat follows the sacrificial cake of that animal;
indeed, his sacrificial cake belongs to Agni Ānīkavat.
The first *sāvitrī* follows that; the animal sacrifice is concluded in the established manner. Then, at midday, he immolates the *saṃtapana* animal.
The *sāṃtapana* oblation follows his animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*). Indeed, his animal-cake becomes the *saṃtapana*. The middle *sāvitrī* verse follows that.
The animal sacrifice is completed in the prescribed manner.
Then, in the afternoon, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ Āsavitṛ;
that well-known iṣṭi is completed.
Then, in the evening, he performs the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice;
then, in the latter part of the night, he performs the Pūrṇadarvya offering;
then, in the morning, he immolates the Kraiḍina animal victim.
The oblation for Kriḍin follows the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) of that [sacrifice].
Or rather, the animal-cake of this [sacrifice] belongs to Kriḍin;
the first offering to Savitṛ follows it.
The animal sacrifice concludes in the established manner.
Then, at midday, they immolate the animals for the Sākamedha offerings.
The great oblations follow those animal-cake offerings;
indeed, for these [sacrifices], the great oblations themselves become the animal-cake offerings.
The middle Sāvitrī follows them.
The animal sacrifices are concluded as established.
Then, in the afternoon, he proceeds with the Pitṛyajña;
having performed the Pitṛyajña, he proceeds with the Traiyambaka offerings.
Having performed the Traiyambaka offerings, he immolates an animal dedicated to Āditya. The oblation for Āditya follows its animal-cake offering (paśupuroḍāśa).
Indeed, the animal-cake offering for this [animal] belongs to Āditya.

The excellent *sāvitrī* follows that; the animal sacrifice concludes in the established manner. Then, having performed the *paurṇamāsa* and *vaimṛdha* sacrifices, he returns in the established manner.
Then, when the next day has dawned, he begins with the *sāvitrī* oblations.

Performing in this very manner day after day with the *sāvitrī* oblations, he passes three and a half months; at his will, he may perform an *iṣṭi*, at his will a *paśubandha*, or at his will the *vrīhyāgrayaṇa*.

Then, on the day of the fast (*upavasatha*) of the new moon, having performed the *sāvitrī-iṣṭi*, having offered the *agnikāni* and *sāvitrāṇi* oblations, and having gathered the fire-pans (*ukhā*) and the heads of the sacrificial animals, he immolates the animal dedicated to Vāyu.
For that [sacrifice], a hornless he-goat dedicated to Prajāpati is to be offered.
Having performed the ritual with the omenta of those two in the established manner, he offers the two animal-cake oblations (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
The central *Sāvitrī* verse follows those two.
The two animal sacrifices conclude in the established manner.
Then, in the afternoon, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ Āsavitṛ; that sacrifice concludes in the established manner.
Then, when the next day has dawned, he begins with the *sāvitrī* offerings.

In this very manner, performing the *sāvitrī* offerings day after day, the sacrificer proceeds through this half-month—either by means of an *iṣṭi* sacrifice or, at his will, by means of an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*).
Then, when four months have elapsed, having performed the *sāvitrī-iṣṭi*, [he continues].
They immolate the animals for the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice; the oblations of the Śunāsīrīya follow their animal-cake offerings, or rather,
the animal-cake offerings themselves become the Śunāsīrīya oblations.
The middle *Sāvitrī* follows them; the animal sacrifices conclude in the established manner.
Then, in the afternoon, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ Āsavitṛ.
That Prasiddheṣṭi comes to a conclusion.

Then, having performed the Full-moon sacrifice and the Vaimṛdha sacrifice, he sits down in the sacrificer’s place and, with a three-striped porcupine quill and a razor of red iron, he shaves the hair on his head and has it shaved all around—first on the front, then on the south, then on the west, then on the north, and finally on top.
The Cāturmāsya animal sacrifices come to a conclusion; the Sāvitra offerings come to a conclusion.
(15.13:217.9) Then they tie the horse in the stable.
(15.13:217.9) Having brought it from the bathing place and purified it, he performs the Agni-dīkṣaṇīyā offering consisting of three oblations.
(15.13:217.10) Of that [offering], as many [elements] are omitted as there are for the Dīkṣaṇīyā.

(15.13:217.11) Then the Adhvaryu, having turned to the right and hastened westward, having performed the offerings for the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*), having gone eastward and replenished the *dhruvā* ladle, offers three prior Vaiśvadeva oblations with: "Svāhā to the fire, to that which has been kindled, svāhā!

(15.13:217.13) Then he offers seven oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with: "To the out-breath, svāhā! To the diffused breath, svāhā! (15.13:217.14) He offers the twenty-one-fold initiation oblation with: "To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā!"

He offers five oblations for the consecration of the sacrifice (*adhvara-dīkṣā*): "Six are the consecrations of Agni, one is the consecration of the seasons (*ṛtu-dīkṣā*), [performed] by the action of the gods, O Bhuvas. He sacrifices with this offering for seven days.
Thus, he offers three *vaiśvadeva* oblations each time, and each subsequent one corresponds to a subsequent consecration of the seasons.
(15.13:217.19) On the two final days, he offers the seasonal consecration oblations with the verses "The Great One" and "Well-Protecting.
(15.13:217.19) On this very day he undergoes consecration;
(15.13:218.1) for a year he carries the fire in the pan.
There are twelve *upasads*. At this point, these subjects settle around him according to the traditional injunction:
carpenters, chariot-makers, mat-makers, potters, and two kinds of smiths—those who work with nails being the seventh. These craftsmen draw near to him ever more closely.
(15.13:218.4) Then he gives instructions to the carpenters regarding these [chariots].

(15.14:218.5) "Cut one hundred and one *bilva* logs, bound with wood; having made them into *pravakala* pieces, pile the fire-altar. Cut twenty-one sacrificial posts: twenty-one cubits long for the central post of *rājjudāla* wood, two flanking posts of *pautudrava* wood, six of *bilva*, six of *khadira*, six of *pālāśa*, a *pālāśa* resting-post (*upaśaya*), a *pālāśa* post for the *pātnīvata* offering, a *pālāśa* wide post, and wooden vessels of a single type."

"Make thirty-six ladles with long handles, thirty-six stirring-sticks with long handles, four or eight *indrāṇasas*, and four wheels with large hubs that are equal in size to the tops of the sacrificial posts; make an unlimited number of ascending platforms and kitchens; and make one mat of reeds for the horse to lie upon.
