Then he instructs the chariot-makers: "Construct a chariot for yourself; construct an unlimited number of chariots."

(15.14:219.1) Then he instructs these leather-workers: "Prepare an unlimited amount of leather. (15.14:219.2) Then he instructs these potters: "Make bricks for a fire-altar of twenty-one types; make three large jars; cook these—the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal—along with their limbs; and make an unlimited number of cooking-pots."

(15.15:219.6) Then he instructs these objects made of black iron: "Make an arrow, a *sittima*, an *aṅkopa*, a black one with a black hilt, and a golden one with a golden hilt; four [arrows] of black iron with bronze hilts, four of bronze with black-iron hilts, thirty-six golden ones with silver hilts, thirty-six silver ones with golden hilts, and three hundred and thirty-three golden needles, and three hundred..."
"Make thirty-three [spoons] of silver, three hundred and thirty-three of lead, and one water-pot of black iron for the cooking of the horse's fat."

(15.15:219.13) Then he gives instructions to the goldsmiths: "Make more than a hundred *niṣkas* weighing a hundred *palas* each; make two vessels for the *mahiman* cups out of gold and silver; make single-layered vessels of gold; make as many golden *upaśayas* as there are wives; make as many golden *kumbakurīras* with silver knots or silver [vessels] with golden knots as there are wives; [make] silver pegs or silver [objects]."

"Or [make] golden pegs; as many as there are wives, so many golden water-pots (kamaṇḍalu) with silver bands, or silver ones with golden bands; make one golden fan (vidhavana); make three golden whisks (dhavitra) with silver handles, or silver ones with golden handles; make a thousand golden glass-beads (kāca), a thousand silver ones, and a thousand from the sea; [make] a golden mattress (kaśipu), a golden six-sided seat (ṣaḍbīśa), and a golden tether (saṃdāna). Thus [he said].
(15.16:220.6) Then he instructs those [grains] prepared on the nails: "Make them in unlimited groups of eight.

(15.16:220.6) Now, these other things are prepared for him: a hundred skins of ghee, a hundred skins of honey, a hundred skins of rice, a hundred skins of flattened grains (*pṛthuka*), a hundred skins of parched grain (*lāja*), a hundred skins of groats (*karambha*), a hundred skins of fried grains (*dhānā*), a hundred skins of barley meal (*saktu*), a hundred skins of lentils (*masūrī*), and a hundred skins of millet (*priyaṅgu*) grains.
(15.16:220.10) Now, twenty-one Pratiprasthātṛs are instructed for him, making himself the twenty-second.
(15.16:220.11) They collect animals from various regions; they recognize those that are similar in form and those that are dissimilar.

(15.16:220.12) They guard the domestic animals in the villages, the wild animals in the forest, the mountain-dwellers on the mountains, the river-dwellers in the rivers, the birds in cages, and the reptiles in jars.
The pouring together [of the grains] is well known.
Then he proceeds with the introductory offering;
having proceeded with the introductory offering, he proceeds with the footprint.
Having walked with a footstep upon a bull's hide and having purchased the King Soma for a thousand [cows], he brings him forward and performs the guest-offering (*ātithya*).
Having performed the guest-offering, he then proceeds day by day with the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites;
this indeed is the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
The fire is established in twenty-one forms;
its *sadas* has twenty-one roofs.
Then he leads forward the *āhavanīya* fire.
Having led forward the Āhavanīya fire, he erects the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds.
Having erected the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds, he leads forward Agni and Soma.
Having led forward Agni and Soma, he raises the sacrificial post according to the procedure for the post.
Having set aside the Agniṣṭha post made of Rājjudāla wood and provided with a *svaru*, he dedicates the animal victim for Agni and Soma.
Having performed the well-known procedure with its omentum, he takes the Vasatīvarī waters;
then he offers the sacrificial cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) belonging to that animal.

Eight *devasū* oblations follow that [main sacrifice], namely those beginning with "To Agni Gṛhapati. And this ten-oblation *iṣṭi* beginning with "To Agni Gāyatra" follows; for it, these become the *yājyā*s and *puronuvākyā*s: "The kindling-stick of the quarters, may it find light for us through our hope.
The animal-cake offerings conclude with the *iḍā*.
The animal sacrifice ends with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings;
some say it ends with the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*).
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters, they set aside the milks and observe the fast.
(15.17:221.13) Now, therefore, they wake up at the very dead of night.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
He applies [the formulas] over the enclosing sticks: "Who yokes you? Let him yoke you. Six times over the middle stick, six times over the southern one, and five times over the northern one.
Then, having brought down the King [Soma], he begins the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*).
When the morning litany has been concluded, he goes toward the waters;
he emerges from the waters.
He enters upon the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
The pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner;
the cups are drawn in the established manner.
The ritual procedure up to the *pavamāna* [laud] is the same.
When he intends to heat the *pavamāna* [vessel], he requests sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and a hundred-pala weight of gold.
Then he says: "O Udgātṛ, may this sacrificial grass and this hundred-pala weight of gold cause my horse to sing the *udgītha*."

They take hold of the horse's tail [with the words]: "O steed, may Agni be your yoke-fellow; I take hold of you; convey me safely across. O steed, may Vāyu be your yoke-fellow; I take hold of you; convey me safely across. O steed, may Āditya be your yoke-fellow; I take hold of you; convey me safely across.
Then they creep toward the *pavamāna* [laud] facing north. To the north, this enclosure for the mares stands, having been raised and surrounded.
They explain this:
"The mares neigh toward the stallion;
the stallion neighs toward the mares."
The horse is the *udgītha*;
therefore, they utter auspicious words concerning it.

"Upward has this sacrificial horse risen! Life has risen upward! Prosperity has risen upward! Spiritual luster has risen upward! This has risen upward! This has risen upward!"—thus do auspicious voices cry out.
They release the mares;
they tether the horse in the stable.
At this point, they scatter food for him intended for both this world and the next.
Then he says: "O Udgātṛ, [I give] to you a hundred cows and a hundred palas; sing the *udgītha* for me.
For him, there are four *bahiṣpavamāna* chants.
There are eight *ājya* chants each;
the midday *pavamāna* consists of twelve verses; and the *pṛṣṭha* chants consist of sixteen verses.
The Ārbhava Pavamāna has twenty-one verses; the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the Caturviṃśa;
they call that the Catuṣṭoma.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup.
Having taken the Āśvina cup and having taken eleven cords, he approaches the sacrificial post.
Having set aside the Svaru-splintered Rājjudāla post standing nearest the fire, he dedicates the animals of the eleven-fold set.
Having performed the ritual with their omenta in the established manner, they proceed to the morning pressing; that concludes in the regular way. They proceed to the midday pressing.
The pressing of the Soma is well-known;
the cups are drawn in the established manner;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the offerings for the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having offered the *dākṣiṇā* oblations, he offers eight *saṃvarga* oblations with the formula: "May the sacrifice come hither.
He gives away a third of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having offered the *vaiśvakarmaṇa* oblations, he offers nine *paryāpti* oblations with the formula: "The past, the present, the future."
(15.18:223.7) There is no consecration by fire here.
(15.18:223.7) He effects the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice. (15.18:223.7) The midday pressing concludes in a straightforward manner.
They proceed to the third pressing.
Having performed the rite with the Āditya cup in the established manner, he draws the Āgrayaṇa cup;
the ritual procedure up to the Pavamāna chant is the same.
Having performed the Pavamāna rite, he proceeds with the animal offerings in their own place.

For these, there are separate *manotā* hymns, separate deities, separate touchings, and separate *vasāhoma* offerings; the *vanaspati* offering is common, as is the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering accompanied by the *praiṣa* call, the *iḍā* portion is common, and the directions are common.
Some say the directions are separate.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
This Agniṣṭoma, which consists of four stomas, concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings at the very moment it is being performed.
(15.19:223.16) Then, these hundred ox-hides are spread out for him, joined along the wings to the north of the northern hip.
(15.19:223.17) Then, having removed twenty or twenty-four of those butter-skins, they mix the foods with the others.
(15.19:223.18) Then, having piled twenty or twenty-four of those wood-covered [skins] in the middle of the fire-altar, they cut up the others and scatter them about.
He extends this square city of the gods over the inner self.
Alternatively, he constructs wings and a tail so that it may be level with the tips of the sacrificial posts; then, having raised it up, they enclose it, making its door face the north.
They bring these *indrāṇasā* vessels; four are placed toward the cardinal directions and the others in the intermediate directions, provided there are eight of them.
Of these, four persons mount each one, while ten others are the performers of the night-rites.
Then they bring clarified butter for them in pots, and food with the eighth [portion].

Then the Adhvaryu takes up the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) with a long handle and the large ladle (*darvī*) with a long handle. Twenty-one Pratiprasthātṛs take them up—ten others being the night-ritual officiants.
Then the Adhvaryu, having dipped the *sruva* into the clarified butter (*ājya*), offers the three first Vaiśvadeva oblations.

"Oblation to the one intent on the vow, oblation to the one who has undertaken the vow!"—with these words they offer the clarified butter with *sruva*-ladles; "Oblation to the toothed," with these words they offer the foods with *darvi*-spoons; "Oblation to the toothless.
In this very manner they recite this section (*anuvāka*); when they reach the end of this section, he then interposes it with this [next] section.
(15.20:224.14) First the *stokīyā* verses, then this section;

(15.20:224.14) then this section, then the subsequent *stokīyā* verses; then this section, then the twenty-one-fold initiation; then this section, then the seasonal initiations; then this section, then the *sāvitra* formulas for the horse; then this section.
(15.20:225.1) Thus, in this very manner, these sections [are recited] with this very section.

When they reach the end of these sections (anuvākas), they then proceed to these [subsequent] sections: those dedicated to the Viśvedevas and the limbs of the horse; two [sections] on the forms of the horse, the herbs, and the trees; two [sections] on the joints of water and the names [of the parts]; and one [section] on the confluence. The oblation of the khārī has been explained. They [proceed] through these sections in this very manner, by means of this very section.
When they reach the end of these sections, they then turn back to those same sections.
"OṂ *ekasmai* svāhā! OṂ *dvābhyām* svāhā!"—with these words, they offer these very sections (*anuvāka*) again and again, repeating the introductory invocation with this same section.
Then, at the time of carrying around the *vasatīvarī* waters, they run toward them.
When the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around and the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, they run back again.
In this very manner, offering oblations with this same *anuvāka* while repeatedly approaching them, they complete these *anuvākas*.
Indeed, these are called "the full lifespans of the horse."
"Some say these are for completion, for with these they offer throughout the entire night.
Then, as the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ are about to commence the Prātaranuvāka, they both step down; two others who have been performing the rites of the night step forward."
Then, having brought down the King [Soma], he begins the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*).
When the morning litany has been concluded, he goes toward the waters;
he emerges from the waters.
He enters upon the Ukthya rite;
the ritual procedure up to the Upāṃśu offering is the same.

Intending to offer the Upāṃśu cup, having run up to the *indrāṇasa* vessel, he offers four spoonfuls with the formulas: "Svāhā to Uṣas! Svāhā to the Dawn! Svāhā to her as she is about to rise! Svāhā to her as she rises!"
The pressing is well-known;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the Antaryāma cup.
When about to offer the Antaryāma, having run over the *indrāṇasa* vessel, he offers four spoonfuls with the formulas: "Svāhā to the risen one! Svāhā to heaven! Svāhā to the world! Svāhā to all!"
When the sun has risen at this point, those performing the nocturnal rites cease their work;
they dismantle the enclosures and turn back the *indrāṇasas*.
(15.22:226.4) The cups are drawn with golden vessels as is well known.
(15.22:226.5) The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āgrayaṇa cup.
Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he draws two Mahiman cups with gold and silver vessels, [reciting]: "He who breathes," and "He who gives himself."
(15.22:226.7) Then he draws the Ukthya cup.
(15.22:226.7) The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup.
Having drawn the Āśvina cup and having taken twenty-four cords, they proceed toward the sacrificial posts; four other assistants take four cords each.
Having set aside the Svarvat post made of Rājjudāla wood as the one standing nearest the fire, he first raises the Upasthāvāna post made of Pūtudru wood to the south of it.

(15.23:226.12) Then follows the subsequent part: (15.23:226.12) three posts of *bilva* wood to the south, three to the north; three of *khadira* wood to the south, three to the north; three of *pālāśa* wood to the south, three to the north.
(15.23:226.14) At this point, he silently places that *pālāśa* resting-post to the south.

Having set out the sacrificial posts provided with wooden rings, the Adhvaryu then dedicates these three animals belonging to Prajāpati at the post standing nearest the fire: a horse, a hornless goat, and a gayal.

Then he dedicates the animals bound to the flanks: one marked with black spots on the forehead for Agni and Indra, one for Indra and Pūṣan, one for Pūṣan, two for Agni with black necks, two for Tvaṣṭṛ with hairy thighs, two for Bṛhaspati with white backs, one speckled-bellied for Dhātṛ, and a white-footed ram for Sūrya.
(15.23:226.18) Then the Adhvaryu dedicates [the victims] at the post standing nearest the fire with eleven [animals], beginning: "To Agni Anīkavant, a red-marked ox.
(15.23:227.1) Then the Adhvaryu dedicates [the victims] at the post standing nearest the fire with pairs, beginning: "To Soma Svarāj, two oxen that draw carts.
(15.23:227.2) Then the Adhvaryu dedicates eleven wild animals at the post standing nearest the fire, beginning: "To Indra Rājā, a boar."
This very [set] consists of sixty animals at the central post.
Then there are the ten sections of eighteen [animals each], beginning with "The ruddy one, the smoke-colored ruddy one.
Of these, they station the first nine on the southern posts, and the latter nine on the northern posts.
The offerings to Agni and Indra are the principal ones for those on the south; those to Indra and Sūrya are for those on the north.
Now, [the offering] to Mayu, the son of Prajāpati—these are the ten sections of ten [offerings] each.
Of these, they present five at a time upon the southern sacrificial posts, and the remaining five upon the northern ones.
The animals for Soma and Pūṣan are the foremost among those on the south side; those for Indra and Pūṣan are the foremost among those on the north side.
Then, upon this *upaśaya* (the spare animal), he dedicates with his mind alone whichever person he hates;
if, however, he does not hate anyone, he assigns it [to the animal] saying, "A mole is your victim."
At this time, he offers a spoonful of oblation into the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: “Svāhā to the one who has been brought forward!”

(15.24:227.13) Then he yokes this horse to his own chariot in front of the sacrificial posts with the verse: "They yoke the ruddy, bright one who moves around those who stand still. (15.24:227.14) Then he strokes its back with the verse: "The luminous realms shine in heaven. (15.24:227.15) In this very same manner, he yokes the subsequent animal to the yoke.
In this very manner, he fastens the side-horse to the north of that [chariot].
He strokes the backs of those two [horses] with the verse: "They yoke his two beloved bay steeds to the chariot on both sides, the ruddy, bold ones that carry the hero.
Then, with the words, "Making a signal for the signalless," he attaches the banner.

(15.24:228.2) Then he equips the sacrificer with the armor-binding verses, using fourteen [verses] according to their form, beginning with: "Like the face of a cloud... (15.24:228.3). Then he pays homage to the chariot with three verses in their proper meter, beginning with: "O Lord of the Forest, may you be firm-limbed... (15.24:228.5). Then he causes the drum to resound with three verses in their proper meter, beginning with: "Make the earth and the sky resound... (15.24:228.5).
Then he proceeds toward the southern lake with three sections: "The sky is your back," "The steed has stepped across with his strides," and "The steed has stepped forth.
They drive the horses toward the horses' chests.

Then, having turned this chariot clockwise, he brings it to the hall with [the verses]: "As the wind went to the waters, the beloved body of Indra; O singer, by this path bring back to us this horse again."
The Adhvaryu follows them with the subsequent *stokīyā* verses: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā!"—with this section, repeating the introductory call again and again until these drops cease.
Then, having unyoked this horse from its own chariot in front of the sacrificial posts and having bound it with a golden halter, they lead it twice around to the Adhvaryu’s dwelling.
Then the Mahiṣī, the Vāvātā, and the Parivṛktī approach the horse, bringing for him perfumes, aromatic powders, and amulets.

(15.24:228.15) That part of it which is in front of the chest, the chief queen anoints with [ointment] from the wood of the *pūtudru* tree while the wives of the deputies are present, saying: "May the Vasus anoint you with the Gāyatrī metre.
(15.24:228.17) Then that part which is behind the chest as far as the navel, the favorite wife anoints, saying: "May the Rudras anoint you with the Triṣṭubh metre."

(15.25:228.19) With *gulgulu* resin, he anoints [the horse] together with the wives of those who are not kings. Then, that part which is behind the navel up to the tail, the *parivṛktī* anoints with the words: "May the Ādityas anoint you with the Jagatī metre! with the juice of the *musta* grass, together with the wives of the charioteers, the village headmen, the *kṣattṛ*s, and the *saṃgrahītṛ*s.
(15.25:229.3) On those hairs of his which are in front of the back, the *mahiṣī* causes a thousand golden beads to be woven, with the word "Earth!", together with the wives of the deputies.

(15.25:229.4) Now, upon those hairs of the *vahasa* that flow westward, the favorite wife fastens a thousand glass beads (*kāca*) from silver, saying, "Bhuvaḥ," together with the wives of those who are not kings. (15.25:229.6) Then this discarded wife (*parivṛktī*) fastens a thousand glass beads from sea-foam upon her tail-hairs, saying, "Suvaḥ," together with the wives of the charioteers (*sūta*), the village headmen (*grāmaṇī*), the attendants (*kṣattṛ*), and the collectors (*saṃgrahītṛ*).
(15.25:229.8) The wives depart as they came.
Then the chief queen, the favorite, the discarded wife, and the slave-girl from the kitchen—these women scatter for him parched grains mixed with honey.

"Lājīñ chācīñ yaśo mamāṃ; for the sake of barley and for the sake of cattle, O gods, eat this food; eat this food, O Prajāpati!"—thus it is known: "Whosever food one eats, his offspring become prosperous.

Then, having released this horse from its tether, he proceeds with the fire-drilled (nirmanthya) fire according to the ritual procedure for the fire-drilled fire, having cast the oblation and offered the libation.

(15.26:229.14) Then the Adhvaryu binds the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal to the post standing nearest the fire. (15.26:229.15) Then he binds to it the animals for the flanks: a black-spotted one for Agni-Indra, one for Indra-Pūṣan, and one for Pūṣan—these three on the forehead.
Two black-necked ones for Agni he binds to the necks.
Two belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ with hairy thighs are for the two thighs;
two with white backs belonging to Bṛhaspati are for the back; one with a speckled belly belonging to Dhātṛ is for the belly.
(15.26:230.2) "A white-spotted ram for Sūrya, [and] a tail.
(15.26:230.3) Then the Adhvaryu binds [the animal] to the post standing nearest the fire with the formula: "For Agni Anīkavant, a red-marked ox.
(15.26:230.4) Then the Adhvaryu binds [the animals] to the post standing nearest the fire with the formula: "For Soma Svarāj, two oxen that draw carts."
(15.26:230.5) Then the Adhvaryu binds [the victim] right at the Agniṣṭha post, saying: "For King Indra, a wild boar!
(15.26:230.6) By this very act of binding, he follows through with all the forest animals, both those which he intends to release among the domestic animals and those that are wild.
(15.26:230.7) Then the Pratiprasthātṛs bind their victims on the south side.
Then the northern ones.
Then, having sprinkled this horse with the regular sprinkling, he sprinkles it with the additional sprinkling [with the verse]: "The seed was born.
He sprinkles the other animals with the regular sprinkling alone.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛs sprinkle the southern [posts],
then the northern ones;
then he causes this horse to smell the sprinkling waters in front of the sacrificial posts.

"Agni was the sacrificial animal; with him they sacrificed, and he won this world in which Agni dwells. That is your world; you shall win it. Now, smell [it]. Vāyu was the sacrificial animal; Āditya was the sacrificial animal. Thus [he says].

If he does not smell it, he causes him to smell it again: "Agni was the sacrificial animal; with him they sacrificed; he won this world in which Agni dwells. That is your world; therefore I shall exclude you from it if you do not smell it. Vāyu was the sacrificial animal... Āditya was the sacrificial animal. Thus [he says].

If he does not smell it, he makes him smell it again [with the words]: "Agni was the victim; with him they sacrificed; he won this world in which Agni dwells. That is your world; you shall win it if you smell it. Vāyu was the victim. Āditya was the victim.
At that time, he offers a spoonful into the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "To the one who has been seized, svāhā!"
(15.28:231.3) Then, taking a fuel-stick from the faggot, he says: "Recite for the fire as it is being kindled.
(15.28:231.4) He places the faggot [on the fire] and leaves one fuel-stick remaining.
(15.28:231.4) He fans [the fire] with the Veda. (15.28:231.4) When the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, he pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* spoon;
once it has been wiped clean, he pours the second [libation] with the two *sruk* ladles.
Then, without letting the two offering-ladles touch each other, he steps across toward the north and anoints with the *juhū* the horse, the hornless goat, and the *gomṛga*;
then the animals bound to the limbs (*paryaṅgya*);
then the others.
Then [he takes coals] from the southern [fire], then from the northern; then, having placed the two offering-ladles in their respective places, he chooses the *pravara*.
He chooses the officiating priests in the established manner;
the Hotṛ sits down;
he awaits the impulse.
(15.28:231.9) Having been urged, he takes the two offering-spoons, steps across, causes the announcement to be made, and says, "Prompt for the kindling-sticks!
(15.28:231.10) "Kindled, anointing the belly of the hymns"—these are the *apri* verses of the horse.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering. Saying "Prompt! Prompt!", he pours together [the butter] at the fourth and eighth [oblations], and at the eighth, he pours all of it together.
He retains the remnants of the *saṃsrāva* for the *svāhākṛti* offerings.
Having performed ten *prayāja* offerings and stepped across to the north, he asks for a golden arrow-head and a shaft.
Having anointed those two with clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle, he anoints the horse, the hornless goat, and the *gomṛga* with them.
(15.28:231.15) The animals tied to the sacrificial posts are bound with iron rings; the others with copper ones; those on the south with gold, and those on the north with silver.
(15.28:231.16) Then, having placed the two offering-ladles in their respective places, he says: "Recite for the fire being carried around!

(15.28:231.17) He continues with the constant formula for the carrying of fire around: "May the ram protect thee with cooked offerings; may the red-necked one with goats; may the *śalmali* tree [protect thee]!"

When these animals have been carried around the fire, they release two ewes, two cows for the Earth, two mares for the Quarters, two cows for the Earth, one cow for Vairāja, and one female human for the Earth; and for Indra the King, a boar—thus all the wild animals are released here.
Then, with the animals that have been carried around the fire, they proceed toward the north.
Among them, those belonging to Indra and Sūrya occupy the northernmost positions.
(15.28:232.4) Regarding the horse:
(15.28:232.4) the Adhvaryu takes hold of the horse itself with the two omentum-spits.
(15.28:232.5) The other assistants lead the others separately toward the north, one after another, without letting them touch each other.

(15.28:232.5) Then he asks for sacrificial grass (*barhis*), a hundred-pieces-of-gold ornament (*śatapala*), a skin (*kṛtti*), an upper garment (*adhīvāsa*), a mattress (*kaśipu*), and a linen cloth (*tārpya*).
(15.28:232.7) To the north, this [place] is strewn thickly with grass;
there he throws down for the horse as it is being slaughtered these five items: the sacrificial grass, the hundred-pieces-of-gold ornament, the skin, the upper garment, and the mattress.
While the victim is being slaughtered with a garment of fine cloth, the Prastotṛ priest stands behind it while reciting the Yāma Sāman;
he does so separately from the others.
Thereafter, they strike the other victims either toward the east or toward the north.
"Make them cry out; cause them to be quietened. Having said this, they return by the same way they came and sit down at the place where the speckled butter is kept.
Then the Hotṛ and the Brahman engage in the *brahmodya* (theological debate) between the sacrificial post and the Āhavanīya fire;
the Brahman stands to the south.
The Hotṛ stands to the north;
the Hotṛ asks the Brāhmaṇ.
"What was the first thought? What was the great bird? What was Piśaṅgilā? What was Pilippilā?
To him the other replied: "The sky was the first thought; the horse was the great bird; the night was Piśaṅgilā; the sheep was Pilippilā."

The other asks him: "Who indeed wanders alone? Who indeed is born again? What is the remedy for the cold? What is the great receptacle? The other replies to him: "The sun wanders alone; the moon is born again; fire is the remedy for the cold; the earth is the great receptacle."

The other asks him: "I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth; I ask you about the navel of the world; I ask you about the seed of the stallion; I ask you about the highest heaven of speech. The other replies to him: "They call the altar the furthest limit of the earth; they call the sacrifice the navel of the world; they call Soma the seed of the stallion; Brahman indeed is the highest heaven of speech."
They announce that the animals have been immolated. He offers the oblation for the immolated animals with the verse: "When the animals have uttered their cries...
Then he offers the seven oblations to the vital breaths: "To the out-breath, svāhā! To the diffused breath, svāhā! and so forth.

He offers thirty-six *aśvastomīya* oblations with [the verses]: "When you first cried out at birth," "May Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman [protect us]," "Those who look upon the horse as cooked," and "And indeed, of him as he runs, as he hastens.
Then they approach with [the call]: "O slaughterers, come near!"

He consecrates the animals as they are being released from the nooses with the mantra: “May Aditi release these nooses. Having fastened them separately with branches that do not fork, they cast them out toward this direction [the south] with the mantra: “I make him who acts as an enemy low; upon him whom we hate, I fasten the nooses.”
Then these wives go forth carrying golden water-vessels;
they proceed along the back of the horse, replenishing its vital breaths, and then follow the other animals in order.

(15.29:233.16) Then this chief queen, having cast off her hair and put on a garment, fanning herself with a golden fan, circumambulates the horse three times moving counter-clockwise, [reciting]: "You are protectors; may the protectors protect you. You, the beloved among the beloved, the most excellent among kinsmen. We invoke you, the lord of treasures, as a treasure among treasures—O my wealth! (15.29:234.1) Having circumambulated three times, she stands to the north together with the wives of the deputies.
In the same way, she stands together with the wives of the favorite queens.
In this manner, the discarded wife (*parivṛktī*) goes together with the wives of the charioteers, the village headmen, the attendants, and the collectors; the wives depart as they came.
Then, having adorned this horse with all its ornaments, they enclose it.
They make its door face the north.

Then, having adorned the queen with all her ornaments, the Adhvaryu leads her forward while she conceals herself and reproaches him, saying: "O Mother, O Ambālī, O Ambikā! No one leads me away; the horse sleeps. Having lain down to the north together with the horse, she places a cloth over his head.
The Adhvaryu covers them both with a garment made of *tārpya* wool, saying: "O fortunate ones, you who dwell in Kāmpīla, may you both be covered in the heavenly world.
Then the chief queen places her phallus in his lap, saying: "I have become pregnant; you have become pregnant. May we two together extend our four feet."

The Adhvaryu consecrates her with the formula, beginning with, “May the bull, the bestower of seed, bestow seed upon you,” and continuing up to, “He who struck down the destroyer of the herd at their dark mark.
Then the wife reproaches him.
(15.30:234.14) “O Ambā, O Ambālī, O Ambikā! No one at all copulates with me; the horse sleeps,” [saying this] the sacrificer addresses her. “Lift her up!
[he says]. She reproaches him in that very same way.
The favorite wife reviles her, saying: "When the doe eats the barley.
She, in turn, reviles her in that same manner. The discarded wife reviles her, saying: "This little bird..."
She reproaches him in that very manner;
all the members of the group revile her, saying, "He is your mother and he is your father!"—
in this case, she does not reproach him.

Having lain down beside the horse for a moment and then having stood up and put on his garment, he purifies himself with water, reciting the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss" according to their meter, and the fourth verse, "I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan.
All those who speak what is impure at the sacrifice mutter the Surabhimatī verse;
they lead away the wife.
They dismantle the enclosure.
They carry away the horse’s ornaments to the Adhvaryu’s dwelling.
Then, having mixed the fine flour of *śalmali* wood with curds, they smear the horse [with it] in the direction of its hair.
(15.30:235.7) Then the chief queen (*mahiṣī*), the favorite (*vāvātā*), and the discarded wife (*parivṛktī*)—these women approach the horse, bringing for him bundles (*gaṇa*) and needles (*sūci*).

Upon that part of his body which is anterior to the chest, the chief queen, together with the wives of those who have been appointed as attendants, fashions incisions (*asipatha*) with golden needles, reciting two verses: "The Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Dvipadā, and the Catuṣpadā.

(15.30:235.11) Then, upon that part which extends from the chest backward to the navel, the favorite queen, together with the wives of those who are not kings, fashions incisions with silver needles, using the next two verses.

(15.30:235.12) Now, that which is from behind the navel to the tail—that part [of the animal] the discarded wife (*parivṛktī*) [cuts] with leaden knives, together with the wives of the charioteers, the village headmen, the attendants, and the collectors, using the two following [verses].
(15.30:235.14) The wives go back the way they came.
(15.30:235.15) They carry the needles to the residence of the *adhvaryu*.
Then he asks for gold and an arrow;
with these two, he rubs the chest of the horse [with the formula]: "Thus dissect the horse!
He causes the sacrificer to recite this hymn of six verses beginning: "Who cuts you? Who dissects you?"
When he has reached the end of this hymn, then the Adhvaryu scrapes the flesh from the chest of the horse, saying: "Thus one should dissect the horse, thus!
There is no omentum (*vapā*) for the horse;
its fat (*medas*), being separated, is like the moon—that is the horse's omentum.
The omentum of the hornless goat is thus, as is that of the gayal;
[the entrails] of the animals bound to the limbs are made of black iron, those of the others of red iron; those of the southern ones are of gold, and those of the northern ones of silver.
The Adhvaryu begins with the omentum of the horse first;
they bring the others in succession.
While the omentum of the horse is being heated, he throws a tip of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) into the fire.
They hand over the remaining [portions].
To the north, they cook the omenta of the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal; to the south, those of the other animals.
Of the horse alone, he makes an offering with a spoonful over its omentum.
They hold the other [utensils] close.

Then, having proceeded with the *svāhākṛti* call according to the direction, he sprinkles the clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with the residue of the oblation and sprinkles it upon the omentum of the horse itself.
They hold the other [utensils] close.

(15.31:236.11) Then, having offered a spoonful of oblation with the *svāhā*-utterance in front, he offers the *mahiman* [libation] with gold, saying: "The sky is your greatness. (15.31:236.12) Then, having spread an underlayer of ghee twice with the *sruva*-ladle, while cutting off the omentum of the horse itself, he says in a whisper: "For Prajāpati"; and aloud: "Recite for the fat of the omenta being cut off—the horse, the goat, and the ox"—as many times as the ladle can hold. (15.31:236.15) Then they lift up the other [omentum pieces] either with a vessel or with the *vedasūna*.
He pours the clarified butter over [the omentum] twice.

Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says in a whisper, "To Prajāpati," and aloud, "Prompt the [hotṛ] for the fat and omentum of the horse, the goat, and the ox that has been set forth.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers the omentum.
(15.31:237.2) Then, from above, he offers the Mahiman oblation with silver, [reciting]: "The earth is your greatness.
(15.31:237.4) Then he proceeds with the omenta of the animals tied to the limbs of the horse; then those of the others;
then the Pratiprasthātṛs proceed with the omenta of the southern animals; then those of the northern ones.
He offers the oblations from the ladle for those domestic animals and wild animals that he has released; he makes offerings corresponding to their omenta.

They proceed with the omenta of these classes of animals in a low voice (*upāṃśu*): those dedicated to Prajāpati, to Savitṛ, to Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Yama, to the Pitṛs as deities, to Heaven and Earth, to Vāyu, to Sūrya, and to Viśvakarman.

Then, having offered the *svāhākṛti* oblation with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) above, and having cast the omentum-spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*) into the fire, they step out and purify themselves at the *cātvāla* pit.

(15.31:237.11) Then he gives instructions regarding the victims, saying: "O *śamitṛ*! Do not cut away the hair of the horse; do not crush the bone of the horse. Having dissected him limb by limb, have him placed together in a pot upon the *śāmitra* fire. Do so for the hornless goat (*tūpara*) and likewise for the *gomṛga*. Then, cook the right horse-hoof and the neck of the *gomṛga* on the *śāmitra* fire. Cook the horse-whip in an iron vessel. (15.31:237.15) Then, having offered the *sāvitra* oblation, they proceed to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).
That concludes in a straightforward manner.

Then, having offered the *sāvitra* oblation, they proceed to the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*). The pressing of the soma is performed in the established manner; the cups (*graha*) are drawn in the established manner.
The ritual procedure up to the *dakṣiṇā* offerings is the same.
Having offered the *dakṣiṇā* oblations, he offers eight *saṃvarga* oblations with the mantra: "May the sacrifice come hither.
He gives the sacrificial fees as he desires.
Having offered the Vaiśvakarman oblations, he offers nine Paryāpti oblations with the formula, "The past, the present, the future. The consecration of the fire is performed in the established manner;
he thereby ensures the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice.
The midday pressing concludes in the regular manner.
Then, having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, they proceed to the third pressing. Having performed the rite with the Āditya cup in the established way, he draws the Āgrayaṇa draught.
Then he draws the Ukthya cup.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Pavamāna laud.
Having performed the Pavamāna rite, he then requests these animals: a horse, a hornless goat, and a gayal.
Then [they bring] the animals tied to the horse's body, then the others, then those on the right, then those on the left.
To the north of the horse, the ram, the hornless goat, and the gayal, they set down the sacrificial oblations; to the south, those of the other animals.
Then, having placed the horse's heart upon a mat of reeds, while cutting off portions from its front with a golden needle, he says:
"Recite for the *manotā* as the oblation is being cut off. With these words, he cuts off the eleven portions.
He does so for the hornless goat (*tūpara*) in this manner, and for the *gomṛga* in this manner.

For the animals bound to the flanks, the vessels are made of black iron; for the others, they are made of copper. For those on the right side, they are made of gold; for those on the left, they are made of silver.
He does not cut off portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt* from the horse, the hornless goat, or the gayal;
he cuts off portions from the other animals.
He does not cut off the *iḍā* portion from the horse, the hornless goat, or the gayal.
He cuts portions from the other animals. Then he arranges this horse limb by limb upon a mat of reeds; he causes the hornless goat to stand facing west in front [of the horse].
To the west, facing east, [he places] the *gomṛga* skin.
Then, taking up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles, he says: "For Prajāpati," in a low voice; "Recite the invitatory verse for the oblation of the horse, the goat, and the ox," loudly.

Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "For Prajāpati," in a low voice; "Prompt the offering of the oblation of the horse, the goat, and the ox which has been set forth," loudly.
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he throws them all together with the mat into the fire.
With the three sections beginning, "Heaven is your back," "The steed has stepped out with his strides," and "The steed has stepped forth," [the Adhvaryu] proceeds.
Then he performs the oblations for the animals tied to the limbs of the horse, then for the others;
then the Pratiprasthātṛs perform the oblations for those on the south side, then for those on the north side.
(15.34:239.10) And for those domestic animals which he has released and for the wild ones, he offers oblations corresponding to their respective sacrificial portions.

(15.34:239.12) It has already been stated that they proceed with the offerings of these classes of animals in a whisper. Then, prior to the offering to Vanaspati, he performs sacrifices toward the common quarters.
Then he proceeds with the Vanaspati offering.
Then, prior to the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he offers the first horse-whip with the neck of a Gomṛga.
Then he proceeds with the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
At this time, he offers a spoonful of oblation into the Āhavanīya fire with the words: "To the offered, svāhā!"
(15.35:239.17) Then he places this *praseka* (water-sprinkler) upon the fire, either to the south facing north, or behind facing east.
(15.35:239.18) Its front half is like a *sruk* ladle;
its middle part is exactly the same.
(15.35:239.18) Its base is like a cup.

Upon it, spreading four [portions of ghee], he says: "Bring [the milk] continuously and without negligence; I shall recite the *stega* verses. (15.35:240.1–2) When the stream reaches the fire, he begins there with: "The *stegas* with his two tusks; the frogs with his jaws. He recites fourteen sections beginning with "To *prayāsa*, svāhā! and the fifteenth.

Then he offers two oblations: “To Iluvarda, svāhā! To Balivarda, svāhā! [He recites] the thirty-six *aśvastomīya* verses, the three *dvipadā* verses, and [the verses] beginning with “May we now bring these worlds to completion” (*imā nu kaṃ bhuvanā sīṣadhema*) and “O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss” (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*).
At this point, he throws that sprinkling-vessel into the fire. Then he makes an offering over it with the residue of the oblation.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the after-offerings (*anūyāja*s).
Then, prior to the final after-offering, he offers a kindling-stick (*samidh*) made from horse-dung with a piece of horse-hoof.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the offerings to the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*s).
(15.35:240.9) Then, before the final Patnīsaṃyāja offering, he offers the horse’s tail-feather with an iron water-pot.
(15.35:240.11) The Ukthya sacrifice, characterized by twenty-one [verses], concludes straightaway with the Patnīsaṃyājas.
Then, having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters and set aside the milks, they fast.
Then, at that very time of the great night, they wake up;
having taken the portions of clarified butter in the morning and having brought down King Soma, he begins the Prātaranuvāka recitation.
When the Prātaranuvāka has been concluded, he goes toward the waters.
He rises with water;
he enters upon the Atirātra sacrifice; the pressing is performed in the established manner.
The cups are drawn in the established manner;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup.
Having drawn the Āśvina cup and having taken eleven cords, he approaches the sacrificial post.

Having set aside the *rājjudāla* post provided with a *svaru*-chip as the one standing nearest the fire, he dedicates eleven bovine animals for Prajāpati in the morning. Having proceeded with their omenta in the established manner, they move forward for the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). That concludes in the regular way.
They proceed for the midday pressing;
the pressing is well-known;
the cups are drawn in the established manner.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the offerings for the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having offered the *dakṣiṇā* offerings, he offers the eight *saṃvarga* oblations with the formula: "May the sacrifice come hither.
He gives away the remainder of the sacrificial gifts.
Having offered the Vaiśvakarman oblations, he offers nine *paryāpti* oblations with the formula: "The past, the present, the future. The consecration of the fire is thus concluded;
he does not perform the continuity of the *ahīna* sacrifice here.
The midday pressing concludes in the regular manner.
They proceed to the third pressing.
Having performed the rite with the Āditya cup in the established way, he draws the Āgrayaṇa draught.
Then he draws the Ukthya cup.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Pavamāna laud.
Having performed the Pavamāna rite, he proceeds with the animal offerings in their own place.

For these [offerings], the *manotā* is common, the deity is common, the touching back is common, the *vasā-homa* is common, the *vanaspati* is common, the *sviṣṭakṛt* with its *praisha* is common, the *iḍā* is common, and the directions are common.
The ritual procedure up to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings is common.

Having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings and having gone forward to the east, he replenishes the *dhruvā* ladle and offers the *abhūti* and *anubhūti* oblations with these two sections: "May my houses be prosperous" and "By means of Agni, he experienced fervor."
Then he offers two oblations for what has been and what is to be: "To what has been, svāhā! To what will be, svāhā!
Then, having offered the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations pertaining to the *adhvara*, he offers the ten oblations pertaining to the fire-altar.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).

(15.36:241.19) Now, at this *avabhṛtha* bath, having offered the second *avabhṛtha* oblation, he offers ten *vāruṇa* oblations with the formulas: "Homage to the King! Homage to Varuṇa! (15.36:241.20) Then he offers ninety oblations with the formula: "To Death, svāhā! To Death, svāhā! and eleven [oblations] with the formulas: "To Prayāsa, svāhā! To Āyāsa, svāhā!
(15.36:241.22) "Man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; the self is the hundred-and-first. As great as man is, from that much he expiates death," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then this Ātreya—dispersed, white, moist, marked with spots, tawny-eyed, bald, deformed, with deformed nails, humpbacked, afflicted with skin disease, naked—dives down.
Upon his head he offers [an oblation], saying: "To Jumbaka, svāhā!
At this point, he gives him this hundred [of coins] on a byway.
(15.37:242.6) Then they blow [the breath] out from him with the arrow-winning [formula]: "May you not thrive in my kingdom.
(15.37:242.7) The ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*) is performed in the established manner.
Having sacrificed with the *udayanīyā* offering, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.
For this [offering], nine white barren cows dedicated to Sūrya are to be immolated.

Having proceeded with their omenta in the established manner, he erects the Pātnīvata post in front of the Gārhapatya fire. Upon it, he dedicates the Tvaṣṭṛ-related animals: a spotted goat, a *kikidīvi* bird, and a *vidīgaya* bird.
Having released them after they have been encircled by fire, he completes the rite with clarified butter.
Then he offers the animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśa*), or two animal-cake offerings.
Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the animal-cake, he performs ten oblations of barley-grains (*yavya*) with the formulas: "Homage to the King! Homage to Varuṇa!

Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the animal victim, he performs ten oblations of cow-products (*gavya*) with the formula: "May the wind blow pleasantly upon us; may the dawns... and so forth.
The animal sacrifices conclude in the established manner.

Then, having performed the Udavasānīyā offering, he erects a wide sacrificial post in front of the Āhavanīya fire and dedicates these animals to it: one for Agni, one for Indra-Agni, and one for the Aśvins. Having proceeded with their omenta in the established manner, he offers the animal-cake oblations.

These are followed by the eight *devasuvām* oblations: "To Agni, the deliverer from distress (*amhomuc*), a cake on eight potsherds"—this is the sacrifice of ten oblations, and these are its *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses.
(15.38:243.8) “I meditate upon Agni, the first, the wise,” he says.

Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), he offers ten oblations for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) with the formula: “O Brahman, may a Brāhmaṇa be born endowed with spiritual luster. (15.38:243.10) Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the animal victim (*paśu*), he offers ten *saṃnati* oblations with the formula: “He has bowed down to Agni; he has bowed down to the Earth.”
The animal sacrifices conclude in the prescribed manner. At this point, he performs the twelve *brahmaudana* offerings day by day;
the procedure for these has been explained, as it was [described] previously regarding one [offering] elsewhere, with the exception of the two cords.
At this point, he gives them more than a hundred gold coins weighing a hundred *pala*s each; he gives two vessels for the *mahiman* cups made of gold and silver;
he gives single-vessel sets made of gold, as well as a golden cushion, a golden foot-fetter, and a golden tethering-rope.
Then he gives a hundred cows to the two lute-players.

Then he sacrifices with the seasonal animals (*ṛtu-paśu*), either according to the sequence of the seasons or all together in the same fire-places: three tawny ones for spring, three dappled ones for summer, three speckled ones for the rainy season, three spotted ones for autumn, three spotted-thighed ones for winter, and three smeared-colored ones for the cool season—thus for the year.
Then he sacrifices with the Devikā oblations.
Then he performs the Traidhātavīya sacrifice;
then he performs the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. The Aśvamedha is completed in three years.
The Aśvamedha is completed; the Aśvamedha is completed.
Whether one person or many are about to perform the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*),
for even a single person performs it with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Whether it be one or many, they undergo initiation (*dīkṣā*) after the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) by means of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*).
They agree regarding the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) of the householder, or they do so separately.
If they agree regarding the householder’s two kindling woods, having churned [the fire], they draw out the *gārhapatya* and the *āhavanīya*;
they bring the *vrata*-cooking [fire] from the village.
But if they indeed agree to act separately, the householder alone churns first;
then the others, sitting around him, churn repeatedly and then together pour the Gārhapatya fire into one place.
From that which has thus become a single entity, they draw out the Āhavanīya fire.
Having brought the sacrificial fuel for the vow from the village, they pour it together.

Now, if another person arrives later, he churns fire and pours half onto the Gārhapatya and half onto the Āhavanīya; having brought the sacrificial fuel for the vow from the village, he places it there. They summon him to participate in the preceding rites.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the purification itself.

The Adhvaryu purifies first the Gṛhapati, then the Hotṛ, then the Brahman, then the Udgātṛ. The Pratiprasthātṛ purifies the Adhvaryu, the Prastotṛ, the Praśāstṛ, and the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. The Āgnīdhra purifies the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Acchāvāka, the Neṣṭṛ, the Potṛ, and the Sadasya. The Unnetṛ purifies the Āgnīdhra, the Grāvastut, the Subrahmaṇya, the Pratihartṛ, and finally himself.
If they should say, "The Adhvaryu alone is the purifier of all; let him purify us all," then he indeed purifies them all. Or rather, they purify one another if they are studying together.
For them, the well-known Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi is performed.

When the *āśrāvaṇa* has been uttered once, at the point where he says, "Like Bharata," he first chooses the *ārṣeya* (lineage) of the householder, then that of the Hotṛ, then his own, then that of the Brahman, then that of the Udgātṛ, then that of the Pratiprasthātṛ, then that of the Prastotṛ, then that of the Praśāstṛ, then that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, then that of the Acchāvāka, then that of the Sadasya, then that of the Āgnīdhra, then that of the Potṛ, then that of the Neṣṭṛ, then that of the Grāvastut, then that of the Unnetṛ, then that of the Subrahmaṇya, and finally that of the Pratihartṛ.
"Brahmaṇvat"—this is the same [as before].
All of them take hold of one another during the consecration oblations;
the Adhvaryu makes only the Gṛhapati recite aloud while on the black antelope skin.
The others follow after him,
or they cause one another to recite if they are already learned;
they approach the cow that yields the vow-milk according to their ability, whether it be one or many.
For them, just as there is a specific order for the *pravara* selections, so too is there an order for the remnants of the *gharma*, the consumption of the *atigrāhya* cups, and the *ṣoḍaśin*.
On the sixth day of the *upasads*, they pile up the *uttaravedi* altar if the sacrifice is one without the piling of fire-altars (*anagnicitya*).
However, if it is a sacrifice with the piling of fire-altars (*sāgnicitya*), they pile up the *uttaravedi* on the very first day of the *upasads*.
For them, there are twelve initiation days (*dīkṣā*), twelve preparatory days (*upasad*), and the Soma-pressings (*prasuta*) last for twelve days.
Regarding this, some say, "One should not pile the fire-altar (*agni*) during the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*)," while others indeed do pile it.
They proceed from the Upavasatha day by means of the well-known ritual.
For them, the Vaiśvānara Jyotiṣṭoma Atirātra is performed as the introductory sacrifice (*prāyaṇīya*).

When, at the midday pressing, he pours [the water] from the Vasatīvarī waters for the third pressing, then—having run to the Āgnīdhra shed and leaving just enough water remaining in the Vasatīvarī jar—he draws [the water] at the junction of shade and sunlight, saying: "These waters are rich in oblation; the divine sacrifice is rich in oblation; he desires to win with oblation; may Sūrya be rich in oblation."
"This is the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice; we shall urge this very same [rite] again and again," they say.
Thereupon, he mutters the *punarālambha* formula either at the *yajñāyajñiya* stotra or at the *śaṃyuvāka*.
For them, the Jyotiṣṭoma Vaiśvānara Atirātra concludes as the introductory rite (*prāyaṇīya*).
When that [offering] has been completed, they turn over the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and cast the grass-bundle (*prastara*) into the fire. It concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
(16.3:248.2) By means of the *atipraiṣa* call, the Brahman restrains his speech.
(16.3:248.2) When the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, and the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, the Brahman releases his speech.

(16.3:248.3) He proceeds with the morning *prātaranuvāka*; as he moves toward the day, the Hotṛ recites the meters. Closing his eyes, the Adhvaryu offers the *upāṃśu* oblation, saying, "This is the form of night."
The threefold Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, having the Rathantara as its Sāman, is performed.
At the Māhendra hymn, a yoked chariot rushes forward;
with the sound of the chariot, he begins the Māhendra hymn.
On this day, only this much artistic performance (*śilpa*) is performed.
He thereby effects the continuity of the *ahīna* sacrifice.
Then, on the following day, the fifteen-fold *ukthya* sacrifice with the *bṛhat* sāman is extended.
On this day, the Adhvaryu introduces the Mahendra-stotra with the drum.
On this day, only this much artistic performance (*śilpa*) is carried out;
he thereby ensures the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice.
Then, on the following day, the seventeen-fold *ukthya* sacrifice with the *vairūpa* chant is performed.
On this day, the Adhvaryu priest introduces the hymn for Mahendra by means of the *ādhāva*.
Only this much artistic elaboration (*śilpa*) is performed on this day.
He ensures an uninterrupted lineage.
Then, on the following day, for him there is a twenty-one-fold Ukthya sacrifice with the Vairāja-sāman; there is an Āgneya-ṣoḍaśin and two Atigrāhya cups.
Some say that there is no Atigrāhya cup for the ṣoḍaśin.
This twenty-first day is to be chanted with the *nyūṅkha* insertion.
There is one view that they insert the *nyūṅkha* either at the beginning of the *virāj* verses or during the *śastra* recitation;

then there is another view that they insert the *nyūṅkha* during the *prātaranuvāka*, at the call for the *haviṣkṛt*, when both [the cups] have been set forth, and at the announcement (*āśrāvaṇa*) for the *māhendra* cup.
(16.3:249.2) They do not perform the *nyūṅkha* chant beyond that point.
(16.3:249.3) On this day, the Adhvaryu, holding the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) in his hand, introduces the *stotra* for Mahendra;
he then rubs them upon the right thigh of the Udgātṛ.
As soon as he is born, everyone utters the sound *abhihiṅkṛ*.
Regarding its ritual application: one who desires a firm foundation should cast it into the Gārhapatya fire; one who desires progeny should cast it into the Āgnīdhra fire.
"On the *śāmitra* fire for those desiring cattle; on the *āhavanīya* fire for those desiring heaven.
Disregarding that, he throws [the heart-spike] onto the *āhavanīya* itself with the formula: "May you two be of one mind toward us."
Having struck [the fire], he makes an offering with the verse: "Fire moves within fire, having entered it.
On this day, only this much artistic performance (*śilpa*) is performed;
thus he ensures the continuity of the sacrificial session (*ahīna*).

(16.4:249.10) Then, on the following day, a Triṇava Ukthya sacrifice is performed, featuring the Śākvara Sāman and an Aindra Atigrāhya cup. (16.4:249.11) On this day, the Adhvaryu introduces the Mahendra Stotra with water mixed with Avakā plants. (16.4:249.12) This is the deliberation regarding those waters.
"One should pour them into the *cātvāla* pit, pour them onto the *āstāva* platform, prepare the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling waters, and knead the flour for the sacrificial cakes.
Disregarding that, one should instead place them under the control of the *udgātṛ*s;
for the *udgātṛ*s consider themselves to be pacifying the affliction (*śuc*) of the *sāmans* sung in the forest by means of these [waters].
If they should announce this to the Adhvaryu, he should simply say, "Carry the waters down.
This much is the artistic performance (*śilpa*) performed on this day;
he thereby effects the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice.
Then, on the following day, the Trayastriṃśa Ukthya sacrifice is performed with the Raivata Sāman; the Saura cup is the Atigrāha.
On this very day, the Adhvaryu introduces the chant for the Mahendra cup with water mixed with Dūrvā grass.
The investigation of these has already been stated.
On this day, the *ṛtuyāja* is performed by oneself;
on this day, they do not perform one another's *ṛtuyāja*.

When he says, "O two Adhvaryus, sacrifice," then the two Adhvaryus, having sat down behind the two *havirdhāna* carts, themselves perform the *ṛtuyāja*: "We who are sacrificing to the Aśvins, the two Adhvaryus, for their office as Adhvaryus; let them drink the Soma according to the season. Yoke today your hitherward-turning chariot that carries heroes, which is easy to drive;

here is your place of unyoking. Mix the oblations with honey, for indeed, come hither! Then drink the Soma, O you who possess abundant wealth! Let them drink the Soma according to the season—*vauṣaṭ*! Thus.

When he says, "O Gṛhapati, sacrifice," then the Gṛhapati, having sat down behind the Gārhapatya fire, himself performs the Ṛtu-offering: "Ye, we sacrifice to Agni Gṛhapati from the Gārhapatya. O Agni, may these pressers and sacrificers be good householders through you; may you be a good householder with these pressers and sacrificers. May Agni Gṛhapati drink the Soma with the Ṛtu from the Gārhapatya."

"O Agni, accept the fuel; accept the oblation; accept the prayer of the people; accept the well-spoken hymn. O Vasu, with all [the gods] and according to the season, being great, desiring [them], make the desiring gods drink the oblation.
Drink the Soma according to the season—*vauṣaṭ*! On this day, there is this mutual agreement (*sāṃvāśina*).
To the north they hold the calves, and to the south the mothers.
During the *māhendra* hymn, having caused the calves to low between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds, they join the calves with their mothers and tie them up.
They release the mothers.
He introduces the chant for the Mahendra cup. Then, in the afternoon, during the Ukthya rounds, the artistic performances are carried out.
The Hotṛ recites the Pārucchepī verses;
the Maitrāvaruṇa arranges the Vālakhilyas; the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin recites the Vṛṣākapi hymn; and the Acchāvāka recites the Evayāmarut hymn.
The Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha is concluded.
He effects the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice.
Then, having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters and having set aside the milks, they fast.
Then, on the following day, they enter upon the Caturviṃśa Chandoma, having the Bṛhat-sāman as its chant.
Then, on the following day, they enter upon the Catuścatvāriṃśa Chandoma, having the Rathantara-sāman as its chant.
Then, on the following day, they enter upon the Aṣṭācatvāriṃśa Chandoma, having the Bṛhat-sāman as its chant.

Then, on the following day, they perform the Caturviṃśa Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, which has the Rathantara as its Sāman. This day is one on which no dispute is permitted; on this day, they do not speak to one another when someone has committed an offense.
"One should recite either with a *gāthā* or with a *nārāśaṃsī*," they say.
Regarding this, they also say: "The sacrifice is certainly not completed if one does not recite [them]. "One should recite them," is indeed what our *brāhmaṇa* states.
One should not pay heed to this;
"one should not pay heed" is the established rule.
This day consists of verses other than the *anuṣṭubh*.
The *anuṣṭubh* verses are not recited.
If they should nevertheless extract *anuṣṭubh*s, the Adhvaryu should extract the *anuṣṭubh*s.
He should take the *vasatīvarī* waters with this *gāyatrī* verse addressed to Sūrya: "Those [waters] which are near the sun, or those with which the sun is joined—may they impel our sacrifice."
Having removed [the verses] "For the heart thee! For the mind thee!", he should bring down the King [Soma] with another Gāyatrī verse addressed to Soma:
"O Viṣṇu, you are our nearest [kinsman]. Having removed this [verse], he should worship the King with another Gāyatrī verse addressed to Viṣṇu.
If, however, being ignorant, he utters an Anuṣṭubh verse, he says to the Hotṛ: "I have overstepped."
The Hotṛ is the one who causes what has not been obtained to be obtained;
the Hotṛ weaves that [sacrifice] of his with syllables.
And if he should think, "I am indeed one whose desire is limited, for that which consists of Ṛg verses in the Veda is likewise limited, and that which consists of Yajus formulas is likewise limited."
"One should ensure that the two Vedas have exactly the same number of syllables"—one should not heed this;
"one should not heed it" is the settled rule.
This twenty-four-fold Agniṣṭoma, having the Rathantara as its *sāman*, is completed.
When that [offering] has been completed, they go to fetch fuel-sticks. Having brought them, they place the fuel-sticks on the Āgnīdhrīya fire.
While they maintain contact with him, he offers a spoonful into the Āhavanīya fire, mentally reciting: "To Prajāpati, svāhā!"
(16.7:254.2) Then they proceed to the *sadas* for the *tūṣṇīṃstoma*.

Having perceived that they have entered, the Adhvaryu, having hastened eastward with his mind alone and having mentally fashioned this [cup] as a vessel, mentally draws another draught for Prajāpati, saying: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Prajāpati.
(16.7:254.5) With "Whatever there is here," he wipes it around mentally and sets it down, saying: "This is thy womb; for Prajāpati, thee!"
(16.7:254.6) Then, having touched water and taken two blades of *barhis* grass, restraining his speech, he hastens westward and introduces the *stotra* with the mind alone;
he gives the impulse with the mind;
he chants the *prastāva* with the mind.
He chants the *udgītha* with the mind;
he performs the *pratihāra* with the mind; [he gives] to the *hotṛ* with the mind. "This is the last," they say.
(16.7:254.10) The Hotṛ invokes with the mind; (16.7:254.10) the Adhvaryu responds with the mind; (16.7:254.10) he recites with the mind.
He responds mentally; when he reaches the conclusion of this mental recitation (*śastra*), then the Hotṛ recites the Caturhotṛ formulas aloud,
and the Adhvaryu responds to him.
"Oṃ, Hotṛ! So be it, Hotṛ! Truth, Hotṛ!
We have succeeded, Hotṛ!"—if indeed the Hotṛ does not know [the response], another who is a reciter of the *hotrā* formulas recites for him, and the Pratiprasthātṛ responds for him.
When they reach the end of these [libations], then the Adhvaryu, having hastened eastward by mind alone, lifts up that cup by mind alone;
he causes the announcement by mind alone; he responds to the announcement by mind alone.
Having offered the oblation with the mental *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ*, he carries away the portion for consumption. Having mentally invited one another, they consume it.
Having mentally rinsed the vessel, he hands it back.
This *tūṣṇīṃstoma* sacrifice is concluded.

Then he asks the officiating priests: "Will you release your speech when the sun is above the trees, or under the stars?"—"When the sun is above the trees," they reply. For such indeed is our Brāhmaṇa.
They release their speech only when the sun has reached the tops of the trees; while they remain seated right there, they enclose them,
and they enclose the wives in the wife's hall.

Then, without stepping across, the two Adhvaryus, with two blades of sacrificial grass, take hold of the Audumbarī post, saying: "Here is support; here is separation; here is delight; here is enjoyment.
Thereupon, they release their speech as they had previously agreed.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the creeping.
They should creep along beneath the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.
By this means, indeed, the serpents crept away.
"Then indeed they cast off their worn-out bodies.
Regarding this, they also say: "He who sets out by a wrong path either strikes against a stump, falls into a pit, or comes to ruin.
Therefore, they should proceed only by the path of the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
(16.9:256.4) "This indeed is the path leading to heaven, namely the path of the *vaṣaṭ*-call," they say.
But regarding this, they also say: "The path of the *vaṣaṭ*-call is, as it were, turned away and unappeased.
They should rather proceed by the path of the *adhvaryu*; for this path of the *adhvaryu* is the path leading to heaven that goes both hitherward and thitherward."
They creep along by the very path of the *adhvaryu*.

When they have taken hold of one another, he offers a spoonful (*sruvāhuti*) into the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra: "Let him, supporting and suckling, unite the calf with its mother; may he bestow upon us abundance of wealth, food, and vigor—*svāhā*!"

Having stepped out to the location of the *cātvāla*, they mutter: "May speech come; may speech approach; may speech come to me. What we have done and what we have not done, what we have overstepped and what we have not overstepped, what we have left in excess and what we have not left in excess—may that merge into Prajāpati, the father.
Thus, they finally find their firm footing in speech.
For them, the *atirātra* sacrifice which serves as the opening (*prāyaṇīya*) is also the concluding (*udayanīya*) one.

Having concluded the sacrificial session (*sattra*), each individual should perform the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice as an *agniṣṭoma*, consisting of four stomas, serving as a rite for the pacification of the *pṛṣṭha* chants, with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
(16.10:257.3) Now, therefore, follows the investigation into the arrangement of the cups (*graha*).
(16.10:257.3) On the first day, the cup for Indra and Vāyu comes first; on the second day, the cup for the *śukra* comes first.
The third and fourth days have the Āgrayaṇa cup as the first;
the fifth day has the Aindravāyava cup as the first; and the sixth and seventh days have the Śukra cup as the first.
The eighth day has the Āgrayaṇa cup as its first;
the ninth and tenth have the Aindravāyava cup as their first— thus, indeed, from the perspective of the Adhvaryu.
Now, according to the Chandogas and Bahvṛcas:
the first three-night period has the Gāyatrī at the morning pressing, the Triṣṭubh at the midday pressing, and the Jagatī at the third pressing;
the second three-night period has the Jagatī at the morning pressing, the Gāyatrī at the midday pressing, and the Triṣṭubh at the third pressing.

The morning pressing of the third three-night rite is in the *triṣṭubh* metre, the midday pressing is in the *jagatī*, and the third pressing is in the *gāyatrī*; therefore, they employ [the days] with their respective metres.
(16.11:258.1) Now, therefore, follows the investigation concerning the preparation of the sacrificial animal. (16.11:258.1) Some say that the animals should belong to Indra and Agni.
(16.11:258.2) For this world belongs to Agni, the intermediate space to Vāyu, and yonder world to Indra.
(16.11:258.2) In that the animal sacrifice is dedicated to Indra and Agni, and the fat-offering is for Vāyu, they proceed pleasing these very worlds and establishing themselves in these worlds.
(16.11:258.4) Now, those who undertake sacrifices not dedicated to Indra and Agni—just as if one were to bring [goods] for a superior without first bringing them for an inferior, such is that act.
(16.11:258.5) Therefore, the animal sacrifices should be dedicated to Indra and Agni; this is one view.

The sacrificial animals for the Atirātra are those dedicated to Indra and Agni on both sides with those dedicated to Indra and Agni in the middle; or, there may be sets of eleven animals on both sides with those dedicated to Indra and Agni in the middle;
or, they may all be dedicated to Agni—this is one view.
(16.11:258.8) "They should all belong to Indra"—this is one view.
(16.11:258.8) "They should all belong to Prajāpati"—this is another.
(16.11:258.9) "They should all be sets of eleven"—this is yet another.

For those who proceed with all the sets of eleven, it is well known that on the first day they immolate the first set of eleven; they make the animal dedicated to Varuṇa the secondary victim for the one dedicated to Agni.
In this way, these ten intermediate days pass without the animals being left over.
It is well known that on the final day they immolate the final set of eleven.
They perform the rite of the animal sacrifice dedicated to the Viśvedevas by sacrificing an animal belonging either to Agni or to Varuṇa.

Regarding this, they say: "Since there are twelve initiations (*dīkṣā*), twelve *upasad*s, and the soma-pressings (*prasuta*) last for twelve days, how do these days of his become possessed of offerings (*iṣṭa*), of propitiation (*āprīta*), and of animals (*paśumat*)? [The answer is: There are three sets of eleven victims (*ekādaśinī*): the one for Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*), the one for the Viśvedevas (*vaiśvadeva*), and the final victim (*anūbandhyā*).
These are thirty-six animals, and these are thirty-six days.
(16.12:259.8) "In this way, these days of his become offered, consecrated with the Āprī hymns, and possessed of animal sacrifices.

(16.12:259.9) Regarding this, they say: "Since there are twelve initiations (*dīkṣā*), twelve preparatory rites (*upasad*), and twelve days of the *prasuta* extraction, how is the year attained through the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*)?
(16.12:259.11) [The answer is: There are twelve full-moon days, twelve eighth-day rites (*aṣṭakā*), and twelve new-moon days.
These, indeed, are the longest days of the year;
following these, the year is attained,
and the twelve-day rite is completed.
(16.12:260.1) The one who desires a year [of life] has reached completion.
(16.12:260.2) Thus, by means of the twelve-day rite, the year is attained.
Those who are about to undergo initiation for the year-long rite settle together.
Indeed, it was the practice of the ancients to settle for the year in this manner, dwelling together while seeking to understand one another’s Vedic recitations as well as their worldly affairs;
for indeed, there may be only a single maker of the peace-chariot among them.
(16.13:260.5) Four days before the full moon of Māgha, they undergo initiation.
(16.13:260.6) For them, the purchase of the Soma falls on the Ekāṣṭakā.
(16.13:260.7) This is the case if they undergo initiation without having ascertained the year.
(16.13:260.7) Or rather, if they desire to determine the year within this very Ekāṣṭakā, they undergo initiation four days before either the full moon of Phālguna or Caitra.
For them, the purchase of the Soma falls on the eighth day of the waning fortnight;
thus, they do not treat the Ekāṣṭakā as a failure.
Their Soma-pressing falls on the first fortnight; the months coincide with the first fortnight;
the commencement is in the first fortnight, the Viṣuvat day is in the first fortnight, and the rising is in the first fortnight.
The ritual procedure of the twelve-day sacrifice is the same.
Likewise, on the sixth *upasad* day, they pile up the *uttaravedi* altar if there is no piling of fire-altars (*agnicityā*).
However, if there is a piling of fire-altars, they pile up the *uttaravedi* on the very first *upasad* day.
For them there are twelve initiation days and twelve Upasad days; the Soma-pressings continue for a year.
Regarding this, some say, "One should not pile the fire-altar during the year," while others indeed do pile it.
They proceed from the fast-day by means of the well-known ritual.
For them, the *vaiśvānara* *jyotiṣṭoma* *atirātra* as the introductory sacrifice (*prāyaṇīya*) is concluded in the established manner.
When that has been completed, they enter upon the twenty-four-fold *ukthya*, the introductory rite (*ārambhaṇīya*), which possesses both *sāmans*.
Then they enter upon the Abhiplava six-day period:
the Jyotis Agniṣṭoma, the Gauḥ Ukthya, the Āyus Ukthya, the Gauḥ Ukthya, the Āyus Ukthya, and the Jyotis Agniṣṭoma;
they perform it four times.
The *rathaṃtara* and the *bṛhat*— the *rathaṃtara* and the *bṛhat*— alternate as the *pṛṣṭha* chants.
This constitutes the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), which makes up that month.
With that very [sacrificial session] thus completed, they proceed for five months.
Then, during this sixth month, they collect the *saṃbhārya* materials:
three *abhiplava* six-day periods, which constitute eighteen days.
The Prāyaṇīya and Ārambhaṇīya [offerings],
those twenty days,
the Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha, the Abhijit, and the three Paraḥsāman [days].
That is one month.
Then comes the Vaiṣuvata day; on this Vaiṣuvata day, they perform the Ekaviṃśa Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, for which the Bṛhat-sāman is chanted.
For this [sacrifice], there is an *atigrāhya* cup for Sūrya, and an animal victim for Sūrya is to be immolated.
Regarding this, some begin this very day with it even while the sun is still up, saying, "The day of the *divākīrtya* [stotra] is when the sun has risen.
Maudgalya says that one should commence it in the same manner as for other days.
For that [sacrifice], the Mahādivākīrtya is the *pṛṣṭha* chant for the Hotṛ, the Vikarṇa is the *brahmasāman*, and the Bhāsa is the *agniṣṭoma*.
Then, after the Vaiṣuvata day, they proceed with three recurring *svarasāmans*.
Then they proceed with the Viśvajit.
Then they perform the reversed *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period.
This day begins with the *trayastrimśa* stoma and has the *āgrayaṇa* cup as its first.
Then they perform the reversed *abhiplava* six-day period.
The Jyotis is the Agniṣṭoma; the Āyus is the Ukthya; the Gauḥ is the Ukthya; the Āyus is the Ukthya; the Gauḥ is the Ukthya; and the Jyotis is indeed the Agniṣṭoma.
They enter upon it in that very same manner.
The Bṛhat and the Rathantara serve as the Pṛṣṭha-stotras in alternation: "Bṛhat, Rathantara; Bṛhat, Rathantara. Thus they alternate.
The Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha is placed at the beginning; that constitutes one month.
By means of that completed [period], they proceed for five months.
Then, during this sixth month, they collect the *saṃbhārya* materials:
two *abhiplava* six-day periods, which constitute twelve days;
the *go* and *āyus* [days], which bring the total to fourteen.
There are four [days] after the Vaiṣuvata; these make eighteen, including the ten-night period, the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra.
That constitutes a month.
This is the Gavāmayana sacrifice, characterized by the Māsa-pṛṣṭhas.
(16.16:262.11) Having performed the *anutsarga* with the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [sāmans], they should perform the *pṛṣṭha* days once in the final month;
that is the second *Gavāmayana*. The third is ten-monthly.

The *abhiplava* days and the *akṣīyanti* days—that is the way of the Aṅgirases. The *pṛṣṭhya* days and the *akṣīyanti* days—that is the way of the Ādityas. The *agniṣṭoma* days and the *akṣīyanti* days—that is the way of Prajāpati.

The Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya [sacrifices] on both sides with the Agniṣṭoma in the middle—that is the second way of Prajāpati. (16.16:262.16) Or rather, they should all be Agniṣṭomas; that is the third way of Prajāpati. Now, therefore, follows the investigation concerning the arrangement of the cups (graha).

Regarding this, some take two cups for Sarasvatī and Viṣṇu from the very beginning of the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra up until the Udayanīya, saying: "Sarasvatī is indeed speech, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; having thus encompassed both speech and the sacrifice in the middle, we shall proceed to the conclusion without harm.
But concerning this they also say: "In that the sacrifice is performed by means of speech, Sarasvatī is thereby attained; and in that it is the sacrifice itself, Viṣṇu is thereby attained.
Indeed, there is no Brāhmaṇa text [authorizing] this for us."
"One should take the two cups for Sarasvatī and Viṣṇu"—this one should not heed;
"one should not heed it," such is the settled rule.
Now, therefore, follows the drawing of the *aṃśu* and *adābhya* cups.

One should draw the *adābhya* at the *prāyaṇīya* [day], the *aṃśu* at the *vaiṣuvata*, and the *adābhya* at the *mahāvrata*. Both [cups] at the *prāyaṇīya*, both at the *vaiṣuvata*, and both at the *mahāvrata*.
"One may draw these two wherever one wishes"—this is another view.
(16.17:263.11) Now, therefore, follows the drawing of the Paraḥsāman cups.

These Paraḥsāmans are drawn day by day for three days prior to the Vaiṣuvata day, proceeding from here outward: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the waters and the plants.
