"Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the plants and to offspring. "Thou art taken with a support; [acceptable] to offspring..."
"I take thee, acceptable to Prajāpati. Thus [he says].
Now, on the Viṣuvat day, the cups are drawn beginning with the Śukra;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the Āgrayaṇa cup.

Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa cup, he draws the three Paraḥsāman cups [with the formulas]: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the waters and the plants. "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the plants and to offspring. "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to offspring and to Prajāpati. Thus.
Then, with a verse addressed to Sūrya, he draws the *atigrāhya* cup dedicated to Sūrya.
Having recited, "The deliverer, visible to all," he says, "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the radiant Sūrya.
Having wiped [the vessel] around, he sets it down, saying, "This is thy womb; for the radiant Sūrya, thee!"

(16.18:264.10) Then he draws the non-repeated cups: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the creatures for Prajāpati. "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the plants and the creatures. "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the waters and the plants. Thus.
"Seven *atigrāhya* cups are drawn on this day," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, after the *vaiṣuvata* day, for three days he draws them every day in reverse order, alternating between those for Viśvakarman and Aditi:
"Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the subjects and to Prajāpati. Thus [he says].
Then follows the offering for Viśvakarman.
Having recited: "O Viśvakarman, increasing by means of the oblation," he continues: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the plants and to offspring.
Then follows the offering for Aditi.
(16.18:264.18) Having recited, "May Aditi protect us," [he says]: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the waters and the plants.
(16.18:264.19) Then [he takes] the cup for Viśvakarman, and then the cup for the Ādityas.
Then, after three days from the Vaiśvakarman [offering], one proceeds with the reversal of the Āditya cups up until the Mahāvrata;
both of those are taken together at the Mahāvrata.
Then, on the day of the Mahāvrata, he takes this Prājāpatya *atigrāhya* cup.
Having recited, "All [gods] turn their will toward you," he says, "You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Prajāpati.
Having wiped it around, he sets it down with, "This is your womb; for Prajāpati, you."
(16.19:265.5) Now, therefore, follows the investigation concerning the preparation of the animal sacrifices.
(16.19:265.5) The praise of the sacrifices dedicated to Indra and Agni has already been stated.
(16.19:265.5) The Atirātra animal sacrifices consist of those for Indra and Agni on both sides, with others in the middle.
(16.19:265.6) On both sides [of the central set] there are the *aikādaśina* animals, and in the middle are the *aindrāgna* ones.
(16.19:265.7) "They should all be dedicated to Agni"—this is one view. "They should all be dedicated to Indra and Agni"—this is another view.
(16.19:265.8) "All [the animals] should belong to Prajāpati"—this is one view.
(16.19:265.9) "All [the animals] should be sets of eleven"—this is another.

For those who proceed with all sets of eleven, it is well known that on the third day of the final ten-night period (*daśarātra*), the *ekādaśinī* consisting of seventeen animals is obtained as an *ukthya*.
Nine days remain for him without animals;
on these [days], they immolate these nine animals accompanied by Brāhmaṇas, beginning with "a dwarf for Viṣṇu.
When they proceed in this manner, the animal sacrifice for Bṛhaspati becomes the Savanīya offering on the Vaiṣuvat day.
For that [sacrifice], they perform the offering of a sun-deer (*saurya*).
However, if they do not find these nine animals accompanied by Brāhmaṇas, they perform the offerings of animals for Indra and Agni on these nine central days of the year-long sacrifice.
As they proceed in this manner, the animal sacrifice for Indra and Agni becomes the *savanīya* at the Viṣuvat day.
For that [sacrifice], they perform the offering of a sun-colored animal;
at the Mahāvrata, a Sāvitra [animal]; for that [Mahāvrata], there are two animals to be offered: a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati and a bull dedicated to Indra.

(16.20:266.5) "Tomorrow is the Mahāvrata," [he says]; he prepares an unlimited number of chariots and an unlimited number of drums, as many as there are runners, as well as a hide, a *ceḍa*-cover, and a ground-drum; a bull-hide with its tail, a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra, and a fresh piece of leather.
The Hotṛ prepares a swing, the Adhvaryu two mats, the Hotrakas cushions, and the Udgātṛ prepares a throne-seat made of Udumbara wood.
He also prepares a lute with a hundred strings, cymbals, flutes, and gongs; these are for the wives.
A mat as a covering, a pair [of slaves], and an unlimited number of female slaves, as many water-jars as there are [slaves].
Then, on the day of the Mahāvrata, they perform the Pañcaviṃśa Agniṣṭoma, having the Rathantara as its Sāman.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the drawing of the Māhendra cup.
Having drawn the Māhendra cup, he then causes these materials to be brought forward.
Having caused a pit to be dug behind the Āgnīdhra fire-shed, they cover it with the hide of a bull, rough to the touch, with the hair side up.
Having pulled out its tail, the slayer stands over it.
At this point, he has these drums suspended in every direction.
While they are not being struck with drumsticks, these slayers stand by them. Then these chariots, having gone around the sacrificial ground on all sides, stand to the north.
Among them, the prince Tisṛdhanvin becomes the leader.
Therefore, in front of the Āgnīdhra shed, he spreads out a piece of leather at the place where the *iḍā* is brought back.
At that very moment, the slaughterer cuts it with a knife.
Then, a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra stand between the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds, holding a piece of moist leather.
The Hotṛ spreads out the *pleṅkha* seat; the Adhvaryu spreads out two *kūrca* grass mats; the *hotraka*s spread out *bṛsī* seats.
The Udgātṛ ascends the throne-seat made of Udumbara wood.
The Udgātṛ takes up a lute with a hundred strings;
the wives sit down around him with *āghāṭīs*, *piñcholās*, and *karkarīkās*.
Then, at the southern edge of the altar, enclosed by mats, two couples play together.
(16.21:267.11) Then these female slaves, having set down water-pitchers, sit around the *mārjālīya* fire-altar.
(16.21:267.12) Then the *adhvaryu*, seated on two grass-bunches (*kūrca*), introduces the chant for the Mahendra cup (*māhendrasya stotram*).
(16.21:267.13) They chant for the Mahendra cup.

When the *sāman* has been introduced, he issues the command: "O race-runners, run the race! Beat the drums! O pressers, press! O *agnīdh*, pour out the *āśira* mixture and make the mortar resound! O *pratiprasthātṛ*, attend to the *saumya* offering!
They act according to the command; the race-runners run.
They beat the drums, and voices cry out;
with clappers, cymbals, and karkarīka lutes, the wives sing in accompaniment to the Udgātṛ.
There is a Sāman named Bhadra;
it is sung by means of speech.
Now, this prince, armed with three bows, pierces the hide.
The Brāhmaṇa stands behind him [the Śūdra], saying: "May you not fail; may you not overreach!
In that very manner, he pierces through with three [stones] which have been placed in between.
Then the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra strive together over a moist hide-cutter, [saying]: "These have succeeded; these have performed well," says the Brāhmaṇa.
"These are those who cause [the fire] to go out; these have brought about misfortune," says the *vṛṣala*. The *brāhmaṇa* conquers; the *vṛṣala* perishes.
The two pairs move together.

Then these female slaves, having set down water-jars, dance around the Mārjālīya fire, striking their thighs and stamping their right feet while singing "Idam madhu. When they have completed one circuit, he makes her recite the first verse.
"The cows are indeed fragrant; the cows have the scent of guggulu resin. The cows are the mothers of clarified butter; may they be more numerous here. This honey belongs to the Haimahās.
Having caused them to perform the ritual salutation (*upasthāna*), they strike down only the right feet.

As they pass around for the second time, he causes the first [cow] to recite: "Did not the cows of Maṅkīra drink the water of the Gaṅgā? They drank from the river Sarasvatī; they have emerged moving eastward. This honey belongs to the Haimahās."
Having performed the *upasthāna* rites, they strike down only the right feet.

When the third [verse] has been recited, he makes him recite the first [verse] of those that follow: "When the two Rākhandyas speak, Maṅkīra and Dāśaka, they settle for security in the village; the ox does not weary while drawing; this honey is from the Haimahā."

(16.23:269.4) Then, while standing to the north of the *mārjālīya* fire, he makes them recite: "This indeed is the honey of the *sāragha* bee; this is the great pressed *soma*. O Indra, you have fully satisfied yourself with that; this is the honey of the *himavat* mountains.
(16.23:269.6) From that point upward, they proceed around [the fire] saying only: "This is the honey, this is the honey, this is the honey.
For them, that which was the opening *atirātra* sacrifice is also the concluding one.

Having emerged from the sacrificial session (*sattra*), each individual should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma* consisting of the *Agniṣṭoma* and the *Catuṣṭoma*, which serves as the *Pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* rite and for which a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is given.
One who desires heaven undergoes initiation for the Dvirātra sacrifice. Its initiation period is unlimited, and there are twelve Upasad days.
He purchases the King Soma in such a way that he thinks: "Since this is my Dvirātra, may the first day coincide with the Upavasatha day of the new moon, and the second day on the following day."
For him it is accomplished in this manner:
the Abhiplava becomes the first day, and the Gati the subsequent day;
the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma becomes the first day.
By that he wins splendor.
The *atirātra* sacrifice with all the *stomas* is the final one;
it is for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything.
On the first day, the *gāyatra* is the *sāman*;
on the second day, the *traiṣṭubha*.
On the first day, the *rathaṃtara* is the *sāman*.
The Bṛhat is on the later day; on the first day, the Vaikhānasa Sāman occurs,
and the Ṣoḍaśin is on the later day.
The first day has the *haviṣmat* as its *nidhana*, and the latter day has the *haviṣkṛt* as its *nidhana*.
"They belong to two different half-months; they possess distinct powers," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
The two-night rite is completed.
One who intends to sacrifice with the three-night rite prepares a thousand [cows].
Among them, there are those that are humpbacked, hornless, or dwarf.
Now, this thousandth cow of his is a piebald that has been marked with spots and prepared;
he undergoes initiation.
He purchases Soma with a reddish-brown, one-year-old cow;
there are twelve Upasad days.
On the first day, the Agniṣṭoma is performed.
Its morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) is the *trivṛt*, the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) is the *pañcadaśa*, and the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) is the *saptadaśa*.

Having offered the oblations for the sacrificial fees (*dākṣiṇāni*), he offers a spoonful (*sruvāhuti*) in the Āgnīdhra fire with the verse: "Bring a thousand! O Exalted One, [drive] Vala open from all sides; O Skin, grant me a share of a thousand, together with offspring and cattle; let wealth enter me again."
(16.25:270.13) Of these three groups of three hundred [verses], the first is led forth as the *unnata*.
(16.25:270.14) He effects an uninterrupted continuity;
on the second day, the *ukthya* sacrifice is performed.
For him, the morning pressing consists of fifteen verses, the midday pressing consists of seventeen verses, and the third pressing consists of twenty-one verses.

Having offered the *dākṣiṇā* oblations, he offers a spoonful (*sruvāhuti*) in the *āgnīdhra* fire with the mantra: "Thou art strength, belonging to Aṅgiras, soft as wool; grant me strength; protect me; do not harm me. Grant me a share in a thousandfold [prosperity], together with offspring and cattle; let wealth enter me again.
Of these three groups of three hundred, the first is led forward by a cow that has miscarried (*vehad*).
He makes his lineage undiminished; it is extended. On the third day there is an *atirātra*.

Its morning pressing has the *saptadaśa* stoma, the midday pressing the *ekaviṃśa*, the *ārbhava-pavamāna* the *triṇava*, and the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* the *trayastrimśa*; the *uktha* chants, including the *ṣoḍaśin*, are in the *ekaviṃśa* stoma.
The *Ṣoḍaśin* is the first *rātrisāman*; the others are *pañcadaśa*. The *trivṛt* *rathaṃtara* is the *sandhi*.

Having offered the *dākṣiṇā* oblations, he offers a spoonful (*sruvāhuti*) in the *āgnīdhra* fire with [the verse]: "Thou art the foundation of a thousand; thou art Vāmana, belonging to Viṣṇu. Grant me a share of a thousand, together with offspring and cattle. May wealth enter me again.
Thus, among these three [groups] of four thousand [cows], the dwarf (*vāmana*) is led first.
In this case, he does not effect a continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice.

(16.26:271.9) Then, having led this thousandth cow around the north of the Āgnīdhra fire-shed, he should cause her to smell the wooden trough (droṇakalaśa) at the edge of the Āhavanīya fire, [with the mantra]: "Smell the vessel, O great one; you who possess wide streams and are full of milk! May the drops enter into you, as rivers flow into the ocean. Grant me a share of a thousandfold, together with offspring and cattle; may wealth enter back into me! Thus.
(16.26:271.12) “Verily, he endows him with progeny, cattle, and wealth; he becomes possessed of progeny, cattle, and wealth, who knows thus. So says the Brāhmaṇa.
(16.26:271.14) Now, it is further said: (16.26:271.14) “Having gone together with her to the Āgnīdhra shed, one should offer while she stands facing west in front [of him]. So it is said.

Having gone with her to the Āgnīdhra shed, he offers while she stands in front facing westward: "Both of you have conquered; you two are not defeated. Neither of these two has been vanquished. O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you strove together, you two distributed the thousandfold in three ways.
For in the three-night rite, the thousandfold is indeed divided into three parts;
thus he makes her possess a thousandfold.
"He makes her measure equal to that of a thousand," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then he offers oblations for her forms, saying: "To the speckled one, svāhā! To the black one, svāhā! To the white one, svāhā!

Then, having approached her, he whispers into her right ear with her names: "O Iḍā, Rantī, Aditi, Sarasvatī, Priyā, Preyasi, Mahī, Viśrutī—these are your names, O inviolable one. Proclaim me as a doer of good deeds among the gods."
"He announces him to the gods; the gods take notice of him," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(16.27:272.8) Then, as she who is the thousandth is being led northward between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, he addresses her with the mantra: "May she cause me to go to the heavenly world; may she cause me to go to the luminous world; may she cause me to go to all the meritorious worlds; may she cause me to go to a firm foundation, together with offspring and cattle; may wealth come back to me again.
(16.27:272.12) Thus, by means of offspring, cattle, and wealth, he establishes him in a firm foundation.
"He who knows thus becomes possessed of offspring, cattle, and wealth"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"One should give her to the Āgnīdhra, or to the Brahman, or to the Hotṛ, or to the Udgātṛ, or to the Adhvaryu."

(16.27:272.14) "A thousand have been given by him; a thousand have been received by him"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is also said: (16.27:272.15) "He who receives her without knowing this—let him receive her [with this formula]: 'Thou art one, not a thousand; I receive thee as one, not as a thousand; enter me as one, not as a thousand. (16.27:272.16) Thus it is.
"He who knows thus accepts her as being truly one, not a thousand," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it further occurs:
"Thou art pleasant, easy to sit upon, and most gracious; enter me as the pleasant one, enter me as the easy-to-sit-upon one, enter me as the most gracious one," he says.
"Like a pleasant, comfortable, and auspicious seat, she enters him and does not harm him," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is indeed said:
"The exponents of the Veda say: 'Does the thousand follow the thousandth? Or does the thousandth follow the thousand?'"
(16.27:273.1) "If he were to release [the thousandth cow] toward the east, the thousandth would follow along;
that thousand would be indistinguishable,
and it would not recognize the world of heaven."
(16.27:273.3) <He releases her toward the west.> (16.27:273.3) <He turns around her a thousand times.> (16.27:273.3) <Knowing the way, she goes to the heavenly world.>
"He releases it toward the sacrificer," so [it is said].
He releases it from the east toward the west toward the sacrificer.
"Quickly a thousand [offspring] are born; as the last she is led away, as the first she goes to the gods," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
With this very [rite], Rauhiṇeya Krotunī, Kaulāśva, and Yāska performed the sacrifice at the beginnings of the seasons by means of the *vihṛta* arrangement.
Then Maśaka Gārgya, a pupil of Āruṇi, arrived; seeing that the conclusion had not been reached, he said, "Is it not so, sir? Is this a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*)?"
"No," he replied to him.
He went to him,
and he spoke to him.
With that entire [sacrifice] he used to perform the rite;
they call this the Garga-trirātra.
Desiring to win four heroes, he undergoes initiation for the Four-night sacrifice.
Its initiation period is unlimited; there are twelve Upasad days.
Its days are indeed Agniṣṭomas, with twenty-four-fold Pavamāna chants that have rising stomas—this is one view.
There is one Agniṣṭoma, two Ukthyas, and then an Atirātra.

Now, the Chandogas might ask about the alternative arrangement of the Sāmans; this is another [point]: "Four powers did not come to the sacrificer Atri, whose deity was Faith: brilliance, sensory power, Vedic luster, and the eating of food."
Desiring to obtain these desires, he undergoes initiation for the four-night sacrifice.
Its initiation period is unlimited, and there are twelve Upasad days.
Its days are indeed Agniṣṭomas; these should be Catuṣṭomas—this is one view.
There is one *agniṣṭoma*, two *ukthya*s, and then an *atirātra*.
Furthermore, the *chandoga*s might ask about the variation of the *sāman*s; this is another point.
One who desires prosperity undergoes initiation for the four-night sacrifice.
For that [sacrifice], there are unlimited initiation days (*dīkṣā*) and twelve *upasads*. Now, it is indeed said: "The *upasads* consist of sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśinī*)."

In the first four-night period, having placed additional portions of clarified butter belonging to Agni and a cake on eight potsherds belonging to Agni into the fire, he offers them morning and evening.

In the second four-night period, having placed additional portions of clarified butter belonging to Soma and a cake on four potsherds belonging to Soma into the fire, he offers them morning and evening.

In the third four-night period, having placed additional portions of clarified butter belonging to Viṣṇu and a cake on three potsherds belonging to Viṣṇu into the fire, he offers them morning and evening.
For this [sacrifice], the *trivṛt* and *saptadaśa* *stomas* alternate.
The *trivṛt* is indeed breath;
the *saptadaśa* is Prajāpati.
(16.28:274.15) "Indeed, having grasped both the vital breaths and the food, Prajāpati was born;
(16.28:275.1) having likewise grasped both the vital breaths and the food, the sacrificer is born.
Its days should be Agniṣṭomas with thirty-four-fold *pavamāna* lauds; this is one view.
There is one Agniṣṭoma, two Ukthyas, and then an Atirātra;
they should ask the Chandogas regarding the alternative arrangement of the Sāmans—this is another [view].
One who desires offspring, or one who desires distinction, or one who desires cattle, or one who wishes to master the end of speech, undergoes initiation for the five-night sacrifice.
Its initiation period is unlimited, and there are twelve *upasads*.

Its days consist of: an *agniṣṭoma* with the *trivṛt* stoma; an *ukthya* with the *pañcadaśa* stoma; an *ukthya* with the *saptadaśa* stoma; an *agniṣṭoma* with the *pañcaviṃśa* stoma accompanied by the *mahāvrata*; and a *viśvajit atirātra* with all the *pṛṣṭha* chants.

Those intending to perform the Sārasvata-ayanam prepare two sets of cows: one set of eleven bulls and another set of one hundred and one bulls. For them, the Havirdhāna and Āgnīdhra sheds are made of Aśvattha wood, for that indeed leads to heaven.
The two [sacrificial posts] are provided with rings.
Their sacrificial post has a mortar-base.
They undergo initiation by the waters of the Sarasvatī that flow downstream.

For them, this very Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma comes to a conclusion. When it has concluded, they carry [the sacrificial materials] toward the sacrificial post and toward the Dhiṣṇiya hearths; they collect together on the cart standing at the Āgnīdhra fire whatever of theirs is to be collected. They proceed by means of this very Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha.
Day after day, at each throw of the *śamyā*-stick, the sacrificers, crying out and desiring non-defeat, perform ten throws; then there is one rising.

When they perform a hundred, then there is one rising. When they perform a thousand, then there is one rising. Or, when one among them dies, or when they are defeated, then there is one rising, or at the Plākṣa spring.
(16.30:276.7) Now, therefore, they call this the "Course of the Sage" (*munyayana*).

A wandering ascetic (*śramaṇa*) carrying a load of a *khārī* measures of grain offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati at the Sarasvatī where the water flows downstream. That well-known sacrifice is completed.

(16.30:276.9) Then he offers this Savaneṣṭi sacrifice: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, one on eleven potsherds for Indra, and one on twelve potsherds for the Viśve Devas. (16.30:276.11) He begins with it either as a unified whole or with its parts separated. Day after day, at each setting down of the *śamyā* pegs, the sacrificer, desiring non-defeat, cries out; whenever they overcome him, or whenever they cut off his *khārīvivadha* load, then there is one rising at the Plākṣa tree or at a spring.
One who desires cattle undergoes initiation for seven nights.

His period of initiation is unlimited, with twelve Upasad days. Its days consist of: an Agniṣṭoma with the Trivṛt stoma; an Ukthya with the Pañcadaśa stoma; an Ukthya with the Saptadaśa stoma; an Ukthya with the Ekaviṃśa stoma; an Ukthya with the Triṇava stoma; an Agniṣṭoma with the Pañcaviṃśa stoma accompanied by the Mahāvrata; and a Viśvajit Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras.
Having approached the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] in the preceding days, they perform the Pṛṣṭha-stotras directly in the Viśvajit.
One who desires spiritual luster undergoes initiation for the eight-night sacrifice;
its initiation period is unlimited, and there are twelve Upasad days.

Its days consist of a *trivṛt* Agniṣṭoma, a *pañcadaśa* Ukthya, a *saptadaśa* Ukthya, an *ekaviṃśa* Ukthya, a *triṇava* Ukthya, a *trayastriṃśa* Ukthya, a *pañcaviṃśa* Agniṣṭoma accompanied by the Mahāvrata, and a Viśvajit Atirātra with all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras.
When his offspring are afflicted by hunger or when he has been long ill, he undergoes initiation for the nine-night sacrifice.
Its initiation period is unlimited, and there are twelve *upasad* days.
For that [sacrifice], they perform three times the three-day period consisting of the Jyotis, Go, and Āyus days.
Of these, the Āyus Atirātra constitutes the final day.

One who desires progeny, or one who desires distinction, or one performing malevolent magic, or one against whom malevolent magic is being performed, or one about to undergo initiation for the ten-night sacrifice, should offer the Daśahotṛ oblation and then undergo initiation for the ten-night sacrifice.

Its consecrations (*dīkṣā*) are unlimited; there are twelve preparatory days (*upasad*). Its days consist of a *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma* performed with verses addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*), and a fifteen-versed (*pañcadaśa*) *ukthya* performed with verses addressed to Indra (*aindrī*).
The *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma* is performed with verses addressed to the Viśvedevas;
the *saptadaśa* *agniṣṭoma* is performed with verses addressed to Prajāpati as the *tīvrasoma*;
the *ekaviṃśa* *ukthya* is performed with verses addressed to Sūrya.
The seventeenth [day] is an Agniṣṭoma with verses addressed to Prajāpati; the Upahavya sacrifice; two Agniṣṭomas with twenty-seven verses on each side, using verses addressed to Indra;
and a Trayastriṃśa Ukthya with verses addressed to the Viśve Devas.
The Viśvajit is an Atirātra sacrifice characterized by all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras.
Those desiring offspring undergo initiation for the eleven-night sacrifice.
Its initiation period is unlimited, with twelve Upasad days. Its constituent days consist of the Jyotis Atirātra.
The Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha, three Chandomas, and then an Atirātra.
Now follows the procedure for the Ahīna sacrifice: the Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha,
three Chandomas, and the tenth day.
Then follows the Atirātra.
Then this Pauṇḍarīka, a sacrifice of eleven nights, with a sacrificial fee of ten thousand, or a sacrificial fee of a thousand horses;
its consecrations are unlimited, and there are twelve Upasad days.
Its days consist of the Abhyāsaṅgya, the Ṣaḍaha,
the three Chandomas,
and the tenth day.
Then follows the Atirātra sacrifice. Day by day he gives a thousand [cows];
on the final day, he gives a thousand horses.
Now, therefore, they speak of the "Jyotirayana" (the Year of Light).
Some say it is the Bharata-dvādaśāha (the Twelve-Day Sacrifice of the Bharatas).
He undergoes initiation.
Its initiation period is unlimited; there are twelve *upasads*. Its days consist of a *jyotis* *atirātra* and a *jyotis* *agniṣṭoma*.
There are eight *jyotis* Ukthya sacrifices;
the *agniṣṭoma* is indeed light;
the *atirātra* is indeed light.
The twelve-day rite has been explained.
He interposes the tenth day and the Atirātra between [the first and second days] by means of the Mahāvrata;
that indeed constitutes the thirteen-night rite.
Now follows the first fourteen-night sacrifice:
an Atirātra and a Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha.
The six-day period is performed in reverse order; then follows the Atirātra;
then follows the subsequent fourteen-night rite.
The Atirātra;
the three-day period consisting of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus;
and the Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha.
(16.33:278.16) A three-day period directed westward; (16.33:278.17) then an Atirātra;
(16.33:278.17) then the first fifteen-night rite.
The Atirātra;
the three-day period consisting of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus;
and the Daśarātra.
(16.33:278.18) Then there is the Atirātra.
(16.33:278.18) He interposes the Mahāvrata between the tenth day and the Atirātra. (16.33:279.1) That very [sacrifice] is the sixteen-night rite for one who is not a Brāhmaṇa.
(16.33:279.1) Now follows the fifteen-night rite: (16.33:279.2) an Atirātra,
a Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma.
The three-day period consisting of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus;
the Pṛṣṭhya six-day period; and the three-day period in reverse order.
(16.33:279.3) Then the Atirātra.
(16.33:279.4) Then the Saptadaśarātra.
The Atirātra.
(16.33:279.4) One [sacrifice] lasts five days; (16.33:279.4) there is a ten-night [sacrifice]; (16.33:279.5) and then an atirātra.
He inserts the tenth day and the Atirātra between [the ninth day and] the Mahāvrata;
thus, indeed, that eighteen-night rite is not for a Brāhmaṇa.
Now follows the twenty-night rite.
An *atirātra*;
three *tryahas* consisting of the *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus* [sacrifices];
and a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*).
The three-day period is performed in reverse order;
then follows an Atirātra sacrifice;
then follows a twenty-one-night sacrifice.
The Atirātra,
the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha—
these seven are the middle days of the year-long sacrifice.
The six-day period is performed facing west;
then follows the Atirātra.
Now follows the first twenty-four-night rite:
an *atirātra*, four three-day periods consisting of the *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus* sacrifices, then a ten-night period, and finally an *atirātra*.
He inserts the *mahāvrata* between the tenth day and the *atirātra*.
That indeed is the non-Brāhmaṇa twenty-five-night sacrifice.
Then follows the subsequent twenty-four-night sacrifice,
which concludes with a Jyotis Atirātra.
The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period; from the thirty-three-fold [stoma] they proceed to the thirty-three-fold.
Then they undertake the undefined *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period.
In the place of the *trivṛt*, they perform the *ukthya* sacrifice with the *trayastrimśa* stoma, having the *rathantara* as its *sāman*.
Its *pavamāna* lauds are in the *caturvimśa* stoma.
In the place of the *pañcadaśa*, they perform the *ukthya* sacrifice with the *triṇava* stoma, having the *bṛhat* as its *sāman*.

Its *pavamāna* stotras consist of twenty-eight verses. In the place of the seventeen-versed (*saptadaśa*) stoma, they proceed to the twenty-one-versed (*ekaviṃśa*) *ukthya*, having the *vairūpa* as its *sāman*. Its *pavamāna* stotras consist of thirty-two verses.
In its own place, they perform the twenty-first Ukthya with the Vairāja as its Sāman;
its Pavamāna stotras consist of thirty-six verses.
In its own place, they perform the twenty-seven-fold Ukthya with the Śākvara as its Sāman.
Its *pavamāna* stotras consist of forty verses;
they proceed to the *ukthya* sacrifice with the *trayastrimśa* stoma at its own proper place, having the *raivata* as its *sāman*.
Its *pavamāna* stotras consist of forty-four verses.
From the Trayastriṃśa they proceed to the Trayastriṃśa;
its Pavamāna stotras consist of forty-eight verses.
Then they proceed to the reversed Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha.
From the *trivṛt* they proceed to the *trivṛt*; it is for the attainment and mastery of the *stomas*.
They proceed to the *jyotis-agniṣṭoma*.
Then the Atirātra;
then the thirty-night sacrifice;
the Jyotis Atirātra.
The Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha;
from the Trayastriṃśa they go to the Trayastriṃśa;
they go to the Triṇava.
They perform the twenty-one-fold stoma; they perform the Agniṣṭut consisting of the nine-fold stoma; they perform the Indra-stoma consisting of the fifteen-fold stoma.
They proceed with the seventeen-fold [stoma];
they proceed with the twenty-one-fold; they proceed with the twenty-four-fold.
They proceed from the twenty-four-fold [stoma] to the *pṛṣṭha* chants;
they proceed from the thirty-three-fold to the thirty-three-fold; they proceed to the twenty-seven-fold.
They proceed with two twenty-one-fold stomas;
they proceed with four fourfold stomas;
then follows the Atirātra.
Now follows the thirty-two-night sacrifice:
an Atirātra,
and nine three-day periods consisting of Jyotis, Go, and Āyus.
(16.35:280.19) A three-day period in reverse order;

An Atirātra; three Pañcāhas;

Then follows an Atirātra;

then an Atirātra.

The Atirātra;
the introductory day; three six-day periods consisting of abhiplava days.

Now, the Sahasrarātra: it consists of an Atirātra; ninety-nine Trivṛt Agniṣṭomas; one hundred Pañcadaśa Ukthyas; one hundred Saptadaśa Ukthyas; one hundred Ekaviṃśa Ukthyas; one hundred Triṇava Ukthyas; one hundred Trayastriṃśa Ukthyas; one hundred Caturviṃśa Ukthyas; one hundred Catuścatvāriṃśa Ukthyas; one hundred Aṣṭācatvāriṃśa Ukthyas; then ninety-nine Trivṛt Agniṣṭomas; and finally an Atirātra.

Intending to perform an Atirātra sacrifice, he prepares four Atirātra victims: a reddish-brown horse, a sacrificial cup made of Udumbara wood with four corners, larger *ambhṛṇa* vessels, and larger *ekadhana* jars.
He undergoes initiation;
he purchases the Soma with a one-year-old cow that is reddish-brown.
There are twelve *upasads*.
He proceeds from the fast-day (*upavasatha*) according to the established ritual procedure.
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and having set aside the milks, they observe the fast.

(17.1:283.5) Now, therefore, they wake up at the very dead of night. Having taken the morning portions of clarified butter and having brought down King Soma, he begins the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*).
When the morning litany has been concluded, he goes toward the waters.
He emerges with water;
he enters the Atirātra rite; the pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner.
The cups are drawn according to the established rule;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the Āgrayaṇa cup.
Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he draws the Ṣoḍaśin, reciting: "Mount the chariot, O slayer of Vṛtra! and then: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra Ṣoḍaśin."
Having wiped it around, he sets it down with: "This is thy womb; for Indra, the Ṣoḍaśin, thee!
Then he draws the Ukthya cup.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup.
Having drawn the Āśvina cup and taken four cords, he approaches the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

Having set aside the post provided with a wooden cup (*svaru*), he dedicates four animals for the Atirātra sacrifice: one for Agni, one for Indra-Agni, one for Indra, and a ewe for Sarasvatī. Having performed the ritual for them in the established manner regarding the omenta, they proceed to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).
That concludes in a straightforward manner. They proceed to the midday pressing.
The pressing is well-known [to be performed] in the established way.
The cups are drawn according to the established rule;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the Āgrayaṇa cup.
Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he draws the Ṣoḍaśin, reciting: "Indra indeed his two bay steeds carry," and then: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra Ṣoḍaśin."
Having wiped it around, he sets it down with the formula: "This is thy womb; for Indra, the Ṣoḍaśin, thee!
Then he draws the Ukthya cup.
The midday pressing concludes in the regular manner.
They proceed to the third pressing.
Having performed the established rite with the Āditya cup, he draws the Āgrayaṇa.
Then he draws the Ṣoḍaśin, reciting: "The Soma has been pressed for you, O Indra," and following this, "You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Indra Ṣoḍaśin."
Having wiped it around, he sets it down with the formula: "This is thy womb; for Indra, the sixteenfold, thee!
Then he draws the Ukthya cup.
The ritual procedure up to the *pavamāna* is the same.
Having performed the *pavamāna*, he proceeds with the animals in their own place.

For these, there are separate *manotā* hymns, separate deities, separate touchings, and separate *vasāhoma* offerings; the *vanaspati* offering is common, as is the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering accompanied by the *praisha* call, the *iḍā* portion is common, and the directions are common.
"From various directions," say some.
The ritual action is the same up to the *camasa* cups associated with the *dhruva*.
Having proceeded with the *camasa* cups associated with the *dhruva*, he proceeds with the three *ukthya* rounds: "To Indra and Varuṇa," "To Indra and Bṛhaspati," and "To Indra and Viṣṇu."
(17.2:285.2) Now, when about to perform the *ṣoḍaśin* rite, while moving forward, he says: "Fill the cups following the Hotṛ’s cup; O Unnetṛ, prepare the Soma!
(17.2:285.3) They fill the Hotṛ’s cup first, and the others as they come.
Having drawn it out, they place it upon the high altar;
then they place this *ṣoḍaśin* cup together with it. Then he pays homage to it.
(17.3:285.7) "Since there is no other born who is higher [than he], who has entered into all beings—Prajāpati, in harmony with his offspring, he dwells with the three lights; he is the Ṣoḍaśin.
(17.3:285.9) "This is the Brahman who is timely; he is the one renowned by the name Indra in the host.
(17.3:285.10) "I shall proclaim your two bay steeds at the great assembly; I win for you that which is timely, the desirable exhilaration of the winner."
(17.3:285.11) "Indra by name, who like ghee is poured out beautifully with his bay horses; may the celebrated host enter you—the songs that have the form of the bay horses.
Having touched water, taken two blades of *barhis* grass, and restrained his speech, he hastens westward. When the sun has reached the meridian, he introduces the *ṣoḍaśin* chant with gold.
To the east, they hold a reddish-brown horse facing west, or a dark one.
Having presented gold, they chant the hymn of praise.
"To the Hotṛ: 'This is the last [verse],' they say. After the time of the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu turns away;
the Hotṛ calls out to him.
The Adhvaryu calls back; he recites; he responds.
(17.4:285.19) Now, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting, “May the bay steeds bring thee hither,” he responds with the *ubhayatomoda*: “Othā moda iva made / madā moda ivom atha.
(17.4:286.1) Then, when he recognizes the Hotṛ reciting, “Forth, forth your Triṣṭubh,” having responded to that well-known *uktha*, he goes forward and lifts up this *ṣoḍaśin* cup;
the goblets are lifted up after it.
Then he causes [the Āgnīdhra] to announce: "O, cause to hear! "Let there be a hearing! "O reciter of the *uktha*, offer the *soma*s!
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the *ṣoḍaśin* cup with the formula: "O Indra, Lord of lords, you are the lord of the gods; make me, long-lived and full of splendor, a lord among men.
At both the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* calls, he offers twice.
In the same manner, they offer all the cups twice each.
Then they run toward the west with the portions for consumption. The formula for the consumption at each pressing is: "Of that which was drunk by Indra, accompanied by the Ṣoḍaśin."
His portion is set aside.
For the portion belongs to the will of the sacrificer, and that of the Hotṛ belongs to the will of the Hotṛ.
If those two should announce it to the Adhvaryu, he should say only: "The portion belongs to the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*."
In this way, he does not exclude himself from the portions;
that is his portion.

(17.5:286.11) "Indra the sovereign and Varuṇa the king—those two made this your portion first. Following their consumption, I consume it. May Speech, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma. Having thus rinsed the vessel, he hands it over.

(17.5:287.1) These three, having invited one another, consume from the *hotṛ*’s cup alone; they consume from their respective cups according to the cup.

Then he issues the direction: "O Pratiprasthātṛ, guard the third portion of the Āgrayaṇa, the third portions of the rectum, the tails, and the speckled butter! O Agnīdh, let your cake on two potsherds for the Aśvins remain cooked even during the latter part of the night."
(17.5:287.5) They perform their duties according to the directions.

Having filled them all, they set them down on the Uttaravedi.
(17.6:287.10) Then, having touched water and taken two blades of *barhis* grass, restraining his speech, he hastens westward and introduces the chant.
(17.6:287.11) They chant for the Hotṛ; they say, "This is the last [verse]."
The Adhvaryu turns away from the Hotṛ’s time;
the Hotṛ calls out to him,

He recites; he responds.
Having responded to the *uktha* in the established manner, he goes forward and lifts up this cup of the Hotṛ.
The cups are lifted up; then he causes the announcement to be made: "O, cause [the Āgnīdhra] to hear! "Let there be hearing! "O reciter of the hymn, offer the Soma-libations!
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* and at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ*, he offers twice.
In the same manner, they offer all the cups twice each.
Then they run toward the west with the portions for consumption. The formula for consuming at each pressing is: "Of that which was drunk by Indra."
(17.6:287.17) Having invited one another, these three consume [the Soma] in a manner equal to that of the Hotṛ's verses; they consume from their respective goblets according to the order of the cups.

They do not swell the cups;
having consumed the entire contents, they perform the ritual purification (mārjana).
Then, as they proceed toward the east, he says:
"Fill the cups following the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa; O Unnetṛ, prepare the Soma!

Then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he, restraining his speech, hastens westward and introduces the chant (*stotra*);

The Adhvaryu calls back,
recites, and responds.

the other cups are lifted up after it.
Then he causes the announcement to be made: "O, cause [the Āgnīdhra] to hear! "Let there be hearing! "O reciter of the *uktha*, offer the *soma* libations!"
At the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ*, he offers twice;
in the same manner, they offer all the *camasa*s twice each.
Then they run back toward the west with the portions for consumption.
The formula for the consumption at each pressing is: "Of that which has been drunk by Indra.
Having thus invoked one another, these three consume the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa; the others consume their respective cups according to their own vessels.

Then he says, "O Pratiprasthātṛ, proceed with the two sets of cups.
