Thus they fill the cup of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin first, and the others as they come.
Having lifted it up, they set it down on the *uttaravedi*.
Then, having touched water and taken two blades of *barhis* grass, he, restraining his speech, runs westward and introduces the *stotra*;
they chant the *stotra*.
"To the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin [he says]: 'This is the last,' they say.
From the time of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Pratiprasthātṛ turns away;
the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin calls out to him.
The Pratiprasthātṛ calls back; [the Hotṛ] recites;
[the Adhvaryu] responds.
Having responded with the established *uktha-pratigara*, he goes forward and lifts up this cup of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
The other cups are lifted up after it.
Then he causes the announcement to be made: "O, cause [the Āgnīdhra] to hear! Let there be hearing! O reciter of the *uktha*, offer the Soma libations!"
At the *vaṣaṭ* and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ*, he offers twice;
in the same manner, they offer all the *camasa*s twice each.
Then they run back toward the west with the portions for consumption.
The consumption at each pressing is with the formula: "Of that which has been drunk by Indra.
Having invited one another, these three consume the cup of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin alone, and the other cups according to their respective vessels.
With the words, "Impel me," they touch themselves; they do not swell the cups; having consumed the entire contents, they perform the ritual purification.
Then, as they proceed toward the east, he says:
"Fill the cups following the cup of the Acchāvāka; O Unnetṛ, cause the Soma to swell!
Thus [he says]. They fill the cup of the Acchāvāka first, and the others as they come.
Having lifted them up, they place them upon the *uttaravedi*.
Then, having touched water and taken two blades of *barhis* grass, he, restraining his speech, hastens westward and introduces the chant (*stotra*).
They chant the hymn.
"To the Acchāvāka: 'This is the last,' they say.
From the time of the Acchāvāka, the Pratiprasthātṛ turns away;
the Acchāvāka calls out to him.
The Pratiprasthātṛ calls back; [the Hotṛ] recites;
[the Adhvaryu] responds with the *pratigara*.
Having responded to the *uktha* in the prescribed manner, he goes forward and lifts up this cup of the *acchāvāka*.
The other cups are lifted after it.
Then he causes the announcement to be made: "O, cause [the response] to be heard! Let there be a hearing! O reciter of the *uktha*, offer the sacrifice of the Soma-draughts!"
At the *vaṣaṭ* call and the subsequent *anuvaṣaṭ* call, he offers twice;
likewise, they offer all the *camasa* cups twice each.
Then they run back toward the west with the portions for consumption.
The formula for the consumption at each pressing is: "Of that which has been drunk by Indra.
These three, having invited one another, consume the cup of the Acchāvāka; the others consume their respective cups according to their own vessels.
With the words, "Impel me," they touch themselves;
they do not cause the cups to swell; having consumed the entire contents, they perform the ritual purification.
The *hotṛ* chants first, then the *maitrāvaruṇa*, then the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, and then the *acchāvāka*.
The *adhvaryu* proceeds with the two preceding groups of cups, and the *pratiprasthātṛ* with the two subsequent ones.
All the cups and the groups of *camasa*s belong to Indra.
(17.9:290.5) Thus, indeed, this first fourfold cycle concludes.
(17.9:290.5) In the same way, the second concludes;
(17.9:290.6) in the same way, the third.
In the middle manner, they proceed as if possessed of artistic skill;
then, having gone forth, they advance for the *rāthaṃtara* junction.

Having recognized that they have all moved forward, the Adhvaryu, walking eastward, says: "Fill the cups following the Hotṛ's cup! O Unnetṛ, draw up the King [Soma] entirely; do not leave any remainder.
Thus, they first fill the Hotṛ's cup, and the others as they come along.
Having drawn out all the King Soma, they set it down upon the high altar (*uttaravedi*).
Along with that, they set down this cup for the Aśvins, which has been spread with a base of ghee and sprinkled over with ghee.
Then, having touched water and taken two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he, restraining his speech, runs westward and introduces the chant (*stotra*).
They say to the Hotṛ while he is praising, "This is the last [verse].
At the moment of the Hotṛ's [utterance], the Adhvaryu turns away.
The Hotṛ calls out to him; the Adhvaryu responds;
[the Hotṛ] recites.
He responds with the *pratigara*. It is recited up to the *mahāhava* verse. "The *āśvina* [śastra] consists of more than a thousand [verses]," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Having responded with the established *uktha*-response, he steps forward to the east and says: "Recite for the Aśvins the [Soma] drawn on the day before yesterday (*tiroahniya*).
Having stepped forward to the east, he lifts up this *hotṛ*’s cup; they lift up the cup for the Aśvins after him.
They lift up the cups;
then he causes the announcement to be made: "O announce! "Let there be a hearing! "Give the command for the Somas set forth for the Aśvins belonging to the day after tomorrow!
At the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call, he offers the oblation.
Then they offer this oblation for the Aśvins, which has been spread with under-layering ghee and poured over with ghee;
they offer it twice, at the *vaṣaṭ*-call and the subsequent *anu-vaṣaṭ*-call.
In the same manner, they offer all the *camasa* cups twice each.
(17.10:291.8) Then they run toward the west with the portions for consumption. (17.10:291.8) The formula for the consumption at each pressing is: "Of that which was drunk by the Aśvins...

(17.10:291.9) The formula for its consumption is: "Of thee, who belongest to all the groups, who hast been drunk by the Aśvins, of the Soma of the Tiroahniya rite, well-pressed, honey-sweet, being invited, I, invited, consume. Thus.
Having invited one another, these three consume the *hotṛ*’s cup; they consume the other cups according to their respective vessels.
With the words, "Impel [the breath] within me," they touch themselves.
They do not swell the cups;

having consumed the entire contents, they perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*). Then he issues the direction: "O Āgnīdh, bring the embers for the supplementary offerings (*aupayaja*); O Upayaṣṭṛ, sit down; O Brahman, we shall set forth; O Āgnīdh, having placed a fuel-stick (*samidh*) on the fire, cleanse each of the fires once."
They bring these embers for the supplementary offerings from the Āgnīdhra fire. He scatters them in front of the Hotṛ. The Upayaṣṭṛ sits down with the third portions of the entrails.
At this point, having divided these into eleven portions with the third being the rectum, the *upayaṣṭṛ* performs the *upayaj* offerings.
From here on, the procedure is the same. The *atirātra* sacrifice concludes.

One intending to perform the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice, having offered the oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*), proceeds toward that direction where he intends to find thirteen sacrificial posts.

Having cut them—including the one lying nearby as the twelfth and the one for the *pātnīvata* rite as the thirteenth—he either brings them himself or has them brought. Having brought them, he prepares them.
He fashions the *svaru* chips from the very wood used for the chiseling.
Now, on the day before [the sacrifice], this altar has already been measured out eleven times by means of the axle of a chariot.
When he traces around the hole for the sacrificial post standing near the fire (*agniṣṭha-yūpa*), he then asks for that chariot axle.

With that [cord], he measures to the south and traces around the sacrificial post-hole (yūpāvaṭa) so as to be level with the top. Then he measures to the north and traces around the sacrificial post-hole so as to be level with the top.
In this very same manner, measuring to the south and to the north, he traces around eight sacrificial post-holes.

Regarding this, some erect these sacrificial posts on the very day of the fast (*upavasatha*), saying, "The sacrificer is indeed the one nearest the fire (*agniṣṭha*); the others are the limbs; [the posts] are his form.
If they were not to erect them at that time, one might say of him, "This sacrificer will surely become limbless," and so it would indeed be.
However, they also say: "If these sacrificial posts were to stand like lifeless stakes, it would be like a desecration of the sacrificial ground, like a ruin of the sacrifice."
"On the day after tomorrow, one should erect these sacrificial posts. Thus, on the day after tomorrow, they erect them;
having encircled the eleven sets of sacrificial stakes with cords at the one nearest the fire, they leave them standing.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the drawing of the Āśvina cup.
Having drawn the Āśvina cup and taken eleven cords, he approaches the sacrificial post.
Then these sacrificial posts—washed, set in place, and fitted with their tops (caṣāla)—lie down to the east of the pits.
Having set aside the central post which has a wooden ring (*svaru*), he first erects the southern attendant post and then the northern one.
In this very manner—first the southern, then the northern—he erects eight posts.
Now, there is indeed this [instruction]:
"One should fix [the sacrificial post] level with its base for one who desires the world of the ancestors"; thus they are level at the bases.

"One should fix it level with the girdle for one who desires the world of men"; thus they are level at the girdles. "One should fix it level with the top-ring for one who desires sensory power"; thus they are level at the top-rings.

(17.12:293.13) “For one desiring a firm foundation, [he should perform] all [the verses] in their regular order. Thus he performs all [the verses] in their regular order for one desiring a firm foundation. (17.12:293.14) “Those three which are in the middle, those he should perform in their regular order for one desiring cattle. Thus he performs those [three] in their regular order for one desiring cattle.
(17.12:294.1) “He should interweave the others. Thus he interweaves them.
In this very manner, he interlinks eight sacrificial posts, alternating between the southern and the northern ones.

Now, it is indeed said: "If one should desire of someone, 'May he be short-lived,' one should set up his [sacrificial post] as one dug into a pit, with the northern half being the tallest and the southern half shorter.
In this case, he sets up the northern half as the tallest and the southern half as shorter.
“This is indeed the ‘pit-fall’; he who erects [the posts] in this manner perishes quickly,” so says the Brāhmaṇa.
“One desiring heaven should erect the southern one as the tallest, and the other as shorter.
Thus, here he erects the southern one as the tallest and the northern one as shorter.

"The sacrificer thus makes that very stepping-stone, a bridge, for the attainment of the heavenly world," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is further said: "Because he winds two cords around a single sacrificial post, therefore one man finds two wives."

(17.13:294.11) "Because one does not encircle two sacrificial posts with a single cord, therefore one woman does not find two husbands"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is further said: (17.13:294.12) "If he should desire of someone, 'May a female child be born to him,' he should intertwine the cords near the ends of his [two posts]."
At its end, he interlinks [the verses];
"A female child is born to him," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it occurs as follows:
(17.13:294.14) "If he should desire, 'May a male be born to him,' he should cause [the mixture] to enter him to the very end.
(17.13:294.15) He causes it to enter him to the very end;
"A male is indeed born to him," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
At this point, he silently spreads out this sacrificial bed to the south.
Having set aside the sacrificial posts provided with *svarkas*, he dedicates the animal for Agni at the post standing nearest the fire.

To the north [he offers] to Sarasvatī; to the south, to Soma; to the north, to Pūṣan; to the south, to Bṛhaspati; to the north, to the Viśvedevas; to the south, to Indra; to the north, to the Maruts; to the south, to Indra and Agni; to the north, to Savitṛ; and to the south, to Varuṇa. Now, it is indeed said: "If he should desire, 'May he who has been excluded be reinstated, and may he who is reinstated be excluded,' he should offer the animal to Varuṇa in the place of the one for Indra, and the animal to Indra in the place of the one for Varuṇa."

"He who has understood is excluded; he who is excluded understands," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is further said: "If he should desire, 'May the offspring become bewildered,' he should intermingle the animals."
"In this [rite], he interlinks the animals;
verily, he confuses the offspring," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said:
"If one were to offer an animal to Varuṇa facing upstream, Varuṇa would seize his offspring.
He offers it facing north from the south, flowing downstream, so that Varuṇa does not seize his offspring"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, upon this resting-place, he dedicates with the mind alone him whom he hates.
If, however, he does not hate anyone, he assigns [the victim] with the formula: "The mole is your animal. The ritual procedure is the same up to the carrying of fire around [the victims].
Having brought forward five of these animals on the southern side and having stationed them, he leads two of them past [the fire] and then interlinks them with the others.
Then, having performed the rite of carrying fire around the animals, they proceed toward the north.
Among them, the animal dedicated to Varuṇa is placed at the northern end;
the one dedicated to Agni follows by way of ritual order.

The Adhvaryu takes hold of the two omentum-roasting spits for the offering to Agni alone; they lead the other assistants separately toward the north, one after another, without letting them cross paths. Having performed the ritual with their omenta in the established manner, they proceed to the morning pressing.
That concludes in a straightforward manner.
Now, it is indeed said:
"The offering with the omentum is performed; the offering with the *vaśā* cow is not yet performed; then one proceeds with the *pātnīvata* [offering].

When, at the time of the *ekādaśinī*, the offering with the omentum of the *anūbandhya* has been performed but the offering with the *vaśā* cow has not yet been performed, he carries away the *stambayajus* from behind the *gārhapatya* fire onto the *aupasadā* altar.
This very procedure is established by the *Pauroḍāśika* [Kalpa-sūtra]:
he performs it three times with the sacrificial formula (*yajuṣ*) and the fourth time silently;
he performs the first tracing of the altar (*parigrāha*).
He mutters the Karaṇa formula. He digs up [the earth]. From the dug-up spot, the Āgnīdhra carries away [the earth] three times.

When the Āgnīdhra has carried [the fire] three times, he then traces around the pit for the *pātnīvata* sacrificial post in front of the *gārhapatya*. The ritual procedure is the same up to the placing of the offering spoons (*sruk*). Having placed the spoons and having raised the *pātnīvata* post in front of the *gārhapatya*, he dedicates a whole-hoofed goat to Tvaṣṭṛ as the victim.
Having released that [animal] after the fire has been carried around it, he completes the rite with clarified butter.

Then, taking four portions of clarified butter, he says "To Tvaṣṭṛ" in a low voice, and "Recite the invitatory verse" loudly. Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says "Tvaṣṭṛ" in a low voice, and "Sacrifice" loudly.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.
Thus he proceeds with the omentum.
Taking four portions of clarified butter, he says "For Tvaṣṭṛ" in a low voice; "Recite the invitatory verse" loudly.
Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says "Tvaṣṭṛ" in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) and "Sacrifice! (*yaja*) aloud (*uccais*).
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering. Thus he performs the counter-rite for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
Taking four portions of clarified butter, he says "For Agni" in a low voice and "Recite the invitatory verse" loudly.
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says "Agni" in a low voice and "Sacrifice" loudly.
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering in the eastern part of the northern half, passing over the previous offerings.
Thus he performs the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
Taking four portions of clarified butter, he says “To Tvaṣṭṛ” in a low voice; “Recite the invitatory verse” loudly.
Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says “Tvaṣṭṛ” in a low voice; “Sacrifice” loudly.
At the utterance of "vaṣaṭ," he offers the oblation. Thus he performs the counter-offering for the sacrificial food. He offers the butter-oblations to the quarters.
He cuts portions of the speckled butter for Vanaspati,
of the clarified butter for Sviṣṭakṛt,
and of the clarified butter for the Iḍā.
He performs the after-offerings with speckled butter;
having performed the offerings to the wives right here, he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations right here. The rite for the wife’s portion is thus completed.
Now, it is indeed said: "He who does not prosper after the establishment of the fires performs the re-establishment; he who does not prosper after piling the fire-altar performs the re-piling.
Having piled the fire-altar and being in decline, he prepares twelve bricks: eight *yājuṣī* bricks and four *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks.

When the northern altar has been sprinkled with clarified butter and the ritual materials have been scattered upon it, he then takes the fire into himself with two verses: "I first take Agni into myself," and "The Agni who is ours.
He mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "O Agni, those logs of thine, those dwellings...
Having touched the white horse, he lays down eight bricks with the formulas beginning, "By which the seers sat for a sacrificial session through austerity."
There are four *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with the formula: "Fill the world; fill the gap.
Then he touches the layer with the *citiklpti* verse: "May the wise one distinguish between thought and thoughtlessness.
Having touched this layer with a *gāyatrī* verse addressed to Agni, he descends with two verses: "May speech be in my mouth; may the breaths be in my nostrils."
Either a Paśubandha or an Agniṣṭoma is performed; it is completed in the well-known manner.

Jarvara was the *gṛhapati*, Dhṛtarāṣṭra the *brahmán*, Airāvata the *tāpasa*, Datta the *hotṛ*, Pṛthuśravas and Dūreśravas the *udgātṛ*, Glāva and Ajagāva the *prastotṛ* and *pratihartṛ*, Śitipṛṣṭha the *maitrāvaruṇa*, Takṣaka Vaiśāleya the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, Upariti Tārkṣya the *sadasya*, Śikha and Atiśikha the *neṣṭṛ* and *potṛ*, Aruṇa Ahiya the *acchāvāka*, Cakrapiśaṅga the *āgnīdhra*, Ajira Māheya the *subrahmaṇya*, and Arbuda the *grāvaṣṭut*.

The Grāvastut was Sāṇḍa, the Unnetṛ was Paśukra, the Dhruvagopa was Kautustau, and the two Adhvaryus were Arimejaya and Janamejaya. These indeed were the kings and princes of the serpents who performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*) at Khāṇḍavaprastha in human form, desiring poison.
For them, some days consisted of the tenfold hymn-form (*daśastoma*), while other days consisted of the twelvefold hymn-form (*dvādaśastoma*) and the *ākṣīyanti* chants.
Because he says "ten by ten," therefore snakes are biters and possess the power of biting.
This is the sacrificial session (*sattra*) of Laukya Pautrīya, which is beneficial for cattle;
snakes do not harm those who undertake it.

(17.19:298.11) < Austerity is the householder; Food is the wife; the Veda itself is the Brahman priest; Truth is the Hotṛ; Immortality is the Udgātṛ; the past and the future are the Prastotṛ and Pratihartṛ; Right is the Maitrāvaruṇa; the seasons are the Sadasyas; the seasonal periods are the Upagātṛs; Splendor is the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; Glory is the Acchāvāka; Radiance and Honor are the Neṣṭṛ and Potṛ; Fire itself is the Āgnīdhra; Speech is the Subrahmaṇya; Fortune is the Grāvastut; Vitality is the Unnetṛ; Strength is the Dhruvagopa; Mind is the Adhvaryu; and Sight is [the assistant].
The Pratiprasthātṛ was Sedi, Āśanayā was Idhmavāha, Diṣṭi was the Viśastṛ, and Mṛtyu was the Śamitṛ.

These, indeed, were the first creators of the universe who performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*). Their consecration (*dīkṣā*) lasted for a hundred years, their *upasad* rites for a hundred years, and their *prasuta* offerings for a thousand years.

Regarding this, the [following] verse declares: "The first creators of the universe performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*), proceeding with a thousand-fold libation. From that, the blinking and the non-blinking came into being; from that, the guardian of the world was born.
Indeed, they went by means of *agniṣṭoma*s.
This journey (*ayana*) is prosperous and productive, namely the *agniṣṭoma*s.
Those desiring to perform the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana undergo initiation;
there are five *sarvato-dhur* days,
and for them, this very [period] is known as the year-long initiation.
The ritual procedure is the same as from the *ārambhaṇīyā* [offering] onwards.
Having performed the *ārambhaṇīyā*, he causes the milk for Indra to be milked—either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* or silently.
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and having set aside the milks, they observe the fast.
Then, when the next day has dawned, they sacrifice with the new-moon oblation;
by that they proceed for twenty-eight days, including the Prāyaṇīyā and Ārambhaṇīyā offerings.
That month:
they proceed for a month with the Full-moon oblations;
they proceed for a month with the Vaiśvadeva oblations.
They proceed for a month with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings;
they proceed for a month with the Sākamedha offerings;
they proceed for twenty-six days with the Śunāsīrīya offerings.
The three Abhijits and the three Paraḥsāmans constitute that month; [then] the Vaiṣuvata day.
There are three *arvāksāman* days; then the *viśvajit*. They proceed for a month with the *trayastrimśa* stoma.
They proceed for a month with the twenty-sevenfold [stoma];
they proceed for a month with the twenty-onefold;
they proceed for a month with the seventeenfold.
They proceed for a month with the fifteenfold [stoma];
they proceed for twelve days with the ninefold [stoma],
and [they perform] the Go and Āyus [sacrifices].
These are fourteen;
four are above the Vaiṣuvata,
making eighteen in total.
The ten-night rite, the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra constitute that month.
Now, as for their *kuṇḍas*:
in that they are all indeed masters of the three Vedas (*trivedasa*), that is their *kuṇḍa*;
and in that they cause one another to sacrifice by moving around in succession, that is their *kuṇḍa*.
Now, when they consume from cups without handles, that constitutes their *kuṇḍa* vessel.
Of these, he who is the *brahman* is also the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* and the *potṛ*.
Then, he who is the *hotṛ* is also the *maitrāvaruṇa* and the *acchāvāka*.
Now, he who is the Udgātṛ is indeed the Prastotṛ, and he is the Pratihartṛ.
Now, he who is the Adhvaryu is indeed the Pratiprasthātṛ, and he is the Neṣṭṛ.
Now, he who is the Āgnīdhra is indeed the Grāvastut, he is the Subrahmaṇya, and he is the Unnetṛ.
(17.21:301.2) Now, the Upaniṣads:
(17.21:301.3) "Agni is the four-hotṛ; Vāyu is the five-hotṛ; Candramas is the six-hotṛ; Prajāpati is the seven-hotṛ; yonder Āditya is the nine-hotṛ.
(17.21:301.4) "These indeed are the deities; they have gone by this very path."
(17.21:301.4) < Then indeed they prospered; they went to the heavenly world.> (17.21:301.5) < Those who, knowing thus, go by this path, certainly prosper and go to the heavenly world.>
Those who intend to perform the Utsarginām Ayana undergo initiation;
for them, this very well-known initiation lasts for one year. The ritual procedure is the same up to the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha.
Having sacrificed with the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite, he causes the milk for Indra to be milked, either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* or silently.
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and having set aside the milks, they observe the fast.
Then, on the morning of the next day, having concluded the day's ritual, they immolate an animal for Prajāpati at the place of the *jyotis* [stotra].
The cake-offering for the animal sacrifice follows that [of Agni]; there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Vasumat.
At the midday pressing, they offer a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra Marutvat and the *sāṃnāyya* for Indra. Thus this sacrifice consisting of two oblations is completed.
At this point, having invited one another, they consume this *sāṃnāyya* offering dedicated to Indra.
Then, in the afternoon, they offer a cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśvedevas and a pap for the Viśvedevas.
They proceed with these two offerings, beginning with the deities and ending with the *iḍā*.
(17.22:302.1) Then he proceeds with the animal sacrifice, beginning with the *manotā* and ending with the *neḍā*.

(17.22:302.1) Then, having performed the after-offerings (*anūyāja*), having turned to the right, having hastened westward, having performed the offerings to the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*), and having gone eastward, having replenished the *dhruvā* ladle, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters, and having set aside the milks, they fast. (17.22:302.3) Then, on the following day, they proceed with the cow.
Proceeding in this very manner, omitting [the rites] month by month, they omit five *jyotis* sacrifices.
Then, having turned back from there, they omit four *trayastrimśa*-stoma sacrifices and one *jyotis*.
Then, on the following day, they commence with the *āyus* sacrifice itself.
Desiring to attain the *ayanam* of those who have accumulated austerity (*tapas*), they undergo initiation (*dīkṣante*).
For them, this very [procedure] is the well-known initiation for the fires; the ritual action is the same up to the mixing of the grains (*saṃnivāpa*).
The *saṃnivāpa* is well known.
Then he performs the *prāyaṇīya* offering;
having performed the *prāyaṇīya*, he proceeds with the footprint rite.
Having proceeded with the *pada* and having purchased the King Soma, he carries him away and performs the guest-offering (*ātithya*).

Having performed the guest-offering, he then offers this sacrifice consisting of five oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, a cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśvedevas, a pap for Bṛhaspati, and a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu.
Regarding this, some say that once they have sacrificed with it, they need not pay further heed to it.
(17.23:302.14) Some say that they should sacrifice with this very [rite] day after day for a year;
(17.23:302.15) on the first day with all [the offerings], on each subsequent day with one by one, and on the sixth day again with all [the offerings], on each subsequent day with one by one.
(17.23:302.16) Some say that one should pile the fire-altar during the first twelve-day period.
Regarding this, they say: "This Agni is indeed Rudra;
he is born at this time when he has been completely piled up. Just as a newborn calf seeks the teat, so does he at this time seek his portion."
"The year itself is his portion from this point on;
one should not go beyond its expectation. "One should pile the fire-altar during the final twelve-day rite"—this is another [view].

Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the daily piling (*aharahaś cayanam*). They complete the piling in a single day. Then, laying down the space-filling bricks (*lokaṃpṛṇā iṣṭakāḥ*), he proceeds for a month.
In the first month, he performs the *tayādevata* rite; in the second month, there is the piling of the loose earth (*purīṣaciti*); they complete the piling in a single day.
Then, for Muṣṭhin, the month proceeds in its regular sequence;
in that month he performs the rite dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ; in the third month is the Vaṇḍaciti.
In the fourth month is the layer of loose earth;
in the fifth month is the middle layer;
in the sixth month is the layer of loose earth.
In the seventh month, the Vaṇḍa layer;
in the eighth month, the Purīṣa layer;
in the ninth month, he lays down the seven Skandhyā bricks up to the Nakṣatra bricks.
In the tenth month, there is a layer of loose soil (*purīṣaciti*).
In the eleventh month, one lays down these [bricks] beginning with "Saṃyac and Pracetas" up to the *vikarṇī*.
For twenty-eight days of the twelfth month, there is loose soil.
On the twenty-ninth day, the Śatarudrīya;
on the following day, the Vasordhārā.
(17.25:304.3) Now, they say that [this period] is "above a month.
On the first day of the month, they complete the *sadyaścit* (immediate piling), including the *satyādevatā* and the *sasūdadohas*.
For a month, they proceed with the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites.
On the first day of the second month is the layering of the loose soil (*purīṣaciti*).
They complete the *sadyaściti* with the *satyādevatā* and the *sasūdadohas* verse.
For the second month, they proceed with the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites.
On the first day of the third month is the Vaṇḍaciti;
on the first day of the fourth month is the Purīṣaciti;
on the first day of the fifth month is the middle layer (madhyamā citiḥ).
On the first day of the sixth month is the layer of loose earth (*purīṣaciti*);
on the first day of the seventh month is the layer of bricks with broken ends (*vaṇḍaciti*);
on the first day of the eighth month is the layer of loose earth.
On the first day of the ninth month, he lays down the seven *skandhya* bricks up to the *nakṣatra*-bricks.
On the first day of the tenth month, there is the layer of loose earth (*purīṣaciti*).
On the first day of the eleventh month, he lays down these [bricks] beginning with “*Saṃyac ca pracetāś ca*” up to the *vikarṇī*.
On the first day of the twelfth month is the layering of the loose soil (*purīṣaciti*); on the twenty-ninth day is the *Śatarudrīya* offering;
on the following day is the *Vasordhārā*.
Now, they say that [this period] is "the month before.
For one month they proceed with the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites.
On the last day of the month, they complete the *sadyaściti* (the immediate piling), together with the *satyādevatā* and the *sasūdadohas* verse.
They proceed with the Pravargya and Upasad rites for the second month.
On the last day of the second month, there is the piling of the soil (purīṣaciti).
They complete the piling in a single day, together with the Satyādevata and Sasūdaoha formulas.
On the final day of the third month is the Vaṇḍaciti;
on the final day of the fourth month is the Purīṣaciti;
on the final day of the fifth month is the middle layer (madhyamā citiḥ).
On the final day of the sixth month is the layering of loose earth (*purīṣaciti*);
on the final day of the seventh month is the Vaṇḍa-layer;
on the final day of the eighth month is the layering of loose earth.
On the last day of the ninth month, he lays down seven *skandhya* bricks up to the *nakṣatra*-bricks. On the last day of the tenth month, there is the layering of the *purīṣa*.
On the last day of the eleventh month, he lays down these [bricks] beginning with "Saṃyac and Pracetas" up to the *vikarṇī*.
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month, the *purīṣa*;
on the twenty-ninth, the *Śatarudrīya*;
on the following day, the *Vasordhārā*.

(17.27:305.14) Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the ritual terminations (*utthāna*). (17.27:305.14) "They should terminate after performing the *Abhijit* sacrifice"—this is supported by the Brāhmaṇa. (17.27:305.15) Or alternatively, having performed the *Abhijit*, they then offer this *Savana* sacrifice: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, and a cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśve Devas.
They proceed with that [formula] either combined or divided.
Having placed a lump of clay into the *vasatīvarī* waters, they go about carrying the *vasatīvarī* waters around day by day.
Now, this is called "the Brahman’s journey," which is completed in a year.
They proceed for four months with consecrations (*dīkṣā*), for four months with the *upasad* rites, and for four months they press the Soma.

Regarding this, they say: "Who else, having performed such austerity, would make it his own exclusive property? He should seek an invitation among his pupils, or they should cause him to sacrifice with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."
He seeks an invitation from his pupils, or they cause him to sacrifice with sacrificial fees.
Now, it is indeed said: "One who desires cattle should pile the Chandaściti.
Thus, he piles the Chandaściti.
Wherever an oblation comes, there he indeed offers it.

Now, whatever other sacrificial formula (*yajus*) there is besides the oblations—which is like a body—he mutters that very *yajus*: the *yajus* for the two cords, the *yajus* for the horse and the donkey, and the *yajus* for the heating of the cauldron (*ukhā*).
He sacrifices with an animal victim dedicated to Vāyu.
He undergoes initiation. Having measured out the fire-altar and dug a trench, he mutters the *yajus* in the place of water; he offers the *śatarudrīya* at the laying down of all the bricks.
He performs the stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*).
"One who desires heaven should pile the *śyena-cit*," it is said;
this very [altar] is the *śyena-cit*.
"One who desires, 'May I be possessed of a head in yonder world,' should pile the Kaṅkacit.
While it is of this very same form, he projects a head-like portion toward the east by the measure of a cubit.
It is thus measured out so that the sacrificial post does not stand outside the altar.
"One desiring stability should pile the *alaja-cit* with four furrows.
Of this very [pile], the tips of the wings become narrower by the measure of a cubit (*aratni*);
by that same measure, the wings themselves become broader.
When those two have receded slightly, they become smaller than the [original] atom.
He ploughs each furrow with a single *ṛc*:
"One who has rivals should pile the *prauga-cit*."
(17.28:307.8) Having taken up this very same [altar], he extends it eastward. It is measured out in such a way that the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) shall not be outside the altar-ground (*vedī*).
(17.28:307.9) "One who desires, 'May I drive away my born enemies and those yet to be born,' should pile the *ubhayataḥprauga* [altar]."
Having taken up the two buttocks of this very [shed] that exists, he extends them toward the west;
it is thus measured out so that the sacrificial post shall not be outside the altar.
"One who has rivals should pile the *rathacakracita* (chariot-wheel-shaped altar)," so it is known from scripture.
This is a modification of the shape due to its connection with the specific word.
Having made a circular area of ground as large as the fire-altar itself—measuring one *aratni* and one *prādeśa*—he piles the bricks around it, including pebbles on the outside and pebbles within.
(17.29:307.16) Then at the end, then from within;
likewise for the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick itself; then all around the *svayamātṛṇṇā*.
He makes it like a navel in the middle;
he causes bricks to extend toward the cardinal and intermediate directions from it like spokes around a rim. This is the chariot-wheel altar, to be dragged around for one who has enemies.
"One desiring food should pile the Droṇacit.
Of this very [altar], he scoops out a space like a stall for cattle to the extent of a cubit toward the east;
then, in the middle, he makes it as if depressed.
This very Droṇacit is to be constructed by one desiring food.
"One desiring cattle should pile it as a *samūhya*," so it is known.
They declare that the lotus leaf, the gold plate, the golden man, and the two offering-ladles (*srucau*) constitute its characteristic features.
One should indeed do that. Furthermore, one brings together the bricks of the loose soil (*purīṣa*). This [altar] is to be piled up for one who desires cattle; it is to be ploughed over.
"One desiring a village should pile the *paricāyya* fire-altar," it is said.
He piles the bricks around the pebbles, with pebbles inside;
first on the outside, then on the inside.
In this very manner [he proceeds] with the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
Then he piles up bricks around the *svayamātṛṇṇā*;
this is the *paricāyya* altar for one who desires a village, which is to be drawn around.
(17.30:309.1) "One who desires, 'May I prosper in the world of the fathers,' should pile the Śmaśānacit.
There are six men facing east; three are transversely placed in front, two transversely behind—that is the body (*ātman*). These are its measurements.
If it is neck-high in front, it should be navel-high behind;
if it is navel-high in front, it should be knee-high behind;
if it is knee-high in front, it should be ankle-high behind.
If it is ankle-deep in front and level with the ground behind, that is the Śmaśānacit for one desiring the world of the fathers; now,
this Kūrmacit is for one who is not a Brāhmaṇa.

Having drawn it out from the middle with its back turned upward, he carves out what exists as this very [altar] like a head toward the east, measuring one cubit. He extends the bricks like feet toward the intermediate directions.
This very one is the tortoise-consciousness, the non-Brahmin, with a back arched in the middle, who is to be drawn around.

One is about to perform the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. He procures the following: the hide of a red bull, lead, and a eunuch; young grass shoots, sprouts of grain, and *vrīhi* rice; *nagnahu* flour reduced to powder; three vessels made of different kinds of wood; three types of groats; three kinds of hair; a sacrificial post; a hawk’s wing-feather; a pregnant mare; a stool; a *iṇḍva* (a type of vessel); a jar; a *kārotara* (a filter); two side-branches; a long bamboo pole; a sling; a hundred-holed sieve; a weight of gold (*śatamāna*); a hundred [pieces of] wool; and a Brāhmaṇa.

If he does not find a Brāhmaṇa to drink the remnants of the oblation, [he should offer it] into an anthill. Or, having sacrificed with the New Moon oblation or under a lunar mansion, the *surā-soma* remains mixed together in front of the hall on a red hide.
A eunuch sits beside it from the south.
He buys the shoots with lead, saying, "This is yours; this is mine. [The formula continues:
"Surā-Soma has been bought.
Then, taking it and having caused him to enter the hall by the eastern door, he places it down behind the Gārhapatya fire.
Then they thresh half of these rice grains.
Then, having placed the other [half] on the *gārhapatya* fire, they roast them in a single pot-sherd (*ekakapāla*); those among them which burst open become parched grains (*lāja*).
Now, those [plants] that do not bear fruit are the *tari* plants.
Having placed a new pot over the *gārhapatya* fire, they cook rice with plenty of water. Then, having drained it, they attach it either to a wooden board or to a mat.
Then they pound those *bhṛṣṭa* grains;
whatever small pieces and husks there are among them, they pour out into the overflow vessel (*utseka*).
This they call *māsara*.
Then, taking a measure, he measures it out: one part of young grass-shoots (*śaṣpa*), two parts of sprouts (*tokman*), three parts of parched grain (*lāja*), and four parts of *nagnahu* seeds.
Then, while sprinkling this boiled rice with flour and moistening it with *māsara*, he prepares it.
"Sweet thee with sweet, sharp thee with sharp, immortal thee with immortal—I mingle with Soma.
Having thus [spoken], he carries this stool around the front of the Āhavanīya fire and places it to the south.
Upon the stool he places the *iṇḍva* vessel; upon the *iṇḍva* vessel, the jar (*kumbha*); and upon the jar, the filter (*kārotara*).
(17.32:311.5) Then he surrounds this rice-porridge with a *kārotara* filter.

(17.32:311.6) Having covered it, he touches it, saying: "Thou art Soma; be cooked for the Aśvins; be cooked for Sarasvatī; be cooked for Indra the Good Protector. (17.32:311.8) It remains mixed for three nights.
"The purchased Soma remains for three nights," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then, when three nights have dawned, the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) of three or four animals is performed.
Now, on the day before that, his *sautrāmaṇī* altar has already been measured out.
Having strewn it around, he performs the *stambayajus* rite.
This very [procedure] is established as that pertaining to the sacrificial cake (*pauroḍāśika*).
He [sows] three times with the *yajus* formula and a fourth time silently. He performs the first tracing of the altar.
He mutters the *karaṇa* formula. He digs up [the earth]. From the dug-up spot, the Āgnīdhra carries away [the earth] three times.
When the Āgnīdhra carries [the earth] three times, he then traces around the *cātvāla* pit according to the procedure for the *cātvāla*.
He pours out the *uttaravedi* altar according to the procedure for the *uttaravedi*.

Having leveled the *uttaranābhi* and dug the post-hole (*yūpāvaṭa*), the two fires are led forward according to the procedure for the fire: the Adhvaryu from the Āhavanīya and the Pratiprasthātṛ from the Anvāhāryapacana.

Having performed the second tracing of the altar while it contains fire, having leveled it, and having held the wooden sword (sphya) crosswise, he issues the call: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the dipping-spoon (sruva), the knife (svadhiti), and the offering-ladles (sruc); [cleanse] the vessel for the speckled butter silently; gird the wife; bring the clarified butter and the curds; O Pratiprasthātṛ, take note of the Surā-Soma!
The Adhvaryu alone performs the well-known ritual actions pertaining to the animal sacrifice.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having purified the surā and taken it along with the vessel, carries it out by the eastern door and places it within the altar.

While the Adhvaryu is occupied there, the Pratiprasthātṛ purifies the *surā* with a tuft of wool whose fringes point northward, [reciting]: "May the daughter of Sūrya purify your *parisrut*, the *soma*, with the eternal, continuous fleece. [He continues:
"Vāyu, purified by the filter... if he has been over-purified by the *soma*.
Then he takes up a vessel made of *parṇa* wood.

With that [cup], he draws [the Soma] while reciting, "O, surely, those who possess barley... and having run through the rest, [he says]: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to the Aśvins.
Having placed two blades of *barhis* grass between [the cup and the vessel], he mixes it with flour of *kvala* beans and with hair from a lion's tail.
Having removed the two blades of *barhis*, he wipes [the cup] with a hawk's wing-feather and sets it down, saying: "This is thy womb; for the Aśvins, thee!"

Then he takes a vessel made of *nyagrodha* wood. With that, having recited the verse, "O, surely, those who possess barley... (*kuvid aṅga yavamantaḥ*), he draws [the juice], saying: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Sarasvatī.
Having placed two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) between [the vessel and the mixture], he mixes it with *badara* flour and with the hair of a tiger.

Having removed the two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and wiped [the vessel] with the "hawk's wing" [formula], he sets it down with: "This is thy womb; for Sarasvatī, thee! Then he takes a cup made of *aśvattha* wood. With that he draws [the Soma], reciting: "O surely, they who possess barley... and continuing: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra the Good Protector."
Having placed two blades of *barhis* grass in between, he mixes [the soma] with jujube flour and the hair of a wolf.
Having removed the two blades of *barhis*, he wipes it around with a hawk’s wing-feather and sets it down, saying: "This is your womb; for Indra Sutrāman, you!"

He causes those [handles] to extend behind the handles of the offering-ladles, either towards the east or towards the north. Then, taking this *surā* together with its dregs, he approaches the southern fire.
He has two pits dug on both sides of it.
He places near it two Viśākhā branches, a long bamboo pole, a sling, a hundred-holed stone, a hundred-measure weight of gold, and a tuft of wool.
Then, to the east of the southern fire, he prepares a mound from old ashes.
He places near it a Brāhmaṇa who is to drink the remnants of the oblation.

If he does not find a Brāhmaṇa, [he takes] an anthill-clod. Then, having touched water, he raises the sacrificial post according to the procedure for the post. Having set up the post provided with a wooden cup (*svaru*), he then dedicates these animals: a smoky-grey one for the Aśvins, a ram for Sarasvatī, and a bull for Indra.
If one has exceeded the Soma draught, there is a fourth animal sacrifice dedicated to Bṛhaspati.
Having performed the offering of their omenta in the established manner, the Adhvaryu takes the portions for the Aśvins and Sarasvatī,
and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the portion for Indra.
Taking up the two cups and rising, he says: "Recite for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman the pressed *surā*-Somas.
He recites this verse: "O Aśvins, you [two] [drink] the *surā*...
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Command the offering of the *surā*-Somas set forth for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman."
The Maitrāvaruṇa [says]: "Let the Hotṛ worship the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra the Good Protector.
He performs the sacrifice with the words, "May both Aśvins [be like] parents to their son.
At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the oblation with the words, "O Agni, the oblation has been poured into your mouth."

Having offered at the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call with the verse, "In whom the horses, bulls, and oxen... he pours the residue of the offering for the Aśvins into the vessel for Sarasvatī, and the residue of the offering for Sarasvatī into that for Indra.
A Brāhmaṇa consumes that [residue] with the two verses: "For separate indeed is the divine ordinance for you two," and "Whatever is here..."
(17.36:314.8) If he does not find a Brāhmaṇa, he pours [the substances] into an ant-hill with this same mantra.
(17.36:314.9) Then, having filled these vessels with bark-fiber, he hides a hawk-wing feather in one made of *parṇa* wood.

(17.36:314.10) Having raised two cross-pieces, he pushes the bamboo pole forward with its tip pointing south; he fastens a sling to the bamboo pole, a hundred-holed sieve to the sling, a tuft of hair to the sieve, and a gold piece weighing a hundred *mānas* to the tuft of hair.
Then, taking this *surā* together with its residue, he pours it into the hundred-holed vessel (*śatātṛṇṇā*) with the words: "O Fathers, whose faces are Soma, be satisfied!
They stand by [the vessel] with the verse, "The hundred-holed one flows," and with this eight-verse hymn beginning, "Pavamāna, who dwells in heaven."

Now, if one has exceeded the Soma offering, they worship with the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyānuvākyā*) of the ancestors: "May those below and those above rise up; I have found the benevolent ancestors. Let this homage be for the ancestors today. Thus the Adhvaryu, the Hotṛ, and the Brahman worship.
"Wherever he holds the hundred-holed [stone], there he sets it down for stability," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Having set that very [stone] down, he places it to the south.
Then he places these vessels upon the mound of old ashes.

"To the fathers who partake of the *svadhā*, *svadhā*! Homage! To the grandfathers who partake of the *svadhā*, *svadhā*! Homage! To the great-grandfathers who partake of the *svadhā*, *svadhā*! Homage! Having said this, he gives a pregnant mare. Then, having touched water, he requests the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) dedicated to Bṛhaspati.
He proceeds with that [offering] beginning from the deities and ending with the *iḍā*. Then he proceeds with the animal sacrifices, beginning from the *manotā* and ending with the *iḍā*.
Then he asks for these sacrificial cakes: one on eleven potsherds for Indra, one on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, and one on ten potsherds for Varuṇa.
He proceeds with those offerings beginning with the deities and ending with the *iḍā*.

Having performed the after-offerings (*anūyāja*), having turned to the right, having hastened westward, and having performed the offerings for the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*), he goes eastward, replenishes the *dhruvā* ladle, and offers the three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations belonging to the animal sacrifice with the formulas: "O Sacrifice, go to the Sacrifice! This is thy sacrifice, O Lord of Sacrifice! O gods who know the way!
At this point, they set down the *avabhṛtha* (purificatory bath) materials—whatever has been smeared with *surā* liquor—and these are placed together with the heart-spikes (*hṛdayaśūla*).
Having taken this [ladle], they go out toward the north between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*.
"I have heard of two paths of the fathers—the one of the gods and the other of mortals. Along these two, this entire world moves, between the former and the latter signpost. (RV 10.88.15)

Having performed the *hṛdayaśūla* offerings as prescribed, he then places these vessels facing away at the edge of the water with the formula: "O divine Varuṇa, that noose of yours which is established in the *brahman* and has the *gāyatrī* metre—by this [offering] I release it for you. Thus [he addresses] the one made of *parṇa* wood.

"O divine Varuṇa, that noose of yours which has the *triṣṭubh* meter and is established in the *kṣatra*, I release it from you with this [offering]. With these words, he offers the fruit of the *naiyagrodha* tree.

(17.38:316.5) “O God Varuṇa, that noose of yours which has the *jagatī* metre and is established among the people—that I release for you with this. With these words, he offers an *aśvattha* branch. (17.38:316.6) “O God Varuṇa, that noose of yours which has the *anuṣṭubh* metre and is established among the cattle—that I release for you with this. With these words, he offers a *śatātṛṇṇā* (a hundred-holed vessel).
He offers a hundred hairs silently.
The *avabhṛtha* rite is well-known;
however, he does not recite the *sāman*, nor the verse: "O divine waters, this is your embryo.
Then they return without looking back, for the sake of escaping Varuṇa.
On the road, they prepare the fuel sticks with the formula: "Thou art fuel; may we prosper.
Having arrived, he places them on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "Thou art a kindling-stick; thou art brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me.
Then they worship the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "I have followed the waters; we have united with their essence. Rich in milk, O Agni, I have come; unite me with splendor."
Then he performs the offering of groats with the Kusīda formula.
Then, having paid homage to the deities, he pays homage to the sacrificial post. The Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice is concluded.

(17.39:316.16) Having studied the Veda, one who is about to perform the ceremonial bath (snāna) should prepare: a grass mat and a pillow, a barber, a razor, pieces of wood for a seat, *vṛkala* twigs, a tooth-stick, warm water and cold water, powder of all fragrant substances, collyrium, a garland, a mirror, an unwashed garment, an upper cloak, an inner garment, a jujube-seed amulet with a gold setting, a cord, two ear-rings, a staff, sandals, an umbrella, and the hide of a bull entirely red.
These materials for him are prepared.
Regarding the consideration of the bath:
one view is that he should bathe under the asterism Rohiṇī.
This lunar mansion belongs to Prajāpati;
thus, his bath takes place under a lunar mansion belonging to Prajāpati.
Furthermore, [he bathes] thinking, "May I ascend all ascents."
"One should bathe under Tiṣya"—this is one view.
For this lunar mansion belongs to Bṛhaspati;
thus, he has effectively bathed under the very lunar mansion belonging to Bṛhaspati.
"Furthermore, may I be impelled by Bṛhaspati"—with this thought, one should bathe under the two Uttaraphalgunīs; this is one view. For this lunar mansion is indeed the constellation of fortune.
Thus, he has bathed under a constellation presiding over fortune (*bhāgya*); furthermore,
thinking "May I be fortunate," he should bathe under the *hasta* asterism— this is one view.
This lunar mansion belongs to Savitṛ;
thus his bath takes place under a lunar mansion belonging to Savitṛ.
Furthermore, he thinks, "May I be impelled by Savitṛ."
"One should bathe under Citrā," so says one [view].
This lunar mansion belongs to Indra;
thus, his bath takes place under a lunar mansion that is indeed Indra's own.
"Furthermore, [one should think], 'May I be variegated,' and one should bathe under the Viśākhās; this is one view.
For this lunar mansion belongs to Indra and Agni."
Thus, his bath takes place under the constellation Aindrāgna;
furthermore, [he bathes] thinking, "May I be possessed of branches through offspring and cattle.
During one of these waxing fortnights, before the rising of the sun, he enters the cow-pen.
On this day, the sun does not scorch him; rather, on that day, he indeed shines with brilliance and glory over those who have bathed. They enclose the pen with a skin having the hair turned inward.
Having kindled the fire in the middle of the eastern half of the pen and strewn grass around it, they bring all these ritual materials at once.
"Whatever [is done] together with all human beings"—from this *brāhmaṇa* passage [it follows that]:
a Brāhmaṇa sits to the south;
to the north, he places a water-pot and a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood.
To the west of the fire, having spread out an erakā-grass mat with its fringes pointing northward and covered with a fine cloth, he sits upon it facing east.
To the north stands the barber;
to the north is the pillow.
He should give alms until midday.
He may even cook a cow here, provided he possesses one.
At this point, having anointed a fuel-stick of *pālāśa* wood with clarified butter, he places it on the fire at midday.

(17.40:319.6) “Let us fashion this hymn with our intellect for the worthy Jātavedas, like a chariot; for his providence toward us is auspicious in the assembly. O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm—Svāhā! (17.40:319.8) Then, on an Erakā plant, he lies down facing north, reciting: “The triple life-span of Jamadagni, the triple life-span of Kaśyapa, the triple life-span of Agastya, the triple life-span of the Ṛṣis, that which is the triple life-span of the gods—may that triple life-span be mine.”

He consecrates the hair being raised [from the head] with: "Be auspicious to me when touched. He consecrates the razor with: "Razor is your name; the axe is your father. Homage be to you; do not harm me. He consecrates the hair being shaved with: "When you shave with the razor, when you shave the hair and beard with the shaver, make my face radiant; do not steal away my life-span."
He first shaves the beard, then the armpits, then the hair of the head, and then the other parts of the body down to the feet.
For it is from these that they depart first when old age comes at the end of life; those who, knowing this, have their body hair shaved, become eaters of food at the beginning of life.
If he should be about to have his body hair shaved, he should have his hair and beard shaved first, then gather the body hair together, and finally have his nails clipped.
Then, having gathered these together, while handing them over to the student, he says: "Having taken these, deposit them on a clump of *darbha* grass or at the root of an *udumbara* tree.
He deposits them there. Sitting down to the west of the fire facing east, he loosens his girdle with the mantra: "I loosen this bond of Varuṇa."

To whoever there is his son or pupil in that [household], giving it to him, he says: "Having taken this, deposit it at the foot of a *nyagrodha* tree or at the root of an *udumbara* tree. He then deposits it there, saying: "Here I bury the sorrow and the evil of such-and-one, the descendant of such-and-one, for the sake of his future enemies."

Having run about with *vṛkala* plants, he cleans his teeth [with them], saying: "Drive away [all obstacles] for the sake of food; King Bhaga has arrived. May he enter my mouth for the sake of splendor and fortune.
He pours together both kinds of water;
he pours cold water into the hot for the sake of distinguishing between the divine and the human.

Having taken some of those [waters] with his joined palms, he sprinkles him with the three verses beginning, “O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss,” and with the three verses beginning, “Golden-colored, pure, purifying.
This is according to the Brāhmaṇa passage: “Man is indeed divided sixfold.
Then, having mixed together all the fragrant powders, he sprinkles him over three times.

"Salutation to Śāka and Jañjabha! Salutation to those deities who are the seizers! With these words, he anoints himself: "Whatever fragrance is among the Apsarases, whatever glory is among the Gandharvas, whatever divine and human fragrance there is—may that enter into me here!
Then he puts on an unwashed garment, saying: "May my own body enter me; may an auspicious body enter me!"
In this very manner he wears the upper garment;
in this very manner from this point onward.

Then, having strung that jujube seed-gem (*bādara-maṇi*) upon a thread with gold placed beneath it, having placed it on a ladle and having wound a thread around the handle of the ladle, he offers it with the mantra: "This herb, the protecting one, the conquering, the powerful—may she make me possessed of the luster of Soma, possessed of the luster of the Sun; may she make me radiant with sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*), an eater of food, svāhā! Thus.
Then he causes him to float in a vessel of water with the verse: "And may we, through thee, cross over all enemies like flowing streams of water.

Having said, "Thou art a releaser from bonds," he carries [the vessel] across diagonally; for, according to this Brāhmaṇa passage, "they fasten the victim facing backward for the sake of distinction."

Then, having threaded these two ear-rings onto a string, placed them on the ladle, and wound the string around the handle of the ladle, he offers [the oblation] with: "Long life, splendor, great heroism, increase of wealth, and prosperity—may this gold enter this man for the sake of splendor and victory; [this] wealth, svāhā! Thus.

He offers the second oblation with: "I have called for the dog of gold; I have grasped the name of my father. May that make me resplendent with Soma, resplendent with the Sun, endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*), and a consumer of food—*svāhā*!
He offers the third oblation with: "O high-flying steed, conqueror of armies, victor in the assembly, winner of wealth! Prosper all prosperities that are concentrated in this gold—*svāhā*!"
He offers the fourth oblation with: "The Virāj and the Svarāj, the favor that is in our house, the fortune that is at the head of the kingdom—with that we unite thee, svāhā!

(17.41:322.7) He offers the fifth oblation with: "Bestow glory upon me among the Brāhmaṇas, bestow glory upon me among the Kṣatriyas, glory upon me among the Vaiśyas and Śūdras; I am thy glory, svāhā! (17.41:322.9) Then he causes the two of them to float in a water-vessel with this verse: "And all [prosperity] through thee... (viśvā uta tvayā vayam).
Taking one of those two, he ties it to the right ear with these five verses beginning, “Bestowing long life, bestowing luster.
Then he causes him to turn around [the fire] with the formula: “With the seasons, with the seasonal periods; with the nourishment of the year; with these, I follow after you.
In the same manner, he ties on the second amulet.
Then he puts on the wreath.
"O auspicious one, ascend my head, beautifying my face; indeed, beautify my face and increase my fortune.
You whom Jamadagni took away for Śraddhā and Kāmāyanī—her, this very one, I now fasten upon myself for splendor and for fortune."

He anoints his eyes with collyrium from Mount Trikakud, saying: "The collyrium from Trikakud, born upon the Himavat, with that I anoint you both; may there be mountain-like luster in me. He gazes into a mirror, saying: "My mind which has gone away, as I gaze into the mirror—this very thing I see within myself; may it be life-prolonging and bestowing luster upon me.
Then he puts on his two sandals, saying "Thou art heaven" over the right foot, and "Thou art earth" over the left.
Then he takes up the staff with the words, "O friend, protect me. He takes up the parasol with the words, "Thou art divine, thou art the fair-winged bird; protect me from the intermediate space.
He remains right there until the rising of the stars.
Then, when the stars have risen, he goes outside and worships the quarters with: "O six goddesses, wide ones, make wide space for us; O All-Gods, display your heroism here!
(17.42:323.16) "May we not be abandoned by our offspring nor by our bodies," [he says] to the stars. "May we not be delivered over to the enemy, O King Soma," [he says] to the moon.
"Having performed the formal attendance [upon the teacher], he goes wherever he desires"—
this is the *samāvartana* (the rite of returning home).
Then, as for the other [rites]:

having bathed silently at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), he emerges. Now, if he obtains a chariot, he touches the right wheel with the words, "Thou art the *Rathantara*"; the left wheel with "Thou art the *Bṛhat*"; and the middle [part] with "Thou art the *Vāmadevya*."
(17.43:324.5) Then he consecrates the moving chariot with the mantra: "O Aśvins, may this chariot of yours not suffer harm, neither in distress nor in prosperity.

(17.43:324.6) Now, if he intends to make it a stationary chariot, he touches water and then touches this [chariot] with the mantra: "Here is support; here is firm support; here is delight; here is pleasure; may it find rest here.
(17.43:324.8) Then the teacher brings him a seat of grass (kūrca).

Having circumambulated it clockwise, he sits down facing north, or he pushes him toward the east while facing westward, [saying]: "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom; thou art the teacher’s seat; may I not be separated from thee. Then he causes water to be brought for him, and with that he washes his feet.
He rubs the hands of the one who has washed them, saying: "In me be greatness; in me be fortune; in me be splendor; in me be glory.
Having touched water, he touches his own chest, saying: "In me be sensory power and vigor. Then he causes him to bring another [portion].
He receives it with the formula: "Come to me with splendor and glory; unite me with milk and brilliance! Make me beloved among subjects, a lord of cattle"—thus for a Brāhmaṇa.
"Make me beloved among cattle, a lord of subjects"—thus for a Rājanya.
Having touched it, he says: "Sprinkle [the water] eastward."
He consecrates the *madhuparka* with the mantra: "May he protect me; may he guard me; may he be pleased with me.
He receives it with both hands.
"Come to me with splendor and glory; unite me with milk and brilliance! Make me dear to all creatures, the lord of cattle"—thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
"Make me dear to cattle, the lord of creatures"—thus says the Rājanya.

If anything should fall upon it, he takes it up with his thumb and ring finger and casts it away toward this direction, saying: "O Neṣṭṛ, I cut away what has been struck; with that body of yours which is terrible, enter him who hates us and whom we hate.

Then, having touched water and stirred it together, he eats three times, saying: "O Breath, I bring this offering to you; make me the best, the overlord. "You are Soma; make me a drinker of Soma," he says a second time.
(17.44:325.10) "Thou art food; make me an eater of food," he says for the third time.
(17.44:325.11) Having drunk three times, he gives the remnant.
To whomever he desires to be superior to himself, to him he should give the remainder.
He consecrates the cow that has been brought near with the mantra: "Slay my evil and that of the one who brings [me] near.
They then either cause her to perform work or release her.
If he intends to have her work, he says, "Work!"

(17.44:325.14) Now, if he intends to release her, he addresses her with this mantra: "The cow is to be a milch-cow; she is the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, and the navel of immortality. I shall proclaim it to the people who understand: do not slay the innocent cow, the Aditi!
(17.44:326.1) "Let her drink water; let her eat grass; Om, release her! Then he causes him to bring cooked rice for him.
He eats it [saying], "May Brahman eat you; may Brahman eat you.
This consists of four ingredients: curds, honey, ghee, and water;
some say it consists of five: curds, milk, honey, ghee, and water.

(17.45:326.5) A Brāhmaṇa, traveling for the sake of Soma, encountered on the road a man with white skin, tawny eyes, and a split head from which matter was oozing. (17.45:326.6) He said to him, "How may I know you, O Blessed One? (17.45:326.7) He replied to him, "I am King Soma."

(17.45:326.7) "May that wicked Adhvaryu, who does not know the rites of the *naiṣṭyayana*, not press me! Wherever that wicked Adhvaryu, who does not know the rites of the *naiṣṭyayana*, presses me, there I shall flow away.
That and that Brahmin knows the *naiṣṭyayana* rites."
"I shall go to him;
he will cause these castes to be established for me.

Where they perform the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), there they offer oblations over the *ṛjīṣa* with a branch of *udumbara* or a branch of *palāśa*, or with a *sruva* ladle not smeared with clarified butter, using curds, milk, or honey-mixed [liquids], accompanied by the *naiṣṭyayana* verses.

With the section beginning, “O King Soma, that which they have cut from you with the pressing-stone,” and with the verse, “By these songs, whatever of ours is deficient here,” they offer the *ṛjīṣa* fourteen times. When they have completed the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), he should say to them: “Those who, having pierced the skin of the King [Soma] and having committed a cruel act here with the pressing-stones, go forth without having appeased [the offense] by means of the *naiṣṭyayana* rites—they indeed depart as those who have committed such a transgression.”

(17.46:327.3) "Those Soma-sacrificers who, having concluded the Soma-rite, purify themselves with water, yet return [to worldly life] saying, 'Our rite is finished'—he strikes them down in the hereafter. (17.46:327.5) "They pierce him with sword-blades at his place of rest—he who, without having pacified himself through the *naiṣṭyayana* rites, then ascends to the firmament (*nāka*).
(17.46:327.6) "Having become Vāyu, he blows toward the third heaven, the highest firmament—he who, having pacified himself through the *naiṣṭyayana* rites, then ascends to the firmament."
(17.46:327.8) “For the Adhvaryu, the Sacrificer, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Agnīdh, the Brahman, the Hotṛ, and the Udgātṛ—the King seizes their world, for they have not offered fourteen [oblations].
(17.46:327.9) “But those who offer these fourteen spoonfuls of curds—neither their world, nor their progeny, nor their vigor does the King seize.”
(17.46:327.11) “Satisfying the King with the pressing-stones, the officiating priests, appeasing his harshness with milk—thus offer the fourteen [verses]. So it is said.
Now, it is indeed said:
"The exponents of the Veda say, 'He alone should perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices who performs them together with Indra.
The Vaimṛdha offering is to be performed subsequently at the Full Moon sacrifice."
(17.47:328.1) "By that, the Full Moon sacrifice is accompanied by Indra; the curd for Indra is at the New Moon;
by that, the New Moon sacrifice is accompanied by Indra. Thus it is said.
“By what means, indeed, do both [the sacrificer] and Indra become possessed of oblations for one who has not sacrificed?
“One should say: ‘By means of the cake (puroḍāśa) dedicated to Indra and Agni. Now, it is also said:
(17.47:328.3) "Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did that too.
(17.47:328.4) "The gods saw this offering:
a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu, a pap for Sarasvatī, and a pap for Sarasvant."
Having completed that Full Moon sacrifice, they performed this subsequent offering. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
He who has a rival should, having completed the Full Moon sacrifice, perform this subsequent offering.

"By means of the Full-moon sacrifice itself, having hurled the thunderbolt at his rival, he appropriates both the deities and the sacrifice of his rival through the offering to Agni and Viṣṇu"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
This is the performance according to one's desire for one who has a rival.
"He [offers] paired animals to Sarasvat and Sarasvatī."
"He takes away everything that he has," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it occurs as follows:
"One who has rivals should sacrifice only at the full moon, not at the new moon"—thus [it is said]. He [performs] the full moon sacrifice.
"One who has rivals should sacrifice only at the full moon, not at the new moon."
"Having slain the rival, he does not cause him to swell again," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"This [act] is either submerged during the spreading [of the grass] or submerged during the exclusion," so it is said.
Now, indeed, there occurs [this]:
"One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Sākaṃprasthāyīya.
Intending to perform this sacrifice, he prepares a large vessel made of Udumbara wood and abundant clarified butter.

Then, having performed the introductory formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, and the Sāṃnāyya offering for Indra.

Having performed the well-known rite with the oblation for Agni, he then takes portions from the other two oblations into a large vessel made of Udumbara wood and says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra," or "for Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra. [He adds: "It should be offered full with a large [ladle]. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Indra," or "to Mahendra," if he is a sacrificer to Mahendra.
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers together with the cup:
"Indra, being satisfied, satisfies him with offspring and cattle"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said:
(17.48:329.6) "He offers with a wooden vessel;
for an earthenware one does not receive the oblation.
It is made of udumbara wood."
"The udumbara is strength; cattle are strength. By means of strength he wins for him strength and cattle," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"This [place] is either reachable by swimming or reachable by despair," so it is said.
Now, indeed, there is this [text]: "It comes to pass."
"One who has not attained prosperity should not sacrifice to Mahendra.
"There are indeed three who have attained prosperity: the learned man, the village headman, and the nobleman; for them, Mahendra is the deity.
Thus, he who, other than these, should desire to sacrifice to Mahendra, having sacrificed to Indra for a year, offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati.
That well-known sacrifice is completed.
Then, when the new moon day arrives, he sacrifices to Mahendra on that day;
from that point forward, he becomes a sacrificer to Mahendra alone.
Now, it is indeed said: "One should sacrifice to Indra for a year;
for one does not overstep the vow for a year."
"The very deities being sacrificed to kindle him with prosperity; he becomes more wealthy," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, it is further stated: "After a year has passed, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati."
"Agni, the lord of vows, causes him who has slain Vṛtra to adhere to his vow for a full year;
thereafter he may sacrifice according to his desire"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, indeed, it is said:
"One who does not sacrifice with Soma should not perform the *saṃnayya* offering. "The milk of one who does not sacrifice with Soma has not yet arrived.
"If one who does not sacrifice with Soma were to perform the *saṃnayya*, that would be mere theft; he commits a falsehood."
(17.50:330.6) "Moreover, it is poured out further;
