"He places milk in himself by means of milk," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Now, it is indeed said: "He who, for whom the oblation has been set out, sees the moon rise in the east, is deprived of offspring and cattle; he causes his enemy to prosper."
(17.50:330.9) "One should divide the rice grains into three parts.
Those that are of medium size, one should make into a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Dātṛ. Those that are the largest, one should make into a pap of curdled milk for Indra Pradātṛ."
(17.50:330.11) "Those [grains] that have not been husked, for those he prepares a pap of boiled milk for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.

For this sacrifice, these are the verses: "O Agni, give wealth to the donor"; "Give us, O Agni"; "We invoke the giver"; "The wielder of the thunderbolt is the giver"; "Forth that [gift] of yours today"; "What indeed, O Viṣṇu, is to be concealed from you?"—these belong to one who has already sacrificed.
He sacrifices with the former verse as one that has already reached its goal, and with the latter as one that has not yet reached its goal.

"One should not sacrifice with two [formulas]. For if one were to sacrifice immediately with the first, he would make a failure (*chambaṭ*) with the second; if he were to sacrifice immediately with the second, he would make a failure with the first."
"There is the *neṣṭṛ*-offering, but no sacrifice.
Consequently, one is born timid and lacking in confidence.
One should perform only a single [offering]; then a confident son is born to him."

(17.50:331.1) <Disregarding that, he should sacrifice with only two [verses].> (17.50:331.1) <With the first, he seizes the very mouth of the sacrifice;> (17.50:331.2) <he sacrifices with the second.>
"By the first [verse] he wins the deities; by the second, power (*indriya*). By the first he conquers the world of the gods; by the second, the world of men.
He approaches more numerous sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*)," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is said:
"This sacrifice is named Sumanā.
For him who performs this sacrifice today and the moon rises behind him, there shall be prosperity for him in this very world. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, indeed, it is so stated.
"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Dākṣāyaṇayajña.
At the full moon, one should offer the *saṃnaya*; at the new moon, one should sacrifice with the *maitrāvaruṇī āmikṣā*. One who is about to perform this sacrifice prepares an unwashed garment.
Then, on the fast-day of the full moon, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati; that well-known sacrifice is concluded.
Then, on this day, the calves are driven away for Indra.
Having caused the milk for Indra to be milked, he observes the fast either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* offering or silently.
Then, in the morning, he offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and the *sāṃnāyya* for Indra. Thus this sacrifice of two oblations is completed.
At this point, having invited one another, they consume this *sāṃnāyya* offering dedicated to Indra.
Then, having put on a new, unwashed garment, he observes the vow for the latter half of the month.
His vow is as follows: he does not speak untruth, he does not eat meat, he does not approach a woman, and they do not wash his garment with alkaline lye.
Then, when the new moon day arrives, on its fast-day he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati. That sacrifice concludes in the established manner.
Then, on this day, the calves are driven away for Mitra and Varuṇa.
Having caused the milk for Mitra-Varuṇa to be milked, he observes the fast, either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* or silently.
Then, in the morning, he offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for Mitra-Varuṇa. This sacrifice of two oblations is thus completed.
At the time for the *vājina*, he proceeds with the *vājina*; he sets aside the garment;
he releases the vow.
Having released his vow, he enters this first fortnight.
Then the full moon arrives;
the lord of the vow departs.
Whatever [portion] remains above, O Lord of Vows, with that he begins;
this is the Soma-sacrifice established for a year.
Now they call this the *iḍādadha*.
The procedure for the garment and for the *vratapati* is the same.
Likewise, having caused the milk for Indra to be milked, he observes the fast according to the ritual procedure for the *sāṃnāyya*, either silently or [according to the prescribed rule].

Then, in the morning, he offers an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, one on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma, and the *sāṃnāyya* to Indra. This sacrifice consisting of three offerings is completed.
At this point, having invited one another, they consume that *sāṃnāyya* dedicated to Indra.
Having put on a garment that has been beaten [with perfume], he observes the vow during the dark fortnight.
When the new moon arrives,
he performs the sacrifice on its fast-day (upavasatha).
Likewise, having caused the milk for Mitra and Varuṇa to be milked according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya*—either with the prescribed ritual formula or silently—he observes the fast.

Then, in the morning, he offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, and curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa. This sacrifice consisting of three oblations is thus completed.
At the time for the *vājina*, he proceeds with the *vājina*; he puts away the garment;
he releases the vow.
Having completed his vow, he enters this first fortnight. Then the full moon arrives;
the Lord of Vows departs.
Whatever [rite] follows the *vratapati*, with that he begins;
this constitutes the Soma-sacrifice submerged within the year.
Now, the sacrifice of one who has rivals consists of four wheels.
It is the same for both the garment and the Vratapati [offering].
Likewise, having caused the milk for Indra to be milked, he observes the fast either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* or silently.

Then, in the morning, he offers an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, a silent sacrifice (*upāṃśuyāja*) to Sarasvat, an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma, and the *sāṃnāyya* offering to Indra.
This sacrifice of four oblations is completed. At this point, having invited one another, they consume that *sāṃnāyya* offering dedicated to Indra.
Having put on a new, unwashed garment in the same manner, he observes the vow during the waning fortnight.
When the new moon day arrives,
he does not perform the sacrifice on the fast-day itself.
In the same manner, having caused the milk for Mitra-Varuṇa to be milked according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya*—either silently or with the prescribed ritual formula—he observes the fast.

Then, in the morning, he offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a silent sacrifice (*upāṃśuyāja*) for Sarasvatī, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, and curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for Mitra-Varuṇa. Thus this sacrifice of four oblations is completed.
At the time for the *vājina*, he proceeds with the *vājina*; he lays aside the garment;
he releases the vow.
Having concluded his vow, he enters this first fortnight. Then the full moon arrives;
the Lord of the Vow departs.
Whatever [rite] follows the *vratapati* sacrifice, with that he begins; this is the *saṃvatsarāvagada*, which is a form of the Soma sacrifice.
This is that four-wheeled sacrifice for one who has rivals.

Just as here on earth a four-wheeled chariot goes along crushing [its way], even so does he, having performed this sacrificial rite, go along crushing evil and his rival. This is the sacrifice of Vasiṣṭha, the sacrifice of Keśin, the sacrifice of Sārvaseni.

"When Vasiṣṭha performed sorcery against the Saudāsas, he indeed overcame them by means of that very [rite]. When Keśin performed sorcery against Khāṇḍika, he indeed overcame him by means of that very [rite]. When Sārvaseni performed sorcery against his rivals, he indeed overcame them by means of that very [rite]."
He is about to perform the Cāturmāsya Soma sacrifices. He prepares two sets of materials: those for the Agniṣṭoma and the materials for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
Having performed the New Moon sacrifice before the full moon of Phālguna or Caitra, he undergoes initiation.
His consecrations (*dīkṣā*) are unlimited; there are three *upasads*.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the full-moon day, the day fit for sacrifice.
For him, it indeed turns out accordingly.
He proceeds from the Upavasatha day with the well-known ritual procedure.
Now, on this day, the calves are driven away for the Viśvedevas;
he causes the milk for the Vaiśvadeva to be milked according to the procedure for the Sāṃnāyya, or silently.
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milks, they fast.
Then, in the morning, there is the threefold sacrificial grass (*barhis*); he spreads it as if it were a single unit.
Then he dedicates the animal victim for Agni;
for that [victim], one to be offered to the Viśvedevas is to be seized as a supplementary offering. The oblations for the Viśvedevas follow the morning *savana* offerings of that [victim].
The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa*-calls.
For the other oblations, [the calls are] "Recite! and "Sacrifice!
Thus, the *trivṛt* *agniṣṭoma* concludes in its regular manner.
Before the *dhānāsoma* offerings, he proceeds with the *vājina*.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the *avabhṛtha* bath;
the *avabhṛtha* is performed in the established manner.
Having performed the *udayanīya* sacrifice, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.

For that [cow], there is an animal to be immolated for Heaven and Earth. Having proceeded with the two omenta of those two in the established manner, he offers the two sacrificial cakes belonging to the animal victims.
The animal sacrifice concludes in the same manner as the two-animal rite (*dvipaśu*).
Now, it has been stated that one should perform the Full-moon sacrifice and the Vaimṛdha sacrifice;
this being so, then, after four months have passed...
One who is about to sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa and Soma offerings undergoes initiation;
his initiation period is of unlimited duration, and there are twelve Upasad days.
He purchases [the Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "On the full-moon day, which is the sacrificial day for me, the second day will be accomplished.
For him, it is accomplished accordingly;
he proceeds from the fast-day (upavasatha) by means of the established ritual procedure.
Then, on this day, the calves are driven away from their mothers for the Maruts.
He causes the milk for the Maruts to be milked either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* or silently.
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milks, they observe the fast.
Then, in the morning, he dedicates an animal victim for Agni;
for that, there is one to be immolated for the Maruts.
Following those [dedications], the seven oblations of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice follow the morning pressing.
When he distributes the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), he makes the *mārjālīya* hearth perpetual.
When the oblations have been placed near, having performed the circumambulation with fire around the *karambha* vessels at the *gārhapatya*, he proceeds with them at the *mārjālīya*.
The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by ritual calls (*praiṣa*).
"Recite the invitatory verse! Perform the offering!"—with these words for the other oblations, the fifteen-verse Ukthya sacrifice is completed in the regular manner.
He thereby ensures the continuity of the Ahīna rite.
Then, on this day, the calves are driven away for Varuṇa.
He causes the milk for Varuṇa to be milked either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* or silently.
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milks, they observe the fast.
Then, in the morning, he dedicates an animal victim to Agni.
For that [offering], one to Varuṇa is to be seized as an additional victim.
Following the morning pressing offerings of that [victim], there follow two additional victims: one for Varuṇa and one for Ka.
The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa* calls.
For the other two oblations, [the calls are] "Recite! and "Sacrifice!
The *ukthya* sacrifice, consisting of seventeen [stotras], concludes in the regular manner.
Before the *dhānāsoma* offerings, he performs the ritual with the two *vājina* portions.
The procedure is the same up to the *avabhṛtha* bath.
Now, at this *avabhṛtha*, they take up the scrapings for Varuṇa and the husks.
For the offering to Varuṇa, there is a portion of the *āmikṣā* for Varuṇa that is to be cut off.
They scatter the husks together with the *ṛjīṣa*. The *avabhṛtha* rite is performed in the established manner.
Having performed the *udayanīyā* sacrifice, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.
For that [cow], there is a goat to be seized for the Kāya [deity]. Having proceeded with the two omenta in the established manner, he offers the two animal-cake oblations (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
The animal sacrifice with two animals is concluded in the same manner as [the standard] animal sacrifice.
Now, it has been stated that one should perform the Full Moon sacrifice and the Vaimṛdha sacrifice;
thereafter, after four months have passed.
One who is about to sacrifice with the Sākamedha Soma offerings undergoes initiation.
His period of initiation is unlimited, and there are twelve Upasad days.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "On the full-moon day, which is the sacrificial day for me, the third day shall be completed.

Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and having set aside the milks, they fast.
Then, in the morning, he dedicates an animal victim to Agni; for that [victim], one dedicated to Agni Anīkavant is to be seized as an additional offering.
The Ānīkavata offering follows the morning *savana* offerings;
the *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praisha* calls.
For the Ānīkavata, [the calls are] "Recite! and "Sacrifice! (*anubrūhi*, *yaja*).
The Sāṃtapana sacrifice follows the midday pressing;
the Savanīya offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa* calls.
For the Sāṃtapana, [the calls are] "Recite! and "Sacrifice!"
The Ukthya sacrifice, characterized by the twenty-one-fold stoma, concludes in a straightforward manner.
He performs the Ahīna-saṃsati rite.
Then, having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters and set aside the milks, they observe the fast-day.

this being so, then, after four months have passed...
One who is about to sacrifice with the *śunāsīrīya* Soma performs the consecration (*dīkṣā*).
Its consecrations are unlimited; there are three *upasad* days.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the full-moon day, which is fit for sacrifice";
and it happens for him accordingly.
He proceeds from the Upavasatha day by means of the established ritual procedure.
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milks, they observe the fast.
Now, on this night, the calves are driven away for Vāyu.
In the morning, he causes the milk for Vāyu to be milked either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* or silently.
Then he dedicates the animal victim for Agni;
for that [offering], a bull for Indra is to be seized as an additional victim.
The oblations of Śunāsīra follow the morning pressing offerings of that [victim].
The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa* calls.
For the other oblations, [the calls are] "Recite! and "Sacrifice!
The *jyotiḥ-agniṣṭoma* concludes in a straightforward manner.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the *avabhṛtha* bath;
the *avabhṛtha* is performed in the established manner.
Having sacrificed with the *udayanīya* offering, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa.
For her, a victim for Sūrya is to be immolated. Having proceeded with the omenta of those two in the established manner, he offers the two animal-cake oblations.
It concludes in the same way as an animal sacrifice involving two animals.
Now, it has been stated: "Having performed the Full-moon sacrifice and the Vaimṛdha sacrifice..."
(17.59:339.3) Now, therefore, they call this the "Jyotis-ayana. One is about to sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva* *soma*. The opening rite (*pratipad*) is the same [as in the preceding sacrifice].
Only this much is different.
The *trivṛt* is the *agniṣṭoma* there;
the *jyotis* is here.
Now, therefore, after four months, he becomes one who intends to sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsa Soma sacrifice.
He undergoes initiation.
His initiatory period is unlimited; there are six *upasads*.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the full-moon day, the day fit for sacrifice."
For him it succeeds in this manner;
he proceeds from the fast-day with the well-known ritual. Now, on this day, two sets of calves are driven away for the Maruts and for Varuṇa.
He causes two [cows] to be milked for the *sāṃnāyya* according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya*, either with the prescribed formulas or silently.
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milks, they fast.
Then, in the morning, he dedicates the animal victim to Agni.
For this [sacrifice], two animals to be seized for offering are prescribed: one for Māruta and one for Vāruṇa.
Following the morning libations (*prātaḥsavanīya*), seven oblations for the Varuṇapraghāsa rites take place.
When he distributes the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths at the morning libation, he then makes the *mārjālīya* fire perpetual.
When the oblations have been brought near, having carried fire around the *karambha* vessels at the *gārhapatya* fire, he proceeds with them at the *mārjālīya* fire.
The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by formal calls (*praiṣa*);
for the other oblations, [the calls are] "Recite! and "Sacrifice! (17.59:339.17).
The offerings to Varuṇa and Ka are followed by those of the midday pressing;
the *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa* calls, while for the other two oblations, [the calls are] "Recite! and "Sacrifice! respectively.
The Jyotirukthya sacrifice concludes in a straightforward manner;
the subsequent ritual procedure is the same as that of the Dvirātra.
Now, therefore, after four months.
One who is about to sacrifice with the Soma of the Sākamedha undergoes initiation. His initiation periods are unlimited; there are six Upasad days.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the full-moon day, the day of sacrifice";
for him, it happens accordingly.
He proceeds from the Upavasatha day by means of the established ritual procedure.
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and having set aside the milks, they fast.
Then, in the morning, he dedicates the animal victim for Agni. For that [sacrifice], there are animals to be seized: one for Anīkavant, one for Kraiḍin, and a hornless goat for Prajāpati.
The *ānīkavata* offering follows the morning *savanīya* offerings;
the *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa* calls.
For the *ānīkavata*, [the calls are] "Recite! and "Sacrifice! (*anubrūhi*, *yaja*).
The Sāṃtapana [offering] follows the midday [pressing];
the Savanīya offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa* calls.
For the Sāṃtapana, [the calls are]: "Recite the invitatory verse! and "Offer the oblation! (*anubrūhi*, *yaja*).
The great oblations (*mahāhavīṃṣi*), beginning with the *gṛhamedhīya*, follow the offerings of the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavanīya*).
When he distributes the fires to the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths at the third pressing, he makes the *mārjālīya* fire perpetual.

Having performed the rites with the great oblations and having cooked the oblations for the Great Sacrifice to the Ancestors (*mahāpitṛyajña*) on the *gārhapatya* fire, he proceeds with them at the *mārjālīya*.
The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa* calls.
For the other oblations, [the calls are] "Recite! and "Sacrifice! Thus, the *jyotiḥ-ukthya* concludes in a straightforward manner.
The subsequent ritual procedure is the same as that for the Trirātra; thus indeed is the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice.
(17.61:340.17) Now, therefore, they call this the Great Sacrifice (*mahāyajña*). Some say it is the Jyotiratirātra.
He undergoes initiation (*dīkṣate*).
His consecration period is unlimited, and there are twelve Upasad days.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the full-moon day, the sacrificial day.
For him, it indeed turns out accordingly.
He proceeds from the Upavasatha day with the well-known ritual procedure. Now, on this day, three sets of calves are driven away for the Viśve Devas, the Maruts, and Varuṇa;
he causes three [cows] to be milked, either according to the procedure for the Sāṃnāyya or silently.
(17.61:341.5) Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the milks, they fast.
(17.61:341.6) Then in the morning, he spreads the threefold sacrificial grass as if it were a single unit.
Then he dedicates the animal victim for Agni.

For that [sacrifice], there are animals to be immolated: one for the Viśvedevas, one for the Maruts, one for Varuṇa, one for Ānīlavat, one for Krīḍin, a hornless goat for Prajāpati, and a bull for Indra.
The oblations for the Viśvedevas follow its morning pressing.
The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa* calls.
For the other oblations, [the calls are] "Recite! and "Sacrifice!". All the Varuṇapraghāsa oblations follow those of the midday pressing.
When he distributes the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths at the midday pressing, he makes the *mārjālīya* hearth perpetual.
When the oblations have been set down, having carried fire around the *karambha* vessels at the *gārhapatya*, he proceeds with them at the *mārjālīya*.
The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by ritual calls (*praiṣa*).
(17.62:341.15) For the other oblations, [the calls] are "Recite! and "Sacrifice! (17.62:341.15). The Mahāhavis offerings, beginning with the Ānīkavata, follow the Tṛtīyasavana offerings.
(17.62:341.16) When he distributes the fires to the Dhiṣṇiya hearths at the Tṛtīyasavana, he makes the Mārjālīya fire perpetual.
Having performed the Mahāhavis offerings and having cooked the oblations for the Mahāpitṛyajña on the Gārhapatya fire, he proceeds with them on the Mārjālīya fire.
The Savanīya offerings are accompanied by formal calls (*praiṣa*);
for the other oblations, [the calls are] "Recite the invitatory verse! and "Offer the oblation! (*anubrūhi*, *yaja*).
The Jyotiratirātra sacrifice is concluded in the straightforward manner.
Having performed the Vājina offerings prior to the Dhānāsoma offerings, he performs the Traiyambaka rites.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Avabhṛtha bath.
Then, at this *avabhṛtha* rite, they take up the scrapings of the *vāruṇī* [curd] and the husks.
Of the *vāruṇa* [oblation], there is a portion of the *vāruṇī āmikṣā* to be cut off.
Together with the *ṛjīṣa*, they scatter the husks.
The *avabhṛtha* bath is well-known.
Having performed the *udayanīya* sacrifice, he dedicates a barren cow to Mitra and Varuṇa;
for that [cow], there are animals to be seized for Dyāvāpṛthivī, Ka, Viśvakarman, and Sūrya.
Having performed the ritual with their omenta in the established manner, he offers the animal-cake oblations (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
These are followed by the *Śunāsīrīya* oblations beginning with that for Āditya; the animal-cake oblations are accompanied by formal calls (*praiṣa*).
(17.62:342.11) For the other oblations, [the calls are] "Recite! and "Sacrifice! (17.62:342.12).
The animal sacrifice with five victims concludes in the same manner as a single-animal sacrifice.

(17.62:342.13) Then, having performed the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices, the sacrificer sits down in his place and, with a three-striped porcupine quill and a razor of red iron, he has his hair cut and shaved on the head—first in front, then on the south, then on the west, then on the north, and finally on top.
The Cāturmāsya Soma sacrifices are completed; the Cāturmāsya Soma sacrifices are completed.

One is about to sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava. He procures the sacrificial fees consisting of four horses of thirty-four years of age, a black antelope skin, two gold and silver plates, a vessel made of *parṇa* wood, and clarified butter for the consecration.
Now, indeed, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage:
"The Hotṛ is one wearing a garland, ruddy, mirmira, and possessing three tufts of hair.
Now, he who is bald but has hair growing around his head is indeed "one wearing a garland" (*parisrajī*). Furthermore, he who is white, perspiring, covered with moles, and tawny-eyed is "mirmira."
Now, this [sacrificer] who possesses the three Vedas is the "three-pointed" one;
he undergoes initiation,
and for him, when he has fasted for one night, they purchase the Soma.
There are three *upasads*.
A threefold (*trivṛt*) *agniṣṭoma* is performed, having the *rathantara* as its *sāman*, accompanied by the *pravargya* ceremony;
it has a single *stoma* in *gāyatrī* verses.
The preparation of the oblations for the Devasū is well known. For this [sacrifice], there is an *atigrāhya* cup dedicated to Bṛhaspati;
an animal dedicated to Bṛhaspati is to be immolated.
The procedure is the same up to the time of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
At the time of the consecration, he spreads a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) on the sacrificer’s seat with its neck toward the east and the hair facing upward.

Having seated the sacrificer upon it facing the east and having placed gold and silver disks on either side of him, he pours clarified butter (*ājya*) into a vessel made of *parṇa* wood and sprinkles [him] while reciting: "Bṛhaspati, being first born from the great light in the highest heaven, Seven-mouthed and many-born, with his roar, He, with seven rays, blew away the darkness."
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I consecrate you with the Bṛhaspatisava.
Thus it is said when he has been wiped all over; "they cry out together"—this is the same [formula] up to the wiping of the face.
At his morning pressing, when the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been set down, eleven sacrificial gifts are led forth;
at the midday pressing, when the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been set down, eleven [gifts are led forth];
and at the third pressing, when the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been set down, twelve including a horse.
"One should give the horse at the midday pressing alone," so said Maudgalya.
This, indeed, is the Naimārjana sacrifice.
Just as this river from the mountains sweeps away [impurities], even so does he, having performed this sacrificial rite, go forth sweeping away evil and his rival.
In this very first fortnight, he should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma consisting of four stomas for the sake of peace before any mishap occurs.

When a king, having performed the Rājasūya, desires, "May I be consecrated by means of the Bṛhaspatisava," they say regarding this: "One who has been consecrated by the Rājasūya must not be consecrated by any other sacrificial rite."
"He becomes one who does not descend again.
"Having been consecrated by both the Brahman and the Kṣatra, he should indeed be consecrated"—
thus he undergoes initiation.
For this [sacrifice], there are three initiation days (*dīkṣā*) and three *upasad* days; [the ritual] is the same up until the time of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
At the time of the consecration, they proceed while wiping the cups (*camasa*) belonging to the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinīya*).
This is the twenty-fourth [section]. When a king,
intending to perform the Rājasūya sacrifice, reflects, "I would have myself consecrated among the three classes— the domestic priest (purohita), the chariot-maker (sthapati), and the herald (sūta)"—
then the domestic priest undergoes initiation.
For this [sacrifice], there are three initiation days and three *upasads*, identical [in procedure] up to the time of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
At the time of the consecration, he sprinkles him with the residue of the *śukra* and *manthin* cups.
This is a Catuṣṭoma sacrifice.
(18.3:345.6) A *sthapati* is about to sacrifice with the *Sthapatisava*.
He procures a bull’s hide, two gold and silver plates, and a vessel made of *udumbara* wood for the consecration with curds;
he then undergoes initiation.
For this [sacrifice], there are three initiation days (*dīkṣā*) and three pressing days (*upasad*).
A spotted heifer (*pṛśni*) dedicated to the Maruts is to be offered as a sacrificial animal (*paṣṭhauhī*) for the [deity] Agni.
Seven oblations follow the morning-pressing offerings: "In that there is an offering to Agni, it is because prosperity has Agni as its mouth"—these are the [details].
It is the same up to the time of the consecration.
At the time of the consecration, he spreads a bull’s hide with its neck pointing eastward and its hair side upward upon the sacrificer’s seat.

Having seated the sacrificer there facing eastward and having placed gold and silver ornaments on both sides of him, he brings curds into a vessel made of Udumbara wood and sprinkles him with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I sprinkle you with the Sthapatisava. Thus.
When he has wiped his face, they cry out together; this is the same [procedure] up to the wiping of the mouth.
This very sacrifice is the Sthapatisava, a seventeen-fold Agniṣṭoma;
this indeed is the Sthapatisava.
This is the Vaiśyasava;
this is the Māsasava. By means of this, the months sacrificed before this time.
The charioteer (*sūta*), being about to sacrifice with the *Sūtasava*,
prepares a black antelope skin, two gold and silver plates, a vessel made of *parṇa* wood, gold, and clarified butter for the consecration;
he then undergoes initiation.
For this [sacrifice], there are three initiation days (*dīkṣā*) and three pressing days (*upasad*).
Eight oblations follow the morning pressings: "In that there is an offering to Agni, for the Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni"—these [details] remain the same until the time of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
At the time of the consecration, he spreads a black antelope skin on the sacrificer’s seat with its neck pointing eastward and the hair side up.

Having seated the sacrificer upon it facing eastward and having placed gold and silver ornaments around him, he pours clarified butter into a vessel made of *parṇa* wood, purifies it with gold, and sprinkles [the sacrificer] while reciting: "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the controller of speech, I sprinkle you with the Sūtasava."
When he has wiped his face, they cry out together; this is the same [procedure] up to the wiping of the mouth.
This very sacrifice is the Sūtasava, a seventeen-fold Agniṣṭoma;
this indeed is the Sūtasava.
This is the Grāmaṇī-sava;
this is the Ṛtu-sava. By means of this, the Ṛtus sacrificed previously.
One is about to sacrifice with the Soma-sava.
He procures a cow that has recently calved for Soma, a black antelope skin, two gold and silver ornaments, a vessel made of Palāśa wood, and milk for the consecration.
Now, there is indeed a Brāhmaṇa passage on this.
"Whatever belongs to the Rājasūya, excluding the Soma sacrifice, all that is included here.
Having performed the New Moon oblation, he proceeds for eight days with the Ānumata and subsequent rites; for a year he performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, beginning with the Saptendraturīya.
Then he performs the offerings of the Ratnins.
(18.5:346.20) Then he sacrifices with the oblations of the *devasū*.
(18.5:347.1) Then he immolates this cow, the calf of a Soma-cow (*saumī sūtavaśā*).
Before she has been slaughtered, he spreads a black antelope skin on the sacrificer’s seat with its neck toward the east and the hair side up.

(18.5:347.3) Having seated the sacrificer facing east and having placed gold and silver plates on both sides of him, he pours milk into a vessel made of *parṇa* wood and consecrates him [with these words]: "The invincible one in battles, the protector in armies, the winner of light, dwelling in the waters, the guardian of the enclosure; born for the fray, with good habitation and great renown—thee, O Soma, conquering, may we rejoice after!"*

(18.5:347.6) "<In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I consecrate you with the Soma-consecration."> (18.5:347.8) Thus, when he has been wiped clean, they cry out together; this is the same [procedure] up to the wiping of the face. (18.5:347.9) Then he performs the sacrifice with the *saṃsṛp* oblations.
(18.5:347.9) Then he performs the Diśām Aveṣṭi sacrifice consisting of five oblations. (18.5:347.10) Then he performs the animal sacrifice with two animals.
(18.5:347.11) Then he performs the sacrifices with the oblations of the Sātyadūtas.
(18.5:347.11) Then he sacrifices with the first *prayuja* oblations.
(18.5:347.12) Then, having sacrificed with the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha offerings, he sacrifices with the subsequent *prayuja* oblations.
(18.5:347.13) Then he sacrifices with the Devikā oblations.
Then he performs the Traidhātavīya sacrifice;
then he performs the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. The Soma-sava is completed in thirteen and a half months.
One who is about to sacrifice with the Pṛthisava procures a red bull’s hide, two gold and silver plates, a four-cornered trough made of Udumbara wood, and water collected from the four quarters.
Now, indeed, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage:
"Whatever belongs to the Rājasūya that does not require a high altar, all that is performed here."
Having sacrificed with the New Moon oblation, he proceeds for eight days with the offerings beginning with the *ānumata*, and for seven days with those beginning with the *indraturīya*.
Then he sacrifices with the oblations of the *ratnins*;
then he sacrifices with the oblations of the *devasū*s.
Then he offers this sacrifice of four oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, a cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśvedevas, and a pap for Bṛhaspati.
Before the [oblation] has been placed together, he spreads out a red bull's hide upon the sacrificer’s seat, with the neck toward the east and the hair side up.

Having seated the sacrificer facing east and having placed gold and silver plates on both sides of him, he pours together four kinds of water into a trough made of *udumbara* wood and consecrates him with the verse: "They who gave me fifty horses—may they be the object of joint praise! O Agni, bestow brilliant, great, and lofty glory upon the wealthy patrons; O Immortal One, grant it to men like heroes among men."

(18.6:348.11) “At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I consecrate you with the wide-flowing consecration.
(18.6:348.13) When he has been wiped clean, they cry out together; the procedure is the same up to the wiping of the face. (18.6:348.14) Then he performs the sacrifice with the *saṃsṛp* oblations.

Then he performs the Diśām Aveṣṭi sacrifice consisting of five oblations. Then, having passed over it, he performs the animal sacrifice of two animals and sacrifices with the oblations of the Sātyadūtas.
Then he sacrifices with the oblations of the Pūrva-prayujas.
Then, having performed the Full Moon sacrifice and the Vaimṛdha sacrifice, he sacrifices with the subsequent Prayuja oblations;
then he sacrifices with the Devikā oblations;
then he sacrifices with the Traidhātavīya offering.
Then he performs the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice;
the Pṛthisava is completed within one and a half months.

One who is about to sacrifice with the Gosava prepares ten thousand cows as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), two ornaments of gold and silver, a vessel made of *parṇa* wood, and a *pratidhuk* [milk] for the consecration (*abhiṣecana*).
He undergoes initiation;
it has six days of initiation and six days of *upasad*.
It is the same up to the time of the consecration.
At the time of the consecration, a portion of the sacrificial altar equal in size to a black antelope skin remains unexcavated at the place where the sacrificer will stand.

(18.7:349.5) Having seated the sacrificer facing eastward and having placed him between two plates of gold and silver, he pours the *pratiduh* milk into a vessel made of *parṇa* wood and consecrates him during the *Bṛhat* chant with [the mantra]: "Born with wealth, increased by power, the best sustainer of dominion among dominions, the bestower of vital strength; great, established in greatness, be watchful over the dominion and the kingdom! I consecrate you with the sovereign rule of Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin."
"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, I consecrate you with the Gosava.
When he has been wiped clean, they cry out together; this is the same [procedure] up to the wiping of the face.
This very Gosava consists of thirty-six [stomas], is entirely Ukthya, possesses both Sāmans, and involves abundant sacrificial fees.
During the Pavamāna laud, they perform the Kaṇvarathantara.

One who is about to perform the Odanasava sacrifice prepares the following: the hide of a red bull, two gold and silver plates, a *pravarta* weight of one hundred *mānas*, four men of the [four] castes—a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra—four liquids—honey, *surā* liquor, milk, and water—four vessels made of gold, silver, bronze, and clay, four sacrificial fees—a piece of gold weighing one hundred *mānas*, a bow with three arrows, a goad, and a water-pot filled with beans.

Four sticks—two made of *parṇa* wood, two of *nyagrodha*, two of *aśvattha*, and two of *phālgunapācya*—four vessels made of various kinds of wood, groats, three bunches of *darbha* grass, a four-cornered trough (*droṇa*) made of *udumbara* wood, four hundred measures of water collected from the various quarters, and a chariot. With these materials prepared, he waits for the arrival of Rohiṇī. Then, [at the time] of Rohiṇī, the *śālīna* householder settles by the eastern fire, and the one who has established the sacred fires settles by the *uttapanīya* fire and the *anvāhāryapacana*.
(18.8:350.8) Then, having hastened there in the latter part of the night, the Adhvaryu gives the command: "Cook the *ekaudana*!
(18.8:350.9) They cook it in such a way that it is ready before the rising of the sun.
(18.8:350.10) "It must be prepared by the rising sun," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

(18.8:350.10) Then, having cooked this rice-mess and poured clarified butter over it, he removes it toward the north. (18.8:350.11) Then, having washed this vessel and spread a layer [of ghee] within it, he draws the rice into it as if without striking it,
(18.8:350.12) having made a hollow for pouring ghee and having brought a large quantity of clarified butter.
(18.8:350.13) Then he causes these four castes to sit down to the south, facing north.

(18.8:350.14) Then, while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, he offers four spoonfuls with the verse: "In the lion, in the tiger, and also in the adder... (18.8:351.1) Having offered each oblation, he pours the remnants over the Pravarta stone with the formulas: "Thou art the ruler (rāṭ), thou art the far-ruler (virāṭ), thou art the sovereign ruler (samrāṭ), thou art the self-ruler (svarāṭ)."
(18.8:351.2) Then, having carried this Pravarta around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it to the south.
Then he asks for this golden vessel.
Having poured honey into it across a strainer and having added groats, he stirs it with two sticks made of *parṇa* wood, saying: "For Indra, the radiant one, I mix thee, the radiant.
Saying, "Thou art radiance," he hands it to the Brāhmaṇa.
"I give this to you," says the Brāhmaṇa as he accepts it.
Then the sacrificer wipes his face, saying: "May my face be radiant; may my head be radiant; may I be radiant on all sides; do thou endow me with radiance.
Having sipped water three times, he offers praise.
To him he gives this very vessel and a hundred-measure weight of gold.
Then he asks for this silver vessel.

Having poured the *surā* through a filter into it and having added barley meal, he stirs it with two sticks made of *nyagrodha* wood, saying: "For Indra, the powerful one, I mix thee, the powerful one."
(18.9:351.13) “Thou art vigor,” with these words he hands it to the Rājanya. (18.9:351.14) “I give that to thee,” with these words the Rājanya receives it.
Then the sacrificer wipes his face, saying: “May my face be full of vigor; may my head be full of vigor; may I be vigorous in every direction; do thou endow me with vigor.”
Having sipped water three times, he praises him; he gives him this very vessel and a bow with three arrows.
Then he asks for this bronze vessel.

Having poured milk across the strainer into that [vessel] and having added barley meal, he stirs it with two sticks of *aśvattha* wood, saying: "I mix thee, who art full of milk, for Indra, who is full of milk. He hands it to the Vaiśya, saying: "Thou art milk.
The Vaiśya receives it, saying: "I accept this from thee."
Then the sacrificer wipes his face with the mantra: "May my mouth be full of milk; may my head be full of milk; may I be full of milk from every side; nourish me with milk.
Having sipped water three times, he pronounces a benediction.
To him, he gives this very vessel as well as a goad.
(18.9:352.4) Then he asks for this earthen vessel.

(18.9:352.5) Having poured water into it across the strainer and having added barley meal, he stirs it with two stirring-sticks made of *phālguna* wood, saying: "For Indra the long-lived, I mix you, the long-lived.
(18.9:352.7) Saying, "You are life," he hands it to the Śūdra.
(18.9:352.7) “I give this to you,” saying this, the Śūdra receives it.

(18.9:352.8) Then the sacrificer wipes his face, [saying]: “May my face be endowed with long life; may my head be endowed with long life; may I be endowed with long life from every side; do thou nourish me with long life.
(18.9:352.10) Having sipped water three times, he praises himself.
To him he gives this very bowl and a water-pot filled with beans; then, having moved toward this rice, he eats it.
Whatever of it he cannot endure, that he throws into the water.
Then he drinks the clarified butter from the gold vessel.

As he drinks, [the officiant] consecrates him with the mantra: "O Agni, make this man fit for long life and splendor; O King Soma and Varuṇa, make his seed dear. O Aditi, grant him protection as a mother; O All-Gods, may he reach old age.
Then, having washed this earring (*pravarta*) with water, he fastens it on the right ear with the mantra: "Bestowing long life upon you from every side."
(18.9:352.17) Then he causes him to turn around [the fire] with the words: "Thou art life; thou art all-encompassing life; thou art complete life; thou art every life.

(18.9:352.18) Then he purifies him with three bunches of *darbha* grass with the verse: "From whence the wind is swift as thought, and from whence the rivers flow—by the splendor of them all, I sprinkle thee with luster."

Then he pours [the water] down upon his right eye-socket with the verse: "Like the ocean art thou in depth; like Soma art thou inviolable; like Agni art thou turned toward all; like Sūrya art thou resplendent with light."

While the Adhvaryu is busy there, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours together four kinds of water into a wooden trough made of Udumbara wood and draws four cups with the following formulas: "The essence of the waters that is in their flow—that I draw for this [sacrificer], the son of such-and-such, for the sake of splendor and Vedic luster," with a cup made of Parṇa wood. "The essence of the waters that is in their wave—that I draw for this [sacrificer], the son of such-and-such, for the sake of vitality and heroism," with a cup made of Nyagrodha wood.
(18.10:353.8) "The essence of the waters which is within them—that I take for this [sacrificer], the son of such-and-such, for nourishment and procreation," with [a cup] made of *aśvattha* wood.
(18.10:353.9) "The essence of the waters which is worthy of sacrifice—that I take for this [sacrificer], the son of such-and-such, for life and long-livedness," with [a cup] made of *udumbara* wood.
(18.10:353.11) Then he spreads out this red bull-hide with its neck to the east and the hair side up.

Having seated the sacrificer facing eastward and having placed him around with two gold and silver plates, he sprinkles him [with water] from a vessel made of *parṇa* wood, saying: "That which is the essence in the flowing of the waters—with that I sprinkle this [son] of such-and-such lineage for splendor and for the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). Then, [he sprinkles him] from a vessel made of *nyagrodha* wood, saying: "That which is the essence in the wave of the waters—with that I sprinkle this [son] of such-and-such lineage for vigor and for heroism."

(18.10:353.16) "With that essence of the waters which is in their midst, I consecrate this [son] of such-and-such lineage for prosperity and procreation"—with these words, he sprinkles him with [water from] an *aśvattha* vessel. (18.10:353.17) "With that essence of the waters which is fit for sacrifice, I consecrate this [son] of such-and-such lineage for life and long-livedness"—with these words, he sprinkles him with [water from] an *audumbara* vessel.
(18.10:354.2) When he has been wiped all over, they cry out together; [the ritual] is the same up to the wiping of the face.
To the north, this smoke rises, and a hundred [men] and a chariot stand there.
He approaches it, saying: "Go forward, show your heroism! You are fierce, a watcher, a slayer of rivals. Ascend, you who increase our friends; may the gods speak in your favor!
Then he touches the two sides of the chariot, saying: "The two hooks, the two side-hooks, which are on both sides of the chariot."

He mounts the chariot, beginning with the verse, "Mount, O slayer of Vṛtra," and continuing as far as, "May he fill the two worlds and the lap. Then, having circumambulated it three times to the right and having placed it in front, he brings it back;
that he gives to the Adhvaryu.
This Odanasava is a sacrifice for a king, a Brāhmaṇa, or a Vaiśya who desires prosperity.
One who is about to perform the Pañcaśāradīya sacrifice prepares seventeen castrated yearling bulls.
Having performed the New Moon oblation prior to the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, he immolates seventeen spotted heifers dedicated to the Maruts.
Having sprinkled water over them and set aside the young bulls, they release them;
then they complete the ritual with the other animals. When the year has elapsed, he immolates seventeen spotted young cows for the Maruts Sāṃtapanas.
Having sprinkled water over them, they set aside the young bulls and release them;
then they complete the rite with the other animals. When the second year has elapsed, one sacrifices seventeen dappled heifers to the Maruts, the householders.
Having sprinkled water over them and set aside the young bulls, they release them.
Then they complete the rite with the other [cows]. When the third year has elapsed, he sacrifices seventeen unanointed heifers to the Maruts, the Playful Ones.
Having sprinkled water over them, they set aside the young bulls and release them;
then they complete the ritual with the other [cows]. When the fourth year has elapsed, he sacrifices seventeen striped heifers to the Maruts, the possessors of wealth.
Having sprinkled water over them, they set aside the young bulls and release them;
then they complete the ritual with the other [animals].
On this very day, he undergoes initiation.
He carries the fire-pan for a year;
there are twelve Upasad days. Its days consist of a Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma, a Pañcadaśa Ukthya, a Saptadaśa Ukthya, a Pañcadaśa Ukthya, and a Saptadaśa Atirātra.
For this [sacrifice], there is a Māruta-stoma.
Now, of these animals, on the first day, three bulls dedicated to Indra and the Maruts are offered as the Savanīya victims;
likewise on the second, likewise on the third, and likewise on the fourth.
On the final day, five [animals] are sacrificed;
for they consider this day to be the most exalted, and [the sacrificer] becomes the most exalted among his peers—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, if any of these animals is lost or dies, one performs whatever expiation (*prāyaścitti*) is prescribed for the Aśvamedha, and then sacrifices another animal in its place, having the same deity, the same appearance, and belonging to the same species.
This Pañcaśāradīya sacrifice belongs to either a king or a Brāhmaṇa. He who should desire, "May I become more than much," let him sacrifice with this sacrificial rite, the Pañcaśāradīya.
Verily, he becomes more than much.
One is about to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut.
For that [sacrifice], everything is entirely the same;
only the *puroruc* verses are different.
(18.12:356.4) For the cup for Indra and Vāyu: "O Agni, you purify the life-spans of this [sacrificer] who is ageless.
(18.12:356.5) For the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa: "Sacrifice for us to Mitra and Varuṇa.
(18.12:356.5) For the cup for the Aśvins: "O Aśvins, drink the pressed [juice]."
"Two of different forms move; by means of *māyā*, these two move one after the other"—this is for the *śukrāmanthin* cups.
"Three hundred, three thousand [beings] [attend] Agni"—this is for the *āgrayaṇa* cup; he assigns them for the *ukthya*.
The *nityā* verses belong to the *dhruva* cup.
“By fire is fire kindled” is for the offering to Indra and Agni;
“Agni is the belly of the gods” is for the offering to the Viśvedevas.
(18.12:356.9) < *agniśriyas* >, < *yad uttame* >, and < *īḍe agniṃ svavasam* >—these three are for the Marutvatīya cups.
(18.12:356.10) < *śrudhi śrutkarṇa vahnibhis* > is for the Māhendra cup.
(18.12:356.11) < *viśveṣām aditir yajñiyānām* >, < *tve agne* >, and < *tvām agne* >—these three are for the Āditya cup.
With the verse, "I bind you, the accomplisher of the sacrifice," he performs the binding for the Sāvitra, the Pātnīvata, and the Hāriyojana offerings as a constant rule.

This very Agniṣṭut sacrifice in threefold form is a means of purification. Just as these plants here, scorched by a forest fire, rise up again fresh when rained upon, even so does he, having performed this sacrificial rite, become pure, cleansed, and fit for sacrifice.
If he should consider himself a wrongdoer in respect of his mouth, he should perform the Trivṛt.
(18.12:356.17) Indeed, he commits a sin with his mouth who understands what is difficult to understand from one who is learned in the Vedas or from a sage.
(18.12:357.2) If one should perform the Pañcadaśa-stoma with the arms,
(18.12:357.2) indeed, he commits a sin with his arms who makes a violent assault upon a Brāhmaṇa.
(18.12:357.3) If one should perform the seventeen-fold [stoma] with the belly,
(18.12:357.4) for he indeed acts wickedly with his belly who eats the food of one whose food should not be eaten.
(18.12:357.5) If one should perform the twenty-one-fold [stoma] with the feet...
It is indeed this [self] that commits evil by means of the feet.
If one goes to the Āraṭṭas, or the Gāndhāras, or the Sauvīras, or the Karaskaras, or the Kaliṅgas,
and if he considers himself entirely a doer of evil, he should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma consisting of four stomas.
With this very [sacrifice], Ṛtuparṇa Bhāṅgāśvinī, the king of the Śaphālas, sacrificed.
"Having sacrificed with that [offering], he set out on a hunt.
Indra, having observed him, reflected: 'I must indeed cause him to suffer for this, since he has obstructed my sacrifice.
He, being distressed with sweat, went down into the water."
(18.13:357.11) He made her into a woman right there.
(18.13:357.12) She was named Sudevalā.
(18.13:357.12) She ascended to that very kingdom.
(18.13:357.13) < Though she was a woman, she gave birth to sons.> (18.13:357.13) < Against them Indra stirred up a conflict.> (18.13:357.14) < They were slain, utterly shattered, and lay prostrate.>
(18.13:357.14) "He made them both weep in between.
(18.13:358.1) "Then Indra came;
he approached her."
He said to her, "Sudevalā! She replied, "Venerable sir.
He said, "This is dear to you."
"What will be pleasing to me, O Blessed One? [he asked].

"Indeed, it was most displeasing to me that you chose to obstruct my sacrifice; choose now whichever of your sons shall live," [said the other]. "Those whom I, being a woman, conceived, O Blessed One," she replied.
"Therefore they say: 'Sons are dearer than a wife.
He should perform the Catuṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma sacrifice during this very first fortnight, before any mishap occurs, for the sake of peace.
He is about to sacrifice with the Indrastut."
For that [offering], everything is the same except for the *puroruc* verses.
For the cup for Indra and Vāyu, they are: "Stand by your two bay steeds; whose bull [art thou] at the pressed juice?
For the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa: "We [invoke] Indra in the great contest."
(18.14:358.11) For the draught for the Aśvins: "He who is doubly the greatest slayer of Vṛtra.
(18.14:358.12) For the Śukra and Manthin draughts: "That sun brought forth light and Indra; and that famous deed of the two Aśvins.
(18.14:358.13) For the Āgrayaṇa draught: "Indra in battles."
For the obligatory Ukthya sacrifice, he binds [the victim] for the Dhruva;
for the one dedicated to Indra and Agni, [he binds it] with the verse: "A great field, many-shining."
"O Knower, you lead us to a wide world"—this is the fixed verse for the Vaiśvadeva;
the fixed verses are those of the Marutvatīyas;
the fixed verses are those of the Māhendra.
(18.14:359.1) “With all your aids,” “Never art thou barren,” and “For Indra the cows [bring] the milk-mixture”—these three [verses] are for the draught of the Āditya cup.
(18.14:359.2) “This prayer of thine”—this is for the Sāvitra cup.
(18.14:359.3) He yokes [the verses] for the Pātnīvata cup.
The *hāriyojana* cup is constant.
This very sacrifice consists of fifteen [stomas] for one who desires power (*indriya*).
Or, whoever may be a senior kinsman who has been deprived of his status, he should perform this sacrificial rite.
He indeed attains preeminence.
One who is about to sacrifice with the Aptoryāma undergoes initiation;
his initiation periods are unlimited, and there are twelve Upasad days.

The *bahiṣpavamāna* is threefold; the *ājya* of the Hotṛ is fifteenfold; that of the Maitrāvaruṇa is seventeenfold; that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin is twenty-onefold; that of the Acchāvāka is twenty-sevenfold; and the *mādhyandina-pavamāna* is thirty-threefold.
The *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ is twenty-fourfold; the *sāmans* are the *rathantara* and the *vairāja*, and they chant around one or the other with either of these two.
(18.15:359.12) For the Maitrāvaruṇa, they chant around the forty-four-versed hymn with either of the two Sāmans, the Vāmadevya and the Śakvara.

(18.15:359.13) For the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, they chant around the forty-eight-versed hymn with either of the two Sāmans, the Naudhasa and the Vairūpa. (18.15:359.15) For the Acchāvāka, they chant around the twenty-one-versed hymn with either of the two Sāmans, the Kāleya and the Raivata.
The Chandogas call this very sacrifice the *aṣṭāpṛṣṭha*.

The *ārbhava-pavamāna* chant has twenty-seven verses; the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* has thirty-three verses; the *ukthya* chants have twenty-one verses along with the *ṣoḍaśin*; the others have fifteen verses; and the *sandhi* based on the *rathaṃtara* has nine verses.
Because of that, small cattle passed beyond [the reach of the sacrifice].
(18.15:360.1) "Soma indeed went forth as something that was left over," they say.
(18.15:360.2) "The gods said, 'This has been left over by the Aptyas; what is its course? (18.15:360.3) That is why the Aptoryāma is called Aptoryāma."

Therefore, they arranged these additional *stotras*: the *Trivṛt* for the *jarābodhīya* of the Hotṛ; the *Pañcadaśa* for the *sauhaviṣa* of the Maitrāvaruṇa; the *Saptadaśa* for the *udvaṃśīya* of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; and the *Ekaviṃśa* for the *vāravantīya* of the Acchāvāka. Regarding this, they say: "If the sacrifice were to conclude with the cup of the Acchāvāka, one would bring the sacrifice to its end;
moreover, the sacrificer would be liable to go to his end."
(18.15:360.8) “The Hotṛ-priests alone should chant the stotras, and the Hotṛ should recite the śastras; in this way, the sacrifice is restored from the middle.
(18.15:360.9) Regarding this, they also say: “All the stotras and śastras should belong to the Aśvins.
Whatever exceeds the night, all that belongs to the Aśvins. This is one view.
Next, there are others: the Trivṛt, the Pañcadaśa, the Saptadaśa, and the Ekaviṃśa.
Now, their deities are Agni, Indra, the Viśve Devās, and Viṣṇu.
He is about to sacrifice with the Mṛtyusava.

He procures a tiger skin, two gold and silver plates, sandals made of tiger skin, sandals with leather soles, a garment of ram's wool, a linen garment, a bow with three arrows, a throne-seat with a coverlet, a drum, a shed, a four-cornered trough made of Udumbara wood, four kinds of water collected from the various quarters, and a hundred [cows] and a chariot.
With these items prepared, he waits for the arrival of the Citrā constellation.

(18.16:361.8) Then, [with the words] "With the *citrayā*," the *śālīna* sacrificer settles down by the eastern fire (*pūrvāgni*), and the *āhitāgni* settles down by the *uttapanīya* and the *anvāhāryapacana*.
(18.16:361.9) Then, while the sacrificer maintains contact [with him], he offers six spoonfuls with the formula: "This tiger moves about, having entered into the fire."

(18.16:361.10) Then, on the sacrificer’s seat, he spreads out a tiger skin with its neck toward the east and its hair upward, [reciting]: "O Kaśyapa, that artifice of yours which is radiant, powerful, abundant, and of wondrous luster; upon that in which the seven suns are placed together—on that let us establish this king. (18.16:361.13) Then he puts on two sandals made of tiger skin: with "Thou art heaven," on the right foot; with "Thou art earth," on the left.

(18.16:362.1) Then, having bent his right knee, he creeps forward [with the words]: "A tiger indeed [art thou]; upon the tiger-skin, take thy station! May the great quarters [of the sky] support thee; may all the people desire thee; let not the kingdom fall away from thee.
(18.16:362.3) Then he hands him a bow, as in the *Rājasūya*.

Having seated the sacrificer facing east and having placed gold and silver plates on both sides of him, he pours together the four kinds of water into a trough made of *udumbara* wood and consecrates him with them.
(18.17:362.6) "The divine waters which have come together with milk—those that are in the intermediate space and those that are on earth—with the luster of all of them, I sprinkle you with splendor.
(18.17:362.7) "I have sprinkled you with splendor, together with the milk of heaven; may Savitṛ make you such as to increase the kingdom.
(18.17:362.9) "All songs have magnified Indra, who is as vast as the ocean—the best of chariot-warriors among chariot-warriors, the true lord and master of spoils."
(18.17:362.10) “May the Vasus sprinkle you from the east with the Gāyatrī metre,” thus [he says] in the east.

(18.17:362.11) Having recited these same three [verses], he says, “May the Rudras sprinkle you from the south with the Triṣṭubh metre,” thus in the south. (18.17:362.13) Having recited these same three [verses], he says, “May the Ādityas sprinkle you from behind with the Jagatī metre,” thus in the west.

Having recited these same three [verses], he sprinkles him from the north with the formula: “May all the gods sprinkle you from the north with the *ānuṣṭubh* metre. Having recited these same three [verses], he sprinkles him from above with the formula: “May Bṛhaspati sprinkle you from above with the *pāṅkta* metre.
Then his chest is wiped upwards with the formula: “The ruddy, fierce wolf, the stirrer of the battle-dust.”
Then he strokes his arms with [the verse]: "Stretch forth your arms that we may live.
Then he brings them down with [the formula]: "I bring down your two arms, which perform Indra’s heroic deeds.
At this point, he hands him a bow, if one has not already been handed to him previously.
When it has been wiped clean, they cry out together; the procedure is the same up to the wiping of the face. To the north stands this smoking [object] and a hundred chariots;
he approaches it with the mantra: "Go forth, show your heroism! You are fierce, a watcher, a slayer of rivals. Ascend, O best slayer of Vṛtra; the gods have spoken in favor of you."

(18.17:363.3) Then he touches the two sides of the chariot with the verse: "The two hooks, the two side-hooks on both sides of the chariot, which move along the darkness at the edge of the wind; may those fires—the far-shooting, powerful, winged ones—carry us across to safety. (18.17:363.5) Then he pays homage to the chariot with the formula: "Homage to thee, O Seer, speak! (18.17:363.6) Then he takes hold of the reins with the verse: "So be it, O Brahman; let this be thine. Stand upon the chariot when thou art thunderbolt-handed; O God of good horses, thou dost take hold of the reins."

He mounts the chariot with the verse: "Mount the chariot, O slayer of Vṛtra; mount its front. May Indra rejoice after you as you mount; all [the gods] have made Indra grow. With these words he concludes.
At this point, he strings the bow with two verses: "May the shouts of the army pass around me; may Anumati grant me her approval. Thus with both verses.

Then, having circumambulated this hundred [of cows] three times from left to right and placed them in front, he comes forward. At this point, he places a throne for him to descend upon; he descends upon it in the same manner as in the Rājasūya sacrifice.
While the Adhvaryu is occupied here, the Pratiprasthātṛ waits with the cooked offering to Varuṇa.
There are two verses for the offering to Varuṇa, and two containing the word "well-sacrificed" (sviṣṭavat) for the Sviṣṭakṛt.
At this point, he gives him this hundred.
Then they cover it with a canopy;
he fastens a drum to its northern half,
and they beat it when the sun has set.
Then he instructs him: "O sacrificer, restrain your speech; remain watchful for the kingdom.
Thereafter, he remains restrained in speech.
Whatever he utters, he utters only: "I give."
The charioteers, village headmen, kṣattṛ-gatherers, and artisans from Rājagṛha approach him;
to them he gives a four-year-old cow that has not yet calved.
While cooking it, they remain there amusing themselves and keeping watch.

Then, at the latter part of the night, the Adhvaryu, having hastened there, stirs a mash in the remnant of the fourfold waters; having smelled it or not having smelled it, he hands it to him. He consumes it silently.
Then he anoints him with fresh butter [with the verse]: "Embracing this tiger..."

Then he worships the rising sun with: "May that Sūrya rise; may this word of mine rise. Rise, O divine Sūrya, together with my voice! May I be the one who utters speech; may speech be firmly established in me.

(18.18:365.3) He addresses those departing from the royal palace: "May the rivers flow; may the rain-clouds pour forth; may the plants bear good fruit. May I become the king of these [people] who possess food, who possess cooked rice, and who possess curdled milk."
During this time, he observes this twelve-day vow.
If he goes out toward the east or the north, he wears linen garments with wings made of leather.
But if he goes toward the south or the west, he wears garments of bull-hide with wings made of tiger-skin.
Then, when twelve nights have passed, he offers two oblations with the *sruva*-ladle, using the two verses beginning, "Those who are long-haired," and "Without a rival.
Then he mounts the couch with the verse, "Mount the couch; overcome your enemies.
Then he loosens his hair with the verse, "That parting which the comb has marked for you."

(18.19:365.11) Then he shaves his hair with [the verse]: "With that razor wherewith Savitṛ shaved [the hair]... (18.19:365.12) As he is shaving, he recites over him: "May this luster not depart following after thy hair.
(18.19:365.13) Then, having gathered them together, he places them upon a clump of Darbha grass with [the verse]: "For them they have sought a manifold resting place."
Then he bathes him with warm water, [reciting]: "May Savitṛ bestow strength upon your two arms.
With this very [rite], Mṛtyu performed sacrifice, thinking, "May I attain sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over offspring.
Thereupon, indeed, he attained sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over offspring.
(18.19:365.17) He who should desire, "May I attain sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship among my peers," let him sacrifice with this sacrificial rite;
he attains sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship among his peers.
(18.19:365.18–19) "Now, Suratha Śaivya sacrificed with this [rite], thinking, 'May I reach the highest eminence.'"

(18.19:366.1) "From that, indeed, he attained preeminence as the *ātiṣṭhīya*. He who should desire, 'May I attain preeminence as the *ātiṣṭhīya*,' let him sacrifice with this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*).
Verily, he attains preeminence as the *ātiṣṭhīya*."

One who intends to perform the Sadyaskrī sacrifice cuts down both a tree suitable for a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and one suitable for a plough (*lāṅgala*). He has a shaft made from the sacrificial post-tree and a plough from the plough-tree.
The two of them consume it together or set it aside.
Now, for him, a shed has already been prepared on a chosen sacrificial ground, measured to the size of the altar.
He plows around that [spot] with this plow.
Having sown inferior barley in that [pit], he causes it to be plowed over.
Then these chariots are prepared for him: one yoked with four, one drawn by mules, one yoked with two, and the *sthūri* [ox-cart].
At the proper time, they attach curds and reeds to them.

(18.20:366.11) During the final days of the summer season, when the barley has been harvested, he causes the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) to summon him by foot, saying: "Either you shall perform a sacrifice for me, or I shall provide you with food. (18.20:366.13) When they have assembled, at the proper time, he performs the morning *agnihotra* oblation. These officiating priests then approach him.
Then he says to them, "Sacrifice for me with the Sadyaskrī [offering].
They reply to him, "So be it," and they construct a hall for him immediately at that very time for the performance of the Sadyaskrī.
Having brought that very [water] from the bathing-place at that very moment and purified it, he performs the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice.
When that sacrifice has been completed, he neither forms his fists nor restrains his speech;
they set aside for him this remnant of the oblation as his vessel for the vow-food (*vrata*).

(18.20:367.4) Then he performs the *prāyaṇīyā* offering. (18.20:367.5) He releases his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*). At this point, they present him with this remnant of the oblation; it is the vessel for his vow-food (*vratabhājana*).
(18.20:367.6) These chariots, once set in motion, run the race:
four yoked together for a *yojana* to the east; a three-legged chariot drawn by side-horses as the sacrificial fee for a *tripada*; and a two-yoked chariot for a *gavyūti* to the west.
"A cart-pole [is used] for a distance of one *krośa*," they say.

Whomever they encounter along the way, they announce to him: "This man is performing the sacrifice; he is the son of so-and-so, the grandson of so-and-so, the great-grandson of so-and-so, performing the *sadyaskrī*.
The chariots arrive.
When the chariots have arrived and are without poles, the butter that remains solid is melted, strained, and poured into a jar of clarified butter with the formula: "For immediate expansion."
Then he performs the Prāyaṇīya offering;

having performed the Prāyaṇīya, he performs the rite with the footprint; having performed the rite with the footprint, having purchased the King [Soma] for a three-year-old castrated bull that is still a calf, and having conveyed it, he offers the Ātithya.
Having performed the *ātithyā* offering, the *upasad* rites are conducted in single groups.
Having performed the middle *upasad*, at the time for the high altar (*uttaravedi*), he has the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) measured out.
Then, having yoked oxen and having scattered barley, they thresh it.
The high altar (uttaravedi) consists of barley chaff.
Then, having yoked oxen in the middle, they proceed toward the east while holding up barley;
thus this great altar (mahāvedi) becomes one with a barley-strewn sacrificial grass (yavabarhis).
Then he leads forward the Āhavanīya fire.
Having led forward the Āhavanīya, he erects the Sadas and the two Havirdhāna sheds.
Having erected the Sadas and the two Havirdhāna sheds, he leads forward Agni and Soma.
Having led forward Agni and Soma, he takes the Vasatīvarī waters;
having carried them around at that very moment, he introduces the Prātaranuvāka.
When the Prātaranuvāka has been concluded, he goes down to the waters.
He emerges with water;
he enters the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; the pressing of the Soma is performed in the established manner.
The cups are drawn in the established manner;
the ritual procedure is the same up to the Āśvina cup.
Having drawn the Āśvina cup and having taken three cords, he approaches the ploughshare.
For her, there is a vessel for the *caṣāla* made of a mat, as it were, at the very top.
Having discarded the ploughshare-shaped piece with its edges intact, he then dedicates these animals: one for Agni-Soma, one for Agni, and the *anūbandhya* victim.
They run after them in succession with their omenta.
The Adhvaryu enters with the first omentum of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma;
the others bring them in succession.
When the drops have been poured out and the omenta of the Agni-Soma animal have been cooked, he proceeds with the offering of that omentum.
They cause the others to lie down;
the animal cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for Agni and Soma belonging to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) is the principal one.
When the midday *pavamāna* has been chanted, he proceeds with the offering to Agni and Soma.
Without interruption, he proceeds with the omentum of the victim for Agni;
he proceeds with the victim for Agni in its own place;
and without interruption, he proceeds with the omentum of the Anūbandhya victim.

The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) belonging to the animal victim of the Anūbandhya sacrifice is the primary offering among those of the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana). He performs the rite with the Anūbandhya before it has been fully concluded; thus the Sadyaskrī sacrifice is completed.
Whatever of his is performed out of sequence is indeed unsuccessful for him; that is merely a renewed sacrifice for him.
Now, it is said that the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases contended with one another in the world of heaven.
Those Aṅgirases approached the Ādityas with Agni as their messenger, saying, "We shall perform the Soma-pressing tomorrow."
(18.22:370.2) "Now, let there be our pressing today.

That which is the white horse is the form of the Sun.
Now, as for the fact that he has reins of gold surpassing [all others], that belongs to his rays.
Of him who is thus threefold, the Mādhyandina and Ārbhava [pavamānas] consist of twenty-four-fold stoma;

everything else is Trivṛt.
He gives a white horse as a gift.

Everything else is indeed threefold.
He gives according to his faith.

It is completed in four days: one day up to the purchase [of the Soma], one day from [the purchase] up to the high altar (uttaravedi), one day up to the fast-day (aupavasathya), and one day for the pressing (sutyā).
This sacrifice consists of the Catuṣṭoma stoma.
One is about to perform the Vrātyastoma sacrifice.
They seek a gift from either a king or a Brāhmaṇa for a month or for a year. Whomever they agree upon, him they appoint as the *sthapati*.
He observes their vows:
he sleeps on the ground, abstains from meat, and avoids women;
for that is the vow of one who has been consecrated.
Now, when he puts on a black garment with a black fringe, that is the form of the garment of the consecrated one (*dīkṣita*).
Now, when he wears two skins, a black and a white one, that is the form of the two black antelope skins (*kṛṣṇājina*).
Now, when he wears two golden and silver ornaments (*rukma*), that is the form of the two [plates] for the *gharma* vessel.

Now, when he wears a black turban, that is the form of the turban of the consecrated one (*dīkṣita*). Then, when he carries a triple-bow with arrows made of leather, that is the form of the staff of the consecrated one. Then, when he utters the speech of a *vrātya*, that is the form of the speech of the consecrated one.
Now, as for why he wears shoes with wooden soles: it is lest, being consecrated, he should stand upon what is impure.
Of this very form of sacrifice, the staff of the goad is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and the handle of the goad is the top-ring (*caṣāla*).
The front of the chariot is the *āhavanīya* fire;
the pole is the *vedī*;
the yoke is the *uttaravedī*.
The northern yoke-pole is the *uttaranābhi*; the two bow-ends are the *havirdhāna* sheds;
the two wings are the *āgnīdhrīya* and *mārjālīya* hearths.
The *kūbara* is the assembly hall (*sadas*);
the *kiṃkarāvatāna* are the hearths (*dhiṣṇiya*);
the *bandhura* is the wife’s chamber (*patnīśāla*).
The interior of the chariot is the Gārhapatya fire; the seat is the ancient Gārhapatya. The goat which they cook as a victim—that is their sacrificial animal.
The cake (*apūpa*) and the cooked rice from the pot (*sthālīpāka*) are the *caru* and the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
That which he calls out as the *pariṣkanda* is the invitatory verse (*puro’nuvākyā*); that which he brings forward is the offering verse (*yājyā*).
That which they eat is the *vaṣaṭkāra*;
the vessel (*kumbā*) that they measure out is the *puro’nuvākyā*; the vessel that they speak over is the *yājyā*.
That which the *vigaṇa* calls out is the response (*pratigara*) to the recitation;
that which they shout out is the *udgītha*.
Those who, having approached this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) indirectly, do not approach it directly—[they are the ones so described].

Just as those who have been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) but have broken their vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), or whose Soma-drinking has been interrupted (*vicchinna-somapītha*), are not to eat [the food of others], therefore the food of one who stands as a *vrātya* but has not yet performed the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice is not to be eaten.
For he is like one whose Soma-drinking has been interrupted; his food is not to be eaten.
Among them, those who have not maintained the sacred fires go back to their respective homes, establish the fires, and then approach the *sthapati* with thirty-three sacrificial gifts each.

Among these, there is a *brahmabandhu* who is not a Magadhan but speaks like a Magadhan; a *brahmabandhu* who is not a harlot but speaks like a harlot; and a decrepit chariot-yoker (*jaratkadratha*) yoked with two decrepit draft-animals (*jaratprayogya*).
Indeed, he who is a *brahmabandhu* who is not a Magadhan but speaks like a Magadhan is one whose ritual success has failed.
One who is a Brahmin in name only is unsuccessful; a woman who is not an unchaste woman is unsuccessful when she utters the words of an unchaste woman.
A dilapidated old chariot is unsuccessful when yoked with two dilapidated old draft-animals.

One expiates for the unsuccessful by means of that which is itself unsuccessful: this is the wealth of the Vrātya—namely, the staff, the sandals, and the skin of a black antelope, all of which have been completely worn out.
Standing on the chariot, the Subrahmaṇya priest invokes the Subrahmaṇyā formula.
At the time of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), this same duty of his is performed;
the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) distribute the sacrificial fees.
The oblations for the *saṃjñānī* follow the morning pressing offerings of that [sacrifice]. For those who practice the *vrātya* conduct move about as if they are unknown;
[with these oblations] they make them known.
The cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and the Maruts follows the midday offerings.
For the Vrātya belongs to Indra and the village belongs to the Maruts;
verily, by means of the village, he makes them harmonious.
The *caru* for the Ādityas Bhavadvat follows the third-pressing offerings.
Those who practice as *vrātyas* move about as if they have not yet come into being;
[this offering] leads them to prosperity.
The rice-pap offering (*caru*) for Aditi follows the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of the Anūbandhya sacrifice.
Those who lead the life of a Vrātya indeed wander as if they are without a firm foundation.
This earth, however, is Aditi.
In this very [world] they find firm support.
This very [sacrifice] is the Agniṣṭoma of the elders;
it has four Ṣoḍaśin cups, two Pavamāna chants, and both Stotras for the Acchāvāka. Being thus, it is the Ukthya of the younger ones.

For that [sacrifice], there are six *ṣoḍaśin* cups; all the *pavamāna* chants and all the *stotras* belong to the *acchāvāka*. "By means of this very [rite], the Maruts sacrificed. Viṣṇu was their architect (*sthapati*)."
(18.26:374.7) "Now, moreover, by means of this, the divine Vrātyas sacrificed; Budha Saumya was their *sthapati*. Moreover, by means of this, the sons of the Kuru-Brahmans sacrificed."

Having sacrificed with him, they set out toward the Pañcālas as *vrātyas*.

(18.26:374.11) Disregarding them, they set out.
(18.26:374.12) They arrived at the sacrificial residence of Keśin Dālbhya.

(18.26:374.14) Now, there was once among the Pañcālas a man named Vāleya Āgniveśya, a descendant of Gandharva, who was well-versed in the Vedas.

"Among you, who is the architect?
"I am Viṣṇu," replied Aupoditi Gaupālayana Vaiyāghrapadya.
"Whatever you have done, who has performed that?"—thus he pointed out the vow in its unmanifest form.
He said to them, "I have censured you who are ignorant; we shall exclude you from the water.
They said to him, "It was indeed the father who censured his sons; your offspring will become more wretched. And so it came to pass.

Whoever would revile a Vrātya, one should revile him in just this way."

the Trivṛt is the recurring [stoma], the Pañcadaśa is the Agniṣṭoma-sāman, and all the Pavamāna [laudatory stotras] are Ṣoḍaśas.
The *pañcadaśa* turns back to the *saptadaśa* as the *agniṣṭomasāman*; all the *pavamāna*s are *ṣoḍaśa*.

The *saptadaśa* turns back to the *ekaviṃśa* as the *agniṣṭomasāman*; all the *pavamāna*s are *ṣoḍaśa*. The *ekaviṃśa* turns back to the *triṇava* as the *agniṣṭomasāman*; all the *pavamāna*s are *ṣoḍaśa*.
The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the Triṇava, revolving toward the Trayastriṃśa; all the Pavamāna-stotras are Ṣoḍaśins.
