The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the Ekaviṃśa, revolving toward the Triṇava; all the Pavamāna-stotras are Ṣoḍaśins.
The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the twenty-one-fold [stoma] repeated; all the Pavamāna-stotras are sixteen-fold.

The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the seventeen-fold [stoma] repeated; all the Pavamāna-stotras are sixteen-fold. The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the fifteen-fold [stoma] repeated; all the Pavamāna-stotras are sixteen-fold. The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is the nine-fold [stoma] repeated; all the Pavamāna-stotras are sixteen-fold.
Now, it is indeed said:

Then, where he says, "To the wives of the gods," [he should say] "To the great wives of the gods"; there he says this. Then, where he says, "To Indra, the possessor of bay horses," [he should say] "To Śakra, the bountiful one"; there he says this.

"The horse belongs to Prajāpati;

This is also the underlying principle for the midday pressing elsewhere:
he should pour out the boiled *kalaśa* of the *ekadhana* waters at the morning pressing,
and curds at the midday pressing.

it is for the attainment of Prajāpati.
A pregnant mare with a white spot on her forehead is the sacrificial fee.
The embryo is indeed the sense-organ;
the spotted [bull] is the sense-organ,
for the sake of possessing the sense-organs.

Its *atigrāhya* draught is offered with the verse: "O Indra, strike down our enemies; cast low those who attack us; place beneath our feet him who seeks to harm us. You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Indra Vaimṛdha.
Having wiped it around, he sets it down with: "This is your womb; for Indra Vaimṛdha, you.

He beheld this sacrificial rite."

Its *atigrāhya* draught is: "Indra has won the plants, the days; he has won the trees and the mid-region. He split Vala and drove away the disputants; then he became the subduer of those who act with hostile intent. "You are taken with a support; I take you, acceptable to Indra, the breaker of Vala. Thus.

there are three *upasads*,

(18.45:400.13) "Whoever should desire to acquire wealth, him one should cause to sacrifice with the Śada."
For that [sacrifice], there are ten *bahiṣpavamāna* [stotras]. One by one they are added for the sake of the twenty-one-fold [laud]; he presses [the Soma] right here.
Now, if one should wish to remove what is unpleasant, one should cause him to sacrifice with the *aupaśada*.
(18.45:401.2) Its *bahiṣpavamāna* chant consists of twenty-one verses.
(18.45:401.3) One verse is omitted at each step until ten remain.
Then there are the two [stotras] named *prājāpatya*, namely the *śada* and the *upaśada*.
In that [rite], there are three *bahiṣpavamāna* chants;
for each of these three, thirty-six verses are added until they reach thirty-six,
and in those thirty-six, the *bahiṣpavamāna* is performed.
Three [verses] fall away from three;
then there are the *śada* and *upaśada* of Kaśyapa Naidhruva;
his *bahiṣpavamāna* is in four [verses].
Four by four verses are added up to forty-eight;
in the forty-eight [verses] is the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant.
Four by four verses are subtracted down to four.
When the gods and the Asuras engaged in a great battle, then these beings indeed split into two parties: some followed the gods, others followed the Asuras.

Bṛhaspati was the domestic priest of the gods, and Uśanas Kāvya was that of the Asuras. The gods were possessed of sacred knowledge (*brahman*), and the Asuras were also possessed of sacred knowledge.
(18.46:402.2) "They, not being victorious in many battles, took counsel together.
(18.46:402.3) None among them perceived the future;
(18.46:402.4) only the Gandharva Sūryavarcas perceived the future."
Indra was laughing at his wife.
He said to her, "O lady with unblown limbs, go ask this Gandharva: 'For what reason do the gods and the Asuras not conquer one another?
She replied to him, "So be it," and added, "You too must come tomorrow."
(18.46:402.7) "He, being within the ocean, sported with his own daughter, the golden ship Kumārī.
Then Indra arrived;
having become a golden bird, he perched upon the prow of the ship."
(18.46:402.10) Having recognized that he had arrived, he asked him with his limbs thrilled: "Tell me this: for what reason do neither the gods nor the asuras conquer?
"Do not speak too loudly," he said. "A boat is indeed hollow, O waters.
"The gods possess the *brahman*," he said. "The asuras possess the *brahman*."
(18.46:402.13) Having heard that, Indra assumed the form of a tawny boar and sprang up.

(18.46:403.1) As soon as he saw him, [Uśanas] said, "O Maghavan! Whichever of these two tawny ones yours shall win, they will conquer. (18.46:403.2) He went and entreated Uśanas Kāvya for his daughter Jayantī and for four wish-fulfilling cows.
(18.46:403.3) Having been thus commanded, he went from among the Asuras to the gods. (18.46:403.4) It was then that the gods won a great battle against the Asuras.
(18.47:403.6) Having accepted much wealth from the Asuras, he felt as heavy as if he had swallowed poison.

He said, "I am like one who has swallowed poison; having accepted much wealth from the Asuras, I have ingested poison as it were. Come, perform a sacrifice for me. Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa performed a twelve-stoma Agniṣṭoma sacrifice for him.
Having sacrificed with it, he vomited up gold.
(18.47:403.10) Having seen that, he reflected: "Come now, I shall carry this away from the Asuras.
(18.47:403.11) Indra, having understood that, turned it into stone. (18.47:403.12) These very stones, known as the *auśanasa*, are found on the mountains in Kurukṣetra.
"He began to behave as if he were light and without support. He said, "I am indeed as if light and without support;
come, perform the sacrifice for me."
(18.47:404.2) Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa caused him to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma consisting of twenty-one stomas.
(18.47:404.3) Thereupon, he indeed became firmly established;
moreover, Indra secured for himself the wish-fulfilling cows.
"He said to him in the evening, 'It is this one in the morning';
he said to him in the morning, 'It is that one in the evening.
In this very manner, he led him about for a year."
He said, "You said, 'Come this morning,' but you did not say that in the evening. You said, 'Come this evening,' but you did not say that in the morning. Who is this *eta*? Which one is this *etas*?"
"O Maghavan, having said, 'This very one whom you speak of,' he departed.
Then Indra made the hymns yield all desires;
he gave them to Varuṇa, saying, 'This is yours, this is mine, and this belongs to both of us together.'"
"To Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa, this [sacrifice] we have declared for you both; may you two maintain it; may you two protect this [world] of ours"—thus [he says] "to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.
This indeed is the creation of the *ukthas*, this is their foundation. Moreover, Manu Vaivasvata himself was his friend when he was being emptied [of his essence].
He gave the fourth [daughter] to him;
he deposited her in this [earth],
and she is indeed this cultivated land.
"This is the creation of cultivation; this is its foundation.
Indeed, these two *punastoma* sacrifices are called the "Aushanasa.

If one should consider himself as having swallowed poison—as if having swallowed poison after officiating at a sacrifice for one who should not be sacrificed for, or having accepted a gift from one whose gifts should not be accepted—one should cause him to perform the *agniṣṭoma* with the twelve-fold chant (*dvādaśastoma*).
He indeed attains lightness. Now, if one who is as if light should act without a firm foundation, one should cause him to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma consisting of the twenty-one-fold stoma;
he thus finds a firm foundation.
(18.48:405.9) Now follows the *praṇoda* rite.
(18.48:405.9) The procedure for the malevolent rite (*abhicaraṇīya*) is the same.
(18.48:405.9) It follows the morning libation cakes; there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Pravata.
This [stoma] is threefold;
then follows the *vibādha*.
The ritual art for the purpose of exorcism is the same.
It follows the midday [pressing]: there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Vibādhavat; this indeed consists of three layers.
Now follows the Pratinoda.
The ritual art for the practice of exorcism is the same.
It follows the offerings of the third pressing; there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Pratīkavat, and this [offering] consists of the Trivṛt stoma.
(18.48:405.15) Now follows the piercing of Agni.
(18.48:405.15) The ritual procedure for sorcery is the same. (18.48:405.16) It follows the animal-cake offering of the Anūbandhya sacrifice: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Vasumat.
This [sacrifice] is indeed threefold;
then there is the Indra-vajra.
The ritual technique for performing malevolent magic is the same.
This [sacrifice] consists of fifteen [stomas].
Śunaskarṇa Śaivya was indeed a king who performed meritorious deeds and had many officiating priests.
Having observed that his subjects were becoming increasingly wicked, he asked his priests: "Is there perhaps some sacrificial rite by which, having sacrificed, I might depart [in peace]?"
"It is so," the officiating priests replied to him.
Therefore, the *adhvaryu* drew the cups without their proper bases and without *puroruks*; the *udgātṛ* sang the *sāmans* without the *iḍā* and without the *nidhana*.
"The Hotṛ recited the invitatory verse with his face turned away;
he died immediately upon rising from the *avabhṛtha* bath.
One should perform the sacrifice for someone whom one hates in this manner, or one should officiate as the priest for such a person."
"He indeed departs quickly from this world.
Now, they call them the *rāśimarāya* offerings;
at the *catuṣṭoma*, one gives grain that has been made into heaps.
That is the heap.
The Catuṣṭoma itself is made of bronze;
that is bronze.
(18.48:406.9) Now, they speak of "the collyrium and the ointment. (18.48:406.10) Having anointed their eyes and being adorned, the officiating priests proceed; that is the collyrium.
Anointed and wearing garments of *śāmūla* grass, that is the anointing. Now, for one who has rivals, the sacrifice is performed with the hall facing in all directions (*viṣūcīnaśāla*).

He chooses the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) in such a way that it slopes eastward from the *āhavanīya* fire and westward from the *gārhapatya* fire. They measure out these two sheds facing opposite directions; they perform the rites moving eastward and westward.
The Gārhapatya fire is in the middle; they bring the portions for consumption to him as he sits in the middle.
"The two *stomas* should be according to the directions"—this is one view.
Disregarding the statement that "there should be two [stomas] of twenty-one," they perform only the two Catuṣṭoma stomas.
(18.49:407.9) When the gods and the Asuras were engaged in a great battle, Śibi Auśīnara won the Asuras from the ranks of the gods. Indra granted him a boon for his victory.
He said, "May I not encounter the fear of death."
(18.49:407.11) "He caused him to perform the *sarvatomukha* sacrifice on the Varṣiṣṭhīya plateau.
(18.49:407.12) "Consequently, this fear of being deprived of one's position does not come upon Śibi Naiṣṭhya.
(18.49:407.13) Whomever one should desire, thinking, "May he conquer unconquerably," one should cause that person to perform the *sarvatomukha* sacrifice on the Varṣiṣṭhīya plateau.
He conquers that which is truly unconquerable.
Therefore, they have these four sheds measured out according to the cardinal directions.
They proceed toward the east; they proceed toward the south; they proceed toward the west; they proceed toward the north.
The Gārhapatya fire is in the middle;
they carry the portions of food for him while he is seated in the middle on mule-drawn chariots.
"The Stomas should correspond to the directions"—this is one view.
"One should have [sacrifices] with twenty-one [stomas]"— this is one view;
disregarding that, the Pārthas perform only those with four stomas.
"Pārthī, the carpenter, desired to win over the gods. He pressed the Soma with a thousand-fold sacrificial fees for those who had already pressed it;
he indeed attained the gods."
(18.49:408.7) Intending to bring these Soma-offerings, he prepares halls—thousands [of them], thousands [of other materials], and a thousand chariots drawn by mules.
Then they measure out these halls according to the directions: two hundred and fifty to the east;
likewise to the south, likewise to the west, and likewise to the north.
They proceed toward the east; they proceed toward the south; they proceed toward the west; they proceed toward the north.
The Gārhapatya fire is in the middle.
Seated in the center, they carry the portions of food around on mules-drawn chariots.
"The Stomas should follow the directions"—this is one view;
"They should be twenty-one-fold"—this is another.
Disregarding that, they perform only the Catuṣṭomas.
When one is about to sacrifice with these two *stomas* for the *Yamas*,
he selects a sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) such that there would be a path toward the north between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*. Therefore,
they measure out the two sheds side by side.
Having settled upon the southern hall, kindled the fires by friction, and distributed the sacred fires, he performs the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering.
Then, having settled upon the northern hall, kindled the fires by friction, and distributed the sacred fires, he performs the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering.
Having performed it here, he then performs it there.
Here he offers the initiation oblations, and there [he offers them];
here he performs the introductory sacrifice (*prāyaṇīyā*), and there [he performs it]. Having performed [the rites] here, he then performs them there.

Having performed here with the *pada* and having purchased and carried away the King Soma, he performs the guest-offering (*ātithya*); then, having performed there [with that], he performs here, and then he performs there.
He performs here first with the two *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, and then there.
(18.50:409.7) Here he performs the two middle Pravargya and Upasad rites, and there [he performs them] later.
(18.50:409.7) Here he performs the first tracing out of the Mahāvedi, and there [he performs it] later.
(18.50:409.8) Here he performs the two final Pravargya and Upasad rites, and there [he performs them] later.
Here he carries forward the Āhavanīya fire, and there [he does so]. Here he erects the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds, and there [he erects them].
Here he carries forward Agni and Soma, and there [he does so].

(18.50:409.10) Here, he erects the sacrificial post according to the procedure for the post; having set aside the post provided with a wooden chip, he dedicates the animal for Agni and Soma. Then, over there.

(18.50:409.12) Having performed the well-known rite here with its omentum, he takes the Vasatīvarī waters; then, over there. (18.50:409.12) Here he offers the cake belonging to the animal sacrifice; then, over there.
Having performed [the rites] here, he performs them there.
Here he performs with the offering to Agni and Soma, and then there.
Having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters here and having set aside the milks, they fast; then there.
But here indeed they settle down.
Having brought down the King [Soma] here, he begins the morning litany; then there [in the next world].
Here, the pressings are completed in their proper sequence until the rising of the sun.
In this very manner, the pressings are completed in the northern hall until the final gathering. Here he performs the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), and there he does so.
Here he offers the concluding oblation (udayanīyā-iṣṭi), and there he does so.
Having performed [the rite] here, one performs it there. Right here one dedicates the cow for Mitra and Varuṇa, and then there.
Having performed [the rite] here, one performs it there.
The Udavasānīya sacrifice is the same [as the preceding one].
Now, because the ritual acts are performed intertwined prior to the pressings (*savana*), therefore the twins lie together, intertwined within the womb;
and because the pressings conclude in regular succession, therefore they are born in regular succession.

Now, because the ritual acts are performed in an interconnected manner following the pressings, therefore they cause [the fires] to lie down together, they cause them to drink together, and they move about together.
And because the two kindling woods are common, therefore their womb is common.
Indeed, Agni and Āditya, desiring to win the same world, perceived this sacrificial rite; they fetched it and sacrificed with it.
Thereupon, indeed, those two came to share the same world; they went to a common world.
He who should desire, "May I go to the same world as Agni and Āditya," let him sacrifice with this sacrificial rite.
Verily, he goes to the same world as Agni and Āditya.
One is indeed a performer of the *vāja* sacrifice, and another is a performer of the *vājapeya*.

He is truly a performer of the *vāja* sacrifice who, without having sacrificed with the *peyas*, then sacrifices with the *vāja*; and he is a performer of the *vājapeya* who, having sacrificed with the *peyas*, then sacrifices with the *vāja*.
Therefore, one should indeed sacrifice with the *vāja* only after having sacrificed with the *peyas*.

When one is about to sacrifice with the Peya offerings, he undergoes initiation even without having performed the Full Moon sacrifice. For him, there are an unlimited number of initiation days and twelve Upasad days.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the new moon day, the day of sacrifice";
for him, it happens accordingly.
He proceeds from the Upavasatha day by means of the established ritual procedure.
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and having set aside the milks, they observe the fast.
Then he offers this *savanīya-iṣṭi*: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, and a cake on twelve potsherds for the Viśve Devas.
With that, he sacrifices for twelve days.
Then, on the thirteenth day, he sacrifices with the full-moon oblation (*paurṇamāsa-havis*) which has not yet been offered by him;
then, on the fourteenth day, he sacrifices with the new-moon oblation (*āmāvāsya-havis*) which has not yet been offered by him;
then he performs one of these sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*).
Then he undergoes initiation again;
he performs the sacrifice in this very same manner for a year.
Its days are: the Trivṛt-Pañcadaśa, then the Trivṛt-Saptadaśa, then the Trivṛt-Ekaviṃśa, then the Trivṛt-Triṇava, then the Trivṛt-Trayastrimśa, and then the Trivṛt-Catuṣṭoma.
The gruels are the form of the months;
the sacrificial groats are the form of the year. Thus this year is sought after for her, and thus it becomes attained.
Now follows the rule for the *ahīna* sacrifice:

its days are the *trivṛt*, the *pañcadaśa*, the *saptadaśa*, and the *catuṣṭoma*; then the *trivṛt*, then the *ekaviṃśa*, then the *triṇava*, then the *catuṣṭoma*; then the *trivṛt*, then the *trayastrimśa*, then the *catuṣṭoma*; then the *trivṛt*, then the *catuścatvārimśa*, then the *catuṣṭoma*, and finally the *atirātra*.
There are twelve months and seventeen sacrificial rites (*kratu*).
During nine months he undertakes nine sacrifices. Then there remain three months and eight sacrifices;
he performs two *trirātra* rites and one *dvirātra* rite.
If, however, he should pass beyond this, he should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma consisting of four stomas.
The stotras and śastras are the form of the months; the Agniṣṭoma is the form of the year and the prize.
Thus this year of his is sought around, and thus it becomes attained.
Now, therefore, regarding both the odd and the even [stomas]:
they chant on one verse, then on three; such are the odd ones.
Now, the even ones.
"They chant on four verses, then on eight"—thus they are in pairs.
Those who proceed by this path and those who know it thus attain union and co-residence with the divine, whether they be odd-numbered or even-numbered.
Now, therefore, regarding the quarters themselves:
the threefold [stoma] belongs to the eastern quarter, and the fifteenfold [stoma] belongs to the southern quarter.
The seventeenfold [stoma] is for the west;
the twenty-onefold is for the north; the twenty-sevenfold is for that which extends upward from here.
The thirty-three-fold [stoma] from here is beyond words;
it is the fourfold-stoma of all [the stomas].
Those who proceed by this path and those who know it thus attain union with and residence in the same world as the quarters of space.
Now, therefore, concerning the seasons:
the Trivṛt belongs to spring; the Pañcadaśa belongs to summer.
The seventeenth [is] of the years; the twenty-first [is] of the autumns; the twenty-third [is] of the winter.
The thirty-third [stoma] belongs to the cool season;
for all [the seasons], it is the fourfold-stoma (*catuṣṭoma*).
Those who proceed by this course and those who know it thus attain union with and residence in the same world as the seasons.
Now, therefore, concerning the seers:
the *trivṛt* belongs to Vasiṣṭha; the *pañcadaśa* belongs to Bharadvāja.
The seventeenth [stoma] belongs to Viśvāmitra; the twenty-first belongs to Jamadagni; the twenty-third belongs to Kaśyapa.
The Trayastriṃśa belongs to Gautama;
the Catuṣṭoma belongs to Agastya;
indeed, the Catuṣṭoma belongs to all.
Those who proceed by this path and those who know it thus attain union with and residence in the same world as the seers (*ṛṣi*).
Now, therefore, concerning the deities:
the threefold [stoma] belongs to Agni.
The fifteenfold belongs to Indra;
the seventeenfold belongs to Prajāpati;
the twenty-onefold belongs to yonder sun that shines.
The Triṇava belongs to the Moon;
the Trayastriṃśa belongs to the Viśve Devas;
the Catuṣṭoma belongs to all [the gods] indeed.
Those who proceed by this path, as well as those who know it thus, attain union with and residence in the same world as the deities themselves.
Now, therefore, they call this the "course" (*ayana*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
some say it is the course of the sun and the moon.
One who is about to perform the Soma sacrifice with the Full Moon [rite] becomes [prepared].
He undergoes initiation.
His period of initiation is unlimited; there are six *upasads*.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "On the full-moon day, which is fit for sacrifice, my *sutyā* will take place."
For him it is accomplished in that manner;
he proceeds from the fast-day with the well-known ritual.
Then, having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters and having set aside the milks, they observe the fast.
Then, in the morning, he dedicates an animal sacrifice to Agni.
For that [offering], an animal for Agni-Soma is to be immolated.
The full-moon oblations follow the morning pressing offerings of that [animal sacrifice].

The *savanīya* offerings are accompanied by *praiṣa* calls: "Recite the invitatory prayer (*anubrūhi*); recite the offering prayer (*yaja*)! For the other oblations, the *ukthya* sacrifice concludes directly with the *jyotis* form.
One is about to perform the *soma* sacrifice of the new moon (*āmāvāsya*).
He undergoes initiation.
His period of initiation is unlimited, and there are twelve Upasad days.
He purchases the King [Soma] in such a way that he thinks, "My Soma-pressing will coincide with the new moon day, which is fit for sacrifice."
For him it is accomplished in this manner;
he proceeds from the fast-day with the well-known ritual.
Now, on this day, the calves are driven away for Indra.
He causes the milk for Indra to be milked either according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya* offering or silently.
Then, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters and set aside the various portions of milk, they fast.
Then, in the morning, he dedicates the animal victim to Agni.
For this [sacrifice], a bull dedicated to Indra is to be offered.

For this [bull], the new-moon oblations follow the morning-pressing oblations; the *savanīya* oblations are accompanied by *praisha*-calls, while for the other oblations, [the calls are] "Recite! and "Sacrifice!"
The Atirātra sacrifice concludes with straight light.

Those who proceed by this path, and those who know it thus, and those who know it thus—verily they attain union with and residence in the same world as the sun and the moon. Those who know it thus, and those who know it thus.
One desiring heaven should pile the Sāvitra altar.

If it is piled at an animal sacrifice, having offered the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ oblation, having offered the oblation for the sacrificial post, and having performed the ritual for the sacrificial post with its formulas, he measures out the altar. It is known from scripture: "One should sacrifice on a third of the altar."
The measurement for that [altar] is the same as that of the Soma sacrifice; there is only this difference:

the *prakrama* shall be one-third of the *prakrama* used in the Soma sacrifice. With that [measurement], he measures out the altar. Alternatively, the side-measurement is a foot across the diagonal, and the cross-measurement is a foot across the animal-track; of these two, the *prakrama* which corresponds to the corner is intended.
(19.1:415.7) Or, the ninth [step] from the foot is its diagonal; that which is equal to the ear of those two is the measure for a *prakrama*, and by that the Soma-altar is to be measured.
(19.1:415.8) He should add fuel to the fires, enter upon the vow, bind together the sacrificial grass and faggot, and perform the *stambayajus* rite.
(19.1:415.9) This is exactly as established in the *Pauroḍāśika* section.
He performs the first tracing of the altar three times with the sacrificial formula (*yajuṣ*) and the fourth time silently;
he mutters the *karaṇa* formula.
He digs up [the earth].
From the dug-up spot, the Āgnīdhra carries it away three times.
When the Āgnīdhra has carried it away three times, he then measures out this fire toward the west from the peg at the sacrificial post-hole.
"It should be piled as large as a wing," it is said; this refers specifically to the size of a chariot wheel.
Furthermore, they quote: "The first wheel is two cubits; the middle one is two and a half; the uppermost is three minus a third."

Having made a rope of one of those measures with loops at both ends, having driven a stake in the middle of the site for the high altar (*uttaravedi*), and having fastened the two loops to it, he throws another stake at that end and traces a circular line around it by means of that [rope], moving clockwise.
Having removed the cord, they dig the trenches (*karṣū*).
They raise the water-channels (*apasyā*).
(19.1:416.2) They make them higher toward the south and the west.

(19.1:416.3) Then he asks for the vessel of clarified butter together with the *sruva*-ladle, the wooden sword (*sphya*), a bunch of *darbha* grass, a water-pot, the materials for the northern altar, curds mixed with honey, gold, pebbles, sand, and *darbha* grass.
(19.1:416.5) Having taken all this, they set it down on the northern half [of the altar].
Then, with two verses, he takes the fire into himself: "I take Agni first into myself; that Agni who is ours...

With these words, he mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "Those logs of thine, O Agni, those abodes... Having touched the white horse, he places this [brick] upon the gravel with the formula: "May Prajāpati seat thee; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!"
Then, having pulled out the peg and poured out a vessel of water, he places a bunch of darbha grass down, either with the formula, "May Vāc place thee upon the ocean," or silently.
Then he makes offerings over it with five spoonfuls, [using the formulas] beginning with, "In harmony with the year, with the months...
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he performs the *sūdadohas* verse.
Then, according to the procedure for the *cātvāla*, he traces around the *cātvāla* pit.
According to the procedure for the *uttaravedi*, he pours out the earth for the *uttaravedi*.

Having leveled the *uttaranābhi*, dug the post-hole, sprinkled it with water, poured clarified butter over it, and adorned it, he scatters sand while reciting the six verses beginning with "O Agni, yours is glory and vigor," in their respective meters.

(19.2:417.1) Then he lays down the upward-facing bricks (*ūrdhvacit*) with the formula: "You are piled, you are piled around; as upward-piled ones, take your place! By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm! (19.2:417.2) Then he spreads them out: for a Brāhmaṇa, with the *gāyatrī* verse, "Swell up" (*āpyāyasva*); for a Rājanya, with the *triṣṭubh* verse, "May thy milks... (*saṃ te payāṃsi*). He spreads them out according to the [shape of the] bricks and according to the gravel.
Upon it, he draws nine circular lines.
Then, having mixed sugar with curd and honey and anointed [the vessel], and having offered the evening *agnihotra* and strewn grass around the fires, he observes the fast.

(19.2:417.6) Then, in the morning after the Agnihotra has been offered, he asks for a water-pot, ashes, soil, saline earth, sand, and as many gold bricks (*hiraṇyeṣṭakā*)—or pebbles smeared with ghee—as there are finger-joints up to the topmost one, measured by the sacrificial joint (*yajñaparu*); that is, one hundred and eighty-five. There are an equal number of *lokapṛṇā* bricks, or an unlimited number; four *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks; and a thousand pieces of gold, provided they exceed three. Regarding this, some say they should be unlimited.
If there are a thousand [bricks], two hundred each are woven into the leaf-veins.
Then, when the sun has risen, he takes the fire into himself with two verses: "I first take Agni into myself," and "The Agni who is ours.
He mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula: "O Agni, those logs of thine, those abodes of thine..."

Having touched the white horse, he mutters the *adhidravaṇa* formula with two verses: "This is the gathering-place of the waters; homage to thee! (19.2:417.16). Then, in the rear half, he places a water-vessel with the formula: "O Speech, I place thee as the ocean, winning good progeny, winning abundance of wealth, for me, the sacrificer" (19.2:418.2).
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.

(19.2:418.2) Then he pours out the ritual materials: with "Thou art the ash of Agni," he pours out the ash; with "Thou art the soil of Agni," he pours out the soil; with "Thou art consciousness, the upholder of desires," he pours out the saline earth (*ūṣān*); with "May thy upholding of desires be in me," he pours out the sand (*sikatās*).
(19.2:418.5) Then he mixes them together with: "Those bodies of yours which are dear, let your hearts be united; let your soul be dear to you, and let your bodies be dear to me."

(19.2:418.6) Then he arranges them with the formula: "May heaven and earth be in harmony; may the waters and plants be in harmony; may the fires be in harmony separately for my preeminence, being of one vow.
(19.2:418.8) He arranges them in such a way that the lines do not overlap, either by performing everything at once or at the time of the *sadyaskāla* sacrifice.

(19.3:418.11) Then, on the final line of the eastern fortnight, he lays down fifteen *iṣṭakā*s for the days with the formulas: "Consciousness; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! Discernment; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras!

(19.3:418.13) In the intervals between them, he lays down fifteen *muhūrteṣṭakā*s for the *muhūrta*s of those very days with the formulas: "The Bright One; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! The Banner; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! Thus fifteen.
At the end of all [the lines], he recites the *sūdadohas* verse.

Then, on the inner line, he lays down the bricks of the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the formula: "O *darśā*, by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras; O *dṛṣṭā*, by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras. Thus, fifteen [bricks].

In the intervals between them, he places fifteen Muhūrta-bricks belonging to these very nights, with the formulas: "The Giver; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! The Bestower; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!
At the end of all of them, he performs the *sūdadohas* verse.

(19.3:419.2) Then, within the inner line, he lays down the day-bricks (*dineṣṭakā*) of the dark fortnight with [the formulas]: "With that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases; praised, with that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases"—thus fifteen.

(19.3:419.4) In the intervals between them, he lays down the moment-bricks (*muhūrteṣṭakā*) of those very days with [the formulas]: "Savitṛ; with that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases; Prasavitṛ; with that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases"—thus fifteen.
At the end of all [the lines], he performs the *sūdadohas* verse.

Then, on the inner line, he lays down fifteen bricks representing the nights of the waning fortnight with the formulas: "The pressed one; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! The pressing one; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! and so forth.

In the intervals between them, he lays down the Muhūrta-bricks of these very nights: "The Accuser; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! "The Permitter; by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! Thus fifteen [bricks].
At the end of all of them, he performs the *sūdadohas* verse.

Then, on the inner line, he lays down the bricks of the bright fortnight with the formulas: "By that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras; purifying, by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras. There are twelve [of these].
At the end of all [the formulas], he performs the *sūdadohas* rite.

(19.3:419.16) Then, on the inner line, he lays down the bricks of the dark fortnight with the formulas: "O powerful one! By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! and "O more powerful one! By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!"—thus twelve [bricks].
At the end of all [these], he performs the *sūdadohas* rite.

(19.3:419.19) Then, upon the inner line, he lays down the month-bricks with the formulas: "The ruddy one—by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! The ruddy-dust one—by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! Thus thirteen [bricks]. At the end of all [the bricks], he performs the *sūdadohas* verse.
(19.3:419.21) Now, some here pour sand into the intervals between the lines with the formula: "The moving ones, the living ones."

Then, on the inner line, he lays down the Muhūrta-bricks for each of the Muhūrtas: "Now, by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! At that time, by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! Thus fifteen [bricks].
At the end of all of them, he performs the *sūdadohas* formula.

Then, within the inner line, he lays down the *ṛtu*-bricks and the *artu*-bricks: "The *agniṣṭoma*; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases! The *ukthya*; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases!"—thus six.
"Agni is the season; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases! Sūrya is the season; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases!"—thus three.
At the end of all these, he performs the *sūdadohas* verse.

(19.3:420.9) Then, in the middle of the navel, he lays down four *saṃvatsara*-bricks with the formulas: "Prajāpati; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! The year; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras!
At the end of all [the bricks], he performs the *sūdadohas* verse.

He asks for these four *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks. He places them in the quarters: with "Bhūḥ! Agni and the earth," he places one in the east; with "Bhuvaḥ! Vāyu and the intermediate space," he places one in the south; with "Svaḥ! Āditya and the sky," he places one in the west; with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Candramas and the quarters," he places one in the north. At the end of all [the formulas], he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.
(19.4:420.16) Then he lays down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks with the formula: "Fill the world, fill the gap; then sit down, you who are auspicious. May Indra, Agni, and Bṛhaspati seat you in this womb.

(19.4:420.18) He performs the *tayādevata* rite with the formula: "By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm. (19.4:420.19) Then he performs the *sūdadohas* rite with the verse: "These dappled cows, yielding milk for him, mix the Soma; they are the clans at the birth of the gods, in the three luminous realms of heaven."

(19.4:421.2) Here, he pours out [the earth] with a Lokampṛṇā brick facing east; they completely cover the fire-altar with bricks facing east. (19.4:421.3) Once it is completely covered, he draws a line around it with a Palāśa branch, saying: "Fill the space! Fill the gap! (19.4:421.4) Then it becomes untouched by the *citikḷpti* formula.
Then he touches the fire with two verses: "That which of thee is unheaped... that which has been heaped of thee, O Agni.
Here, he touches it with the *citikḷpti* verse: "May the wise one distinguish between thought and thoughtlessness.

Having touched this layer with the Gāyatrī verse addressed to Agni, "O Agni, bring the gods hither," he mutters the two *avadravaṇa* formulas: "May speech be in my mouth; may the breaths be in my nostrils."
(19.4:421.8) Then, having touched the black horse, he places the *tanūpurīṣa* [earth] with the verse, "He who is asked in heaven" (*pṛṣṭo divi*).
Having performed the *tayādevata* rite, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula.

(19.4:421.10) Then, having poured water into a vessel and scattered gold chips therein, he sprinkles [the earth] with two hundred [chips] at a time: with "Thou art the measure of a thousand," in the east; with "Thou art the image of a thousand," in the south; with "Thou art the span of a thousand," in the west; and with "Thou art the counter-measure of a thousand," in the north.
(19.4:421.14) Then he sprinkles the middle part with two hundred [stalks], saying: "Thou art thousandfold; for a thousand, thee!

(19.4:421.15) Then, standing on the northern half, he makes the bricks into milch-cows, reciting from "O Agni, may these bricks of mine be milch-cows" until the end of the section. (19.4:421.16) At this point, some offer goat's milk upon the final brick using an *arka* leaf.

If he is about to perform this [rite], then, having made a funnel-shaped cup from an *arka* leaf with an inner channel, standing facing north and holding it at the level of his mouth, he says: "Bring!
Fetch! When he reaches the *dhāreṣṭakā*, he begins there with the verse, "Thou, O Agni, art Rudra," reciting until the end of the section.
At this point, he throws that *arka* leaf upon the path where the cattle of the one whom he hates pass.
If, however, he does not hate anyone, he casts [the bone] into a rat's hole.
Then he worships it with this anuvāka: "Thou thyself knowest thyself; who thou art, that thou art.
Then he worships it with the two [anuvākas] on gathering and wandering: "Thou art the Saṃvatsara; thou art the Parivatsara. With this anuvāka he worships it.
Then he says, "O Hotṛ, recite the *uktha* for Agni after [the praise of] Agni.

If the Hotṛ does not desire to do so, the sacrificer himself, having spread grass behind the fire and sat down upon it, recites the *uktha* for Agni after [the praise of] Agni. He recites each of these two verses—"bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ"—three times each, with the *praṇava* (the syllable *om*) as the connection between them. In the same way, wherever there is a connection between verses, the connection is made by means of the *praṇava* alone.
In this regard, if one were not to bring sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to those Brahmins who are learned in many branches of knowledge, the sacrifice would be ill-performed;
they might even seize his fire-altar. Therefore, one should give to them according to one's faith.
"Thus this is performed as a well-sacrificed offering; 'they do not exclude his fire,' so says the Brāhmaṇa."
(19.5:422.15) Now, the ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) is carried out, beginning with the placing of the firewood.

Having completed the established rites up to the carrying forward of the fires, having carried forward the fire, kindled it, and offered the *adhvara* oblations, he offers these following oblations with separate fourfold portions:
(19.5:422.17) "O Agni, you are Rudra"—this is the form of the *Śatarudrīya*.
(19.5:423.1) “O Agni and Viṣṇu,” for the stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*). (19.5:423.1) “O Lord of Food,” for the oblation of food (*annahoma*).
(19.5:423.2) “Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues,” for the *viśvaprī* offering.
Then, dipping the *sruva* ladle each time, he offers twenty-one oblations with the formula: "To Asu, svāhā! To Vasu, svāhā!
Having offered them one by one, he pours the remnants of the offerings into the hollowed palms of the sacrificer.
With these, the sacrificer wipes his face with this section of the text beginning: "The Queen, the Virājī..."
(19.5:423.6) From the second tracing out of the altar onwards, the ritual procedure pertaining to the animal sacrifice is carried out.

Having performed the established rites up to the *manotā*, and having recited the *manotā* and touched the portions of the victim, he takes the *mṛtyugraha* (the cup for Death) of the broth in a vessel made of *udumbara* wood, reciting: "Sing to the wise Pavamāna! Having recited this, [he says]: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Death.
Having wiped it with *darbha* grass, he places it on the northern altar, saying: "This is thy womb; for Death, thee!"
Then he proceeds with the animal sacrifice;
then he proceeds with the Vanaspati offering;
then, prior to the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, when about to offer this cup, he touches water, saying: "Thou art lightning; dispel my evil."
(19.5:423.13) Then he offers [the oblation]: "Away with death, away with hunger; drive away the curse from here! And so, O Agni, bring to us thousandfold abundance of wealth.
(19.5:423.15) "O Death, those thousands and tens of thousands of snares of yours intended for the slaying of mortal man—all these we unbind by means of the power of the sacrifice, svāhā!
(19.5:423.16) Having offered, he should then touch water, saying: "You are rain; cut away my evil."

(19.5:423.17) Then he proceeds with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. (19.5:423.17) While the *iḍā* is being invoked, they hold the cup close. (19.5:424.1) Once the cup has been invoked, the sacrificer consumes it, saying: "Thou art food, the drink of immortality. Of thee, who hast been drunk by Death, who art possessed of nectar, who hast been made *svagā*, who art honeyed, and who hast been invoked—I, being invoked, partake. Thus he says.
Having consumed [the portion], he touches himself with the formula, "The mild, overpowering banner of sacrifices," up to the end of the section.
From the after-offerings (*anūyāja*) onwards, the ritual procedure pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśubandhika*) is performed;
it is established [to proceed] up to the time of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
At the time for the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), having given a milch cow, a bull, and a draft ox, he gives twenty-one sacrificial fees;
he gives a hundred;
he gives a thousand.
He gives sacrificial gifts corresponding to each brick;
if he cannot find them, he should give as many stirred-drink mixtures (mantha) or cooked rice dishes (odana), but he must give a pregnant heifer.
He gives gold; he gives a garment.
"By that he extends his life," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
If one should pile it at the Soma sacrifice, the preparation of the site occurs during the first *upasad*;
the laying down of the bricks takes place between the middle and the last *upasads*;
and the carrying forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) occurs at the [proper] time.
At the time for the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*), the gifts are given.
At the time of the broth of the *savanīya* animal, there is the Mṛtyugraha cup.
If one should pile [the fire-altar] during an *ahīna* or a *sattra*, the gifts are on the first day, and the Mṛtyugraha cup of broth is on the first day.
No sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are led forth at the *sattras*.
"The *nāciketa* fire-altar itself should be the seizing of death"—this is another [view].
"Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the *sautrāmaṇī*, or with the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. Thus [it is said].
When the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, the evening milking takes place; when the morning *agnihotra* has been offered, the morning milking takes place.
The cooking is performed together with the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*). The ritual procedure is not to be performed until the sun has risen.
The Sāvitra [rite] is completed.
Now, the preparation of the sacrificial ground for the Nāciketa fire is well known to be the same as that for the Sāvitra;
only this much is different.

No lines are drawn here. Then he lays down the Yājuṣī bricks with the formula, "Thou art the world; thou art heaven. With his joined palms, he lays down twenty-one [bricks] wherever they fall. This is the rule for the laying down of those scattered bricks elsewhere as well.
(19.6:425.5) If it is fivefold (*pāṅkta*), there are five [bricks] in the east, five in the south, five in the west, five in the north, and one in the middle.
(19.6:425.6) Now, if it is threefold (*trivṛt*), there are seven in the east, three in the south, seven in the west, three in the north, and one in the middle.
(19.6:425.7) Now, as for those that are upright, they begin from the rear corner and extend upward until the space of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
Now, if they are oriented toward the east, [the procedure] starting from the space for the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks is as established;
from the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks onwards, it is as follows:
"If he should desire, 'May I be radiant, glorious, and possessed of spiritual luster,' he should creep forward as far as the *hotṛ*'s hearth," that is, from the vicinity of the *āhavanīya* fire.
"May this glorious one who has come from the east cover me with splendor, glory, and the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*).

Thus he says; "He indeed becomes possessed of splendor, glory, and the luster of sacred knowledge. Now, if he should desire, "May they have the greatest faith in me; may they bring the most abundant sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*)," then while the sacrificial gifts are being led forward, he should offer an oblation in the *āhavanīya* fire, having dipped the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) [into the butter] with the formula: "Come from the east, come from the east! May the eastern quarter, rejoicing, partake of the clarified butter, Svāhā!"
"They place the greatest faith in him;
they lead away the most abundant sacrificial fees"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Thus the Nāciketa fire-altar is completed.
Now, regarding the piling of the Brahman-fire:
the preparation of the site is well known, as it is for the Sāvitra fire;
only this much is different.
No lines are drawn here.

Then, in front [of the altar], he lays down ten *daśahotṛ* bricks facing north: "The thought (*citti*) is the ladle; by that divinity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases! The thought is the clarified butter; by that divinity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases!"—thus ten.
(19.7:426.8) Then he lays down the heart-brick, reciting: "He knows the golden Gharma, the longing one... and continuing until "...that mind-born self of men, together with the gods.

(19.7:426.10) Then he lays down two Yajus-bricks: "Agni with the Yajus-formulas... by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! and "Savitṛ with the Stomas... by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! Thus.

(19.7:426.12) Then he lays down two *patnī* bricks with the formulas: "The army of Indra; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! and "The speech of Bṛhaspati; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras!
(19.7:426.14) At the end of all [these formulas], he performs the *sūdadohas* rite.

(19.7:426.15) Then, to the south, he lays down four *caturhotṛ* bricks facing eastward with the formulas: "Earth is the Hotṛ; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! and "Heaven is the Adhvaryu; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras!"—thus four.
(19.7:426.17) Then he lays down the Heart-brick, reciting: "Brahman, Indra, Agni... and continuing until: "...the sages have perceived this sacrifice, the self of the Caturhotṛs.

(19.7:426.19) Then he lays down two Yajus-bricks with the formulas: "O Indra, with the hymns of praise; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! O Mitra and Varuṇa, with the blessing; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!"
Then he places the two Patnīṣṭakā bricks with the formulas: "The path of Pūṣan; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! Speech of Vāyu; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!
At the end of all these, he performs the *sūdadohas* rite.

(19.7:427.3) Then, behind [the previous layer], he lays down five *pañcahotṛ* bricks facing north: "Agni is the Hotṛ; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! "The two Aśvins are the Adhvaryus; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!"—thus four [bricks].
Or rather, with this mantra alone, "The two Aśvins are the Adhvaryus," he lays down two bricks that share the same deity.
He modifies the mantra: “With that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit firm.
Then he lays down the heart-brick, reciting: “He knows a hundred teams,” and continuing until: “The breath is the caul; by that I am fashioned with immortality.”

(19.7:427.9) Then he lays down two *yajus* bricks with the formulas: "O Aṅgirases, with the fires of the *dhiṣṇiya*s; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases! O Maruts, with the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases!

(19.7:427.12) Then he lays down two *patnī* bricks with the formulas: "The consecration (*dīkṣā*) of Soma; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases! The earth of Agni; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases! (19.7:427.14) At the end of all these, he recites the *sūdadohas* verse.

(19.7:427.14) Then, to the north, he lays down six *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*-bricks facing eastward: "Vāc is the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases! Dīkṣā is the wife; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of the Aṅgirases!"—thus six.
(19.7:427.17) Then he lays down the *hṛdayeṣṭakā*, reciting: "The golden casket, enveloped by the dust... and continuing until: "...the self of Indra moving in a hundred ways."

(19.7:427.18) Then he lays down two *yajus*-bricks with the formulas: "The waters with the sprinkling-vessels; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! The plants with the sacrificial grass; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! (19.7:427.20) Then he lays down two *patnī*-bricks with the formulas: "The *gāyatrī* of the Vasus; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras! The *triṣṭubh* of the Rudras; by that deity, sit firm in the manner of Aṅgiras!
(19.7:428.3) At the end of all [these formulas], he performs the *sūdadohas* verse.

(19.7:428.3) Then, above [the previous layer], he lays down seven *hotṛ*-bricks facing eastward: "The Great Oblation is the Hotṛ; by that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm! "True Oblation is the Adhvaryu; by that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm! Thus six [bricks].
(19.7:428.5) Or alternatively, with the mantra, "Unassailable and Unassailable are the two announcers of the sacrifice," he lays down two bricks that share the same deity.
He adapts the mantra to: "By that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit ye both firm! (19.7:428.7) He modifies the mantra accordingly.
(19.7:428.8) Then he lays down the heart-brick with the formula: "Indra is the king of the world who rules," reciting the entire section until its end.

(19.7:428.9) Then he lays down thirteen Yajus-bricks with the formulas: "Aditi by the altar; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! Soma by consecration; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! and so on for the thirteen.

(19.7:428.11) Then he lays down the Patnīṣṭakā bricks with: "The Jagatī of the Ādityas; by that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit thou firm! The Anuṣṭubh of Viṣṇu; by that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit thou firm!"—thus eighteen [bricks].
At the end of all [the formulas], he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse.

(19.7:428.14) Then, according to the available space, he lays down the *graha* bricks with the formulas of the Daśahotṛ: "O Lord of Speech, ordainer, [my] name"; with those of the Caturhotṛ: "O Lord of Speech, by the power of speech"; with those of the Pañcahotṛ: "Soma is the leader of Soma"; with those of the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar"; and with those of the Saptahotṛ: "O Lord of Speech, ordainer of the heart, [my] name. At the conclusion of all these, he performs the *sūdadohas* verse.
Then, according to the available space, he lays down the *pratigraha* bricks.
Having recited, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," [he says], "This is your sacrificial fee, O Kāma; may Uttāna Āṅgirasa receive you. With this formula, he places nineteen bricks.

Alternatively, with the mantra, "For the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the garland and ornaments," he places two bricks that share the same deity. He modifies the mantra to: "By that deity, sit firm like the Āṅgirases."
(19.7:429.4) From the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks onwards, it is established; from that point upward, (19.7:429.5) the *brahmacit* is completed.
Now,
the preparation of the sacrificial site for the combined [rite] is well known, as it is for the Sāvitra [rite].
Only this much is different.
The first layer is the Agni of Savitṛ;
the second is the Lokampṛṇā;
the third is the Nāciketa.
The *lokaṃpṛṇā* is the fourth;
the *brahmacit* is the fifth;
in all layers, there is a *svayamātṛṇṇā*.
The layers end with the loose soil (*purīṣa*).
With the verses beginning, "O Agni, bring the gods here," he touches the five layers.

If he should pile [the fire-altar] at the very end of the Soma sacrifice, he should worship with the *divaḥ śyenī* verses before the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, and with the *apāghā* verses after the *udavasānīyā*.
Having performed it once, he combines them; thus, when combined, it is completed.
Now, regarding the Vaiśvasṛja [sacrifice],
the preparation of the sacrificial ground is well-known, being the same as that of the Sāvitra;
only this much is different.
There are three lines.
Then, upon the innermost line, he lays down eighteen [bricks] with the verse, "That which is immortal and that which is mortal.
At the end of all [the bricks], he performs the *sūdadohas* rite.
(19.9:430.4) Then he places [the bricks] upon the inner line with the formula, "All quarters in the quarters," fifteen times.

(19.9:430.5) At the end of all [these formulas], he performs the *sūdadohas* rite. (19.9:430.5) Then he places [the bricks] upon the inner line with the formula, "{F All}{FN TB.3.12.8.1. BI: s;arvān. AnSS, BS: s;arvāṃ.}{BI sarvān} the heavens, all the gods in heaven," nine times.
At the end of all [the layers], he performs the *sūdadohas* verse.
From the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks onwards, the procedure is established as already explained.

If one should pile this altar during an *ahīna* or a *sattra* sacrifice—such as the *Śatarātra*, the *Viśvajit*, or the *Sarvapṛṣṭha*—then at the time for the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the Brahman priest, seated in the *sadasya* shed, recites the *vaiśvasṛja* verses: "The eastern direction of the *ṛc*s is called the great one," reciting them quarter by quarter, half-verse by half-verse, and sentence by sentence according to the Brāhmaṇa.
The Adhvaryu responds to him: "Om, the Great! The Great is the Cosmic Order (Ṛta)! The Great is Truth! We have succeeded, O Great One!
In its final round, the phrase "We have succeeded, O Great One" is fulfilled;
thus the Vaiśvasṛja rite is completed.
By this, the Āruṇaketuka fire-altar is explained.
As far as the mantra extends, so far are the bricks;
and the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks and the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks are indeed water.
A lotus leaf, a gold plate, a golden man, and a tortoise—these are [the items].
"The rain-clouds shine," as recited in the traditional text;
"those of the pools" means those that do not dry up.
At the time of throwing up the *uttaravedi*, having dug it knee-deep silently, he pours earth elsewhere;
the formula beginning with "Agni has found [thee]" (*vider agniḥ*) is omitted,
and he begins with "Thou art firm" (*dhruvāsi*).
Taking them by the hand, he should place the bricks that are not made of clay.
Having performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the two verses beginning, "May we hear what is auspicious with our ears," he places them with those two.
With the five *Mahānāmnī* verses beginning, "The waters, the waters," he [places] the warm water.
"May they be auspicious to us, most peaceful," [with these words] he gives the waters together with the herbs to the Adhvaryu.
Having accepted them, he lays them down with the words, "Auspicious to us. He should lay down one containing the word *sumṛḍīkā* facing the earth; these [bricks] are placed in the east.

"Smṛtiḥ pratyakṣam" and so forth—eight [verses] in the middle; "śukraṃ te anyat" and "sākaṃjānām"—these eleven [verses] in the east. To the south: "akṣiduḥkhotthitasyaiva"—six [verses]; and "iheha vaḥ svatapasas."
(19.10:431.13) Having performed the pacification at the beginning and end as in the Pravargya rite, [he recites] the four [verses] beginning with “*atitāmrāṇi*”;
(19.10:431.14) the three *ṛtumaṇḍala* verses beginning with “*atyūrdhvākṣas*,” and also “*ava drapsas*”;
(19.10:431.15) the eight [names] beginning with “*ārogas*,” word by word, using the names of the Sun; and also “*yat te śilpam*.”
Having murmured the *vyāhṛtis*, the sacrificer worships [the waters] with the formula: "The waters are yours.
In the same way, he performs the subsequent worship after murmuring the *vyāhṛtis* with the four solar verses:
"Seven suns," "Seven directions with various suns," "When the heavens," and "The splendor of the gods"; and finally, one verse beginning with "Where is this cloud?"
(19.10:432.4) "The half-months," [this is] above;
(19.10:432.4) "The times enter into the waters," [this is] on the south;
(19.10:432.5) "What indeed is here?"—these five verses addressed to Viṣṇu.
"I ask you about death beyond" (19.10:432.6)—these four are the verses concerning death.
"I ask you about the evildoers" (19.10:432.7)—these four are the verses concerning hell.
"In whom [the gods]... and "O Agni, lead us..."—these two [verses].
"Agni and Jātavedas"—these eight are for the quarters. "The quarters be yours," says the sacrificer. "The resplendent ones"—these eleven are the Rudras.
"The resplendent females"—these eleven are the Rudrāṇīs; they are placed step by step in the middle.
"O Vasus, [accept] the forms," says the sacrificer.
"The resounding, shining ones"—these are the eleven groups of Gandharvas, [recited] word by word from behind.
"The Gaurī has lowed"—this is one [verse].

(19.10:432.12) “The boar-like ones, self-heated”—these are the seven winds, word by word. (19.10:432.13) “This is common”—this is the verse concerning rain. (19.10:432.13) “That which is the syllable”—this is the world.
"Jamadagni"—thus it is strengthened; "That [be] auspiciousness"—thus it is the *śaṃyu*; "The thousand-fold"—these are the eight *saṃyānī* verses.
(19.10:432.15) “*sa saṃgrāmaḥ*” (and) two [verses];

(19.10:432.15) “*pavitravantaḥ*,” “*pavitraṃ te*,” “*brahmā devānām*,” and “*asataḥ sadye*” (four verses)—these four beginning with *pavitram* are on the north side. (19.10:432.17) “*amī ya ṛkṣāḥ*” (seven verses) are in the middle.
The five verses beginning with "Andho maṇim" are dedicated to the Viśvedevas;
the next [set] consists of three verses beginning with "Ā tam agne ratham," and four verses beginning with "Ā tanuṣva."

The sacrificer should lay down one brick with the formula: “< {F ā}{FN TĀ.1.12.2. BI, BS, AnSS var.g: ;ā. AnSS: m;ā.}{TĀn m;ā}{TĀn(g) ;ā}{TAbi ;ā}{TAbs ;ā}{BI ā} mandrais >”; two bricks with the formula: “< aṇubhiś ca >”;
and one brick with the formula: “< subrahmaṇyom >”.
"O ruddy horses!"—these are the four *revatī* verses.
"Thou art the womb of Brahman"—these are the four *brahmasadana* verses.
"The eightfold source"—these are the eight *diśyā* verses.
"Mitra and Varuṇa"— with these [verses], eight [bricks] belonging to the quarters [are placed].

Having placed the lotus-leaf, the gold plate, the golden man, and the tortoise just as in the Mahāgni, he places two *dūrohaṇa* bricks with the verse "The swan dwelling in purity," on both sides of the man.
(19.10:433.7) He places two [bricks] in the middle with the words, "That is the step," and eight to the north with the words, "Of the Vasus" and "of the Rudras.
The sacrificer [recites], "O rays, be ye."
(19.10:433.9) “Of the healthy one”—these eight [verses] are recited above.
(19.10:433.9) “O Waters, you are”—thus the sacrificer [recites].
(19.10:433.9) “Of the brilliantly shining ones”—this is one [verse]; and “of the brilliantly shining women”—these eleven [verses] are recited in the middle.
(19.10:433.11) "O forms, [be] yours," says the sacrificer;
(19.10:433.11) "Of Agni, [the one] belonging to the eastern direction," [he says]; thus [are] the eight directional [offerings].
(19.10:433.12) "O directions, [be] yours," says the sacrificer.
"In the south-eastern [quarter]"—four [verses] containing the word *narakavatī*, according to their respective characteristics;
"In which [the waters]... and "O Śatakratu, the senses..."—two [verses] to the south;
"Indraghoṣā vaḥ" and "Saṃjñānam"—six [verses] pertaining to the quarters.
(19.10:433.14) “O Āditya, all!”—these five [verses] belong to the quarters.
(19.10:433.15) “For thus indeed, thus indeed!”—these six [verses] belong to the quarters.
(19.10:433.15) “Water, water!”—these nine [verses] follow after.
(19.10:433.16) He recites once, "The essence of the waters.
(19.10:433.16) He recites the verse containing the word *saṃkalpa*, "Desire was there in the beginning.
(19.10:433.17) He recites the verse containing the word *ogha*, "The waters, indeed, when..."
(19.10:433.17) “Having fashioned the worlds”—this is the *stambhanavatī*. (19.10:433.18) “The banners”—this is one verse.
(19.10:433.18) “Now these”—these are three verses.
(19.10:433.18) “Āplavasva” — these are seventeen *kṣapaṇyās*.
(19.10:433.19) “Viśīrṣṇīm” — these are two.
(19.10:433.19) “Parjanyāya” — these are three.
"May he come back to me again"— with these three [verses], and the subsequent procedure is the same starting from the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick; with the *sāvitra* formula, there are the *svayamātṛṇṇā*,
the *lokaṃpṛṇā*s, and these waters— these constitute the five layers (*citayaḥ*).
The layers are covered in each direction with lotus leaves and other materials.
The others are like the first layer;
there are no lotus leaves and so forth.

To the north, he leaves a space for the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks. Having constructed a platform with long pieces of wood, he performs the spreading of the loose earth (*purīṣa-vyūhana*) with the verse "Thou art asked in heaven," and at the final brick, he performs the *śatarudrīya* oblation.
At the conclusion of the recitation of the benefits (*anuśaṃsanānta*), there is the leading forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*).

While the oblation is being offered, the Vaiśravaṇa sacrifice is explained by the Brāhmaṇa for one desiring food or for one desiring all things; the Vaiśravaṇa sacrifice is performed at every *parvan* [festival].
"One should pile [the fire-altar] during sacrifices that have an *uttaravedi*," according to the Brāhmaṇa.

(19.10:434.10) "His vow is this"—thus, according to the Brāhmaṇa, there are various combinations of vows. (19.10:434.11) One should not loathe water, as stated in the Brāhmaṇa; whether desiring one thing or all things, (19.10:435.1) it is known from the Brāhmaṇa: "Water indeed is all this. "The waters are indeed Brahman; when the waters are laid down, he places Brahman within himself. He who piles this fire attains union with and residence in the same world as Brahman. Thus it is said.
The Āruṇaketuka is completed; the Āruṇaketuka is completed.
"The fast-day," he says.

(20.1:1.1) How indeed should one recognize the fast-day? Should the junction [of day and night] be brought about, or [should it be when] the moon has not yet been seen because it was not full? (20.1:1.2) It is indeed well that the junction is so; it is well that the junction is brought about.
"But surely, the *saṃdhya* [period] is easy to establish for everyone, as it were; yet for all, it is indeed like the *saṃdhya*.

Baudhāyana used to say: "When those observing the fast, after the sun has set, see the moon rising in the east appearing as if reddened, one should recognize that too as the day of fasting (*upavasatha*).
Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "This [lunar conjunction] has indeed already passed."
He should either perform the *saṃdhyā* rite or sacrifice with the full moon offering (*pūrṇāhuti*).

If, while he is observing the fast and the sun has set, the moon should rise in the east appearing as if reddened, he should say, "Let us desist from the *agnihotra*," and proceed with the *pārvaṇa* rite. When the *pārvaṇa* rite is completed, he should offer the *agnihotra*.
"Thus indeed regarding the full moon day;
now, regarding the new moon day," [it is said].
Baudhāyana used to say: "One should observe the fast while [the moon] is still invisible, not when it is visible."
"One should indeed act in this very manner," says Śālīki; "however, there is also a visible *upavasatha*:
when the moon has become thin through these nights and the stars have faded at dawn, and it is not seen on the following day—one should recognize that too as an *upavasatha*."
(20.1:3.4) Regarding the adding of fuel to the fires.
The Sūtra belongs to Aupamanyavīputra.
Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say that one should add fuel to the fires with the *vihavyā* verses—three for each fire—if they recite nine such verses.
Now, those who have eight [verses] should repeat either the first or the last one twice.

(20.1:3.7) Now, as for those who say that one should place each of the ten [logs] with three verses each, and then, standing to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, recite the tenth verse—(20.1:3.8) regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "That which has been placed once is indeed the Gārhapatya; the Anvāhāryapacana has its origin in the village."
"One should enkindle only the Āhavanīya fire with the *vihavyā* verses;
then, standing to the north of the Āhavanīya, one should recite the remaining verses," so it is said.
Regarding this, Aupamanyava used to say: "One should enkindle the fires with the *vihavyā* verses alone, adding each verse to each individual fire."
(20.1:3.12) Now, standing to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, he should recite what remains [of the formula].

(20.1:3.13) Regarding this, Maudgalya used to say: "One should add fuel to the Āhavanīya alone with [the verse]: 'I take hold of Agni, the good chariot, who is a source of bliss; he who ascends the rising sun for the sake of the day; the Āditya, the highest light among lights; may he rest for the sacrifice tomorrow for the sake of the deities.
(20.1:3.16) 'The Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas—the deities together with Indra—I first enclose them within my own abode with my mind.'"

(20.1:3.18) "Those gods who have entered this fifteenfold strength, them I first encompass; may Agni, the bearer of oblations, bring them here; let this full-moon offering be for them within me"—thus at the full moon. (20.1:4.2) "Let this new-moon offering be for them within me"—thus at the new moon. (20.1:4.3) Regarding this, Maitreya used to say: "One should enkindle only the Āhavanīya fire with the *vihavya* verse, while the other two fires remain silent; then, standing to the north of the Āhavanīya, one should recite the remaining verses."
Rāthītara says that one should add fuel to the fires with the *vyāhṛtis* alone.
Regarding the curdling agents.
Baudhāyana used to say, "These are the substances for curdling the sacrificial oblation.
Regarding this, Śālīki used to say, "Indeed, curd is seen as the substance for curdling; if that is unavailable, one should curdle [the milk] with any one of these."
Regarding the undertaking of the vow: thus it is said.

Baudhāyana used to say that one should undertake the vow (*vrata*) at the time of *saṃgava* (the second of the five divisions of the day), or when the cows are being milked, or when the *praṇītā* waters have been carried forward, or when the oblations (*havir*) are about to be carried forward, or when the oblations have been set down.

Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "The undertaking of the vow indeed belongs to the time of the previous day; for the Brāhmaṇa states, 'On the full moon day he undertakes the vow with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), on the new moon day with the calves. Therefore, he should undertake the vow precisely at the time of *saṃgava*. Aupamanyava says it begins from the *anvādhāna* (the preliminary placing of fuel).
Regarding the Abhyuditeṣṭi sacrifice.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "Having performed the sacrifice with the established New Moon oblations, and having fasted again, one should, on the following day, perform the timely sacrifice when it has not dawned upon [the moon] and is unimpaired.

On this point, Śālīki used to say: "One should perform that sacrifice which is the *brāhmaṇajā* sacrifice for the sake of distinction; having sacrificed with it, and having fasted again, one should, on the following day, perform the timely sacrifice when it has not dawned upon [the moon] and is unimpaired.
This, indeed, is the rule for one who is offering the *saṃnāyya*.
Now, regarding one who does not perform the *saṃnayya* offering, the ritual procedure is the same according to Baudhāyana.

On this point, Śālīki used to say: "Having cooked these oblations in water itself and having fasted again, on the following day, when the moon has not risen and the time is appropriate, one should sacrifice; or else, one should extend the fast-day (*upavasatha*) even further."
"Covering," so it is said.
Baudhāyana used to say: "One who has restrained his speech should cut the branch; one who has restrained his speech should carry it. "In this very manner one should carry it," so [he said].
And indeed, one should act exactly thus, according to the Brāhmaṇa: while smiling inwardly, one may converse with a Brāhmaṇa, but not with a non-Brāhmaṇa.
(20.1:5.13) "Regarding the cutting off of a branch."
Baudhāyana used to say: "One should cut the branch with the formula, 'For food, thee! One should either wipe along it or look at it with the formula, 'For strength, thee!
Śālīki says: "One should only look at it."
(20.1:6.1) Regarding the driving away of the calves: //

Baudhāyana used to say: "With the formula, 'Ye are for Vāyu,' one should set aside the males; with 'Ye are approaching [Vāyu],' the females. Now, if there should be only one or the other, one should not abandon the mantra at all; rather, one should do so with the combined formula, says Śālīki.
Regarding the "path for the branch":
Baudhāyana says that one should move it along the front of the Āhavanīya fire;
Śālīki says [one should move it] behind the Gārhapatya fire.
(20.2:6.5) This is the movement for the branch in all ritual procedures, as well as for the milk offerings, except for the Prāvargya rite.
(20.2:6.6) Aupamanyava says that one should cause the Prāvargya to proceed behind both [the fires].
"The duties of the sacrificer for one who is away on a journey."
Baudhāyana used to say: "The sacrificer indeed travels while accompanied by his sacrificial formulas;
wherever he may be, he should mentally contemplate that [sacrifice].
If he should arrive while the rite is still incomplete, he should consecrate what has been performed and proceed with the remainder of the ritual."
Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "If he has a son or a pupil who is capable of performing the ritual, he should send him there.

If he should return while the rite is still unfinished, or depart after it has been completed, or if one should disregard him, both [the sacrificer and the one sent] should nevertheless consume the sacrificer’s portion."
(20.2:7.1) Regarding the preparation of the fuel and the sacrificial grass: thus it is said.
The Sūtra belongs to the two teachers.

Āñjīgavi says that one should bind the fuel and sacrificial grass after having offered to the ancestors in the afternoon. Aupamanyava says that this should be done on the following day, ending with the call to the preparer of the oblation.
"The heating of the knife."
Baudhāyana used to say: "One should indeed heat both the knife and the horse-rib for the purpose of striking away the Rakṣas.

Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "One should not heat brilliance against brilliance; for these mantras are seen to apply specifically to the horse-rib. Therefore, one should heat only the horse-rib, not the knife, for the purpose of striking away the cruel [Rakṣas]."
"At the steps," so it is said.

Baudhāyana used to say: "One should first take three or four steps eastward from the Āhavanīya fire, and then proceed toward that direction where one thinks one will find the sacrificial grass (barhis).
Śālīki says: "One should go directly from the Āhavanīya as required, but not by way of the southern door."
Regarding the "pariṣavaṇa" (the act of pouring out).
Baudhāyana used to say: "One should recite the mantra three times and perform the ritual action three times.
[He says this] regarding the tracing around the pit for the sacrificial post, the footprint of the Soma-purchase cow, the pit for the Audumbarī post, and the Uparava holes.
Śālīki, however, says: "One should recite the mantra only once and perform the ritual action three times."
"In cases of seizure," so it is said.
The rule is that of Baudhāyana:
"Indeed, this mantra is seen to contain a blessing directed toward oneself.
Śālīki says, "This should rather be a touching performed with the mantra."
Regarding the binding of the *prastara* grass-bundle.
Baudhāyana used to say that one should gird this [sacrificial grass] both at the midpoint and elsewhere;
from this [midpoint], one should perform the *nidhana* chants in an uneven manner.

Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "Indeed, because the *prastara* receives the mantra, the entire *barhis* receives the mantra; therefore, one should not gird it at the midpoint, and this [girding] should be done in the most uneven manner."
(20.2:8.4) "The making of the cord."
Baudhāyana says that the fourth section should be the *adhikaraṇa*;
Śālīki says that the third [section] itself should be the *adhikaraṇa*.
"The covering of the sacrificial grass."
Baudhāyana used to say: "Having first gathered together with a mantra those other *nidhana*s that belong to the Yajurveda, one should then gather the subsequent Yajurvedic *nidhana* with a mantra.

Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "Having first gathered together silently those other *nidhana*s that belong to the Yajurveda, one should then gather the subsequent Yajurvedic *nidhana* with a mantra."

Regarding this, Aupamanyava used to say: "Just as at the beginning of the cutting, so too at the gathering; having first gathered [the grass] with the mantra accompanied by the *yājus*, and having silently gathered the others, one should gather them together, loosen the knot, and then tie it."
(20.3:8.13) Regarding "the making of knots":
The rule is Baudhāyana’s; Śālīki says that one should mutter this mantra while actually drawing the cord together.
"From behind, she embraces him while he faces eastward."
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana;
Śālīki says it should be from the east toward the west.
Regarding the placement of the sacrificial grass (barhis): //20.3.8.17//

Baudhāyana used to say: "Having placed either the wooden sword (sphyam) or a wood-chip (śakalam) within the altar (antarvedi), and having established it there with the mantra, one should then place [the other items] as is most convenient.
Śālīki says: "One should place them with the mantra only at the very spot where one intends to place them."
Regarding the laying down of the enclosing sticks.
Baudhāyana used to say that the middle [post] should be measured by the chest, while the other two should be the length of an arm;
Śālīki, however, says that all of them should indeed be the length of an arm.
(20.3:9.6) Regarding the preparation of the sacrificial fuel.
Baudhāyana says that one should prepare the fuel for the *sāmidhenī* verses;
Śālīki says it should be of unlimited quantity.
"Regarding the composition of the Veda."
"One should make [the sacrificial post] calf-knee-shaped," says Baudhāyana;
"it should be made of *mūtaka* wood," says Śālīki; "it should be threefold [in its dimensions]," says Aupamanyava.
"With the tip pointing upwards," says Aupamanyavīputra.
(20.3:9.11) "The sacrificial grass for the Pitṛyajña."
Baudhāyana says that this sacrificial grass (*barhis*) should have its roots, because of its similarity to the Pitṛyajña; for this very feature is observed specifically in the Mahāpitṛyajña.
Śālīki says that this sacrificial grass should be rootless.
(20.3:9.14) "The convergence of sacrifices."

Baudhāyana used to say: "Whatever sacrifices should coincide on the same day, the cutting of the sacrificial grass for them should proceed for each individual performance (*tantra*), or one should set aside the cut grass for each; having entered upon the vow for each performance, one should release the vow at the conclusion of that performance. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "Whatever sacrifices should coincide on the same day, the cutting of the sacrificial grass for all of them together should take place only once, or one should set aside the cut grass all at once; having entered upon the vow for them at the beginning, one should release the vow at the completion of all of them."
"The pouring out of the parṇatsaru blades."
Śālīki says that one should follow the Sūtra.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "One should throw a third part [of the earth] into the fire-hall (*agnyagāra*), one third within the altar (*antarvedi*), and with the third part one should perform the shaking of the calves;
for in this way, it becomes closer to the cattle."
(20.3:10.9) On the full moon day, the making of the *upaveṣa* [is performed].
"One should perform it," says Baudhāyana;
"one should not perform it," says Śālīki.
(20.3:10.11) Regarding the preparation of the milking-strainer: |||

Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "Having tied the roots together at the root, one should stretch out a double-fold cord and tie it at the tip; in this way, its tip becomes joined with the tips. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "Having tied the roots together at the root, one should stretch out a double-fold cord, wrap it around the root, then stretch out a triple-fold cord and tie it at the tip."
In this way, its summit becomes joined with summits.
Regarding the performance of the *agnihotroccheṣaṇa* rite.

Baudhāyana used to say: "If his [Agnihotra] should have been commenced with clarified butter or with vegetable food, he should offer milk for that night; he should likewise make the remnant of the Agnihotra from milk. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "One should not interrupt the ritual when it is not yet completed.
