but if all the smearings have been poured out together, then one should act in this manner," so says Śālīki.
Thereupon, he mutters the *punarālambha* formula for the sacrifice, either at the *yajñāyajñīya* chant or at the *śaṃyuvāka*.
The former alternative is that of Baudhāyana; the latter is that of Śālīki.
They turn the enclosing-sticks (paridhi) and he throws the grass-bundle (prastara) after them.
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana. Śālīki says that one should indeed throw the prastara and the paridhis into the fire at this point.
"The Adhvaryu, having closed his eyes, offers the oblation silently."
The rule is that of Baudhāyana.
Śālīki says that one should offer the oblation without even looking back.
"The commencement [of study] by means of the arts."

Baudhāyana used to say that one should perform the *upākaraṇa* rite with both—the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the ritual implements (*śilpa*). Śālīki, however, says it should be performed with the ritual implements alone.
Regarding the *nyūṅkhana* (the low-toned chanting): [it is as follows].
One performs the *nyūṅkha* either at the introductory verses (*pratipad*) of the *virāj* meters or during the recitation (*śastra*).
The former alternative is that of Baudhāyana; the latter is that of Śālīki.
Regarding the fire produced by friction, there is the question of whether it is accompanied by mantras or without mantras.
Baudhāyana says that it should be accompanied by a mantra; Śālīki says it should be performed silently.
(23.10:165.7) "The offering for the sacrificial gifts."

Baudhāyana used to say: "One should indeed offer the oblations, but one should mutter the formulas for the responses. Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "One should indeed offer the oblations, but one should not mutter the formulas for the responses.
And Aupamanyava said: "Whatever formulas are connected with the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), one should pay no heed to them at all."
"One who is beyond reproach."
"On this day there should be no recitation," says Baudhāyana;
"one should indeed recite," says Śālīki.
Regarding the extraction of the *ṛc*s.
The rule is Baudhāyana’s: the Adhvaryu should perform [the rite] exactly according to the archetype;
Śālīki says that only the Chandogas and Bahvṛcas should perform the counter-rite.
(23.11:166.1) Regarding "creeping": [it refers to] the act of gliding.
Baudhāyana says that they should move along with the edges of their black antelope skins and touch the northern *havirdhāna* cart;
Śālīki says that they should not touch it.
"In the case of those sacrifices where the Āgrayaṇa cup comes first."
Baudhāyana says that the Adhvaryu, restraining his speech, should draw the cups for the preceding deities;
Śālīki says he may do so after releasing his speech.
Having drawn the *śukra* cup, he holds it until he draws the other two cups.
The Sūtra is Baudhāyana’s:
"Whichever [cup] he should take, having wiped it all around, he should set it down," says Śālīki.
(23.11:166.8) Regarding the phrase "having walked along after [the sacrificer] during the drawing and placing of the cups."
"One should follow after [the fire]" says Baudhāyana;
"one should not follow after it" says Śālīki.
"In the animal sacrifice manuals."
(23.11:166.10) All the ritual procedures are according to Baudhāyana;
Śālīki, however, maintains that the Ahīna sacrifices, the Rātri-sattras, and the animal sacrifices for Indra and Agni are indeed performed with [the specific] animal offerings for Indra and Agni.
(23.11:166.12) Regarding those [sacrifices] which have the Mahāvrata, they are accompanied by the piling of the fire-altar;
however, for the others, Baudhāyana says they should be performed on the northern altar-ground.
Śālīki, however, says that the fire-altar is indeed that of the one-day sacrifice (aikāhika).
"In the cases of the *ākṣīya* [verses]," so it is said.
Baudhāyana says that the Abhijit, the Viṣuvat, the Viśvajit, the tenth day, and the Mahāvrata—these are the ones that do not decrease.
Śālīki says that they are those other than the Pṛṣṭhya and the Abhiplava. Aupamanyava says that they are those other than the Pṛṣṭhya and the Abhiplava, as well as the tenth day.
Gautama says that these eight—the Prāyaṇīya, the Ārambhaṇīya, the Abhijit, the Viṣuvat, the Viśvajit as the tenth day, the Mahāvrata, and the Udayanīya Atirātra—are non-depleting.
"In the animal sacrifice rituals."
All the ritual procedures belong to Baudhāyana.
Śālīki, however, maintains that the annual sacrificial sessions (*sattras*) consist exclusively of animals belonging to the set of eleven (*aikādaśina*).
"The lute has a hundred strings," it is said.
The rule is Baudhāyana’s; Śālīki says that this very lute should have a hundred strings.
(23.11:167.10) Regarding the performance of the artistic crafts belonging to the Mahāvrata in a multi-day sacrificial session (ahargaṇa).
"One should perform it," says Baudhāyana;
"one should not perform it," says Śālīki.
(23.11:167.12) Regarding the shaving of the tufts in a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*).
"They should follow [the fire]," says Baudhāyana;
"they should not follow it," says Śālīki.
"The two-night [rite]," it is said.
The rule is that of Baudhāyana.
Śālīki says that on the day of sacrifice, the preceding day is the first [part] and the following day is the latter [part].
In that regard, it is said: "There are those who are tall, those who are barren, and those who are dwarfish."
"B These [cows] should indeed be the regular ones in a thousand," says Baudhāyana;
"These very ones should be the thousandth," says Śālīki.
(23.12:168.6) Regarding the smelling of the *droṇakalaśa* vessel: [the rule is as follows].
"One should cause [the horse] to smell [the offering] inside the enclosing sticks," says Baudhāyana;
"outside the enclosing sticks," says Śālīki.
"The oblation of forms," so it is said.
The rule is that of Baudhāyana.
Śālīki, however, says that one should also offer the oblations belonging to the Aśvamedha here.
"When the hymns are being raised," so it is said.
The former alternative is that of Baudhāyana; the latter is that of Śālīki.
Regarding the sacrificial cakes of the *aupasada* offerings, there is the question of whether they are accompanied by mantras or are mantra-less.
Baudhāyana says that they should be accompanied by mantras; Śālīki says they should be silent.
Aupamanyava says that one should offer the cakes on single potsherds dedicated to Agni together with a spoonful of oblation all at once.
"They prepare two kinds of cows," so it is said.
The sūtra is that of Baudhāyana.
Śālīki says that one should also prepare goats for this occasion.
"The sacrificial post has its base in a mortar," so it is said.
"One should perform all the ritual acts," says Baudhāyana;
"having sprinkled it, one should raise it," says Śālīki.
Having sprinkled water and held up a chip of the sacrificial post, one should raise it; so says Aupamanyava.
"The gathering up of the dust."

Baudhāyana says that one should carry away the earth from the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths, from the pit for the *audumbarī* post, from the *uparava* holes, from the rubbish heap (*utkara*), and from the *uttaravedi*.
Śālīki says that one should not carry it away.

(23.12:169.7) Now, if they should report an obstacle during the consecrations or the Upasad days, Baudhāyana says that they should disperse and rise [from the session] after performing the Udavasānīya offerings. Śālīki says that they should rise after pressing the Soma for a one-day sacrifice.
Aupamanyava says that they should not rise until the Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha has been completed.
"At their rising," so it is said.
"They should go [to the end] of the *āvabhṛtha*," says Baudhāyana;
"to the end of the *apsuṣoma*," says Śālīki; "to the end of the *dhruva*," says Aupamanyava.
Regarding the Janaka-saptarātra, Baudhāyana says it consists of an Atirātra and a Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha;
Śālīki says it consists of a Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha and an Atirātra.
"One who is about to undergo initiation for the ten-night sacrifice, having offered the Daśahotṛ oblation, undergoes initiation for the ten-night sacrifice."
The rule is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says that after having offered the Saptahotṛ, one should offer the Daśahotṛ.
Thus, indeed, is one possessed of the Brāhmaṇa.
Then there is the *gobalada* ten-night rite, an *atirātra*, a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, a *vājapeya*, and a *mahāvrata* followed by an *atirātra*; on the eighth day, there is a *vājapeya*.
In that regard, there is the performance of the oblations of the *devasū* sacrifice.
"One should perform it," says Baudhāyana;
"one should not perform it," says Śālīki;
"they should follow the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) of the animal sacrifice of the thirty-threefold [stoma]," says Aupamanyava.
When the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period is being omitted, there is the performance of the arts.
"One should perform it," says Baudhāyana;
"one should not perform it," says Śālīki.
In the sixty-first night, there is the taking of the cups for Viśvakarman and Āditya.
Baudhāyana says that one should draw [the cups] during the latter thirty-night period;
Śālīki says that these two are seen [to be prescribed] for the year itself, and therefore one should draw them only during the year.
"The cup for the *ṣoḍaśin* [oblation] is made of udumbara wood."
The rule is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says it must be made of khadira wood alone.
Regarding the dedication of the animals for the Atirātra sacrifice.
The rule is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says that one should dedicate the Sārasvata [animal] alone.
The consumption of the cups belonging to the sixteen officiants.
Baudhāyana says that one should consume [the portions] as manifest;
Śālīki says they are those drunk by Indra.
(23.13:171.3) Regarding the touching of the principal cups during the night rounds.
Śālīki says that one should recite the *sūtra* [as given].
Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "One should touch each principal cup with the formula, 'For Indra Āpiśarvara, thee!'"
(23.13:171.6) Regarding the Āśvina [cup], there is the question of whether it is accompanied by a mantra or without a mantra.
Baudhāyana says that one should perform it with the mantra, while Śālīki says it should be done silently.
Regarding the performance of the Āśvina cup.
The Sūtra is that of Śālīki.
Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "Before the performance of the cups for the day after the Soma-pressing, one should perform the rite with the Āśvina cup there."
Regarding the consumption of the cups belonging to the day after [the Soma pressing].
"One should consume [the portion] with the *anuṣṭubh* metre," says Baudhāyana; "with the *jagatī* metre," says Śālīki.
"In those where the anus is the third," it is said.
Baudhāyana says that one should perform the *upayaja* offerings after dividing [the portions] into eleven parts. Śālīki says [they should be offered] by cutting them off individually.
Aupamanyava says that having thrown all of them into the fire together, one should consecrate them with all the formulas.
"Regarding the dedication of the set of eleven [sacrificial animals]."
Śālīki holds that there should be one set of eleven.
Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "There should be eleven Agniṣomīya victims, eleven Savanīya victims, and eleven Anubandhya victims."
Regarding the sacrificial bed, there is the question of whether it is accompanied by a mantra or without a mantra.
"One should obtain [the sacrificial fire] in a village, not in the forest," says Baudhāyana; "one should obtain it in the forest, not in a village," says Śālīki;
"neither in a village nor in the forest," says Aupamanyava.
"The worship of the couch."
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana.
Śālīki says that one should deposit it right here to the north.
"The tracing around for the Pātnīvata [offering]," so it is said.
"One should trace around the Śālāmukhīya peg," says Baudhāyana;
"one should erect the Pātnīvata post to the north of the set of eleven posts," says Śālīki.
"Regarding the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, [the question is] whether there is a mantra or no mantra."
Baudhāyana says that it should be accompanied by a mantra; Śālīki says it should be performed silently.
"The release of the son of Tvaṣṭṛ."
Śālīki says that one should [perform] the *sūtra*.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "Having carried it around the fire, having led it out northward between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, and having sprinkled it with water, one should release it among the goats of the sacrificer."
"Of the performance of the rite for Tvaṣṭṛ."
"One should perform it in a whisper," says Baudhāyana;
"aloud," says Śālīki.
"Regarding the phrase 'at the re-piling'."
The Sūtra is that of Śālīki.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "If one who is building the fire-altar should lose his way, he should pile a *punar-citi* (re-piling) upon it, and he should set up a sacrificial post to the north of the [original] post."
"In the Kauṇḍapāyinīya sacrifices," so it is said.
Baudhāyana says that the rites beginning with the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) and ending with the *iḍā* offering should be completed;
Śālīki says they should begin with the portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) and end with the *iḍā*;
Aupamanyava says they should include the pouring out of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) and the strides of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇukrama*).
The giving of the piṇḍapitṛyajña is [the first].
"One should give [the gift] day by day," says Baudhāyana;
"at the beginning and at the end of the month," says Śālīki.
This is the exposition of the Hotṛ priests.
"One [version] is: 'together with the grahas, without the svāhā-calls';
another is: 'without the grahas, with the svāhā-calls within';
and another is: 'all [of them]'."
The first option is that of Baudhāyana; the latter two are those of Śālīki.

(23.15:173.11) Sacrificing at each full moon, he should sacrifice twelve times in a year; this is one view. (23.15:173.12) At each new and full moon; this is another. (23.15:173.13) At all [the new and full moons]; this is yet another.
The first option is that of Baudhāyana; the latter two are those of Śālīki.
"In the altar consisting of thirty-three layers."
Śālīki prescribes the Sūtra [as follows].

Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "One should perform all these rites—the taking of the fire, the self-piling, the touching of the white and black [spots], the ascending, and the descending—in accordance with the ritual procedure."
"Day by day at the sacrificial pile."
Śālīki [follows] the Sūtra.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "The taking up of the fire, the self-piling, the touching of the white and black [spots], the ascending, and the descending—one should perform all these rites with the repeated ritual procedure."
Regarding the layering of the loose earth on the chariot-wheel-shaped altar: it is as follows.
Baudhāyana says that one should form the edges of the loose soil;
Śālīki says that one should reach the end of the loose soil only upon the bricks themselves.
"On a red hide," he says.
The sūtra is that of Baudhāyana.
Śālīki says that it may even be without a mounting-block.
"In the case of a document executed by both parties. (23.16)
"Baudhāyana says that one should repeat both verses twice;
Śālīki says that while saying them only once, one should utter each twice."
"Soma facing east, Soma facing west; Soma facing west, Soma facing east."
The former alternative belongs to Baudhāyana; the latter belongs to Śālīki.
"For the mixing of the *sautrāmaṇī* liquor."
The Sūtra belongs to the two teachers.
Regarding this, Aupamanyava used to say: "One should have it brought from wherever the *surā* may be."
Regarding the taking of the cups of Surā.
The rule is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says that one should also take the milk-draughts (payograhāḥ) here.
He causes them to extend behind the handles of the offering-ladles, either towards the east or towards the north.
The former alternative is that of Baudhāyana; the latter is that of Śālīki.
"The mixing of the *surā* and *soma*."
"One should carry it to the south and deposit it to the north," says Baudhāyana; "one should carry it to the north and deposit it to the south," says Śālīki;
"one should deposit it from the very same place from which one carries it," says Aupamanyava.
"One should perform the worship with the Pāvamānī verses."

Baudhāyana says that after worshipping with the Pāvamānī verses, they should worship with the invitatory and offering verses (yājyānuvākyā) for the ancestors; Śālīki says that they should worship with the invitatory and offering verses for the ancestors alone, and not with the Pāvamānī verses.
"The purificatory bath," he says.
The Sūtra belongs to the two teachers.
Regarding this, Aupamanyava used to say that one should go to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with the spits and the *māsara* mixture.
The throwing back [of the water] at the edge of the water has been explained.
The ritual bath has been explained.
The preparation of the fuel-sticks has been explained.
"The subsequent offering of the Vaimṛdha cake."
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says that one should not perform the subsequent offerings without having first sacrificed with the Soma.
"One who has rivals should sacrifice only on the full moon day, not on the new moon day."
Baudhāyana says that one should sacrifice with the full-moon oblations on both occasions.
Śālīki says that one should not perform any form of sacrifice on the new moon day.
Aupamanyava says that one should perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
"One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Sākaṃprasthāyīya. Thus [it is said].
Śālīki says that one should recite the *sūktavāka* formula.
Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say that one should offer the *puroḍāśa* with the two offering-ladles (*sruc*) and the *sāṃnāyya* with the cup (*camasa*).
"One who has not attained prosperity should sacrifice to Mahendra.
"There are indeed three who have attained prosperity: the learned man, the village headman, and the nobleman.
For them, Mahendra is the deity," so it is said.
(23.17:176.11) "If anyone other than these [should wish to sacrifice to Mahendra], he must first sacrifice to Indra for a year and then obtain the right to sacrifice to Mahendra," says Baudhāyana.
(23.17:176.13) "Even from this very point, having sacrificed to Indra for a year, one may obtain the right to sacrifice to Mahendra," says Śālīki.
"One should sacrifice to Indra for a year;
for one does not overstep the vow for a year. Thus [it is said].
Śālīki holds that this is the rule of the Sūtra.

Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "On whichever new moon day one first begins to sacrifice to Indra, when that year has elapsed, on that same day he should sacrifice to Mahendra; from that point forward, he shall indeed be a sacrificer to Mahendra."

Regarding this, Aupamanyava used to say: "The year indeed becomes fully completed for him who begins to sacrifice to Indra on a particular new-moon day; when the year has elapsed, he should sacrifice to Mahendra on whichever new-moon day occurs prior to that [original starting point].
From that time forward, he shall be a sacrificer to Mahendra alone."
"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Dākṣāyaṇayajña;
at the full moon he should offer the *saṃnaya*, and at the new moon he should sacrifice with the *āmikṣā* dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. Thus [it is said].
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says that one should also offer the Vaimṛdha cake on this occasion.
Regarding the consumption of the *sāṃnāyya* offering.
The Sūtra is that of Śālīki.
Regarding this, Baudhāyana used to say: "The sacrificer himself, having set this half-month aside, should consume the Sāṃnāyya."
(23.17:177.13) "Regarding the *āmikṣā*, [the question is] whether there is a mantra or no mantra."
"It should be accompanied by mantras," says Baudhāyana;
"it should be silent," says Śālīki.
(23.17:177.15) He offers the *iḍā*; the four-wheeled [chariot] is the instrument for the *upāṃśuyāja*. Thus it is said.
"One should perform it," says Baudhāyana;
"one should not perform it," says Śālīki.
At the Bṛhaspatisava, there is the offering of the sacrificial fees.

"One should offer the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) at each pressing," says Baudhāyana; "one should offer the sacrificial gifts only at the midday pressing," says Śālīki; "in the other two pressings, one should simply say, 'I give,'" says Śālīki.
"With gold he purifies the clarified butter."
Baudhāyana says that this clarified butter should be poured out with a mantra; Śālīki says it should be done silently.
On an unraised altar to the south of the Āhavanīya fire, he consecrates him with the Bṛhat-sāman chant.
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says that one should sprinkle [the sacrificer] after having spread out even a black antelope skin there.
"A water-pot filled with beans."
"It should be made of gold and filled with gold *māṣa* beans," says Baudhāyana;
"it should be made of clay and filled with grain *māṣa* beans," says Śālīki.
"He offers seventeen spotted heifers to the Maruts."
Baudhāyana says that for these [animals], there should be separate *manotā* hymns and separate animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśa*).

Śālīki says that for these, there should be separate *manotā* hymns but a single animal-cake offering. Aupamanyava says that for these, there should be only one *manotā* hymn and a single animal-cake offering.
The Agniṣṭut and the Indrastut.
The rule is Baudhāyana’s: the Adhvaryu should perform the rite exactly according to the archetype, while only the Chandogas and Bahvṛcas should perform the modifications; so says Śālīki.
"In the case of additional stotras."
The former alternative is that of Baudhāyana; the latter is that of Śālīki.
Regarding the bestowing of the bow.
The former ritual procedure belongs to Śālīki; the latter belongs to Baudhāyana.
"At the end of the one-day sacrifices."
The rule is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says it ends with the Mṛtyusava.
They set aside for him this sacrificial remnant as his portion of the vow-food.
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana.
Śālīki says that one should not place the remnants of the oblation here as a portion for the vow-food.
Then, regarding this Pravargya rite, there are the following options: performing it on the same day, performing it subsequently, performing it with a fee, or performing it beyond the standard time.
"One should perform it," says Baudhāyana;
"one should not perform it," says Śālīki.
The two pressing-boards are the two shoulder-blades of the corpse; the two press-stones are the two testicles of the man.
The rule is that of Baudhāyana.
Śālīki says that one should also prepare the two fire-drills from the chariot-axle wood in this case.
Whatever cup he draws, he draws it in this very manner; and whatever vessel he sets down, he sets it down in this very manner.
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana.
Śālīki says that whichever cup one may draw, one should wipe it all around and then set it down.
He gives a white horse;
he gives a white mare;
he gives a black horse.
He gives a pregnant mare with a white spot on her forehead;
he gives a hundred oxen;
he gives thirty-three gold coins.
He gives a Soma-cup;
he gives a golden cup;
he gives grain heaped up in a mound.
"He gives grain that has been treated with poison."
Baudhāyana says that one should offer both these [optional] oblations and the obligatory ones;
Śālīki says that one should offer only these.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the Sarvatomukha [fire-altar].
"One should pile the fire-altar facing all directions," says Baudhāyana;
"one should not pile it," says Śālīki.
Regarding this, Maudgalya used to say that while the piling of the fire-altar occurs only in the first case, in the others there should be the Sāvitra rites.
Āñjīgavi says that one should not even do this.
(23.19:180.9) "The mounting [of the fires] onto the two kindling woods."
The Sūtra belongs to the two teachers.

Regarding this, Gautama the Householder used to say: "In the case of a sacrificial session (*sattra*), the householder alone should first consign [the fires] into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*); the others [should do so later]."
"Of the hall," [he said].
One should measure it according to the standard unit of measurement;
the Gārhapatya fire-altar is in the middle.
The rule is that of Baudhāyana.
Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "By a step of three paces on all sides."
The *trivṛt* is in the eastern direction, the *pañcadaśa* to the south, the *saptadaśa* to the west, and the *ekaviṃśa* to the north;
or rather, the *jyotiṣṭoma* is on all sides, for all [the sacrificial fees] belong to the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
Regarding the performance of the *pravargya* rite.
The rule of the Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says that one should not perform the Pravargya rite at an Ukthya sacrifice.
"The duties of the sacrificer," he says.
Baudhāyana says that one should perform the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) by reciting the names [of the fires] individually.
Śālīki says that one should perform the duties of the sacrificer according to the occasion.
Aupamanyava says that those which are refinements of the fire (*agni-saṃskāra*) may be performed at will, while the others may be done by means of the common ritual procedure (*tantra*).
Regarding the "adding of fuel to the fires" (agnyanvādhāna).
The rule is that of Baudhāyana.

Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "The Gārhapatya fire should be enkindled once; the Anvāhāryapacana fire should have its source in the village; having enkindled the Āhavanīya fire once, one may then proceed according to the requirements."
Regarding the consumption [of the sacrificial portion].
The rule of Baudhāyana is that one should consume it all at once after having gathered everything together; Śālīki says that one should consume it only once.
(23.19:182.5) "The cleansing," it is said.
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says it should be done once in a single [vessel].
Regarding the carrying away of the world-fires.
The Sūtra belongs to the two teachers.
Regarding this, Dīrghavātsya used to say: "The sacrificial duties (yājamāna) should belong to the former alone."
Regarding the performance of the animal sacrifices for the seasonal rites.
The rule is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki holds that the sacrificial animals of the seasonal rites (*kratupaśu*) and those of the set of eleven (*aikādaśina*) are optional alternatives.
The Sūtra of Aupamanyavīputra is as follows:
"One should anoint [the oblation] with the *pracaraṇī* spoon as many times as there are *stomas*," says Baudhāyana.
(23.19:182.13) [It is called] the *dadhigraha* (curd-offering).
The sūtra of Maudgalya states:
"With milk or with clarified butter."
The former alternative is that of Baudhāyana; the latter is that of Śālīki.
Regarding the drawing of the Aṃśu and Adābhya cups.
The rule is that of Baudhāyana.

Regarding this, Śālīki used to say: "In the Vājapeya, in the twelve-day sacrificial session (*sattrā*), in the *tāṇḍinām ayana*, in the *udbhid*, and in the *valabhid*—for him there should be [the offering] with the *pṛśnigrahas* and the *prāṇagrahas*. Thus it is.
Regarding the taking up of the sixteen cups (*ṣoḍaśigraha*).
The rule is that of Baudhāyana.
Śālīki says that they should draw [the cups] at each pressing.
The offering of the *atigrāhya* cups.
The rule of Baudhāyana is that one should offer the secondary oblation (*anuvaṣaṭkāra*) for the Mahendra cup; Śālīki says they should do so.
"He initiates the *ṣoḍaśin* chant."
The Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says it may be with whatever [wood].
(23.19:183.9) Regarding the removal of the heart-spikes: thus it is said.
"One should remove them one by one," says Baudhāyana; "all of them together," says Śālīki.
"The purificatory bath," he said.
The rule is that of Baudhāyana; Śālīki says that they should go toward the Avabhṛtha bath facing eastward.
(23.19:184.1) "The mounting [of the fires] onto the two kindling woods."
The Sūtra belongs to the two teachers.
Regarding this, Gautama the householder used to say: "One should consign the two fires into the two kindling woods; then the other [should do so]."
One should examine the ritual procedure by means of five factors: by the *chandas*, by the *brāhmaṇa*, by the *pratyaya*, by the *nyāya*, and by the force of the *saṃsthā*.

Regarding "by the *chandas*," which we have already mentioned, it refers to the application according to the traditional recitation (*āmnāya*), such as "this is the preceding part" and "this is the subsequent part.
Furthermore, sometimes the *mantra* itself explicitly declares the ritual action.

It is a restatement of the ritual action (*karmānuvāda*), as for example: "The prayer has gone forth toward the sacrificial grass; follow the wide mid-air! At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I offer what is pleasing to Agni.
Whatever one may not be able to arrange by means of a *chandas* verse, that one should arrange by means of a *brāhmaṇa* passage.

Indeed, the Brāhmaṇa prescribes these mantras that are not [otherwise] known, stating, "One does this with this," and "One does that with that," so that it may come to pass: "For sap thee! For strength thee!"—with these words he cuts off a branch; "Ye are winds! Ye are near-winds!"—with these words he drives away the calves. Moreover, it also prescribes ritual acts that are without mantras.

(24.1:185.10) As for this matter: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fire at eight steps, a Rājanya at eleven, and a Vaiśya at twelve"—this is the settled rule because of its connection with specific social classes (*varṇa*). (24.1:185.12) As for the statement "by means of conviction," this refers to the conviction derived from the *Chandoga*, *Bahvṛca*, and *Ādhvaryava* [Vedic schools]. (24.1:185.13) And as for the statement "by means of logic": when one does not find the standard logic within the archetypal ritual procedure (*prakṛta-tantra*), one should resort to the logic of common practice (*grāman-nyāya*), thinking, "This is the appropriate undertaking here."
Regarding this point concerning the determination by the *saṃsthā*: when the Soma has been carried away, one should press *ādāra* and *phālguna* plants.

There are four ways in which mantras function: by way of praise (*stuti*), by way of designation (*nirdeśa*), by way of benediction (*āśis*), and the fourth is neither by praise, nor by benediction, nor by designation.
Now, these are the five forms of oblation: plant-offering (*auṣadha*), milk (*payas*), animal-offering (*paśu*), Soma, and clarified butter (*ājya*).
Their ritual duties (*dharma*) are distinct and their legal cases (*adhikaraṇa*) are distinct. Since the mantras have been observed according to each respective case,
one should not combine them with one another, as there is no injunction to do so.

(24.2:186.1) By whatever means a particular oblation may be successfully prepared, one should perform it by that very means; that constitutes its proper application (*adhikaraṇa*). (24.2:186.2) The applications have been explained. (24.2:186.3) [This concludes the section on] the sacrifice.
(24.2:186.3) "What is the origin of sacrifice? Faith is its origin; what is the origin of auspiciousness? (24.2:186.3) "And where, indeed, is sacrifice?
(24.2:186.4) "In the person."
(24.2:186.4) "Who, indeed, is the deity of consecration?
"Speech.
(24.2:186.5) "And who, indeed, is Pathyā Svasti?"
"It is speech indeed.
"What then is the one-syllable Gāyatrī?
"It is speech indeed."

"What indeed is the beginning of the sacrifice? What is its foundation? It is known from scripture: "Svāhā! I begin the sacrifice with the mind; svāhā! [I begin] for Heaven and Earth; svāhā! From the wide atmosphere; svāhā! I begin the sacrifice from the wind.
Thus, the wind alone is the beginning of the sacrifice; the wind is its foundation.
(24.3:186.11) How, indeed, should one know this: "This is the *tantra* (the main body of the ritual), this is the *āvāpa* (the insertion)"?
(24.3:186.11) From the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) until the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*), excluding the herb-offering, is the *tantra*.

(24.3:186.12) While that *tantra* exists, there are the points for insertion (*āvāpasthāna*), such as: the milking of the cows, the placing of the potsherds (*kapāla*), the carrying away of the *stambayajus*, the taking of the butter-portion (*ājyagraha*), and whatever else one pours in.

(24.3:186.14) After the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, this insertion (*āvāpa*) occurs in the middle; whatever oblations are poured into that [fire] are subject to the rules of the inserted portion (*āvāpaja*), just as the *prāśitra*, the sacrificer’s portion, the Brahman’s portion, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, the *iḍā*, and so forth.
(24.3:187.3) The insertion pertains to the cutting of the portions (*avadāna*), but the ritual framework (*tantra*) pertains to the offering (*pradāna*).
(24.3:187.4) Where, indeed, does the framework become subject to the inserted portion, or the inserted portion become subject to the framework?
In the Maitrābārhaspatya sacrifice as well as in other rites, the *tantra* indeed begins from the pouring out [of the oblation], while the *āvāpa* occurs at the offering.
Alternatively, in the Vāruṇī offerings and the *saṃjñānī* sacrifice, the *āvāpa* occurs from the pouring out, but the *tantra* occurs at the offering.
The *tantra* extends from the *anūyāja* offerings up to the offering of the *samiṣṭayajus*.
"What deities indeed do the after-offerings (anūyāja) belong to?
"One should say they belong to Agni," he replied.
For it is known from scripture: "The gods found him through the oblations in the after-offerings; in that he performs the after-offerings, he thereby kindles Agni."
"The *prayāja* offerings indeed have the seasons as their deities."
"How many are the forms of the *pākayajña*, how many are the forms of the *haviryajña*, and how many are the forms of the *soma* sacrifice?
"The *huta*, *prahuta*, *āhuta*, *śūlagava*, *baliharaṇa*, *pratyavarohaṇa*, and the *aṣṭakāhoma*—these are the seven forms of the *pākayajña*.
Some, however, declare them to be unlimited."
And whatever else is offered elsewhere than in a monastery, all those are forms of the *pākayajña*.

Now, the forms of the *haviryajña* are: the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*), the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the first-fruits offering (*āgrayaṇa*), the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice, and the Kauṇḍapāyina sacrifice;
some, however, include the Sautrāmaṇī among them.
(24.4:188.2) Now, the Soma-saṃsthās:
the Agniṣṭoma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśī, the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma—these are the seven Soma-saṃsthās.
Whatever constitutes the ritual performance (*kratukaraṇa*) of the Agniṣṭoma, that same applies to the Atyagniṣṭoma.

Whatever [is prescribed] for the Ukthya, that applies to the Ṣoḍaśin and the Vājapeya; whatever [is prescribed] for the Atirātra, that applies to the Aptoryāma. Thus, among the seven Soma-sacrifices, two do not belong to the category of *sattras*: the Vājapeya and the Aptoryāma.
How, indeed, should one know that "this is the first layer" and "this is the upper layer"?
That which is the archetype (*prakṛti*) is the first layer;
then, what he enjoins is the upper layer.
The establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) is the first series; the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) is the subsequent series.
The new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are the first series among the *iṣṭi* offerings; all optional (*kāmya*) *iṣṭis* are the subsequent series.
The offering to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*) is the first series among the independent animal sacrifices (*nirūḍhapaśubandha*); all optional animal sacrifices are the subsequent series.
The Jyotiṣṭoma is the first series among the Soma sacrifices; all other Soma sacrifices are the subsequent series.
The Śyenacit is the first series among the fire-altars; all optional fire-altars are the subsequent series.
The Dvirātra is the first series among the Ahīna sacrifices; all Ahīna sacrifices are the subsequent series.

The twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is the first series of multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*); all other multi-day sacrifices are the subsequent series. The *gavāmayana* is the first series of year-long sacrificial sessions (*sattrāṇi*); all other year-long sacrificial sessions are the subsequent series.
Now, how many *gavāmayanas* are there?
It is known: "Just as in this month the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] are performed, in the final month they should perform the *pṛṣṭhas* once; the third [period] consists of ten months.
"There are seven cultivated plants and seven wild plants;
there are seven domestic animals and seven wild animals."
(24.5:189.2) "The seven meters increase by four syllables each.
Thus, there are seven cultivated plants: sesame, beans, rice, barley, millet, small grains, and wheat; some say that lentils are the seventh.
The seven wild grains are *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, *jartila*, *gavīdhuka*, *gārmuta*, *vāstūka*, and bamboo-barley (*veṇuyava*); some, however, say that *kuruvinda* is the seventh.
The seven domestic animals are the cow, the horse, the goat, the sheep, the human, the donkey, and the camel; the camel is the seventh.

Some, however, say that the "ass" (*aśvatara*) refers to the seven wild animals: the two-hoofed, the beasts of prey, the birds, the reptiles, the elephant, and the monkey, with the river-dwelling creatures as the seventh.
There are the seven meters increasing by four syllables each: the *gāyatrī*, the *uṣṇih*, the *anuṣṭubh*, the *bṛhatī*, the *paṅkti*, the *triṣṭubh*, and the *jagatī*.
Now, there are these three types of repetition (*abhyāvartin*): repetition of the ritual act (*karman*), repetition of the deity (*devatā*), and repetition of the number (*saṃkhyā*).
Indeed, this ritual act of the Sāvitra [offering] involves repetition.
Now, that which involves repetition of the deity consists of the *dhruvājya*, the *droṇakalaśa*, and the "all-pṛṣṭha" [stotra].

(24.6:189.14) Then he asks three times, repeating the count each time: "O slaughterer, is the oblation cooked? (24.6:189.15) Now, regarding the measurement of the King [Soma]: where indeed should one apply a mantra that has been omitted?
One should seek to determine [the proper order] either by position or by suitability or by excellence.

Regarding "by position," as we have stated, one should arrange it together with whichever mantra is recited immediately preceding it, whether by means of an earlier time or a later time. As for what was said regarding "by suitability," it is as follows: "Hoping for great heroism, abundance of wealth, and possession of good horses; consecrated by Bṛhaspati with wealth, stand firm for me, the sacrificer."

As for this [objection] regarding "by means of a beam," this ritual manual for the fire-altar (*agnikalpa*) is indeed taught as consisting predominantly of bricks; therefore, whatever mantra might be omitted there, one should cause it to attain the state of being a brick.
Now, this Aśvamedha is traditionally taught as consisting largely of oblations; therein, whatever mantra might be omitted, one should cause that very mantra to become an oblation.
One should not initiate what has not been commenced, nor should one step beyond what has been commenced; one should complete the rite silently through the performance of the action itself.

(24.7:190.9) Regarding what we said, "it is not for that which has not been commenced": this mantra for the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is indeed recited as short, yet the ritual act (*karman*) is long.
The mantra does not recur merely on account of the stepping (*kramaṇa*).
Now, this mantra for the dismembering of the animal is recited as short, yet the ritual act is long.
A mantra should not be brought into operation merely for the sake of the ritual action.
Now, on this *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, a long mantra has been traditionally handed down, while the ritual action is short; the mantra should not be discontinued merely for the sake of the ritual action.
Regarding this [statement], "three times with the *yajuṣ* formula, once silently"— and regarding those *lokāgni*s, having heard [the rule] concerning the *stambayajus*—
and regarding this [other statement], "five times with the *yajuṣ* formula, five times silently"— [this refers to] having heard the measurement of those [stakes] for the King [Soma].
Regarding the statement, "once with the sacrificial formula, once silently," this refers to measuring the King [Soma] while listening to those [formulas].

Regarding the statement, "he pours out four handfuls of rice," two are for the deity, the third for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and the fourth for the *iḍā*; all of these indeed have their corresponding Brāhmaṇa explanations.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the rites performed according to specific instructions.
The fire-altar is not [otherwise] prescribed.

Rather, it is as follows: "He offers on the gambling-ground; he offers at the front of the chariot; he offers on the pole of the chariot; he offers at a crossroads; he offers on the two tracks; he offers on a stump; he offers on a footprint; he offers on a she-goat; he offers in the right ear of a goat; he offers on the right horn of a goat; he offers in the right hand of a Brāhmaṇa; he offers on a bunch of *darbha* grass; he offers in the waters."

"He offers on the Audumbarī post; he offers on the mound of an anthill; he offers on the Āvasathya fire; he offers on the Uttapanīya fire; he offers on the Śāmitra fire; he offers on the Āgnīdhrīya fire; he offers on the Anvāhāryapacana fire; he offers on the Gārhapatya fire. Thus it is said.
When no specific fire is prescribed, one should offer only in the Āhavanīya; when no specific priest is prescribed, the Adhvaryu [is the officiant].
But rather, it happens as follows: "The Unnetṛ offers; the Pratiprasthātṛ offers.
When no one has been specifically assigned by the Adhvaryu, he alone must offer; the vessel is likewise unassigned.

Moreover, it is as follows: "He offers with his joined palms; he offers with a winnowing basket; he offers with a pouch made of a black antelope skin; he offers with the middle leaflet; he offers with the innermost leaflet; he offers with an *arka* leaf; he offers with a ladle made of *parṇa* wood; he offers with a ladle made of *udumbara* wood; he offers with his two thumbs; he offers with two stalks that have fallen apart; he offers with the throat of a *gomṛga*; he offers with a horse's hoof;
he offers with a metal water-pot. Thus it is said.

(24.8:192.5) When no specific instruction has been given, one should offer with the *sruk* ladle; the fuel-stick (*samit*) is likewise unassigned. One should recognize the fuel-stick only from a specific instruction.
It is known from scripture: "One should not offer [an oblation] into one that lacks fuel; if one were to offer into one lacking fuel, it would be as if one were to give food to one who has no tongue.
Therefore, one must offer only into that which possesses fuel.
When no specific fuel is prescribed, one should offer after having added fuel.
(24.9:192.9) Now, therefore, follows the ritual for the portions (*avadāna*).
(24.9:192.9) "He draws out four times; it becomes a fourfold portion.
(24.9:192.9) When no specific instruction is given, one should offer by merely cutting off the portions.
The sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is unspecified.
One should understand that anything other than rice and barley is [only] known through a specific injunction. However, they indeed say that clarified butter (*ājya*) is the most quickly prepared.
The animal sacrifice is not specifically prescribed.
From the specific injunction alone, one should understand that it is other than the goat [dedicated] to Indra and Agni.
Whatever ritual procedure involves an addition, one should perform it with that addition.
The New and Full Moon sacrifices are characterized by the bringing forward of the fire;
the Soma sacrifice is characterized by the bringing forward of Indra;
and the offering of the medicinal plant to Savitṛ is observed [as its characteristic].
"What indeed is the [equivalent] for the *sāṃnāyya* and for the animal sacrifice? "The milking is for the *sāṃnāyya*; the dedication (*upākaraṇa*) is for the animal."
That which he measures out for the *upāṃśusavana* stone belongs to the King;
the carrying of fire around the other oblations is well known.
What, then, belongs to the King?
That which he carries around as the Vasatīvarī waters at the beginning, that belongs to the King.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).
All of them are dedicated to Agni and consist of eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*), except for those belonging to the re-establishment of the fires (*paunarādheyika*).
All of them are dedicated to Indra and Agni and consist of eleven potsherds (*ekādaśakapāla*), except for those of the *āgrayaṇa* and the *śunāsīrīya* sacrifices.
All [the offerings] for Indra consist of eleven potsherds, except for the Śunāsīrīya;
all [the offerings] for Agni and Soma consist of eleven potsherds, except for that of śyāmāka grain; all animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśa*) consist of eleven potsherds, except for that of Vāyu.
The animal cake (paśupuroḍāśa) belongs to the same deity as the animal victim, except in the case of the offering to Vāyu.
All [animal cakes] belong to Agni-Viṣṇu and consist of eleven potsherds, except for that performed according to the model of the Adhvara sacrifice;
in that case, there are both an eight-potsherd and a twelve-potsherd cake.
All Sāvitra offerings consist of twelve potsherds, except for those belonging to the Aśvamedha;
in that [Aśvamedha] sacrifice, there are both an eight-potsherd and an eleven-potsherd offering, according to the rule: "The Sāvitra is an eight-potsherd.

All Māruta offerings consist of seven potsherds, except for the animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the twenty-one-potsherd Māruta cake of the Rājasūya, and the animal-cake offerings of the Pañcaśāradīya sacrifices.

"What indeed are those 'anukhyā' potsherds that are to be drawn? It is known from scripture: 'One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara in the deer-trap; [it is] a potsherd of the earth. These are the *anukhyā* potsherds. Now, the previously established forms (*pūrvasaṃsthā*).
The *prayāja* offerings consist of five, nine, or eleven; these are the preceding terminuses (*pūrvasaṃsthā*).
There is the carrying of fire around the animal (*paryagnikaraṇa*), the silent pressing (*upāṃśvabhiṣava*), and in the *agniṣṭoma*, the twenty-fourth day of the *gavām ayana*.
Regarding this, it is also known: "It has three hundred and sixty *stotrīya* verses."
"There are as many nights in a year. Thus [it is said].
(24.11:194.5) Now, the royal sacrifices (*rājayajña*):

the *rājasūya*, the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), the human sacrifice (*puruṣamedha*), the universal sacrifice (*sarvamedha*), the *somasava*, the *pṛthisava*, the *mṛtyusava*, the *kānāndhayajña*, and the *śunaskarṇayajña*.
(24.11:194.7) Now, the deities beginning with Aditi.
At the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), however, the first *caru* is offered;
at the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the second;
and at the introductory (*prāyaṇīya*) and concluding (*udayanīya*) rites, as well as at the consecration of the fire (*agnidīkṣaṇīyā*).
(24.11:194.8) There are three [cases]: in the Rājasūya, in the Ratnimāna sacrifices, and in the Prāyuj sacrifices, according to the rule "one should immolate a dewlapped pregnant Aditi-cow.
(24.11:194.10) One [case] is in the iṣṭikalpa; one [case] is in the Vrātyastoma.
In the Aśvamedha, there are four offerings: a pap for Aditi, the wife of Viṣṇu; a haṃsasāci for Aditi; and three reddish-brown ewes for the Ādityas.
In the Sautrāmaṇī, there are two: a ewe for the Ādityas and a barren cow.

And regarding the statement "the draughts are eighteen," there are three ritual systems (*tantra*) dependent upon the sacrifice: that with five *prayāja*s, that with nine *prayāja*s, and that with eleven *prayāja*s.
By means of the five-*prayāja* system, the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) and the optional offerings (*kāmyeṣṭi*) proceed.
The Cāturmāsya sacrifices are performed with nine fore-offerings;
the animal sacrifice and the Soma sacrifice are performed with eleven fore-offerings. These six [rites] are applicable to all ritual manuals and serve all purposes.

(24.11:194.17) Just as this [is taught regarding] the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*), the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and the Soma sacrifice—(24.11:195.2) that too is known: "Now, when he takes out his fire, by that he obtains a thousand wish-granting cows (*kāmadughā*).
(24.11:195.3) And when he performs the fire-oblation, by that [he obtains a thousand]; for indeed, this is the measure (*mātrā*) of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
This, indeed, is the lowest of these [sacrifices];
from this, each subsequent one becomes better.
One who performs the animal sacrifice conquers all the worlds.
(24.11:195.5) Indeed, other sacrificial rites are undertaken for a single desire, but the animal sacrifice and the Soma sacrifice are for all desires.
(24.11:195.6) "The animal sacrifice and the Soma sacrifice are for all desires."
One who is about to establish the sacred fires should make himself prosperous;
by whatever means he might be unprosperous, by that same means he should make himself prosperous.
Whatever debts may have become due, he should either settle them or obtain permission regarding them.
Now, we shall first cite the selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) specifically for the *agnyādheya* rite.

If they have been selected by his ancestors, he should not select others, provided that their lineage of Vedic study has not been interrupted and they are endowed with human qualities, good character, and proper conduct.
Regarding this, what indeed constitutes "over-selection" (*ativaraṇa*) or "selection" (*varaṇa*)?

“He has committed theft,” “He has accepted [an improper gift],” “He has officiated for one for whom one should not officiate,” “He has performed a censurable rite,” or “He has persisted in such [conduct]”— if there is either an over-selection or a selection among these,
and if he should select them, he should select only those whose limbs are unimpaired. But which of these should he select first?
He should choose first that one who is his most highly esteemed; with him as an associate, he should seek the others.
Or, indeed, if he chooses according to seniority, he should choose the Brahman first, then the Hotṛ, then the Udgātṛ, and then the Adhvaryu.
Either immediately after the Brahman or before him, whichever comes first according to the ritual action;
he should dwell together with the officiating priests using the wealth distributed [by the patron].
There are three legal cases concerning officiating priests (*ṛtvij*): "I shall sacrifice even without a priest"; "He did not appoint his wife as the *ājyāśis*" [priest];
and "What indeed is the duty toward the priests?"—[the answer being] "He who is the teacher (*ācārya*)."
"How is one worthy? [he asked].
"Āgama-āgama" is one [formula];
"ṛtumukha-ṛtumukha" is one;
"saṃvatsarasya pāra" is one.
(24.13:197.4) "The attainment of sacrifice"—this is another [point].
(24.13:197.4) What indeed is the duty (*dharma*) of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)?
(24.13:197.5) One should not perform the office of an officiating priest once it has been relinquished.
One should not officiate as a priest for one who has not been meditated upon; one should not officiate for one who has not been purchased;
one should not officiate for one who has not been chosen.
One should not officiate at a sacrifice for one who has exceeded the prescribed age limit;
one should not officiate for one whose specific purpose is not declared; one should not officiate for one for whom the sacrificial fees have already been taken.
One should not officiate at a sacrifice during the dark fortnight; one should not officiate for one who is afflicted; one should not officiate for one who is deceased.
One should not officiate at the sacrifice of one who has three scars;
one should not officiate at the sacrifice of one who has crossed a moat;
one should not officiate at the sacrifice of one who has gone to the end [of his life].
One should not officiate at a sacrifice for an outcaste (*antyaja*).
One should not officiate at a sacrifice for one who has not studied the Vedas (*ananūcāna*).
Or rather, among these, one may officiate for that person who, while living by looking for a livelihood, should break the sacrificial potsherds (*kapāla*).
This is also known from the *Daśataya*: "In distress, I cooked the entrails of a dog; I found no comforter among the gods. I saw my wife being dishonored; then the hawk brought me honey.
Regarding these [verses], it is said: "There is no one unfit for sacrifice who gives a thousand-fold fee."
Regarding the phrase "salt and sand":
if there should be salt that resembles ashes, one should have it brought;
one should also have it brought from the dung of a wild boar.
One should fetch [the material] from the heap of an aranyakhara (wild rat).
One should fetch it from the one who is a non-negligent cook;
if no such cook is available, one should fetch it from the hollow of a crab.
If wood struck by lightning is unavailable, one should bring wood struck by frost or wind;
[as for the phrase] "of a variegated *aśvattha* tree," one should fetch it from a place where a village, a city, a river, or a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) is known.
"A horse that has drawn before" means "a young one"; this is what is expressed by the phrase "three chips of gold."
One should have these six made:
those for the purpose of worship should be of gold, and those for the purpose of giving away should be of silver.
Both are adorned with human ornaments and dressed in new, unwashed garments.
Every other human ornament is indeed different from the *nalada* [grass];
they prescribe this specifically for one who is afflicted.
Some, however, prohibit the wearing of a garland.
"One should place them a year in advance," [it is said].
[If they are placed] on the third day, the sixth day, or the twelfth day,
and the year has not yet elapsed and the fire goes out, what should one do in that case?
He should once again prepare the *brahmaudana* until the placing of the fuel-sticks.
He should not have his hair or beard shaved;
however, he should look toward this [period] for a year beforehand.
This has been stated for the purpose of expiation.
As many times as it should go out, one should act in this very manner; even when it has gone out completely, one should not initiate [the student] again, but should act in this very manner.
The ritual procedure beginning with the cow for the Upavasatha day is performed.
Some say there are two *brahmaudana* offerings: the one to be consumed as leftovers is the first, and the one for the *sāntva* rite is the second.
Then, while pouring the saline earth (*ūṣa*) among the ritual materials, he should meditate mentally on that which is black in the moon, thinking: "That also is here."
If he has not studied the Sāmans, he should recite the Yonis, or else the Vyāhṛtis, or else the Hiṃkāra.
With the light of the Praṇītā water, he should set the chariot wheel in motion.
If the moon should appear to him while he is establishing the fires, what should he do in that case?
Whatever ritual task may have been commenced, one should bring it to completion and then cease according to the proper sequence. [The rule is: "On the following day, one should complete it.
Now, if the sacrificial fuel (idhma) should be seen [already] placed on the fire, how should one act in that case?
Having performed the ritual up to the final full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should conclude at the end of that rite; on the following day, he should bring it to complete fulfillment.
(24.16:200.3) Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the seasons and the lunar mansions. We shall first explain the seasons, and then the meters:
"In spring, a Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires; in summer, a Rājanya; in autumn, a Vaiśya; and in the rainy season, a Rathakāra."
The establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) belongs to all [classes], and it may be performed by all under the asterism Rohiṇī.
However, the Vedic meters (*chandas*) are assigned according to the respective caste (*varṇa*). Nevertheless, the rites for establishing the fires are indeed not restricted by specific desires.
As it is said:
"One should establish the sacred fire under the Kṛttikās;
one should establish the sacred fire under Rohiṇī."
One should establish the sacred fires under the two Punarvasus, or under the two former Phalgunīs,
or under the two latter Phalgunīs.
(24.16:200.9) "Under Citrā," it is said;
these [sacrifices] are to be performed on the same day.
(24.16:200.10) "In summer, a Rājanya [should sacrifice]."
"A Vaiśya [should establish the fires] in autumn"—these two [rules] do not apply to the immediate (*sadyaskāla*) performance.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the fire-establishments resulting from distress (*ārtijāny agnyādheyāni*).
[They are performed] during the bright fortnight in one half of the year and during the dark fortnight in the other half of the year.

One who establishes the sacred fires during the waxing fortnight of the month of Vipakṣa may establish them within whatever interval of time is available; however, on the full moon day, it must be performed as a single-day rite (*sadyaskāla*). One who establishes the fires during the waning fortnight of the month of Vipakṣa finds no such interval for waiting.
One should perform this entire day as a single-day rite (*sadyaskāla*), including the Caturhotṛ formulas, the two Sārasvata oblations, and the Anvārambheṣṭi.
Then, having performed the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha sacrifices, he should wait for the New-moon day.
If it is the New-moon day, he should perform the rites of that very day ending with the New-moon sacrifice;
then he should offer the two Sārasvata oblations and join verse with verse.
Thus for the *pūrṇadarvī* offering;
thus for the *vāstoṣpatīya* offering.
How, indeed, should one offer the *pūrṇāhuti*?
(24.17:201.4) He should offer with the formula: "To Agni, to the Earth, to Vāyu, to the Atmosphere, to Sūrya, to the Sky, to Varuṇa, to the Waters, Svāhā!
(24.17:201.5) Now, this silent Agnihotra is seen as being for the purpose of consecrating the fire;
that he should offer with clarified butter alone.
Having wiped downward, he wipes upward.
He considers both of these as being offered at the morning and evening *agnihotra* until the night of the fast-day (*aupavasathikā*).
When about to recite the *sāmidhenī* verses, having explained the *daśahotṛ* formula and uttered the *vyāhṛti*s, he should then utter the sound *hiṃ* and then recite; this is the sequence here.

(24.17:201.10) How, indeed, does one proceed with the Soma sacrifice at the establishment of the fires? Having performed the sequence up to the full-offering (pūrṇāhuti), he should enter the sacrificial hall. The cake on eight potsherds for Agni should follow the initiation offering (dīkṣaṇīyā); the cake for Indra-Agni and the pap for Aditi should follow the introductory offering (prāyaṇīyā); the cake on eight potsherds for Agni Pavamāna should follow the guest reception (ātithyā); the animal-cake for the victim dedicated to Agni-Soma should follow [the offering]; and the Anvārambhaṣṭi offering should follow the morning pressing cakes for Agni Pāvaka and Agni Śuci.
Alternatively, having completed all the oblations pertaining to the establishment of the sacred fires (*āgnyādheya*), he should enter the hall;
this is the *anvārambheṣṭi* following the *udavasānīyā*.
Now follows this re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*).
What, indeed, constitutes the re-establishment?

It is when, after having established the fires, one becomes worse off, thinking, "I have not prospered; my son has died"—it is upon seeing such a thing within this very year that the re-establishment occurs.

"At what time, indeed, should one establish this [sacred fire]? That new moon which occurs before the full moon of Āṣāḍha coincides with the *punarvasu* constellation once a year; on that day, one should establish it."

On the day of preparation (*upavasatha*) for that [sacrifice], having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*), having moved away, having churned out the fires, and having spread them out, he should perform the *udvāsanyā iṣṭi*; having sacrificed, he should consign the fires again and go. He should have this fire-hall repaired or have another new one built; he should have these sacrificial vessels scraped clean or have other new ones made.
"A chariot renewed is the sacrificial fee"—by this, it is said to be one that has been repaired; "a garment re-sewn"—by this, it is said to be one that has been repaired.

The "bull let loose again" is said to be one that has already been worn out. Now, these follow the procedure of the *upāṃśu* (whispered) rite: namely, the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*), the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*), the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), the consecration offering (*dīkṣaṇīyā*), the introductory offering (*prāyaṇīyā*), the guest-offering (*ātithyā*), the Upasad rites, the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*), the offerings to the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*), the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), the concluding offering (*udayanīyā*), the offering at the settling of the altar (*udavasānīyā*), the rite for carrying forth the fire-altar (*citipraṇayanīya*), the rite for the post of Tvaṣṭṛ (*tvāṣṭra*), the rite for the sprouting of the sacrificial post (*yūpavirohaṇīya*), the eight-footed cow, and the pregnant cow;
these are performed with the conviction that they are auxiliary acts.
As for this, they teach the ritual procedure according to the manual of Baudhāyana.

"One should establish the Gārhapatya fire with the verses of the Serpent Queen (*sarparājñī*). Having extracted the *gharmaśiras* verse, one should insert the verses of the Serpent Queen in its place. Having performed the regular worship, one should perform the worship pertaining to the re-establishment of the fires (*paunarādheyika*).
(24.19:203.10) It is established from this point forward for one who has sacrificed and is re-establishing the fires: "Should he perform the *saṃnayya* offering or not?
(24.19:203.11) Some say that he should perform the *saṃnayya*.

Now, some say that one should not bring [the fire] together; for the sacrifice is one that touches the body. Only when one is to sacrifice again should one then bring them together. "They consist of a hundred syllables," so it is said.
These four Akṣarapaṅkti verses each consist of twenty-five syllables; that makes one hundred. Now follows this third piling.
"Now, which of these two does this depend upon: the initial establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) or the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*)?
One should say, "The initial establishment of the fires.
Now, for one whose fires have been carried away or whose kindling woods (*araṇī*) are lost, he proceeds by means of the *brahmaudana* alone.
The establishment of the sacred fires is accomplished.
(24.20:204.6) Now, regarding these New and Full Moon sacrifices, the teachers declare that they begin with the full moon and conclude with the new moon.
(24.20:204.7) In this regard, they cite: "After midnight on the full moon night, the moon becomes full;
it remains full for the remainder of that night, for the entire following day, and until midnight of the subsequent night."
Now, on the day of preparation for the new moon sacrifice, after midday, the sun overtakes the moon.
Having overtaken it during this afternoon, as well as throughout the entire night and until midday of the following day,
one should perform the sacrifice toward this junction.
The night is to be joined with the full moon day, and the day with the new moon day.
There are two full moon days and two new moon days;
[one should perform the rites] on each preceding full moon day and each succeeding new moon day.
"The earlier full moon is Anumati, the later is Rākā; the earlier new moon is Sinīvālī, the later is Kuhū.
"Anumati is indeed the Gāyatrī, Rākā is the Triṣṭubh"—these are the names of the full moon. "Sinīvālī is the Jagatī, Kuhū is the Anuṣṭubh"—these are the names of the new moon.
Now, this moon consists of sixteen digits; fifteen of its digits are arranged as the fortnights,
but this sixteenth digit has entered manifoldly into the Brahmins, the waters, the plants, the trees, and the animals.
In that these [rites] are performed at the sacrifice, by that means it is gathered together.
Now, the days of the Upavasatha are the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the sixteenth; however, the thirteenth and seventeenth do not occur.
On the day of the fast, this *āhitāgni* should set out the fire-sticks intended for the *anvādhāna* before the morning *agnihotra*; he should have the food for entering the vow cooked;
of that, two portions remain for him to eat.
Mixed with ghee, mixed with curds, free from pungent salt and meat—
on this entire day he should avoid all such cultivated grain except for sesame; having offered it to a Brāhmaṇa, he may eat.
On this day, one should not give the remains of the meal to a Śūdra;
on this day, one should give the remains of the meal only to one's wife.
One should not sleep on a couch, nor should one have sexual intercourse with a woman.
He may sleep on a raised surface at will, but he must not approach a woman; rather, he should remain one who observes his vow.
If he intends to have his hair and beard shaved, then after having his hair and beard shaved, he should have his body hair clipped and trim his nails.
He should bathe, anoint himself with oil, and apply collyrium to his eyes.
One should assume the form of the consecration (*dīkṣā*).
Having placed the fires in order—one should kneel on the right knee before the *gārhapatya*, squat before the *ānvāhāryapacana*, and stand before the *āhavanīya*—one should recite the tenth [verse].
If the fires that have been established should go out, the *savanīya* offering belongs to the *gārhapatya*.

If the *āhavanīya* goes out, one should remove the ashes, smear the ground with a lump of dung, draw out the flaming *āhavanīya*, deposit it, add fuel, re-establish it, and worship it with the *vyāhṛti*s.
Now, if the *anvāhāryapacana* should go out, one should carry it away in exactly the same manner.
"For this deity, namely the Anvāhāryapacana fire, is indeed not afflicted.
Having thus rekindled [the fire], he should worship it with the *vyāhṛtis*.

Now, if the sun should set or rise while his fire has not been lifted out, he should either act according to the sūtra or offer the *saṃtanī* oblations: "May the mind, the light, enjoy [the offering]; thirty-three are the threads. Having offered these two spoon-oblations (*sruvāhuti*), he should worship [the fire] with the *vyāhṛtis*.

Then, when the sun has set, having offered a *sruva*-oblation to Varuṇa, he should worship with the *vyāhṛtis*. Then, when the sun has risen, having offered a *sruva*-oblation to Mitra, he should worship with the *vyāhṛtis*;
and [he should worship] the *anvāhāryapacana* fire with the *vyāhṛtis* alone.

(24.22:206.18) Now, when the fires have been mounted upon the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) or within oneself, and one has set out on a journey, the teachers declare that there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Regarding this, they cite an example: "If the fires have been mounted within oneself, one may at will cause them to descend into the two kindling woods and churn [the fire].
Or else, having spread the fires over the attendants (*amātya*), one should cause them to descend into that [fire] and offer oblations.
Then, once the fires have been mounted upon the two kindling woods, he should churn them out, distribute the fires, and offer oblations.
Alternatively, having distributed the fires among the attendants and placed the kindling woods between them, he should offer oblations.
As it is for the fire of a king or a Vaiśya, so it is for the *nirmanthya* fire used for non-sacrificial purposes;
some declare that this is established by tradition.
The minimum extent of a dwelling site for one traveling on a journey is as much ground as a black antelope could lie upon.
He should add fuel to the fires, enter upon the vow, and once he has entered upon the vow, he should cut a branch of the *parṇa* tree; this is the sequence here.
There are three kinds of *palāśa* trees: the smooth, the hairy, and the creeper-like.
Of these, it is the hairy one that must be cut.
One should cut no further than the distance a cow would graze;
beyond that, it would be unfavorable for cattle.
If, however, one should be negligent regarding the remnants of the *agnihotra* oblation, he should simply offer the *agnihotra* again.
Now, these six lowest [cows] for milking the *sāṃnāyya* are traditionally handed down;
if there should be only three of them, one should draw [the milk] four times from either the first or the last. But if there should be only two, one should draw from each of them three times.
If, however, there should be only one [cow], he should divide that very one six times.
"Having released his speech, without touching [the cow], he should milk the subsequent ones"—this is said to apply specifically to the case of an unlimited number [of cows].
There are twelve pairs in the New and Full Moon sacrifices; these are to be accomplished [as follows]:
"The wooden sword and the potsherds" constitutes five.
"He releases the calf and places the cooking pot on the fire"—these are seven; together with those [previously mentioned], they make twelve.
This applies only to one who performs the *saṃnayya* offering at the new moon sacrifice, not to one who does not.
Now, this altar for the New and Full Moon sacrifices is either as large as the sacrificer or of unlimited size.
Its crosswise dimension is such that it may encompass the oblations as they are placed;
he raises the two longitudinal sides of the altar to enclose the Āhavanīya fire.
He digs out the two buttocks facing west for the sake of enclosing the Gārhapatya fire.

It is wider in front, broader behind, and more deeply concaved in the middle; for such indeed is a woman. He says of it: "He digs it to this extent, measured by Prajāpati who is the mouth of the sacrificer; he digs it for the sake of a firm foundation."
Some say it should be dug two finger-breadths deep;
some say three finger-breadths deep;
others say four finger-breadths deep.
According to some, it should be the measure of a furrow; according to others, the measure of a chariot track;
according to others, as far as the white [mark] on the heel of the hoof.
This very [space] becomes more deeply excavated than others;
one should not dig deeper than these measures.
One makes it broader toward the south.
"He makes it filled with loose earth, sloping toward the east and the north, and well-finished," [the text says]; "he takes this much," thus he speaks regarding the prastara-bunch.

According to some, it should be taken up as large as the nail of the thumb; according to others, it should be taken up as a spreading [blade of grass]; according to others, it should be taken up as large as the handle of a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*).

(24.25:210.1) According to some, it should be taken as long as the handle of a *sruva* ladle; according to others, it should be taken as long as a thigh bone; according to others, it should be taken as measured by a joint of the thumb.
"An unlimited number should be taken," say some; "There are this many," he says regarding the fuel-sticks.
These [reeds] are said to be exactly a span in length;
they say they should be made measured by this [span],
for "by means of this, Prajāpati first created offspring."
"To which deity do the two strainers belong, and by whom are they purified?
One should reply: "They belong to Viṣṇu and are purified by Vāyu.
They should not be cut with the fingernails.
While leading forward the *praṇītā* waters, he should meditate on the earth with his mind, thinking: "With this [verse] I lead forward the waters.

He should perform these [rites] in common: the *praṇītā* waters, the *āhavanīya* fire, the *brahmán*, and the fuel and sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*). They say that this constitutes the head of the sacrifice.
Now, what indeed makes the sprinkling waters (*prokṣiṇyaḥ*) truly sprinkled?
It is known: "The exponents of Brahman say, 'With water have you sprinkled the oblations; with what [did you sprinkle] the waters? "'With the Brahman,' [they reply].
Thus they become indeed sprinkled by the Brahman."

"O *haviṣkṛt*, come!"—thus he says for a Brāhmaṇa; "O *haviṣkṛt*, arrive!"—thus for a Rājanya; "O *haviṣkṛt*, hasten here!"—thus for a Vaiśya. (24.25:210.14) This [call] is addressed to Parjanya himself.
Furthermore, they also cite: "He speaks thus to her who prepares the oblation (*havis*)."
"It is known from the Brāhmaṇa: 'One should strike the grinding stones loudly with a bull's roar. [The text continues: 'He says, "Strike loudly," for the sake of victory;
as many enemies as hear the sounding of his sacrificial implements, they perish.'"
Twice on the lower grinding stone and once on the upper grinding stone;
"he completes it nine times," so it is known from tradition.
"O Agni, drive away the raw-eating fire from the fire!"—
what indeed is this "raw-eater"?
It is said to be another fire.

"Drive away the flesh-eater"—by this, the fire of the cremation ground is meant. "Bring hither the one who sacrifices to the gods"—by this, the Āhavanīya fire is meant. But who indeed is the Kavyavāhana? One should say: it is the Anvāhāryapacana fire.
It is known from scripture: "O Agni Kavyavāhana, you who increase the cosmic order, you shall worship the ancestors.
From where, then, should one pour out the flour? One should say: "From the black antelope skin.
While pouring out the flour, he restrains his speech.
"Without letting it burn, cook it"—thus he releases his speech.
"That which is burnt belongs to Nirṛti; that which is uncooked belongs to Rudra;
that which is well-cooked belongs to the gods"—by this it is meant that he cooks it so that it is properly cooked.
"Be united with the *brahman*," it is known; "Speech indeed is the *brahman*; verily by speech he thus unites him. But where, indeed, is the mixed oblation cooked?
At the very moment he pours this out for the Āpyas, [he recites]: "Svāhā to Ekata! Svāhā to Dvita! Svāhā to Trita!
Now, who indeed is Ekata, who is Dvita, and who is Trita?
Some say they are the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather.
Some say they are earth, the intermediate space, and heaven;
others say they are fire, the sun, and lightning.
Some say that Agni had three elder brothers;
some say they were sages who bore these names.
These gods wiped themselves on the Āpyas, and thus the gods come to have the name Āpya.

(24.27:212.6) "Where, indeed, is it offered to the ancestors on the full moon day? (24.27:212.7) "It is when one pours [the remains] down upon the two hips. (24.27:212.7) "But how, indeed, does the clarified butter become sprinkled?"
One should say, "Sprinkled with truth.
It is known from scripture: "I sprinkle thee with truth; may I partake of that which is thine. [And one says:
"I take thee for the restraint and support of the five winds. Thus the winds are directed toward each quarter.

The Viṣvagvāta wind indeed becomes their fifth. With the formula, "I take you for the restraint and support of the five seasons," the winter and the cool season here enter into a single unit. With the formula, "I take you for the restraint and support of the five directions," this very upward direction becomes their fifth.

"I take you for the restraint and support of the five classes of beings. These are the gods, humans, asuras, rakṣases, and the gandharvas are the fifth among them. "I take you for the restraint and support of the five-holed cauldron. This very sky is that five-holed cauldron.
"The five directions are its cavities; the wind is the stirring-ladle.
Regarding this, they also cite: "The year itself is the sacrificial porridge (caru); it has five cavities. The seasons are its cavities; the wind is the stirring-ladle."
(24.28:213.5) Now, the entrance of both the Adhvaryu and the Hotṛ:
the Adhvaryu enters from the east, having turned back toward the west, while the Hotṛ enters from the west, having turned back toward the east.
The Adhvaryu should remain closest to the fire.
If one does not know his ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*), when told, "Recite the *pravara*," he should simply say, "In the manner of Manu, in the manner of Bharata, in the manner of Manu.
For it is known from the Brāhmaṇa: "For all creatures are descended from Manu. Or, for a king, the *pravara* of his domestic priest (*purohita*) may be used.

Now, if one whose lineage is unknown should recite the *pravara* for his teacher’s teacher (*ācāryāmuṣyāyaṇa*), he should indeed choose that very person as the preeminent teacher; then he should choose the *hotṛ*.
He should augment the portion for the deity with milk and the *sviṣṭakṛt* portion with curds. Having interlaced his fingers, he should take the portions.
The portions for the deity are the size of a thumb-joint; those for the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *aiḍa* portions are larger.

Having offered the fourfold portions with the formula, "The Brahman is the foundation," and having filled the *sruva* ladle with water for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he should pour it out inside the enclosing sticks with the formula, "I offer this oblation in Vaiśvānara. Regarding the question, "What indeed constitutes that which has not been recited together? one should say: "Everything prior to the call (*saṃpraiṣa*) for the *anūyāja* offerings."
What is the sacrificial fee for the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the optional offerings, and the animal sacrifice?
Some say that the Agnihotra has a small gift as its fee;
others say that the Agnihotra has a ladleful of grain as its fee.
In that he offers in the evening, he thereby makes the night worthy of the sacrificial fee; in that he offers in the morning, he thereby makes the day worthy of the sacrificial fee;
and what he gives from there, that is the sacrificial fee.
When it is said that "he gives during the day and night," this is precisely what is meant.

Now, regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, there is the fourfold division of both the *anvāhārya* rice and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). It is known from scripture: "This [gift] is indeed his sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."
(24.29:214.10) "Furthermore, he thus closes the breach of the sacrifice.

(24.29:214.10) Just as in that Soma sacrifice the sacrificial fees are led to the officiating priests according to instruction, even so here, having divided the southern cake into four parts, he places it upon the sacrificial grass.
Garments are the sacrificial fees for optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) for which no specific fee has been prescribed.
The animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) has a cow as its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The *anvāhārya* mess of rice is obligatory.
