Regarding this ritual procedure taught by Śālīki—that at the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings everyone should walk around the north side of the *gārhapatya* fire—it follows that the offering of husks (*phalīkaraṇahoma*) should be performed here without returning [to the starting point].

(24.29:214.16) Now, some offer oblations to Rākā, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, and Anumati, as well as the Patnī-homas and the two Nāriṣṭha-homas, before the Gṛhapati: "May the wife go together with her husband through good deeds; may they both become the two yoke-animals harnessed to the sacrifice. Being in harmony, may they cast off their enemies; may they grasp the undecaying light in heaven, Svāhā!"

(24.29:215.3) "O sacrifice, these ten forms of yours are worthy of worship; may the sacrificer gratify them with clarified butter. Praising the instruction of the two *nāriṣṭha* [sacrificial ladles], the sacrificer has become immortal within the divine assembly of the gods—*svāhā*!
(24.29:215.5) O you two of a hundred powers, that portion of strength which the gods ordained for you—by this I gratify you; by this, may you two be satisfied from distress—*svāhā*! Thus.
Now, the teachers declare that this Agnihotra begins in the evening and concludes in the morning;
regarding this, they cite the example: "These two lights, those of the sun and of the fire, have come together;
one should not let them be separated."

When taking out the Āhavanīya fire in the evening, he should pour it out from the east while facing west; when taking out the Āhavanīya fire in the morning, he should pour it out from the west while facing east.

When about to offer the evening Agnihotra, he should circumambulate by the front and make the offering; when about to offer the morning Agnihotra, he should circumambulate by the rear and make the offering.
In this way, these two lights of his remain unseparated.

Now follows this mantra for the lifting [of the fire]: "With speech as the *hotṛ*, with breath as the *udgātṛ*, with the eye as the *adhvaryu*, with the mind as the *brahman*, and with the ear as the *āgnīdhra*—with these five divine officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), I lift you up. Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! While being lifted, lift me away from evil."
"Whatever evil I have done, whether unknowingly or knowingly, whatever sin has been committed by day—release me from all that, O Deliverer! Thus at evening.
"Whatever sin has been committed by night—release me from all that, O Deliverer! Thus at dawn.

He places the fire [on the altar] with the mantra: "I offer the immortal oblation into the immortal; Agni on earth for the winning of immortality. Through this, may we win from here our infinite desire, that which Prajāpati first won. I offer the immortal into Agni Vaiśvānara, Svāhā! Thus at evening. At morning, he says: "I offer the immortal into Sūrya Vaiśvānara, Svāhā!
This indeed is the Agnihotra of Agni; the other is the milk-oblation.
One who is about to sacrifice should sprinkle water around the fires as they were established; having sacrificed, he should sprinkle water around the Āhavanīya alone.
One who is about to sacrifice and one who has sacrificed should sprinkle water around the Āhavanīya alone. Or rather, he should not sprinkle water at all; this is another [view].

(24.30:216.6) Now follows this worship performed in absentia: "O Agnis, while remaining right here, I support you who are there with breath, speech, and mind; may life not desert me while I am away; I worship you with the Vaiśvānara light.
(24.30:216.8) Then, when about to depart on a journey, he should silently place this fuel-stick upon the fire;
thus, while traveling, he performs the sacrificer's duty.
(24.31:216.10) Now, regarding this combined oblation (*samastahoma*), the teachers declare it to exist according to the *yāyāvara* rule.
(24.31:216.11) On this point they cite an example: "There were indeed sages named the *yāyāvaras*.
While on their journey, they became exhausted."
They offered it all together;
therefore, according to the practice of the *yāyāvara*, one should offer everything together while on the road.
That is the offering without a specific occasion.
He should conceal [the fire] by lying down, or by closing his eyes, or by extinguishing it.

One should not offer the *agnihotra* with the milk of a *śūdra* woman; nor with that of one who has not been consecrated (*anāhitāgni*), nor of one whose calf is dead, nor of one that is very young (*vahala*), nor of one that is barren (*vāhinī*), nor of one that is estranged from her husband (*anyā*), nor of one whose calf belongs to another, nor of one received as a gift for a funeral feast (*anudeśya*), nor of one received as a gift for a sacrificial animal to be immolated (*anustaraṇī*).
Many should not offer with the milk of a single cow, nor should a single person offer with the milk of many cows.
For one who obtains milk, the consecration of what has been spilled takes place starting from the act of placing it near the fire.
While the fires are blazing but no offerings have been made, he should count how many *agnihotra* oblations have been omitted and offer them again in succession.
If he should offer while the sun has not yet set, he must offer again once the sun has actually set.
Now, if one should offer at the dead of night, one should offer again at dawn.
How, indeed, is the offering of rice balls performed for one whose father is still living?
To those very ancestors to whom the father gives, the son gives;
however, one whose father is living gives to two.
(24.32:217.11) One whose grandfather is still living gives [the offering] to one person.

Some say that one should not give while [the father] is living. (24.32:217.12) If one should inherit the estate of a paternal uncle who belongs to the same *gotra*, how is the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) performed in that case?
At the same time that he offers the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to his father, at that same time he should offer a rice-ball for him [the adopted son].
Now, if he should receive an inheritance from one who is not of his own *gotra*, how is the offering of the rice-ball performed in that case?
Having given [rice-balls] to his own [kinsmen], he should spread sacrificial grass (*barhis*) near the neighbor and offer the rice-ball starting with the sacrificial grass.
Alternatively, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* in the fire-chamber itself, one should offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) starting with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
How, indeed, does the offering of the rice-ball take place for the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*)?

[The formula is: "This is for you, O father of such-and-such a name, my grandfather, and those who follow you; this is for you, O grandfather of such-and-such a name, my great-grandfather, and those who follow you; this is for you, O great-grandfather of such-and-such a name, my great-great-grandfather, and those who follow you."

Or he may give according to the procedure for the *pravidāna* offering: "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling on earth; svadhā to the fathers dwelling in the intermediate space; svadhā to the fathers dwelling in heaven.
If one does not know the names of the father, grandfather, or great-grandfather, how then should the offering of the rice balls (*piṇḍa*) be performed?
One should give according to the procedure for the *pravidāna* offering.

Or alternatively: "This for you, father, and for those who follow you; this for you, grandfather, and for those who follow you; this for you, great-grandfather, and for those who follow you. [Thus it is said.
"One should have the hair cut in the latter part of life.
At what time, then, should this cutting be performed?
After sixty-six years and eight months—only at this time is it to be cut off.
Now, how indeed does the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* of one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) take place?

Having cooked an unoffered *sthālīpāka*, having kindled the fire and strewn grass around it, and having offered the oblations, he should spread sacrificial grass with its tips pointing south to the south of the fire; beginning with the spreading of the grass, he should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*).
Alternatively, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* in the very same shed, he should offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) starting with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), he should worship this fire with the verse addressed to Prajāpati.

Regarding this point which they teach according to Baudhāyana’s ritual manual—that one should release speech with the call to the *haviṣkṛt* and then offer the *ājyānī* oblations—at what time, indeed, should one offer them? Having performed the ritual actions up to the point of the spilling [of the grain], one should offer them at that time.
Furthermore, how does the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice come to be for one who has not established the sacred fires?

Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* that has not been previously poured out, having kindled the fire, strewn it all around, offered the two *āghāra* libations, and sacrificed the two *ājyabhāga* portions, he should offer oblations to the deities of the *Āgrayaṇa*, with the *Sviṣṭakṛt* as the fourth.
He may, at his will, offer the *ājyānī* oblations before the *Sviṣṭakṛt*.
He should eat of this [remnant] with this very mantra: "O gods, you have led us from good to better."
Alternatively, one may seek to obtain it from the remnants of the oblation of a learned Brāhmaṇa;
the mantra for consuming it is the same.
How, indeed, should one know [the distinctions of] the *antarvirāja*, the *bahirvirāja*, and the *antarbarhirvirāja*?

Having performed the regular worship, he should perform the worship with the *virāj* formulas; having returned from a journey abroad, having performed the worship with the *virāj* formulas, he should perform the worship with the regular [formulas] alone.
By this very [method], both the external *virāj* and the internal-external *virāj* have been explained.
He travels abroad after sleeping on the ground, abstaining from meat and avoiding women.
This [offering] has a reversed name.
Should this expiation, which has fallen in the middle, be for the two-potsherd offering to the Aśvins, one should conclude it at that very end.
If it should be lost during the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [initiation offering], one should follow through with the *prāyaṇīyā* [opening offering].
If it should be lost during the *prāyaṇīyā* [offering], one should follow the procedure of the *ātithyā*.
If it should be lost during the *ātithyā*, one should follow each subsequent ritual framework (*tantra*) of the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for the Agni-Soma sacrifice.
Now, if it should be lost during the *agnidīkṣaṇīyā*, at what time indeed should one perform its offering?

Having offered the initiation oblations (*dīkṣāhuti*), one should offer this [oblation] at this time; or rather, before the drawing of the *audgra* cups. As they teach according to the ritual manual (*kalpa*) of Baudhāyana regarding one who is traveling abroad: "One should throw the sacrificer’s portion into the fire together with the *prastara* grass-bundle. Having spread a layer of clarified butter from the *dhruvā* vessel and having placed it in the *juhū* ladle, one should offer it. Thus the sacrificer’s portion attains the status of the *prastara*. Therefore, for one who is traveling abroad, one should indeed throw the sacrificer’s portion into the fire together with the *prastara*.
Now, this animal sacrifice includes the *upavasatha* day.
What is the commencement of its ritual procedure?

Having moved away with the perpetual fires (*ajasra*), having offered the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* oblation, having offered the *yūpāhuti* oblation, having consecrated the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with its formulas, and having measured out the altar (*vedi*), one should consume the food for entering the vow (*vratopāyanīya*) and then add fuel to the fires.

He should undertake the vow. Having bound together the sacrificial fuel and the grass, he should fast. Then, in the morning, he should sacrifice with an offering on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni; such is the ritual procedure of Baudhāyana.
He should not add fuel to the fires, nor should he undertake a vow; he should rub his hands together and strew grass around the altar.
Having washed the vessels, he should set them down.
He should seat the Brahman priest silently to the south. However, once the fire has been carried forward onto the high altar, he should sit down with the mantra.
Having prepared the sprinkling waters, he should sprinkle the vessels.
Having poured out the clarified butter, placed it on the fire, and carried fire around it, he should go forward to the east with the wooden sword in his hand and perform the *stambayajus* rite.
From this point onward, the procedure is established.
Now, according to Śālīki:

Having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods, having descended [to a new site], having churned out the fires, and having spread them out, one should offer the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ oblation in this very same manner, offer the oblation for the sacrificial post, prepare the sacrificial post with its formulas, measure out the altar, and add fuel to the fires.
One should then enter upon the vow.
He should bind together the fuel and the sacrificial grass; he should rub his hands together;
he should strew the sacrificial grass around.
Having washed the vessels, he should set them down.
He should seat the Brahman priest silently to the south. But once the fire has been carried forward upon the high altar, he should sit down with the mantra.
Having prepared the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he should sprinkle the vessels.

Having poured out the clarified butter (*ājya*), placed it on the fire, carried fire around it, melted the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya*, purified it, and taken four spoonfuls into the *sruc* ladle, he offers a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) in the *āhavanīya* while a fuel-stick is held [in the hand]. Then, with the wooden sword (*sphya*) in his hand, he goes eastward and should perform the *stambayajus* rite.
From this point onward, the procedure is established.
"The wooden sword (sphyā) becomes the sacrificial post (yūpa). But how, indeed, do its splinter (svaru) and the two chips used for the churning (adhimanthana) become [the post]?
One should plane off [these] from this very same [wooden sword].

Alternatively, one may make it from another tree of the same species. This [post] is without a crest-piece (*caṣāla*). One should perform the ritual recitations beginning with the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) up until the third time of encircling; at that third time, one should encircle it.
In this way, [the measurements] are commensurate with the *upara* stone.
The sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) range from five *aratni*s up to nine *aratni*s.
The sacrificial posts for the *agniṣṭoma* range from nine *aratni*s up to twenty-one *aratni*s.
For one who has performed the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice, the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is made of *pālāśa* wood and is three or four *aratnis* in length.
Now, regarding one who is away on a journey: is the Paśubandha sacrifice accomplished for him, or is it not accomplished?
Some say it is accomplished.
Now, some indeed say, "It does not succeed.
For they call these world-fires a second establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*); yet, for one who is traveling abroad, the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) certainly does not succeed.
"What indeed constitutes the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*?
[He replies: "The undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*), the release from the vow (*vratavisarjana*), and the re-grasping of the sacrifice (*yajñasya punarālambha*).
Some, however, say that the opening of the clarified butter (*ājyāvakāśa*) and the calls for the *praipas* and *āśrāvaṇas* constitute them.
"What deity indeed presides over this?
one should reply, "It has Death as its deity.
Now, in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), there are these six sprinkling waters: three are accompanied by mantras and three are silent.
The sprinkling waters for the animal sacrifice are those accompanied by the *yavamati* and *indraghoṣavatī* verses,
while those for the sacrificial cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), the vessels, the fuel and sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*), and so forth, are consecrated with mantras.
If one wishes to offer the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) in an animal sacrifice, at what time, indeed, should one offer them?
Having performed the ritual according to the *svāhākṛti-praiṣa* before the offering of the omentum (*vapā*),
[one reflects that] some gods have their *svāhākṛti* offerings first, while others have their *svāhākṛti* offerings later.
These rays of the sun indeed extend both eastward and westward.
Now, as for this animal cake-offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*):
what is the commencement of its ritual procedure?
One should place the wooden sword (*sphya*) behind the *gārhapatya* fire.
(24.36:223.6) The vessel is placed upon the wooden sword (sphyá). (24.36:223.6) One should pour the rice grains into the vessel.
The ritual action extends from the taking up of the winnowing basket until the end, concluding with the pouring out of the water for the *āpya* libations.
He should pour out [the water] for the Āpyas behind the Gārhapatya fire.
With the remainder of the sprinkling-water, he should mix the flour for the sacrificial cakes. This is likewise for the Savanīya offerings.
As for this, they teach the ritual procedure according to the manual of Baudhāyana.

(24.37:223.10) One should cut off the *iḍā* portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering from this [cake] without having first made a base-layer of ghee; how, then, does the fourfold cutting (*caturavatta*) come to be here?

(24.37:223.11) Having spread a base-layer of ghee, one should divide the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) into two parts and pour ghee over them. In this way, the fourfold cutting is accomplished for him.

Now, some teachers eliminate eleven ritual elements from the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*): the adding of fuel to the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*), the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*), the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, the *praṇītā* water, the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāgau*), the portion for the *prāśitra*, the portions for the sacrificer and the Brahman (*yajamānabhāga-brahmabhāgau*), the fourfold division of the cake (*caturdhākaraṇa*), and the strides of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇukramān*).
But how many *darvihoma* offerings are actually seen in the animal sacrifice?
They are: the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula, the oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*), the *stokyā* verses, the offerings to the quarters (*diśāṃ-pratījya*), and the *upayaja* offerings.
"What deity, indeed, does the Manotā have?
"One should say: 'Agni's.
What deity, indeed, does Vanaspati have?"
One should say simply, "It belongs to Viṣṇu.
For it is known: "The trees indeed belong to Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, they cite: "Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice."

Now, this animal sacrifice is entirely in the Triṣṭubh metre: there are eleven *prayāja* offerings, eleven *anuyāja* offerings, the animal cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is on eleven potsherds, there are eleven cuttings (*avadāna*), and there are eleven *upayāja* offerings. Regarding this, they teach the ritual procedure of Śālīki: having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), one should depart for the final bath (*udavasyet*). If the sun should set while he is performing the rites there, how is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) accomplished in that case? Is it accomplished or not? Some say, "It is accomplished."

Now, some indeed say, "It does not succeed," for this space is encompassed by the sacrifice; it certainly does not succeed. But indeed, this animal has been explained as being entirely connected with the *triṣṭubh* metre.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the animals for optional sacrifices. Which ones among these, indeed, have their [mantras] pronounced in a whisper?
Those belonging to the Aśvamedha: those dedicated to Prajāpati, to Savitṛ, to Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Yama, to the Pitṛs, to Heaven and Earth, to Vāyu, to Sūrya, and to Viśvakarman.
(24.38:224.13) "The women become pregnant. How, in this case, is the expiation accomplished? Is it accomplished or not?
(24.38:224.14) Some say it is accomplished; others, however, say it is not accomplished.
"These [sacrifices] lead to prosperity;
they do not fail to succeed. Regarding the injunction, "One sacrifices a speckled, pregnant female goat to Āditya," this is indeed merely the name of a seer.
"She has teeth that have not fallen out"—by this it is meant that she has not lost her teeth.
Now, this [cow] is assigned for ten bulls over the course of a year;
among them, Kadrū is the tenth, belonging to Prajāpati.
(24.38:225.3) "In this matter, how is the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) accomplished or not accomplished?
(24.38:225.4) "It is accomplished," say some; then others indeed say, "It is not accomplished."
"It concludes;
it does not succeed at all," [he says],
"she is one who has borne a child by a paramour."
Some say she is "one who brings about the avoidance [of calamity]. Now, others say that this very one is called "the younger" (*anujā*),
and they designate her as "the barren cow" (*vehat*).
"One should sacrifice a three-year-old animal dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan"—this is said to refer specifically to those who have reached their third year;
and they also cite: "he who sucks at three [teats]."
"One should sacrifice a stallion belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ"—this refers to that very male whom one mounts; he is the stallion.
"One should sacrifice on uneven ground"—thus it is said.
"Either the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) may be uneven, or one should immolate the animal on whatever [ground] one chooses;
however, one should immolate it at the junction of water and plants.
Regarding this, some say: "At the edge of the water."
Now, some say it should be performed either in the rainy season or in autumn:
"If the sun does not become visible while the *Aśvina* śastra is being recited, one should offer a multi-colored animal to Sūrya.
If [the sun] should not be seen during the *Prāyaṇīya* Atirātra, one should perform the animal sacrifice for the *Savanīya* of the *Ārambhaṇīya* day.

If, however, [the moon] should not appear at the *udayanīya* *atirātra* or at the one-day sacrifice, they should perform the selection of the *anūbandhya* animal; or else, having performed the *udavasa*, they should sacrifice with this animal.
Thus have these optional animals been explained.
How, indeed, is there a subsequent performance (*anuprayoga*) of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices that have been undertaken for as long as one lives?
On the full moon day of either Phālguna or Caitra, one should sacrifice with the *Śunāsīrīya* section.
Then one should fast for the *Vaiśvadeva*.
Having performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, one should perform the Full-moon sacrifice and the Vaimṛdha sacrifice.
Now, if one should sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, an animal sacrifice, or the Soma sacrifice, how should one act in that case?
Having drawn back [the ritual sequence], one should sacrifice with the *śunāsīrīya* section of this very fortnight.
Then one should sacrifice with one of these;
then one should fast for the Vaiśvadeva;
having sacrificed with the Vaiśvadeva, one should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsa and Vaimṛdha offerings.

(25.1:227.7) Regarding this, they teach Baudhāyana’s ritual manual: "The Cāturmāsya sacrifices should indeed be performed throughout one's life, with the sexual unions occurring within [the intervals].

However, in the very first year, one should observe the vow. [Question: "How then are the *iṣṭis* and animal sacrifices [to be treated]? [Answer: "At will by means of an *iṣṭi*, at will by means of an animal sacrifice."
(25.1:227.10) Where, indeed, do the Cāturmāsyas find their synthesis?
(25.1:227.11) One should say: "In the Rājasūya, in the Cāturmāsyas, and in the Soma sacrifices.
(25.1:227.12) Moreover, they also cite: "One may also sacrifice with the Cāturmāsyas during the Dvādaśāha."
"One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva on the fourth day, with the Varuṇapraghāsas on the eighth, with the Sākamedhas on the ninth, and with the Śunāsīrīya offering on the twelfth"—
thus it is known. "The twelve nights are indeed a representation of the year," and "the sacrificial grass is threefold."
"The intermediate [offerings] are indeed silent," it is said; thus, this very [procedure] involving the recitation of mantras is external.
This same rule applies elsewhere except when there is a conjunction with an *iṣṭi*, in which case it becomes the reverse.
Where, then, do the *karambha* vessels first receive a mantra?
One should simply say "sprinkling.
One should carry fire around the *karambha* vessels together with the sacrificial offerings.
Now, what are the deities of the *karambha* vessels?
One should say, "Belonging to Varuṇa. It is known from scripture: "He offers sacrifice to another Varuṇa indeed.
By the words, "Go home, O bounteous ones," it is meant that he should look toward his house.
The two of them should exchange the *stambayajus* formulas as they go back and forth. The Pratiprasthātṛ should follow the Adhvaryu from behind as he goes hither and thither.
Having poured out water from the vessel that was filled together, the Pratiprasthātṛ should cause the Adhvaryu to recite over the clarified butter.
Then, having taken up their respective fuel-sticks before the carrying forward [of the fires], the Adhvaryu stands aside after stepping away with his own fuel-stick.
Then this Pratiprasthātṛ, having passed between the fuel-pile and the Āhavanīya fire, should take up his own fuel-pile.
They both should turn around by circling counter-clockwise and carry the two fuel-piles.

Then, having turned clockwise from that point and having set down the two fuel-piles, they return by the same way they came; the Pratiprasthātṛ turns back, and the carrying of the supporting ladle proceeds eastward between the two altars.
(25.2:229.2) Then the Adhvaryu, having taken these sprinkling waters around the Pratiprasthātṛ by the right, should set them down.
(25.2:229.3) In this way, he is not bypassed by them.
Then this offering for the Maruts goes to the southern altar; it is the seventh of the oblations to be placed on the fire.
How do these [offerings] become unseparated by this?
Having drawn it back, one should remove it from the front, to the south of the oblations, before it has been sprinkled with clarified butter.
Then, having placed it on the fire again and removed it after it has been sprinkled, one should set it down within the altar.
In this way, these [formulas] become uninterrupted.
Then this Pratiprasthātṛ should cause the recitation for the deity Marut to be performed only once and should cause the announcement to be made only once.
Now, elsewhere it is said that he acts as an imitator of the Adhvaryu.
In that regard, when he causes the announcement here and performs the sacrifice here, the Pratiprasthātṛ acts as a mere imitator.

Then, having taken this stirring-stick for the Maruts around the fire on the northern part of the altar, he should throw it into the fire. Furthermore, according to the ritual procedure of Aupamanyava which they teach—one should go to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with the husks and the scrapings—he should, after offering the portion to the deity, hand over the husks for the Sviṣṭakṛt; having scattered them, he should cast them into the water at its edge.
(25.2:230.2) From this point onward, it is established.
(25.2:230.3) Now, this Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice concludes with the Ājyabhāgas, the Pratipat, and the Iḍā.
(25.2:230.4) In that rite, there is no Prāśitra portion.
(25.2:230.4) He should silently throw the anointed śākala-sticks and enclosing sticks into the fire.
(25.2:230.5) If a cow that suckles another's calf is not available, he should have the milk of a *saṃdhinī* cow milked.
Now follows this Mahāpitṛyajña. What is the commencement of its ritual?

One should prepare the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the *yajus* formula: "Thou art cut for the gods and the fathers; O divine-fatherly sacrificial grass, do not [fall] lengthwise upon me, nor crosswise. May I succeed in [cutting] thy joint. "Araru is driven away from the earth, the place of sacrifice for the gods and the fathers. "Araru, the non-sacrificer to the gods and the fathers, is driven away from the earth. In this manner one should act in these instances wherever the gods and the fathers come together.
He should rub his hands together,
strew the sacrificial grass around,
and, having washed the vessels, set them down.
Having seated the Brahman priest to the south and having placed a vessel of water right there to the north, he should set down the wooden sword (sphya) behind the Gārhapatya fire;
upon the wooden sword, a shallow bowl (pātrī);
and into the bowl, he should pour rice grains.
The ritual action extends from the taking up of the winnowing basket until the end of the Āpya offerings. He should pour out the Āpya waters behind the Gārhapatya fire.
These officiating priests walk around in a counter-clockwise direction.

The Adhvaryu should be closest to the fire, then the sacrificer, then the Brahman, then the Āgnīdhra. Or alternatively, the Āgnīdhra alone should be closest to the fire, then the sacrificer, then the Brahman, then the Adhvaryu.
They carry the oblations around in front of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*): the parched grains (*dhānā*) behind it, and the groat-mash (*karambha*) behind the parched grains.
When these oblations have been thus exchanged, one should set aside each one individually.
Where, indeed, are the Traiyambaka offerings set aside?
Having set aside the oblations, [one does so] with the formulas belonging to whose [ritual] they are: "I set aside what is pleasing to Rudra and Ambikā."
"Kāya"—with these words he should offer the oblation; "Recite for Kāya"—with these words he should recite the invitatory verse; "Sacrifice to Ka"—with these words he should perform the offering.
(25.3:231.6) "Where, indeed, does the offering to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt for the Traiyambaka cakes take place?
(25.3:231.7) "It is when he attaches [the cord] to the bundle from this very point.
(25.3:231.8) "He gives a bull that has not yet been united with a cow."
This [offering] is to be given at the Mahāhavis sacrifices when they have not yet been combined;

otherwise, the entire ritual duty of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) would perish in the Pitṛyajña, the Paśubandha, and the Soma sacrifice, except where there is a specific scriptural injunction to the contrary.

All the duties of the sacrificer pertaining to the fire belong to the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicaya*); all the duties of the sacrificer pertaining to the meters belong to the laying of the fires (*agnyādheya*).
One who is about to perform the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice should make himself ready for battle.
Whatever may be unfavorable for him, he should turn that into something favorable.
Any debts whose time for payment has arrived, he should either settle or obtain permission regarding them.
(25.4:231.15) He prepares beforehand a large quantity of *ṛṇavaṃśa* wood, sacrificial butter, a pot, a vessel, a water-jar, and a *kurīra* head-net.
(25.4:232.2) The water-jar is made of split bamboo, and the *kurīra* is a net.
There are one hundred and twelve sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

It is known from the Chandoga Brāhmaṇa: "He who presses the Soma is indeed a slayer of the heroes of the gods. Thus, with a hundred [cows] he makes atonement for the hero, and with ten [cows] for each of the ten vital breaths.
The eleventh [offering] is for that purpose;
the twelfth itself is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Now, some indeed sacrifice with a twenty-one-fold fee, saying, "The *yajñāyajñiya* chant is twenty-one-fold."
Now, some perform the sacrifice with seven cords: the cow for the purchase of Soma, the guest-cow, the Anūbandhyā cow, and four in the middle.
This is also known from the *Daśataya*: "The wise one, of sevenfold lineage, whose thoughts are fixed on the Truth."

(25.5:232.10) Now, therefore, follows the ritual for selecting the sacrificial ground (*devayajanakalpa*). He chooses this sacrificial ground: one that has water to the east, is not saline, not filled with debris, free from fissures, not hollow, not prone to breaking, devoid of ant-hills, and abundant in herbs where various kinds of plants grow intertwined; it should slope toward the northeast so that the waters flow toward the *cātvāla* pit, yet not so steeply that they would flow away; nor should he choose it if he cannot find another sacrificial ground more proximate to the east. On such a site, they cause a hall (*śālā*) with its ridge-pole facing east to be measured out.
"These Kṛttikās indeed do not abandon the eastern quarter.
"One should measure by the appearance of them"—this is one view. "One should measure by the appearance of Śroṇā"—this is another view.
"Between Citrā and Svātī"— this is another [explanation].
"It has openings toward the quarters" means that it indeed has openings toward the quarters by means of its doors.
Moreover, they also cite: "One should make the openings of the bamboo tubes themselves.
Two *stomas* carry the morning pressing;
the *trivṛt* and the *pañcadaśa* carry the morning pressing.
The midday pressing consists of the fifteenfold and seventeenfold stomas;
the third pressing consists of the seventeenfold and twenty-onefold stomas. This very sacrifice becomes a *catuṣṭoma*.
For there are four *stomas*;
although it is this very [sacrifice], it becomes a twelve-fold *stoma*,
for there are twelve *stotras*.

Regarding this, they teach the ritual procedure of Aupamanyava: one should settle upon the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) only after the threefold [sacrificial fires] have been established; for it is known from scripture: "This earth is indeed the entire altar."
(25.6:233.15) Now, some say that this offering to Agni and Viṣṇu should be performed either before the consecration water or after it.
(25.6:234.1) Where indeed should one perform the *barhis*-formula for the consecration-offering? Having set down the ritual materials, [one should do so] prior to the touching of the hands.
(25.6:234.2) He does not lead the sacrificer to the vow, nor does he gird the wife; thus he dispels the vow for the sake of the consecration of the *adhvara*.
This entire sacrifice is one for undertaking the vow (*vratopāyanīyā*); however, the binding of the wife’s girdle comes first.
He does not set aside a portion for the sacrificer nor a portion for the Brahman; these two [portions] are mentioned only as being connected with the prayer for blessings (*āśis*).
Why? Because when about to commence the sacrifice, should he utter a prayer for blessings?
Furthermore, it is said that there is an abundance of food for one who has undertaken a vow.
To whom, then, should one offer from this abundance?
Indeed, by the removal of the sacrificer’s portion, the Brahman’s portion is also removed.
"For these two, the sacrificer's portion and the Brahman's portion, are indeed connected," [it is said].
"He does not place the sacrificial cake on the *barhis* grass, nor does he ask for the *anvāhārya* rice"; thus, when the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is mentioned, these two are already included.
(25.6:234.10) Furthermore, other sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are indeed prescribed here;
(25.6:234.11) he does not perform the *phalīkaraṇa* oblation, nor does he offer the *samiṣṭayajus*. These two [acts] are said to be those that conclude the ritual.
(25.6:234.13) Why should one who has begun a sacrifice bring it to its conclusion?

He does not cause the sacrificer to recite over the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*), nor does he perform the *viṣṇukrama* strides; for indeed, the full vessel is prescribed specifically for the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). Indeed, a different purificatory bath is intended here;
the *viṣṇukrama* strides belong to one who goes around the end.
(25.6:235.2) "How should one bring a sacrifice to its conclusion after having commenced it? he asked.
"He offered twelve *vātsabandha* oblations.
What indeed are these *vātsabandha* oblations? They are these very *sruva*-oblations, excluding the utterance of *svāhā*.
Moreover, they cite this: "The fire has an equal number [of verses]; there are three deities in the *ṛc*; these make twelve.
Now, this black antelope skin is explained etymologically:
having bent the knee, one should crawl along its side toward the right opening, as if toward a boat.

If he should see something impure at night, he should worship the Āhavanīya fire with this very *yajus* formula. Now, these vows pertaining to the initiation (*daikṣa*) begin in the evening and conclude in the morning;
whereas those pertaining to the Upasad days begin in the morning and conclude in the evening.
Now, one should observe this vow of initiation only after having enclosed the fire-altar;
for previously, the Agnihotra was offered in the Āhavanīya fire itself, lest it should become human.
Now, regarding this Prāyaṇīya [offering],
what is the commencement of its ritual action?
One should prepare the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with a *yajus* formula, provided that it has not already been prepared without a *yajus* formula beforehand.
He should rub his hands together,
strew the sacrificial grass around,
and, having washed the vessels, set them down.
Having seated the Brahman priest to the south and having placed a vessel of water right there to the north, he should set down the wooden sword (sphya) behind the Gārhapatya fire,
with the bowl upon the wooden sword.
He should pour the rice grains into the bowl.
The ritual action begins with the taking up of the winnowing basket and extends until the pouring out [of the grain].

Having performed the ritual actions ending with the pouring out, having offered a spoonful in the Āhavanīya fire, having gone out and issued the call, having entered again and poured water across the strainers, and having placed it over the fire, he should pour the rice grains across the strainers.
Then he should pour out the clarified butter.
Then he should place the clarified butter over the fire.
Having carried fire around both [the butter and the oblation], and having gone forward to the east with the wooden sword (*sphya*) in his hand, he should perform the *stambayajus* rite.
From this point onward, the procedure is established.
The Prāyaṇīya sacrifice concludes with the Śaṃyu-formula.
What, indeed, remains of this ritual?
[It remains] until the releasing of the offering-spoons.

(25.8:236.11) "The pouring out of the water for the *caru* oblations is not prescribed," [says one view]. (25.8:236.12) "One should offer the *caru* using the very cooking-pots (*sthālī*)," such is the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) of Baudhāyana.
(25.8:236.13) "To which deity, indeed, does the foot-oblation (*padāhuti*) belong? [he asks].
Some say it belongs to Agni;
some say it belongs to Viṣṇu; some say it belongs to Prajāpati.
One should say, "It has Vāc as its deity. With a tuft of black wool, he pierces the two eyebrows of the Soma-seller from behind; the sacrificer then uncovers the King [Soma].
(25.9:237.1) With the verse, "The fair-winged birds have approached Indra," [he performs the rite].

(25.9:237.1) Now, if there should be no Soma-seller, having driven in a Palāśa branch at the spot where the sacrificial post-hole is to be, and having bound the King [Soma] together and suspended him upon that Palāśa branch, he should sit waiting.
(25.9:237.3) Then, if someone should utter something connected with an impulse—such as "Quickly!", or "Hurry!", or "Do it!"—then he should take up the King [Soma].
The agreements shall not recur;
he would then be a seller of Soma.
Now, this first Subrahmaṇyā formula is said to end with the syllable *oṃ*.
Now, regarding this guest-offering (*ātithya*):
what is the commencement of its ritual procedure?
One should prepare the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with a *yajus*-formula, provided that it has not already been prepared without a formula beforehand.
He should rub his hands together,
strew the sacrificial grass around,
and, having washed the vessels, set them down.

Having seated the Brahman priest to the south and having unyoked the southern ox, he should place a vessel of water right there to the north; behind the Gārhapatya fire, he should set down the wooden sword (sphya), and upon the wooden sword, a shallow bowl (pātrī).
Into the bowl, he should pour rice grains.
The ritual action begins with the taking up of the winnowing basket and extends until the scattering [of grain].
Having performed the ritual actions ending with the scattering, and having unyoked the northern ox, he should cause the King Soma to be brought forward.
One should understand that the Agniṣṭoma ritual is established here up until the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*).
One performs the guest-offering (*ātithya*) by means of the shaking of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*); from this point onward, the procedure is established as standard.
"He pulls out a bunch of *darbha* grass"—
what indeed is this bunch of *darbha* grass?
It is that very one which he places upon the two *godāna* locks.
"Having pierced the seven mountains"—
what indeed are these mountains? They are said to be the *prayāja* and *anūyāja* offerings, namely those of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, the *prāyaṇīyā*, the *ātithyā*, and the *agnīṣomīya* [sacrifices].
Moreover, they cite: "The *dīkṣaṇīyā*, the *prāyaṇīyā*, the *ātithyā*, the *upasads*, and the *agnīṣomīya* as the seventh. [And they ask:
"The sacrifice fled away from the gods;
which one, indeed, is this sacrifice?"
That very Ātithya sacrifice which concludes with the *iḍā*— it is said,
"The gods, having grasped their hands together, desired it.
This refers to the fact that they touch the *tānūnaptra* together.
"Indra passed over him from above," so it is said;
"because they perform these Upasad rites," so it is said; "the sacrifice itself brought the sacrifice to them," so it is said.
"What indeed was that sacrifice which brought the sacrifice? [He replied:
"The *dīkṣaṇīyā*, the *prāyaṇīyā*, and the *ātithyā*—this very sacrifice brought the sacrifice."
"This boar steals what is desirable for you two"—
this refers to the most excellent day among the days of the Soma-pressing.
Thus, it steals desirable wealth from the sacrificer.
"What indeed are the after-offerings (*anūyāja*) of the guest-offering (*ātithya*? "One should say: 'The Upasad rites. "Of what deities, then, are the Upasad rites?"
One should simply say, "They belong to Agni. Now, how indeed does the commencement of the *upasads* take place?
One should perform the rite with the *barhis*-formula, provided that it has not previously been performed without a formula.
He should rub his hands together,
strew the sacrificial grass around,
and, having washed the vessels, set them down.
Having prepared the *madantī* water, he should sprinkle the vessels.
Having poured out the clarified butter, placed it on the fire, and carried fire around it, he should go eastward with the wooden sword (*sphya*) in his hand and perform the *stambayajus* rite.
From this point onward, the procedure is established.
(25.10:238.17) Just as in the archetype, so should he set down the offering-spoons at the first *upasad*.
(25.10:239.1) They are pushed forward at the second; they are pushed further forward at the third.
(25.10:239.2) They should proceed with the *upasads* as if in great haste; they should not concern themselves with what has not been performed.
With all his fingers joined together, having taken up the *sruva* ladle, he should offer the *upasat* oblation as if about to eat.
Where indeed should one perform the *barhis*-formula for the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma?
Having removed the *pravargya* vessel before the carrying forward of the *āhavanīya* fire, one should bring the calves away for the sake of the *savanīya* offerings.
When the Āhavanīya fire has been separated [from the Gārhapatya], he should scatter a third of a footprint [of soil] upon the Gārhapatya; likewise upon the supporting stones (*upayamanī*).
Now, this pillar of *udumbara* wood must be made equal in height to the sacrificer.
Furthermore, this sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is measured by the cubits (*aratni*) of the sacrificer.
Some say [the rites] should be performed together.

In this case, however, one should perform these very acts after tracing around the pit for the sacrificial post (*yūpāvaṭa*), but one should rub one's hands together and strew the grass around the fire.
Having washed the vessels, he should set them down;
having prepared the sprinkling waters, he should sprinkle the vessels.
Having poured out the clarified butter, placed it on the fire, and carried fire around it, he cleanses the ladles.
They carry away the earth for the high altar and the sprinkling waters.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ should gird the wife with the cord used for the cake-offering.
Then he should cause her to look at the Gārhapatya fire.
(25.11:240.1) Then, having caused her to look at the clarified butter, he should run toward it with the clarified butter.

He should take hold of what has been looked at by his wife [with the formula]: "Thou art brilliance. (25.11:240.2) Then, having taken hold of it with a chip of wood, he should carry it away [with the formula]: "Follow after the brilliance."
Then he should place it over the Āhavanīya fire with [the formula]: "May Agni not take away thy brilliance.

Then, having held it and placed it to the north of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he should look at it or purify it; [he should purify] the *prokṣaṇī* waters with the two [spoons] containing clarified butter (*ājyavatī*).
It is well known that he should take the portions of *pṛṣadājya* and the clarified butter in the vicinity of the Āhavanīya fire.
(25.11:240.6) From this point on, it is established.

(25.11:240.6) As for that ritual procedure which they teach according to Śālīki— that one should take the clarified butter portions for Agni and Soma in the wife’s hall itself and place them on the mound—
having brought forward either a garment or having brought forward the old Gārhapatya fire, he should rub his hands together over it.
He should strew the sacrificial grass,
wash the vessels, and set them down;
having prepared the sprinkling water, he should sprinkle the vessels.
Having poured out the clarified butter, placed it on the fire, and carried fire around it, he cleanses the offering-spoons.
They set those spoons down right here together with the *prokṣaṇī* waters.
The Pratiprasthātṛ should not gird the wife with the cord used for the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika*).
One should not let her look at the *gārhapatya* fire.
Then, having had her look at the clarified butter (*ājya*), one should move forward with the clarified butter.
One should take up that which has been looked at by the wife [with the formula]: "Thou art brilliance."
Then, having approached it with a chip of wood, he should carry it away [from the fire] with the formula: "Follow after your brilliance.
Then he should place it over the Gārhapatya fire with the formula: "May Agni not take away your brilliance.

Then, having lifted it up and set down the *prokṣaṇī* waters to the north, he should look at it or purify it. Having taken the clarified butter for the two [offerings] containing *ājya* and the *prokṣaṇī* waters in the established manner, and having taken the *pṛṣadājya* and the *ājya*s near the Gārhapatya fire—
Having handed over [the king] to the attendants, he should hand him over to the Brahman priest.
When they have covered him, he should offer two oblations with the *sruva* ladle.
And they should proceed while remaining covered, from the *āhavanīya* fire.
The King Soma should be in the southern half, then the fire, then the pressing-stones and the Vāyu-vessels in the northern half, as well as the clarified butter offerings.
Alternatively, the fire may be in the southern half, then the King Soma, then the pressing-stones and the Vāyu-vessels in the northern half, likewise the clarified butter offerings.

Having gone out by the eastern door, having circumambulated the *sadas* to the north, and having placed the fire in the Āgnīdhra shed and offered oblations into it, he proceeds with the *prokṣaṇī* water in his hand to the north of the Āgnīdhrīya hearth.
(25.12:241.9) He follows with the clarified butter offerings.

Having offered in the Āhavanīya fire, having sprinkled the fuel, having sprinkled the altar, having sprinkled the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and having sprinkled the sacrificial grass that has been set down, and having poured water over it, he takes up the *āśvavāla* grass as the *prastara* from the front, spreads the fivefold sacrificial grass, and, holding the *prastara* in his hand, steps forward toward the east. Having laid the enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood around, having placed two upright kindling sticks upon the fire, and having taken up the handful of sacrificial grass, the two separating blades (*vidhṛti*), and the *prastara*, he turns to the right and enters the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door.
Having stepped forward, he should spread a handful of sacrificial grass on the northern half of the seat of the donkey;
upon the sacrificial grass, he places the two separating blades,
and between the two separating blades, the prastara-bunch made of *aśvavāla* grass.
He places the *juhū* on the *prastara*,

and the other two ladles on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Having touched them all together with the formula, "These have sat down," and having touched water, he takes the King [Soma] from the Brahman and causes it to enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, as if turning himself around.
(25.12:242.1) From this point onward, it is established.
"But where, indeed, does the sacrificial fuel and grass go to its completion like a craft?
"One should say: at the Agniṣomīya [offering].
"But where, indeed, does the Agniṣomīya follow the day of the Soma-pressing?"
One should say, "The *sadyaskrī* [sacrifice].
Where indeed does the *pravargya* ceremony follow upon the day of the Soma-pressing? One should say, "Upon the *sadyaskrī*."
(25.13:242.6) "Which deity, indeed, is invoked first as the Subrahmaṇyā?
"Speech itself invokes speech," [he said].
(25.13:242.7) "Where, indeed, is the Pitāputrīyā Subrahmaṇyā invoked first?"
When the omentum of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma has been offered, when the Vasatīvarī waters have been carried around, there is a second [recitation] during the morning litany;
the third occurs at the time for the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*); thus say some regarding the calls.

Now, when it says, "He asks for that firm jar," this is simply a way of saying "solid. When it says, "Prepare milk and groats," these two are stated for the purpose of mixing. There are four cords, four omentum-spits, and two sets of fuel and sacrificial grass; these belong to both the *savanīya* and the *anūbandhya* offerings.
(25.13:242.14) What are the four vessels for Vāyu that are used for drawing the Soma?
They are: the Āditya vessel, the Ukthya vessel, the Āgrayaṇa vessel, and the Dhruva vessel.

(25.13:242.15–16) Now, there are these twelve upright cups: the cup for the Dadhi-graha, the two cups for the Aṃśu and Antaryāma, the two cups for the dual-deity offerings, the two Ṛtu-cups for the Śukra and Manthin, the resting cup for the Āditya vessel, and the resting cup for the Ukthya vessel.

Now, there are these eleven cups for the sacrificer, the Brahman, the Hotṛ, the Udgātṛ, the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Acchāvāka, the Sadasya, the Āgnīdhra, the Potṛ, and the Neṣṭṛ. One should have their handles made of the same material from *nyagrodha* wood.
It is known [from scripture]: "In the subsequent performance, when they consume [the soma] with cups that have handles, they do so with *nyagrodha* cups."
From this [tree], they are made of *nyagrodha* wood alone.
With the words, "And my rein," this is said to be the *adābhya* cup.
With the words, "And my overlord," this *dadhi-graha* belongs to Prajāpati.

"May there be for me [the offering] to Sarasvatī, and may there be for me [the offering] to Pūṣan"—thus some say regarding the *vasatīvarī* waters. Now, others say that this is the great draught (*mahāgraha*) belonging to the *Rājasūya*;
it is called "Pauṣṇa" because of nourishment (*poṣaṇa*), and "Sārasvata" because of being taken up (*grahaṇa*).
Now follows this ritual of the great night (*mahārātrika*).
What is the commencement of that rite?
Having washed their hands and feet, they enter the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap.
Their ritual acts are performed according to the respective directions.
Then the Adhvaryu should touch the Āgnīdhra shed with a verse addressed to Agni, and the Havirdhāna shed with one addressed to Viṣṇu. Thereupon he ceases.

(25.14:243.16) Then this Āgnīdhra, having first run to the wife’s hall (*patnīśālā*), having kindled the fires, strewn around them, washed the vessels, and set them down, melts the clarified butter (*ājya*) and waits upon it.
(25.14:244.2) The other, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having prepared the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), should sprinkle the vessels.
Having poured out the clarified butter, placed it on the fire, and carried fire around it, he cleanses the offering-spoons (*sruk*).

They carry away the *uttaravedi* and the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*). Then the Adhvaryu touches the spoons with a verse addressed to Agni, thinking, "The vessels have been cleansed; they are now to be touched twice."
With a verse addressed to Vāyu he sets down the Vāyavya cups; with a verse addressed to Indra, the Sadas.

Then this Unnetṛ, having washed the Grāvovāyavya cup and having placed the fringe of the *daśāpavitra* filter into the *droṇakalaśa*, sets it down in front of the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.
The Pratiprasthātṛ prepares curds for the *pṛṣadājya*.
The Āgnīdhra places the fuel and the sacrificial grass down.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ should bind the wife with the cord used for the cake-offerings.
Then he should cause her to look at the Gārhapatya fire.
Then, having caused her to look at the clarified butter, he should run toward it with the clarified butter.

He should cause the wife to take that very portion she has looked upon, saying, "Thou art brilliance. Then, having approached it by way of a side-path, he should carry it away, saying, "Follow after the brilliance."
(25.14:244.12) Then he should place it over the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "May Agni not take away thy brilliance.

(25.14:244.13) Having held it up and set down the *prokṣaṇī* waters to the north, he should look at it. He should purify the *prokṣaṇī* waters with two strainers used for the clarified butter (*ājyavatī*). In the established manner, he takes the portions of *pṛṣadājya* and clarified butter near the Āhavanīya; from this point onward, the procedure is established.

Now, according to Śālīki: In this very manner, their ritual acts are performed according to the respective directions. Then the Adhvaryu should touch the Āgnīdhra shed with a verse addressed to Agni, and the Havirdhāna shed with one addressed to Viṣṇu.
Then he ceases.

Then this Āgnīdhra, having first run to the hall of the wives (*patnīśālā*), having kindled the fire, strewn it around, washed the vessels, and arranged them, having melted the clarified butter (*ājya*), waits nearby.
The other, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having prepared the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), should sprinkle the vessels.
Having poured out the clarified butter, placed it on the fire, and carried fire around it, he cleanses the offering-spoons (*srucaḥ*).
They carry these, as well as the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇīḥ*), to the Āgnīdhra.
Then the Adhvaryu touches the spoons with a verse addressed to Agni.
"The vessels have been wiped; they are now to be smeared twice.
With a verse addressed to Vāyu he smears the vessels for Vāyu, and with one addressed to Indra, the Sadas.

Then this Unnetṛ, having washed the pressing-stones and the vessel for Vāyu, and having placed the fringe of the *daśāpavitra* filter into the *droṇakalaśa*, sets them down in front of the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.
The Pratiprasthātṛ prepares curds for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*).
The Āgnīdhra places the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmabarhis*) nearby.
The Pratiprasthātṛ should not gird the wife with the cord used for the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika*).
One should not let her look at the *gārhapatya* fire.
Then, having had her look at the clarified butter (*ājya*), one should proceed with the clarified butter.
One should take hold of that which has been looked at by the wife, saying: "Thou art brilliance."
(25.15:245.16) Then, having approached it with a chip of wood, he should carry it away [with the formula]: "Follow after the splendor!
(25.15:246.1) Then he should place it over the Āgnīdhrīya fire [with the formula]: "May Agni not take away your splendor!

(25.15:246.2) Then, having lifted it up and having set down the *prokṣaṇī* waters to the north, he should look at it; he should purify the *prokṣaṇī* waters with the two [spoons] containing clarified butter, as in the case of the *ājya*.

(25.15:246.3) Having taken the clarified butter portions containing clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*) near the Āgnīdhrīya hearth and handed them over to the attendants, he proceeds northward past the Āgnīdhrīya hearth with the *prokṣaṇī* water in his hand. (25.15:246.6) The others follow behind him with the clarified butter.

(25.15:246.6) Then, having sprinkled the fuel, having sprinkled the altar, having sprinkled the sacrificial grass, and having sprinkled the sacrificial grass that has been set down, having poured water down [upon it], having taken the *prastara* from the front, and having spread the single-layered sacrificial grass, he— holding the *prastara* in his hand and moving forward to the east— should lay the enclosing sticks of *udumbara* wood around [the fire], place two upright kindling sticks upon it, take up the handful of sacrificial grass, the two separating blades (*vidhṛti*), and the *prastara*, turn to the right, enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door, and should spread the handful of sacrificial grass on the northern half of the *khara*. He should place the two separating blades upon the sacrificial grass.
He places the *prastara* on the two *vidhṛtī*s;
the *juhū* on the *prastara*;
and the other spoons on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Having touched them together with the formula, "These have settled," he joins them by means of the *yoga* formula;
from this point onward, the procedure is established.
Is the consecrated one (*dīkṣita*) an *agnihotra* performer? Is he an *aupasada*? Is he one for whom the soma has been pressed (*prasuta*)?
It is known from scripture: "The *vratya* [fasting] itself is the *agnihotra* of the consecrated; the remnants of the *gharma* [milk offering] are the *aupasada*."
The Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups belong to the *prasuta* [soma-pressing].
That which is offered before sunrise has the character of the evening Agnihotra;
that which is offered after sunrise has the character of the morning Agnihotra.

Regarding the question, "What is the Darśapūrṇamāsa? it is known from scripture: "They performed the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice with the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma; they performed the Darśa sacrifice with the animal dedicated to Agni.

Furthermore, as they teach the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) of Aupamanyava: "At the morning pressing itself, one should offer the *savanīya* oblations for all the pressings; the potsherds (*kapāla*) should be placed [on the fire] only once."
(25.16:247.4) Up until the final covering, the combined ritual action is maintained.
(25.16:247.5) One should remove each of those [pots] at each pressing, whichever one he intends to use for the performance.
(25.16:247.6) Or rather, he should let the remaining lumps of the [grains] that have been touched rest during the other two pressings.

If a cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) is intended to be prepared, he should proceed with the rites belonging to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) until the end of the established procedure; then he should resume the ritual pertaining to the sacrificial cake (*pauroḍāśika*). For the other two pressings, at each respective pressing (*anusavana*), he should begin with the potsherds by merely placing embers upon them.
From this point onward, the rite is established.

(25.17:247.11) As for this point, they teach Baudhāyana’s ritual procedure: "One should draw the *vasatīvarī* waters so that they are bright on both sides and contain the sun; those [waters] are bright, and with them one should cause [the Soma] to swell, and with them one should press.
(25.17:247.13) Having placed the *hotṛcamasa* cup above the half [of the vessel], one should proceed by means of this very third [method].

(25.17:247.14) One should cause the three kinds of water—the water for the *hotṛcamasa*, the *vasatīvarī* water, and the water for the *maitrāvaruṇacamas*—to enter the *havirdhāna* shed through the eastern door. Having taken hold of them to the south of the *hotṛ*, one should bring in the *ekadhana* waters through the western door.

And at this time, he should pour out the contents of the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup entirely; he should pour down one-third of the *vasatīvarī* waters and one-third of the *ekadhana* waters. In this way, his *śukra* cup becomes exclusively [Soma] beforehand.
"One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should draw the *soma-graha*," so it is said.
This king [Soma] is to be taken only when he has not yet been poured out.
As for which deities indeed consume the Soma first—one should say:
"The waters."
It is known [from scripture]: "Invited, drink of the Soma; invited, let your Soma drink.
Where, indeed, does the drinking of the Soma take place? It is known: "O Soma, that invincible, watchful name of yours which belongs to Soma—for that Soma of yours, svāhā!"
This indeed is the drinking of the Soma for Soma;
this is the sequence for those who have assembled.
Having caused them to recite over the *nigrābhya* waters, he should proceed with the *ādābhya*.
(25.17:248.9) Then he should take up the *upāṃśusavana* stone.
(25.17:248.10) Then he should pour out the *rājā* (Soma).
One should understand that the ritual procedure pertaining to the *agniṣṭoma* is established here up until the touching of the two fruit-bearing boards.
Having touched the wooden board, he should proceed with the *pṛśni* verses;
then he should proceed with the *prāṇagraha* formulas;
then he should take hold of the *aṃśu* stalks.
Then he should proceed with the Aṃśu cup;
then with the Upāṃśu cup;
at the proper time, with the Antaryāma cup.
(25.17:248.13) From this point onward, it is established.

Regarding this point, they teach Baudhāyana’s ritual procedure: at the drawing of the Āgrayaṇa cup, one should draw two streams at the morning pressing, three at the midday pressing, and four at the third pressing. Furthermore, the residue from the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups and the continuous stream of the Śukra cup—these two are for the morning pressing;
and the continuous stream of the Śukra cup together with the Āgrayaṇa and the Udacanapātra are for the third pressing at the midday session.
The remnant left in the Āditya vessel and the residue of the Āditya draught, as well as the Āgrayaṇa, are mixed with the drawing-spoon at the third pressing as the fourth [portion].
One should mix the purified King Soma with three things: milk, parched barley flour, and gold.
Whatever draught he draws, he makes it have its bottom upwards on both sides and its mixing-vessel made of gold.

"The cups should be offered while standing, except for the one for Prajāpati and the remnants of the *manthin* cup"—thus they teach the ritual procedure of Śālīki regarding the verses for the consecration of the drops (*drapsa*). One should offer these as oblations with the *sruva*-ladle. At what time, indeed, should one offer them?
Having offered the *saṃtanī* oblations, one should offer them at this time.

(25.18:249.9) Then he says, "O Unnetṛ! Cause the King [Soma] to flow through the filter toward the Pūtabhṛt; having wiped the Ādhavanīya with the fringes, turn it upside down. This is the formal instruction (saṃpraiṣa) that remains in effect until the Avakāśa offerings.
Having worshipped with the Avakāśas, he wipes it with the fringes and turns it upside down.
"The ritual procedure is the same from the Āśvina cup onwards.
(25.19:249.13) "Up to the pouring of the remnants over the Dhiṣṇiya hearths"—this is the general heading.
But how, indeed, is the pouring over the Dhiṣṇiyas performed according to the order in which they were cast?

Having sprinkled [the butter] with the formula, "To the all-pervading Pravāhaṇa, svāhā!", he chooses seven [priests] with the mantra, "O Agni, protect me with your fierce countenance; carry me across; do not harm me. Of these, the Hotṛ himself becomes the seventh.
(25.19:250.4) Regarding the *ahargaṇa* sacrifice, how should the morning pressing procession (*prasarpaṇa*) be conducted on the subsequent days?
(25.19:250.5) One should say: "Starting from the worship of the *āhavanīya* fire," and the worship of the *sphya* and *vighana* stones is performed only once.
(25.19:250.7) But how indeed should their movement through the sacrificial ground (*saṃcara*) be arranged?
Between the *dhiṣṇya* of the Hotṛ and that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin are those [priests] who have no *dhiṣṇya*.
Then, those who possess *dhiṣṇyas* should circumambulate their respective *dhiṣṇyas* by the north.
Now, these two Adhvaryus do not have cups (*acamasa*).
"Where, indeed, does the consumption of these two take place?
"One should say: 'In the Hotṛ's cup.
"And which of the officiating priests, indeed, do not consume the Soma at the one-day sacrifice?"
One should say: "The Unnetṛ, the Grāvastut, and the Subrahmaṇya.
Now, at what point indeed in the Sattra should those who have been consecrated consume [the Soma]?
The Unnetṛ should consume from the Neṣṭṛ’s cup; the Grāvastut from the Acchāvāka’s cup; and the Subrahmaṇya from the Udgātṛ’s cup.

Alternatively, all may consume [the Soma] from the Āgnīdhra’s cup. It is known from scripture: "In the subsequent performance, he who is the Āgnīdhra is the Grāvastut, he is the Subrahmaṇya, and he is the Unnetṛ."

(25.20:250.17) As for this which they teach as the ritual manual of Baudhāyana: one should remove the *savanīya* offerings onto a single vessel; this is seen to be the adornment of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) itself.

(25.20:251.2) One should remove the sacrificial cake from the middle, having spread a base of clarified butter and poured butter over it; the parched grains (*dhānā*) to the east, the groat-mash (*karambha*) to the south, the parched flour (*parivāpa*) to the west, and the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) to the north.
(25.20:251.3) But how, indeed, should this [arrangement] be a common practice?
The path for the oblation is well-known.
Now, another [procedure]:

having carried it out through the eastern door and led it into the *sadas* through the western door, one should carry it around in front of the performers (*kartṛ*), behind the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths, and past the north of the *ācchāvāka’s* *dhiṣṇiya*. Having handed it over to another, one returns by the same way one came, goes around the north of the *sadas*, carries it out through the eastern door, carries it around the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth, and should set it down within the altar (*antarvedi*).
If the Adhvaryu has entered the *havirdhāna* shed, he should say: "Come forth; let me not pass you by.

As for that which they declare to be the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) of Baudhāyana—namely, that he hands over the secondary portions (*pratinirgrāhya*) to the Pratiprasthātṛ standing to the north of the offerings for the dual deities—the Adhvaryu, when he carries the sacrificial cakes westward, should take hold of the Pratiprasthātṛ as he enters the *havirdhāna*.
Having taken the two cups, he goes out.
As soon as he has gone out, the Adhvaryu takes the two cups.
Having walked around by the rear, he hands over the *pratinirgrāhya* cup to the Pratiprasthātṛ standing to the north.
Having offered the oblation and poured out the remnants, the Pratiprasthātṛ should turn to the right and take hold of the Adhvaryu from behind.
Then the Adhvaryu, running westward toward the Pratiprasthātṛ with the vessel, [performs the rite];
from this point onward, it is established.
Now, these offerings to the dual deities are without the *anuvaṣaṭ* call.
Where, then, does their *anuvaṣaṭ* call occur?

It is known from scripture: "The dual-deity offerings, the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtuyāja*), the cup for the wives' husband (*pātnīvata*), the Āditya cup, and the Sāvitra cup—do not offer the *anuvaṣaṭ* call for these."

As for this ritual procedure of Aupamanyava which they teach: one should consume the cups dedicated to dual deities using the long *bhakṣa*-formula. Having begun with "Consume! Enter me!", he then touches [the cup] from that point onward with: "For power, for skill, for the increase of wealth, for heroic offspring;
O King, do not terrify me; do not strike my heart with thy brilliance; for virility, for strength, for life, for splendor.
Then, one should consume the cups belonging to the openings of the pressings (*savanamukhīya*) using the very formula for the consumption at each pressing.
(25.21:252.12) Where, indeed, does the *vasatīvara* [water] have its participation in the *stotra* and its participation in the *śastra*?
(25.21:252.13) Its participation in the *stotra* is in the *viśvarūpā* verses, and its participation in the *śastra* is in the *prātaranuvāka*.
(25.21:252.14) And where, indeed, do the *upāṃśu* and *antaryāma* [libations] and the *dvidevatya* [cups] have their participation in the *stotra* and their participation in the *śastra*?
That which he recites in a whisper belongs to the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups;
[it belongs] to the Prauga-uktha and to the dual-deity offerings.
Now, this Pratiprasthātṛ becomes the attendant to the north of the Adhvaryu during the seasonal cups.
The Pratiprasthātṛ should follow the Adhvaryu as he moves from here and there.
Then the Adhvaryu, running westward toward the Pratiprasthātṛ with the vessel, [proceeds];
from this point onward, the procedure is established.
(25.21:253.5) "Of what deities, indeed, are the seasonal offerings (*ṛtuyāja*)? (25.21:253.5) 'The seasons are the deities'—this is one view; now another."
The Hotṛ priest sacrifices to Indra;
the Potṛ priest sacrifices to the Maruts;
the Neṣṭṛ priest sacrifices to the Gnas.
The Āgnīdhra priest sacrifices to Agni;
the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin sacrifices to Indra;
the Maitrāvaruṇa [sacrifices] to Mitra and Varuṇa.
Four [verses] for the god Draviṇodas;
the two Aśvins as Adhvaryus, the Adhvaryus; Agni Gṛhapati, the Gṛhapati.
"Where, indeed, does the portion of the *stotra* for the offering to Indra and Agni occur?
"One should say: in the *bahiṣpavamāna*.
"Whatever cups (*graha*) there may be that lack a *stotra*, their *stotras* occur in the *pavamāna* itself."
"Where, indeed, are the *savanīya* offerings of the midday pressing offered?
"One should say: 'At the stotra of the minor *vaiśvadeva*. Where are those of the third pressing?"
One should say, "The stotra for Mahendra."

One should take the *nārāśaṃsa* cup from the very oblation already offered in the *hotṛ*-cup. There are two *nārāśaṃsa*s at the morning pressing and the midday pressing, and one *nārāśaṃsa* at the third pressing.
Thus, there are four *unnīyamāna-sūkta*s (hymns recited while the soma is being drawn).
At the openings of the pressings and at the cup of the Acchāvāka,
there are three long recitations (*dīrghabhakṣa*).
Where, indeed, does the *pravargya* rite follow the day of the Soma-pressing?
One should simply say, "The curd-heat offering" (*dadhigharma*).
What [is the purpose] of the *upasad* offerings?
It is for the complete performance of the Soma sacrifice.
"One makes the pressing-stones resound upon a wooden board covered with leather"—
this they call the "dry pressing.
But how, indeed, should one take the Māhendra cup when the Rathantara is the *pṛṣṭha* chant?
One should draw the Māhendra cup with this Gāyatrī verse: "Great is Indra, who by his might... (RV 8.6.1).
Now, when the Bṛhat is the Pṛṣṭha-stotra, one should draw the Māhendra cup with this Triṣṭubh verse: "Great is Indra, man-like, the protector of the people...
(RV 8.6.2). When both [the Bṛhat and the Rathantara] are the Pṛṣṭhas, one should draw it with whichever [verse] corresponds to the Pṛṣṭha-stotra, and use the other as the Puroruc.
(25.23:254.11) How, indeed, does the performance of the Savanīya animal sacrifice commence?

(25.23:254.12) Having spread out the *iḍasūna* grass, having divided the clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*) and poured it into the *juhū* ladle, having gone out northward between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), he should call for the formal announcement (*saṃvada*), baste [the butter], and set down the sacrificial animal. With the *pañcahotṛ* formula, he spreads [grass] in the four [ladles];
he should perform the rites beginning with the *manotā* and ending with the *iḍā*.
(25.23:254.15) It is established from this point forward.
Now, regarding the divisions of the Ukthya: whichever is the formula for drawing the cup at the morning pressing, that same one is used for the midday pressing and the third pressing.
One should merely manifest the deity.
For each cup (*camasa*), one should cast three pieces of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) into it, saying, "Nine for the *hotṛ*-cup.
This is said to apply to exactly three [cups].
Now, this *āgrayaṇa* cup is drawn for thirty-three deities.

"But where indeed are these [verses] known to be used at the offering? "They are known to be used at the Pātnīvata [offering], as it is stated: 'Of the husband of the wives, the thirty and the three gods.'"
(25.23:255.6) How, indeed, should one consume the *pātnīvata* [cup]?

(25.23:255.7) <O divine Soma, belonging to the troop of Aditi, who knowest the mind, of thee who art drunk by Agni Vaiśvānara accompanied by the wives [of the gods] and by Tvaṣṭṛ, at the third pressing, with the *jagatī* metre, being invited, I, invited, consume thee, the sweet-scented!> Thus.
(25.24:255.10) How, indeed, does the *antarukthya* sacrifice come to be?
(25.24:255.10) Having taken the *āgrayaṇa* cup at the established third pressing, one should take the *ukthya* cup.

(25.24:255.11) Then, having set this down near the *dhruva* cup, one should divide it among three upright vessels with [the formula]: "Thou art taken with a support; for the gods thee, the god-loving; for the *ukthya*s thee, the *uktha*-loving; for the life of the sacrifice, I take thee, acceptable to Indra and Varuṇa. Thus.

(25.24:255.14) Again, [saying] "Thou art the oblation," he touches the *ukthya* vessel; having wiped it around, he sets it down [with], "This is thy womb; for Indra and Varuṇa, thee. At that very moment, he draws another [cup] [with]: "Thou art taken with a support; for the gods, thee, the god-loving; for the *ukthya*s, thee, the *uktha*-loving; for the life of the sacrifice, I take thee, acceptable to Indra and Bṛhaspati."

Again, with the words, "Thou art the oblation," he touches the *ukthya* vessel; having wiped it around, he sets it down with, "This is thy womb; for Indra and Bṛhaspati, thee! At that very moment, he draws another portion with, "Thou art taken with a support; for the gods, thee, the one who yearns for the gods; for the *ukthyas*, thee, the one who yearns for the *ukthyas*; for the life of the sacrifice, I take thee, acceptable to Indra and Viṣṇu."
(25.24:256.5) Here, however, he does not touch the *ukthya* vessel with the formula, "Thou art the oblation.
(25.24:256.6) Having wiped it with the fringes [of the cloth], he turns it face down;
having wiped it all around, he sets it down with the words: "This is thy womb; for Indra and Viṣṇu, thee!"
Then, having poured them into the *dhruva* cup, he should pour them into the *hotṛ*’s cup.
He should pour the *stotra*s into the *stotra*s and the *śastra*s into the *śastra*s.

Of that which has been offered, the consumption is performed with the formula: "Of that which has been drunk by Indra-Varuṇa, Indra-Bṛhaspati, Indra-Viṣṇu, Agni Vaiśvānara, and the Maruts; of the sweet, the invited, I, being invited, partake. Or he may consume it with this very [formula].

Or rather, [he may do so] with the permanent formula: "O God Soma, belonging to the troop of Aditi, knower of the mind, of thee who art drunk by Indra and Varuṇa, by Indra and Bṛhaspati, by Indra and Viṣṇu, by Agni Vaiśvānara, and by the Maruts—at the third pressing, having the Jagatī as its metre, being sweet and invited—I, being invited, partake. Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, regarding this ritual procedure of Aupamanyava which they teach, one should offer the two Mindā oblations beforehand.
"Having offered the two *mindā* oblations, one should draw the *hāriyojana* cup," so it is said.

Now, some, having placed the *avabhṛtha* at the site of the *cātvāla*, offer the *ṛjīṣa* with curds, milk mixed with honey, using the *naiṣṭyayana* verses: "O King Soma, that which they have cut from thee with the pressing-stone...
He then offers the *avabhṛtha* sacrificial formulas (*yajus*).

"What indeed are these *avabhṛtha*-oblations? [The answer is: "When they perform the rite with wood-shavings (*śākala*) in the *āhavanīya* fire, [saying]: 'Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the gods; thou art the expiation for sin committed against men; thou art the expiation for sin committed against the ancestors.
Thus it is regarding the *avabhṛtha* oblation."
"What indeed is this *avabhṛtha* oblation? [he asks].
Taking up water, he offers it with the mantra: "O Lord of the Sacrifice, we worship thee with the oblations of the sacrifice; in the *sūktavāka* and the *namovāka*, we pay homage—*svāhā*!
Standing right there, they should proceed with the *avabhṛtha*.
Turning his back, he should push the water away with the tip of his big toe; from this point onward, the procedure is established.
Now follows this Udayanīya [offering].
What is the commencement of its ritual?
One should perform it with the *barhir-yajus* formula.
He should rub his hands together,
strew the sacrificial grass around,
and, having washed the vessels, set them down.

Having seated the Brahman priest to the south, and having placed a water-pot right there to the north, he should set down the wooden sword (sphya) behind the Gārhapatya fire, with the vessel upon the wooden sword.

He should pour the rice grains into the vessel; the ritual procedure, beginning from the taking up of the winnowing basket, extends until the end of the rite, up to the point of the scattering [of the grains].
Having performed the ritual actions up to the pouring out [of the grains], he should pour water across the strainer, place it over the fire, and then pour the rice grains across the strainer.
Then he should pour out the clarified butter;
then he should place the clarified butter over the fire.
Having carried fire around both [the animal and the sacrificial post], one should carry away the *stambayajus* from the *aupasadā* altar behind the *gārhapatya*.
