From this point onward, the procedure is established;
[this concludes] the setting down of that cooked [animal].

Having loosened the western joint of the southern enclosing-stick, or having moved the southern enclosing-stick forward along its front, he should place the *prāyaṇīya* oblation facing east and the *udayanīya* oblation facing west.
Here the deities are worshipped beginning with Agni;
the *udayanīya* concludes with the *śamyu*-verse.
Now, if an animal has been prepared, he should rub his hands together,
strew the sacrificial grass around the fire,
and, having washed the vessels, set them down.
Having prepared the sprinkling waters, he should sprinkle the vessels.
Having poured out the clarified butter, placed it on the fire, and carried fire around it, he should take up the wooden sword (*sphya*).
From that point, beginning with the formal summons (*saṃpraiṣa*), the ritual procedure pertaining to the animal sacrifice (*pāśubandhika*) is performed.
(25.26:258.6) From this point onward, it is established.

(25.26:258.7) Regarding that which they declare as the ritual procedure of Śālīki—that one should sacrifice with the curdled milk (āmikṣā) for Mitra and Varuṇa—for that [offering], the driving away of the calves is performed together with the Savanīya offerings, and the evening milking is performed together.
Having performed the Udayanīya offering, he should rub his hands together.
He should strew the sacrificial grass,
wash the vessels, and set them down. Having prepared the sprinkling waters, he should sprinkle the vessels.
(25.26:258.10) Then he should have the cows milked for the morning milking.
(25.26:258.11) Then, having cooked it over the Gārhapatya fire, he should remove it from the heat without pouring clarified butter over it.
(25.26:258.11) Then he should pour out the clarified butter.
Then he should place the clarified butter on the fire.

Having carried fire around both [the butter and the victim], having laid the fencing-sticks of split bamboo around the Āhavanīya fire, and having again placed [the butter] on the fire, poured the clarified butter over it, and removed it from the heat, he should set it down within the altar.
Having performed the ritual up to the portioning of the clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), he has his hair and beard shaved and his nails clipped at the southern edge of the altar.
(25.26:259.1) Then it concludes with the *ājyabhāga* offerings and ends with the *iḍā*.
(25.26:259.1) Now, this *udavasānīyā* offering is performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), for it follows the ritual procedure of the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*).
(25.26:259.2) There is a single removal of the *stambayajus* from the great altar (*mahāvedi*).
The unarmored wife sits beside the tail of the sacrifice.
Now, they pile this fire-altar with three *upasads*, six *upasads*, or twelve *upasads*.

If he intends to pile one consisting of a thousand bricks with three *upasads*, having performed the *pravargya* and the two *upasads* in the forenoon, he piles the first layer together with the *purīṣa* and offers the *saṃcitāhuti* oblations;
having piled the second layer together with the *purīṣa*, he offers the *saṃcitāhuti* oblations.

On the following day, having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites, and having laid down the third layer, the fourth layer, the fifth layer, and the sixth layer together with the loose earth (*purīṣa*), he offers the *saṃcita* oblations.
The third [layer] is indeed that of the Upavasatha day.

Now, if one is about to pile a thousand-brick fire-altar with six Upasads, having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites in the forenoon and having laid down the first layer together with the loose earth, he offers the *saṃcita* oblations.
On the following day, having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites and having piled the second layer together with its loose soil, he offers the Saṃcita oblations.
He proceeds in this very manner for five days; the sixth day is indeed the day of the fast (Aupavasathika).

(25.27:259.15) Now, if he is about to sacrifice with a thousand [bricks] and twelve *upasad* days, it is to be done according to the sūtra. (25.27:259.16) But if he is about to sacrifice with two thousand [bricks] and three *upasad* days, having performed the *pravargya* and the *upasad* rites in the forenoon, and having laid down the first layer together with the *purīṣa* and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he lays down the *āhāryā* brick together with the *purīṣa*. Having laid down the second layer together with the *purīṣa* and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he lays down the *āhāryā* brick together with the *purīṣa*.

On the following day, having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites, and having laid down the third layer, the fourth layer, the fifth layer, and the sixth layer together with their soil-coverings, and having offered the Saṃcita oblations, he lays down the Ahāryā brick together with its soil-covering.
The third [layer] is indeed that of the Upavasatha day.

(25.27:260.7) Now, if one is about to pile a fire-altar of two thousand bricks with six *upasad* days, he performs the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites in the forenoon; having piled the first layer together with its *purīṣa* and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he piles the *āhāryā* layer together with its *purīṣa*.

On the following day, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, having piled the second layer together with its *purīṣa* and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he piles the *āhāryā* layer together with its *purīṣa*.
In this very manner, he proceeds for five days.
The sixth day is indeed the day of the fast (*aupavasathika*).

Now, if one is about to sacrifice with a two-thousand-brick altar involving twelve *upasads*, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites in the forenoon and having laid down the first layer (*citi*) and spread the loose earth (*purīṣa*), he dwells for that night.

On the following day, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, having spread the loose earth and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he lays down the *āhāryā* brick together with the loose earth.
Proceeding in this very manner according to the sūtra, having laid down layer after layer of loose soil and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he lays down the *āhāryā* brick together with its soil.
The twelfth day is indeed the day of fasting (*aupavasathika*).

Now, if he is about to pile a three-thousand-brick altar with three *upasad* days, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites in the forenoon, having piled the first layer together with its *purīṣa* and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he piles two additional layers together with their *purīṣa*.
Having piled the second layer together with its *purīṣa* and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he piles two additional layers together with their *purīṣa*.

On the following day, having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites, and having laid down the third layer, the fourth layer, the fifth layer, and the sixth layer together with their soil-covering (purīṣa), and having offered the Saṃcita oblations, he lays down two by two the removable bricks (āhārya) together with their soil-covering.
The third [layer] is indeed that of the Upavasatha day.

Now, if he intends to pile a three-thousand-brick altar with six *upasad* days, he performs the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites in the forenoon; having piled the first layer together with the *purīṣa* and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he piles two additional layers together with the *purīṣa*.

On the following day, having performed the *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, having piled the second layer together with the *purīṣa* and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he piles two additional layers together with the *purīṣa*.
He proceeds in this very manner for five days.
The sixth day is indeed the day of the fast (aupavasathika).

Now, if one is about to perform a sacrifice consisting of three thousand [bricks] with twelve Upasad days, he performs the Pravargya and Upasad rites in the forenoon, lays down the first layer, and having spread the loose soil (purīṣa) over it, he dwells for that night. On the following day, having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites, having laid down the loose soil, and having offered the Saṃcita oblations, he lays down two additional bricks together with the loose soil.

Proceeding in this very manner according to the Sūtra, having laid down layer after layer of soil and offered the *saṃcita* oblations, he lays down two by two the removable bricks together with the soil.
The twelfth day is indeed the day of the fast (*aupavasathika*).
How, then, should one understand [the sequence] as "with an inner *upasat*," "with an outer *upasat*," or "with both inner and outer *upasats*"?

When twelve days remain of the year-long consecration (*daikṣa-saṃvatsara*), one should purchase the King (Soma); that [rite] has the Upasad days within it. When the year has fully elapsed, one should purchase the King; that has the Upasad days outside it. When six days remain of the year-long consecration, one should purchase the King; those shall be the Upasad days, as well as the subsequent six-night period; that has the Upasad days both within and without.
"He makes this clay level with the opening" means that he places it level with the ground; this is what is being stated here.
Then he stations these two, the horse and the donkey, either to the north or in front, facing westward.
If the horse is to the south and facing west and the donkey is to the north,
or if the horse is to the north and the donkey is to the south,
[he performs the sacrifice] according to the rule: "He immolates the animals for the fires."
There is a Brāhmaṇa passage concerning five animals:

"If he indeed dedicates these animals, having performed the ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) up to the laying down of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), they should cut off the heads and cast the bodies into the water.
'They cast the bodies into the water,' so it is known."
For this month he practices celibacy (*brahmacarya*); sleeping on the ground, abstaining from meat, and avoiding women, he maintains the former consecration (*pūrvadīkṣā*)—this is what they call it.
He considers this very thirteenth month as his consecration.
At this point, he causes the sacrificer to recite over the black antelope skin: "He neither forms his fists nor restrains his speech.

This ritual procedure, beginning with the black antelope skin and ending with the announcement (*āvedana*), takes place during the first *upasad*. He measures out the altar (*vedi*) and carries away the *stambayajus* grass-bundle.
(25.29:263.6) This is brought about solely by the power of karma.
(25.29:263.7) Now, while pouring the saline earth among the ritual materials, he should meditate with his mind on that which is black in the moon, thinking, "That too is here."
(25.30:263.9) "Plowing each successive furrow while driving the oxen one after another, and sowing all kinds of herbs, he should not step upon the place of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*.
(25.30:263.10) Now, some indeed sing a *sāman* both over the man and the *svayamātṛṇṇā*.
(25.30:263.11) But what, indeed, is the significance of the *svayamātṛṇṇā-nikotha*?
One should call a gold brick a "circle-brick" and a "seminal brick.
Whichever group of bricks one lays down, one should not separate them; the southern [group] by the south and the northern [group] by the north.
If one were to lay down the bricks from the south or from the front, one should turn back there with the fingers drawn inward.
Now, if one were to turn clockwise from the north or from the west and lay down the bricks facing the *svayamātṛṇṇā* itself, [one would ask]:
"He lays down the *kṛttikās*";
but which indeed are these *kṛttikās*?
One should say "lightning" (*vidyut*) alone.
Regarding the purpose of non-hearing, Baudhāyana says there is a repeated piling (*punaścit*) for every fire;
that is not a piling with earth (*purīṣacit*), but rather a sixth [piling] characterized by increase.
"It is by means of growth," says Śālīki.
Regarding the bringing forward of the sixth covering, at what time indeed should one bring it?
One should say: "after having laid down the star-bricks."
He proceeds by means of three rites: by the laying down of the loose earth, by the sprinkling accompanied by the *sāhasravat* formula, and by the making [of the bricks] into milch-cows.

He proceeds by means of eight rites: the two *saṃcita* oblations on the final layer, the *Śatarudrīya*, the prostrations (*namaskāra*), the sprinkling around, the dragging [of the cord], the *sarpa* oblations, the worship with Sāman chants, and the recitation.
Now, regarding the question of whether there is a *tantra* (common ritual procedure) for the pouring out of various seeds:

the taking up of the offering-ladle (*sruk*) is a *tantra*; the taking up of the winnowing-basket (*śūrpa*) is a *tantra*; and all the mantras for the cart, beginning with the yoke-pole (*dhur*), constitute a *tantra* up until the *Sāvitra* [rite].
With each individual seed, however, the *Sāvitra* rite is repeated.
The *tantra* consists of the Daśahotṛ formula, the departure, and the entrustment; thus it is the *tantra*.

The *tantra* includes the beating of the black antelope skin, the placing of the mortar, the pouring of the grains for the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), the setting down of the pestle, the winnowing with the basket, and the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*). From the mantra used at the pouring onwards, the formula is repeated for each individual seed until the end of the scattering.

Regarding that which they teach as the ritual procedure of Śālīki—that one should step across together with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering—this is appropriate for the eleven *prayāja*s, not for the five *prayāja*s.

Regarding that which they teach as the ritual procedure of Aupamanyava—that one should consecrate [the sacrificer] before the *sviṣṭakṛt* according to the traditional injunction; that here there is no black antelope skin, no two gold plates, and no *pārtha* offerings; but having spread out *kuśa* grass, he should consecrate him upon them—how indeed is the consecration of the performers of a sacrificial session (*sattra*) to be repeated?

The consecration and the announcement take place on the first day; the consecration is on the first day; the horse is made to smell [the offerings] at the beginning and at the end; they should chant the *bahispavamāna* in the *āstāva*; and day by day, during the *yajñāyajñiya* chant, he should touch [the horse] with two verses.
(25.32:265.11) How, indeed, does the performance of the eleven animals commence?

(25.32:265.12) Having spread out the *iḍasūna* grass, having divided the speckled butter and poured it into the *juhū* ladle, having gone out northward between the *cātvāla* and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), he should call for the *saṃvāda*, baste [the portions], and set down the animal. With the *pañcahotṛ* formula, he spreads [grass] in the four [ladles].
Having taken the portion for the deity of the principal animal, and having placed the fat of the kidneys into the broth, he should cover the *juhū* with that.
He should sprinkle it with broth and then pour clarified butter over it.

Then, for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, having taken a single portion from each of the three parts [of the organs] into the *upabhṛt* ladle, he should place the fat of the kidneys into the broth and cover the *upabhṛt* with that.
He should sprinkle it with broth but not pour clarified butter over it.
Then, having placed the heart, the tongue, the breast, the two kidneys, and the rectum together in a vessel, and having sprinkled them with broth, he should not pour clarified butter over them.
Then, having taken the fat-oblation in a bronze cup or a wooden bowl, and having sprinkled it with broth, he should pour clarified butter over it.
He should touch the animal.
He should proceed with the offering of the fat (*vasāhoma*) by the side, using the *maṃs* and *kumbata* vessels.

Having circumambulated the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) from behind, he should call for the *āśrāvaṇa*; at the half-verse of the *yājyā*, the Pratiprasthātṛ should offer the fat. He should also sprinkle it toward the quarters.
(25.32:266.10) Then he should pour the remainder into the *vasāhoma* ladle.
(25.32:266.10) At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the oblation.
(25.32:266.11) Without yet having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he steps across toward the north and spreads an underlayer of ghee both in the *juhū* and in the *vasāhoma* ladle.
Having cut the portion for the deity from the second animal, he should place the fat of the kidneys into the broth and cover the *juhū* ladle with it.
Having sprinkled it with broth, he should pour clarified butter over it.
Then, having taken one portion each from all three organs for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering into the *upabhṛt* ladle, he should place the fat of the kidneys into the broth and cover the *upabhṛt* with it.
This [omentum] having been cut out, one should pour broth over it but should not sprinkle clarified butter upon it.
Alternatively, one should take the fat-oblation in a bronze vessel or a wooden cup, pour broth over it, and then sprinkle clarified butter upon it.
One should touch the animal.

One should offer the fat-oblation from the side, from the shoulder and the hip. Having walked around the back of the northern altar, the Pratiprasthātṛ should cause the announcement to be made; at the half-verse of the *yājyā*, he should offer the fat-oblation, and he should leave a remnant for the quarters.
At the utterance of "vaṣaṭ," he offers the oblation;
he does exactly the same for all the animals. When he cuts off the portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering of the animal dedicated to Varuṇa, he should pour clarified butter over it twice.
Having poured broth over that which has been cut off, he should sprinkle it with clarified butter.
In the same manner, he should take the fat-oblation in a bronze vessel or a wooden cup, pour broth over it, and sprinkle it with clarified butter; then he should touch the animal.
He should offer the fat-oblation (*vasāhoma*) from the side, [using] the *maṃstaḥ* ladle and the *kumbha* vessel.

Having circumambulated the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) by its rear, he should cause the announcement (*āśrāvayet*). At the half-verse of the offering-formula (*yājyā*), the Pratiprasthātṛ should offer the fat-oblation;
and he should leave a remnant for the quarters.
(25.32:267.11) Then he should pour the remainder into the *vasā-homa* ladle.
(25.32:267.12) At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the oblation.
(25.32:267.12) Then, prior to the offering to Vanaspati, he should offer sacrifices to the common quarters.
Then he should proceed with the offering to Vanaspati;
then with the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
From this point onward, the ritual is established.

Regarding this, they teach the ritual procedure of Aupamanyava: "One should sacrifice with a *nirūḍha* curd-mixture dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. One should understand that the ritual duties of the fast-day (*aupavasathika*) are established here, just as they are for one who performs the *saṃnayya* offering on the new moon day, except for the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*.

For one year, he should not descend to anyone [in status], nor should he eat the flesh of the head, nor the flesh of birds, nor, having piled the fire-altar (*agni*), should he approach a woman with reddish-brown hair (*rāmā*). One who has piled the fire-altar should not run while it is raining; if he should run, he should turn back.
"He turns toward food itself," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, in this Vājapeya sacrifice, there are three horses for each of the seventeen chariots; these amount to fifty-one.
One should yoke a side-horse to the north.
"Twenty-four animals"—thus both the animal for Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*) and the subsequent sacrificial animal (*anūbandhya*) become twenty-four-fold.
Now, indeed, it is said: "One offers an oblation to Savitṛ before each and every ritual act."
"One who is about to offer the *dīkṣaṇīyā* oblation offers the *sāvitra* oblation"— thus,
from the *sāvitra* itself, it becomes *sāvitra*.
"One who is about to offer the *dīkṣā* oblations offers the *sāvitra* oblation."
Having offered the *sāvitra* oblation, one should offer the *dīkṣā* oblations;
for it is said, "When about to pour out the *prāyaṇīyā* [oblation], he offers the *sāvitra*.
Thus, from the *sāvitra* itself, the *sāvitra* [nature] arises.
"One who is about to offer [the oblation] with gold inside offers to Savitṛ";
having offered to Savitṛ, he should offer [the oblation] with gold inside.
"Having proceeded with the footprint-rite, having purchased and carried back the King Soma, and being about to pour out the guest-offering (ātithya), one offers to Savitṛ."
The Sāvitra [offering] arises from the Sāvitra [rite] itself;
for it is said, "When about to proceed with the first Pravargya and Upasad rites, he offers the Sāvitra.
Having offered the Sāvitra, he should proceed with the first Pravargya and Upasad rites.
"One shall offer the oblation to Savitṛ when about to perform the first tracing of the Mahāvedi";
having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, he should take up the wooden sword (*sphya*).
"One offers the oblation to Savitṛ when about to lead forward the Āhavanīya fire."
Having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, he should take up the fuel.
Intending to erect the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds on the chariot-stand, he offers the oblation to Savitṛ;
having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, he should erect the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds on the chariot-stand.
"One who is about to lead forward Agni and Soma offers an oblation to Savitṛ";
having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, he should lead forward Agni and Soma.
"One who is about to erect the sacrificial post offers an oblation to Savitṛ."
Having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, he should take up the sprinkling waters.
Having set aside the sacrificial post provided with a wooden chip, and being about to dedicate the animal victim for Agni and Soma, he offers the oblation to Savitṛ;
having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, he should take up two blades of sacrificial grass.
Having performed the well-known rite with its omentum, and being about to take the *vasatīvarī* waters, he offers the oblation to Savitṛ;
having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, he should take up the water-jar.
He offers the oblation to Savitṛ when he is about to pour out the sacrificial cake for the animal victim.
From the Sāvitra [offering] itself, the Sāvitra [portion] comes into being.
"The hornless goat is four-cornered. Having established the corners in the intermediate directions, he should join together the corner facing the fire and the corner facing the sun.
"He draws five *atigrāhya* cups for Indra."

All of these must be taken with their respective *upayāma* vessels. Having performed the rite for the Maruts, one should cause them to be immolated. The carrying of the firebrand is common to all; the *adhvaryu’s* call to the *adhrigu* should be repeated for each.

At the *saṃjñaptahoma*, he should break the two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) that are held upright; at the *svāhākṛti* call, he should divide the clarified butter into two parts, as the drops belong to both portions.
Now, this chariot wheel is raised one span above the ground.
Having gone around by the rear, [the text says] "he touches the two wings"; it is indeed these two chariot wheels that he touches.
Then he says: "The race-runners pass by on the southern path. By this, it is the Sūtas and Rājanyas who are meant.
"The Māruta [chariots] go around the front of the Āhavanīya fire. By this, it is the Kṣattṛs and Saṃgrahītṛs who are meant.
Then he causes the sacrificer to put on a garment of silk cloth (*tārpya*).
Thus, this garment becomes satisfied by the clarified butter alone.
Furthermore, they cite: "There are trees named *tṛpa*;
it belongs to them."
(25.34:270.6) Now, some say that this Vājapeya is entirely characterized by the number seventeen.
(25.34:270.7) According to the specific instruction, they should chant the Bṛhat-sāman on twenty-one verses, using verses addressed to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.
Now, this Rājasūya concludes in fifteen and a half months, or in fourteen and a half months.
In it, there are five Soma-sacrifices consisting of single-day rites, an Ahīna of two nights, and six sheds.
There are eight sacrificial posts; indeed, six belong to the Agniṣṭoma, while in the animal sacrifice involving two animals and in the Sautrāmaṇī, there is an eighth.
There are just as many Avabhṛtha rites.
Where, then, is the oblation for the oblation poured out?
He should say, "It is approved. A black garment with a black border is the sacrificial fee;
by this, it is meant that it has a black fringe.
"One may perform [the sacrifice] at will by means of an *iṣṭi* or an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*).
Having performed the *saṃtanī-ṣṭi*, one should sacrifice with either the *āgrayaṇa* or the *pārvaṇa*.
But how indeed is the *sākamedhaparvan* [to be performed]?
The first *saṃtani* [offering] is at the deep of night; the second, on the following day, at the onset of evening.
What indeed constitutes that which has not yet arisen?
One should say: "Prior to the formal call (*saṃpraiṣa*) for the *anūyāja* offerings."
He offers a *caru* oblation to Bṛhaspati in the house of the Brahman;
that is, any other Brāhmaṇa who is not connected with the duties of the sacrificer.
He offers a *caru* to Bhaga in the house of the favorite wife.
Whichever woman among the queens becomes most fortunate, [it is said] "for the rival wife,
a *caru* offering to Nirṛti in her house";
by this she is declared to be unfortunate.
"The *pauṣṇa* oblation in the house of the *bhāgadugha*"—this refers specifically to the cook (*mahānasika*).
Furthermore, they cite: "He who milks for his share—that one is referred to here."
The oblations of the Ratnins take twelve days;
on the thirteenth day is the offering to Mitra and Bṛhaspati. When two days remain of this very same bright fortnight—
In that [sacrifice], he should sacrifice with the two *saṃtanī* offerings.

Now, if he should pile the fire-altar during the *ukthya* consecration ceremony (*abhiṣecanīya*), then in this very two-night rite, having offered the *āgnika* and *sāvitra* oblations, having gathered the fire-pans (*ukhā*) and the heads of the sacrificial animals, he should sacrifice with the animal dedicated to Vāyu.
"Thou art the lord of waters," with these words [he offers] the oblations to the Lord of Waters;
these are said to be for those belonging to the ocean.
"Ye are the vigor of the Maruts," with these words [he offers] the Niveṣṭya oblations.
These are said to be for whirlpools;
"Ye are sun-bright," [is said] when they are visible;
these are said to be for clear waters.
"Ye are Śakvarīs"—thus these [verses] are said to be for the cow's caul.

"He should sacrifice right here with a cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni"—this is the rule for the Ukthya sacrifice when it is completed on the same day; but if it should be extended beyond that, then he should sacrifice with a cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni at that very time.
On the following day, with the Sārasvata [offering], they agree upon ten cups for each; thus there are seven cups in the Hotṛ’s cup and seven in the Udgātṛ’s cup.
(26.2:273.2) Now, in the other [sessions], these consist of nine [stomas] each, beginning with the *prasarpaṇa* and ending with the *apsuṣoma*.
(26.2:273.3) Then this *keśavapanīya* Atirātra sacrifice follows, characterized by the *pratīcīnastoma* and the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.

For him, the *agniṣṭoma* chants are reversed: the *bahiṣpavamāna* is the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*), the *ājya* chants and the midday *pavamāna* are seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*), the *pṛṣṭha* chants and the *ārbhava-pavamāna* are fifteen-fold (*pañcadaśa*), and the *yajñāyajñiya* is threefold (*trivṛt*).
Then he undergoes initiation for the *atirātra* sacrifice known as the *keśavapanīya*, which has chants directed backward (*pratīcīnastoma*).
For this, there are six days of initiation, six *upasads*, the pressing on the thirteenth day, and the concluding ceremony (*udavasāna*) on the fourteenth day.
(26.2:273.9) Now, during this very remaining half-month, he undergoes initiation for the two-night Vyuṣṭi sacrifice.
He remains initiated for one night of the first fortnight and two nights of the latter fortnight; for those nights, there are twelve Upasad days.
(26.2:273.12) Then he observes the fast-day.
(26.2:273.12) Now, on the day of the fast for the new moon, the first day occurs, and the second day occurs on the following day; thus concludes the Vyuṣṭi Dviraatra.
(26.2:273.13) Then he should take up residence in the northern hall.
(26.2:273.14) Then, having churned the fire and distributed the sacred fires, he undergoes initiation for the *udayanīya* *agniṣṭoma*.
(26.2:274.1) For that sacrifice, there are three days of initiation (*dīkṣā*), three days of *upasad*, and the pressing of the Soma occurs on the seventh day.

This Udayanīya Agniṣṭoma, for which a thousand-fold sacrificial fee is given, is concluded. Then, during the remainder of this very fortnight, he performs the Kṣatrasya Dhṛti, the Devikā offerings, the Traidhātavīyā, and the Sautrāmaṇī.
Thus the Rājasūya is completed in sixteen and a half months.
Now, according to Śālīki, those [sacrifices] ending with the Keśavapanīya consist of fifteen and a half [stomas].
(26.3:274.7) Now, therefore, the *añjasava* sacrifices. (26.3:274.7) The first half-month is completed in the established manner.

The *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices are performed in five days; the *Saṃtanī* sacrifice in two days; on the eighth day, the *Indraturīya*; on the ninth day, the former *Devikā* oblations; on the tenth day, the latter ones; on the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth [days, the remaining rites]. On the fourteenth day, with the *Triṣaṃyukta* offerings, there is a cake for Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds; on the fifteenth day, a porridge of barley for Varuṇa—this constitutes the month.

(26.3:274.11) With a twelve-day period, there are the oblations of the Ratnins; on the thirteenth day, the offering to Mitra and Bṛhaspati; with a two-day period, the Saṃtanī; with a half-month, the Abhiṣecanīya Ukthya—this constitutes two months. (26.3:274.13) With a half-month, the Saptadaśa Daśapeya; for a half-month, one remains consecrated, observing the vows of consecration—this constitutes three months.
(26.3:274.15) With a half-month, the Pratīcīnastoma Keśavapanīya Atirātra; with a half-month, the Vyuṣṭi Dvirātra—this constitutes four months.
"By half a month is the support of the Kṣatriya," so they say;
thus there are four and a half months.
Now, according to Śālīki:

The *agniṣṭoma* is purified in seven days; in that very manner, the remainder of the fortnight is accomplished up to the *vāruṇa* offering by means of the twelve-day *ratninām havīṃṣi*. On the thirteenth day, there is the *maitrābārhaspatya*; with two days, the *saṃtanī*—this constitutes one month. (26.3:275.3) With half a month, the *abhiṣecanīya ukthya*; with half a month, the *saptadaśa daśapeya*—these constitute two months.
(26.3:275.4) With half a month, the *pratīcīnastoma keśavapanīya atirātra*; with half a month, the *vyuṣṭi dvirātra*—these constitute three months.
"By half a month [is] the support of the Kṣatriya"—
thus they are three and a half;
then the *patantaka*.
There are twelve initiation days and twelve Upasad days; the Rājasūya is a seven-day Ahīna sacrifice.
He performs the other Rājasūya oblations according to the available space.
(26.3:275.8) Then he sacrifices with the Devikā oblations; (26.3:275.9) then he sacrifices with the Traidhātavīya offering;
then he sacrifices with the Sautrāmaṇī.
The Rājasūya sacrifice is completed.
(26.4:275.11) Now we shall set forth this ritual procedure for the bricks (*iṣṭikalpa*), involving both fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses and seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.
In that regard, the ritual duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) are established according to the *kalpa* of Baudhāyana;
[they are] according to the traditional recitation (*yathāmnāyam*) in the school of Śālīki.
"One should recite three triplets," it is said;
having recited the first verse three times, one should recite the next three verses once each, and the last verse three times.
These amount to fifteen [verses].
"One should recite fifteen [verses]," it is said.
We recite these eleven *sāmidhenī* verses;
of these, one recites the first three times and the last three times.

These are fifteen. One should recite seventeen; one should recite twenty-one; one should recite twenty-four; one should recite thirty; one should recite thirty-two; one should recite thirty-six; one should recite forty; one should recite forty-four; one should recite forty-eight. These are the *dhāyyā* verses in this context; they are to be inserted. All are addressed to Agni and are in the *gāyatrī* metre.
"One should recite all the meters; one should recite them in unlimited measure"—it is precisely in the place of the *dhāyyā* verses that these are to be inserted.
Not all of these are *gāyatrīs*;
the *puro'nuvākyā* is a *gāyatrī*, while the *yājyā* is a *triṣṭubh*.
The *puro'nuvākyā* has its mark at the beginning, and the *yājyā* has its mark at the end;

the *puro'nuvākyā* contains the word "head" (*mūrdhan*), and one sacrifices with a verse containing the word "team" (*niyutvatī*); "one performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between"—this applies only to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) and not elsewhere.
(26.5:276.8) Now, these optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) must be performed by one who is free from bodily excrement (*niṣpurīṣa*).

(26.5:276.9) He should observe a vow of milk for a year, or for twelve days, or for as long as he might prescribe. (26.5:276.10) Among those [sacrifices], if one were to offer even one of those that have the same ritual connection (*samānasaṃyojana*), all of them indeed must be offered. And as for this matter: one who tends the sacred fires (*agniparicara*) without being engaged [in other duties], having drawn out a small amount [of fire], draws it out again.
(26.5:276.12) "How is it in this case that the expiation succeeds or does not succeed?
(26.5:276.13) "It succeeds," say some; (26.5:276.13) but others indeed say, "It does not succeed."
"One of these two has a specified portion, while the other has an unspecified portion.
But indeed, both of these have unspecified portions;
thus, it is not established at all.
The taking of the *dhṛṣṭi* is the *tantra*.
One should take the *dhṛṣṭi* from the vicinity of the *gārhapatya*;
with it, one should place the potsherds for Vaiśvānara upon the *āhavanīya*.

(26.5:276.17) Having turned clockwise, having poured together the flour-preparations for the Maruts upon the Gārhapatya fire, having mixed them, touched them, and formed two lumps, he should carry one lump around the front of the Maruts' [fire] and smear the Vaiśvānara cake upon the Āhavanīya fire.
(26.5:277.3) Having turned clockwise, having caused the skin to form on the Maruts' [cake] over the Gārhapatya, he should cause the skin to form on this one.
Having carried fire around that one, he should carry fire around this one.
Having cooked that [other] one, he should cook this one.
Or rather, he may perform both actions in both places.
As for the placing of that cooked [offering], having released the rear joint of the southern enclosing-stick, or the front of the southern enclosing-stick, he should place it there.
(26.5:277.6) It is established from this point forward:
(26.5:277.7) "In this case, these two wipe themselves clean on each other—he who eats the food of two people who hate one another.
(26.5:277.8) By this, it is said that one [is wiped] by the other.
"Those against whom enemies might tremble, or whose realms might come together in conflict"—the neighboring kings are the *mṛdha*s;
their own districts are the *rāṣṭra*s; and the subjects are the *viśa*s.
"One who is dejected in mind should be like one who has committed a sin himself.
Thus, even when possessing strength, he should be dejected in mind as if he had committed a sin himself;
that is, he should be like one who has committed a sin himself within a family of virtuous appearance.

(26.5:277.12) “That which has been offered as it were, but is not actually given”— this refers to that which has been offered but not yet formally presented, and is thus being obstructed. Now, in this *adhvarakalpā* sacrifice, one should perform the first ritual sequence (*tantra*) ending with the *iḍā*.
With the third [offering], he should proceed with what remains.
Regarding the question, "How are the portions (bhakṣas) here?",
one may consume them at each respective place.
Alternatively, having made an offering by taking portions from all [the oblations] together, he should consume [the remainder] at the end.
"An ox is to be given by the Hotṛ"—
this [ox] must be given by the sacrificer himself from his own herd.
Having enclosed the altar, one should throw up half of it and not the other half;
or rather, the southern half of the altar or the western half. Having taken a portion for Indra, one should take a portion for the Viśve Devas, and then [another] portion for Indra on top of that.

These two portions for cutting off are indeed prescribed. "The garment worn previously by the teacher is the sacrificial fee"— either from the upper part or from the lower part of it, threads of copper-colored or blue hue are attached.
Or rather, this is said to be merely the cord for the supporting-wood.
Then, during this Sajñāneṣṭi, he should cause the invitatory verse to be recited only once and cause the call for the offering to be made only once;
for she has two invitatory and offering verses.
Now, it is indeed said:

"If he should not obtain [the consent], he should offer [the oblation] with the formula: 'I offer this portion to the Ādityas so that they may come to an agreement for such-and-such a person from such-and-such a clan. Having offered and ceased, and having performed the ritual up to the point of the entrustment (*paridāna*), he should then pour these rice grains onto a black antelope skin and place them on the northern part of the fire-hall."
(26.6:279.4) Then, once it has been understood, he should collect [the remains];
he should proceed with the ritual beginning from the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
From this point onward, the procedure is established.
Just as when [the gold] has been broken by the fingernails, even in the case of the hundred *kṛṣṇala* pieces;

or he should place the gold plate (*rukmam*) before the pouring of the rice grains, or even after it has been cooked— though it should indeed be cooked— he should set it down within the altar (*antarvedi*), having grasped it on both sides with two gold and silver plates,
and he should cause the portions for Agni and Soma to adhere together in that for Indra.
The portions of the balls that have been touched must be joined together before the final sprinkling;
"cutting off while causing all [the portions] to reach [the fire]"—this is said with reference to the offering that includes both the deities and the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
Furthermore, it should be of such a size as he thinks will last for as many years as he intends to live.
If he should be thirty years old, he should make it seventy measures;
if he should be forty years old, he should make it sixty measures.
This indeed is the rule for its increase.

Alternatively, in the case of the offerings to Varuṇa and the *saṃjñāneṣṭi*, one should cause the invitatory verses (*anuvāka*) to be recited only once, cause the call for the *śrauṣaṭ* to be made only once, and offer the oblations only once, since they share the same deity. Having returned, one should offer a pap (*caru*) dedicated to Apām Napāt.
Now, who indeed is this Apām Napāt?
One should say "of lightning" alone;
and regarding "black honey," this refers specifically to that which comes from bees.
"Without triple cords" means that it is said to have three folds;
furthermore, they also cite: "with three coverings," which is precisely what is meant by this.
(26.6:280.6) Just as in the case of the threefold oblation, such is the rule for the cutting of the sacrificial cake when it is doubtful.
"He created serpents"—
these, it is said, are the months.
"He created birds"— thus [it is stated].
These are indeed said to be the *chandāṃsi* (Vedic meters).
"He should indeed be so," they say, pointing to the ancient *gārhapatya* fire.

At the time for the animal sacrifice, having taken a firebrand from that [Ahavanīya], having carried it out by the southern door, having gone around the south of the Sadas, having carried it around the south of the Mārjālīya hearth, having brought it between the sacrificial post and the Āhavanīya, and having carried it out northward between the Cātvāla pit and the rubbish-heap (utkara), they should cook the animal with it.
Now, if the firebrand were to come from the Āhavanīya, they should carry it away together with the omentum (vapā).
"To which deity, indeed, do the Apāvya offerings belong? [he asked].
(26.7:281.1) There are two offerings dedicated to Prajāpati, and [one each] to Agni, Vāyu, and the Viśve Devas.
(26.7:281.2) Or rather, the Adhvaryu is the one who causes the sacrificer to prosper; he is the "prosperity-bringer" for the sacrificer.
(26.7:281.3) By this, what is meant is simply that the top [of the ladle] is warm.
Moreover, they also cite this: "This very one is called the Adhvaryu. [He recites:
"Protect me from the mantra of the mouth, from every curse.
For the mantra of the mouth is indeed a verbal assault.
Therefore, this is what is meant by "protect me from that";
thus, one must not enter upon the sacrificial site.
"Day and night" constitutes one [alternative].
(26.7:281.6) "Until the fires have become cold"—this is one [view].
(26.7:281.7) "Until rain falls upon him"—this is another.
(26.7:281.8) "Two oceans, vast and undecaying. Thus [it is said].
These two are said to be day and night.
"They turn around like feet within the belly"—
by this it is meant that the feet are within the belly.
(26.7:281.10) "Beholding one of them, they pass beyond; not beholding the other, they pass beyond by means of the bridge.
(26.7:281.10) "Beholding the day, they pass beyond the night; by means of sleep as the bridge, they pass beyond the other. (26.7:281.12) "One [wind] clothes the two firm, continuous [worlds]."

"The sun clothes himself in day and night"—this is what is meant by this. "Having clothed himself in black, he goes away; having left behind the old, he takes up the bright" (RV 1.115.5)—this means that, having clothed himself in the night, he goes away, and having left behind the old, he takes up the day. This is what is meant by this.
Regarding the phrase "of that which is infested with insects" (kīṭāvapannasya):
what indeed is this insect?
It is that very one who rolls the balls of rice.
Regarding the rule that "one follows the Vaiṣṇava verse during the constant drawing [of the cup]," this verse is to be recited specifically over the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya).
Now, therefore, we shall explain the *atigrāhya* cups.
These very *pṛṣṭhya-atigrāhya*s are five for Indra at the *vājapeya*:
those with the *paraḥsāman* chants and those with the *arvāksāman* chants, and the one for Sūrya at the *vaiṣuvata*.
The Vaiśvakarman and Āditya [offerings] are at the Gavāmayana;
the Prājāpatya at the Mahāvrata;
and the Bārhaspatya at the Bṛhaspatisava.
In the *vaimṛdha* and the *udbhid* sacrifices, [the verses] are "tviṣim," "ati ca," and "vṛṣā so 'ṃśuḥ pavate.
In the *aśvamedha*, there are two *mahiman* offerings;
one should offer the omentum of the horse around with the two *mahiman* verses according to the specific instruction.
How, indeed, does the consumption of the *paraḥsāman* [cups] take place?

"O God Soma, belonging to the troop of Rudra, who knowest the mind, of thee who art drunk at the midday pressing, whose metre is the *triṣṭubh*, drunk with waters and plants, drunk with plants and offspring, drunk by Prajāpati, full of sweetness, being invited, I, invited, consume thee.
This is the formula for the consumption of the *arvāksāman* cups when they have been turned back.
"Gold with eight protuberances is the sacrificial fee"—
by this it is meant that there are eight knobs.
If there should be two embryos, there should be twelve protuberances.
There should be one large vessel and two intermediate vessels.

Then, having gathered these bones together with clarified butter from the woman whose fetus has perished, he should pour them inside the enclosing sticks with the middle leaf of a Palāśa branch, saying: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ."
Regarding the statement, "If it becomes cloudless when [the animal] has been seized":
if it should become cloudless once the animal has been seized, one should indeed conclude the rite.

However, if it should become cloudless after the animal has been brought forward for dedication (*upākṛta*), they should dedicate another animal in that same place and proceed with this sacrifice when the subsequent day is free from clouds.

Now, these *jayas*, *abhyātānas*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛts* are seen to be prescribed for both the one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and the one who has not, except in the case of the sacrificial fire-enclosure (*vihāra*).
However, the teachers prescribe that they should be offered before the *sviṣṭakṛt* from the beginning of the undertaking.
"The eight Vasus... [and so forth].
"Who indeed are these Vasus?
"The earth, the intermediate space, the sky, fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the waters—these eight are the Vasus.
Indeed, everything that exists here is established upon them."
He who knows thus stands firm.
"The eleven Rudras"—
these are said to be the vital breaths.
"The twelve Ādityas"—
these are said to be the months themselves;
they are taken as five, they are taken nine by nine, and they are divided fivefold.
There are nine fresh shoots.
Now, this tenth mantra is seen as intended for the grasping of these very [shoots]:
"Having milked her, one should give her to a Brāhmaṇa whose food one would not eat. Thus it is said.
This [portion] is to be given only to one who has stood ready for alms.
Now, of what deity are the *atirikta-soma* draughts?
Whichever draught they may exceed, those [excesses] should belong to that very deity; this is one view.
(26.9:284.5) Now, furthermore:
It is indeed known from their Brāhmaṇa: "But why is the sacrifice dedicated to Indra completed [only] at the end? Because of this, they belong exclusively to Indra and Viṣṇu;
by means of that which has become cooled, they may desire the completion of the six-day period.
This is indeed the *Ṣaḍahabrāhmaṇa*.
Now, if a conjunction of days should occur such that even the nine middle days of the twelve-year cycle coincide, then at that very time, having cooled them down, they should pile them up.
And if this occurs on the *udayanīya* *atirātra*, it is exactly the same.
"‘The creatures indeed performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*), performing austerity while not offering oblations.
Regarding this, they ask: ‘Which is that sacrificial session?
[The answer is: ‘That which those who have not established the sacred fires perform as a futile exertion—that is the sacrificial session.’"
Regarding the statement, "The Āśvina cup is before the Āśvina [cup]," one might ask: "How far indeed does the Āśvina extend? It is two *yojanas*, or as far as a horse can travel in a day.
"The altar is twice as large [as the fire-altar].
One should take the diagonal measurement of the square *prakrama* used for the fire-altar;
that shall be the *prakrama*.
With that [measure], one should measure out the altar (vedi).
Alternatively, one should take a twenty-fourth part of twenty axle-lengths of a chariot, twenty-one foot-steps, and eight finger-breadths;
that shall be the *prakrama*.
With that [measure] he measures out the altar.
"Agni becomes threefold in praise," thus there are three [altars] of sevenfold [construction].
It is of twenty-one kinds.
Now, regarding the instruction that "one should select these two ponds in the middle of the sacrificial ground," for what purpose indeed do these two ponds exist?
Aśvaplāvana is the southern *udavabhṛtha* vessel, and the other is the northern.
There are two slaves: the son of the mother born after [the father], and the son of the mother born after [the wife].
He who is the son of his father’s junior wife he leads first; then he who is the son of his mother’s junior wife follows behind.
(26.10:285.14) "Having wrapped his left knee with a worn-out garment"—this refers to the *upadhāna* rope. (26.10:285.15) For it is said:
"There are indeed a hundred princes worthy of a couch."
These are said to be merely deputies; as for the verse "A hundred fierce kings," these are indeed *rājanya*s who are not to be consecrated.
(26.10:286.2) Now, regarding the injunction: "In the morning, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Savitṛ.
(26.10:286.3) This is the first offering to Savitṛ; the second occurs in the section concerning the Vaiśvadeva.
In the afternoon is the third [offering]. One should understand that this is the ritual procedure for a one-day sacrifice (*aikāhika*) here.

And from the north of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), one should conclude the Cāturmāsya rites; in this same manner for the animal sacrifice to Vāyu, and likewise for the hornless goat (*tūpara*).
"One should sacrifice with this iṣṭi for seven days. Regarding this, [the question is] "How are the portions [to be consumed] here? [The answer is:
one may consume them at each respective point, or rather, one should [consume them] already at the beginning of these seven days.

(26.10:286.8) Regarding the sacrificial post, the traditional injunction states: "He erects the one made of *rājjudāla* wood at the fire-altar. (26.10:286.9) By this, it is actually meant that it is made of *śleṣmātaka* wood.
Furthermore, they cite: "He erects the *rājjudāla* post at the fire-altar for the removal of the sin of killing an embryo."
"Two [spoons] made of *pautudrava* wood are on both sides for the attainment of a holy fragrance"—
thus he gives the third of the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇās*).
Indeed, the third of the items belonging to the fire-altar is given together with the *kāmapra*, the third at the *atirātra* sacrifice, and the third [in general].
This is a Catuṣṭoma;
this Catuṣṭoma consists of four Uttarāyas.
(26.11:287.1) “Svāhā to one! Svāhā to two!”—thus [it is said]. How, indeed, should one offer these sections? They should be offered in their natural sequence, one after the other.
Having taken twenty-four cords, they approach the sacrificial posts—four each for the other assistants. [The question arises: "How should one bind the animals to these?
The horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal—these three share a common cord.
Three on the forehead-marked [animals], five on the animals bound around the frame;
eight on those [dedicated] with the formula, "To Agni Anīkavant, a red-spotted ox."
"To Soma, the self-ruling one, two oxen that draw a cart"—in these [formulas], there are seven.
Now, among these, three by three have identical cords;
of these, the fourth belongs to the principal [animal] alone.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the carrying of fire around [the animals]. Of these animals that have been carried around with fire, nineteen are released, and forty-one remain.
There are forty-two cords for them; here, two are joined together on the horse.
(26.11:287.11) Then, for the other animals, they are provided individually: "For Indra and Agni, the givers of vigor, two camels.
These two are indeed said to be the yoke-animals (*prāsaṅgya*).
Then, regarding this [animal], one mixes the flour of the *śalmali* tree with quick-cooking flour.
These are the flour of those very *āśuka* rice grains mixed with the sap of the *śalmali* tree.
The Pratiprasthātṛs portion them out separately.
For these, the Maitrāvaruṇas alone should recite the invitatory verses.
There are exactly these four offerings:
"Svāhā to Iluvarda! Svāhā to Balivarda!
By this, the sun and the moon are indeed meant.
Moreover, they also cite: "The *saṃvatsara* is indeed the *iluvarda*, the *parivatsara* is the *balivarda*.
Upon its head he offers with: "To Jumbaka, svāhā!
Now, to which deity does this oblation belong?
One should say "belonging to Varuṇa" (*vāruṇī*);
[one should say] "the *kikidīvi* bird, the *vidīgaya*. Because it cries "vididihī vikīdīha," it becomes the *kikidīvi*.
The spotted antelope, the locust, and the *vidīgayas*.
Then he dedicates these animals: one for Agni, one for Indra and Agni, and one for the Aśvins;
these goats are of the same origin as Yama.
The performance of these has been explained in the same manner as that of the eleven sacrificial animals.
Now, regarding the seasonal animals (*ṛtupaśu*): what are their deities?
One view is that the seasons themselves are their deities.

(26.11:288.13) Now, furthermore: the first [sets] are dedicated to Agni; the second to Indra; the third to the Viśvedevas; the fourth to Mitra and Varuṇa; the fifth to Bṛhaspati; the sixth to Savitṛ; and those for Prajāpati are dedicated to the Year with the verse beginning "saṃvatsarāya nivakṣasaḥ."
Now, this twelve-day sacrifice is of two kinds: either an *ahīna* or a *sattra*.
If indeed only one person undergoes initiation, it is an *ahīna*;
but if many do so, it is a *sattra*.
Whether it be an *ahīna* or a *sattra*, in both cases it has *atirātra*s on both sides.
For *ahīna*s have *atirātra*s on one side only, whereas *sattra*s have *atirātra*s on both sides.

An *ahīna* has *atirātra*s on both sides only by specific injunction; but a *sattra* may lack *atirātra*s on both sides by specific injunction, as for example the *agniṣṭomāyana*, the *sārasvatam ayana*, and the *viśvasṛjām ayana*.
(26.12:289.7) How indeed should the mixing of these [fires] be performed?
(26.12:289.8) First they should mix the fires for the Sāvitra offerings; having offered the Sāvitra oblations and having transferred the fires, they should offer the Agnihotra oblations.

Alternatively, they may combine [the fires] for the animal sacrifice to Vāyu. Having sacrificed with the offering to Vāyu and having descended from the sacred fires, they should then perform the Agnihotra oblations.
But if they were to combine them for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* initiation offering, those fires would remain combined until the *vyudavasānīyā* concluding rite.
Having made a division, the neighboring priests should perform the tail-portions of the sacrifice.
But how indeed should those who have been consecrated together perform the Viṣṇu-strides?
They should either perform them while encircled by the great cords.
Alternatively, having fastened the cords, there should be a stepping forward; then he says, "Step forward," and again, "Step forward. Such a ritual procedure would be excessively burdensome.
As for this rule in the Sūtra: "On the sixth day, having approached, they pile up the Uttaravedi; or else on the eleventh day."
This applies only to the *anagni-caya* (the rite without the piling of the fire-altar), not to the *sāgni-caya*.
How, indeed, does the continuity (*saṃtati*) of these [rites] come about?

The Adhvaryu maintains the continuity by the taking up of the *vasatīvarī* waters and by the preparation of the fuel and sacrificial grass; the Brahman by the milks and the distribution of the portions; the Hotṛ by the restraint of speech and the subsequent call (*atipraiṣa*); the Udgātṛ by the repetition; and the Sacrificer by the re-undertaking of the sacrifice through the *subrahmaṇyā* formula.
While proceeding with this, they take up the clarified butter from the *dhruvā* vessel. Then they should collect these sacrificial grasses for the pressings;
having risen during the deep of night, they should cause the fires to blaze while taking up the clarified butter in the *āgnīdhra*.
(26.13:290.11) How, indeed, does the commencement of the day’s *prātaranuvāka* take place?

(26.13:290.12) Having concluded that day’s ritual either with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings or with the *hṛdayaśūla*, having bound up King Soma, having taken up the *vasatīvarī* waters at the proper time, and having ensured the continuity of the *ahīna* sacrifice, they wash the pressing-stones and the *vāyavya* cups, place the *daśāpavitra* strainer into the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, run to the *āgnīdhra* shed, and proceed with the fuel-bearers.
Having brought back the fuel-sticks, they set them down near the *āhavanīya* fire.

When the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, and the fuel-sticks for lying down (*saṃveśanīyāḥ samidhaḥ*) have been placed on the fire, he should bind together the sacrificial grass and faggot (*idhmābarhis*), set aside the milks, run to the *āgnīdhra* shed, prepare the forms for lying down in the *āgnīdhra*, and proceed with the morning ritual according to the established procedure of the deep night. From this point onward, it is accomplished as prescribed.
"The *atigrāhya* cups are indeed the support of the sacrifice, as are the *pṛṣṭha* chants.

The threefold and the twenty-onefold [stomas] are the wheels; the cup for Agni is the support. The fifteenfold and the twenty-sevenfold [stomas] are the wheels; the cup for Indra is the support. The seventeenfold and the thirty-threefold [stomas] are the wheels; the cup for Sūrya is the support.

Regarding this point, they teach Baudhāyana’s ritual manual: "The fire produced by friction is accompanied by mantras. In this case, only the mantras belonging to the office of the Adhvaryu are repeated here, not those for the churning of the fire.
On this day, the Ṛtu-offering is performed by oneself; on this day, one does not perform the Ṛtu-offering for another.

(26.14:291.13) Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, the Adhvaryu hands the cup to another, returns by the same way he came, sits down behind the two *havirdhāna* carts, utters the *ṛtusaṃpraiṣa*, stands up, offers the oblation, pours out the remnants, turns to the right, and—sitting facing east where he previously offered—should consume the portion belonging to the Hotṛ; sitting facing west, he should consume the portion belonging to the Adhvaryu.
(26.14:291.16) The Hotṛ recites the *pārucchepī* verses; the Maitrāvaruṇa arranges the *vālakhilyā* hymns; the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin recites the *vṛṣākapi*; and the Acchāvāka recites the *evayāmarut*.
"What, then, is the duty of the *adhvaryu*? "He should simply respond," one should say.

Those *anuṣṭubh* verses which the *adhvaryu* extracts and brings forward—those four [verses] are actually *gāyatrīs*, and those three are *anuṣṭubhs*. With only a single foot of this *gāyatrī* verse, "O King Soma, come hither; descend," he should cause the King [Soma] to descend.

How indeed does the tenth day, by way of its ritual application (*bhakti*), become entirely characterized by the *caturviṃśa* stoma and yet remain a *triṣṭoma*, except for the *tūṣṇīṃstoma*? The *bahiṣpavamāna* is twenty-fourfold, the *brahmasāman* is fifteenfold, and the *agniṣṭomasāman* is thirty-threefold; thus, nine of those [stomas] do not come into play.
These amount to twenty-four.

Thus, by way of ritual application (*bhakti*), even this tenth day becomes entirely characterized by the twenty-four-fold stoma (*sarvacaturviṃśa*) and the *triṣṭoma*, except for the silent stoma (*tūṣṇīṃstoma*).
[The verses are: "Approaching the mother with the calf," and "Sustaining, the supporter, sucking."
"To which deity, indeed, does this oblation belong?
"One should say: 'To Prajāpati.'"

(26.15:293.4) Now, we shall arrange this twelve-day rite by means of the foremost cups (*grahāgra*) alone. Then, nine days of it proceed as an arrangement, namely those other than the introductory day (*prāyaṇīya*), the concluding day (*udayanīya*), and the tenth day.
Next are the *Chandomas*.
That consists of exactly six [pressings].
For the first three-night period is its own proper place.
At the morning pressing of the Gāyatrī [chant] during the first three-night period, one should first perform the silent pressing eight times.
The second [draught] eleven times;
the third twelve times.
One should draw the draught for Mahendra with this Triṣṭubh verse: "Great is Indra, manly, the protector of the people."
With the verse, "O Savitṛ, with thy undeceivable protections," he should prepare the cake on eight potsherds for Savitṛ at the morning pressing;
[he should prepare] cakes on eleven potsherds for the midday pressing.
One should consume the twelve-potsherd cakes of the third pressing with the *vasumadgaṇa* formula and the *gāyatrī* metre;
the morning-pressing cakes with the *rudravadgaṇa* formula and the *triṣṭubh* metre.
"With the *ādityavat* group, with the *jagatī* metre, for the [soma-pressings] belonging to the third extraction.
Now, at the morning extraction of the second three-night period, one should first perform the silent pressing (*upāṃśu-abhiṣava*) twelve times with the *jagatī* metre;
the second time, eight times.
The third [libation] eleven times.
One should take the Māhendra cup with this Gāyatrī verse: "Great is Indra, who by his might...
One should take the Sāvitra cup with this Triṣṭubh verse: "O Savitṛ, may that which is lovely today..."
One should prepare twelve-potsherd cakes for the morning pressing,
eight-potsherd cakes for the midday pressing,
and eleven-potsherd cakes for the third pressing.

One should consume the portions of the morning pressing with the *ādityavadgaṇa* and the *jagatī* metre; those of the midday pressing with the *vasumadgaṇa* and the *gāyatrī* metre; and those of the third pressing with the *rudravadgaṇa* and the *triṣṭubh* metre.
Now, at the morning pressing of the third three-night rite, one should perform the first silent pressing eleven times;
the second twelve times; and the third eight times.
One should repeat this *gāyatrī* verse, "Great is Indra who [rules] by might," three times without the *upayāma* formula.
It becomes a *jagatī*;
with that [verse], one should draw the *māhendra* cup.
With this *gāyatrī* verse, "The golden-handed for aid," one draws the *sāvitra* cup.
One should prepare cakes on eleven potsherds for the morning pressing,
cakes on twelve potsherds for the midday pressing,
and cakes on eight potsherds for the third pressing.
One should consume the portions of the morning pressing with the Rudravat-gaṇa and the Triṣṭubh metre;
those of the midday pressing with the Ādityavat-gaṇa and the Jagatī metre; and those of the third pressing with the Vasumat-gaṇa and the Gāyatrī metre.

(26.16:295.1) Now, some say that this Vaiṣuvata day should be obtained as the middle of the series of months: seventeen days of initiation (*dīkṣā*), twelve days of preparatory rites (*upasad*), and the Vaiṣuvata as the thirtieth.

(26.16:295.2) But how indeed do the *stomas* come to be for the Go and Āyu sacrifices? (26.16:295.3) For the Go sacrifice, the *bahiṣpavamāna* is fifteenfold, the *ājya* chants are ninefold, the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina savana*) is entirely seventeenfold, and the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) with its *ukthya* stotras is entirely twenty-onefold.

(26.16:295.5) Now, for Ayus, the *bahiṣpavamāna* is threefold (*trivṛt*), the *ājya* stotras are fifteenfold (*pañcadaśa*), the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina savana*) is entirely seventeenfold (*saptadaśa*), and the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) is entirely twenty-onefold (*ekaviṃśa*), together with the *ukthya*.
(26.16:295.7) Now, these two, the Viśvajit and the Abhijit, are *agniṣṭoma*s included in the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
(26.16:295.8) What indeed are the *stomas* of these two?
Now, indeed, the Abhijit has three risings and four turnings;
then the Viśvajit has four risings and three turnings.
How, then, does it come to have the Ekaviṃśati as its womb?
Having reached the Abhijit, they should perform the Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha;
then three Paraḥsāman days; then the Vaiṣuvata day; then three Pratyaksāman days; then the reversed Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha; and then the Viśvajit.
How, indeed, should one understand the Go and Āyus days as being separated?
"One should approach the *gavyūti* before the *Abhijit*; thus one's life remains in its own place.
"How many *agniṣṭoma*s are there indeed in the *Gavāmayana*?

"The *Jyotis-agniṣṭoma*, the *Trivṛt-agniṣṭoma*, the *Viśvajit-agniṣṭoma*, and the two *Abhijit-agniṣṭoma*s; the *Vaiṣuvata* as the tenth day, and the *Mahāvrata*—thus, they say, this *Gavāmayana* consists of seven [sacrifices] with well-known *stoma*s."
On its northern wing, there is a reversal of everything other than the Go-āyuṣ and the ten-night period; therein one should draw the Tryanīka cups in their unreversed order.
Now, these thirty-two sets of eleven [cattle] are for the Gavām Ayana.
Of these, sixteen are completed in the first fortnight; seventeen remain for the set of eleven [cattle] at the Vaiṣuvata day, where the Savanīya animal sacrifice belongs to Bṛhaspati.
For that [set], nine days remain over without cattle.
"What indeed are these days?

[he asked]. "The latter three days of the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, the three *chandomas*, the tenth day, the *mahāvrata*, and the *udayanīya atirātra*—these, together with the *abhiplavas* and the *akṣīyantis*, constitute the *Aṅgirasām Ayana*."
In this place, he places the *abhiplava* days instead of the *pṛṣṭhya* days;
thus they diminish the *pṛṣṭhyas*, and that is called the "Course of the Ādityas.
In this place, he places the *pṛṣṭhya* days instead of the *abhiplava* days.

"The Agniṣṭomas also diminish; that is the course of Prajāpati. Here, in place of both the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava [six-day periods], he establishes only Agniṣṭomas, [using] *āghāṭīs*, *piñcholās*, and *karkarīkās*.
The *āghāṭyas* are indeed *koloṣṭhas*;
the *piñcholās* are indeed *vīṇākāṇabhrasas*; and the *vīṇās* are indeed *karkarīkāḥ*.
"At that very moment he cuts with the knife"—
this means that he should indeed cut it.
Now, it is indeed said:
"The exponents of sacred knowledge say, 'He truly should sacrifice who, having sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma, then sacrifices with the Sarvastoma.
Thus, there are four *ājya* stotras consisting of fifteen verses each.
Those two are the two groups of thirty.
Of those two, he offers three oblations in the other group of thirty;
those two are the two [groups] of twenty-nine and thirty-three.

"On the first day the Gāyatra is the Sāman, on the next the Triṣṭubh"—thus one should prepare these [verses] for the Hotṛ’s Ājya-stotra; in the same way on the subsequent day, [they belong] to the Hotṛ’s Ājya alone.
Now, this thousandth [cow], a piebald, has been prepared and made ready;
by this it is meant that she has been "fully served" (saṃsevita).
"At what time, indeed, should one give a six-year-old cow that has calved for the first time and is a slayer of enemies?
Having won a battle, a member of the royal caste should give her.
And how, indeed, should one sacrifice with the Garga-trirātra, as it is expanded at the beginnings of the seasons?"

In the fortnight of Āṣāḍha or Śrāvaṇa, he should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma. Having performed that day ending either with the Patnīsaṃyājas or with the Hṛdayaśūla, having bound the King Soma, and having taken up the Vasatīvarī waters at the proper time, he ensures the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice. Having washed the pressing-stones and the Vāyavya cup, and having placed the *daśāpavitra* strainer into the Droṇakalaśa, they run to the Āgnīdhra shed; carrying fuel-sticks, they proceed. Having brought the fuel-sticks, they place them near the Āhavanīya fire.

When the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around and the *saubrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, he should place the *saṃveśanīyā* fuel-sticks on the fire, bind together the sacrificial grass (*idhma*) and the *barhis*, and having set aside the milk products, they observe the fast.
Then, on the following day, he should perform the *savanīyeṣṭi*;
thereafter, he carries away the *stambayajus*.
In this very manner, carrying the *vasatīvarī* waters around day after day, he performs the *savaneṣṭi* sacrifices for four months.
He does not offer the *agnihotra*, nor does he sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

Then, when the four months have elapsed and the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, once the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, they add the daily *saṃveśanīyā* fuel-sticks, bind the sacrificial grass (*idhma*) and the altar-grass (*barhis*), set aside the milk offerings, and observe the fast.
Then, when the next day has dawned, he performs the Ukthya sacrifice.

Having performed that day’s rites either ending with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings or ending with the heart-spit ceremony, having bound the King Soma, and having taken up the Vasatīvarī waters at the proper time, he ensures the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice. Having washed the pressing-stones and the Vāyavya cups, and having placed the fringe-cloth (*daśāpavitra*) into the Droṇakalaśa, he hastens to the Āgnīdhra shed; they go forth carrying the fuel-sticks. Having brought the fuel-sticks, they place them near the Āhavanīya fire.

When the *vastīvarī* waters have been carried around, the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, and the *saṃveśanīyā* fuel-sticks have been added to the fire, he binds together the sacrificial grass (*idhma*) and the *barhis*, and having set aside the milk products, they observe the fast.
Then, on the following day, he performs the *savanīya* sacrifice.
In that rite, he does not perform the *stambayajus* in the same manner as before.
In this very manner, performing the *vasatīvarī* water-carrying rite day after day, he performs the *savanesti* sacrifice for the remaining four months.
During this time, he neither offers the *agnihotra* nor sacrifices with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

Then, when the four months have elapsed and the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, once the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, they add the daily *saṃveśanīyā* fuel-sticks, bind the sacrificial grass (*idhma* and *barhis*), separate the milk products, and observe the fast.
Then, on the following day, he performs the Atirātra sacrifice together with the tail of the sacrifice.
Then, having turned this thousandth cow toward the east or the north, he should not pass between her and the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) nor between her and himself.
"What indeed are the sacrificial fees for the Ahīna sacrifices?
"Each individual day of the multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*) should have a thousand as its fee; this is one view.
Each single day should have a thousand as its fee; this is another."
"It should have a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of twelve hundred" is one [view];
"it should have a sacrificial fee according to one's faith" is another, based on the specific injunction.
In this *Atirātra* sacrifice, he gives a thousand [cows] as prescribed.
The *ahīna* sacrifices begin with the two-night rite and extend up to the eleven-night rite.
Now, these *sattra* sessions are encompassed by the *ahīna*s, such as this eleven-night rite which contains the year within it.
For the Bharata-twelve-day rite is of both kinds.
There are twelve Agniṣṭomas with the Rathantara-sāman; that indeed is the Bharata-dvādaśāha.
Now, regarding those sacrifices with rising stomas: the first day should have the Trivṛt-stoma, the second the Pañcadaśa, the third the Saptadaśa, and the fourth the Ekaviṃśa—this is one way.

(26.20:300.13) Now, another [form]: the morning pressing of the first day is the *trivṛt*, the midday pressing is the *pañcadaśa*, and the third pressing is the *saptadaśa*. (26.20:300.14) Then, for the second day: the morning pressing is the *pañcadaśa*, the midday pressing is the *saptadaśa*, and the third pressing is the *ekaviṃśa*. (26.20:301.2) Then, for the third day: the morning pressing is the *saptadaśa*, the midday pressing is the *ekaviṃśa*, and the third pressing is the *triṇava*.
Now, for the fourth day, the morning pressing consists of the twenty-onefold stoma, the midday pressing the twenty-sevenfold stoma, and the third pressing the thirty-threefold stoma.

Now, these *aupasada* sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), beginning with the taking up of the winnowing basket and ending with the *āpyā* libations, he should offer them all together with a single oblation from the *sruva*-ladle according to the ritual procedure of Aupamanyava; likewise for the single-pot-sherd offerings to Agni.
[The priests] proceed eastward along the Sarasvatī river.
One should throw a *śamyā* from the vicinity of the *āhavanīya* fire; where it falls, that shall be the location of the *gārhapatya*. From there, the *āhavanīya* is to the east.

Now, if they should encounter water that is not yet crossed, they should perform a *caru* offering to Aponaptr at the third pressing as a subsequent oblation (*anunirvāpya*) to the offerings of the third pressing.
(26.21:301.12) Then, on the following day, having indeed completed [the rite], he should throw the *śamyā* [sacrificial pin].
"They are three-day periods; they are five-day periods," [it is said].
These are indeed the omissions (*apaccheda*) of the *abhiplava* [six-day] periods.
"On the eighth day, the Vājapeya.
In that regard, one should perform whatever ritual actions pertaining to the Vājapeya are encompassed by the *sutyā* day. Now, this *saṃsadāmayaṇa* is performed without the *acchandomas*.
Indeed, its metrical portions are known to be the twenty-fourfold, the forty-fourfold, and the eight-twenty-fourfold.
Now, this Atirātra sacrifice is of two kinds: either an Ahīna or a one-day (Ekāha) rite.
However, it indeed possesses the form of an Ahīna alone;
for it has twelve Upasad days and extends over more than a single day.
(26.22:302.6) Now, this is the form of the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*):
he takes the *vasatīvarī* waters once; he dedicates the animals once;
there is a single performance of the ritual act.

"When the sun has reached the meridian, he begins the *ṣoḍaśin* stoma with gold"—this means that it is said [to be performed] when the sun has half-set. If the sun should set before it has been commenced, one should offer three spoonfuls of oblations on the *gārhapatya* fire, saying: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ."
(26.22:302.10) Now, regarding one for whom there might be a surplus in the Ukthya, it is said: "He should perform an Atirātra.
(26.22:302.11) For him, the Dīkṣā and Upasad rites have already passed, the Kratukaraṇa has passed, and the drawing of the Ṣoḍaśin cup has passed.
(26.22:302.12) Therefore, having prepared the Ṣoḍaśin vessel at that very moment, he should draw [the juice] with three Ṛg-verses.
(26.22:302.13) Now, one should perform [the rites] prior to the night-rounds by means of this [offering].

In that case, the summons is exactly as follows: "O Pratiprasthātṛ, guard the third portion of the Āgrayaṇa vessel, the third portions of the rectum, the tail-ends, and the speckled butter! O Agnīdh, let the two-potsherd offering for the Aśvins be cooked even during the latter part of the night!
(26.22:303.2) At what time, indeed, is the two-potsherd offering for the Aśvins to be poured out?
Either with the cakes belonging to the third pressing, or even before the final round of the night, [he offers].

"The *trivṛt* is indeed the lowest of the *stomas*, the *trivṛt* is the highest"—this is the *Atirātra-brāhmaṇa*. Now, this *sautrāmaṇī* liquor is either made from the foot-ferment (*pādakiṇva*) or it is fivefold (*pañcikā*).
"Grass-shoots and sprouts"—the grass-shoots are of barley, and the sprouts are of rice; but the *māṣa* beans are *nagnahu*.
Now, this *kārotara* [filter] may be made of wood, or of split bamboo, or of clay; however, it must indeed be covered with a skin.
"This is pressed and unpressed"—
for him there is indeed what has been pressed in the other world, and what has been unpressed in this world.
Now, in this Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice, one should perform the Upāṃśu offering.

Now, in this set of eleven sacrificial posts (*ekādaśinī*), the ritual procedure for the oblation to the post (*yūpāhuti*) is that which is offered in the fire. Then, there is the portable post made from the fresh-cut wood (*avraścanaja*); that is the rite involving the touching (*saṃsparśaka*).

One should strike the corner-post (*agniṣṭhā*) of the first [post] once, twice that of the second, and thrice that of the third; in the same manner for the others, according to the sequence for the purpose of marking the cuts.
Now follows the measurement of the altar (*vedi*):
one should take a twenty-fourth part of ten chariot-axles, eleven foot-steps, and eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
That shall be the step;
with it he should measure out the altar.
Now, these two *upasthāvān* [corner-posts] should be separated by a distance of exactly four finger-breadths.

(26.23:304.7) "Then the others should be at the same distance as the intervals between the chariot axles. (26.23:304.8) Now, indeed, it is said: "<One should measure [the post] level with the top for one who desires the world of the ancestors>."
"As long as the post standing nearest the fire is, so long are the others.
"For one desiring power, [the others] should be equal to the *caṣāla* [top-ring]. Thus, as long as the girth-rope of the post nearest the fire is, so long are the others.
"All should be equal for one desiring a firm foundation. Thus, for one desiring a firm foundation, he makes them all equal.

(26.23:304.12) “Those three which are in the middle, he should make them equal for one who desires cattle. Thus, he makes those three equal for one who desires cattle. (26.23:304.13) “He should interlace the others,” it is said; thus he interlaces the eight sacrificial posts (yūpa), placing the southern one above the northern one.
Now, indeed, there is this [text]:

"If one should desire of someone, 'May he be short-lived,' one should erect for him a *gartamit* [post] such that the northern one is the tallest and the southern one is shorter. Thus, here he erects the northern one as the tallest and the southern one as the shorter.
"This indeed is the *gartamit*; for whomsoever one erects it in this manner, he quickly perishes," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"One should erect the southern one as the tallest for one who desires heaven, and the northern one as the shorter."
One should erect each successive sacrificial post (*yūpa*) so that it is shorter than the preceding one by the measure of a thumb-joint (*aṅguṣṭhaparvan*).
Alternatively, one may dig the sacrificial post-pits (*yūpāvaṭa*) to these very measures.
Or else, they simply place the reserve post (*upaśaya*) [in its place].
One should perform these actions with those same measures.
How indeed should one’s movement be while tracing around the pits for the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), erecting the posts, and dedicating the animals?

Having passed between the post standing nearest the fire (*agniṣṭha*) and the one standing near the *upasthāvana* pit, and having walked around behind the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), one should again pass between the *agniṣṭha* and the *upasthāvāna* post and then trace around, erect, or dedicate each one individually.
Alternatively, whichever [post] one should trace around, erect, or dedicate, one should not pass between it and the next; the southern [post] by the south, and the northern [post] by the north.
Or rather, having gone around all the posts from the front, one should trace around, erect, or dedicate each one individually;
by that method, they become interconnected in the east.
