In this manner, having commenced with the five animals on the southern side among these animals arranged in an interlocking pattern, they should cause them to stand.
They should lead the animal dedicated to Varuṇa across first, and then the others in successive order.
Having gone out toward the north between the Cātvāla pit and the Utkara mound, they should either immolate the victims after setting them down, or else after arranging them in a circle.
Having extracted their omenta, they should carry them out in such a way that they do not separate the sacrificial enclosure from themselves by means of the omenta.

Now, this [victim] for Pātnīvata should be shorter than the northern part of the sacrificial post by the measure of a thumb-joint; or rather, as prescribed in the Brāhmaṇa, it should be below the navel, without a top-ring, and not spread with grass.
Now, this Sarpāṇām Ayana is modified in its Stomas.
Now, one might ask: "How can this sacrificial session of the creators of the universe (viśvasṛjām ayana) be performed by people of the present day? [The answer is:
there are a hundred initiation days (dīkṣā), a hundred attendant days (upasad), and a thousand days of Soma-pressing (prasuta).
(26.25:306.10) Now, regarding this Kuṇḍapāyināmayana, some say it is preceded by the Agnihotra; others enter upon it as preceded by the Soma-sacrifice.

Having performed that day ending either with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings or with the heart-spikes (hṛdayaśūla), and having bound up the King Soma, they take up the Vasatīvarī waters at the proper time, ensure the continuity of the Ahīna sacrifice, wash the pressing-stones and the Vāyavya cups, place the fringe-filters (daśāpavitra) together in the Droṇakalaśa, run to the Āgnīdhra shed, and proceed carrying the fuel-sticks.
Having brought the fuel-sticks, they place them near the Āhavanīya fire.

When the Vasatīvarī waters have been carried around, when the Subrahmaṇyā has been invoked, and after he has added the "bedding" fuel-sticks, he binds together the sacrificial grass and faggot; then, setting aside the milk products, they fast.
Then, on the following day, he performs the sacrifice with the New Moon oblation.
In that case, they do not perform the *stambayajus* rite.
Carrying the *vasatīvarī* waters around in this very manner day after day for twenty-eight days, they sacrifice with the new-moon oblation;
they do not offer the *agnihotra* oblations, nor do they perform the full-moon sacrifice.
When he distributes the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths at the third pressing, he makes the *mārjālīya* hearth perpetual.
When the oblations have been set down, having carried fire around the *karambha* vessels over the *gārhapatya*, he proceeds with them at the *mārjālīya*.
Having cooked the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* on the *gārhapatya* itself, he proceeds with it at the *mārjālīya* itself.
He chooses the *pravara* ancestors for each of them individually.
For each one of them there are three *piṇḍas*; these amount to fifteen.

In the Mahāpitṛyajña, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is already spread; he does not trace the altar, he does not carry away the *stambayajus* clod, nor does he take portions of clarified butter (*ājya*). When he distributes the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths at the third pressing, he makes the *mārjālīya* hearth perpetual.
Once the oblations have been set down, having cooked the Mahāpitṛyajña oblations on the *gārhapatya* fire, he should proceed with them at the *mārjālīya*.
One should perform the offering to the Maruts at the Āhavanīya fire.

The final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) should follow immediately. The sacrificial altar (vedi) is one-third [of the size]; for indeed, it is one-third of the strides (prakrama), while the ninth part belongs to the ground.
Then, having performed the five-oblation sacrifice, one should sacrifice with each oblation in turn, repeating the cycle day by day.
If, however, only one or two oblations should remain when the year is completed, how should one act in that case?
One should draw back [the ritual] and perform the five-oblation sacrifice for this [remaining] fortnight.
Now, on the final day of the year there should be five oblations;
"one should pile the fire-altar during the first twelve-day period.

Thus, while piling the fire-altar during the first twelve-day period, one should proceed for four days with the first *upasad* rite, for four days with the middle one, and for eight days less than a year with the last one.
(26.26:308.12) Then, regarding the other four-day periods, he should take up four months at a time by means of one [Upasad] day for each;
he should proceed for four days with the first Upasad, for four days with the middle one, and for four days with the last one.
Or rather, he may proceed for exactly four months at a time with each individual Upasad.
"One should pile the fire-altar during the final twelve-day rite.
Piling the fire-altar during the final twelve-day rite, he should proceed for eight deficient months with the first *upasad*, four days with the middle one, and four days with the last one.
Then, for the other deficient months, he should take up four deficient months at a time, each consisting of four days.
One should proceed for four days with the first *upasad*, four days with the middle one, and four days with the last;
or alternatively, one may proceed for exactly four months with each individual *upasad*.
Now, it is said: "One goes through a month laying down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks.
Having gone through a month laying down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks, on the thirtieth day one should cover the entire covering.
Or alternatively, having left space for thirty [bricks], one goes through a month laying down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks.

"How should one proceed for this month? [The answer is: First, the *iṣṭi*; then, in the forenoon, the *pravargya* and the *upasad*s; then the bricks; then, in the afternoon, the *pravargya* and the *upasad*s; [and] monthly, the *vasordhārā*. "For a month they proceed with the *purīṣa*."
"How should one pass this month?
[The answer is: First there is the *iṣṭi*; then, in the forenoon, the *pravargya* and the two *upasad*s; then the *purīṣa*; then, in the afternoon, the *pravargya* and the two *upasad*s.
Thus, for four months, he proceeds with the *upasad*s.
"What one performs there in a month, one performs here in ten nights;
'he presses for four months'—
which, indeed, are these months?"

Regarding the first and last months of the Gavāmayana, as well as those two months on either side of the Viṣuvat together with the Viṣuvat itself, [the rule says]: "One should place a lump of clay into the Vasatīvarī waters.
For what purpose, then, is this lump of clay used?
"This [rite] serves the purpose of continuity," he says.
When the jar has been broken, one should place this lump of clay into another jar and bring water.

Having performed that day's rites ending either with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings or the *hṛdayaśūla*, having bound up the King Soma and at the proper time taken up the *vasatīvarī* waters, having ensured the continuity of the *ahīna* sacrifice, having washed the pressing stones and the *vāyavya* cups, and having placed the *daśāpavitra* strainer together in the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, they run to the *āgnīdhra* shed bringing fuel-sticks.
Having brought the fuel-sticks, they place them near the Āhavanīya fire.

When the Vasatīvarī waters have been carried around, the Subrahmaṇyā has been invoked, and the fuel-sticks for the lying-down ceremony have been added, they bind together the sacrificial grass and fuel, and having set aside the milk products, they observe the fast.
Then, on the following day, they perform the sacrifice with the Savana-istis.
In that case, one does not perform the *stambayajus* offering.
Carrying the *vasatīvarī* waters around in this very manner day after day for a year, they sacrifice with the *savanesti*.
They do not offer the *agnihotra* oblations, nor do they sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* rites.

Then, when the year has elapsed, when the *vasatīvarī* waters have been carried around, and when the *subrahmaṇyā* has been invoked, they should daily place the kindling woods for retiring upon the fire, bind together the sacrificial fuel and the *barhis* grass, set aside the milks, and observe the fast. Then, on the following day, having performed the *abhijit* sacrifice, they rise from the session.
Now, it is indeed said: "One who desires cattle should pile the Chandaściti.
One should perform the rites beginning with the taking up of the wooden shovel (abhri) up to the Vāyavya [offering] with the appropriate mantras.
He should perform the sacrifice with the animal dedicated to Vāyu directly, and the initiation rite (*dīkṣaṇīyā*) directly.
He should recite the formulas beginning from the heating of the fire-pan (*ukhā*) up to the *vātsapra* and *viṣṇukrama* steps.
Having stepped with the *vātsapra* and *viṣṇukrama* steps directly, he should then recite the remaining formulas.
He should dwell near a fire;
he should display forms;
he should go to a barren wasteland.
There he should recite the Nairṛta mantras;
he should worship the Gārhapatya fire directly,
just as one does directly with the Prāyaṇīyā offering.
The *ātithyā* [offering] is performed directly;
one should accomplish the mantras beginning with those for the black antelope skin up to the plowing and sowing.
The plowing and sowing are performed directly.
One should recite the first layer together with its loose soil;
likewise the second, and likewise the third.
One should recite every layer together with its loose soil and every layer together with its clods. As for those oblations that are performed within the hall, one should indeed offer them.
Now, as for those mantras pertaining to the high altar (uttaravedi), he should simply recite them.

"The Agnihotra is indeed the source of the Daśahotṛ, and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are the source of the Caturhotṛ"—thus some declare their sequential order. Furthermore, they cite: "The establishment of the sacred fires (*āgnyādheya*) occurs in the first half of the month; the eleven fore-offerings (*prayāja*) arise all together;
the seasons are the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ."
This animal sacrifice is said to be performed every six months.
Moreover, they quote: "The one who has established the sacred fires must sacrifice with an animal every six months;
he should perform the sacrifice at both solstices."

"In the month of Māgha, the sun moves northward with the *dhaniṣṭhā* [nakṣatra]; in the middle of the month of Śrāvaṇa, it turns southward. These two are the solstices (*kāṣṭhe*). Therefore, one who has not performed the sacrifices should not let a year pass by. Now, in the *cāturmāsya* [sacrifices] and the *soma* sacrifices, the *pañcahotṛ* [formula] takes the place of the *saptahotṛ*.
Now, as for this fire produced by friction which is used for the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and goes out, it serves precisely as the means for binding the sacrificial animals.
"One should tie the animals to the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*)," so says the Brāhmaṇa; thus, for us, those [sticks] become the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*).

Now, in the Mahāpitṛyajña, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is already spread; one does not draw lines on the altar, one does not carry away the *stambayajus*, and one does not take up the clarified butter (*ājya*).
When he distributes the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths at the third pressing, he makes the *mārjālīya* hearth perpetual.

Having performed the *mahāhavis* offerings and when the oblations have been set down, he cooks the oblations for the Great Pitṛyajña on the *gārhapatya* fire and proceeds with them at the *mārjālīya*.
He should proceed with the offering to the Maruts at the *āhavanīya* fire.
The final bath should indeed conclude [the rite].
"Its first layer is provided with loose earth and accompanied by mantras," it is said; thus, his very first layer becomes provided with loose earth and accompanied by mantras.
The others, however, are silent.
Whichever layer they designate as having both the loose earth (*purīṣa*) and the formulas, that very layer of his becomes possessed of loose earth and possessed of formulas;
the others, however, remain silent.

Now, regarding these one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*): one should understand that those days among them for which no specific rite is prescribed are *agniṣṭoma*s. Furthermore, regarding the *ahīna*, *rātri*, and *sattra* sacrifices: one should understand that those days among them for which no specific rite is prescribed are *ukthya*s.
"The cup-bearers of the midday pressing go along, wiping [the cups] for him.
Indeed, while he is seated in the *sadas*, the cup-bearers of the midday pressing go along, wiping the cups for the purpose of consumption.
This [rite] is the twenty-fourfold one.
"He sprinkles him with the residue of the *śukra* and *manthin* cups," it is said.
Having brought together the residue of the *śukra* and *manthin* cups while [the sacrificer] is seated in the sacrificer’s station, he sprinkles him.
This [sacrifice] consists of the *catuṣṭoma*.
"Seven oblations follow the offerings of the morning pressing," it is said.

They are: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Pūṣan, a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, a cake on eight potsherds for Tvaṣṭṛ, a cake on ten potsherds for Varuṇa, a pap for the Viśve Devas, and a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts.
"Eight oblations follow the offerings of the morning pressing," it is said.

An offering on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, an offering on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Bṛhaspati, an offering on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma, a pap for Sarasvatī, an offering on ten potsherds for Varuṇa, and an offering on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth— whatever belongs to the Rājasūya, excluding the Soma sacrifice, all that is performed here; however, he prohibits the cake on twenty-one potsherds for the Maruts and the Aupasadā rites.

This sacrifice is completed in thirteen and a half months; it includes everything that constitutes the Rājasūya, except for that which requires a high altar (uttaravedī). Furthermore, it prohibits the animal sacrifice involving two animals as well as the Cāturmāsya offerings.
(26.30:314.15) It concludes with one month and a half.
(26.30:314.15) "The lion, the tiger, and also the viper...
(26.30:315.1) To which deity, indeed, does this oblation belong?
One should say that Indrāṇī is the deity.

Having performed the animal sacrifice with seventeen animals and having collected the fire-pans (*ukhā*) and the heads of the sacrificial animals, one should sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Vāyu.
Or rather, having previously collected [the materials] silently, and having collected the clay accompanied by mantras, one should smear [the pans] with that [clay].

He joins [the cup] for the Ukthya: "Thou art taken with a support; for Agni, the mighty, the vigorous, the seeker of the Ukthya; that which is thy great vigor, O Agni—for that thee! For Viṣṇu thee, I take thee as one who is well-pleased. Thus.
Having wiped it around, he sets it down: "This is thy womb; for Agni thee, who is eager for the hymn.

Thus he joins the *dhruva* cup: "The head of heaven, the messenger of earth, the bounteous one born for the sake of Truth, Agni—the sage, the sovereign, the guest of men—the gods generated as a vessel in their mouth.
"Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Indra Maghavan. Thus he says.
Having wiped it around, he sets it down with: "This is thy womb; for Indra Maghavan thee! Thus he joins the cup for the Patnīvata.

He takes hold of it with: "Thou art taken with a support; of thee, pressed by Bṛhaspati, belonging to Indra and endowed with power, I take the draught for the Patnīvats. "Indra, O thou who hast a wife... (he says).

He pours out [the draught] for the Hāriyojana cup: "Thou art taken with a support; thou art the ruddy one (*rohit*), whose yoke is ruddy; thou art the rider of the ruddy one, the bearer of the thunderbolt, the precursor of the speckled cow (*pṛśni*). For thee, O divine Soma, for whom the *yajus* has been offered, the *stotra* sung, and the *uktha* recited, I take this draught accompanied by the ruddy one. Ye are the ruddy ones; the parched grains are for the ruddy ones, together with the Soma. To Agni, Svāhā!
Thus, he should set aside that which is the contact of Indra in the Agniṣṭut, and he should set aside that which is the contact of Agni in the Indrastut.
"The other deities are eternal;
of which deity, then, are the additional stotras?
One should say: 'They belong to the Aśvins.'"
And whatever exceeds the night, all that belongs to the Aśvins; thus is one [view].
Now another:
the first is for Agni, the second for Indra, the third for the Viśvedevas, and the fourth for Viṣṇu.
"In the latter days of summer, when the barley has been harvested"—
this means "when it has been trampled";
this is what is expressed by the locative case.
"He causes the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) to call out by means of their titles"—this [rule] applies either previously or [later].
Then, having anointed him and purified him, he leads him forward;
one should understand that the ritual procedure pertaining to the *agniṣṭoma* is established here until the subsequent incidental occurrence.

And at this time, one should perform three *barhis*-spreads with a *yajus* formula—namely, those for the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, the *prāyaṇīyā*, and the *ātithyā*. Then one should offer the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and the *prāyaṇīyā*; from the *ātithyā* onwards, one should proceed with clarified butter (*ājya*) until the chariots arrive. One should divide the clarified butter that was poured out together into three vessels.
That which is the conclusion of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, by means of that one should bring the *dīkṣaṇīyā* to its completion.
One should proceed with the *prāyaṇīya* [offering] using the *praṇītā* waters.
This very [procedure] constitutes the commencement of the *ātithyā*.
Having purchased the King [Soma] with a three-year-old bull that has not yet been castrated, one should bring it forward and perform the *ātithyā* oblation.
By the phrase "with a three-year-old [bull]," this very thing is expressed.
How, indeed, should one adapt its mantras?

"You are a Kṣatriya. "You are Aditi, with heads on both sides. "May you be well-disposed toward us from the east, well-disposed toward us from the west—be thus!
Thus [he says].
"The Upasad rites consist of single groups," so it is said.
These are said to be the very same rites performed in the forenoon;
"the threshing-floor post becomes the sacrificial stake"—
it is this very [post] that they make into their central pivot.
The threshing-fence post is the sacrificial stake;
for it, a mat serves as the vessel for the *caṣāla*—
this is what is meant by the term "piling up."
(26.32:318.2) Then he dedicates these animals: the one for Agni-Soma, the one for Agni, and the Anūbandhya;
(26.32:318.3) these goats are indeed Yamas, being of a common origin. (26.32:318.4) Their ritual performance has been explained.
(26.32:318.4) Now, for this [cow], there is the *sadyaskrī*, the *anukrī*, the *parikrī*, and the *atikrī*; from the *avabhṛtha* onwards, the tail of the sacrifice [is performed] after sunset.

(26.32:318.5) Of these, only the first has the chariot, the first is accompanied by the *somakrayaṇī* cow, and the first has the remnants of the *agnihotra* as its vow-food (*vrata*). (26.32:318.6) Then, for this [cow], they perform the forms of the vows of three teats, two teats, and one teat, [respectively] corresponding to the *sadyaskrī*, the *anukrī*, the *parikrī*, and the *atikrī*.
"But where, indeed, is the *saṃnivāpa* seen in a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*)?
"One should say: 'In the Vrātyastoma and in the Kulāya of Indra and Agni.
Now, in this Vrātyastoma, many undergo initiation for the sake of one [sacrificer].
They cause these very persons, who have not been initiated, to perform the sacrifice.
[The items are] a staff, sandals, and a *śāmūla* antelope skin; for the *śāmūlaka*s, there are blankets mixed with hair, and that [skin] is white and from a black antelope.
This same sacrifice is an Agniṣṭoma for those who are senior;
being the very same, it is an Ukthya for those who are junior.
The first day consists of four stomas, while the subsequent day consists of five stomas.
The chariot is the *havirdhāna*. One should make the northern *havirdhāna* in the form of a bed;
thus the formulas for the cart would not be sublated.
"There are two *triṣṭhomas* with thirty-three verses each in the middle," [it is said].
These two *pṛṣṭhya-stomas* thus occur in reverse order both from here and from there.
Then, on the new moon day, having combined [the elements], one should offer the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* dedicated to Candra.
Sitting around him as he is [the embodiment of] Brahman, they consume [the food]; because they consider it to be *ṛta*, by that [act] he becomes a Brāhmaṇa.
"The Brāhmaṇa is indeed the best of the social classes, Agni the best of the gods"—with this [formula], or else with the *vyāhṛtis*, he may consume it.
"This is a *catuṣṭoma*," they say; this *diśāṃ catuṣṭoma* consists of fourfold increments.
Now, in this sacrifice that blinds the forest, from the *avabhṛtha* bath onwards until sunset is the tail of the sacrifice.

For it, having recited the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant ten times, a hundred times, a thousand times, ten thousand times, a hundred thousand times, a million times, ten million times, a hundred million times, a billion times, ten billion times, a hundred billion times, a trillion times, and so on—up to a *padva*, a *palva*, and eternally—even while praising with the mind alone, one considers: "My praise has reached this much.
Then, there is a single *pravargya* rite and only one *agnihotra*.
Now, at this Śunaḥkarṇa sacrifice,
having eaten food mixed with sesame seeds and having consumed fish, one should drink only alkaline water.
Then, one should lie down on the path of the Sāmans.
From dream itself one goes into a dream;
"he gives grain made into a heap" and "he gives grain made into a measure"—
this is what is meant by "made into a measure."
"They move forward and they move backward"—
that which is the westward arrangement (*vihāra*) with the ritual procedure (*upacāra*) from the south, this is it.
By this very [explanation], the "facing all directions" (*sarvatomukha*) is also explained.
(26.33:320.10) By this [means], there are a thousand halls.
(26.33:320.11) "Having purified him here, they purify him there"—
one should understand that the ritual procedure pertaining to the Agniṣṭoma is established here for the northern hall alone.
He performs two three-night rites and one two-night rite; by means of the consecrations (*dīkṣā*) and the attendant ceremonies (*upasad*), he thus extends these days for him.
He should perform them according to the rules of the *ahīna* sacrifice, lest he should overstep the sacrifice.
This which has been declared is that which was not prescribed by the Sūtra.

However, regarding the ritual application, Baudhāyana says that one should observe sacrifice within sacrifice according to the convention; Baudhāyana says that one should observe sacrifice within sacrifice.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the expiations prescribed in the collection of mantras.

In every case, if that which was performed with a mantra above should fall below, one should establish it with the verse, "Brahman is the foundation of the mind," and with this same verse offer a spoonful of oblation (*sruvāhuti*). Having offered the oblation, one should establish it; or, having established it, one may perform the subsequent rite immediately after the offering.
The same applies to other [omissions] as well.
One should not take heed of a rite that has been passed over if it is rendered redundant by the purpose [of another].

In all cases involving the *āśrāvita*, *pratyāśrāvita*, and *vaṣaṭkāra*—whether they are uttered too early, not uttered at all, or omitted—one should offer a spoonful (*sruvāhuti*) with the formula: "The *āśrāvita* has been over-uttered."

(27.1:322.7) In all cases where one might pronounce the name of a deity, if one should pronounce the name of another deity instead of the deity to whom the portion belongs, one should offer a spoonful with the verse: "O gods, that which I have overstepped in your regard... (27.1:322.9). In all cases of invoking deities, if one should invoke another deity instead of the deity to whom the portion belongs, one should offer a spoonful with this same verse. Wherever one remembers [the error], one should rise and mentally invoke that [correct] deity; then one should sacrifice the surplus with clarified butter according to the order in which they were invoked.

(27.1:322.11) In all cases, if drops should fall from the *praṇītā* waters—whether they have already been led forward, are being led forward, or have already been led forward—or if they should leak into the cup (*camasa*), one should fill it with water while reciting the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*). Then, with the verse "That [work] has been performed for me by the waters; that is performed again," one should offer a spoonful (*sruva-āhuti*) of oblation.

(27.1:323.1) In every instance, if the sun does not appear during the performance of the sacrificial rite, except when otherwise prescribed, one should offer spoonfuls of oblation with these verses: "Up from the darkness we [have risen]," "Up that [sun]," and "The bright [face]."
If an eclipse of the sun or the moon occurs, this very [rite] is performed.

Furthermore, if there should be an emission of semen by the sacrificer or by the officiating priests in a dream, one should offer two spoonfuls with these two [verses]: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa" and "That I implore of thee."

In all cases, when there is an omission or displacement regarding the oblation, the deity, the *yājyā*, the *anuvākyā*, or the offerings—whether the offering has been made or not—one should offer two spoonfuls (*sruvāhuti*) with these two verses: "Thou, O Agni, for us... and "So thou, O Agni, for us...".

In all cases, when there is cutting, burning, damage, loss, or destruction of the ladle, the brush, the sacrificial grass-bundle, the enclosing sticks, the sacrificial grass, the separating blades, the strainers, the wooden sword, the fuel, or the ritual materials and equipment, one should prepare another item according to its characteristic mark and, having set it down according to its characteristic mark, offer two spoonfuls with these two verses: "O Agni, you are the unswerving one" and "O Prajāpati. This applies everywhere in a sacrifice that has been commenced.

(27.2:323.12) If, prior to the offerings, the embers should roll out beyond the enclosing sticks, one should perform the expiation prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa and offer a spoonful with the verse: "I set up this enclosure for the living.

(27.2:323.14) In every case where a failure in the sacrificial rite occurs during the performance of the sacrifice, one should offer eight spoonfuls with these [formulas]: "To those who have sacrificed, Svāhā! Vaṣaṭ to those who have not sacrificed, Svāhā! and so forth.

(27.2:323.16) If, during the performance of a sacrifice that has been fully commenced, a danger from enemies should arise, one should offer two spoonfuls with the two verses, "From whatever we fear, O Indra... and "The giver of well-being, the lord of the people..."; or, once the danger has passed, one may perform the sacrifice again.

(27.2:324.2) In all cases, regarding the errors in accent, syllable, word, or meter occurring from the *upāṃśu* [whispered] portion up to the suspension of speech (*vācaḥ sthāna*), one should offer a spoonful with this verse: "Whatever of ours is deficient here through these songs..."
In all cases where no expiation has been prescribed, one should offer two spoonfuls with the two verses: "The unknown" and "Measured by the person.

In all rites involving the *idhma* and *barhis*, the *prayāja*s and *anūyāja*s, or in acts performed for the sake of cooked offerings (*pākayajña*), one should offer a spoonful with the verse: "Whatever [fault] was committed by the mind in the cooked offering. In all cases where [an item] is spilled, broken, cut, shattered, lost, scorched, misplaced, burnt up, or deficient or in excess, one should recite: "Whatever injury has occurred to my self; Agni has restored my sight."

With these two verses he should offer oblations with the *sruva*-ladle in all cases of injury to the fires. With the verse, "May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle thee again," he should place a fuel-stick on the fire and offer an oblation with the *sruva*-ladle using that same verse. In all sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*), having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings and having gone eastward, he replenishes the *dhruvā* ladle and offers the *sarvaprāyaścitta* expiations from the *dhruvā* ladle with this entire section beginning, "Brahman is the foundation of the mind," reciting it verse by verse. Now, indeed, there is this [text]:
“He offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations for the completion of the sacrifice.

“Whatever in the sacrifice is cruel, whatever is mangled, whatever it oversteps, whatever it does not overstep, whatever it does in excess, and whatever it does not do—it is precisely these [oblations] that he gratifies with them,” so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Baudhāyana says that these very [oblations], prescribed according to the rule of the Brāhmaṇa, are the restorative offerings accompanied by mantras.
Śālīki maintains that those [rites] prescribed in collections of mantras are occasional (naimittika).

Now, regarding the preparation of the potsherds (*kapāla*), a space the size of a horse’s hoof is prepared in the shape of a chariot wheel. The intention (*saṃkalpa*) constitutes the authority; there may be an increase or decrease of potsherds. If the potsherds do not spread out [as required], one should offer oblations with a *sruva*-ladle into the *āhavanīya* fire using the *vyāhṛti*s: "Bhūḥ! Bhuvaḥ! Suvaḥ! This applies equally to both insufficient spreading and excessive spreading. Now, the expiation for the raw state of the sacrificial offerings, their spilling, their being poured over, or their leaking away is as follows.

(27.3:325.8) If [the oblation] is not cooked, one should offer a spoonful on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "To Rudra, svāhā! If it is liquid, [it is for] Vāyu; if it is burnt, [it is for] Nirṛti.

(27.3:325.10) If it should be partially burnt, one should proceed with whatever part of it remains cooked. But if it should be entirely burnt, having poured water over it, one should offer the two Mindā oblations.
(27.3:325.12) Then he should offer another oblation, or he may proceed with clarified butter; that itself is the expiation for it.

To whichever direction the [spilled] liquid flows, to that deity he should offer a spoonful (*sruva-āhuti*): if to the east, to Agni; if to the south, to Yama; if to the west, to Varuṇa; if to the north, to Soma.

Now, if [the oblation] should spill out from all sides, one should offer spoonfuls (*sruvāhuti*) to all these deities with the two *āpyāyanī* verses: "Swell up" (*āpyāyasva*) and "May it swell for thee" (*saṃ te*).

Then, at the time of taking down the sacrificial offerings (*havir*), in the event of falling, splitting, breaking, crumbling, crawling over, or being handled in a contrary or improper manner, one should offer spoonfuls into the *āhavanīya* fire with the *vyāhṛtis*: "Bhūḥ! Bhuvaḥ! Suvaḥ!"

Then, having gone out northward between the altar and the rubbish-heap, and having crept out northward until he can no longer see, he recites the *vyāhṛtis* and proceeds with the *vyāhṛtis* themselves.
"The *vyāhṛtis*, however, consist of four feet; they have nine parts and six syllables. They are the beginning, middle, and end of all four Vedas.
Whatever may be deficient in a mantra, or redundant, or even improperly performed, they dispel that evil; therefore they are remembered as the *vyāhṛtis*."
(27.4:326.12) If a failure in the sacrifice should occur on account of the *ṛc*, one should offer an oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire with the words, "bhūḥ.

(27.4:326.12) If it occurs on account of the *yajus*, [one should offer] in the *anvāhāryapacana* fire with the words, "bhuvaḥ. (27.4:326.13) If it occurs on account of the *sāman*, [one should offer] in the *āhavanīya* fire with the words, "suvar."
(27.4:326.14) If one should offer all [the portions] from every side, (27.4:327.1) then regarding the case:

"When the sacrificial cake has been lifted up, or when it trembles, or likewise when it flows out, (27.4:327.2) or even when it is broken or slips away—what should be the expiation? Thus [it is asked].
It is known:
"If it is lifted up, he destroys his family; if it trembles, his offspring perish;
and if it breaks or slips away, the sacrificer dies."

Then, having removed [the fire] that is established in falling, splitting, breaking, blowing out, or creeping away, and having made it rest upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he pours abundant clarified butter over it and consecrates it with the mantra: "Why do you fly up? Why have you departed? Being pacified, come here for the sake of peace!
Having become non-terrible and worthy of sacrifice, sit in your own seat; sit in your own seat.
Having given a boon to the Brahman priest, he should place it within the altar (*antarvedi*).
When that [offering] has been completed, one should offer the *surabhimatī*. When that has been completed, one should offer the *tantumatī*.
"But the *āyuṣmatī* offerings must be performed; the subsequent rites are to be carried out according to the meters."
"This is the rule for the mishap of the oblation, as ordained by those who perceive reality. Thus [it is said].

(27.4:328.1) <In the event of spilling, seizing, or pouring out, and in the case of the consecration of substances,> (27.4:328.2) <at whatever time one becomes aware [of the error], one should perform it within the sequence of the ritual action.> (27.4:328.3) <The *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*— this is the sacrifice, both supreme and inferior.*>
"Therefore, whatever in the sacrifice has been spilled, and whatever has become inverted—

that should all be remedied with the *vyāhṛtis*, except for that which has already been consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ* call. And whatever has been done by those acting unknowingly, and whatever has been done by those acting in haste."
"Whatever is performed by means of the application of the *vyāhṛtis*, that indeed is truly performed.
"One should state the measurements of the potsherds (*kapāla*) in the ritual procedure of the Adhvaryu:
they should be equal and square, measuring two finger-breadths on all sides."
Baudhāyana says that one should increase the portions of the sacrificial oblations, whether equal or unequal, according to their measurement.

Now follows the expiation for fires that have gone out—whether they are those located in the *araṇis*, those located within oneself (*ātman*), the perpetual (*ajasra*) fires, the *anvāhita* fires, or the fires belonging to the *savana* sacrifices.

Having churned the fire from the *araṇis* and having established the sacrificial fires (*vihāra*), one melts clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire and purifies it. Having taken four spoonfuls into the ladle (*sruc*), one offers the *saṃtanī* oblation into the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra: "May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this severed sacrifice. Those dawns and sunsets that have passed—I unite them by means of this oblation of ghee, Svāhā! Thus he says.
(27.5:329.3) This is the expiation when [the fire] has gone out, when it has not been offered, or when it has risen before sunrise or set after sunset.
(27.5:329.4) This is for the one who has superseded his younger brother in marriage; this is for the one who has been superseded.

This is for one who has vomited [the Soma]; this is for one who has vomited Soma, for one who has passed the Soma through [excessive vomiting], and for one whose consumption [of the Soma] was interrupted; this is for one who is deprived of the consumption [of the Soma].

This applies to one who has already performed the search; this applies to one who is about to perform the search. This very same rule applies if a man, a chariot, a horse, a cow, a buffalo, a boar, a snake, a wild animal, a dog, or any other beast of prey should pass between the two fires.
This same [penance applies] if they should carry away even a single part of one's fire.
This same expiation by means of the *manasvatī* verse is performed for all calamities of the *agnihotra*.
"Having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, there are four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). If one of them is absent, three or even two may perform the rites.

Furthermore, if there should be only one priest, before the *prayāja* offerings, he offers the expiations pertaining to a single Adhvaryu by dipping the *sruva* spoon into the *ājyasthālī* vessel, [reciting]: "May I be pleasing to speech; may I be pleasing to Vācaspati; O divine Speech!"
(27.6:329.14) < Whatever is honeyed in speech, place me therein; to Sarasvatī, svāhā!
> (27.6:330.1) < O Aśvins, whatever in this sacrifice is deficient in speech, whatever is ill-performed—> (27.6:330.2) < that the two Aśvins shall mend with their healing balm; svāhā! >

(27.6:330.2) < Indra the protector, Indra the helper; at every invocation, I call upon the hero Indra, who is easily invoked. (27.6:330.3) Now I call upon Śakra, Indra who is invoked by many: may the bountiful Indra bestow well-being upon us—svāhā! (27.6:330.5) Whatever flaw there is in my mind, or in my speech, or in my heart...>

(27.6:330.5) < May the gods pacify all that—Soma and Bṛhaspati, svāhā! > (27.6:330.6) < Whatever the priests, whether knowing or unknowing, do in confusion, > (27.6:330.7) < may Agni and the goddess Śraddhā release me from that sin, svāhā! >

(27.6:330.8) <Whatever harm we have done to the atmosphere, to the earth, or to the sky, to our mother or to our father—> (27.6:330.9) <May Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin; may he clear away those misfortunes which we have committed, and make me free from fault, svāhā!> (27.6:330.11) <In the office of the Brahman, the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Āgnīdhra, and the Yajamāna, whatever errors I have made in the sacrifice—may the gods protect me from that; may they not harm my vital breaths, svāhā!>

(27.6:330.13) “I am the Brahman, I am the Hotṛ, I am the Adhvaryu, I am the Agnīdhra, and I am the sacrificer; I alone encompass the ritual duties in this sacrifice. May the gods protect that for me; may they not harm my vital breaths—svāhā!
Having offered these expiations for the single office of the Adhvaryu, it is known from tradition: “While seated within the altar, he sacrifices to all the deities.”

(27.6:330.17) <When the *homa* offerings have been passed over, and when the *parvan* and *āgrayaṇa* sacrifices have been omitted, while the two fire-drills (*araṇi*) are still being maintained, how is it that the ritual framework (*tantra*) is not lost?> (27.6:331.1) <The *Śuci*, the *Pāvamānī*, the *Tantumant*, and the *Pāthikṛt*—these sacrifices should be performed; then the ritual framework is not lost.> (27.6:331.3) <The *Śuci* purifies evil; the *Tantu* should not cause the thread to be broken. The *Pāthikṛt* should ascend the path, and the *Pāvamānī* shall purify.* Thus is the ritual manual (*kalpa*) of Baudhāyana.>

When the new moon sacrifice has been omitted, the Pāthikṛtī offering should be performed; when the full moon sacrifice has been omitted, the Vaiśvānarī offering should be performed; when both have been omitted, both should be performed; Śālīki says that when many have been omitted, the Anvārambhaṇīyā offering should be performed.

Now, if the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) should become worn out—either by insects or by friction—one should procure two other new fire-drills that are identical. Having fasted on the new moon day and performed the *darśa* sacrifice on the following day, one should break the old drill into pieces, cast them into the *gārhapatya* fire, and having kindled it, take the upper drill with the right hand and the lower drill with the left, holding them over the fire while muttering: "Awake, O Agni! Enter another womb, O Jātavedas, in order to carry out the sacrifice to the gods."
"O Forest, pass over to the fire-drill; cast off this worn-out body with your undecaying self. Thus [it is said].

(27.7:331.14) "This is your seasonal womb"—having thus consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), having churned out the Gārhapatya fire according to the procedure for churning, and having arranged the sacrificial hearths (*vihāra*), he melts clarified butter over the Gārhapatya, purifies it, takes four portions in the offering-spoon (*sruk*), and offers the *saṃtanī* oblation into the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this interrupted sacrifice. Those dawns and those sunsets that have been offered—those I unite by means of the oblation of ghee, Svāhā!
Thus.
Then he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumat;
he gives a shallow cup (*śarāva*) as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
that well-known sacrifice is thus completed.

(27.8:332.8) Now we shall explain the destruction of the two kindling woods (*araṇi*). (27.8:332.8) It perishes due to eight causes: through contact with impure matter, a dog, a *caṇḍāla*, a *śūdra*, a crow, a fallen man, a donkey, or a menstruating woman, the two kindling woods are destroyed. (27.8:332.10) Having discarded those two, one should fetch two other new kindling woods that are similar; then, having performed the *agnyādheya* together with the fire, the *punarādheya* takes place when the fire has gone into the kindling woods. If the kindling woods are lost, he immerses them in water [with the mantra]: "May you two be of one mind for us. (27.8:332.10) Thus it is said.

(27.8:332.12) Then, having cut, split, and reduced the northern [araṇi] to pieces, he should perform the rubbing, the placing upon [the lower araṇi], the remaining rubbing, or the secondary rubbing, excluding all the wooden pegs.
(27.8:333.2) Thus concludes the mishap regarding the two araṇis.

(27.9:333.4) Now we shall explain the defects of sacrificial offerings (*havir-doṣa*). These include: if it is infested with blue flies, *śātikā* flies, bedbugs, lice on clothing or the head, nits, or worms that form lumps; or if it is contaminated by small insects, flies, or ants—excluding these [specific small creatures]; or if it is defiled by the excrement of dogs, cats, mongooses, chickens, monkeys, or crows; or by mice, sweat, hair, dead nails, deformed nails, putrid drops, perspiration, blood, oil, tears, coughing, sneezing, or by being touched by a moist nose; or if it has been touched by a menstruating woman; or if it has been seen by one who is impure (*aprayata*) or by a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*); or if it is in an unsuitable vessel (*apapātra*) or in an impure place.
If the sacrificial offering has been spilled or spoiled, they carry it away into the water,
or have it placed in cold ashes.
Having offered the two *mindā* oblations, he should then prepare another [offering], or proceed with clarified butter (*ājya*).
Moreover, indeed, they say that clarified butter is quickly prepared;
having offered the two *mindā* oblations, he offers the *manasvatī*;
that itself is the expiation for that.
Now, therefore, follows the expiation for fires that have gone out.
Oblations are seen to be for the purpose of restoration;
some say they are the *caturhotṛ* formulas.
Some say they are the *vyāhṛtis*;
some say they are the *mindāhutis*;
others say they are the *manasvatī*.
Some say [the verses] are the *mahāvyāhṛtis*.

Now, if all the fires should go out, one should consign the fires from their hearths into the two kindling woods (*araṇis*) and churn out the *gārhapatya* fire according to the procedure for churning: "From here Agni was first born, Jātavedas from his own womb; may he, knowing, carry the oblation to the gods by means of the *gāyatrī*, the *triṣṭubh*, and the *jagatī*.
[The Brāhmaṇa says: "Verily, by means of the meters, he causes him to be born from his own womb. This is the Brāhmaṇa.

(27.10:334.10) Now, if [the fire] should not be produced while being churned, one should fetch another from wherever one sees it and offer the oblation. (27.10:334.11) Then, without hurrying, one should churn again. (27.10:334.11) But if, once produced, it should go out, one should mutter the mantra for the re-depositing of the fires and churn again.
Then he pays homage to it with the words: "Rejoice for the sake of food, wealth, power, splendor, vigor, and offspring.
Then he kindles it with the words: "May the two springs of Sarasvatī kindle thee; thou art the sovereign ruler, thou art the radiant one."

Then, having kindled it, having brought the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, having taken out the blazing *āhavanīya* fire, having established it and kindled it at the *gārhapatya*, having melted the clarified butter (*ājya*) and purified it, and having taken four portions into the ladle (*sruc*), he offers it into the *āhavanīya* while mentally reciting the *daśahotṛ* formula, as the sacrificer maintains contact with him, saying: "Svāhā!

Then, having turned to the right and hastened back toward the west, he offers ten spoonfuls (*sruva-āhuti*) into the *gārhapatya* for the Brāhmaṇa section beginning with "The one Hotṛ is the Brahman" (*brāhmaṇa ekahotā*).

Now, if the *anvāhāryapacana* fire should go out, one should take it up from the *gārhapatya* and offer the *caturhotṛ* formula in the *anvāhāryapacana*, while offering the tenfold formula in the *gārhapatya*.

If the *āhavanīya* fire should go out, one should take it up from the *gārhapatya* and offer the *pañcahotṛ* formula in the *āhavanīya*, while offering the tenfold formula in the *gārhapatya*. If, among the fires belonging to the *savana* rites, the *āgnīdhrīya* fire should go out, one should take it up from the *śālāmukhīya* and offer the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula in the *āgnīdhrīya*, while offering the tenfold formula in the *śālāmukhīya*.

Now, if the Āhavanīya fire on the high altar should go out, one should take it up from the Āgnīdhrīya fire and offer the Saptahotṛ formula into the Āhavanīya on the high altar, and the Daśahotṛ formula into the Āgnīdhrīya.

By this same procedure, when one or two fires have gone out, he should offer the oblations by dividing them among the Hotṛ-priests; and if the *vyāhṛtis* are to be offered, he should offer them both separately and collectively. Likewise, he should offer the *mindā*-oblations, and if the *manasvatī* is to be offered, he should offer it in the Āhavanīya fire. This indeed is the expiation for fires that are perpetually maintained (*ajasra*), those for which fuel has been added (*anvāhita*), those occurring during the Soma-pressings (*savanagata*), and those that have gone out; this very rite applies at the time of the oblation, with the exception of the adding of fuel (*anvādhāna*).

Now, if one's fire has been taken out and should go out before the *agnihotra* has been offered, he should either act according to the *sūtra*, or he may take a fuel-stick from the *gārhapatya* fire and recite these mantras over the churning, the upper churning-stick, and the kindling: "The churning... the upper churning-stick... the kindling... [and so forth].

Or, even during the recitation [of the Śānti], he should perform the Jyotiṣmatī sacrifice; or he should offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with two Jyotiṣmatī verses; or he should offer a spoon-oblation (*sruvāhuti*) with a Jyotiṣmatī verse: "To Agni Jyotiṣmat, svāhā! The teachers declare that among the sacrifices, the full oblation, and the spoon-oblation, each preceding rite is more powerful than the one following it. Regarding this, they cite an example:
"Whatever specific minor rules are observed here and there, one should not perform those actions out of mere habit; rather, that wealth [of knowledge] should be used in times of distress.
One should diligently master the specific rules from all the Vedas for the sake of discerning ritual actions and to resort to them in times of calamity. Thus it is said.

(27.11:337.1) If, by way of incidental occurrence, an oblation has been offered in the common fire by the ignorant or by children, or if it has been spread out by the wife, one should consign those fires into the two kindling woods, move away, churn out the fires, spread them out, and then perform the *pūrṇāhuti* and the *tantumatī* offering.

(27.11:337.3) But if, not by way of incidental occurrence, an oblation has been offered in the common fire by the ignorant or by children, or if it has been spread out by the wife, one should spread them out with the *vyāhṛtis*, and then perform the *pūrṇāhuti* and the *tantumatī* offering.
Now, it is indeed said:
"Nirṛti seizes the sacrifice of him for whom any oblation is burnt; if they find the portions [still intact], they do not perform an expiation here.
For this Adhvaryu burns the portions.
(27.12:337.10) "He satisfies these together.

(27.12:337.10) "Verily, he burns [the offerings] who offers the portions before having offered the clarified butter, and who does not pour clarified butter over them from above. When they are thus burnt, neither the gods nor the sacrificer are satisfied."

Now, he satisfies these [deities] by first offering the clarified butter (*ājya*), then offering the portions (*avadāna*), and finally pouring clarified butter over them from above. When they are thus satisfied, the gods are satisfied, and the sacrificer is satisfied.
Now, if one were to sacrifice to Agni-Soma from the cake for Agni, or to Agni from the cake for Agni-Soma, that would not be a true offering.
One should offer a spoonful (sruvāhuti) into the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "Whatever, O gods, I may have overstepped. This is the purification of the gods.

The invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-puronuvākyā*) dedicated to Agni constitute the purification of the gods; those dedicated to Indra constitute the purification of the gods; those dedicated to Prajāpati constitute the purification of the gods; and the *vyāhṛtis* constitute the purification of the gods.
Now, if the Hotṛ should become confused regarding the invitatory and offering verses, he should sacrifice using all those verses dedicated to Agni.
It is known: "Agni is all the deities.
[The verses] addressed to Indra;
it is known: "Indra indeed is all the deities."
With the verses dedicated to Prajāpati; for it is known: "Prajāpati is all the deities.
With the *vyāhṛtis*.
It is known: "The *vyāhṛtis* are indeed all the *ṛcs*, all the *sāmans*, and all the *yajus*.

Now, if the sacrificer should become confused regarding the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), his entering between the altar (*vedi*) and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*) shall be performed with the *vyāhṛtis* alone; his exiting shall be performed with the *vyāhṛtis* alone; and his consecration (*anumantraṇa*) shall be performed with the *vyāhṛtis* alone.
It is known: "The *vyāhṛtis* are indeed all the *ṛcs*, all the *sāmans*, and all the *yajus*."
The gods indeed wait upon the sacrifice, thinking, "We have been excluded; this oblation of ours has not yet been offered; let us consume it.
Some say [this occurs] until the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering;
others say until the *iḍā*.
Some say [the offering] is until the after-offerings (ānuyāja);
some say until the *śaṃyuvāka*; some say until the *samiṣṭayajus*.
If he should remember [the omission] after the *samiṣṭayajus* offering, he should conclude this sacrifice and perform another sacrifice that is free from defects;
for it is known: "The sacrifice is indeed the expiation for the sacrifice."

Now, if the calves should suckle the cows intended for the *sāṃnāyya* offering, he should sacrifice in the evening with barley gruel prepared with the milk of a cow dedicated to Vāyu. Even if only one cow has been milked, he should not let her suckle.
Having completed the rite with the milk already drawn and having driven away the calves from those not yet milked, he should sacrifice with the *sāṃnāyya* on the following day.
If the evening milking should meet with misfortune, one should set aside rice for Indra and fast, according to the traditional injunction.
Alternatively, having divided the morning milking into two parts and having curdled one of them, one should use it in place of the evening milk, and the other in place of the *śṛta* (boiled milk).
If the morning milking should meet with misfortune, one should set aside a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) for Indra or Mahendra and proceed with the ritual using that together with the curds.

"If both [fires] should suffer distress, one should offer a five-śarāva oblation of cooked rice to Indra. Having performed the rite for Agni in the established manner, one should then perform the rite for Indra.

If all the sacrificial oblations should become spoiled, be lost, or be stolen, one should perform a sacrifice to these deities with clarified butter according to their respective order, and then extend another sacrifice that is free from defects.
"It is known from scripture: 'The sacrifice, indeed, is the expiation for the sacrifice.'"
(27.14:340.10) Now, therefore, we shall explain the consecratory formulas (*anumantraṇa*) for the oblations that are not recorded in the *Chandas* [Vedic meters].

(27.14:340.11) He consecrates the sacrifice to Vaimṛdha Indra with: "Through the sacrifice to the god Vaimṛdha Indra, may I become possessed of power, free from rivals, heroic, and glorious"—or rather, "May I become free from rivals and heroic. (27.14:341.1) Or:
"Through the sacrifice to another god, may I become one who has good pasture."
"Through the sacrifice to Soma, may I be procreated with offspring and cattle; may I be rich in seed and deposit seed. Or:
"Through the sacrifice to Savitṛ, may I become possessed of well-being and cattle;
through the sacrifice to Sarasvatī, may I nourish speech and the eating of food."

"Through the sacrifice to Sarasvatī, may I become possessed of faith in my mind. Through the sacrifice to Pūṣan, may I become prosperous and rich in cattle. Through the sacrifice to the Maruts, may I prosper in my vital breaths."

"By the sacrifice to the Viśve Devas, may I attain union with the vital breaths. "By the sacrifice to Heaven and Earth, may I prosper in both worlds; may I attain abundance and a firm foundation. Or: "By the sacrifice to the Vājins, may I become possessed of seed; by the sacrifice to Varuṇa, may I become a partaker of the sacred law (*dharma*)."
"Through the sacrifice to which god may I become most powerful?
Through the sacrifice to Viśvakarman may I accomplish all works. Through the sacrifice to Aditi may I be released from sin."
"By the sacrifice to the god Vāyu, may I become a partaker of treasure.
By the sacrifice to the god Sūrya, may I become fair to behold.
By the sacrifice to the gods Agni and Viṣṇu, may I become possessed of heroic vigor."
"By the sacrifice to the god Viṣṇu, may I become Śipiviṣṭa"; "By the sacrifice to the god Aryaman, may I go to the heavenly world"—
in this manner he consecrates each offering according to its respective deity.

(27.14:342.2) They declare that cakes on eight potsherds which have not been specifically prescribed are modifications of the offering to Agni; those on eleven potsherds are modifications of the offering to Agni-Soma; those on twelve potsherds are modifications of the Vaiśvadeva offering; and those on one potsherd or with the earth as a potsherd are modifications of the offering to Heaven and Earth; others than these are modifications of the offering to Agni. (27.14:342.5) Caru-offerings are modifications of the offering to Soma; curd, milk, clotted curd, and animal sacrifices are modifications of the Sāṃnāyya offering; and the Vanaspati offering is a modification of the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.

They say that the *upāṃśuyāja* offerings and those which are modifications of the *upāṃśuyāja* are so designated. Furthermore, they cite: "The commonality of the oblation (*havis*), the commonality of the deity, and the commonality of the potsherds (*kapāla*). When there is a commonality of oblation, deity, and potsherds, the commonality of the oblation is more powerful.
Alternatively, the formula "May I attain the verse at the call of this sacrifice" is universal.

Now, it is indeed said: "He who is seized by a malignant wasting disease, or he who is excluded from the gods, the seers, the ancestors, the cows, and the Brahmins—whether already accused or being accused—should perform the Rahasyeṣṭi.
One intending to sacrifice with this offering procures gold.
The day of preparation for that [sacrifice] is well known.

Then, in the morning, after the *agnihotra* has been offered and before the carrying forward of the waters, he melts the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, purifies it, takes four portions into the offering-spoon, and offers it into the *āhavanīya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "With that purifier by which the gods always purify themselves—by that thousand-streamed one, may the *pāvamānī* verses purify me, *svāhā*!"

Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers it in the Āhavanīya fire itself with the mantra: "The purifier belonging to Prajāpati, hundred-stranded and golden—by means of that, we who know Brahman purify the purified Brahman, svāhā!"

Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers it in the Āhavanīya fire itself with the mantra: "May Indra purify me with good guidance; may Soma with well-being, and Varuṇa with concord; may King Yama purify me with those who crush [enemies]; may Jātavedas purify me with the purifying [power]—svāhā!"

Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a sacrifice consisting of ten oblations, beginning with: "To Agni, the deliverer from distress, a cake on eight potsherds. Having cooked them, he places them [on the altar].

For this sacrifice, there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. Between the verse addressed to the one being kindled and the verse addressed to the one already kindled, he inserts two *dhāyyā* verses: "This is the gathering-place of the waters" and "Homage to thee"—these two.
The two *ājyabhāga* offerings are indeed accompanied by the word *pāvaka*.

Having recited the *puro’nuvākyā*: “Agni, the immortal with bright luster, drives away the demons; he is pure, purifying, and worthy of praise,” one then recites: “O Agni, that filter of yours which is spread within your flame...”

(28.1:344.1) He performs the sacrifice with the verse: "By that we purify ourselves, O Brahman. (28.1:344.2) Having recited the *puro'nuvākyā*: "He who, being pressed, flows all around in a purifying stream—the drop like a swift horse," he sacrifices with the verse: "He runs into the jars; he is poured out upon the filter; he grows through the hymns at the sacrifices. (28.1:344.5) Then, for the oblations, the *yājyās* and *puro'nuvākyās* in this section beginning with "I meditate upon Agni, the first, the wise one" are to be used together with their respective *saṃyājyās*.

(28.1:344.6) Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers oblations with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) verse by verse using this section beginning: "The purifying [wind], the winner of heaven. (28.1:344.8) The *iḍā*-portion is performed in the established manner. (28.1:344.8) Then, having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives gold as a gift.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.

Then, prior to the Gṛhapati offering, he offers oblations with the wooden spoon (sruva), verse by verse, with this Anuvāka beginning, "O gods, whatever offense against the gods... This sacrifice concludes with the pouring out of the full vessel (pūrṇapātra) and the Viṣṇu-strides (viṣṇukrama).

He releases the vow. He should perform this very sacrifice if he has transgressed against the seasons, transgressed against his wife, or emitted semen in a place that is not a womb. He should perform this very sacrifice if he is tainted by a *pātaka* or *upapātaka*; if tainted by a *mahāpātaka*, for twelve days; if desiring merit, for a month; or for a year or a season. This [sacrifice] they call the *Mahāpavitreṣṭi*, or the *Mṛgāreṣṭi*, or the *Rahasyeṣṭi*—so says Baudhāyana.

(28.2:345.1) As for the statement, "He may travel abroad for an unlimited time," this means that he does not travel abroad beyond a year; however, if he should travel abroad beyond that, he should sacrifice with the Pavitreṣṭi.
(28.2:345.3) One who is about to perform this sacrifice prepares gold. The fast-day for it is well known.

(28.2:345.4) Then, in the morning, after the *agnihotra* has been offered and before the carrying forward of the water, he melts the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, purifies it, takes four spoonfuls into the offering-ladle, and while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, he offers it into the *āhavanīya* fire with the verse: "With that purifier by which the gods always purify themselves—by that thousand-streamed one, may the *pāvamānī* verses purify me, *svāhā*!"

Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers it in the Āhavanīya fire itself with the mantra: "The purifier belonging to Prajāpati, consisting of a hundred strands, made of gold—by means of that, we who know the Brahman purify ourselves as the purified Brahman; svāhā!"

Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers it in the Āhavanīya fire itself with the mantra: "May Indra purify me with good guidance; may Soma with well-being, Varuṇa with harmony; may King Yama purify me with his crushing powers; may Jātavedas purify me with the *ūrjanyā* [strength-giving] power—Svāhā! Thus.

Then, having spread the *pṛṣṭhyā* grass and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna; [he offers] clarified butter in a low voice to Sarasvatī Priyā. He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pāvaka; [he offers] clarified butter in a low voice to Savitṛ Satyaprasava. He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Śuci; [he offers] clarified butter in a low voice to Vāyu Niyutvat.
He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati; [he offers] clarified butter in a low voice to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa;
he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara; [he offers] clarified butter in a low voice to Dadhikrāvan.
Having cooked them, he sets them down.
For this [offering], there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

Between the verse addressed to the one being kindled (*samidhyamāna*) and the verse addressed to the one already kindled (*samiddha*), he inserts two *dhāyyā* verses containing the word "purifier" (*pāvaka*): "This is the gathering-place of the waters" and "Homage to thee"—these two.
The two *ājyabhāga* offerings likewise contain the word "purifier."

"Agni, the immortal with bright luster, drives away the *rakṣas*—the pure, purifying, and worthy of praise. Having recited this *puro'nuvākyā*, he offers the oblation with: "O Agni, that purifier which is spread within your flame—with that we purify our *brahman*. Thus he sacrifices.

Having recited the *puro’nuvākyā*: “He who, pressed out, flows all around with a purifying stream—the drop (*indu*), like a horse fit for action”—he performs the *yajyā* with: “It rushes into the jars; it is poured around the filter; it grows through the hymns at the sacrifices.
Then, for the oblations, he uses [the verses] for Agni Pavamāna: “O Agni, you purify the lives” and “O Agni, purify yourself.”
(28.2:346.10) “And may our dear [songs] among the dear ones,” and “These offerings being poured for you”—these are for Sarasvatī, the beloved.
(28.2:346.11) “O Agni, purifier,” and “May he, the purifier, [purify us]”—these are for Pāvaka.
(28.2:346.11) “To him who belongs to all the gods,” and “With truth”—these are for Savitṛ of true impulsion.
(28.2:346.12) “Agni is the most pure in his vows,” and “Up, O Agni, thy pure [flames],” for Śuci.
(28.2:346.13) “Vāyu goes first,” and “O Vāyu, the bright [oblation] is offered to thee,” for Vāyu Niyutvat.
(28.2:346.14) “Thou, O Agni, art the protector of vows,” and “Whatever vows of yours we may violate,” for Vratapati.

(28.2:346.15) “*Pratad te adya*... *kim it te viṣṇo paricakṣyam bhūt*” for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa; (28.2:346.16) “*vaiśvānaro na ūtyā pṛṣṭo divi*” for Vaiśvānara; (28.2:346.17) “*dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam ā dadhikrāḥ*” for Dadhikrāvan.

Then follows the consecration formula after the oblation: "By the sacrifice to the god Agni Pavamāna, may I become pure, cleansed, fit for sacrifice, free from evil, endowed with Vedic luster, and an eater of food. By the sacrifice to the god Agni Pāvaka, to Agni Śuci, to Agni Vratapati, and to Agni Vaiśvānara, may I become pure, cleansed, fit for sacrifice, free from evil, endowed with Vedic luster, and an eater of food.
Regarding the Upāṃśuyāja, it is performed as in the case of the Upāṃśuyāja.

(28.2:347.2) Now, before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers oblations with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) using this entire section beginning, "Pavamāna, the winner of heaven," verse by verse. (28.2:347.3) The two *saṃyājyā* verses are those containing the word "guest" (*atithi*) and those containing the word "house-dweller" (*damūnas*): "May the guest, the house-dweller, be pleased in our home; come to this sacrifice of ours, O wise one.
(28.2:347.5) "O Agni, having struck down all assailants, bring hither the enjoyments of those who act as enemies."
(28.2:347.6) “The domestic one, worthy of being groomed, is groomed in his own home; he is our auspicious guest, praised by sages.
The bull with a thousand horns, possessing such vigor—O Agni, by your power you surpass all others. With these words, the *iḍā* offering is performed in the established manner.
Then, having set down the *anvāhārya* rice, he gives gold as a gift.
The ritual procedure is the same up to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Then, prior to the offering for the *gṛhapati*, he offers oblations with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) using each verse of this section: "Whatever offense against the gods... (*yad devā devaheḍanam*).
This sacrifice concludes with the *pūrṇapātra* libation and the *viṣṇukrama* steps; he releases his vow.
One who has been accused or is being accused should sacrifice with this very [rite].
One should sacrifice with this very [rite] in the event of a transgression of the seasons, a transgression regarding one's wife, or having spilled semen in a non-vaginal place.

With this very [rite] one should sacrifice for a year, or for twenty-one nights consisting of half-footed [verses]. It purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and oneself as the twenty-first, as well as the [sacrificial] row; it purifies kinsmen who have entered the womb of animals, those existing in another birth, and those obstructed by evil deeds. One does not return again. Moreover, they cite this: (28.2:347.13) With this very [rite] one should sacrifice for a year, or for twenty-one nights consisting of half-footed [verses], or for twenty-one nights. (28.2:347.14) It purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and oneself as the twenty-first, as well as the [sacrificial] row; it purifies kinsmen who have entered the womb of animals, those existing in another birth, and those obstructed by evil deeds. One does not return again. (28.2:348.2) And they also cite:
"By performing the Vaiśvānarī, the Vrātapatī, and likewise the Pavitreṣṭi sacrifice at every change of the seasons, one purifies ten generations of one's lineage."
Now, therefore, we shall explain the Nakṣatreṣṭis. "Agni, indeed, desired: 'May I be an eater of food among the gods. These have been explained by the Brāhmaṇa.
That new moon which occurs before the full moon of Vaiśākha coincides with the Apabharaṇīs once a year; on that day one should begin.

On the day of preparation (*upavasatha*) for that [sacrifice], having consigned the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), having moved down [to a new site], having churned out the fire, and having spread the fires, or alternatively, having kept them burning continuously, he should fast either on the full moon or the new moon—or on whichever day the characteristic mark occurs. This is the rule for that occasion: "The sacrificer observes the vow of the remnants of the oblation (*havirucchiṣṭavrata*)," so it is known. Or rather, one who desires long life should perform it under his birth-star (*janmanakṣatra*). The performance may last for as long as one lives, or for a minimum of three years.
He offers the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) containing the word "living" (*jīvat*), with the verses: "O Agni, come to us with fair guidance... and "O Soma, you bestow great fortune.
Then he pours out the oblation-grains, saying: "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni and the Kṛttikās.
He issues the direction: "Sacrifice to Agni and the Kṛttikās!"
(28.3:349.6) He attaches [the formulas] "to Agni an oblation on eight potsherds" and "to Anumati a pap" throughout, in the midst of the oblations for the lunar mansions (nakṣatra).
Having cooked it, he places it down.
For that sacrifice, there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

Between the verses for the fire being kindled (*samidhyamāna*) and the fire already kindled (*samiddha*), he places two glorious *dhāyyā* verses: "Whose self-arisen glories are visible," and "The invincible one who goes before.

He performs the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) with verses containing the words "wealth" (*rayimat*) and "prosperity" (*puṣṭimat*): "By Agni may he obtain wealth," and "Increasing the household, the dispeller of disease.

Then, for the oblations, the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-puronuvākyā*) of the two transitional offerings (*saṃcaryau*) are: "Agni is the head," "Of the world," "May Anumati favor us today," and "O Anumati, you indeed [favor us]."
(28.3:350.1) For the oblation to the lunar mansions, [he recites] "May Agni protect us, the Kṛttikās," according to the traditional text.
Then, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he offers oblations with the wooden spoon (*sruva*), [reciting] "To Agni, svāhā! To the Kṛttikās, svāhā! according to the traditional text.
The two *saṃyājyā* verses contain the word *sviṣṭa*; [the first is] "O bearer of oblations, well-sacrificed."
This sacrifice concludes with the *pūrṇapātra* and the *viṣṇukrama* steps;
[the sacrificer] releases his vow.
(28.4:350.6) Thus, one should sacrifice with each subsequent ritual manual on each successive day;
we shall explain the specific differences.
(28.4:350.7) "<Prajāpati is Savitṛ>"—this [he recites] in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
"For the serpents, for the Āśleṣās, a *karambha* [mixture] in clarified butter"—thus it is said;
all the grains are barley.
At the time of placing [the pot] on the fire, having poured the clarified butter across the strainer and placed it on the fire, he pours the *karambha* grains across the strainer.

"For the Fathers associated with the Maghās, a cake on six potsherds"— by this [formula], the acts of pouring out, sprinkling, placing upon the fire, and mixing [the grains] belonging to the sacrifice to the Fathers are explained. The procedure for the performance of the offering to Soma at the third pressing is explained by [the rules for] the *saumya* oblation.
(28.4:351.1) Now, regarding the statement, "This [milk] is for Vāyu, for Niṣṭyā, the milk of a first-calf cow," the preparation of the milk is like that of the morning milking.
Having sacrificed with the Viśākhās, one should immediately thereafter perform the Full Moon sacrifice with clarified butter.

Then, on the following day, having sacrificed with the subsequent *aṣāḍhā* offerings, [namely] "A pap for Mitra and the Anūrādhas," he should immediately thereafter sacrifice with the *abhijit* offering.
Then, on the following day, [he sacrifices] "A cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu and Śroṇā.
With the subsequent *proṣṭhapada* offerings, [he sacrifices] "A cake on earth-potsherds."
Having traced a mere outline of a potsherd on the ground, he places charcoal upon it; its ritual preparation is like that of a single potsherd.
Having sacrificed with the Āpabharaṇī constellations, he should sacrifice with clarified butter at that very time, on the new moon day.

(28.4:351.8) Then, on the following day, [the injunction is]: "A cake on fifteen potsherds for Candramas when he has become visible. (28.4:351.9) Having brought [the materials] forward during the day, one should perform the offering once the moon has risen.

(28.4:351.10) "They two offered this oblation of cooked rice for the day and night, made of two kinds of rice—white and black—and in the milk of two cows that suckle each other, one white and one black. Thus it is said.
Having led [the victim] forward, one should offer the oblation during the day and perform the ritual after sunset;
or alternatively, one may offer the oblation at the very juncture [of day and night] and perform the ritual at that same juncture.
One should proceed according to the procedure for the offering of the oblation.
(28.4:351.14) Now, regarding the oblation for Uṣas:
one should pour it out at night while still bringing it forward, and perform the offering at dawn.
Then he pours out the oblation for this lunar mansion.
"At the time of the offering, the sacrificer, seated on the sacrificer’s seat, mutters: 'As you are among the gods, so may I be among men.
He should offer after having brought [the oblation] forward during the day; he should proceed once the stars have risen.
Then [he offers] with the formula: 'This pap for Sūrya and for the stars.'"
Having brought [the oblation] inside, he should offer it at night; once the sun has risen, he should proceed.
He sacrifices with the formulas: "Now this pap for Aditi," and "Now this pap for Viṣṇu.
"Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus he finds firm support in the sacrifice itself at the very end," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"It is known from scripture: 'The boon is the sacrificial fee.
Or rather, it is the well-known animal that is excluded."
Having performed the Pāthikṛt sacrifice, one should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices; through the Nakṣatra-sattra, splendor leads to infinity.
Having sacrificed with the Jyotiṣām ayana, one casts off evil and the state of light arises; "he conquers repeated death," so indeed said Baudhāyana.
(28.5:352.11) One should sacrifice with new grain either on the new moon day or the full moon day; or one should offer the Agnihotra with new grain.
(28.5:353.1) Or, having fed the Agnihotra cow with new grain, one should offer the oblation with her milk; or one should offer the morning and evening Agnihotra with gruel made of new grain.
(28.5:353.3) Or, having cooked four śarāva-measures of rice on the Gārhapatya fire, one should offer it to the deities of the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, with Sviṣṭakṛt as the fourth.
Or rather, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas with fresh [grains] alone.

This same procedure for the performance of the *iṣṭi* applies to green barley, *śamī*-grain, cultivated plants, wild herbs, trees, roots, fruits, and vegetables: until one has performed the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, one may eat them according to desire, because there is no inequality in their ripening.
Having sacrificed with rice, one should sacrifice again with rice, not with barley; having sacrificed with barley, one should sacrifice again with barley, not with rice.
Or rather, one may sacrifice with either rice or barley; thus the Āgrayaṇa offerings are completed.

(28.6:354.1) Now, therefore, we shall explain the expiations for the sacrificial animal. (28.6:354.1) If the animal, once dedicated, should bleat, he offers this [oblation] with the verse, "That which is beyond the reach of dust... and then offers a second, occasional oblation with the verse: "From whatever you fear, O Bleater, protect us; from that, grant us freedom from fear. Be gracious to all our offspring. Homage to Rudra, the Bountiful! Svāhā! (28.6:354.4) Thus.

(28.6:354.5) “Because of fear from whom you trembled most, fled, were recognized, voided excrement, or passed urine”—in these circumstances, he offers the third oblation with: “Homage to him who did this; to him, svāhā!

(28.6:354.7) If he should sit down, having offered the oblation with: “Because of fear from whom he sat down,” he should make him rise with the staff of Maitrāvaruṇa or with another staff made of Udumbara wood.
(28.6:354.8) “The Udumbara is strength; cattle are strength. By means of strength, he wins for him strength and cattle,” so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"Arise, O bull!"—with these words [he addresses] the bull;
"Arise, O horse!"—with these words the horse; "Arise, O goat!"—with these words the goat.
With the verse, "The ram," he [offers] a ram;
with the verse, "Up for the bull," a cow.

If it should die prior to the carrying of fire around it, one should perform whatever expiation exists for the Aśvamedha, and then sacrifice another animal of the same deity, the same color, the same age, the same appearance, and the same species.

For that [sacrifice], everything beginning with the *upākaraṇa* is repeated, with the exception of the fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*), the *sāmidhenī* verses, the remainder of the *samidh* offerings, the *āghāra* libations, the *saṃpraiṣa*, the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*), the *pravara*, and the *prayāja* offerings.

Now, if one should not find an animal of that same species, [it is said]: "Goats, sheep, cows, and horses are substitutes for one another. Of these, the goat and the ram are to be offered at the *upākaraṇa*.
If [the prescribed animal] is not available, he should sacrifice one of the others.
The ritual procedure for the offering to Tvaṣṭṛ has been explained.
Then he causes its body to enter the waters with two verses: "Verily, you do not die here... and "Thee, the hope of hopes... all the quarters... (RV 10.16.3; 7.100.3).

(28.7:355.5) Now, if the animal is deficient in a limb, whether in form or color, one should offer oblations to Agni, to Agni-Viṣṇu, to Indra, to Vāyu, and to Prajāpati, and then dedicate that very animal. (28.7:355.7) Now, if a hawk should snatch away or cause the loss of the omentum while it is being brought forward, one should take four spoonfuls of ghee, place gold within the vessel, and offer it in the Āhavanīya fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "The well-winged bird shines forth, encompassing all; golden-bellied, seven-headed, he is in the east."
(28.7:355.10) "The All-pervading One has entered all worlds; find a path for the sacrificer in this sacrifice, Svāhā!
(28.7:355.11) Now, whatever fatty substance may remain in place of this omentum, having cut that out, he should proceed with it.
(28.7:356.1) And if he should find it again, he need not pay further heed to it.

Now, if the omentum, the sacrificial offering, or a portion thereof should be spilled, he takes it up with the verse: "I have taken you for glory and for heroism; O inviolable ones, may you bestow upon us sensory power and milk," and offers it with: "That drop of yours, that surge of yours, the divine banner which has entered the entire world—protect us for our safety, Svāhā!"
