(28.7:356.5) Now, if a bird should perch on the *caṣāla* while the animal sacrifice has not yet been completed, one should wash the *caṣāla*, sprinkle the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and offer an oblation with clarified butter in the same manner: "Flow away or speak out for the drinking of Soma; find a path for the sacrificer in this sacrifice, Svāhā! Thus.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the observances for the interval between the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. His observance is this:
he does not speak untruth.
He does not eat meat,
he does not approach a woman,
and they do not wash his garment with alkaline salt.
Drinking from vessels not made of clay, avoiding the leavings of a Śūdra,
he washes his own feet and does not eat salt.
(28.8:356.12) He shall not engage in usury, except for sesame seeds. (28.8:356.13) He shall not sleep on a couch,
nor shall he approach a woman.
(28.8:356.13) He may, at his pleasure, approach his wife during her season, provided he has not yet fathered a son.
(28.8:356.14) At both times, he undertakes the vow beginning with honey;
(28.8:357.1) "He eats honey," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
This is said to be "clarified butter" (*ghṛta*);
it is known as "divine honey" (*daivyaṃ madhu*). [As it is said:
"O Lord of the Forest, those seeking the gods anoint you with divine honey at the sacrifice."
One should not eat the leavings of another;
one should not perform the priestly office for another;
one should not apply ointments.
He should not anoint himself;
he should not eat at a *śrāddha* feast; he should not have his hair shaved.
He does not brush his teeth; he does not clip his nails.
At will, however, he may have his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved on the festival days (*parvan*).
"One should discontinue [the vow] every four months," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
After a year, they prescribe the very same vow as that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, provided that the time for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has not passed.
If it should pass, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vratapati.
That Prasiddheṣṭi concludes with the time of the new moon; thus the [proper] times have been explained.
In the event of a lapse of these times due to misfortune, one should perform the sacrifice.

(28.9:358.1) Now, therefore, we shall explain the expiations for the consecration (*dīkṣā*) of the *adhvara* sacrifice. (28.9:358.1) If one who is consecrated should speak untruth, he should mutter these four verses addressed to Varuṇa: "Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa," "That I implore of thee," "Thou, O Agni, art our lord," and "So thou, O Agni, art our lord. (28.9:358.3) If he is separated from his black antelope skin or his staff, he should mutter: "The sacrifice has gone to the gods, to the people; may the blessing of the sacrifice protect me from there. May prosperity increase through curds and ghee; may the sacrifice release the lord of the sacrifice from distress."
(28.9:358.5) "Having seen something impure or undesirable, he mutters [the following]"—this has been stated.
(28.9:358.6) "When it has rained upon him, or while it is raining, he mutters"—this has been stated.

(28.9:358.7) Having performed his vow and sipped water, he mutters: "O waters, may you be auspicious when drunk; may you be very gracious in our womb and belly. Rich in nourishment, free from disease, and sinless, be a blessing for our life. Thus.
Having vomited or spat out [the food], he mutters: "Whatever of my essence (*rasa*) here I have spat out, being unrestrained—may Agni, Soma, and the Earth restore that to me within myself.
(28.9:358.11) He consecrates the spilled semen with: "That semen of mine which you have cast away through excessive passion, I take that back again, as one takes up the *agnihotra* with Soma."

When about to urinate or defecate, he takes a clod of earth from the ground, saying: "This is your sacrificial body. He then places the clod back down, saying: "I release the waters, not my offspring; released from distress, go to the earth, consecrated by Svāhā!
Be united with the earth!"

"O waters named *bībhatsā*, consecrated by *svāhā*, enter the earth!"—thus [he offers] the tears. "O waters named *kaphasyā*, consecrated by *svāhā*, enter the earth!"—thus [he offers] the phlegm. "O waters named *tapasyā*, consecrated by *svāhā*, enter the earth!"—thus [he offers] the sweat.

Having seen a bad dream, he mutters: "The bad dream turns back, away from the evil dream and from misfortune. I, as the Brahman, create a barrier between [it and me]; for one does not fasten on a dream. Having eaten food in a dream, he mutters: "The food that is eaten at night does not satisfy hunger in the morning. May all that not harm us; for it is not seen by day."
Seeing blood flow out, or having scratched himself, he mutters: "Homage to the waters belonging to Rudra; svāhā!
While it is raining, he should not run.
If he should run, he should mutter this verse: "Homage to Rudra, the lord of the dwelling-place."

One should not associate with another who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*). If one should associate [with such a person], he should mutter this verse: "With what [splendor] has the wondrous one shone upon us? If the sun rises or sets while he is away from the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), he should mutter: "May the god Sūrya protect me from the gods. Thus, indeed, Baudhāyana says that these expiations (*prāyaścitta*) apply to all consecrations for the *adhvara* sacrifice.
Śālīki says [the sacrifice should be performed] up until the release of the intermediate consecration.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the expiations for all sacrifices.

(28.10:360.5) In all cases where the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) has been spilled, cut, split, broken, lost, spoiled, inverted, or deficient; or where it has flowed out, leaked, fallen, or cracked; or when non-twice-born persons, dogs, cats, crows, donkeys, wild animals, domestic animals, birds, reptiles, or other insects have entered between the officiating priests and the fires—one should fill the *sruk* ladle with twelve portions and offer the *durgā*, the *manasvatī*, and the three *mahāvyāhṛti* oblations. [The verse: "We shall press the Soma for Jātavedas; he burns away the wealth of those who act as enemies."
"May he carry us across all difficulties, as Agni carries us across a river with a boat, beyond all misfortunes; Svāhā! (28.10:361.3).

And in the event of a reversal of ritual actions—whether it be merely a mistake in the *mantra* or *brāhmaṇa*, or any reversal regarding the *darbha* grass, fuel, sacrificial grass (*barhis*), enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), separating blades (*vidhṛti*), strainers (*pavitra*), oblation (*havis*), potsherds (*kapāla*), the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the kindling wood (*araṇi*), the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), the water for consecration (*praṇītā*), or the removal of the fire (*agnyudvāsana*)—he offers expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta*) by dipping the *sruva* ladle into the butter-pot (*ājyasthālī*), saying: "To Prajāpati, Svāhā! To Hiraṇyagarbha, Svāhā!"
(28.10:361.7) Then he offers to the Grandfathers with: "To the Lord of the Bhṛgus, svāhā! To the austerity of the Aṅgirases, svāhā!

(28.10:361.8) Then he offers the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*) with: "Bhūḥ! To Agni and to the Earth and to the Great One, svāhā! Bhuvaḥ! To Vāyu and to the Atmosphere and to the Great One, svāhā! Suvaḥ! To Āditya and to the Sky and to the Great One, svāhā! Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! To the Moon and to the Nakṣatras and to the Quarters and to the Great One, svāhā! Thus.
Then he offers the *vyāhṛtis*: "bhūḥ svāhā! bhuvaḥ svāhā! suvaḥ svāhā! bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā! Thus.
If the mantra is deficient or redundant, if it is poorly recited or incorrectly approached;
if the *vaṣaṭ* call is not uttered or has already passed;
if there is a flow of the oblation from the fire, or if the *hotṛ* priest uses a deficient tone—[in these cases, the sacrifice is flawed].
(28.11:362.2) < Also in the case of excessive burning of the oblations; whatever [occurs] upon the breaking of a vessel;

(28.11:362.3) < upon the loss or breaking of a potsherd; when a four-footed animal enters between [the fires]; (28.11:362.4) < upon the destruction of the strainer, or the stirring up of the clarified butter.>
(28.11:362.5) < And there is a transposition of the oblations, and among the officiating priests who have not yet been engaged,
at the time of spreading out the sacrifice when a state of duality has arisen.> (28.11:362.6–7) <The two Mindā oblations are to be offered, followed by the Vyāhṛtis preceded by the Praṇava.>
The *vāruṇī* and *tantumatī* verses, the *anvagni* and *manasvatī*,
the seven *mahāvyāhṛtis*, and likewise those addressed to Prajāpati—
these mantras are proclaimed for the purpose of rejoining the sacrifice.
(28.11:362.11) "For a sacrifice lacking expiation is consumed by the *asuras*.
(28.11:362.12) But a sacrifice consumed by the *asuras* would bring the gods into contact with guilt.
(28.11:363.1) [It deprives] both the officiating priests and the sacrificer of their lifespan and spiritual luster."
"It shall cast away that ill-performed rite; therefore, one should eliminate those defects. Thus it is said.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the favors.
One should offer the evening oblation before sunrise and the morning oblation before sunset, without letting the proper times pass.
It is known from scripture: "The time for the New and Full Moon sacrifices and for the Agnihotra does not fail, nor does it suffer."
The time for the evening oblation should not pass until the time for the morning oblation, nor should the time for the morning oblation pass until the time for the evening oblation.
Now, if it is the evening, having offered the oblation with the formula, "To the evening, to the dwelling, homage, svāhā! he should perform the Agnihotra.
If it is the morning, having offered the oblation with the formula, "To the morning, to the evening, homage, svāhā! he should perform the Agnihotra.

(28.12:363.11) Now, if the Āhavanīya fire should go out after the first oblation has been offered, he should place gold on a piece of wood while reciting, "Fire is in the wood, in the wood is fire," and then offer the subsequent oblation. (28.12:364.2) In cases of the lapse of the proper time, there are oblations for emergencies.

(28.12:364.3) From the time of the New Moon sacrifice, the time for the Full Moon sacrifice must not be exceeded; likewise, from the time of the Full Moon sacrifice, the time for the New Moon sacrifice must not be exceeded.

The time for the Śyāmāka-Āgrayaṇa shall not pass beyond the time for the Vrihi-Āgrayaṇa; the time for the Yava-Āgrayaṇa shall not pass beyond the time for the Vrihi-Āgrayaṇa, the Śyāmāka-Āgrayaṇa, or the Yava-Āgrayaṇa. The time for the Vaiśvadeva shall not pass beyond the time for the Varuṇapraghāsas; the time for the Varuṇapraghāsas shall not pass beyond the Sākamedhas; the time for the Sākamedhas shall not pass beyond the Śunāsīrya; and the time for the Śunāsīrya shall not pass beyond the Vaiśvadeva.

The time for the animal sacrifice of the northern course should not pass beyond the time for the animal sacrifice of the southern course, nor should the time for the animal sacrifice of the southern course pass beyond that of the northern course.
The time for the Jyotiṣṭoma of the later spring should not pass beyond the time for the Jyotiṣṭoma of the earlier spring;
[this applies] until the entire year has passed without a Soma-pressing.
"In former ages, the sages used to practice thus:
every half-month they offered the Agnihotra.
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, in the evening, he draws fourteen portions."
The oblation is offered once;
there is one fuel-stick, one offering, and one act of worship.
(28.12:365.1) He wipes his hands once.
(28.12:365.2) In this same manner in the morning.

(28.12:365.2) Now, for six months, while the *agnihotra* has not been offered, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices have not been performed, and the *āgrayaṇa*, *cāturmāsya*, and *paśubandha* sacrifices have not been performed, he should offer sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) to Agni Pathikṛt, Agni Tantumat, Agni Vaiśvānara, and Agni Vratapati; then, having offered the *agnihotra*, he should perform the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, *āgrayaṇa*, *cāturmāsya*, and *paśubandha* sacrifices.

Then, after a year has passed without having offered the Agnihotra, without having performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa, the Cāturmāsya offerings, or the Animal Sacrifice, he should offer sacrificial cakes to Agni Pavamāna, Agni Pāvaka, Agni Śuci, Agni Pathikṛt, Agni Tantumant, Agni Vaiśvānara, and Agni Vratapati; then, having offered the Agnihotra and performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa, the Cāturmāsya offerings, and the Animal Sacrifice.
Now, for the purpose of the oblations, there are rice and barley;

in their absence, millet (*priyaṅgu*), with the exception of *kodrava*, *udāra*, and *varaka*, as well as *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, bamboo-seeds (*veṇuyava*), *atarasaṃpāka*, tubers, roots, fruits, water, and groats— these are used,
while clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is used for the purpose of the sacrificial fat (*ājya*).
The term "gavya" (derived from the cow) is a specific designation;
if that is unavailable, one should employ buffalo-ghee or [ordinary] clarified butter (*ghṛta*) for the purpose of *ājya*. Some authorities consider it not contradictory to use these in meals.
In the absence of those two, oil is the substitute; in its absence, jartila oil;
and according to the authority of the learned, oils of linseed, safflower, mustard, and tree-fruit may also be used.
(28.13:366.4) Beyond this, in the event that these are unavailable, one should mix barley flour, rice flour, or millet flour with water and use them for the purpose of clarified butter.
(28.13:366.5) Kuśa grass is for the purpose of spreading.

(28.13:366.6) In the absence of these, [one may use] materials made of reeds, kutapa grass, the hair of a sheep’s shoulder, muñja grass, sugandhitejana, arjuna, dāra, dūrvā grass, millet, milky trees, or sugarcane—[from among] these.

The *prastara*, *barhis*, *vidhṛti*, *pavitra*, *yūpa*, *raśanā*, *paristaraṇa*, *antardhāna*, *āsana*, *śayana*, and materials for the *stotra* and *upākaraṇa* should be made from all kinds of grasses, excluding dry *śuṇṭhi*, *nalava*, *balbaka*, black cotton-plant fibers, and wild grasses. The *vedhas* should be made of *pālāśa* or *khadira* wood; if these are unavailable, it may be made from any one of the sacrificial trees. If even those are unavailable, [it may be made from other woods], excluding *aralu*, *kapittha*, *kovidāra*, *śalmali*, *śleṣmātaka*, *nīpa*, *nimba*, *tilaka*, *vādhaka*, *vibhītaka*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *karañja*, and *palāṇḍu*.
Some say that the fuel for all the trees [of the forest] is used;
at the time of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), one should give a cow, gold, or a garment; if these are not available, one should give fruits, roots, or edible foods.

But one must certainly not fail to sacrifice: "One should be constantly engaged in the obligatory rites (*nitya*) as well as in the occasional ones (*ājasrika*); for him by whom the obligatory rites have been omitted, as well as the occasional ones..."

"One who stands on a wrong path does not go to heaven, for he has fallen. Therefore, one should always perform the obligatory rites with roots, fruits, honey, or meat, and one must never let the obligatory rites lapse."
And one should not cause the eternal [rites] to be omitted.

(29.1:368.1) Now, if the *sadas* and *havirdhāna* sheds are burnt, they should be constructed either with the same enclosure as the entire sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) or without an enclosure; according to the opinion of Vādhūlaka, one should first take the *vasatīvarī* waters.
Then the others [the fires] should be taken in their proper sequence.

(29.1:368.3) Now, if all the oblations should fall when the potsherds have broken, there one should take as much clay as is available, mix it with the *vasatīvarī* waters, pour it out, and proceed; in that case, as an expiation, one should offer an oblation with one of the *graha* formulas.

If the *agnīdhrīya* fire-altar is destroyed, one should offer an oblation with a verse addressed to Agni: "Agni is the head of heaven. With a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, namely "O Viṣṇu, you are our nearest," [one offers] in the *havirdhāna* shed.
With a verse addressed to Agni, namely "This Agni [is the lord] of thousands," [one offers] in the offering-spoons (*sruk*).
With the verse addressed to Vāyu, "O Vāyu, [accept] a hundred of thy bay steeds," he offers on the Vāyavya cups;
with the verse addressed to Indra, "All have magnified Indra," he offers in the *sadas*;
and with the verse addressed to the Viśvedevas, "O Viśvedevas, hear this my invocation," he offers on the *prāg-aṃśa* cup.
In all these cases, one should offer the two *mindā* oblations and the *vyāhṛti*s.
Alternatively, one who has suffered a loss should perform an *iṣṭi*: the *kṣāmavatī* when the house is burned; the *tantumatī* in the event of total destruction;

and the *dagdhā* when the *soma* plants have been burnt or lost, or when there is damage to or theft of the *soma*. In such instances, having taken as many stalks as are available and having mixed them with the *vasatīvarī* waters, one should press them and proceed with the ritual.
(29.1:369.5) Having pressed [the Soma] with all-destroying herbs, one should proceed;
having performed that, one should sacrifice again—such is the Śruti.
One should act in this very manner.
"That is the expiation."

(29.2:369.8) Now, if one of the *hotṛ*-priests should urge another, or if they should perform the sacrifice for one another using each other’s *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses, there is an expiation for that. (29.2:369.10) With the first [verse] of this section beginning with "The Brāhmaṇa is the single Hotṛ," the Adhvaryu should offer for the Hotṛ; with the second, for the Maitrāvaruṇa; with the third, for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; with the fourth, for the Potṛ; with the fifth, for the Neṣṭṛ; with the sixth, for the Acchāvāka; and with the seventh, for the Agnīdh. If the Adhvaryu, having failed to utter the name of the principal deity, should utter it in the place of another, [this expiation applies].

(29.2:369.13) With the verse, "Whatever, O gods, I may have transgressed," he should offer a spoonful of oblation. (29.2:369.14) He should perform the previously mentioned expiation with the eighth and ninth [verses] consisting of ten [syllables].

(29.2:370.1) During the Ukthya rounds, he should offer according to the sequence; with the tenth [verse], [he offers] for the Ṣoḍaśin and the Saṃdhi belonging to the Rathantara from the rounds of the night.

Likewise in the Śipiviṣṭa-stotra at the Vājapeya, and likewise in the *atirikta*-stotras, if another should sacrifice as prescribed, the first [priest] should sacrifice or recite; if he himself is enjoined, he alone should sacrifice. In the case of the Soma sacrifice, the second [priest] would be the one for whom the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies. In other cases, one should act thus: the Hotṛ should sacrifice with another [verse], and the Maitrāvaruṇa likewise; or else the previously mentioned expiation should be performed.
Likewise, if the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses are used otherwise, there would be a different expiation.

(29.2:370.7) Now, during the food-oblations of the Aśvamedha, if there is a deficiency, excess, repetition, or contradiction regarding the spoonfuls for the wild animals, one should offer two *mindā* oblations. (29.2:370.9) The same applies when laying down the bricks.

Furthermore, if one should employ a different seed-grain for the oblations of the *devasū* than that belonging to the respective deity, one should abandon that [offering], produce it again, and sacrifice.
One should sacrifice with what remains, or recite it;
or one should perform the previously mentioned expiation.
Now, when the sacrificial rite has been commenced, we shall explain the expiations (*prāyaścitta*).
In that regard, if the medicinal herbs, milk, the animal victim, *soma*, or clarified butter are deficient, lost, or stolen, one should produce them again and take them up.
Wherever one remembers [the omission], the production [of the substance] occurs prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

(29.3:371.4) If one should remember [the correct deity] after the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he should conclude that rite and sacrifice again with this very same [offering], or he may sacrifice together [with the other]. (29.3:371.5) Now, if one should remember [the error] after having poured out [the oblation], he should divide it for another deity, saying, “For such-and-such thee,” touch it, and then offer the whole, saying, “To such-and-such, svāhā! (29.3:371.6) Wherever one should remember [the error], there he should act in this very manner until the placing [of the oblation].

(29.3:371.7) Now, if one should remember [the omission] after having set down the oblation, one should offer it in its proper place after bringing it forward; or one should perform another previously mentioned expiation (*prāyaścitta*). If other deities have been sacrificed to, or if the materials are lost or spoiled, or if the ritual procedure (*tantra*) has become defective, one should repeat the principal rite (*pradhāna*); the entire sacrifice (*sarveṣṭi*) must be performed without remainder.
(29.3:371.10) What is the commencement of that rite?
Having performed the rites beginning with the taking of the winnowing basket for the deity entitled to the portion, and having cooked and set down the offering, one should proceed in its own place.

In that case, as an expiation, one should offer the two *mindā* oblations and the *vyāhṛtis*. Likewise, regarding the animal sacrifice, from the moment of dedication (*upākaraṇa*) until the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, one should perform the previously mentioned expiation.
Now, if the sun should rise while the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) has not yet been commenced, what is the expiation for that? [One should recite:
"May Uṣas with her banner favor the sacrifice accompanied by the gods."
Having offered the two *mindā* oblations with the formula, “To the gods, the most honeyed, svāhā! and having offered the *vyāhṛti*s, he should perform the *upākaraṇa*.

Now, if the sun should rise while the *prātaranuvāka* is being recited, he should offer spoon-oblations (*sruvāhuti*) with these [verses]: “Up from the darkness,” “Up that one,” and “The bright one. Now, if the Soma should not be visible, he should offer spoon-oblations with these two [verses]: “He becomes ever new as he is born,” and “The stalk which the Ādityas cause to swell.”
If an eclipse of the sun or the moon occurs, this very [rite] is to be performed.

(29.4:372.11) Now, if one who is about to draw the cups (*graha*) should draw from the womb-vessel (*yoni*) without having first drawn for the deity who is the rightful recipient, he should at that very moment offer everything with the formula: "To such-and-such, svāhā!
(29.4:372.13) Having drawn again for the rightful recipient, he should offer the two *mindā* oblations.

Or alternatively, he may offer with one of the cups; or he may offer all the cups belonging to the *hotraka*s with the formulas beginning, "O Lord of Speech, Vidhe, Nāman," etc., whether in the cups or in the goblets (*camasa*), provided that no defect previously mentioned regarding the sacrificial food has occurred.

Likewise, having consumed water and offered that expiation, he should take [the draught] again and offer it; or, having poured it back into the cups, he should offer it. Or, having offered it, he should place gold within it, pour water into it, and consume it. That itself is the expiation from that point. Now, if the time for the pressing should pass, he should offer at the morning pressing with the first *gāyatrī* verse of the section beginning, "Agni is the head of heaven."
Likewise, with the *triṣṭubh* metre at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*),
and likewise with the *jagatī* metre at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*).
Beyond this, one should not reach the subsequent day of the *atirātra*.

If he should go away, a failure of the sacrifice would occur; in that case, as an expiation, he should offer oblations for all the *hotṛ* priests. It is known from scripture: "The *caturhotṛ* formulas are indeed the Brahman."
Therefore, one should offer the Caturhotṛ formulas from that point onward; one need not keep track of the number of days in the case of one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*).
Now follows the expiation for the *savanīya* offerings.
If they should have a putrid odor, one should discard them, produce new ones, and proceed with the rite.
Alternatively, having washed it with hot water, placed it in clarified butter, and cooked it again, he should proceed with the ritual.
Even in that case, if a putrid odor should arise, he should discard it, produce it anew, and proceed.
The same applies to the *puroḍāśa* cakes of the *savanīya* offerings.
Likewise regarding the *sāṃnāyya* offerings:
now, if one should omit a *stotra*, a *śastra*, or a *pratigara*, one should offer the two *mindāhuti* oblations and then recite the introductory formula (*upākuryāt*).

Now, if one should omit a single *stotrīyā* verse, a hymn (*sūkta*), a *varcas*, a half-verse (*ardharca*), or a *pratigara*, one should offer the two *mindāhuti* oblations and then mutter [the following].
(29.4:374.3) From the beginning of the *stotra* until the oblation, he should restrain his speech.
(29.4:374.4) If he should release his speech, he should mutter a verse addressed to Viṣṇu.
(29.4:374.5) Furthermore, if he should release his speech after having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he should mutter a verse addressed to Viṣṇu: "O Viṣṇu, you are our nearest [kinsman]."
Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ* again, he should sacrifice.
In cases of deficiency, excess, repetition, contradiction, or other such errors, one should offer the *mindāhutī* as an expiation;
for the scripture states that the *mindāhutī* are the body of the sacrifice in all instances.
Therefore, this is the commendable view of all the teachers.

(29.5:374.10) Now, if the two *soma* offerings, the offered and the unoffered, should become mixed, one should draw out embers from the Āhavanīya fire toward the north and offer upon them: "O Indra and Agni, you two are the seasonal priests of the sacrifice and of consciousness.
Be satisfied with the offered and the unoffered, with the unoffered and the offered, with both the offered and the unoffered, and with both the unoffered and the offered."

"O Indra and Agni, enjoy this Soma; drink it, take pleasure in it—svāhā! With these words, he follows it with his regular formula for consuming: "May darkness not find the sacrificer, nor the priests, nor these offspring. May he who drinks this Soma [be spared]; both [portions] have been made mixed together."
(29.5:374.16) Now, if cups offered by one person were to be mixed with those offered by another, or if one were to pour soma over soma, this same [penance] applies.

(29.5:375.2) Furthermore, if officiating priests engaged by one person were to be mixed with those engaged by another, or if initiated persons were to be mixed with other initiated persons—except in the case of the Vrātyastoma and the Sattra—this same [penance] applies.

Now, if the pressed Soma should be rained upon, he offers two spoonfuls with these two verses: "That very place," and "To him who desires to drink. Having offered them, he follows it with his regular formula for consuming: "The drop has gone to the drop; Indra has drunk of the drop.
Of that [Soma] of yours, O Drop, which was drunk by Indra, which is honeyed and invited, I, being invited, partake."

(29.5:375.7) Now, if the sacrificer should die or fear should come upon him when the Soma has been pressed, he should place all the oblations together in a single vessel, pour the Soma into the *droṇakalaśa*, the clarified butter into the *juhū* ladle, and the animal victim into another; thus he should offer a single oblation with [the verse]: "O gods, to whom this portion belongs, to whom belong the *prayāja*s as well as the *anūyāja*s."

Having offered with the formula, "Svāhā to the gods who have Indra as their chief, Varuṇa as their king, and Agni as their hotṛ," one should thereafter proceed with the rites pertaining to the funeral fire (*paitṛmedhika*). Alternatively, one may sacrifice again when free from danger.
For one who is aged or incapable of performing the duties of the *agnihotra*, the enkindling of the fires within oneself (*ātman*) is prescribed.

When the fires have been mounted upon himself, he should not eat, he should not drink, he should not sleep on a raised bed, he should not immerse himself in water, and he should not engage in sexual intercourse. Alternatively, he may eat at will, drink at will, and indeed sleep on a raised bed; however, he must never immerse himself in water nor engage in sexual intercourse.

Having washed his hands and feet and sipped water, sitting facing the east, he should consume a small amount with the *agnihotra-yajus* formula and then consume more silently while meditating on Prajāpati in his mind.
In this very manner, one should worship until the liberation of the sun from its splendor.
Now, indeed, it is said:

"Just as a son who is born dies, even so does he die whose *ukhya* fire goes out. If he were to produce a fire by friction (*nirmanthya*), he would cause a rupture and would bring forth a rival for himself."
(29.6:376.9) "That very same one is to be girt again. (29.6:376.9) "He generates him from his own womb;
he does not generate a rival for him," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

If the fire-pan (*ukhyā*) should go out, one should cast its ashes into water, smear the pan with a lump of dung, rekindle it once more, hand it over, and having made it capable of bearing oblations, he then makes offerings over it with *sruva*-ladles, saying: "Like heaven is the Gharma, Svāhā! Like heaven is the Arka, Svāhā! Like heaven is the Śukra, Svāhā! Like heaven is the Jyotis, Svāhā! Like heaven is the Sūrya, Svāhā! Thus.
With the two verses beginning with *arkavatī*, he places two *arka* fuel-sticks on the fire, reciting: "The *arka* is the purifier; the purifier is the *arka*, the measurer of the mid-region.
(29.6:377.2) He should proceed with the ritual beginning from the nest of *muñja* grass up until the speech over the black antelope skin.
Now, it is indeed said:
"Darkness indeed seizes him whose fire in the *ukhya* [pot] goes out;
death is darkness.
A black garment and a black cow are the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Thus it is said.
He gives a black garment, a black cow, and gold weighing a hundred mānas.
"By means of darkness itself he strikes away darkness, death";
moreover, gold is indeed brilliance.
"He places brilliance within himself," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, if a couch, a sling, or a house should be burned, one should add fuel-sticks with the verses addressed to Vaiśvānara, using this eight-verse hymn beginning with: "Vaiśvānara, for our aid..."

(29.6:377.8) Now, if the *vasatīvarī* water-jar, the *pānnejana* vessel, the *ekadhana* jars, the *kumbheṣṭakā* bricks, or the *kvathaneṣṭakā* bricks should be spilled; or if the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) should break, the girdle (*raśanā*) should snap, the *caṣāla* top-ring should break, the *audumbarī* post should break, a pressing stone (*grāvan*) should break, the *droṇakalaśa* trough should crack, or any other vessel made of wood or clay should break during the sacrifice—having set it down in its own place with its own *yajus*-formula and having placed it there, he consecrates it [with the formula]: "Bhūs! Āyur..."
"Support my breath; support my life-force; support my offspring; support my cattle; let not my life, breath, offspring, and cattle be spilled away.

(29.6:378.2) Now, if the vessel is made of wood, he should throw it into the Āhavanīya fire; but if it is made of clay, he should cast it into the water with the verse: "The earth has gone to the earth; the mother has gone back to her mother. May we abound in sons and cattle; may he who hates us be shattered. (29.6:378.4)
Now, therefore, we shall explain the worldly procedure for the Agnihotra.

Before the Agnihotra, they consign the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) from the Gārhapatya fire with [the verse]: "This is thy seasonal womb. Having placed the two kindling woods within the altar, one should offer the oblation in the worldly fire.
"It is known from scripture: 'In the evening he draws [the fire] out after having offered the evening oblation; in the morning he draws it out after having offered the morning oblation.
Now, the Agnihotra is omitted by four [rites]: the *homa*, the *upasthāna*, the *vrata*, and the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
Having performed the *tantumati* sacrifice, one should perform the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices."
The rite concludes with the expiation for the interruption performed.
Now, regarding the combination of *agnihotra* offerings in times of distress:

it occurs when there is the upheaval of a kingdom, diseases, travel on a journey, residence in the teacher’s house, the unavailability of place, time, or materials, or when one is unable to perform them due to other circumstances. In such cases, what is the procedure for that ritual?

One may perform it at will in the forenoon, or in the afternoon, or at the time of the *agnihotra*, according to the sūtra, or as is well known, until the sacrificer gives the command (*prasava*). Once commanded, on the first day of the lunar fortnight in the evening, he takes fourteen portions of four spoonfuls each; on the day of the fast (*upavasatha*) or at the *parvan* sacrifice, fifteen.
All the ritual acts from the kindling of the wood onwards are performed as is well known.
Having concluded the mantras as a single unit and having offered the evening *agnihotra* oblations, he should offer the morning *agnihotra* oblations;
the commencement is in the evening and the conclusion is in the morning.
At the time of the *pārvaṇa* sacrifice, he should not sacrifice.
(29.8:379.10) There is no occasion for a compound [of these terms] beyond the [mention of] "occasional" (*pākṣika*), nor for one who lacks faith.
(29.8:379.10) Moreover, they cite this:
(29.8:380.1) "Lack of faith is the supreme evil; for evil is said to be ignorance."
(29.8:380.2) "Through ignorance, dharma is lost; one whose dharma is lost is considered base.
(29.8:380.3) By faith the intellect is purified; by faith the mind is purified. (29.8:380.4) By faith Brahman is attained; faith is the destroyer of sin."
Therefore, one who possesses faith and avoids excessive attachment should sacrifice to Tantumatī when the proper time has arrived.
Thus it is for worldly activities, thus for what has not been offered, and thus in the event of a transgression of the rules.
Moreover, they cite this: "One should not extinguish the fires in vain, nor except in times of distress."

"(29.8:380.7) <(cont) He who extinguishes the fire is indeed a slayer of the heroes of the gods>. Thus, for one who has faith and is not distracted by other pursuits, even elsewhere: "(29.8:380.10) <Whichever specific minor [details] are observed in whatever [context],>"
(29.8:380.11) "One should perform [the rites] upon the sacrificial bed with those [implements], so that it may be endowed with correctness.
(29.8:380.12) For him who, while his own scripture exists, proceeds according to another's scripture—
(29.8:380.13) for him who thus despises his own scripture, it is equal to the murder of an embryo."
"The instructions for one's own Vedic school belong to the lineage of the ṛṣis and are equal in authority to those [of other schools] through their shared qualities;
they should be employed for the purpose of investigating ritual acts and for the sake of completing them in times of distress. Thus it is said.

(29.9:381.1) Regarding this point—that he may travel abroad for an unlimited time, but not beyond a year—it is stated without qualification that this refers specifically to the husband and wife who have maintained the sacred fires; and it is known from scripture: "The wife is indeed half of one's own self.

(29.9:381.2–3) Now, if while the sacrificer is away on a journey some occasion for the wife’s departure should arise, then the Adhvaryu, having offered the oblation to Vāstoṣpati, should consign the fires by reciting: "This is thy seasonal womb."
Wherever he may go, he should take the fire there.

Having reached that place, having churned the fire, and having arranged the sacrificial fires, he melts the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire, purifies it, takes four portions in the offering-spoon, and offers the *saṃtanī* oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: "May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it join together this severed sacrifice.
Those dawns and those sunsets which have passed—those I unite with the oblation of clarified butter, Svāhā! (29.9:381.9). Thus.
Then he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Tantumat; he gives a shallow wooden cup as the sacrificial fee; that well-known sacrifice is thus completed.

(29.9:381.12) Now, if both the sacrificer and his wife should depart [from the hermitage] and dwell at the edge of a village or at the boundary of a village, the Agnihotra alone would be lost; he should perform the Agnyādheya in its unmodified form.
(29.9:381.14) While carrying the fires, they must not breathe over them; if they were to breathe over them, the fires would become worldly (laukika).

(29.9:381.15) One need not pay heed to the cart when the fires have been mounted upon it, because of the precedent seen in the case of the Sattra sacrifice at the distance of a throw of the wooden pin (śamyā-prāsa).

Now, it is indeed said: "He who, having added fuel to the fires, undertakes the vow, places all his desires within the fire; if he were to depart without having sacrificed, [he would lose them]. Thus it is said.

When he is about to depart without having performed the sacrifice, he melts clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, purifies it, takes four portions in the ladle, and offers it into the *āhavanīya* fire while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, [reciting]: "To thee, O best of the Aṅgirases..."
(29.10:382.5) “If the fire goes out for one who has established the sacred fires and entered upon the vow”—this has been explained previously.

(29.10:382.6) “If the fire of one who has established the sacred fires goes out, as far as he might pierce with a pin—if it should go out that far—he should collect it [rekindle it] with the mantra: ‘This is one for thee; yonder is one for thee. (29.10:382.8) Having collected it, he should throw it back into the fire at the times for the *agnihotra* or at other times.
"If the [enemy] should retreat further away, one should advance after him and halt.
One should indeed advance and halt; wherever he halts, there they should dismantle the fires.
"Verily, the plants enter the milk of the cattle of that man whose calves, having been driven away for the sake of the oblation, suckle [their mothers]."
"If he were to milk them, he would sacrifice with an exhausted oblation; if he were not to milk them, he would omit a limb of the sacrifice. Therefore, one should offer a barley gruel to Vāyu."

Then, having had these [cows] milked, having poured water into that [vessel], and having completed the rites beginning with the pouring of rice, from this point onward—now, regarding him whose evening-milk offering has met with misfortune, it is said: "Having set aside rice for Indra, he should fast. Having performed the ritual up to the point of the setting aside of the grain, on the following day, having performed the rite for Agni, he should perform the rite for Indra.

One should prepare that place for boiling. Now, regarding the rule: "If both sacrificial offerings (*havis*) of one should meet with disaster, he should offer five *śarāva*-measures of boiled rice to Indra"—should he offer it according to the original model (*prakṛti*), or with a *śarāva* measure?
Some say that one should offer according to the original model, saying "a *śarāva* [is for the purpose of measuring]" so as to indicate the measure of a *śarāva*;
likewise, they say one should offer using four vessels.
In this case, one should indeed offer in a single vessel and perform it in place of the *sāṃnāyya*.
"If on the day of the vow (*vrātya-ahan*) the wife becomes menstruating (*anālambhukā*), one should perform the sacrifice after having excluded her.
Thus, one should indeed perform the sacrifice after excluding her;
"he sacrifices with the entire sacrifice. Having sacrificed to her, he should call out to her: "I am so-and-so. This is the mantra for approaching her during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*).
One should perform the sacrifice, beginning from the adding of fuel to the fires, without excluding anyone; the same applies to sacrifices lasting a single day.

Now, if [blood] appears during the *dīkṣā* or *upasad* rites, or likewise on other days of a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), or even when three days have passed, it is known from the tradition: "Having said, 'Cut it away! one washes the blood with cow's urine mixed with warm water and purifies [the person] with bunches of *darbha* grass. It is further known: "The *darbha* grasses are indeed the waters; by them one becomes purified after bathing. And: "For he remains having assumed the color of the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*)."
Therefore, one should neither look at nor touch the sacrificial oblation.
Then, when ten days have passed since the birth of the woman who has given birth, having performed the purification as prescribed, one should employ the wife in the ritual duties;
her son or a student (*brahmacārī*) should perform that work.
The sacrificer should mutter that mantra.
If the wife should be unwell, he should have it performed in this very same manner.
Now, if there should be no milk when the *sāṃnāyya* or the *gharma* has begun, he should, by whatever means possible, cause some milk to be milked, mix it with water, and proceed with the rite.
One must not bring in other milk and perform [the rite]; that itself is the expiation for that.
Now, if she becomes unfit for contact after beginning the establishment of the *soma* fire but before the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, and does not offer the *agnihotra*, [this is the rule].
When three days have passed, the procedure from the initiation by water onwards is established; from that point forward [the ritual continues].
Now, if she becomes untouchable before the milking for the vow-milk, she should eat sacrificial food for three days.
If she becomes untouchable after the vow-milk has been milked, she should simply consume sacrificial food as her vow-food, having poured it into water.
When three days have elapsed, the procedure beginning with cow’s urine is established; from that point onward [the rite proceeds].

Now, if she should become menstruating before the *pravargya* ceremony, one should not perform the *pravargya*; rather, having performed the purification starting from the sacrificial oblation (*havirya*) as prescribed, the procedure beginning with cow’s urine is established from that point onward. Now, if she becomes menstruating after the *pravargya* has been commenced, one should conclude that day with only the sacrificial oblation; when three days have elapsed, the procedure beginning with cow’s urine is established from that point onward.

Then, following the summons: "O consecrated one, restrain your speech! O observer of the vow, restrain your speech! O wife, restrain your speech!"—from that point on, beginning with the single-breast [offering], she remains untouchable until the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). Having performed the rites up to the *avabhṛtha*, when three days have elapsed, they go down for the *avabhṛtha*.
On the day of the Soma-pressing, he should sit down after having enclosed the *mārjālīya* shed which is strewn with sand.
On other days, he should sit down in the *patnīśālā* itself.
One should not enter the *prāgvaṃśa* shed.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the compendium of expiations (*prāyaścitta-samuccaya*). In all cases where no specific rule has been prescribed, one should offer the *manasvatī*, the two *mindā* oblations, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *hotṛ* formulas. In all instances of violating the vows, one should offer the two *mindā* oblations; in the case of the omission of the *pitṛyajña*, one should perform the *saptahotṛ* offering as an expiation.

(29.12:385.13) Now, if at the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) they should all go away leaving the *aupāsana* fire behind, he should offer a spoonful (*sruvāhuti*) with the verse, "May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle thee again," and then perform the domestic rites (*gṛhyakarmāṇi*) in a common (*laukika*) fire, provided that half [of the fire] remains. (29.12:386.1) But if the *brahmaudana* fire has been maintained, it should be treated like the *aupāsana* fire. Likewise, if the fire goes out after cooking, one should offer the *jaya* oblations and the others.

(29.12:386.3) Now, if the sun should rise while the Gārhapatya fire has not yet been established, one should begin from the very beginning and establish it at whatever time is appropriate; if the fire is extinguished in the middle, this same rule applies. (29.12:386.5) Furthermore, if one should find his wife in her season, this same rule applies until the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is given. (29.12:386.6) From that point onward, there is exclusion [from ritual duties] in the Agnihotra, in the Soma sacrifice, in the Avabhṛtha bath and other rites, and in all Iṣṭis, Paśubandhas, and Soma sacrifices; either the wife is excluded for that duration, or she is excluded from everything.
Now, if both the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires should go out while the sun sets or rises, the expiation for that is the re-establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*).
Some say it is the re-consecration (*punarādheya*). Furthermore, if the wife goes outside the boundary, there is the re-consecration.

Now, if one should practice what is contrary to the vow while the fires have been consigned within oneself, or if the fault mentioned regarding the destruction of the *araṇis* should occur, the re-establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) must be performed;
for it has been stated that by the destruction of the *araṇis*, the destruction of the fires follows.

Furthermore, if they should carry the fires across the boundary of the village or across a river, the two [the sacrificer and his wife] should maintain contact with these very fires as they are being carried.
When the sacrificer is away on a journey, the wife does not go; there is no expiation for this.
If the Anvāhāryapacana fire should go out while its source is different, one should fetch it from its original source or from separate fire-sticks.

Now, if a cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) rolls away, the Adhvaryu should set it back in its place with the words: "Follow the path of Prajāpati. The sacrificer consecrates it with these two verses: "I am established in power, established in the kingdom; the other has increased everything.
He should offer two spoonfuls with these two verses: "Heaven has settled upon the earth; he has been born, he has procreated."
When [the sacrifice] has been completed, one should perform the Vaiśvānara offering.
It is known from scripture: "If he should step forward [toward the east], he would conquer the world of the gods;
if toward the south, the world of the ancestors."

"If [the oblation] were offered toward the west, the *rakṣases* would destroy the sacrifice; if toward the north, one would conquer the world of men; therefore, it should be offered while firmly established."
(29.13:387.11) Now, if either the animal sacrifice or the Soma sacrifice should be omitted, one should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice and then sacrifice again.

(29.13:387.12) If the entire day of the *sutyā* should be passed over, or if those who have taken hold of one another should be separated before the sitting down [for the meal], one should complete the rite and sacrifice again.
(29.13:387.13) "One initiated for the Soma sacrifice shall not give gifts, nor offer oblations, nor cook food, nor recite prayers."
(29.13:387.14) "One should divide [the sacrificial fees] from the very beginning," they say.
(29.13:387.14) One who is engaged in a vow must not bathe, nor plunge into water, nor discard his garment, nor wash away the dust [from his body].

(29.13:388.2) In all cases, they prescribe a vow for the sacrificer and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as long as the ritual action lasts; however, no other priestly function (*ārtvijya*) exists apart from that of the officiating priests. There is no collective performance (*samāsa*) by the great officiating priests (*mahartvij*), nor is there any priestly function for the sacrificer in any case except during a *sattra* sacrifice.

In all *soma* sacrifices, when there is an omission of the *soma*, a lapse of time, an interruption, a transposition, an intermixture, a combination, or other such defects—whether known or unknown—one should offer the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblations by dipping with the *sruva* spoon from the *ājyasthālī* before the *samiṣṭayajus*.
Some say [one should offer] the *jayas*;
others say the *abhyātānas*.
Some say [they are] the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings;
some say [they are] the *amātya* oblations; some say [they are] the *chandas* meters.
Some say [the verses] are dedicated to Sūrya; some say they are "tanūs";
some say they are the "hotṛ" verses.
Some say they consist of ten [verses];
some say they are the *pauruṣīs*;
others say they are the *vaiṣṇavīs*.
Some say [he should recite] the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
some say the Vyāhṛtis;
others say the Prājāpatyā.
Some say [he should recite] the syllable *praṇava*; the Teacher says he should recite all [the names]; the Teacher says he should recite all.
Now, regarding these fire-altar constructions (*agnicaya*), we shall explain the measurements and the layout of their ground.
Furthermore, as for the measurement of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*): fourteen atoms (*aṇu*) and thirty-four flat, closely joined sesame seeds (*tila*) constitute another [definition].
Ten *aṅgulas* constitute a small foot (*kṣudrapada*).
Twelve [of these] constitute a span (*prādeśa*), which is wider by one in the subsequent pair when thirteen [are used].
The footprint is fifteen [units].
The pole is one hundred and eighty-eight; the axle is four hundred;
the yoke is eighty-six.
The knee is thirty-two [finger-breadths], the two arms extended by the *śamyā* are thirty-six,
and a step (*prakrama*) consists of two feet.
Two *prādeśas* make one *aratni*.

Furthermore, they cite this: "In matters of measurement, one may proceed as one desires regarding the *pada*, the *yuga*, the *prakrama*, the *aratni*, and the *śamyā*. A man is five *aratnis* in height, as is a *vyāma*.
The vyāyāma is four aratnis in length. One who wishes to construct a square, having made a cord of the required length with loops at both ends, makes a mark in the middle;
having drawn a line, he should drive a peg into the middle of that line.
Having fastened the two loops on that [cord], one should mark out the circle with a reference point.
One should drive stakes at the ends of the diameter;
having fastened the loop on the eastern stake, one should mark out the circle with the cord.
In the same way on the other side.
Where the two [measures] should meet, one should stretch the second *viṣkambha* cord;
one should drive stakes at the two ends of the *viṣkambha*.
Having fastened the cord at the eastern point, one should trace a circle around it by means of a mark.
Likewise to the south, likewise to the west, and likewise to the north.
The points where those [circles] meet at their extremities constitute a square.
Now, another [method]:
having made a cord twice the measure [of the side] with loops at both ends, he makes a mark in the middle;
that is for the purpose of the east.
On the other half, at a point one-fourth part from the end, he makes a mark; that is the *nyañcana*,
for the sake of the shoulder-line (*aṃsa*).
Having fastened the two loops at the ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord, one should mark out the hips and shoulders by means of a downward pull using the southern half of the cord.
Desiring to construct a long square, one should drive two stakes into the ground over as much space as one intends to measure;
there should be two stakes on each side of every single [side], equidistant from one another.
Having made a cord as long as the cross-measure with loops at both ends, he makes a mark in the middle.
Having fastened the two loops to the two last pegs of the eastern side, he pulls it southward along the mark and makes a mark upon the mark.
Having fastened the two loops to the middle peg, he pulls it southward above the mark and should drive a peg into the ground upon the mark.
This is the shoulder;
by this, the upper shoulder is explained,
as are the two hips.
Where one would measure out a longer side in front, there he makes a mark at half that length.

Then, having made another cord one and a half times the measurement with loops at both ends, he makes a mark on the third part beyond the sixth division on the other side; that [mark] is turned downwards.
For the sake of the shoulder [of the altar] when it has been measured out:
having fastened the two loops at the ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord, one should carry away the hips and shoulders toward the south by means of a diagonal shift.
A diagonal cord of a square of equal sides makes a space twice as large.
The measurement is across.
The length of the *vikaraṇī* is its diagonal cord; it is three times the [unit] cord.
The third operation is explained by this [same principle].
As for the ninth part of the ground,

it is said that the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayārajju*) of a long quadrangle performs both functions that the side-measuring cord (*pārśvamānī*) and the cross-measuring cord (*tiryaṅmānī*) perform when they are separate.

Their attainment occurs in these [combinations]: the triad and tetrad, the twelvefold and fivefold, the fifteenfold and eightfold, the sevenfold and twenty-fourfold, the twelvefold and thirty-fivefold, and the fifteenfold and thirty-sixfold.
When combining two unequal squares, one should mark off the diagonal of the larger square with the side-measure of the smaller one.
The diagonal cord of the marked-off portion becomes the side-measure of the two combined squares.
When one wishes to subtract a square from a square, one should mark off the diagonal of the larger square with the side-measure of the portion one intends to subtract.
One should extend the side-measure of the *vṛdhra* diagonally along the other side;
where it falls, there one should cut it off. By means of what has been cut off, [the excess] is removed.

If one wishes to make a square that is equal on all sides out of a rectangle, one should cut off a diagonal portion from it, divide that part into two, and place them along the two sides as appropriate.
Alternatively, having combined this square with another square, one should cut off a portion using its diagonal measure; what remains should be placed upon the other.

If one wishes to make a square that is equal on all sides out of a rectangle, one should make the transverse measuring-line the side-measure, divide the remainder into two, and place them along the two sides.
One should fill that gap with an insertion (*āvāpa*);
the removal of that has been explained.

Desiring to make one side of a square smaller, one should take the diagonal measuring-line (*karaṇī*) of the smaller side as the transverse measuring-line, divide the remainder diagonally, transpose it, and place it on the other side.

One desiring to construct a square *prauga* should, having made a rectangular area twice as large as that which one intends to make into a square, drive a peg into the middle of the eastern side-line.
Having fastened two loops to that peg, one should fix them at the southern and northern corners.
One should then cut away the outer cord.

One desiring to construct a quadrangular altar with a *prauga* on both sides should, having made a rectangular area twice as long as the desired length, drive a peg into the middle of the eastern side-line.
Having fastened two loops to that peg, one should drop them at the central points of the southern and northern sides.
One should cut off the outer cord; by this, the other *prauga* is explained.
(30.2:392.9) One desiring to make a square from a circle should strike a diagonal line from the center toward the east.
(30.2:392.10) Whatever remains, one should trace the circle using a cord equal to three parts of that remainder.

(30.2:392.11) One desiring to make a circle from a square should divide the diameter into eight parts, subdivide one part into twenty-nine parts, and set aside twenty-eight parts, as well as the sixth part of a part minus one-eighth.
Alternatively, having divided [the area] into fifteen parts, one should set aside two;
this is the variable side-measure for making a square. One should increase the measurement by a third part, and that by a fourth part less a thirty-fourth part, which is the specific increment.

Now, regarding the sacrificial enclosure for the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*), the location of the *āhavanīya* fire is from the *gārhapatya*. It is known from scripture: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish his fire at eight *prakramas*, a Rājanya at eleven, and a Vaiśya at twelve.
One should cause three squares to be made, following one after another, each being one-third of the total length.
The Gārhapatya fire is at the western left hip;
the Anvāhāryapacana fire is on its southern shoulder; and the Āhavanīya fire is on the northern shoulder of the eastern [altar].

Alternatively, having divided the space between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires into five or six parts, and having added an additional sixth or seventh part to make them equal, he divides it into three equal portions and makes a mark at the end of the first two portions from the front.
Having fixed the two ends of the cord between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires, he extends it toward the south by means of a mark and drives a peg into the ground at that mark;
this becomes the location for the Dakṣiṇā fire. Alternatively, one may extend the measurement by a fifth part.
Having divided all that into five parts, he makes a mark at two of the parts from the further end.
Having fastened loops at the two ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord and having pulled it southward by means of the mark, he drives a peg into the mark;
that becomes the location for the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*).

By this, the *utkara* [mound] has been explained as being inverted. "To the west of the Āhavanīya fire, it is as high as the sacrificer"—this is known from the *Vedi* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
One-third less than that [height] is its transverse measurement at the back.
Half of that same [side] is laid out as a transverse line at the front.
Having thus laid out a long quadrangle that is narrow on one side, one should drive stakes into the corners.
Having made a cord twice the length of the side-measure with loops at both ends, one makes a mark in the middle.

Having fastened the two loops on the two southern sides and having pulled [the cord] southward along the mark, one should drive a peg into the mark. Having fastened the two loops onto that peg, one should trace around the southern side using the mark.
By this, the northern side is explained.
With that [line] doubled, he should trace around the eastern side;
likewise the other [side].
"Ten paces long from west to east, twelve paces long from south to north, and eight paces long from east to west"—thus it is known regarding the altar for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*).
The measurement-yoga for her has been explained. According to some, she is equal to a chariot; according to others, she is perfect as a *virāj*.

"It is a four-cornered [altar] measuring one *śamyā*," thus it is known regarding the *uttaravedi*, because there is no specification to the contrary that it is a square. "The altar is three parts wide," thus it is known regarding the *paitṛkī vedi*.
"The third side of the great altar, which has been made into a perfect square, becomes the third *karaṇī*.
Thus it is said; however, the ninth part of the ground becomes [the measure], according to some, it is four-cornered and equal to the height of the sacrificer.
The corners are formed in the cardinal directions.
They prescribe the Sautrāmaṇī altar as one-third of the Veda;
when the Mahāvedi is made into a square, its side-measure consists of eighteen paces when calculated as one-third of the Mahāvedi.
Regarding that [altar], one may act according to one's desire with respect to its long side and the side provided with a single small corner.
The *prāgvaṃśa* hall is sixteen steps in length and twelve in width;
or alternatively, it may be twelve steps in length and ten in width.
In its center is the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) measuring twelve steps.

"The cross-line at the back consists of thirty paces or steps; the line extending eastward is thirty-six, and the cross-line at the front is twenty-four. Thus it is known regarding the Mahāvedi, and its method of measurement has been explained. The Mahāvedi extends six paces from the Āhavanīya fire.
Then, in one of the *sadas* sheds,
that [measuring] group of ten [cords] is [placed];
it is twenty-seven *aratnis* long, directed toward the north.
According to some, there are eighteen;
from those, the *havirdhāna* [sheds] are placed in four,
making that group of ten or twelve.
The measurement-yoga for those two has been explained.

Leaving half a prakrama beyond the peg at the sacrificial post-hole, one measures out the northern altar (*uttaravedi*), according to the injunction in the *Soma* ritual: "The northern altar is ten paces."
The measurement-yoke for it has been explained. The *cātvāla* pit is either the size of a *śamyā* or of unlimited size.
Then there are the *uparava* pits, with openings one span wide and intervals between them of one span.
Having marked out a square measuring one *aratni* on all four sides, one should drive stakes into its corners.
With intervals of half a *prādeśa* each, one should trace a circle around each [stake].
Leaving a space of two *prakramas* from the eastern half of the *sadas*, the diameter of the *dhiṣṇya* hearths shall be two *prādeśas*.
Likewise, the intermediate spaces.
The side-measure of the Āgnīdhra shed is five *aratnis*.
By this, the Mārjālīya shed is explained.
They make its door face north.
"The sacrificial post-holes are at intervals equal to the axle of a chariot," so it is known in the case of the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice.
From that [measurement], one should take a twenty-fourth part of ten chariot-axles, eleven foot-steps, and eight finger-breadths.
That shall be the basic step (*prakrama*).
With it he measures out the altar (*vedi*).
Now, in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, one should take twenty axle-lengths of chariots, twenty-one foot-steps, and the twenty-fourth part of eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
That shall be the basic step;
with it he measures out the altar.

Then, from the eastern half of the altar, having cut off a piece measuring half a foot in width for the sake of the eleven sacrificial posts in the eastern row, he should place it in front, facing eastward.
In this case, there is no eight-finger-breadth [measurement], nor is there any interlocking.
The sacrificial post-holes have a width of one *pada*, and the upper parts of the posts have a circumference of three *padas*.
The first fire-altar consists of seven and a half men; the second consists of eight and a half men; the third consists of nine and a half men.
In this way, the practice of increasing the number of parts proceeds from elevenfold;

that [series] begins at sevenfold and ends at one hundred and onefold. Beyond this, one should take up only those sacrifices of one hundred and onefold [parts], or one should perform fireless sacrificial rites, except for the Aśvamedha.
If he should bring back the Aśvamedha before it has been completed, from that point onward he should practice the ritual procedure (*vidhā*) and pay no heed to anything else.
If he should bring it back after it has passed [the completion], having brought it back, he should resume it precisely from the point where it was interrupted.
How, indeed, should he practice the ritual procedure?
Whatever else there is beyond the *prakṛti*, one should divide that into fifteen parts; having laid it out, one should combine two parts for each layer (*vidhā*).
With those [parts], which amount to seven and a half, one should pile the fire-altar.
Some authorities prescribe that the height should be increased by a twenty-fourth part of the fifth knee-height.
Now, some indeed pile the altars starting from the one-cell [citi] upwards without wings or tail;
that is not tenable, because it contradicts what precedes and what follows.
Furthermore, regarding this, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage for some: "The first layer of the fires is the Śyena-pile."
(30.5:397.7) Now, as for others [they say]: "Having piled a larger [altar], one should not pile a smaller one.
(30.5:397.8) But as for us: "It becomes winged."
"For that which has no wings is not fit to fly.
By means of a cubit, the two wings become longer. Therefore, birds are called 'pakṣapravayas' (those whose wings extend)."
(30.5:397.10) "The two wings and the tail are each one fathom in length.

(30.5:397.11) Thus, there exists no hawk without wings and a tail; nor do wings and a tail exist for that which is not sevenfold; nor does the sevenfold altar result in the contingency of being singlefold.
Therefore, the first fire-altar consists of exactly seven layers.
One should avoid the divisions;
for they teach that "divisions" refer to the joining of the lower and upper sides.
That [measurement] is not found at the ends of the fire-altars, nor on the corners or sides.
"One building it for the first time should build a *sāhasra*," so it is said;
thus, one should fulfill the number in the fifth layer if one intends to build two hundred [bricks], and one should understand the *nākasad* bricks to be of equal number with the five-ribbed ones.
Agni, indeed, has the nature of a sacrificial animal.

Just as, for a sacrificial animal, that which is the right side of the right ribs is the left side of the left ribs, and that which is the left side of the left ribs is the right side of the right ribs; and what is both downward and upward is the same—so should he lay down the forms of the bricks. Those lines which turn to the right, he should lay down on the south; those which turn to the left, on the north.
The straight lines run both from behind and from the front, while there are three intersecting lines in the middle.

Now, as for those bricks situated in the interspaces: one should understand their placement to be such that they do not extend beyond on one side, nor on the other, just as the backbone of an animal does not protrude on either flank.
Moreover, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage:
"Prajāpati is indeed Atharvan; Agni is Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa; his bones are the bricks.
Therefore, if one were to pile up the body externally, one should join it together from the center of the body-covering by means of the centers of the body-coverings of the limbs.
"One piles this [fire-altar] facing east," so it is known.
One should not complete the count with non-clay bricks that are not *iṣṭakās*.
This is because of the Brāhmaṇa passage: "One fire-altar consists of *iṣṭakās*, while another consists of animals."

"This Agni is indeed an animal, and this sacrificial formula (*yajus*) which is recited prior to the laying of the bricks is indeed the transformation of the womb of the animal. Thus, one should place materials that cause distress to living beings within the pits.
One should recognize the marks on the bricks as the "circle," the "bull," and the "Vikarṇī."
(30.6:399.5) Since the bricks and the formulas are not distinct from the bricks themselves, they result in *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks because there is no fixed measure.
(30.6:399.6) One should place here only those groups of bricks already mentioned:
five *lokaṃpṛṇā*s.
(30.6:399.7) When there is no mantra, one should place pebbles smeared with butter at the joints.
(30.6:399.8) The statement regarding the "flow" (*rīti*) in the case of groups [of bricks], such as "he places them facing east" or "he places them facing west," is a description of the flow.
(30.6:399.9) The statement "he places one facing east" or "he places one facing west" is a description of the agent's orientation.
He places some bricks facing west in the east and others facing east in the west; this constitutes the completion.
This applies specifically to those bricks that are square.
One should not place a broken brick;
one should not place a cracked brick;
one should not place a black brick.
One should not place a worn-out brick.
One should not place a *lakṣmaṇā* brick.
One should not place a *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick on a self-built altar.
One should determine the vertical measurement of the bricks by means of the fifth part of the knee;
likewise for the *nākasad* bricks and those with five *coḍā*s.
Whatever may be diminished through drying or baking, that one should fill up with *purīṣa*, because there is no fixed measure for the *purīṣa*.
"It is of the measure of a man's stride," so it is known from the Gārhapatya altar;
according to some, it is square, and according to others, it is circular.
Having divided the square into seven parts, one should divide it transversely into three parts.
In the subsequent layer, one lays down the bricks running northwards;
if they are to be laid down as equal squares, one should have the bricks made with the sixth part of the diagonal as the fourth and the third [parts].
Of those, he places nine in the first row and twelve in the second in the eastern layout;
five in the third row and sixteen in the first in the western layout.
Having made a square as large as possible within a circular space, one should divide it into nine parts, arranging the *pradhīs* in groups of three each.
One should lay out another layer in such a way that the corners fall upon the *pradhyanīka* bricks.
The *dhiṣṇya* hearths are built in a single layer and are either square or circular.
Having divided the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth into nine parts, one should place a stone in the place of one of those parts.
Then, having divided the *dhiṣṇya* of the Hotṛ into nine parts, one should divide each of the three eastern parts into two.
Then, having divided the others into nine parts each, one should combine the middle and the easternmost two parts.
Then, having divided the *mārjālīya* into three parts, one should divide the eastern and western parts into five parts each.
"One should have bricks made by mixing them with the ashes of the fire-pan (ukhya)," it is said.
This applies only to one who has maintained the fire for a full year, not to one who has maintained it for only a night.
In this way, his construction of the layers is accompanied by the sacred formulas.
One may pile the *chandaścit* beyond three thousand [bricks], according to one's desire for distinction;
its form is that of a hawk.
Now, it is indeed said: "One who desires heaven should pile the Śyena-cit.
Thus, there is a twofold variety of form.
It is known from the Brāhmaṇa that it has both a four-cornered nature and the form of a falcon;
"He places five bricks on the southern hip and five on the northern."
He places [the brick] on the right shoulder with the words, "The goat is the age"; on the left with, "The bull is the age";
and he places [the brick] on the right wing with, "The tiger is the age."
"‘The lion is the age,’ [he says] over the northern [stones];
‘Man is the age,’ [he says] over the middle one. And thus it is said.
Now, another [instruction].
"This Agni is built as a likeness of birds," so it is said;
the meaning is "by means of the shadow of those that fly up.
"He piles the fire with equal squares for the sake of distinguishing between the divine and the human," so says the Maitrāyaṇīya Brāhmaṇa.
One should have bricks made for it [the fire-altar] in the fourth, fifth, sixth, and tenth parts of a man's height.
Then one measures out the fire-altar:
as long as a man with upraised arms is, so long he makes two holes in the bamboo pole at equal intervals, with the third hole in the middle.
What he performs there with the *spandayā* (the vibrating cord), that he performs here with the bamboo pole.
Its body is a square of equal sides, measuring four *puruṣas*; each wing is a square of equal sides, measuring one *puruṣa*.
But it is longer by one *aratni* on the right side; by this, the left wing is explained.
The tail is a square of one *puruṣa*.
One should extend it by one span from below;
thus, with the addition of the *aratni* and the span, the sevenfold altar is completed.
During the laying of the bricks, on the third man’s line to the north of the wing-tip, there are four fifth-sized bricks; on both sides of these, there are two foot-bricks each.
Then, there are eight fourths;
one should cover the remainder of the wing with six-part bricks.
By this, the northern wing is explained.
One should lay down four-part bricks on the two sides of the tail, both at the front and the back.
On the south and north [sides], one should place foot-bricks.
One should cover the remainder of the altar with fifth-part bricks.
This is the first layer consisting of two hundred bricks.
In the subsequent layer, one should lay down the bricks in reverse order: three sixty-brick units and two two-brick units at each half-measure-mark to the north of the tip of the wing;
likewise on the northern side.
On the southern hip, nine squares of sixty finger-breadths each are marked out, and likewise on the northern hip.
One should lay down nine squares of sixty finger-breadths each from the southern shoulder and the northern shoulder, alternating two by two with two-footed squares.

(30.8:402.14) He should cover the remaining space with fire-altar bricks having five parts. This is the two-hundred-brick layer; he should pile them in alternating fashion for as many layers as he intends to construct.
Furthermore,
there are five [fingers] of a man; these same [fingers], taken together, are one and a half.
Of these, some are for the arghya-water and some for the foot-washing water.
On the two side-wings of the front and back [sections], one should lay half-iṣṭakās pointing northward;
likewise on the northern [side].

On the southern and northern sides of the tail, four and four half-bricks are laid facing north. Below the tail, four half-bricks are laid facing north; on both sides of these, two foot-bricks are placed.
Along the rear of the two points where the tail joins, he should place one half-brick each, oriented eastward.
He should cover the remainder of the fire-altar with bricks measuring a fifth part.
This is the two-hundred-brick layering.
In the subsequent layer, one should place four foot-bricks on the body-ridges;
around them, two half-bricks each; and five in the eastern face.
At the tips of the two wings, one should lay three bricks each, measuring one and a half [units], facing north.
In the intervals between them, one should place a single half-brick each, facing east. One should cover the remainder of the fire-altar with bricks measuring a fifth part.
This is the two-hundred-brick layering.
One should pile them in alternating fashion for as many layers as one intends to construct.
Now, for one with curved wings and a fanned-out tail,
he should have bricks made that are one-fourth of a man's height; of these,
some are half-sized and some are one-quarter-sized.
In the absence of a specific instruction, the cutting [of the bricks] should always be diagonal.
One should enclose the foot-bricks with four [parts]: with a quarter-part, a full part, a one-and-a-half part, and a part with a specific addition.
One should have the half-brick made in such a way that those two [halves] would be long and closely joined together.
Then he measures out the fire-altar.
Its body is two puruṣas in length and ten paces in width. From its southern shoulder, he makes a mark one and a half prakramas to the north.
In the same way from the other side, having fastened a cord over those two, one should cut off the shoulder.
By this, the cutting off of the other corners is explained.
That self is the head, measuring five and a half padas in length and half a puruṣa in width.
One should cut off its two shoulders at every successive prakrama.
The tail [of the altar] is six padas long from east to west and two puruṣas wide from north to south. One should cut off its two eastern corners by three prakramas each.
The wing is twelve padas in length and ten padas in width.
From the middle of that [space], having stepped six paces toward the east, one should drive in a peg.
[One should drive] one peg at each of the two hips; then one should enclose it with a cord.
Having cut off the inner vibration, one should place it in front, facing eastward;
that is the *nirṇāma*.
By this, the *nirṇāma* of the northern wing is explained.
Having made five square sections, each measuring one *prakrama*, along the tips of the two wings, one should cut them off diagonally toward the bottom and remove the halves.
In this way, the sevenfold altar, including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, is completed.
During the laying down of the bricks, one should place the fourth brick at the end of the head.
In front, there is a haṃsamukhī brick; on both sides of it, two foot-bricks;
below those two, three square foot-bricks on each side; and the remaining spaces are filled with foot-bricks.
Alternatively, one should place the Haṃsamukhī brick at the front of the head; below that, one should place the fourth brick on both sides of the two foot-bricks;
and below those, on both sides, three square-foot bricks each.
In the remaining spaces, one should lay down the foot-bricks (pādeṣṭakā).
Below the head, one should lay down five foot-bricks interlaced; likewise in front of the tail.
Whatever has been cut off, in that [space] one should lay half-bricks and quarter-bricks.
One should cover the remainder of the fire-altar with fourth-part bricks;
one should complete the count with quarter-bricks and half-bricks.
This is the two-hundred-brick arrangement (*prastāra*).
In the subsequent arrangement, one should join four *haṃsamukhī* bricks with four *pādeṣṭakā* bricks so that it becomes a long quadrangle (*dīrghacaturaśra*).
One should then place that [quadrangle] crosswise in the space of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.

Two chief *haṃsa*-bricks, facing west, are placed at the junction of the tail and the body with one half-brick each. Below them, on both sides, one should place three foot-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*) facing east.
Below the tail, one should place fifteen foot-bricks interlaced with one another.
One should pile the wings and tail with bricks measuring one-quarter and half-bricks, laid out facing east in alternating fashion.
In the space where there is a deficiency, one should place half-bricks and quarter-bricks;
the remainder of the fire-altar should be covered with fourth-part bricks.
