One should complete the count with [the verses] beginning with "pādyābhiḥ" and "sārdhyābhiḥ."
Now, furthermore, another [calculation]:
by means of the fifth parts of a man, one hundred and eighty-seven and a half [parts] constitute the sevenfold [altar] including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*.
Of those, fifty-two are in the self.
He should place three and a half bricks on the head, fifteen on the tail,
and fifty-eight and a half on the right wing.
Then, regarding the northern [side]:
the corners are cut off by half a vyāyāma;
the tail is curved.
One should cut away [the wings] at intervals of three *aratnis* on both sides. One should fashion six feathers with each of the one-and-a-half [cubits].
The shape of the head is constant.
Now, the modifications of the bricks:
there are five [finger-breadths] for the person; these same [fingers] are one and a half on one side.

These same [bricks] on one side are with a quarter [of a finger-breadth], [namely] those belonging to the fifth-part brick, those with a quarter, and those with a half; likewise those with a full and a half.
And one should join the eighth parts of those two in such a way that three sides are formed;
these ten are the eighth parts of the fifth-part brick.
One should lay down the fifth-part bricks with half-bricks upon the body; likewise, one should lay down the one-and-a-half bricks with half-bricks upon the tail and the two wings.
Those [bricks] which are produced on the head:
in the subsequent layer, one should place one of each pair upon each of the two ends of the wings from the previous [layer], and one of each pair upon each of the two [ends] of the other [wings];
two [bricks] each on both sides of the head.
Below the tail, there are one and a half [bricks] facing east as much space as available;
on the two sides, there are quarter-bricks increased by an eighth part; and on the two wings, there are one and a half bricks with their fractional parts.
The remainder he should arrange according to what is appropriate, according to the numerical order, and in accordance with the Dharma.
By this, the Kaṅkacit fire-altar, including its self and tail, has been explained.
One should place five bricks on the head;
its form has been explained.
One should place fifty-seven [bricks] on the right wing and likewise on the left; the bending of the two wings is by means of the span together with the *prādeśa*.
One should fashion six leaves each with pieces measuring one-fifth and one-half [of the span]. One and a half [spans] remain;
with that, one makes two feet at the lower part of the tail, measuring one cubit in length, separated by an interval of one cubit, and one span in width.
Below those two, on both sides, one should place two-eighths each, with their divisions facing east.
In this way, the sevenfold altar, including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, is completed.
Now follow the modifications regarding the bricks.

The fifth-part bricks (*pañcamabhāgīyāḥ*) have fractional parts; one should enclose a quarter-brick (*pādeṣṭakā*) with four [units]: half-a-prādeśa, one and a half prādeśas, one prādeśa, and a prādeśa plus a fraction.
One should enclose a one-and-a-half brick (*adhyardheṣṭakā*) with four [units]: half a vyāyāma, two *aratnis*, and an *aratni* plus a fraction.
These are six;
having laid down four square-foot bricks with an eighth part added to each foot, one should lay down the remainder as appropriate, according to the number, and in accordance with the rule.
By this [method], the head and the tail of the *alaja-cit* are explained; having removed the two feet,
one should place sixty-three bricks on the right wing and likewise on the left.
The man bends down at the two wings.
From this bending, having measured out an aratni toward the east, he fixes a peg there and should extend the cutting of the feathers of the other wing along it.
In this manner, five [lines] are raised for each fifth day.

Having laid down a foot-brick with its corner turned away, one should remove from those bricks four square-foot portions and one-eighth parts, and then lay down the remainder as appropriate, according to number, and in accordance with the rule.
"One should pile the *prauga* altar," it is said.

Having made the *prauga* as large as the fire-altar itself, including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, one should have twelve bricks made from its rear diagonal cord (*karaṇī*), with half that measure as their width; of these, some are half-sized and some are quarter-sized.
Of those [bricks], one should place two half-iṣṭakas with their special parts facing outward at the chin, and two full iṣṭakas at the two ends;
the remainder of the fire-altar he should cover with *bṛhatī* bricks.
He should complete the required number with half-iṣṭakas.
In the subsequent layer, in the subsequent row, one should lay forty-seven foot-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*) interlaced.

One [foot-brick] should be placed on the chin; four others, which are long, should be placed on the *śūlapādī* brick, and four more should be placed in the space of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, with two half-bricks at the two ends.
One should cover the remaining space of the fire-altar with large bricks (bṛhatī) laid facing eastward;
one should complete the required number with half-bricks (ardheṣṭakā).
"One should pile the *ubhayataḥprauga*," it is said.
Having made the *ubhayataḥprauga* as large as the fire-altar including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, the transverse measures for the ninth layer are stated as variations of the *prauga*-piling.
The same applies to the *upadhāna* layer. In the subsequent layer, one should place two *pādeṣṭakās* at the two jaws (*cubuka*), and two long *pādyā* bricks at the ends of the joints.
One should place four [bricks]—both the long and the others—in the space for the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks, and two *ardhyā* bricks at the two ends.
One should cover the remaining fire-altar with large bricks (*bṛhatī*) laid facing east;
one should complete the required number with half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*).
"One should pile it in the form of a chariot wheel," so it is known.
Now, there are indeed two kinds of chariot wheels: those with solid hubs and those joined with rims. Since no distinction is specified, we consider them both to be intended.
"The shape of one or the other.
Then he measures out the fire-altar:

having made a circular area of ground as large as the fire-altar itself plus an *aratni* and a *prādeśa*, and having made a square of equal sides within that space as far as possible, he should have twelve bricks made from the diagonal of that square.
Having laid down six of those [bricks] along the spines (*pradhī*), one should divide the remainder into eight parts.
One should lay out the subsequent layer in such a way that the corners (*srakti*) fall upon the spines.
Now, another [layer].
From half a man's height, one should have fifteen bricks made, equal squares for the purpose of measurement;
two hundred and twenty-five of these, together with a *aratni* and a *prādeśa*, result in the sevenfold [altar].
Among those, one should insert another sixty-four.
With those [lines] he makes it a perfect square.
Of that [square], sixteen bricks form the side-measure;
thirty-three remain over.
With those [spokes] one should enclose the ends on all sides;
the hub consists of sixteen middle sections,
and there are sixty-four spokes.
The altar is sixty-four [square units].
The navel is the remainder; one should trace around the navel at its outer limit.

Having drawn a circle around the rim both from the outside and from the inside, one should divide the space between the rim and the hub into thirty-two parts and mark off the divisions in reverse order.
In this way, the *avāpa* is marked out.
Having divided the rim into sixty-four parts and having drawn lines across it, one should draw [the pattern] in the center.
These amount to one hundred and twenty-eight.
One should divide the spokes into four parts each and the nave into eight parts. This is the first layout.
In the subsequent layout, one should draw the navel toward the edge at the fourth turn, and the rim inward from within.
Having made sixty-four [divisions] from within the rim, one should mark them out;
the division of the spokes is fivefold up to the two points of convergence.
On the rim, two [bricks] are placed in each interval; on the hub, one in each interval.
Whatever remains of the hub, that he should divide into eight parts.
This is the sixteenfold construction, the essence of the chariot-wheel altar.
"One should pile the *droṇacit*," so it is known. Now, there are indeed two kinds of *droṇas*: square and circular.
Because there is no distinction [stated], we consider them both.
"The form of one or the other.
Then he measures out the fire-altar;
its body becomes four-cornered.
Its three men, less by one-third, constitute the side-measurement; its rear handle is one and a half men and ten finger-breadths long, extending eastward.

(30.17:410.4) "A man less by one-third [is the measure] towards the north. (30.17:410.4) In this way, the sevenfold [altar], together with the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, is completed. (30.17:410.5) Now follow the modifications of the bricks.
The sixths of a man are those [same measures] taken together as one and a half;
their halves are the transverse divisions, which are the fourths of a man.
Having laid down sixty-six bricks each in the space between the handle and the buttock of those [bricks], one should cover the remaining fire-altar with *bṛhatī* bricks.
One should complete the count with half-bricks.
On the subsequent layer, one should lay down a brick measuring one and a half units on the southern shoulder, oriented toward the north.
Likewise, in the northern [section],
one should place the bricks measuring six parts in the eastern row;
in the southern and northern [rows], those measuring four parts.
In front of the *tsaru*, one should place two *caturbhāgīyā*s on the two sides.
Below those, on both sides, one should place two *adhyardha*s extending in opposite directions (*viṣūcī*). Below those, in the middle region, one should place two *ṣaṣṭhī*s facing eastward.
One should cover the remaining fire-altar with Bṛhatī bricks laid facing eastward;
one should complete the count with half-bricks.
Now, another [method]:
a man’s height of one hundred and twenty finger-breadths, including the span of the arms and the forearms, becomes sevenfold.
Having removed one of those [parts], he makes the remainder circular.
That has been explained by the preceding [section] regarding the chariot-wheel-shaped altar (*rathacakracit*).
Having placed the *ṣoḍaśī* brick in front and having fixed it, one should trace a circle together with it. Whatever portion is cut off from below, that one should place in the front.
The division of the *pradhīs* is sevenfold;
the widths of the steps at the middle of the *pradhīs* are equal to the side of the square. One should complete the count by means of half-units for those that are square.
In the subsequent layer, having placed the middle brick of the rim on the edge, one should divide that which is below it into two parts. This is the circular *droṇacit* consisting of nine courses.
The *samūhya* and *paricāyya* have been explained previously by means of the chariot-wheel altar (*rathacakracit*).
Having caused pits to be dug for the *cātvālas* in the various directions of the *samūhya*, one should collect the earth from them and pile it up.
In the case of the *paricāyya*, there is a distinction in the locations of the bricks; one should enclose that [fire-altar] with all [the bricks] in a clockwise direction.
"One should pile the *śmaśānacit*," so it is known.
Having divided the entire fire-altar into fifteen square sections, their laying out has been explained.
Having laid out a long rectangle with a width of half a section using three sections, one should draw lines from the center of the eastern side toward the two corners and remove the outer ends.
Its division is tenfold;
those twenty [bricks] constitute the entire Agni.
On the subsequent layer, one should divide [the space] lengthwise in the middle of the *prauga*.
Its division is sixfold; one should place two of those parts on the two sides.
One should have [the remaining parts] made with a length of one-third of a part and a width of one-fourth.
Of those bricks, the half-sized ones are the transverse divisions;
having placed them at the two ends, one should cover the remaining fire-altar with large bricks laid lengthwise.
One should complete the count with half-bricks.
One should increase the height of the fire-altar by one-fifth.
Having divided that entire measurement into three parts, one should have bricks made from one-fourth, one-ninth, or one-fourteenth of two of those parts.
Having laid down four, nine, or fourteen layers with those [bricks], one should cut off the remainder diagonally from above and set aside half.
Its division is constant;
the decrease or increase of the bricks is according to the requirements.
"One should pile the tortoise-shaped altar for one who desires, 'May I conquer the world of Brahman,' so it is known.
There are indeed two kinds of tortoises: those with curved limbs and those that are circular.
Since there is no distinction specified, we consider them both."
"The shape of one or the other.
Then he measures out the fire-altar;
its body becomes four-cornered.
Its side-measure is ten steps;
the cutting off of its corners is by two steps each.
Having made four squares of the measure of one step in the front face, one should cut off those which are the outermost diagonally.
In this manner [he measures] to the south, in this manner to the west, and in this manner to the north.
That is the body; the head is five paces long and half a man's width across.
One should cut off its shoulders step by step. In the case of a cutting at the corner (srakti), one should raise the feet.
Its diagonal measurement across two feet is twice as long as its longitudinal measurement.
One should cut off its front shoulder by means of two diagonal lines. By this, the cutting off of the other feet is explained.
One should cut off the two rear shoulders from the two rear feet.
In this way, the sevenfold altar, including the *aratni* and the *prādeśa*, is completed.
One should have bricks made for it that are one-fourth of a man’s height;
of these, some are half as high and others are one-quarter as high.
One should enclose [the altar] with four [sides], each measuring one and a half pādas; by means of a *prakrama*, two feet, and a specific foot-measure (*padasaviśeṣa*).
One should have one [side] made such that those two [other sides] are long and closely joined;
[and] one [side] as a perfect square, equal to half of a double-footed eye.
In the layering, one should place a square brick at the front of the head.
One should place two "goose-head" bricks below it, five-by-five square bricks [on each side], and two foot-bricks on each of the feet. Thus one should lay them upon the feet.
Whatever has been cut off, one should place half-bricks (*ardheṣṭakā*) upon that; the remainder of the fire-altar (*agni*) one should cover with quarter-bricks (*caturbhāgīyā*).
One should complete the count with half-bricks.
On the subsequent layer, one should place the *haṃsamukhī* brick at the front of the head, with two foot-bricks (*pādeṣṭakā*) on either side.
Below those two, on both sides, one should place two half-and-a-quarter bricks each, oriented crosswise.

Below those two, on both sides, one should place two jointed brick-fragments. Then, one should place three half-bricks for each of the two-footed bricks, making two sets of two-footed bricks. Thus one should lay them down upon the foot-positions.
Whatever has been cut off, one should place half-bricks and foot-bricks in that space.
One should cover the remainder of the fire-altar with quarter-bricks,
and complete the count with half-bricks.
Now, another [method]:
a man’s height, including the span of the arms extended and the forearms, amounts to one hundred and twenty finger-breadths when measured in units of sixteen.
Having removed five of those sixteen-finger units, he makes the remainder circular.
That has been explained by [the description of] the Droṇacit altar above.
Now, those five Ṣoḍaśī bricks: with them he should raise up the feet in the intermediate directions and the head in the east.
Their drawing around has been explained.
The division of the *pradhīs* is sevenfold;
the widths of the steps (*prakrama*) are equal to the diameters of the *pradhis*.
Whatever remains over should be joined with one and a half [units] of squares.
In the subsequent layer, the division of the quarters is like that of the head, and the division of the head is like that of the quarters.
One should pile them in an alternating manner for as many layers as one intends to construct. At the edge of the tortoise-shaped altar, one should place thin loose soil; in the middle, thick.
This very same [arrangement] is reversed in the Droṇa.
Now, some indeed declare that the Praugas and other [stomas] begin with the Ekavidha;
one teacher [says they are] square on all four sides.
One should have twelve bricks made according to its diagonal; of these, some are half-measures and some are quarter-measures.
Now, for the fire of the Aśvamedha, there is no measurement in terms of *puruṣas*, *aratnis*, or *prādeśas*.
"Or the natural [fire] is threefold:
'The fire has a triple stoma,' and 'The fire is twenty-onefold'—both are Brāhmaṇa passages, both are Brāhmaṇa passages."
Now, therefore, we shall explain the *pravara* lineages.
There are branches belonging to seven *ṛṣis*, with Agastya as the eighth.
Among them, there are three branches of the Bhṛgus: the Vatsas, the Vidas, and the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas, each having five *ṛṣis* as their ancestors.

The Aṅgirasas consist of exactly four groups: the Kaumaṇḍas, the Dīrghatamasas, the Raukṣāyaṇas, and the Gargas. For the Gargas, there is an option consisting of three *ṛṣis*. In the lineage of Viśvāmitra, the Pūraṇas have two *ṛṣis*.
The Śunakas and Vasiṣṭhas have a single *ṛṣi* ancestor.
Others than these have three *pravara*s.
Regarding these, Baudhāyana’s opinion is that the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases perform intermarriage unless there should be many who share the same *ṛṣi* ancestors.
(Pr.2:415.8) Now, therefore, the Adhvaryu chooses [the ancestors] from above, and the Hotṛ from below; this is the rule for both in all cases.
(Pr.2:415.9) When there is a meeting of two *ṛṣi*-lineages, there is no marriage among those who have three *ṛṣi*-lineages.
(Pr.2:415.10) When there is a meeting of three *ṛṣi*-lineages, there is no marriage among those who have five *ṛṣi*-lineages.

Marriage is with those who do not share the same *pravara*. As long as even a single *ṛṣi* recurs among the *pravaras*, there is the state of having the same *gotra*, except for the groups of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases; thus, marriage is prohibited due to commonality among three among five, and among two among three.
Even if only one person among the remaining groups of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases should object, [the rite is not valid].
We shall first explain the lineage of the Bhṛgus:

the Mārkaṇḍeyas, Māṇḍūkās, Māṇḍavyas, Kāṃsayas, Ālekhanas, Dārbhāyaṇas, Śārkarākṣas, Daivatāyanas, Śaunakāyanas, Māṇḍūkeyas, Pārṣikas, Sāṅkas, Prāntāyanas, Pailas, Paiṅgalāyanas, Dādhreṣayas, Bāhyakayas, Vaiśvānarayas, Vaihīnarayas, Virohitās, Bārhās, Gauṣṭrāyaṇas, Aiṣṭeṣayas, Kāśakṛtsnas, Vāgbhūtayas, Ṛtabhāgas, Aitiśāyanas, Jānāyanas, Pāṇini, Vālmīki, Sthaulapiṇḍayas, and Śaikhāvatās.

The Jihītayas, Sāvarṇis, Vākāyanas, Bālāyanas, Saukṛtis, Maṇḍavits, Sauviṣṭis, Hastyāgnis, Śauddhakas, Vaikarṇas, Aupajihvyas, Auraśayas, Kāmbalodarayas, Kāṭhorakṛts, Vaihalis, Virūpākṣas, Vṛkāśvas, Uccairmanyus, Daivamatis, Ārkāyaṇas, Mārkāyaṇas, Kāhvāyanas, Vāyavāyaninas, Śāṃkaravas, Kārabavas, Cāndramasas, Gāṅgeyas, Anupeyas, Yājñikas, Jābālis, Bāhumitrāyaṇas, Āpiśalis, Vaiṣṭapureyas, and Lohitāyanas.
The Uṣṭrākṣas, the Nāḍāyanas, the Śāradvatāyanas, the Rājitavāhas, and the Vatsas—some say the Vatsas are [a sub-division] of these;
their *pravara* consists of five ṛṣis:
Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Jāmadagna; this is the Hotṛ's invocation.
"Like Jamadagni, like Urva, like Apnavāna, like Cyavana, like Bhṛgu"—thus says the Adhvaryu.

The Vidas, the Śailas, the Avaṭas, the Śailas, the Prācīnayogyas, the Abhayajātās, the Kāṇḍarathayas, the Vaidabhṛtas, the Pulastayas, the Ārkāyaṇas, the Mārkāyaṇas, the Nāṣṭrāyaṇas, the Krauñcāyanas, the Bhuñjāyanas, and the Jāmalāyanas—these are the Vidas.
Their *pravara* consists of five ṛṣis;
the Hotṛ recites: Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Veda.
"Like Vidavat, like Ūrvavat, like Apnavānavat, like Cyavanavat, like Bhṛguvat," says the Adhvaryu.
The Ārṣṭiṣeṇas, Nairathayas, Grāmyāyaṇas, Kāṇvayas, Cāndrāyaṇas, Prauḍhakalāyanas, Siddhas, Sumanāyanas, Gaurāmbhis, and Rāmbhis—these are the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas. Their *pravara* consists of five ancestors;
the Hotṛ priest recites: "Bhārgava, Cyāvāna, Āpnavāna, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Anūpa."

"Like Anūpa, like Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, like Apnavāna, like Cyavana, like Bhṛgu"—thus says the Adhvaryu. "The Vatsas, the Vidas, the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas"—there is no marriage among these. These are the performers of the five-fold cutting.

The Yaskas—namely Mauna, Mūka, Vādhūla, Varṣapuṣpa, Bāleya, Rājitatāyin, Durdina, Bhāskara, Daivantāyana, Bāṣkaleya, Mādhyameya, Vāśaya, Kauśāmbeya, Kauṭilya, Satyaka, Citrasena, Bhāgantaya, Vārkāśvaka, Auktha, Augraciti, and Bhāgurithya—these are the Yaskas.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: Bhārgava, Vaitahavya, and Sāvetasa; thus says the Hotṛ.
"Like Savitṛ, like Vītahavya, like Bhṛgu," thus says the Adhvaryu.

The Mitrayus consist of the Rauṣṭyāyanas, Śāyaṇḍinas, Sāpiṇḍanas, Surāmbhins, Mālyas, Bālyas, Mahābālyas, Tārkṣyāyaṇas, Aurukṣyāyaṇas, Vājāyanas, Mādāghayas, and Kaitavāyanas; these are the Mitrayus. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
Bhārgava, Vādhryaśva, and Daivodāsa; this is the Hotṛ's invocation.
"Like Divodāsa, like Vadhryaśva, like Bhṛgu," says the Adhvaryu.
The Vainyas, the Pārthas, and the Bāṣkalas—among them, the *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.
The Hotṛ priest says: "Bhārgava, Vainya, Pārtha";
the Adhvaryu says: "Like Pṛthu, like Vena, like Bhṛgu."

The Śunakas, Gārtsamadas, Yajñapayas, Saugandhyas, Khārdamāyanas, Gāṅgāyanas, Matsyagandhas, Caukṣas, Śrotriyas, Taittirīyas, and Palpūlas—these are the Śunakas. Their *pravara* consists of a single *ṛṣi*;
the Hotṛ priest invokes: "Śaunaka."
"Like Śunaḥśepa," says the Adhvaryu;
"Like Gṛtsamada," says the Hotṛ; or "Like Gṛtsamada," says the Adhvaryu.

We shall explain the Aṅgirasas. The Āyāsyas—Āṇīveyas, Kācākṣyas, Mūḍhas, Sātyakayas, Taidehas, Kaumāravatyas, Tāuṇḍis, Dārbhis, Devakis, Sātyamugris, Kaubāhyas, Baudhyas, Naikaris, Svastaiṣakis, Kīlālayas, Kāruṇis, Kāṭoris, and Kāśīvājas; these Pārthivas are the Āyāsyas Gautamas. Their *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis.
The Hotṛ says, "Of Āṅgirasa, Ayāsya,
and Gautama," while the Adhvaryu says, "Like Gautama, like Ayāsya, and like Āṅgirasa."

The Śāradvatas—namely the Ābhijitas, Rauhiṇyas, Kṣīrakarambhas, Saumucayas, Sauyamunas, Aupabindavas, Rāhūgaṇas, Rāṇayas, and Mārṣaṇyas—these are the Śāradvata-Gautamas. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: the Hotṛ recites "Āṅgirasa, Gautama, Śāradvata."
"Like Śaradvat, like Gotama, like Aṅgiras"—thus says the Adhvaryu.
The Kaumaṇḍas, Māmanthareṣaṇas, Māsurākṣas, Kāṣṭareṣayas, Ūrjāyanas, Vanajāyanas, and Vāśayas—these are the Kaumaṇḍa Gautamas.
Their *pravara* consists of five ṛṣis:
Āṅgirasa, Aucathya, Kākṣīvata, Gautama, and Kaumaṇḍa; thus says the Hotṛ.
"Like Kumaṇḍu, like Gotama, like Kakṣīvat, like Ucathya, like Aṅgiras"—thus says the Adhvaryu.
For those of the Dīrghatamas lineage, there is a five-ṛṣi *pravara*:
"Āṅgirasa, Aucathya, Kākṣīvata, Gautama, Dīrghatama"—thus the Hotṛ;
"Like Dīrghatamas, like Gautama, like Kakṣīvat, like Ucathya, like Aṅgiras"—thus the Adhvaryu.

The Auśanasas are those of the Diśya lineage who are praised, having beautiful eyes, large bellies, wide-open mouths, and keen intellects; they are established in the cave. These are the Auśanasa-Gautamas.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
"Āṅgirasa, Gautama, Auśanasa"—thus says the Hotṛ.
"Like Uśanas, like Gotama, like Aṅgiras," says the Adhvaryu.
The Kāreṇupālas, Vāstavyas, Śvetīyas, Pauñjiṣṭhyas, Audajñāyanas, Bāndhukyās, and Ājagandhayas—these are the Kāreṇupālas who belong to the Gautama lineage.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ priest invokes them as "Āṅgirasa, Gautama, Kāreṇupāla."
"Like Kāreṇupāla, like Gotama, like Aṅgīras," says the Adhvaryu.
For the Vāmadevas, the *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ says, "Āṅgirasa, Gautama,
Vāmadeva," and the Adhvaryu says, "as Vāmadeva, as Gautama, as Āṅgiras."
There is no intermarriage among all those belonging to the Gautama lineage.

The Bharadvājas, the Kṣāmyāyaṇas, the Māmaṇḍas, the Devāśvas, the Udvahavyas, the Prāgvaṃśayas, the Vāhalayas, the Bāhyogas, the Vāsināyanas, the Taidehas, the Ājñas, the Aukṣas, the Bhūrayas, the Pāriṇaddheyas, the Śaikheyas, the Śauddhakas, the Ūrūḍhas, the Khārigrīvas, the Aupaśayas, the Vayokṣibhedas, the Āgniveśyas, the Vedhas, the Śaṭhas, the Gaurivāyanas, the Celakas, the Stanakarṇas, the Ūrukṣas, the Māṇabhindavyas, the Kāhvodaṅkas, the Taujvalayas, the Velās, the Khāraṇādayas, and the Bhāruṇḍeyas.

The Mādrapathas, the Saurobhaṅgas, the Śuṅgas, the Daivamatayas, the Īṣumatas, the Audameghayas, the Pravāhaṇeyas, the Kalmāṣas, the Rājastambhis, the Sudhūpakṛdvārāhayas, the Valabhikayas, the Ugrāṃgatas, the Śālāhalayas, the Devavelās, the Mahāvelās, the Niviñcyāyanas, the Dhanyāyanas, the Śālālayas, the Śārdūlayas, the Kātkalas, the Vākkalās, the Saihyakeṣas, the Krauḍāyaṇas, the Krauḍilyas, the Brahmastambhas, the Rājastambhas, the Agnistambhas, the Vāyustambhas, and the Sūryastambhas, as well as the Somastambhas.

The Yamastambhas, the Indrastambhas, the Viṣṇustambhas, the Yajñastambhas, the Āpastambhas, and those others who have "stambha" as their name—such as the Sviṣṭas, the Āruṇasindhus, the Kaumudagandhis, the Śaktis, the Kauśivāyanas, the Ātreyāyaṇas, the Bhāmaṇyas, the Dhūmagandhas, the Kukās, the Kaukākṣayas, the Naitundayas, the Dārbhayas, the Śyāmeyas, the Matsyakrāthas, the Kaukvāyanas, the Kārūpathayas, the Kārīṣāyaṇas, and the Kāmbalyas—these are the Bharadvājas. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: the Hotṛ recites, "Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, Bhāradvāja."
"Like Bharadvāja, like Bṛhaspati, like Aṅgiras," says the Adhvaryu.
For the Raukṣāyaṇas, there is a five-ṛṣi *pravara*:
"Āṅgirasa, Bārhaspatya, Bhāradvāja, Vāndana, Mātavacasa," says the Hotṛ; "like Matavacas, like Vandana, like Bharadvāja, like Bṛhaspati, like Aṅgiras," says the Adhvaryu.

The Gargas—namely the Sāṃbharāyaṇas, Sakhīnayas, Gandhārāyaṇas, Bāhulakayas, Bhraṣṭakas, Bhrāṣṭrabindavas, Krauṣṭukayas, Sauyāmunis, Bhrājinākṣatreyas, Hotrāpacayas, Satyāpacayas, Kāṇāyanas, Aupamatkaṭāyanas, Jāṇavats, Palāśaśākhāvantis, Saṃgrahatulyas, Vaiḍuhas, Nisrohatas, Kārirautis, Kaivalyas, and Rājayas—these are the Gargas.
For them, there is a *pravara* consisting of either five or three *ṛṣis*.
The Hotṛ [recites]: "O descendant of Aṅgiras, of Bṛhaspati, of Bharadvāja, of Śainya, of Garga.
Or alternatively: "O descendant of Aṅgiras, of Śainya, of Garga.
The Adhvaryu [recites] as follows: "Like Garga, like Chinin, like Bharadvāja, like Bṛhaspati, like Aṅgiras."
As in the cases of Garga, Chini,
and Aṅgiras, there is no intermarriage among all the Bharadvājas.

The Viṣṇuvṛddhas are the Śaṭhamarṣaṇas, Bhadraṇas, Madraṇas, Śāmburāyaṇas, Bādarāyaṇas, Vātsaprāyaṇas, Sātyakis, Sātyakāyanas, Naitundyas, Stutyas, Bhāruṇyas, Vaihoḍhas, and Daivasthānayas; these are the Viṣṇuvṛddhas.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ priest invokes them as Āṅgirasa, Paurukutsa, and Trāsadasya.
"Like Trasadasyu, like Purukutsa, like Aṅgiras," says the Adhvaryu.
The Kaṇvas—namely the Aupamarkaṭāyanas, Bāṣkalas, Śailāhalinas, Mauñjis, Mauñjayas, Mauñjigandhas, Vājins, Vājayas, and Vājaśravasas—these are the Kaṇvas.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ priest invokes them as "Āṅgirasa-Ajamīḍha-Kāṇva."
"Like Kaṇva, like Ajamīḍha, like Aṅgiras," says the Adhvaryu.

The Haritas are the Kautsas, Śāṅkhyas, Dārbhyas, Śaibhaṅgas, Bhaimagavas, Manāyus, Lambodaras, Mahodaras, Naimiśrayas, Miśrodanas, Kauṭhapas, Kāroṣayas, Kaulayas, Paulayas, Pauṇḍalas, Māndhūpas, Māndhātṛs, and Mādrakārayas; these are the Haritas.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ priest invokes them as Āṅgirasa, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva.
"As was Yuvanāśva, as was Ambarīṣa, as was Aṅgiras," says the Adhvaryu.

The Saṃkṛtis—namely the Lamakas, Pautyas, Taṇḍis, Śambhus, Śaivagavas, Paribhavas, Tārakādya-s, Hārigrīva-s, Vaitāleya-s, Śrautāyana-s, Cārāyaṇa-s, Āgrāyaṇa-s, Ārṣiya-s, Cāndrāyaṇa-s, Āpaghrāpaya-s, and Pṛtimāṣa-s—these are the Saṃkṛtis.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ priest recites "Āṅgirasa, Sāṃkṛtya, Gaurivīta."
"Like Gaurīvīta, like Saṃkṛti, like Aṅgiras," says the Adhvaryu.
The Rathītaras, Hāstidāsins, Kāṇvāyanas, Naitirakṣayas, Śailālayas, Bhailis, Bhillibhāyanas, Sāvahavas, Bhaikṣavāhas, and Haimagavas—these are the Rathītaras.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
"Āṅgirasa, Vairūpa, Rāthītara"—thus says the Hotṛ.
"O descendant of Aṅgiras, Vairūpa, Pārṣadaśva," or "like Rathītara, like Virūpa, like Aṅgiras"— thus says the Adhvaryu;
or "like Pṛṣadaśva, like Virūpa, like Aṅgiras."

The Mudgalas—namely the Hiraṇyākṣas, the Ṛṣabhas, the Mitākṣas, the Ṛśyas, the Ṛśyāyaṇas, the Dīrghajaṅghas, the Pralambajaṅghas, the Taruṇas, and the Bhindavas—these are the Mudgalas. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: the Hotṛ priest invokes them as "Āṅgirasa, Bhārmyaśva, Maudgalya."
"Like Mudgala, like Bhṛmyaśva, like Aṅgiras," says the Adhvaryu.

The Kapayas—namely the Vaitalas, the Aitiśāyanas, the Patañjalas, the Tarasvins, the Tāṇḍins, the Bhojasinas, the Śāṅgaravas, the Karaśikhaṇḍas, the Mauṣītakis, the Chāgalayas, and the Pauṣpayas—these are the Kapayas.
Their pravara consists of three ṛṣis;
the Hotṛ priest invokes them as: "Of the Āṅgirasas, Mahayya, and Aurukṣaya."
"Like Urukṣaya, like Amahīya, like Aṅgiras," says the Adhvaryu.

We shall now explain the Ātreyas. The Ātreyas are numerous: the Chāndinas, the Chāndogins, the Pauṣṭikas, the Māṅgalayas, the Śaivas, the Chāgalas, the Tṛṇabindus, the Bhāgantayas, the Mālakujas, the Vyāḍalas, the Śāmbavyāyanas, the Kārmaryāyaṇas, the Dākṣis, the Taidehas, the Gāṇispatyas, the Auddālaki, the Droṇabhāvas, the Gaurigrīvas, the Gāviṣṭhiras, the Śiśupālas, the Kṛṣṇātreyas, the Gaurātreyas, the Aruṇātreyas, the Nīlātreyas, the Śvetātreyas, the Śyāmātreyas, the Mahātreyas, the Ātreyas, the Hāleyas, the Vāleyas, and the Śaubhreyas.

The Vāmarathins, the Vaitabhāvyas, the Śaudreyas, the Kaudreyas, the Gopavanas, the Kālapavas, the Ānīṣāyaṇas, the Ānaṅgiras, the Mānaṅgiras, the Dauraṅgis, the Sauraṅgis, the Puṣpayas, the Śaikhayas, the Sāketāyanas, the Bhāradvājāyanas, and Indrātithi—these are the Atris. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ recites "Ātreya-Arcanānasa-Śyāvāśva."
"Like Śyāvāśva, like Arcanānas, like Atri," says the Adhvaryu.
For those of the Vādbhuta lineage, there is a *pravara* consisting of three *ṛṣis*.
The Hotṛ priest pronounces: "Ātreya, Ārcanānasa, Vādbhutaka"; the Adhvaryu priest pronounces: "Like Vādbhutaka, like Ārcanānasa, like Atri."
The *pravara* for the Gaviṣṭhiras consists of three *ṛṣis*.
The Hotṛ says: "Ātreya, Arcanānasa, Gāviṣṭhira.
The Adhvaryu says: "Like Gaviṣṭhira, like Arcanānasa, like Atri."

The Mudgalas—namely the Śālisaṃdhis, Aurṇanābhas, Dākṣis, Vaitavāhas, Śirīṣayas, Śālimats, Vrīhimats, Gaurīṣitas, Gaurikayas, Vāyavanās, and Vāyupūṭas—these are the Mudgalas. Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: the Hotṛ priest recites, "Ātreya-Arcanānasa-Paurvātitha."
"The honoring [of the guest] is like that of a previous guest; [he is] like Atri," says the Adhvaryu.
We shall now explain the Viśvāmitras:

the Kuśikas, the Pārṇajaṅghas, the Vārakyas, the Audarins, the Māṇis, the Bṛhadagnis, the Ālavins, the Āghaṭṭins, the Āpadyapas, the Antakas, the Kāmantakas, the Bāṣpakayas, the Cikitās, the Lāmakāyanas, the Śālaṅkāyanas, the Śāṅkāyanas, the Laukas, the Gauras, the Saugantayas, the Yamadūtas, the Anabhimlātas, the Tārakāyaṇas, the Cauvalas, the Jābālas, the Yajñavalkas, the Vidaṇḍas, the Bhauvanayas, the Saubabhravas, the Aupadahanas, the Audumbaris, the Bhāriṣṭikayas, the Śyāmeyas, the Caitreyas, and the Śālāvatas.
The Mayūras, Saumatyas, Citratantus, Manutantus, Māntavas, and others who have names derived from the word *tantu*, as well as the Bābhravyas, Kalāpas, and Utsarayas—these are the Kuśikas.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ priest invokes Vaiśvāmitra- Daivarāta- Audala.
"Like Udaḷa, like Devarāta, like Viśvāmitra," says the Adhvaryu.
The Lohitas, the Dāṇḍakayas, the Ākravarmāyaṇas, the Jharjhāyanas, the Vāñjāyanas, the Mādāghayas, the Kaitavāyanas, and the Vāśayas—these are the Lohitas.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ priest invokes "Vaiśvāmitra-Aṣṭaka-Lauhita."
"Like Rohita, like Aṣṭaka, like Viśvāmitra," says the Adhvaryu.
The Śraumata-Kāmakāyanas are the descendants of Viśvāmitra, Devaśravas, and Devataras; their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
"Vaiśvāmitra, Daivaśravasa, Daivatarasa"—thus says the Hotṛ.
"Like Devataras, like Devaśravas, like Viśvāmitra," says the Adhvaryu.
The Raukṣakas, the Auḍūhalas, and the Reiṇavas—
their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: "Vaiśvāmitra, Raukṣaka, Reiṇava"— thus says the Hotṛ.
"Like dust, like a rough person, like Viśvāmitra"—thus says the Adhvaryu.
The Katas—namely the Sairindhas, Karabhas, Vājāyanas, Sāṃhiteyas, Kaukṛtyas, Śaiśireyas, Audumbarāyaṇas, Piṇḍagrīvas, Nārāyaṇas, and Nārāṭyas—these are the Katas.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*: the Hotṛ invokes "Vaiśvāmitra Kātya Ātkīli."
"Like Atri, like Kavaṣa, like Viśvāmitra," says the Adhvaryu.
The Dhanañjayas, the Kārīṣayas, the Āśvavatās, the Tulabhyas, the Saindhavāyanas, the Uṣṭrākṣas, and the Mahākṣas—these are the Dhanañjayas.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
"Vaiśvāmitra, Mādhucchandasa, Dhānañjaya"—thus says the Hotṛ.
"Like Dhanañjaya, like Madhucchandas, like Viśvāmitra"—thus says the Adhvaryu.
For one whose lineage is unknown, there is a *pravara* consisting of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ says, "Vaiśvāmitra-Mādhucchandasa-Agastya," and the Adhvaryu says, "like Agastya, like Madhucchandas, like Viśvāmitra."
The Aghamarṣaṇas are Kuśikas;
their pravara consists of three ṛṣis:
Vaiśvāmitra-Aghamarṣaṇa-Kauśika—thus says the Hotṛ.
"Like Kuśika, like Aghamarṣaṇa, like Viśvāmitra," says the Adhvaryu.
The Indrakauśikas have a *pravara* consisting of three *ṛṣis*:
"Vaiśvāmitra, Aindra, Kauśika"— thus says the Hotṛ.
"Like Kuśika, like Indra, like Viśvāmitra," says the Adhvaryu.
The Pūraṇas, who cause [their descendants] to drink water,
have a *pravara* consisting of two *ṛṣis*:
"Vaiśvāmitra Pauraṇa," says the Hotṛ.
"As before, like Viśvāmitra," says the Adhvaryu.
We shall explain the lineage of Kaśyapa:

the Kaśyapas, Chāgasa, Maṭhara, Aitiśāyana, Ābhūti, Vaiśipra, Dhūmra, Dhūmrāyaṇa, Dhaumya, Dhārmyāyaṇa, Audavraji, Agrāyaṇa, Baimbaka, Prāvāhārya, Hṛdroga, Kāśyātapas, Āpāmbānika, Mauṣītaki, Chāgasas, Māṣaśarāvi, Saudhavaya, Sāyasya, Āsurāyaṇa, Chāgavya, Saunadya, Sthaulakeśi, Vārṣaka, Lākṣamaṇi, Kroṣṭṛ, Jīvati, and Khārdamāyaṇa.

The Lohitāyanas, the Mitakumbhas, the Piṅgākṣyas, the Auḍalayas, the Mārāyaṇas, the Vaikarṇeyas, the Kauṣītakeyas, the Dhūmalakṣmaṇayas, the Surās, the Gaurivāyaṇas, the Vimatsyas, the Āgniśarmāyaṇas, the Aukthyāyanas, the Kāmbarodarayas, the Devayātās, the Vaidas, Ambā, Velayā, the Mahācakreyas, the Paiṭhīnasas, the Pānasyas, the Viṣagaṇas, the Dākṣāyaṇayas, the Bhālandanas, the Śāṅkhamitreyas, the Harityas, the Pāñcālās, the Jāramāṇyas, the Vārṣagāṇis, the Sauviśravasas, the Vaiśampāyanas, and the Svairakis.

The Kālaśayas, Auktrāyaṇis, Mārjāyanas, Kāṃsāyanas, Daivas, Hotṛs, Śucis, Kharebhas, Āyasthūṇas, Bhāguris, Pāthikāryas, Gaumāyanas, Hiraṇyapāpas, Āgnidevis, Tathāsūryas, Musalas, Āviśreṇyas, Uttarato-gaṇḍamānas, Mantritas, Vaikarṇayas, and Sthūlabindavas—these are the Nidhrus, who are Kaśyapas. Their *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis: Kāśyapa, Avatsāra, and Naidhruva; thus the Hotṛ priest invokes them.
"Like Nidhruva, like Avatsāra, like Kaśyapa," says the Adhvaryu.
For the Rebhas, there is a *pravara* consisting of three *ṛṣis*:
"Kāśyapa-Āvatsāra-Raibha," says the Hotṛ; "as Raibha, as Āvatsāra, as Kaśyapa," says the Adhvaryu.

The Śāṇḍilas, Kauhaḍas, Pāvakas, Pāryakas, Audameghas, Saudānavas, Sāvacasas, Kāreyas, Kaukuṇḍeyas, Aiṣikayas, Mahodakayas, Kauśrayas, Kāmaśayas, Mauñjāyanas, Jāṇavatsas, Khārvamāyanas, Gāṅgāyanas, Vātsabhālayas, Gobhilas, Vaidāyanas, Vātsyāyanas, Vāhyāyanas, Bahūdara, Bhāguri, Gārdabhīmukha, Hiraṇyabāhu, Taideha, Gomūtra, Vārkakhaṇḍa, Jānantari, Jālandhari, and Dhanvantari— these are the Śāṇḍilas.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ priest invokes them as "Kāśyapa, Avatsāra, Śāṇḍila," or alternatively as "Kāśyapa, Avatsāra, Daivala."
The Adhvaryu priests [recite] either "Kāśyapa, Avatsāra, Asita" or "Śāṇḍila, Asita, Daivala," [saying] "like Śāṇḍila, like Avatsāra, like Kāśyapa."
Either like Devala, like Sārava, or like Kaśyapa;
or like Asita, like Avatsāra, or like Kaśyapa; or like Devala, like Avatsāra, or like Śāṇḍilya.

The Laukākṣayas, Dārbhāyaṇas, Maitravādins, Vaidehas, Kāleyas, Kāpuṭis, as well as the Kalayas, Kāṃsapātrayas, Bhālakāyanis, Nityarasovirs, Odakis, Kauṇāmīs, Sautayas, Saitakis, Sāṃbharis, Āniṣṭis, Aiṣikis, Sausukis, Carandis, Paśubhis, Colapalas, Yauthakālakis, Lokākṣayas, Yauthapālas, and Ajapālas—these are the Lokākṣayas.
Day belongs to the Vasiṣṭhas and night to the Kaśyapas;
their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.
The Hotṛ [recites]: "Kāśyapa, Avatsāra, Vasiṣṭha";
or "Kāśyapa, Avatsāra, Asita.
The Adhvaryu [recites]: "Like Vasiṣṭha, like Avatsāra, like Kāśyapa."
Or [the prohibition applies] as in the cases of Asita, Vatsāra, and Kaśyapa;
among these very [lineages], there is no intermarriage.
We shall explain the Vasiṣṭhas as having a single *ṛṣi* ancestry:

the Vaikalis, the Vārāṭakis, the Sākhalas, the Gauriśravasas, the Āśvalāyanas, the Kāpiṣṭhas, the Śaucivṛkṣas, the Vaiyāghrapadyas, the Vāhyakāyanis, the Vāṭavyas, the Jātūkarṇas, the Auḍulomis, the Kaubhojis, the Kaulāyanas, the Sundaraharitās, the Kāṇṭheviddhis, the Sauyavasāyanas, the Ālambhāyanas, the Laumāyanyas, the Svastyas, the Kārṣitas, the Pārṇakāyanas, the Cauḍakāyanas, the Pārṇavalkas, the Devanas, the Gauravyas, the Śrāviṣṭhāyanas, the Vāhakathayas, and the Āvikṣitayas.
The Śvayājayas, the Pūtimāṣas, and the Saptavailas are Vāsiṣṭhas;
for them, there is a single ancestral invocation (*ekārṣeya-pravara*): "Vāsiṣṭha" is the Hotṛ, and "like Vasiṣṭha" is the Adhvaryu.

The Kuṇḍinas—namely the Lohāyanas, Guggulis, Aupavastis, Vaikarṇayas, Aśmarathas, Bāhavas, Krauñcokyas, Sāmaṅgalinas, Kāpaṭavas, Paiṭhakas, Navagrāmas, Hiraṇyākṣāyaṇas, Paippalādakas, Bhākṣis, Mādhyaṃdinas, Śantis, and Saupatithis—these are the Kuṇḍinas. Their *pravara* consists of three ṛṣis;
the Hotṛ priest invokes them as: Vāsiṣṭha, Maitrāvaruṇa, Kauṇḍinya.
"Like Kuṇḍina, like Mitrāvaruṇa, like Vasiṣṭha," thus says the Adhvaryu.

The Upamanyus, the Aupagavas, the Maṇḍalekhyas, the Kāpiñjalas, the Jālāgatas, the Tapolokas, the Traivarṇas, the Pārṇāgāris, the Surākṣaras, the Śailālayas, the Mahākarṇāyanas, the Vālaśikhas, the Audgāhamānis, the Bālāyanas, the Bhāguritthāyanas, the Kuṇḍodarayaṇas, the Lākṣmaṇeyas, the Kācāntayas, the Vārkāśvakas, the Ānṛkṣarāyaṇas, the Ālabavas, and the Kapikeśas—these are the Upamanyus.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ priest recites, "Vāsiṣṭha, Indrapramada, and Bharadvāja."
"Like Ābhara Vasu, like Indrapramada, like Vasiṣṭha," [thus says] the Adhvaryu.
The Parāśaras: "The Kāṇḍūśayas, the Vājayas, the Vājayantas, and the Vaimatāyanas; Gopāli is their fifth. These are the black Parāśaras."
The Prārohayas, Vaikalayas, Plākṣayas, Kaumudas, and so forth;
Hāryaśvi is their fifth [founder]; these are the Gaura-Parāśaras. The Khalvāyanas, Gopayas, Kālkayas, and Śyātayātayas.
Vāruṇi is the fifth among these; these are the Aruṇa Parāśaras. Bhālukya and Bādari, Kāhvāyana and Kaukuśālaka—Kṣaimiti is the fifth among these; these are the Nīla Parāśaras.
The Kṛṣṇājinas, the Kāpiśubhras, the Śyāmāyanas, the Śvetayūpayas,
and Poṣkarasādi as the fifth— these are the Śveta-Parāśaras. The Vāśyāyanas, the Vārṣṇeyas, the Śyāmeyas, together with the Śrautibhis.
"The fifth among these is Cauli; these Śyāmas are Parāśaras.
Those Parāśaras who are black, fair, ruddy, blue, white, or dark—among them, the *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.
"Vāsiṣṭha, Śāktya, Pārāśarya," says the Hotṛ; "Like Parāśara, like Śakti, like Vasiṣṭha," says the Adhvaryu.
We shall now explain the Agastis.

The Agastis consist of the Viśālas, the Skālāyanas, the Aupadahanayas, Kalmāṣadaṇḍi, Dhāvaṇi, Lāvarṇi, Lavyārbuda, the Bairiṇayas, the Budbudodarayas, the Śaivapathayas, the Śālāvatās, the Mauñjakayas, the Pāṇḍuhṛdas, the Hārigrīvas, the Rauhiṣyas, and the Mausalyas; these are the Agastis.
Their *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*.
"O Agastya, Dārḍhacyuta, Idhmavāha!"—thus the Hotṛ; "Like Idhmavāha, like Dṛḍhacyuta, like Agastya"—thus the Adhvaryu.
The *pravara* for those who carry the Soma consists of three *ṛṣis*.
The Hotṛ says: "Āgastya, Dārḍhacyuta, Saumavāha";
the Adhvaryu says: "Like Saumavāha, like Dṛḍhacyuta, like Agasti."
For those who offer sacrifices, the *pravara* consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ says, "The lineage of Agastya, Dṛḍhacyuta,
and Yajñavāha," and the Adhvaryu says, "Like Yajñavāha, like Dṛḍhacyuta, and like Agastya."
For those of three lineages, there is a pravara consisting of three ṛṣis:
"Mānava-aiḍa-paurūravasa" is the Hotṛ;
"Purūravas-vat, iḍā-vat, manu-vat" is the Adhvaryu.
The *pravara* of the Vaiśyas consists of three *ṛṣis*:
the Hotṛ says, "Bhālandana, Vātsapra, Māṅktila";
the Adhvaryu says, "Māṅktilavat, Vatsapravat, Bhālandanavat."
We shall now explain the *nārāśaṃsa* cups.

The Ātreya, Vādhryaśva, Vādhūla, Vasiṣṭha, Kaṇva, Śunaka, Saṃkṛti, Yaska, Rājanya, and Vaiśya—these are proclaimed as those for whom the cup is dedicated to Nārāśaṃsa; for the others, it is dedicated to Tanūnapāt.

"It is known from scripture that for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, the most excellent priest (*purohita*) is one of the *pravara* lineage of Manu; or rather, [he may be] of any *gotra*, for it is known from scripture that 'all creatures are descended from Manu. Having approached a woman of the same *gotra*, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."

When the vow has been completed, one should not abandon a Brāhmaṇī wife, treating her like a mother or a sister. It is known from scripture: "The embryo is not defiled, O Kaśyapa. Now, if a marriage occurs during such a period of impurity, one should avoid that particular chapter; for the authority of Baudhāyana must be followed in this matter.
"For offspring are indeed Mānavyas," so it is known; and:
"There are thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions of lineages (*gotra*s), yet their *pravara*s are only forty-nine, according to the vision of the seers (*ṛṣi*)."
Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa— these are the seven ṛṣis.
The offspring of these seven ṛṣis, with Agastya as the eighth, is called a *gotra*.
He who knows both his own and others' *pravara* lineages is not one who should be excluded from officiating at sacrifices.
They declare that the *mantra*, the *brāhmaṇa*, and the *veda* [are what define a Brahmin];
therefore, the twice-born must exert great effort in the knowledge of the *pravara*.
(Pr.54:467.10) At a *śrāddha* or a wedding, the officiating priests, the deities, the hymns of praise, and the roots of the lineage are established in the great ancestral invocation (*mahāpravara*).
(Pr.54:467.11) One who constantly studies the Veda on every sacred festival day (*parvan*) is glorified in the world of Brahman; he is glorified in the world of Brahman. Thus it is said.
